From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Biological ability to perceive magnetic fields

"Magnetoception" redirects here. For the Joshua Abrams album, see [Magnetoception (album)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetoception_(album) "Magnetoception (album)").

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/Erithacus_rubecula_-RHS_Garden_Harlow_Carr-8c.jpg/500px-Erithacus_rubecula_-RHS_Garden_Harlow_Carr-8c.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Erithacus_rubecula_-RHS_Garden_Harlow_Carr-8c.jpg)

Experiments on [European robins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_robin "European robin"), which are [migratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bird_migration "Bird migration"), suggest their magnetic sense makes use of the quantum [radical pair mechanism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radical_pair_mechanism "Radical pair mechanism").

**Magnetoreception** is a [sense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sense "Sense") which allows an [organism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organism "Organism") to detect the [Earth's magnetic field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth's_magnetic_field "Earth's magnetic field"). Animals with this sense include some [arthropods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthropod "Arthropod"), [molluscs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mollusc "Mollusc"), and [vertebrates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertebrate "Vertebrate") (fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals). The sense is mainly used for orientation and [navigation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_navigation "Animal navigation"), but it may help some animals to form regional maps. Experiments on [migratory birds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bird_migration "Bird migration") provide evidence that they make use of a [cryptochrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryptochrome "Cryptochrome") protein in the eye, relying on the quantum [radical pair mechanism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radical_pair_mechanism "Radical pair mechanism") to perceive magnetic fields. This effect is extremely sensitive to weak magnetic fields, and readily disturbed by radio-frequency interference, unlike a conventional iron compass. Some [bacteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bacteria "Bacteria") orient passively using [magnetite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetite "Magnetite") crystals; the mechanism has not been reliably detected in [eukaryotes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eukaryote "Eukaryote").

[Cartilaginous fish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartilaginous_fish "Cartilaginous fish") including [sharks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shark "Shark") and [stingrays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stingray "Stingray") can detect small variations in electric potential with their [electroreceptive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electroreception "Electroreception") organs, the [ampullae of Lorenzini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ampullae_of_Lorenzini "Ampullae of Lorenzini"). These appear to be able to detect magnetic fields by [induction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electromagnetic_induction "Electromagnetic induction"). There is some evidence that these fish use magnetic fields in navigation.

## History

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Magnetoreception&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

Biologists have long wondered whether [migrating animals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_migration "Animal migration") such as [birds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bird_migration "Bird migration") and [sea turtles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_turtle_migration "Sea turtle migration") have an inbuilt magnetic compass, enabling them to [navigate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_navigation "Animal navigation") using the [Earth's magnetic field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth's_magnetic_field "Earth's magnetic field"). Until late in the 20th century, evidence for this was essentially only [behavioural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethology "Ethology"): many experiments demonstrated that animals could indeed derive information from the magnetic field around them, but gave no indication of the mechanism. In 1972, Roswitha and Wolfgang Wiltschko showed that migratory birds responded to the direction and [inclination (dip)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetic_dip "Magnetic dip") of the magnetic field. In 1977, M. M. Walker and colleagues identified iron-based ([magnetite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetite "Magnetite")) magnetoreceptors in the snouts of [rainbow trout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainbow_trout "Rainbow trout"). In 2003, G. Fleissner and colleagues claimed to have found iron-based receptors in the upper beaks of [homing pigeons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homing_pigeons "Homing pigeons"), but subsequent studies employing high resolution electron microscopy revealed that the cells identified are in fact macrophages.[[1]](#cite_note-Treiber2012-1) Research took a different direction in 2000, when Thorsten Ritz and colleagues suggested that a [photoreceptor protein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photoreceptor_protein "Photoreceptor protein") in the eye, [cryptochrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryptochrome "Cryptochrome"), was a magnetoreceptor, working at a molecular scale by [quantum entanglement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_entanglement "Quantum entanglement").[[2]](#cite_note-Winklhofer_2010-2)

## Proposed mechanisms

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Magnetoreception&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Proposed mechanisms")]

### Passive iron-based alignment in bacteria

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Magnetoreception&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Passive iron-based alignment in bacteria")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d3/Magnetite_magnetosomes_in_Gammaproteobacteria.png/500px-Magnetite_magnetosomes_in_Gammaproteobacteria.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Magnetite_magnetosomes_in_Gammaproteobacteria.png)

[Magnetite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetite "Magnetite") magnetosomes in [Gammaproteobacteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gammaproteobacteria "Gammaproteobacteria") strain SS-5. (A) Chain of highly elongated magnetosomes. (B) Part of a chain. (C) The magnetosome in the lower right in (B), viewed along the ![{\displaystyle \scriptstyle [1{\overline {1}}0]}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/f99ce4c507bedc2d8c9e600715fe15e2d2666907) direction, with its [Fourier transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform "Fourier transform") in the lower right.[[3]](#cite_note-3)

[Magnetotactic bacteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetotactic_bacteria "Magnetotactic bacteria") of multiple taxa contain sufficient magnetic material in the form of [magnetosomes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetosome "Magnetosome"), nanometer-sized particles of [iron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron "Iron")-containing [magnetite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetite "Magnetite"),[[4]](#cite_note-4) that the Earth's magnetic field passively aligns them, just as it does with a compass needle. The bacteria are thus not actually sensing the magnetic field.[[5]](#cite_note-5)[[6]](#cite_note-6)

A possible but unexplored mechanism of magnetoreception in animals is through [endosymbiosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endosymbiosis "Endosymbiosis") with magnetotactic bacteria, whose DNA is widespread in animals. This would involve having these bacteria living inside an animal, and their magnetic alignment being used as part of a magnetoreceptive system.[[7]](#cite_note-7)

While numerous studies have claimed to identify magnetite-based magneotoreceptors in vertebrates such as birds,[[8]](#cite_note-Fleissner2003-8)[[9]](#cite_note-Falkenberg2010-9)[[10]](#cite_note-Hore_2016-10)[[11]](#cite_note-Solov'yov_Greiner_2007-11) none have been independently replicated; most have been shown to be iron-rich [macrophages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macrophage "Macrophage")[[1]](#cite_note-Treiber2012-1) or environmental contaminants.[[12]](#cite_note-12)

### In animals

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Magnetoreception&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: In animals")]

In animals, the mechanism for magnetoreception is still under investigation. Three main hypotheses are currently being discussed: one proposing a quantum compass based on a [radical pair mechanism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radical_pair_mechanism "Radical pair mechanism"),[[13]](#cite_note-13) one postulating a iron-based magnetic compass with [magnetite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetite "Magnetite") particles,[[14]](#cite_note-Wiltschkojcp-14) and a third that relies on electromagnetic induction.[[15]](#cite_note-15)

#### Cryptochrome

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Magnetoreception&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Cryptochrome")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/29/Quantum_Magnetoreception_in_Birds.svg/960px-Quantum_Magnetoreception_in_Birds.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Quantum_Magnetoreception_in_Birds.svg)

The [radical pair mechanism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radical_pair_mechanism "Radical pair mechanism") has been proposed for quantum magnetoreception in birds. It takes place in [cryptochrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryptochrome "Cryptochrome") molecules in cells in the birds' [retinas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retina "Retina").[[16]](#cite_note-Hore_Mouritsen_2022-16)

According to the first model, magnetoreception is possible via the [radical pair mechanism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radical_pair_mechanism "Radical pair mechanism"),[[10]](#cite_note-Hore_2016-10) which is well-established in [spin chemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spin_chemistry "Spin chemistry"). The mechanism requires two molecules, each with unpaired electrons, at a suitable distance from each other. When these can exist in states either with their [spin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spin_(physics) "Spin (physics)") axes in the same direction, or in opposite directions, the molecules oscillate rapidly between the two states. That oscillation is extremely sensitive to magnetic fields.[[17]](#cite_note-Rodgers_2009-17)[[18]](#cite_note-Steiner_Ulrich_1989-18)[[19]](#cite_note-Woodward_2002-19)[[20]](#cite_note-Rodgers_Hore_2009-20) Because the Earth's magnetic field is extremely weak, at 0.5 [gauss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss_(unit) "Gauss (unit)"), the radical pair mechanism is currently the only credible way that the Earth's magnetic field could cause chemical changes (as opposed to the mechanical forces which would be detected via magnetic crystals acting like a compass needle).[[20]](#cite_note-Rodgers_Hore_2009-20)

In 1978, Schulten and colleagues proposed that this was the mechanism of magnetoreception.[[21]](#cite_note-21) In 2000, scientists proposed that [cryptochrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryptochrome "Cryptochrome") – a [flavoprotein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flavoprotein "Flavoprotein") in the [rod cells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rod_cell "Rod cell") in the eyes of birds – was the "magnetic molecule" behind this effect.[[22]](#cite_note-22) It is the only protein known to form photoinduced radical-pairs in animals.[[10]](#cite_note-Hore_2016-10) The function of cryptochrome varies by species, but its mechanism is always the same: exposure to blue light excites an electron in a [chromophore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromophore "Chromophore"), which causes the formation of a radical-pair whose electrons are [quantum entangled](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_entanglement "Quantum entanglement"), enabling the precision needed for magnetoreception.[[23]](#cite_note-Wiltschko_Ahmad_Nießner_Gehring_2016-23)[[24]](#cite_note-24)

Many lines of evidence point to cryptochrome and radical pairs as the mechanism of magnetoreception in birds:[[16]](#cite_note-Hore_Mouritsen_2022-16)

* Despite 20 years of searching, no biomolecule other than cryptochrome has been identified capable of supporting radical pairs.[[16]](#cite_note-Hore_Mouritsen_2022-16)
* In cryptochrome, a yellow molecule [flavin adenine dinucleotide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flavin_adenine_dinucleotide "Flavin adenine dinucleotide") (FAD) can absorb a photon of blue light, putting the cryptochrome into an activated state: an electron is transferred from a tryptophan amino acid to the FAD molecule, forming a radical pair.[[16]](#cite_note-Hore_Mouritsen_2022-16)
* Of the six types of cryptochrome in birds, cryptochrome-4a (Cry4a) binds FAD much more tightly than the rest.[[16]](#cite_note-Hore_Mouritsen_2022-16)
* Cry4a levels in [migratory birds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Migratory_birds "Migratory birds"), which rely on navigation for their survival, are highest during the spring and autumn migration periods, when navigation is most critical.[[16]](#cite_note-Hore_Mouritsen_2022-16)
* The Cry4a protein from the [European robin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_robin "European robin"), a migratory bird, is much more sensitive to magnetic fields than similar but not identical Cry4a from pigeons and chickens, which are non-migratory.[[16]](#cite_note-Hore_Mouritsen_2022-16)

These findings together suggest that the Cry4a of migratory birds has been [selected](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_selection "Natural selection") for its magnetic sensitivity.[[16]](#cite_note-Hore_Mouritsen_2022-16)

Behavioral experiments on migratory birds support this theory. Caged migratory birds such as robins display migratory restlessness, known by [ethologists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethologist "Ethologist") as *[Zugunruhe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zugunruhe "Zugunruhe")*, in spring and autumn: they often orient themselves in the direction in which they would migrate. In 2004, Thorsten Ritz showed that a weak radio-frequency electromagnetic field, chosen to be at the same frequency as the singlet-triplet oscillation of cryptochrome radical pairs, effectively interfered with the birds' orientation. The field would not have interfered with an iron-based compass. Further, birds are unable to detect a 180 degree reversal of the magnetic field, something they would straightforwardly detect with an iron-based compass.[[16]](#cite_note-Hore_Mouritsen_2022-16)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/62/Effect_of_RF_interference_on_Magnetoreception_in_Birds.svg/960px-Effect_of_RF_interference_on_Magnetoreception_in_Birds.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Effect_of_RF_interference_on_Magnetoreception_in_Birds.svg)

Very weak [radio-frequency interference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electromagnetic_interference "Electromagnetic interference") prevents [migratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bird_migration "Bird migration") robins from orienting correctly to the [Earth's magnetic field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth's_magnetic_field "Earth's magnetic field"). Since this would not interfere with an iron compass, the experiments imply that the birds use a radical-pair mechanism.[[16]](#cite_note-Hore_Mouritsen_2022-16)

From 2007 onwards, Henrik Mouritsen attempted to replicate this experiment. Instead, he found that robins were unable to orient themselves in the wooden huts he used. Suspecting extremely weak radio-frequency interference from other electrical equipment on the campus, he tried shielding the huts with aluminium sheeting, which blocks electrical noise but not magnetic fields. When he earthed the sheeting, the robins oriented correctly; when the earthing was removed, the robins oriented at random. Finally, when the robins were tested in a hut far from electrical equipment, the birds oriented correctly. These effects imply a radical-pair compass, not an iron one.[[16]](#cite_note-Hore_Mouritsen_2022-16)

In 2016, Wiltschko and colleagues showed that European robins were unaffected by [local anaesthesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_anesthesia "Local anesthesia") of the upper beak, showing that in these test conditions orientation was not from iron-based receptors in the beak. In their view, cryptochrome and its radical pairs provide the only model that can explain the avian magnetic compass.[[23]](#cite_note-Wiltschko_Ahmad_Nießner_Gehring_2016-23) A scheme with three radicals rather than two has been proposed as more resistant to spin relaxation and explaining the observed behaviour better.[[25]](#cite_note-Kattnig_2017-25)

#### Electromagnetic induction

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Magnetoreception&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Electromagnetic induction")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/53/Yellow_Stingray%2C_Belize%2C_2007-09.jpg/330px-Yellow_Stingray%2C_Belize%2C_2007-09.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Yellow_Stingray,_Belize,_2007-09.jpg)

The [yellow stingray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_stingray "Yellow stingray") is able to sense the intensity and [inclination angle of a magnetic field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetic_dip "Magnetic dip").[[26]](#cite_note-Newton_Gill_Kajiura_2020-26)

Another possible mechanism of magnetoreception in animals is electromagnetic induction in [cartilaginous fish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartilaginous_fish "Cartilaginous fish"), namely [sharks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shark "Shark"), [stingrays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stingray "Stingray"), and [chimaeras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chimaera "Chimaera"). These fish have [electroreceptive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electroreception "Electroreception") organs, the [ampullae of Lorenzini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ampullae_of_Lorenzini "Ampullae of Lorenzini"), which can detect small variations in [electric potential](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_potential "Electric potential"). The organs are mucus-filled and consist of canals that connect pores in the skin of the mouth and nose to small sacs within the animal's flesh. They are used to sense the weak electric fields of prey and predators. These organs have been predicted to sense magnetic fields, by means of [Faraday's law of induction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faraday's_law_of_induction "Faraday's law of induction"): as a conductor moves through a magnetic field an electric potential is generated. In this case the conductor is the animal moving through a magnetic field, and the potential induced (*V*ind) depends on the time (t)-varying rate of magnetic flux (Φ) through the conductor according to ![{\displaystyle V_{ind}=-{\frac {d\Phi }{dt}}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/44c2f057ca79c6dc644bcaa129ade62cc1ffee90)

The ampullae of Lorenzini detect very small fluctuations in the potential difference between the pore and the base of the electroreceptor sac. An increase in potential results in a decrease in the rate of nerve activity. This is analogous to the behavior of a current-carrying conductor.[[27]](#cite_note-27)[[28]](#cite_note-28)[[29]](#cite_note-Anderson_Clegg_Véras_Holland_2017-29) [Sandbar sharks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandbar_shark "Sandbar shark"), *Carcharinus plumbeus*, have been shown to be able to detect magnetic fields; the experiments provided non-definitive evidence that the animals had a magnetoreceptor, rather than relying on induction and electroreceptors.[[29]](#cite_note-Anderson_Clegg_Véras_Holland_2017-29) Electromagnetic induction has not been studied in non-aquatic animals.[[20]](#cite_note-Rodgers_Hore_2009-20)

The [yellow stingray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_stingray "Yellow stingray"), *Urobatis jamaicensis*, is able to distinguish between the intensity and inclination angle of a magnetic field in the laboratory. This suggests that cartilaginous fishes may use the Earth's magnetic field for navigation.[[26]](#cite_note-Newton_Gill_Kajiura_2020-26)

## Unanswered questions

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Magnetoreception&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Unanswered questions")]

It remains likely that two or more complementary mechanisms play a role in magnetic field detection in animals. Of course, this potential dual mechanism theory raises the questions of to what degree each method is responsible for the stimulus, and how they produce a signal in response to the weak magnetic field of the Earth.[[20]](#cite_note-Rodgers_Hore_2009-20)

In addition, it is possible that magnetic senses may be different for different species. Some species may only be able to detect north and south, while others may only be able to differentiate between the equator and the poles. Although the ability to sense direction is important in migratory navigation, many animals have the ability to sense small fluctuations in earth's magnetic field to map their position to within a few kilometers.[[20]](#cite_note-Rodgers_Hore_2009-20)[[30]](#cite_note-30)

## Taxonomic range

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Magnetoreception&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Taxonomic range")]

Magnetoreception is widely distributed taxonomically. It is present in many of the animals so far investigated. These include [arthropods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthropod "Arthropod"), [molluscs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mollusc "Mollusc"), and among [vertebrates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertebrate "Vertebrate") in fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals. Its status in other groups remains unknown.[[31]](#cite_note-Wiltschko-31)

The ability to detect and respond to magnetic fields may exist in plants, possibly as in animals mediated by cryptochrome. Experiments by different scientists have identified multiple effects, including changes to growth rate, seed [germination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germination "Germination"), [mitochondrial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitochondrion "Mitochondrion") structure, and responses to gravity ([geotropism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geotropism "Geotropism")). The results have sometimes been controversial, and no mechanism has been definitely identified. The ability may be widely distributed, but its taxonomic range in plants is unknown.[[32]](#cite_note-Maffei_2014-32)

### In molluscs

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Magnetoreception&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: In molluscs")]

The giant sea slug *[Tochuina gigantea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tochuina_gigantea "Tochuina gigantea")* (formerly *T. tetraquetra*), a [mollusc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mollusc "Mollusc"), orients its body between north and east prior to a full moon.[[33]](#cite_note-Lohmann_Willows_1987-33) A 1991 experiment offered a right turn to geomagnetic south and a left turn to geomagnetic east (a [Y-shaped maze](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Y_maze "Y maze")). 80% of *Tochuina* made a turn to magnetic east. When the field was reversed, the animals displayed no preference for either turn.[[34]](#cite_note-34)[[35]](#cite_note-Wang_Cain_Lohmann_pp._1043–1049-35) *Tochuina*'s nervous system is composed of individually identifiable [neurons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neuron "Neuron"), four of which are stimulated by changes in the applied magnetic field, and two which are inhibited by such changes.[[35]](#cite_note-Wang_Cain_Lohmann_pp._1043–1049-35) The tracks of the similar species *[Tritonia exsulans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tritonia_exsulans "Tritonia exsulans")* become more variable in direction when close to strong [rare-earth magnets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rare-earth_magnet "Rare-earth magnet") placed in their natural habitat, suggesting that the animal uses its magnetic sense continuously to help it travel in a straight line.[[36]](#cite_note-Wyeth_Holden_Jalala_Murray_2021-36)

### In insects

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Magnetoreception&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: In insects")]

The fruit fly *[Drosophila melanogaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drosophila_melanogaster "Drosophila melanogaster")* may be able to orient to magnetic fields. In one [choice test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preference_tests_(animals) "Preference tests (animals)"), flies were loaded into an apparatus with two arms that were surrounded by electric coils. Current was run through each of the coils, but only one was configured to produce a 5-Gauss magnetic field (about ten times stronger than the Earth's magnetic field) at a time. The flies were trained to associate the magnetic field with a sucrose reward. Flies with an altered cryptochrome, such as with an antisense mutation, were not sensitive to magnetic fields.[[37]](#cite_note-Gegear2008-37)

Magnetoreception has been studied in detail in insects including [honey bees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honey_bee "Honey bee"), [ants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ant "Ant") and [termites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Termite "Termite").[[38]](#cite_note-Pereira-Bomfim_2015-38) Ants and bees navigate using their magnetic sense both locally (near their nests) and when migrating.[[39]](#cite_note-Wajnberg_2010-39) In particular, the Brazilian stingless bee *[Schwarziana quadripunctata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schwarziana_quadripunctata "Schwarziana quadripunctata")* is able to detect magnetic fields using the thousands of hair-like [sensilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sensillum "Sensillum") on its antennae.[[40]](#cite_note-Esquivel_2005-40)[[41]](#cite_note-Lucano_2005-41)

### In vertebrates

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Magnetoreception&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: In vertebrates")]

#### In fish

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Magnetoreception&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: In fish")]

Studies of magnetoreception in [bony fish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bony_fish "Bony fish") have been conducted mainly with salmon. Both [sockeye salmon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sockeye_salmon "Sockeye salmon") (*Oncorhynchus nerka*) and [Chinook salmon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinook_salmon "Chinook salmon") (*Oncorhynchus tschawytscha*) have a compass sense. This was demonstrated in experiments in the 1980s by changing the axis of a magnetic field around a circular tank of young fish; they reoriented themselves in line with the field.[[42]](#cite_note-Quinn_1980-42)[[43]](#cite_note-Taylor_1986-43)

#### In amphibians

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Magnetoreception&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: In amphibians")]

Some of the earliest studies of amphibian magnetoreception were conducted with [cave salamanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cave_salamander "Cave salamander") (*Eurycea lucifuga*). Researchers housed groups of cave salamanders in corridors aligned with either magnetic north–south, or magnetic east–west. In tests, the magnetic field was experimentally rotated by 90°, and salamanders were placed in cross-shaped structures (one corridor along the new north–south axis, one along the new east–west axis). The salamanders responded to the field's rotation.[[44]](#cite_note-:Phillips_1977-44)

[Red-spotted newts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_newt "Eastern newt") (*Notophthalmus viridescens*) respond to drastic increases in water temperature by heading for land. The behaviour is disrupted if the magnetic field is experimentally altered, showing that the newts use the field for orientation.[[45]](#cite_note-Phillips_1986_newt-45)[[46]](#cite_note-Phillips_1986_salamander-46)

Both [European toads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_toad "Common toad") (*Bufo bufo*) and [natterjack toads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natterjack_toad "Natterjack toad") (*Epidalea calamita)* toads rely on vision and olfaction when migrating to breeding sites, but magnetic fields may also play a role. When randomly displaced 150 metres (490 ft) from their breeding sites, these toads can navigate their way back,[[47]](#cite_note-:12-47) but this ability can be disrupted by fitting them with small magnets.[[48]](#cite_note-:6-48)

#### In reptiles

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Magnetoreception&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: In reptiles")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ac/Leatherback_Turtle_eggs_hatching_at_Eagle_Beach%2C_Aruba_%28cropped%29.jpg/500px-Leatherback_Turtle_eggs_hatching_at_Eagle_Beach%2C_Aruba_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Leatherback_Turtle_eggs_hatching_at_Eagle_Beach,_Aruba_(cropped).jpg)

Magnetoreception plays a part in guiding [loggerhead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loggerhead_sea_turtle "Loggerhead sea turtle") hatchlings to the sea.[[49]](#cite_note-Lohmann_et_al_2022-49)

The majority of study on magnetoreception in reptiles involves turtles. Early support for magnetoreception in turtles was provided in a 1991 study on hatchling [loggerhead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loggerhead_sea_turtle "Loggerhead sea turtle") turtles which demonstrated that loggerheads can use the magnetic field as a compass to determine direction.[[50]](#cite_note-Lohmann_1991-50) Subsequent studies have demonstrated that loggerhead and green turtles can also use the magnetic field of the earth as a map, because different parameters of the Earth's magnetic field vary with geographic location. The map in sea turtles was the first ever described though similar abilities have now been reported in lobsters, fish, and birds.[[49]](#cite_note-Lohmann_et_al_2022-49) Magnetoreception by land turtles was shown in a 2010 experiment on *Terrapene carolina*, a [box turtle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Box_turtle "Box turtle"). After teaching a group of these box turtles to swim to either the east or west end of an experimental tank, a strong magnet disrupted the learned routes.[[51]](#cite_note-Mathis_Moore_2010-51)[[52]](#cite_note-Stehli_1996-52)

Orientation toward the sea, as seen in turtle hatchlings, may rely partly on magnetoreception. In [loggerhead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loggerhead_sea_turtle "Loggerhead sea turtle") and [leatherback](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leatherback_sea_turtle "Leatherback sea turtle") turtles, breeding takes place on beaches, and, after hatching, offspring crawl rapidly to the sea. Although differences in light density seem to drive this behaviour, magnetic alignment appears to play a part. For instance, the natural directional preferences held by these hatchlings (which lead them from beaches to the sea) reverse upon experimental inversion of the magnetic poles.[[53]](#cite_note-Merrill_Salmon_2010-53)

#### In birds

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Magnetoreception&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: In birds")]

[Homing pigeons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homing_pigeon "Homing pigeon") use magnetic fields as part of their complex [navigation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_navigation "Animal navigation") system.[[54]](#cite_note-54) [William Keeton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Tinsley_Keeton "William Tinsley Keeton") showed that time-shifted homing pigeons (acclimatised in the laboratory to a different time-zone) are unable to orient themselves correctly on a clear, sunny day; this is attributed to time-shifted pigeons being unable to compensate accurately for the movement of the sun during the day. Conversely, time-shifted pigeons released on overcast days navigate correctly, suggesting that pigeons can use magnetic fields to orient themselves; this ability can be disrupted with magnets attached to the birds' backs.[[55]](#cite_note-55)[[56]](#cite_note-Gould,_J._L._1984-56) Pigeons can detect magnetic anomalies as weak as 1.86 [gauss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss_(unit) "Gauss (unit)").[[57]](#cite_note-ReferenceA-57)

For a long time the [trigeminal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trigeminal_nerve "Trigeminal nerve") system was the suggested location for a magnetite-based magnetoreceptor in the pigeon. This was based on two findings: First, magnetite-containing cells were reported in specific locations in the upper beak.[[8]](#cite_note-Fleissner2003-8) However, the cells proved to be immune system [macrophages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macrophage "Macrophage"), not [neurons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neuron "Neuron") able to detect magnetic fields.[[1]](#cite_note-Treiber2012-1)[[58]](#cite_note-Engels_20180124-58) Second, pigeon magnetic field detection is impaired by sectioning the trigeminal nerve and by application of [lidocaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lidocaine "Lidocaine"), an anaesthetic, to the olfactory mucosa.[[59]](#cite_note-59) However, lidocaine treatment might lead to unspecific effects and not represent a direct interference with potential magnetoreceptors.[[58]](#cite_note-Engels_20180124-58) As a result, an involvement of the trigeminal system is still debated. In the search for magnetite receptors, a large iron-containing organelle (the [cuticulosome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuticulosome "Cuticulosome")) of unknown function was found in the inner ear of pigeons.[[60]](#cite_note-60)[[61]](#cite_note-61)

Areas of the pigeon brain found in a 2011 study to respond with increased activity to magnetic fields are the posterior [vestibular nuclei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vestibular_nuclei "Vestibular nuclei"), [dorsal thalamus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorsal_thalamus "Dorsal thalamus"), [hippocampus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hippocampus "Hippocampus"), and [visual hyperpallium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avian_pallium "Avian pallium"). The vestibular nuclei receive information from the inner ear including the [semicircular canals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semicircular_canals "Semicircular canals"). This suggests that bird sense magnetism in the inner ear.[[62]](#cite_note-62) A 2025 study in *[Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_(journal) "Science (journal)")* presents two lines of evidence that pigeons sense magnetic fields in their inner ears. Firstly, brain mapping found populations of neurons whose activity is triggered by magnetic fields. Neuron activity was measured using a genetic marker. Brain activity of pigeons exposed to a rotating magnetic field was found in the part of the brain linked to the semicircular canals, and other regions that collate sensory information. Secondly, RNA sequencing in single inner ear cells of the semicircular canals found "the molecular machinery necessary for the detection of magnetic stimuli by [electromagnetic induction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electromagnetic_induction "Electromagnetic induction")."[[63]](#cite_note-Nordmann_2025-63)[[64]](#cite_note-Castelvecchi_2025-64)

[Chickens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chickens "Chickens") have iron mineral deposits in the sensory [dendrites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dendrites "Dendrites") in the upper beak and are capable of magnetoreception.[[9]](#cite_note-Falkenberg2010-9)[[65]](#cite_note-Wiltschko_et_al.,_2007-65) Beak trimming causes loss of the magnetic sense.[[66]](#cite_note-Freire_et_al.,_2011-66)

Superparamagnetic macrophages are present in the liver of pigeons. After macrophage depletion, pigeons flying under overcast conditions lacked their usual orientation capabilities. The superparamagnetic macrophages appear to be required for sensing magnetic direction.[[67]](#cite_note-67)

#### In mammals

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Magnetoreception&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: In mammals")]

Some mammals are capable of magnetoreception. When [woodmice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wood_mouse "Wood mouse") are removed from their home area and deprived of visual and olfactory cues, they orient towards their homes until an inverted magnetic field is applied to their cage.[[68]](#cite_note-68) When the same mice are allowed access to visual cues, they are able to orient themselves towards home despite the presence of inverted magnetic fields. This indicates that woodmice use magnetic fields to orient themselves when no other cues are available. The magnetic sense of woodmice is likely based on a radical-pair mechanism.[[69]](#cite_note-69)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/82/Graumull_IMG_4039.jpg/250px-Graumull_IMG_4039.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Graumull_IMG_4039.jpg)

The [Zambian mole-rat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zambian_mole-rat "Zambian mole-rat") is one of several mammals that use magnetic fields, in their case for nest orientation.[[70]](#cite_note-Nemec_2001-70)

The [Zambian mole-rat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zambian_mole-rat "Zambian mole-rat"), a subterranean mammal, uses magnetic fields to aid in nest orientation.[[71]](#cite_note-Marhold_Wiltschko_Burda-71) In contrast to woodmice, Zambian mole-rats do not rely on radical-pair based magnetoreception, perhaps due to their subterranean lifestyle. Experimental exposure to magnetic fields leads to an increase in neural activity within the [superior colliculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superior_colliculus "Superior colliculus"), as measured by immediate [gene expression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gene_expression "Gene expression"). The activity level of neurons within two levels of the superior colliculus, the outer sublayer of the intermediate gray layer and the deep gray layer, were elevated in a non-specific manner when exposed to various magnetic fields. However, within the inner sublayer of the intermediate gray layer (InGi) there were two or three clusters of cells that respond in a more specific manner. The more time the mole rats were exposed to a magnetic field, the greater the immediate early gene expression within the InGi.[[70]](#cite_note-Nemec_2001-70)

Magnetic fields appear to play a role in [bat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bat "Bat") orientation. They use [echolocation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_echolocation "Animal echolocation") to orient themselves over short distances, typically ranging from a few centimetres up to 50 metres.[[72]](#cite_note-72) When non-migratory big brown bats (*[Eptesicus fuscus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eptesicus_fuscus "Eptesicus fuscus")*) are taken from their home roosts and exposed to magnetic fields rotated 90 degrees from magnetic north, they become disoriented; it is unclear whether they use the magnetic sense as a map, a compass, or a compass calibrator.[[73]](#cite_note-73) Another bat species, the greater mouse-eared bat (*[Myotis myotis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myotis_myotis "Myotis myotis")*), appears to use the Earth's magnetic field in its home range as a compass, but needs to calibrate this at sunset or dusk.[[74]](#cite_note-Holland_Borissov_Siemers_2010-74) In migratory soprano pipistrelles (*[Pipistrellus pygmaeus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soprano_pipistrelle "Soprano pipistrelle")*), experiments using mirrors and [Helmholtz coils](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmholtz_coil "Helmholtz coil") show that they calibrate the magnetic field using the position of the solar disk at sunset.[[75]](#cite_note-75)[[76]](#cite_note-76)

[Red foxes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_fox "Red fox") (*Vulpes vulpes*) may be influenced by the Earth's magnetic field when [predating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Predation "Predation") small rodents like mice and voles. They attack these prey using a specific high-jump, preferring a north-eastern compass direction. Successful attacks are tightly clustered to the north.[[77]](#cite_note-77)

There is not yet a consensus on whether humans can sense magnetic fields, but some evidence suggests it.[[78]](#cite_note-Wang_Hilburn_Wu_2019-78)[[79]](#cite_note-Chae_Human_magnetic_sense-79) The [ethmoid bone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethmoid_bone "Ethmoid bone") in the nose contains magnetic materials.[[80]](#cite_note-Carrubba_Frilot-80)[[79]](#cite_note-Chae_Human_magnetic_sense-79) Magnetosensitive cryptochrome 2 (cry2) is present in the human retina.[[81]](#cite_note-Foley_2011-81) Human alpha [brain waves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brain_wave "Brain wave") are affected by magnetic fields, but it is not known whether behaviour is affected.[[78]](#cite_note-Wang_Hilburn_Wu_2019-78)[[81]](#cite_note-Foley_2011-81)

args.summary:
This Wikipedia article (a "Good Article") provides a comprehensive overview of magnetoreception, the biological sense that allows organisms to detect the Earth's magnetic field. The sense is used mainly for orientation and navigation and is found across arthropods, molluscs, and vertebrates (fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals).

**History:** Until the late 20th century, evidence for magnetic sensing was essentially behavioral only. Key milestones: In 1972, Roswitha and Wolfgang Wiltschko showed migratory birds respond to magnetic field direction and inclination; in 1977, M. M. Walker identified magnetite-based magnetoreceptors in rainbow trout snouts; and in 2000, Thorsten Ritz proposed cryptochrome as a magnetoreceptor working via quantum entanglement.

**Proposed mechanisms (three main hypotheses):**
1. **Passive iron-based alignment (bacteria):** Magnetotactic bacteria contain magnetosomes (nanometer-sized magnetite particles) that passively align with the Earth's magnetic field like a compass needle—these bacteria are not actually sensing the field. A possible but unexplored mechanism in animals is endosymbiosis with such bacteria. Numerous claimed findings of magnetite-based receptors in vertebrates have not been independently replicated; most proved to be iron-rich macrophages or contaminants.
2. **Cryptochrome/radical pair mechanism (in animals):** This quantum-based mechanism is well-established in spin chemistry and is currently the only credible way the weak Earth's field (0.5 gauss) could cause chemical changes. Cryptochrome, a flavoprotein in bird rod cells, binds FAD and forms quantum-entangled radical pairs when excited by blue light. Evidence supporting it includes: no other biomolecule capable of supporting radical pairs has been found in 20 years; cryptochrome-4a (Cry4a) binds FAD most tightly and levels peak during migration seasons; European robin Cry4a is more magnetically sensitive than pigeon/chicken versions. Behavioral experiments support this: weak radio-frequency interference (which wouldn't affect an iron compass) disrupts robin orientation, and birds cannot detect 180° reversal of the field. Henrik Mouritsen replicated these findings between 2007 onwards, showing that even extremely weak RF noise disorients robins while aluminium shielding restores orientation.
3. **Electromagnetic induction (in cartilaginous fish):** Sharks, stingrays, and chimaeras use their ampullae of Lorenzini (electroreceptive organs) to detect magnetic fields via Faraday's law of induction as they swim through the field. The yellow stingray (*Urobatis jamaicensis*) can distinguish between field intensity and inclination angle. Induction has not been studied in non-aquatic animals.

**Unanswered questions:** It is likely that two or more complementary mechanisms play a role. Magnetic senses may differ by species—some detecting only north/south while others map position to within a few kilometers.

**Taxonomic range:**
- **Molluscs:** The giant sea slug *Tochuina gigantea* orients between north and east before a full moon; in a Y-maze, 80% chose magnetic east when given a choice.
- **Insects:** Fruit flies (*Drosophila melanogaster*) can associate magnetic fields with sucrose rewards, requiring cryptochrome. Honey bees, ants, and termites also exhibit magnetoreception; the Brazilian stingless bee *Schwarziana quadripunctata* uses hair-like sensilla on its antennae.
- **Fish:** Sockeye and Chinook salmon have a compass sense (demonstrated in 1980s circular-tank experiments).
- **Amphibians:** Cave salamanders respond to field rotation; red-spotted newts use the field for orientation; European and natterjack toads can be disrupted by small magnets.
- **Reptiles:** Loggerhead hatchling studies (1991) showed magnetic compass use; loggerhead and green turtles also use the magnetic field as a map (the first such map ever described). Box turtles (*Terrapene carolina*) were disrupted by magnets in 2010 experiments.
- **Birds:** Homing pigeons use magnetic fields as part of their navigation; time-shifted pigeons navigate correctly on overcast days (attributed to magnetic sensing) but fail on clear days. Pigeons detect anomalies as weak as 1.86 gauss. Former claims of magnetite receptors in the beak were disproven (the cells are macrophages). A 2025 *Science* study found neurons in pigeon inner ears triggered by magnetic fields and molecular machinery for electromagnetic induction in semicircular canal cells. Chickens have iron deposits in upper-beak dendrites.
- **Mammals:** Woodmice use magnetic fields when no other cues are available (likely radical-pair based). The Zambian mole-rat uses magnetic fields for nest orientation, relying on the superior colliculus rather than radical pairs. Bats (big brown, greater mouse-eared, and migratory soprano pipistrelles) use magnetic fields for orientation. Red foxes attack rodents in a preferred north-eastern direction. There is no consensus on human magnetoreception, though the ethmoid bone contains magnetic material and cryptochrome 2 exists in the human retina; human alpha brain waves are affected by magnetic fields, but behavioral effects are unknown.

The article also notes possible magnetoreception in plants (likely cryptochrome-mediated, affecting growth, germination, mitochondrial structure, and geotropism), though no mechanism is definitively identified.

# Further Analysis of the Magnetic Compass of MigratOlY Birds 

> WOLFGANG WILTSCHKO, Fachbereich Biologie der Universitiit, 6000 Frankfurt, FRG

Abstract The orientation behavior of migratory European Robins (Erithacus rubecuZa) during Zugunruhe was used for a further analysis of the characteristics of the birds' magnetic compass. Tests with Robins adapted to field intensities outside the normal functional range of the magnetic compass show that the process of adaptation to fields outside this range is neither a shifting nor a simple enlargement of tpe functional range. Tests in several 1-Hz alternating magnetic fields with rectangular and sine-shaped impulses indicate that a cer-tain constant portion of the impulse is necessary to enable the birds to use it for orientation. A. Introduction Since the sonsory basis for the perception of the magnetic field by birds is still unknown, investigating behavioral responses to different types of magnetic fields appeared to be the best approach to gain more information about how the birds' "gaussmeter" might function. One be-havioral response to magnetic stimuli that is easily studied is the directional orientation of caged migratory birds - especially of European Robins - during Zugunruhe. Their orientational reaction (1) corresponds to the migratory direction of their free-living conspe-cifics as revealed by the banding recoveries and is thus biologically meaningful, (2) is directly correlated to the direction of the magnetic field applied, and (3) indicates whether a given magnetic field is adequate for the birds, since it becomes random if the field cannot be used (Wiltschko 1968, 1972). So it seemed appropriate to continue to use this response for the further analysis of the characteristics of the birds' magnetic compass. B. Materials and Methods All experiments reported here were conducted in the spring. The test birds - European Robins (Erithacus rubecuZa) - were either (1) captured during the preceding autumn migratory season, and their Zugunruhe was induced ahead of time by photoperiodic manipulations (making it pos-sible to start the tests in January, compo Wiltschko, 1968), or (2) freshly trapped and tested during the natural spring migratory season. As in former experiments, octagonal cages with eight radially posi-tioned perches were used for recording the birds' activity. From the amount of activity per perch, the headings of the test nights were calculated. They were comprised in the mean vector of the series with 

K. Schmidt-Koenig et al. (eds.), Animal Migration, Navigation, and Homing 

© Springer-Verlag Berlin Heidelberg 1978 303 the direction am and the length rm; rm was tested for statistical sig-nificance using the Rayleigh Test (Batschelet, 1965). A more detailed description of the experimental procedure, the registration method, and the statistical evaluation is given in Wiltschko (1968) and Wiltschko and Wiltschko (1976). The magnetic fields to be tested were produced by pairs of Helmholtz coils (2 m in diameter, 1 m clearance). All statements pertaining to the characteristics of the magnetic fields apply to the resultant magnetic field as measured inside the orientation cage. For the alternating fields, a pair of such coils with two independent sets of windings was positioned such that the coils' axis lay in the course of the field lines, i.e., in the direction of inclination. One set of windings was then charged with direct current to cancel out the local field; the other set was charged by a Wavetek frequency generator producing the pulses to be tested, the output of which was checked by an oscilloscope. C. Results and Discussion I. Intensity Range of the Magnetic Compass Former experiments (Wiltschko, 1972) had shown that the magnetic com-pass normally functions only in a relatively narrow intensity range. Robins, captured and kept in Frankfurt at the local Earth's magnetic field of 0.46 gauss, could spontaneously orient at 0.43 gauss and at 0.54 gauss, but at 0.34 gauss and 0.60 gauss, random behavior was ob-served. Thus, the normal functional intensity range of these birds' magnetic compass appears to include ca. 0.2 gauss; its lower limit being at approximately 0.38 gauss and the upper limit at ca. 0.57 gauss (Table 1). The study aimed to gain insight into the sensory basis of magnetic field perception by testing birds' responses to various magnetic field types. 

Methodology: Robins were tested in octagonal cages with eight radially positioned perches, with activity recorded to calculate nightly headings. Magnetic fields were produced by pairs of Helmholtz coils (2 m diameter). Tests were conducted in spring using either photoperiodically-induced Zugunruhe (starting January) or naturally migrating birds. Statistical significance was assessed using the Rayleigh Test.

The normal functional intensity range of the birds' magnetic compass includes approximately 0.2 gauss, with a lower limit around 0.38 gauss and upper limit around 0.57 gauss (Table 1).

The abstract states that tests with Robins adapted to field intensities outside the normal functional range show the adaptation process is neither a shifting nor a simple enlargement of the functional range. Tests in several 1-Hz alternating magnetic fields with rectangular and sine-shaped impulses indicate that a certain constant portion of the impulse is necessary to enable birds to use it for orientation.

## Abstract

The avian magnetic compass was analyzed by testing migratory birds, using their orientation as an indicator. These tests revealed some remarkable properties of the avian magnetic compass: (1) It is an inclination compass’, (2) it is light-dependent, with (3) receptors located in the right eye. These characteristics are in agreement with the Radical Pair model proposed by Ritz et al. (2000). Using the same experimental set-up, we tested the model by behavioral spectroscopy’, exposing migratory birds to radiofrequency fields of different frequencies and intensities. Such fields affected the orientation only when applied at an angle to the field lines. Tests with different frequencies led to an estimate of the life time of the crucial radical pair between 2-10 μs. We also could identify an extremely sensitive resonance at the Larmor frequency, which implies specific properties of the radical pair. Cryptochromes, a blue-light absorbing photopigment, has been proposed to be the receptor-molecule; it has been found to be present in the retina of birds.

args.key_excerpts: The avian magnetic compass was analyzed by testing migratory birds, using their orientation as an indicator. These tests revealed some remarkable properties of the avian magnetic compass: (1) It is an inclination compass, (2) it is light-dependent, with (3) receptors located in the right eye.
args.summary:
This webpage presents the peer-reviewed open-access research article "The mechanism of the avian magnetic compass" by Wolfgang Wiltschko, Roswitha Wiltschko, and Thorsten Ritz, published in Procedia Chemistry (Volume 3, Issue 1, 2011, Pages 276-284, DOI: 10.1016/j.proche.2011.08.035). The paper is part of a special issue on the 22nd Solvay Conference on Chemistry, edited by G.R. Fleming, G.D. Scholes, and A. De Wit.

The researchers analyzed the avian magnetic compass by testing migratory birds, using their orientation as an indicator. The tests revealed three remarkable properties of the avian magnetic compass: (1) it is an inclination compass, (2) it is light-dependent, and (3) its receptors are located in the right eye. These characteristics align with the Radical Pair model proposed by Ritz et al. (2000).

Using behavioral spectroscopy, the team tested the model by exposing migratory birds to radiofrequency fields of different frequencies and intensities. Key findings include:
- The fields only affected orientation when applied at an angle to the field lines
- Tests with different frequencies led to an estimate of the lifetime of the crucial radical pair between 2-10 μs
- They identified an extremely sensitive resonance at the Larmor frequency, implying specific properties of the radical pair
- Cryptochromes, a blue-light absorbing photopigment proposed as the receptor-molecule, were found to be present in the retina of birds

Keywords associated with the article: Magnetic compass, inclination compass, Radical Pair model, Larmor frequency, cryptochrome.

The article has been cited 21 times and has 73 Mendeley readers. Related works cited include papers on quantum effects in bird navigation, the biophysics of bird flight, magnetoreception and activated cryptochrome 1a, and magnetite-based receptors in the beaks of birds.

# Radical-pair-based magnetoreception in birds: radio-frequency experiments and the role of cryptochrome

### Christine Nießner

### Michael Winklhofer

Corresponding author.

Received 2017 Mar 1; Revised 2017 May 28; Accepted 2017 May 29; Issue date 2017.

**Open Access**This article is distributed under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License (<http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/>), which permits unrestricted use, distribution, and reproduction in any medium, provided you give appropriate credit to the original author(s) and the source, provide a link to the Creative Commons license, and indicate if changes were made.

## Abstract

The radical-pair hypothesis of magnetoreception has gained a lot of momentum, since the flavoprotein cryptochrome was postulated as a structural candidate to host magnetically sensitive chemical reactions. Here, we first discuss behavioral tests using radio-frequency magnetic fields (0.1–10 MHz) to specifically disturb a radical-pair-based avian magnetic compass sense. While disorienting effects of broadband RF magnetic fields have been replicated independently in two competing labs, the effects of monochromatic RF magnetic fields administered at the electronic Larmor frequency (~1.3 MHz) are disparate. We give technical recommendations for future RF experiments. We then focus on two candidate magnetoreceptor proteins in birds, Cry1a and Cry1b, two splice variants of the same gene (Cry1). Immunohistochemical studies have identified Cry1a in the outer segments of the ultraviolet/violet-sensitive cone photoreceptors and Cry1b in the cytosol of retinal ganglion cells. The identification of the host neurons of these cryptochromes and their subcellular expression patterns presents an important advance, but much work lies ahead to gain some functional understanding. In particular, interaction partners of cryptochrome Cry1a and Cry1b remain to be identified. A candidate partner for Cry4 was previously suggested, but awaits independent replication.

**Keywords:** Radical-pair mechanism, Cryptochrome, Inclination compass, Radio-frequency magnetic fields, Larmor frequency

## Introduction

Birds use their magnetic compass sense to extract directional information from the Earth’s magnetic field (Wiltschko and Wiltschko [1972](#CR70)). With a “magnetic map sense”, they can moreover locate their position (Kishkinev et al. [2015](#CR27)), which together with compass, information is required for magnetic navigation. Here, we focus on the basic principles of functionality of the magnetic compass in birds and on experiments that have been designed to test for the underlying biophysical mechanism.

The magnetic compass in birds is the so-called inclination compass (Wiltschko and Wiltschko [1972](#CR70)), which detects the spatial orientation of the field lines but not their polarity. The functional window of the compass sense is adapted to the naturally occurring geomagnetic field strengths, but can be adjusted to ten times lower field strengths (Winklhofer et al. [2013](#CR78)). The avian magnetic inclination compass is light-dependent, requiring wavelengths between UV and green light (Wiltschko and Wiltschko [2005](#CR72)), and it is localized in the eye (Semm et al. [1984](#CR61); Semm and Demaine [1986](#CR60); Wiltschko et al. [2002](#CR74), [2003](#CR75); Mouritsen et al. [2005](#CR40); Liedvogel et al. [2007](#CR33); Heyers et al. [2007](#CR19); Stapput et al. [2010](#CR64); Zapka et al. [2009](#CR81)). The characteristics of the magnetic compass in birds—polarity insensitivity and light-dependence—are consistent with a photo-activated radical pair (Schulten et al. [1978](#CR58); Schulten [1982](#CR56); Ritz et al. [2000](#CR52); recent review: Hore and Mouritsen [2016](#CR22)) and has guided the search for a molecule that acts as a magnetic field detector when activated by light and that resides in the eye, leading to cryptochromes as structural candidate.

## Radical-pair mechanism

A free radical by definition is a chemical species with an unpaired valence electron. A well-known example from cell biology is the signaling agent nitric oxide ·(NO), which has 5 + 6 = 11 valence electrons, one of which is unpaired. A free radical is a paramagnetic entity, because the electron spin of the unpaired electron is unpaired (uncompensated). However, the magnetic moment of a free radical is many orders of magnitude too small to significantly interact with the comparatively weak Earth’s magnetic field. The situation is different for two radicals originating from the same process, either by bond splitting from the same parent (e.g., hydrogen peroxide decomposition into HO· and ·OH) or by a redox reaction, where an electron is transferred from a donor to an acceptor. In such a geminate radical pair, the electron spins are in a coherent spin state, oriented either antiparallel to each other (singlet state) or parallel to each other (triplet state), and their relative orientation, the so-called spin multiplicity, can be affected even by a moderate-strength external magnetic field (Schulten et al. [1976](#CR57)). A radical pair is relatively short-lived and may recombine by electron back transfer, but only if it is in the correct spin state (Schulten et al. [1976](#CR57)). Spin selectivity of geminate radical-pair recombination, therefore, is essential for the chemical magnetoreception pathway proposed by Schulten et al. ([1978](#CR58)), who also pointed out that it provides a natural explanation for the magnetic compass sense of song birds being insensitive to the polarity of the magnetic field lines (Wiltschko and Wiltschko [1972](#CR70)).

Soon afterwards, Schulten ([1982](#CR56)) suggested a photoexcitation pathway for the formation of the precursor state from which the geminate radical pair descends and thereby redefined the concept of physico-chemical light-dependent magnetoreception that had been proposed by Leask ([1977](#CR31)) to occur through an optical pumping pathway. However, it was not until two decades later that a concrete candidate molecule—cryptochrome—was suggested (Ritz et al. [2000](#CR52)) and which then acted as a game changer for research into radical-pair-based magnetoreception. For details about the radical-pair mechanism and how it could be realized in the avian magnetoreception pathway, we refer to the excellent review by Hore and Mouritsen ([2016](#CR22)). We here discuss physical concepts only to the point where they are essential for grasping the idea behind experiments conducted with radio-frequency magnetic fields, which are the key diagnostic test for radical-pair-based magnetoreception.

### Effects of broadband magnetic fields

Schulten et al. ([1976](#CR57)) emphasized the importance of hyperfine interactions for singlet to triplet interconversion in a geminate radical pair. Hyperfine interaction refers to the magnetic interaction between electron spin and nuclear spin. In a spin-correlated radical pair where each unpaired electron experiences different hyperfine interactions, the two spins precess at different frequencies and thus change their relative orientation, oscillating between singlet and triplet states. This natural interconversion between singlet and triplet is modulated by an external magnetic field (Schulten et al. [1978](#CR58)). Moreover, the singlet–triplet interconversion can be perturbed by an oscillating magnetic field whose frequency matches any of the interconversion frequencies in the radical pair system. The hyperfine splitting frequencies are in the lower MHz radio-frequency (RF) range, but not exactly known yet for the biological radical pair underlying the magnetic sense (Ritz et al. [2004](#CR53)). In a behavioral experiment, this limitation can be overcome by applying an RF magnetic field over a frequency spectrum that covers the lower MHz range. Indeed, European robins subjected to broadband-noise RF magnetic fields were disoriented (Ritz et al. [2004](#CR53)), a key finding that was independently replicated with significantly weaker RF magnetic field intensities: Engels et al. ([2014](#CR11)) and Schwarze et al. ([2016](#CR59)) reported that RF magnetic field intensities of the order of 1 nT (root mean square) were already sufficient for disrupting orientation. At the theoretical level, it is not understood how such low RF levels could affect a radical pair (e.g., Kavokin [2009](#CR23), [2017](#CR24); Hore and Mouritsen [2016](#CR22)) or could have unspecific physiological effects on cells, tissues, or the whole organism. An unequivocal effect of RF magnetic fields on the partitioning of reactive oxygen species has been demonstrated experimentally for very high RF intensities of 20,000 nT (Usselman et al. [2016](#CR67)), but it is not clear if the radical pair mediating that effect has sufficiently long spin-correlation time for the effect to still occur at RF intensities of 20 nT or lower. Likewise, RF-induced heating of magnetic material in a magnetic-particle-based magnetoreception pathway is possible for high RF magnetic field levels (Shcherbakov and Winklhofer [2010](#CR62)), but exceedingly unlikely to occur under 1 nT RF magnetic fields.

### Effects of Larmor frequency RF magnetic fields

Thalau et al. ([2005](#CR66)) and Ritz et al. ([2009](#CR54)) conducted a series of experiments aimed at perturbing a radical-pair-based compass with a magnetic field oscillating at a special RF frequency, the so-called Larmor frequency of the free electron, defined as:

|  |
| --- |
| fL=γB, |

where *γ* = 28,024.95 MHz/T is the gyromagnetic ratio for a “free” electron (i.e., *g-*factor of 2.0023) and *B* is the absolute value of the external magnetic field in units of T (flux density). The rationale for applying this frequency is that it matches the Zeeman splitting induced by the static geomagnetic field (Thalau et al. [2005](#CR66)). Both studies were conducted in Frankfurt in a local magnetic field of between 46,000 and 47,400 nT intensity, with an RF frequency of 1.315000 MHz, i.e., the Larmor frequency for *B* = 46,922.5 nT. Birds turned out to be disoriented in the Larmor condition down to RF amplitudes of 15 nT, while 150 nT administered at non-Larmor frequencies had no effect. These results have been interpreted in terms of a radical pair in which one of the radicals is devoid of hyperfine interactions and thus is only sensitive to the external magnetic field (Ritz et al. [2009](#CR54)). However, the work of Ritz et al. ([2009](#CR54)) has also triggered critical reviews (Kirschvink et al. [2010](#CR26); Kavokin et al. [2014](#CR25)). Kirschvink et al. ([2010](#CR26)) criticized the lack of confound control in RF experiments. An obvious confound would be the usage of two different test chambers, one dedicated to test, the other to controls, so that a statistical meaningful difference between test and control could be due as well to the differences between the test chambers. Equally confounding is electronic equipment that is running during test trials only (Kirschvink et al. [2010](#CR26)). It is clear that the comparison between test and control will be more meaningful if the overall design of the conditions is similar. Schwarze et al. ([2016](#CR59)) implemented a confound control to ascertain that birds from both the experimental group (RF) and control group (sham-RF) experienced otherwise identical conditions in the test setup, housed in an electromagnetically shielded environment. Specifically, the RF amplifier was operating under load for the whole duration of both control and test trials. The vibrations and acoustic noise produced by the cooling fans of the amplifier then is of comparable magnitude and frequency content, no matter whether it delivers electric power into the coil (RF) or into a dummy load (sham-RF). Schwarze et al. ([2016](#CR59)) did not observe complete disorientation in the birds tested under the Larmor condition, that is, the level of non-orientation (*p* value 0.138) was much lower than the one reported by Ritz et al. ([2009](#CR54)) or by the other independent replication study by Kavokin et al. ([2014](#CR25)). Importantly, the orientation data under Larmor-RF were statistically indistinguishable from those under sham-RF conditions (Schwarze et al. [2016](#CR59)). From a statistical point of view, the large number of birds (31 per group) tested by Schwarze et al. ([2016](#CR59)) implies high statistical power and thus a low probability for false negatives, i.e., for not identifying a potentially existing difference between experimental and sham-RF group. Even at higher RF amplitude, in an RF condition similar to Thalau et al. ([2005](#CR66)), Schwarze et al. ([2016](#CR59)) obtained a significant orientation at the group level.

It is unclear why the Larmor-RF condition affected complete disorientation in Frankfurt (Thalau et al. [2005](#CR66); Ritz et al. [2009](#CR54)) and at the Curish spit (Kavokin et al. [2014](#CR25)), but not in Oldenburg, where the most rigorous RF test design was implemented (Schwarze et al. [2016](#CR59)). In Table [1](#Tab1), we have juxtaposed the Larmor frequency experiments in terms of experimental parameters, RF equipment, group sizes, and statistical results. The studies differed in various experimental details (coil design, RF equipment, illumination), bird testing procedures, and analysis protocols. All these differences make it difficult to identify the key factor responsible for the presence or absence of disorientation effects under the local Larmor condition. It is not even clear if the local Larmor-RF condition was always exactly matched in each experimental trial so as to produce the maximum resonance effect. If a 25 nT single-frequency magnetic field is to have an effect on the spin dynamics in a radical pair, it has to act upon the spin-correlated pair for longer than 200 μs (Hiscock et al. [2016](#CR20)), which implies that its resonance frequency is sharper than 5 kHz, ca. 0.5% in terms of the absolute frequency (5/1315). The 0.5% figure defines the accuracy with which the absolute value of the magnetic field has to be measured at the test site before setting the Larmor frequency (see below).
