Could a chemical reaction be used to detect the direction of the Earth's magnetic field? At first sight, most physical chemists would be skeptical. The energy of interaction of a molecule with a ≈50-μT magnetic field is >6 orders of magnitude smaller than the average thermal energy _k_ B _T_, which in turn is 10–100 times smaller than the strength of a chemical bond. It therefore seems inconceivable that the position of a chemical equilibrium or the rate of an activated chemical reaction could be significantly altered by such a minuscule perturbation. Nevertheless, there is growing evidence that the striking ability of birds to detect the direction of the geomagnetic field ([1](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B1)) is based on a chemical reaction whose product yields depend on the orientation of the reactants within the field ([2](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B2)) (for reviews, see also refs. [3](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B3)–[8](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B8)).

It has been known since the 1970s that certain chemical reactions do in fact respond to applied magnetic fields. The key species are radical pairs—pairs of transient radicals created simultaneously, such that the 2 electron spins, one on each radical, are correlated. They have the unique properties that their chemical fate is largely controlled by weak (≪_k_ B _T_) magnetic interactions via their spin correlation and that the electron spins remain far enough from thermal equilibrium for long enough that the _k_ B _T_ objection is irrelevant. Experimental and theoretical studies of the “radical pair mechanism” over the last 30 years have given an extraordinary variety of information on the magnetic properties, kinetics, and dynamics of radicals and their reactions (reviewed in refs. [9](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B9)–[13](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B13)). This field of endeavor has come to be called “spin chemistry.”

The radical pair mechanism [and a few rare variants ([10](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B10))] is currently the only plausible way in which weak magnetic fields can affect chemical reactivity. Most experimental studies have been of photochemically formed organic radicals in solution. The effects are usually not dramatic—typically <50% change in reaction yields or radical lifetimes and, with few exceptions ([14](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B14)), are observed for magnetic field intensities (1 mT–10 T) considerably stronger than the Earth's (25–65 μT). Compared with these chemical studies, there are relatively few reliable examples of magnetic field effects on biological processes, the most notable by far being photosynthetic reaction center proteins where light absorption leads to radical pair formation by sequential electron transfer steps (reviewed in refs. [15](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B15)–[17](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B17)).

Radical pair reactions were first proposed as a magnetoreceptor by Schulten ([18](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B18), [19](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B19)), prompted by the findings that avian magnetic orientation is light-dependent—suggesting a photochemical process—and is responsive to the inclination rather than the polarity of the geomagnetic field ([20](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B20)–[23](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B23)); unlike a magnetic compass needle, birds maintain their orientation when the ambient field vector is reversed ([5](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B5)).

Our aim here is to survey the radical pair mechanism in the context of the avian magnetic compass. We identify the key features required for efficient magnetoreception, comment on the likelihood that they could occur in a biologically plausible receptor, and evaluate the evidence for and against the radical pair hypothesis. Throughout, the focus is firmly on the primary reception mechanism: We make no significant attempt to review the behavioral studies that led to and have since supported the radical pair model, or to comment on (neuro) physiological aspects of magnetoreception, all of which have been covered authoritatively and extensively in recent reviews ([3](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B3)–[5](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B5), [8](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B8), [24](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B24), [25](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B25)). Nor do we presume here to debate the relative merits of the radical pair hypothesis versus proposals based on biogenic magnetite (Fe 3 O 4) ([26](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B26)–[32](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B32)). We close with a discussion of cryptochrome, the photoreceptor protein that is presently the only molecule under consideration as the magnetoreceptor ([2](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B2)), and make suggestions for further research. We hope that the thoughts set out here will be of interest to both physical and biological scientists who may be inspired to contribute to the elucidation of this intriguing and incompletely understood sensory mechanism.

## Key Features of a Radical Pair Magnetoreceptor

### Chemistry.

Magnetically sensitive reactions almost always involve radicals, i.e., molecules that have an odd number of electrons and consequently an unpaired electron spin that may be found in one of 2 spin states: ↑ or ↓. A radical pair is a short-lived reaction intermediate comprising 2 radicals formed in tandem whose unpaired electron spins may be either antiparallel (↑↓, a singlet state, S) or parallel (↑↑, a triplet state, T). As each electron spin has an associated magnetic moment, the interconversion and chemical fates of the S and T states can be influenced by internal and external magnetic fields.

In chemical terms, the minimum requirement for a radical pair reaction to be sensitive to an external magnetic field is that at least one of the S and T states undergoes a reaction that is not open to the other, usually as a consequence of the imperative to conserve spin angular momentum. [Fig. 1](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#F1) shows what is probably the simplest reaction scheme possessing the essential chemical features required to form the basis of a magnetic compass. Imagining for now that the radicals are completely immobile, the individual reaction steps are as follows.

Fig. 1.

Open in Viewer![Image 6](https://www.pnas.org/cms/10.1073/pnas.0711968106/asset/93b0fafb-b372-458d-90cc-4f0c63c382a1/assets/graphic/zpq9990964370001.jpeg)

A simple reaction scheme that could form the basis of a compass magnetoreceptor. The spin-correlated radical pair is depicted in red for the singlet state and blue for the triplet. See _Key Features of a Radical Pair Magnetoreceptor: Chemistry_ for further details.

A and B in [Fig. 1](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#F1) could be portions of the same molecule or distinct molecules held in close proximity by their surroundings (e.g., 2 cofactors or a cofactor and an amino acid residue in a protein). Species C is either the signaling state or leads to the signaling state via subsequent chemical transformations (which are not shown in [Fig. 1](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#F1)). An applied magnetic field can alter the yield of C by regulating the competition between its formation (from the S and T states, step 4) and the regeneration of A B (exclusively from the S state, step 2). If the interconversion of S and T is hindered by the external magnetic field, then less C will be produced and correspondingly more radical pairs recombine directly to A B. The opposite follows if the field enhances S ↔ T interconversion. It is important to note that the external magnetic field is far too weak to initiate new radical reactions.

Variants on the reaction scheme in [Fig. 1](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#F1) are possible, and although the details of the chemistry may differ, the principles remain the same. Some of the more likely alternatives include: an excited triplet precursor state; electron transfer in the reverse direction (to form A•−B•+); and formation of the radical pair via sequential electron transfer steps ([33](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B33)). These and other possibilities are described in the [supporting information (SI) _Appendix_](https://www.pnas.org/cgi/data/0711968106/DCSupplemental/Appendix_PDF.pdf) together with comments on the nature of the reactions that could lead to C and subsequently convert it back to A B.

A well-studied precedent for this kind of magnetically sensitive radical pair chemistry is provided by the initial charge separation steps of bacterial photosynthetic energy conversion, which proceed via a series of radical ion pairs formed by sequential electron transfers along a chain of immobilized chlorophyll and quinone cofactors in a reaction center protein complex ([15](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B15)–[17](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B17)). Provided subsequent forward electron transfer is blocked, the recombination of the primary radical pair responds to magnetic fields in excess of ≈1 mT. In unblocked reaction centers, spin correlation can be transferred along the electron transport chain from the primary to the secondary radical pair ([34](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B34)–[36](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B36)), whose lifetime is also magnetically sensitive ([37](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B37)–[39](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B39)). Similar effects occur in plant photosystems. Other biological radical pair processes are much less well characterized (see [_SI Appendix_](https://www.pnas.org/cgi/data/0711968106/DCSupplemental/Appendix_PDF.pdf)).

### Hyperfine Interactions.

We now turn to the essential magnetic properties of a radical pair magnetoreceptor, focusing first on detecting the presence of an external magnetic field and then its direction. An absolute requirement is that the 2 radicals, between them, have at least 1 hyperfine interaction, i.e., an intraradical coupling between the magnetic moment of the unpaired electron and the magnetic moment of an atomic nucleus such as 1 H or 14 N. Almost all biologically occurring radicals have several potentially suitable hyperfine interactions. Ample data on hyperfine tensors is available from electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy ([40](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B40), [41](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B41)) and ab initio density functional calculations ([42](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B42)).

Hyperfine interactions are crucial because they drive the interconversion of the S and T states of the radical pair and allow it to be modified by an external magnetic field. S ↔ T interconversion is a coherent quantum mechanical process: Radical pairs oscillate between their S and T states at a variety of frequencies determined by the strengths of the hyperfine interactions. 1 H and 14 N hyperfine couplings in organic radicals are typically in the range 10–1,000 μT, corresponding to frequencies of 300 kHz to 30 MHz (the conversion factor is 28 kHz μT−1). The time scale for significant transformation of S into T and vice versa is thus typically 10 ns–1 μs. Sensitivity to an external magnetic field arises because the Zeeman interaction of the magnetic moments of the 2 electrons causes additional periodic S ↔ T interconversion. In a 50-μT field, this oscillation has a frequency of ≈1.4 MHz and a period of ≈700 ns. The calculated time dependence for a prototype radical pair is shown in [Fig. 2](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#F2).

Fig. 2.

Open in Viewer![Image 7](https://www.pnas.org/cms/10.1073/pnas.0711968106/asset/80bde8f9-20bf-47b9-8ad1-53359a547157/assets/graphic/zpq9990964370002.jpeg)

Quantum mechanical spin dynamics simulations for the reaction in [Fig. 1](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#F1), performed as described in ref. [60](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B60). (_A_) In the absence of the magnetic field and with no recombination (green), the fraction of radical pairs that exist in the triplet state, _p_ T(_t_), oscillates at the frequency of the hyperfine coupling (here 14 MHz). (_B_) When a weak magnetic field is introduced (green), _p_ T(_t_) shows an additional, slower, modulation at the frequency of the Zeeman interaction (here 1.4 MHz). The radical pair reactions cause _p_ T(_t_) to be exponentially damped (red) and allow the reaction product (species C in [Fig. 1](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#F1)) to accumulate (blue). The applied magnetic field (50 μT) results in an increased transient conversion of the radical pair into the triplet state, causing C to be formed more rapidly and in higher yield. Faster recombination than shown here would allow scant time for the slow modulation arising from the Zeeman interaction to alter _p_ T(_t_); the yield of C would then be much less affected by the field. For details of the calculation, see [_SI Appendix_](https://www.pnas.org/cgi/data/0711968106/DCSupplemental/Appendix_PDF.pdf).

To act as a compass, a radical pair reaction must respond to the direction of the field and not just its intensity. This is unlikely to occur for solution-phase reactions where rapid molecular tumbling tends to average any anisotropic responses. The radicals must, at least partially, be immobilized and oriented and possess appropriate anisotropic magnetic interactions. As originally proposed by Schulten ([18](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B18)), the most likely source of anisotropy is the hyperfine interaction, i.e., the dependence of the electron–nuclear coupling on the orientation of the molecule in an external magnetic field. Almost every hyperfine interaction has an anisotropic component: As a consequence, S ↔ T interconversion, and therefore the reaction yield, should vary with the direction of the external field. This suggestion has been confirmed by numerical simulations ([2](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B2), [33](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B33), [43](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B43)–[45](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B45)).

Anisotropic magnetic field effects arising from hyperfine interactions have recently been observed experimentally ([14](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B14)). Somewhat related observations at higher magnetic fields, for radical pairs in solids ([46](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B46), [47](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B47)) and in viscous liquids ([48](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B48)–[50](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B50)), appear to have their origins in electron–electron dipolar interactions and _g_-tensor anisotropy. Additionally, time-resolved EPR ([51](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B51)–[53](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B53)) and solid state NMR ([54](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B54)) spectroscopies provide clear evidence for the involvement of anisotropic hyperfine interactions in the spin dynamics of photosynthetic radical pairs.

Ritz _et al._ ([2](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B2)) have suggested that the cells responsible for light-dependent magnetoreception are distributed around and aligned within the retina, in the manner of the visual rod and cone cells. In turn, the magnetoreceptor molecules would be oriented within the receptor cells perhaps by attachment to cytoskeletal proteins ([55](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B55)). Thus, cells at different retinal locations would make different angles to the Earth's magnetic field vector and so respond differently according to the anisotropy of the reactions of the radical pairs within them. The transduction of the magnetic compass information may “piggy-back” the visual reception pathway ([2](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B2), [56](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B56)), so that the bird literally sees the magnetic field as a “signal (or visual) modulation pattern,” reflecting the anisotropy of the radical pair reaction, and perhaps reminiscent of a “heads-up” display in an aircraft ([2](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B2), [57](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B57)).

[Fig. 3](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#F3) shows the results of a few spin dynamics simulations of reaction yield anisotropies and the corresponding signal modulation patterns. Unless the radicals contain very few magnetic nuclei or possess some degree of molecular symmetry or are favorably disordered, the shape of the anisotropy can be complex. There is no clear picture of what would constitute the optimum sensory input for the bird; however, it seems reasonable to suppose that strongly anisotropic but relatively simple directional information would be favored. Simulations and experiments on solution-phase reactions suggest a few simple design features discussed in the section on cryptochromes ([43](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B43), [58](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B58), [59](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B59)).

Fig. 3.

Spin dynamics simulations of anisotropic reaction yields for model radical pairs performed as described in refs. [58](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B58) and [66](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B66) using the reaction scheme of [Fig. 1](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#F1). (_Upper_) Polar plots. (_Lower_) The corresponding signal modulation patterns for a bird looking directly along the Earth's magnetic field vector. The heights of the vertical scale bars in the upper images correspond to singlet yields of 2% (black) or 0.2% (red). (_A_ and _B_) The simulations demonstrate that a relatively simple orientation dependence of the reaction yield (_A_) can be obtained from radical pairs containing a small number of hyperfine interactions or from more complex radicals when a few symmetry-related hyperfine interactions dominate (_B_). (_C_ and _D_) More intricate anisotropy patterns (_C_) can be dramatically simplified if the radical pairs are axially rotationally disordered (_D_). The signal modulation pattern for _C_ is identical to that for _D_ and is only shown once. Note that in all cases the reaction yield is invariant to exact reversal of the magnetic field vector, i.e., the response is that of an inclination compass rather than a polarity compass. See [_SI Appendix_](https://www.pnas.org/cgi/data/0711968106/DCSupplemental/Appendix_PDF.pdf) for details of the calculations.

### Kinetics.

The principal kinetic requirement for a sensitive magnetoreceptor is that the geomagnetic field has sufficient time to modulate the S ↔ T interconversion of the radical pair ([Fig. 2](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#F2)) ([60](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B60)). This condition is met if the spin correlation of the 2 electrons persists for more than ≈1 μs, a requirement that constrains both the reaction kinetics and the molecular dynamics. The rate constants _k_ S b + _k_ S f and _k_ T f ([Fig. 1](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#F1)) must therefore, ideally, be ≈10 6 s−1 and fairly similar to one another (say within a factor of 10) to allow significant competition between the S and T reaction pathways. Such values are certainly achievable, e.g., in electron transfer proteins where rates can be tuned over many orders of magnitude via the reaction Gibbs energy, the reorganization energy and, especially, the donor–acceptor distance ([61](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B61)). The change in the reaction yield produced by a ≈50-μT field grows sigmoidally as a function of the radical pair lifetime, leveling out at ≈1 μs (see [_SI Appendix_](https://www.pnas.org/cgi/data/0711968106/DCSupplemental/Appendix_PDF.pdf)). There is therefore no advantage, and probably serious disadvantages (as a result of spin relaxation, see below), in having a radical pair lifetime much in excess of 1 μs.

Approximate structural constraints can be derived from the simple theory of electron transfer reactions ([61](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B61), [62](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B62)). First, for the lifetime of the radical pair to be ≈1 μs (to allow enough time for S ↔ T interconversion, without excessive spin relaxation), the edge-to-edge separation _r_ e of the 2 radicals in the magnetically sensitive radical pair should be less than ≈1.5 nm. Second, to achieve a high quantum yield of radical pairs, a plausible lower limit on the forward electron transfer rate would be ≈10 9 s−1, implying _r_ e ≤ 1.0 nm for each of the electron donor–acceptor pairs involved in the formation of the magnetoreceptive radical pair. The derivation of these constraints is given in the [_SI Appendix_](https://www.pnas.org/cgi/data/0711968106/DCSupplemental/Appendix_PDF.pdf).

### Geometry.

The separation of the 2 radicals not only has a strong influence on electron transfer rates but also determines the strength of the (exchange and dipolar) spin–spin interactions between the 2 unpaired electrons ([63](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B63)–[65](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B65)). The interconversion of S and T states by a ≈50-μT magnetic field is only possible when the interradical interactions are not much stronger than 50 μT. Given that the dipolar coupling has a magnitude of 500 μT at a radical–radical center-to-center separation _r_ c of 1.8 nm and only falls to 50 μT at _r_ c = 3.8 nm ([58](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B58)), it is not immediately obvious how this requirement can be reconciled with the much smaller separations just estimated from electron transfer rates. Theory suggests that the inhibitory effects of the exchange and dipolar interactions may partially cancel for immobilized protein-bound radicals when _r_ c = 2.0 ± 0.2 nm ([58](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B58)). Such a center-to-center separation would be compatible with the above constraint on the edge-to-edge separation (_r_ e ≤ 1.5 nm) provided the radicals had diameters of more than ≈0.5 nm. The relative orientation of the radicals within the pair may also be important; simulations indicate that alignment of anisotropic hyperfine interactions could be a factor in optimizing the magnitude and shape of the reaction-yield anisotropy ([43](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B43), [66](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B66)). The experimental evidence that the effects of weak magnetic fields are quenched by strong interradical interactions is reviewed briefly in the [_SI Appendix_](https://www.pnas.org/cgi/data/0711968106/DCSupplemental/Appendix_PDF.pdf).

### Disorder and Motion.

As mentioned above, a critical requirement for a functional compass is that the radical pairs must be aligned within the host receptor cells which, in turn, must be spatially ordered within the bird's body ([2](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B2)). We focus here on the former. Rotational disorder would cause the anisotropic responses of differently oriented radical pairs to cancel one another, potentially reducing the directional sensitivity of the receptor. However, perfect ordering, as in a crystal, is not necessary. The compass function would be preserved if the magnetoreceptor molecules tended to be aligned along a common cell-fixed axis (the “director”) and had a reasonably large order parameter. Such alignment would largely preserve components of the magnetic response that are cylindrically symmetric with respect to the director axis, and cancel all others, so simplifying the orientational dependence of the reaction yield and resulting, perhaps, in a more efficient compass ([Fig. 3](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#F3)). This point is illustrated by a recent study of an aligned radical pair whose lifetime was found to have a rather straightforward dependence on the orientation of the molecule in an applied magnetic field, as a consequence of static orientational averaging around the long axis of the rod-like molecule ([14](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B14)).

There are also strict constraints on the dynamics of the radical pair. First, rapid molecular rotation tends to average anisotropic magnetic interactions. For hyperfine and Zeeman interactions of ≈500 μT and ≈50 μT, respectively, motions with characteristic correlation times shorter than ≈1 μs would seriously attenuate the anisotropy of the reaction yield. The other consequence of molecular motion is that it causes the electron spins to relax, i.e., to equilibrate thermally with their surroundings, with concomitant loss of spin correlation. The criterion for a significant magnetic field effect is that relaxation times should be longer than the radical pair lifetime, which was estimated above to be ≈1 μs. This requires rotational motion either to be slower than ≈1 μs or faster than ≈100 ps. The latter, known as the “extreme narrowing limit,” seems implausibly fast for a molecule large enough to host a suitable radical pair and would anyway lead to efficient averaging of anisotropic magnetic interactions. Examples of slowly relaxing spin-correlated radical pairs at physiological temperatures are mentioned briefly in the [_SI Appendix_](https://www.pnas.org/cgi/data/0711968106/DCSupplemental/Appendix_PDF.pdf).

In the light of the above, we may conclude that the ordering and motional constraints can be simultaneously satisfied if the radical pairs are uniaxially ordered with a high-order parameter and if all relevant motions are slower than ≈1 μs.

## Evidence for Radical Pair Magnetoreception

We have presented a rather long list of magnetic, structural, kinetic, and dynamic requirements that must be fulfilled if a radical pair is to operate as a compass sensor. Using well-founded theory and experimental precedents, we have argued that all these conditions are individually plausible, both chemically and physically. The crucial question is whether these constraints can be satisfied simultaneously in a biologically credible magnetoreceptor. We discuss first the extent to which the available evidence supports a radical pair mechanism and then evaluate how well the “cryptochrome hypothesis” stands up against the various criteria.

Much of the evidence in favor of a photochemical radical pair magnetoreceptor is circumstantial. Schulten's original proposal ([18](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B18)) was inspired by 2 behavioral features of the avian magnetic compass: the requirement for light at wavelengths below ≈565 nm ([23](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B23)) and the invariance to reversal of the field direction ([21](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B21)). However, it is conceivable that light has an entirely different physiological effect: Rather than a direct involvement in magnetoreception, it could possibly affect the birds' motivation to act upon magnetic compass information derived from a separate, light-independent mechanism ([7](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B7)). Moreover, although radical pairs cannot form the basis of a polarity compass, one can speculate about magnetite-based receptors that would be consistent with inclination compass behavior ([29](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B29), [67](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B67), [68](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B68)).

Probably the most convincing experimental test of the radical pair model has involved subjecting caged migratory birds to weak radio frequency fields ([2](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B2)). Magnetic fields oscillating at frequencies in the range 1–100 MHz, with or without a static field present, are expected to alter the yields of radical pair reactions by modifying the spin dynamics ([69](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B69)). This has been observed for reactions of organic radicals in solution when the frequency of the applied field matches a S ↔ T interconversion frequency arising from hyperfine and/or Zeeman interactions ([70](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B70)–[72](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B72)). Such resonances are diagnostic for radical pairs: Magnetite particles of sufficient size to function as a compass are too large to reorient in magnetic fields fluctuating as rapidly as 1 MHz ([73](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B73), [74](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B74)).

Linearly polarized radio frequency fields 100 times weaker than the Earth's field (≈500 nT), with frequencies of 7.0 MHz or 1.315 MHz, are sufficient to disrupt the migratory orientation of caged European robins ([75](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B75), [76](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B76)). Moreover, disorientation is found when the angle between the Earth's field and the radio frequency field is 24° or 48°, but not when the 2 fields are collinear. The birds are also disoriented by a broadband (0.1–10 MHz) 85-nT radio frequency field ([75](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B75)). These remarkable observations appear to exclude a number of the more obvious artifacts: it seems unlikely, for example, that the motivation of freely moving birds would be disturbed to different extents after rotation of the radio frequency field axis. That the radio frequency field appears to have little effect on the birds' orientation when it is parallel to the Earth's field can be understood if one of the radicals has (effectively) no hyperfine interactions ([14](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B14), [66](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0711968106#core-collateral-B66)). This is a scientific "Perspective" article published in PNAS (Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences) on January 13, 2009 (Vol. 106, No. 2, pp. 353-360, DOI: 10.1073/pnas.0711968106) by Christopher T. Rodgers and P. J. Hore of Oxford University (edited by Nicholas J. Turro). The article examines the "radical pair mechanism" as the proposed basis for the avian magnetic compass — how migratory birds detect the Earth's magnetic field.

Key content:
- Birds have possessed a magnetic compass for 40 years, but magnetoreception is poorly understood across all levels from biophysical detection to brain processing.
- The paper presents a physical chemist's perspective on how a chemical reaction (involving radical pairs as transient intermediates) could detect the direction of an Earth-strength ≈50 μT magnetic field.
- The energy of interaction with a 50-μT field is >6 orders of magnitude smaller than average thermal energy (k_B T), making magnetic detection chemically counterintuitive; however, radical pairs work because their electron spins remain out of thermal equilibrium.
- The radical pair mechanism (proposed first by Schulten) is the only plausible way weak magnetic fields can affect chemical reactivity. The mechanism was inspired by two behavioral features: avian compass requires light below ≈565 nm (suggesting photochemistry) and is responsive to inclination rather than polarity of the geomagnetic field (unlike a compass needle).

Key requirements for a functional radical pair magnetoreceptor:
1. Chemistry: Radical pairs in singlet (antiparallel spins) and triplet (parallel spins) states, with at least one state undergoing a reaction not open to the other. Precedent exists in bacterial photosynthetic energy conversion via sequential electron transfers.
2. Hyperfine interactions: At least one hyperfine coupling (between electron and nucleus, e.g., ¹H or ¹⁴N) is required—nearly all biological radicals have suitable ones. ¹H and ¹⁴N couplings range 10–1,000 μT (300 kHz–30 MHz frequencies). Radicals must be partially immobilized and oriented for anisotropy/direction sensing.
3. Kinetics: Spin correlation must persist for more than ≈1 μs for the geomagnetic field to modulate S↔T interconversion; rate constants should be ≈10⁶ s⁻¹. Radical separation (edge-to-edge) should be < ≈1.5 nm for ~1 μs lifetime, and ≤1.0 nm for high quantum yield (forward electron transfer ≥10⁹ s⁻¹).
4. Geometry: Inter-radical spin-spin interactions must not exceed ~50 μT (exchange and dipolar interactions); theory suggests partial cancellation of these effects at center-to-center separation of 2.0 ± 0.2 nm.
5. Disorder and motion: Radical pairs must be aligned within receptor cells (uniaxially ordered with high order parameter); motions must be slower than ≈1 μs (or faster than ≈100 ps, implausible) to avoid spin relaxation.

Mechanism: Ritz et al. proposed magnetoreceptor cells are distributed and aligned in the retina like rods/cones, with magnetoreceptor molecules oriented within cells (possibly attached to cytoskeletal proteins). Magnetic compass information may "piggy-back" the visual pathway, so the bird "sees" the magnetic field as a signal modulation pattern ("heads-up display"). The mechanism produces an inclination compass (invariant to field reversal), not a polarity compass.

Experimental evidence: 
- The most convincing test involved subjecting caged migratory birds to weak radio frequency fields (1–100 MHz). Linearly polarized fields 100 times weaker than Earth's field (≈500 nT) at 7.0 MHz or 1.315 MHz disrupted migratory orientation of European robins; the field had little effect when parallel to Earth's field.
- Disorientation occurred when angle between Earth's field and RF field was 24° or 48°, but not when collinear. Broadband (0.1–10 MHz) 85-nT fields also disoriented birds. These resonances are diagnostic for radical pairs (magnetite particles would be too large to reorient at these frequencies).

The article closes by evaluating cryptochrome, the photoactive protein considered the leading candidate magnetoreceptor molecule, and suggests directions for future research. Article metrics show 47,813 total views and 482 citations.

This Semantic Scholar page documents the research paper "Radical-pair-based magnetoreception in birds: radio-frequency experiments and the role of cryptochrome" by Christine Nießner and Michael Winklhofer, published in the Journal of Comparative Physiology on June 13, 2017 (DOI: 10.1007/s00359-017-1189-1). The paper discusses behavioral tests using radio-frequency (RF) magnetic fields to specifically disrupt the radical-pair-based avian magnetic compass sense, and focuses on two candidate magnetoreceptor proteins in birds, Cry1a and Cry1b (two splice variants of the same gene).

The page also lists numerous related, citing papers that provide context on magnetoreception research, including:
- Ritz et al. (2000, Biophysical Journal): showed theoretically that geomagnetic field strength fields can produce different reaction yields for different radical pair alignments with the magnetic field.
- Ritz et al. (2004, Nature): demonstrated that oscillating magnetic fields disrupt magnetic orientation behavior in migratory birds, consistent with a resonance effect on singlet-triplet transitions and a radical-pair mechanism compass.
- Nießner et al. (2011, PLoS ONE): identified avian UV/V-cones as probable magnetoreceptors, supporting Cry1a as the receptor molecule for magnetic direction information.
- Nießner et al. (2013, J. R. Soc. Interface): found that activated Cry1a and well-oriented behavior occur at 565 nm green light, a wavelength not absorbed by fully oxidized cryptochrome, suggesting a state other than the Trp•/FAD• radical pair is crucial for magnetic direction detection.
- Wiltschko et al. (2014, J. Exp. Biol.): showed oriented behavior and activated Cry1a under 373 nm UV, 424 nm blue, 502 nm turquoise, and 565 nm green light.
- Kobylkov et al. (2019, J. R. Soc. Interface): found no disruption of orientation in night-migratory Eurasian blackcaps by 0.1–100 kHz RF fields, implying the spin coherence lifetime is in the range 2–10 µs.
- Pakhomov et al. (2017, J. R. Soc. Interface): found the magnetic compass sensitivity threshold to oscillating magnetic fields (OMF) lies around 2–3 nT.
- Muheim and Phillips (2023, Scientific Reports): showed zebra finches are disoriented by low-level (~10 nT) Larmor-frequency RF fields, indicating RF alters but does not eliminate magnetic input.
- Granger et al. (2022, J. Comp. Physiol.): examined environmental sources of RF noise, concluding solar RF rarely disrupts magnetic orientation but atmospheric RF can sometimes exceed disrupting levels.
- Additional works on cryptochrome expression, human CRY1 functions, and the radical-pair mechanism by Hore and Mouritsen (2016).

This is a lecture by Prof. Peter Hore (University of Oxford) on the "Radical pair mechanism of magnetoreception," presented at the FENS Hertie Winter School 2017 on Neural Control of Behaviour - Series 1: Navigation, held 10-16 December 2017 in Obergurgl, Austria (posted 24 May 2019). The lecture focuses on the physics of how migratory songbirds sense the Earth's magnetic field via a chemical compass.

**Core Mechanism:**
- The proposal (dating to 1978, by Klaus Schulten) is that a chemical reaction in birds contains short-lived intermediates called radical pairs, which are sensitive to magnetic fields as weak as the Earth's (~50 microTesla).
- Radical pairs (lasting ~1 microsecond) can either revert to reactants (singlet) or form products. The branching ratio depends on the strength and direction of the Earth's magnetic field, making it a direction-sensing compass rather than just an intensity sensor.
- The mechanism is light-dependent—blue and green photons provide energy to create the radicals.
- The key energetic paradox: the magnetic interaction with Earth's field is ~10 million times smaller than thermal energy (kT), yet the mechanism works because it applies tiny energy at a precisely non-equilibrium moment (analogous to a fly landing on a balanced stone block), influencing spin dynamics.

**Physics Background:**
- Electrons have quantum spin (quantum number s=1/2) and associated magnetic moments.
- Radicals are molecules with unpaired electrons and are therefore magnetic.
- Radical pairs exist in singlet states (opposite spins, total spin 0) or triplet states (parallel spins, total spin 1).
- Organic radical reactions conserve spin, so singlet radical pairs must come from singlet precursors, and triplet products can only form from triplet radical pairs.
- Hyperfine interactions between electron spins and nuclear spins (of hydrogen and nitrogen, which have ~100% natural abundance) are essential. Carbon-12 and oxygen-16 have no nuclear spin.
- Anisotropic hyperfine interactions (particularly from nitrogen atoms in the central rings of flavin) enable direction sensitivity, with interaction strengths ranging from microTesla to milliTesla—many stronger than the Earth's field.
- For flavin and tryptophan radicals, hyperfine interactions are in the milliTesla range, compared to Earth's field at ~0.05 milliTesla.

**Spin Dynamics:**
- Hyperfine interactions cause coherent oscillations between singlet and triplet states at frequencies determined by interaction strengths (typically ~10 MHz).
- The Larmor frequency for a free electron in Earth's field (50 microTesla) is 1.4 MHz, corresponding to a 700-nanosecond period.
- A magnetic field shifts energy levels and changes oscillation frequencies, with differences becoming visible after ~0.1 microsecond; direction matters because of anisotropy.
- Earth's field effects (~10^-7 of kT) arise from the "low field effect"—pairs of degenerate energy levels split slightly by the field, adding a slow oscillation pathway (a 1.4 MHz beat).
- The final product yield integrates over the radical pair lifetime and thus depends on field presence and direction.

**Key Points on the Mechanism:**
- The mechanism is consistent with birds having an axial compass (not polarity-sensitive), and with light-dependence (evidenced by Wiltschko's findings that blue/green light is required).
- The chemistry is well established—hundreds of radical pair reactions in laboratories are known to be magnetically sensitive at 1 milliTesla or more. The big question is whether it is the actual mechanism in birds.
- In 2002, Ritz and Schulten proposed cryptochrome as the protein hosting this chemistry, likely located in the retina, with aligned/immobilized molecules needed for direction sensing.

**Magnetite Alternative:**
- Magnetite (Fe3O4) is the principal competing mechanism, based on iron atoms' magnetic moments.
- Particle properties depend on size/shape: small crystals (<30-40 nm) are superparamagnetic (fluctuating moments); larger crystals can be single-domain (permanent moments acting like compass needles); too large and they become multi-domain (moments cancel).
- Magnetotactic bacteria make chains of single-domain magnetite crystals (~40 nm each) that passively align their bodies (an alignment mechanism, not sensing).
- Hypothetical magnetite mechanisms include torque-based ion channel activation (polarity-sensitive) and superparamagnetic particle induction (which could give an inclination/axial compass independent of polarity).
- Magnetite is considered less likely for birds (they sense rather than passively respond, and would need enormous numbers of particles to align their bodies), but cannot yet be ruled out.

**Conclusion:** The lecture presents radical pairs as a well-understood, physically valid mechanism (the quantum chemistry is solid), with cryptochrome and light-dependent radical formation as the leading hypothesis for avian magnetoreception, pending further experimental investigation.

# The magnetite-based receptors in the beak of birds and their role in avian navigation

[R. Wiltschko](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/?term=%22Wiltschko%20R%22[Author])

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369)Abstract

Iron-rich structures have been described in the beak of homing pigeons, chickens and several species of migratory birds and interpreted as magnetoreceptors. Here, we will briefly review findings associated with these receptors that throw light on their nature, their function and their role in avian navigation. Electrophysiological recordings from the ophthalmic nerve, behavioral studies and a ZENK-study indicate that the trigeminal system, the nerves innervating the beak, mediate information on magnetic changes, with the electrophysiological study suggesting that these are changes in intensity. Behavioral studies support the involvement of magnetite and the trigeminal system in magnetoreception, but clearly show that the inclination compass normally used by birds represents a separate system. However, if this compass is disrupted by certain light conditions, migrating birds show ‘fixed direction’ responses to the magnetic field, which originate in the receptors in the beak. Together, these findings point out that there are magnetite-based magnetoreceptors located in the upper beak close to the skin. Their natural function appears to be recording magnetic intensity and thus providing one component of the multi-factorial ‘navigational map’ of birds.

**Keywords:**Magnetite-based receptors, Pulse treatment, Trigeminal nerve, ‘Fixed direction’ responses, Magnetic ‘map’ component

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369)Introduction

The literature on the avian magnetic compass, showing its functional properties, the underlying physical radical pair processes and its association with the visual system, has been discussed in several recent reviews (e.g., Ritz et al. [2010](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR41); Ritz [2011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR38); W. Wiltschko et al. [2011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR69)). The other avian magnetoreception system, based on magnetite and associated with the trigeminal system, has received less attention and has not been summarized in a review so far. In the present paper, we will describe the respective findings, mostly behavioral that support the existence of magnetite-based magnetoreceptors in the beak of birds and also provide some insight in their structure, their function and their role in avian navigation.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369)Biogenic magnetite and its possible role in magnetoreception

Lowenstam ([1962](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR34)) described magnetite, a form of Fe 3 O 4 in the denticles of the radula of chitons (Mollusca: Polyplacophora), where they seem to be used for hardening the teeth. This was the first time that magnetic material was found in living organisms and proved in principle that magnetic material can be produced by biological means. In the mid-1970s, Blakemore ([1975](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR8)) found intra-cellular magnetite crystals in bacteria, a discovery that was soon followed by many other reports describing the occurrence of magnetite in other bacterial species, protozoa etc., and also in higher animals (see Kirschvink et al. [1985a](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR32) for a summary up to that date).

Bacteria use their magnetite inclusions for orientation: they become ‘north-seeking’ or ‘south-seeking’; when they are stirred up, they move along the magnetic field lines to reach the ground. This is a mere passive orientation, mediated by the force of the magnetic field acting upon the magnetite crystals. Yet it inspired Yorke ([1979](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR73)) to suggest that magnetite could also be part of magnetoreceptors in higher animals.

The magnetic properties of magnetite depend on the size of the particles: larger particles are multi domain with no net magnetization; smaller crystals are single domains (SD) with a stable magnetic moment, and even smaller ones are superparamagnetic (SPM)—they do not have a stable magnetic moment, but will align their magnetization by an external magnetic field. Kirschvink and Gould ([1981](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR30)) described several ways how magnetite particles could work in a receptor, discussing systems based on single domain magnetite, on superparamagnetic crystals or a combination of both. These first considerations on the function of magnetite in receptors were followed by others proposing modified models and considering various theoretical possibilities how magnetite-based receptors might work and what type of information they might convey (e.g., Kirschvink and Walker [1985](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR31); Shcherbakov and Winklhofer [1999](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR44); Davila et al. [2003](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR10); Fleissner et al. [2007](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR17); Solovyov and Greiner [2007](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR45); Walker [2008](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR52); Winklhofer and Kirschvink [2010](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR71)).

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369)Magnetite found in birds

Birds were a group of special interest, because their ability to use information from the geomagnetic field for orientation had been demonstrated: migratory birds had been shown to use the magnetic field as a compass (e.g., W. Wiltschko [1968](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR56); Keeton [1971](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR28)), and the behavior of pigeons in a magnetic anomaly suggested a possible use of magnetic components in the navigational ‘map’ (Walcott [1978](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR50)).

The first report of magnetite in birds was published in 1979, when Walcott et al. ([1979](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR51)), measuring the remanence with a SQUID magnetometer, found permanently magnetic material, presumably single domain magnetite, in the head of pigeons between the brain and the skull, that is, at a location where a sensory function does not seem very likely. Other iron-rich structures were found in the nasal region of birds: based on histological studies with Prussian blue staining, Beason and Nichols ([1984](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR2)) and Beason and Brennan ([1986](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR1)) described such structures in Bobolinks (_Dolichonyx oryzivorus_: Emberizidae), a passerine migrant, and Williams and Wild ([2001](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR55)) reported similar structures in pigeons. The size of the structures and remanence measurements suggested single domain magnetite. Being associated with the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve, these structures were discussed as possible magnetoreceptors.

Another type of putative magnetoreceptors involving superparamagnetic magnetite was described in the skin of the upper beak of pigeons. Hanzlik et al. ([2000](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR22)) identified the iron-rich particles crystallographically as magnetite; histological and electron microscopic studies revealed the fine structure, indicating clusters of nanocrystals adjacent to or within dentrites of the ophthalmic nerves (Winklhofer et al. [2001](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR72); Fleissner et al. [2003](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR16), [2007](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR17)). An independent histological study and remanence measurements by Tian et al. ([2007](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR47)) supported these findings. Falkenberg et al. ([2010](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR15)) reported similar structures in the beak of domestic chickens (_Gallus gallus_) and two species of migrating passerines, the Garden Warbler (_Sylvia borin_) and the European Robin (_Erithacus rubecula_: Turdidae). These findings have recently been challenged by Treiber et al. ([2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR49)) who claim that the iron-containing structures described as potential magnetoreceptors were merely macrophages.

Magnetic material, presumably magnetite, has also been described in other vertebrates. Cells containing single domain magnetite were also found in the nasal regions of fish from the genus _Oncorhynchus_ (Salmonidae), and interpreted to play a role in magnetoreception (e.g., Kirschvink et al. [1985b](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR33); Mann et al. [1988](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR35); Walker et al. [1997](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR53); Diebel et al. [2000](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR13); Eder et al. [2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR14)). Remanence measurements indicated magnetite in the newts (Brassart et al. [1999](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR9)) and in the heads of bats (Tian et al. [2010](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR48)). Ferrous inclusions, discussed to be magnetite, were also found the cornea of mole-rat (genus _Fukomys_, Bathyergidae) (Wegner et al. [2006](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR54)).

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369)The pioneering studies by Beason and Semm

Beason and Semm ([1987](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR3), [1991)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR4); Semm and Beason ([1990](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR43)) recorded electrophysiological responses to magnetic stimulation from the ophthalmic nerve and the trigeminal ganglion of Bobolinks. Their stimuli consisted of changes in direction and intensity of the magnetic field produced by a set of coils. Figure[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#Fig1)a showed the responses to increases of the vertical components of the magnetic field; in Fig.[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#Fig1)b, the number of spikes is plotted as a function of the magnetic intensity, revealing a logarithmic relationship.Fig.1Electrophysiological recordings from the trigeminal ganglion of the bobolink. _Left_ spontaneous activity and responses to various changes in the intensity of the vertical component of the magnetic field. The _lines_ indicate the 50 ms of stimulation (from Semm and Beason [1990](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR43)). _Right_ recorded activity changes as a logarithmic function of the increased intensity (from Beason and Semm [1991](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR4))

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369)From their findings, Beason and Semm drew two conclusions

The ophthalmic nerve mediates magnetic information,This information is probably the information on magnetic intensity involved in the navigational ‘map’.

The first conclusion, namely that a branch of the trigeminal nerve mediates magnetic information, has been confirmed in a behavioral study with caged Bobolinks by the authors themselves (Beason and Semm [1996](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR5)): injecting an anesthetic in the ophthalmic nerve suppressed the effect of a short, strong magnetic pulse (see Fig.[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#Fig3)a below). A conditioning study by Mora et al. ([2004](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR36)) produced corresponding results: after locally anesthetizing or sectioning the ophthalmic nerve, homing pigeons trained to respond to a small, strong magnetic anomaly could no longer perform the task. Similar results were obtained by Freire et al. ([2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR19)) with young Pekin Ducks (_Anas platyrhynchos_ _domestica_) trained to associate a small, strong magnetic anomaly with food: here, too, anesthesia or sectioning the ophthalmic nerve led to a performance at chance level. A recent ZENK-study with European robins (Heyers et al. [2010](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR24)) likewise confirms the involvement of the trigeminal system in magnetoreception: after magnetic stimulation, a number of ZENK-positive neurons were found in two areas in the trigeminal brain stem, and this number deceased significantly when the ophthalmic nerve was sectioned.

In all studies mentioned above, the magnetic stimuli used do not allow to decide whether the information mediated by the ophthalmic nerve was indeed information on intensity. Behavioral data that will be discussed below support this view, but recent findings show that the situation is rather complex.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369)Pulse experiments to indicate magnetite

The electrophysiological responses recorded in the ophthalmic nerve after magnetic stimulation suggested these responses originate in the iron-rich structures found by the histological studies and the remanence measurements. Yet more direct evidence for an involvement of magnetite in orientation behavior seemed desirable. A diagnostic tool to identify magnetite is the response to a strong, short magnetic pulse, e.g., 0.5 Tesla with a duration of <5 ms: the pulse must be strong enough to remagnetize single domains, and it must be brief enough to prevent the magnetite crystals to rotate and align in the direction of the pulse. Since the orientation of the magnetite particles was unclear, it was to be expected that such a pulse would remagnetize roughly half of the single domains. A pulse would also disrupt clusters and chains of superparamagnetic magnetite, as experiments with model systems of ferrofluids showed (Davila et al. [2005](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR11)). In both cases, receptors based on magnetite would be severely disrupted, and their input would be markedly changed. Other types of magnetoreception, like the radical-pair processes in the eye (Ritz et al. [2000](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR39), [2004](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR40)), are not affected by the pulse, however.

The first birds subjected to such a magnetic pulse were Australian Silvereyes (_Zosterops lateralis_), Australian migrants. In cage studies, the pulse was applied ‘south-anterior’, with the direction of the pulse being towards the beak in birds facing east in the geomagnetic field. This caused a roughly 90° shift to the east during spring as well as during autumn migration (Fig.[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#Fig2)a)—the effect was obviously independent from the migratory direction (W. Wiltschko et al. [1994](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR58), [1998](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR59)). Interestingly, the effect of pulsing was only observed in old, experienced migrants; young birds that had been captured immediately after fledging did not respond to the pulse (Fig.[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#Fig2)b; Munro et al. [1997](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR37)). Treating the ophthalmic nerve or upper beak of birds with the local anesthetic suppressed this pulse effect (Fig.[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#Fig3); Beason and Semm [1987](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR3); W. Wiltschko et al. Beason et al. ([1995](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR6)) pulsed Bobolinks in two different directions, recorded their activity in cages and found that they deviated in different directions: the bird pulsed ‘south anterior’ headed to the right, those pulsed ‘north anterior’ to the left of their directions before pulsing (Fig.[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#Fig2)c). Deflections to different sides were also observed in homing pigeons that had been displaced after being pulsed ‘south anterior’ and ‘south left’ (Beason et al. [1997](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR7)). Here, the observed effect was much smaller, probably because the pigeons were released and had, in contrast to the migrants tested in cages, other navigational factors available.

The pulse was found to alter the behavior of migrants only temporarily. The deviations described above are observed only on the day of pulsing and the two following days; after that the birds in the cage studies were disoriented, and about 8–10 days after the pulse, their orientation was back to normal—they again preferred their seasonally appropriate migratory direction (W. Wiltschko et al. [1994](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR58), [1998](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR59)). This transient nature of the effect proved important when wild migrants were subjected to a pulse before they were released and their starting routes were tracked. A first study in America involving Catbirds (_Dumetella carolinensis_: Mimidae) proved inconclusive because the birds lingered in the area and took off only with considerable delay (Holland et al. [2009](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR27)). In a second study in spring with European Robins and Reed Warblers (_Acrocephalus scirpaceus_: Sylviidae), many birds departed in the first days after pulsing, and here, the treated birds showed a significant deviation from the untreated controls, with the amount and direction of this deviation depending on the direction of pulsing (Holland [2010](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR25)). A subsequent study with robins in autumn showed that juvenile birds were not affected by the pulse and those adult birds that took off within the first 10 days showed a significant deviation from their migratory direction, in contrast to those that departed later (Holland and Helm [2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR26)).

Together, these findings provide some information on the receptors in question: the effect of the strong, short magnetic pulse on the orientation of birds indicates that the receptors are indeed based on magnetic material like magnetite. The observation that the deviations induced by pulsing depended on the direction in which the pulse is applied points out that the pulse does not silence the magnetite-based receptors altogether and that it just alters the information they mediate. At the same time, this observation also suggests that the magnetite particles in the receptors are not evenly or circular-symmetrically arranged, but extend differently to the various sides. From the behavioral point of view, it is interesting that only experienced, but not juvenile birds are affected, as this suggests that the mechanism involved is not innate, but based on experience.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369)Single domains or superparamagnetic particles?

Pulse experiments were first proposed to find out whether the receptors controlling the respective behaviors contained magnetic material like magnetite. The observed effects of pulsing indeed indicate magnetite-based receptors, but it is not clear what type of particles is involved. Any interpretation of behavioral data in view of this question must necessarily remain speculative. Yet some findings give at least some hints.

The observation that the pulse effect is rather short-lived speaks against an involvement of single domain particles, because the new magnetization should be just as stable as the original one. Restoring the remagnetized particles seems rather unlikely, for this would mean that these particles would all have to be replaced within 10 days, the more, since the correct direction of magnetization could be difficult to determine under these circumstances. Recalibration of the altered input could have been possible for free-flying migrants, but seems unlikely for caged birds, because it is hard to see how they could have obtained the necessary information and new experience. The input from the damaged receptors could be simply ignored after a while, but the finding that a second, identical pulse affected the orientation again speaks against this possibility (W. Wiltschko et al. [2007](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR63)). The second pulse, administered on day 16 after the first, led to a brief period of disorientation that lasted only 1 or 2 days; afterwards the Silvereyes again preferred their normal migratory direction. Rearrangement of disrupted clusters of superparamagnetic crystals, on the other hand, could roughly fall into the observed time frame (see Davila et al. [2005](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR11)). The very short duration of the effect of the second pulse could be interpreted in the sense that repairing mechanisms had been activated and could be reactivated faster than after the first pulse.

Another approach involved pulsing the birds while they are exposed to a strong biasing field that aligns single domain particles (if sufficiently mobile) in one direction—in this case, a pulse parallel to the biasing field should have no effect, whereas an antiparallel pulse should remagnetize a maximum of particles, and thus lead to a marked change in orientation. The results of the two such experiments do not agree: Australian Silvereyes, pulsed parallel in a 100 μT biasing field showed the same axial deviations from their migratory direction as those pulsed antiparallel (W. Wiltschko et al. [2002](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR60)), whereas Reed Warblers pulsed in a 320 μT biasing field seemed unaffected by a parallel pulse and showed an axial deviation when pulsed antiparallel (Holland [2010](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR25)). The data of the pulse experiments available so far do not yet allow a decision on the type of particles involved in the magnetite-based receptors.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369)What kind of information is mediated?

Another question concerns the type of magnetic information these receptors provide—directional information for compass use or a component of the navigational ‘map’. Theoretically, magnetite-based receptors could provide information on both, direction and intensity (e.g., Kirschvink and Gould [1981](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR30); Solovyov and Greiner [2007](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR45)). But these are two different qualities of the magnetic field—we humans measure them with different instruments, a compass and a magnetometer. Hence, it would not be surprising if birds had specialized their magnetic sense in a similar way.

The electrophysiological study by Semm and Beason ([1990](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR43)) pointed towards magnetic intensity, and the observations of Munro et al. ([1997](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR37)) that young Australian Silvereyes remain unaffected by the pulse also speaks in favor of a learned system, which suggests the magnetite-based receptors provide a component of the navigational ‘map’ (see also Deutschlander et al. [2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR12)). At the same time, the data of the respective study (Fig.[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#Fig2)b) clearly show that the young birds, despite the pulse treatment that disrupted their magnetite-based receptors, continued in migratory direction: obviously, their magnetic compass mechanism was not affected. This conclusion is also supported by findings that pulse-treated birds preferred their normal migratory direction when the altered input from the magnetite-based receptors was disrupted, either by anesthetizing the ophthalmic nerve (Fig.[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#Fig3)a; Beason and Semm [1996](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR5)) or by anesthetizing the skin of the upper beak with the local anesthetic Xylocain, applied externally (Fig.[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#Fig3)b; W. Wiltschko et al. [2009](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR66)). Testing pulse-treated Silvereyes in a magnetic field with the vertical component reversed showed that these birds located their changed course with their normal inclination compass (W. Wiltschko et al. [2006](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR61)). Furthermore, in otherwise untreated Robins and Silvereyes, local anesthesia of the upper beak—the same treatment that disrupts the pulse effect—did not affect migratory orientation (R. Wiltschko et al. [2007](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR62), [2008](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR64)).[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#Fn2) Zapka et al. ([2009](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR74)) obtained similar results by cutting the ophthalmic nerve.

All these findings clearly show that the magnetite-based receptors are _not_ involved in the avian magnetic compass. The inclination compass represents a different mechanism based on different physical reactions, namely on radical-pair processes in the eye (Ritz et al. [2000](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR39), [2004](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR40)). The magnetite-based receptors in the beak, in contrast, seem to contribute to the processes that determine the course to be pursued, the avian ‘map’ mechanism. In view of this, it appears most likely that the iron-rich structures mediate information on magnetic intensity.

In rainbow trouts, _Oncorhynchus mykiss,_ two findings that might be parallel cases have been reported. In electrophysiological studies from a branch of the trigeminal nerve, Walker et al. ([1997](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR53)) found responses to changes in intensity, but not to changes in direction alone. In a study by Hellinger and Hoffmann ([2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR23)), fish were conditioned to magnetic stimuli; inactivation of the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve by a local anesthetic abolished the response to changes in intensity, but did not affect the response to changes in direction.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369)‘Fixed direction’ responses

The cage experiments with migratory birds reported so far were performed under ‘white’ or under very low intensity monochromatic lights from the short-wavelength end of the spectrum—here, the birds prefer their natural migratory direction. In total darkness, under red light or when short-wavelength light is combined with yellow light, birds change their behavior and head in directions that are different from their migratory direction—since these preferences do not show the seasonal change between autumn and spring, they are characterized as ‘fixed direction’ responses (see R. Wiltschko et al. [2010a](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR67)). In contrast to migratory orientation by the inclination compass which ignores the polarity of the magnetic field (W. Wiltschko and Wiltschko [1972](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR57)), these ‘fixed direction’ responses are polar responses, that is, they orient by the polarity of the magnetic field. This indicates that they must be based on a mechanism that is fundamentally different from the radical pair processes of the inclination compass.

Several such ‘fixed direction’ responses have been described in European Robins and Australian Silvereyes (e.g., R. Wiltschko et al. [2007](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR62), [2008](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR64), [2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR70); Stapput et al. [2008](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR46); for review, see R. Wiltschko et al. [2010a](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#CR67)). The ones analyzed in detail so far could all be disrupted by local anesthesia of the upper beak (for examples, see Fig.[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369#Fig4))—the magnetic information involved appears to originate in the magnetite-based receptors located there. Obviously, under some extreme light conditions, the normal inclination compass is disrupted, and the receptors in the upper beak can take over and control the directional behavior of birds.Fig.4‘Fixed direction’ responses in Robins, observed under certain light regimes, can be disrupted by local anesthesia of the upper beak.
