You are tasked with summarizing the raw content of a webpage retrieved from a web search. Your goal is to create a summary that preserves the most important information from the original web page. This summary will be used by a downstream research agent, so it's crucial to maintain the key details without losing essential information.

Here is the raw content of the webpage:

<webpage_content>
© The Ecological Society of America  Front Ecol Environ doi:10.1002/fee.2029 RESEARCH COMMUNICATIONS 1 Front Ecol Environ 2019; doi:10.1002/fee.2029 T rillions of flying organisms (eg birds, bats, insects) occupy the airspace within the troposphere during different peri-ods of their annual cycles (Diehl 2013). The recent recognition of airspace as vital habitat – one that is subject to increasing modification by humans – highlights the fundamental need to understand how organisms cope with such alterations (Lambertucci et al. 2015), which pose numerous challenges to airborne organisms during periods of transit, including noc-turnally migrating birds. Of the nearly 630 terrestrial species of birds regularly occurring in North America, approximately 70% are considered migratory, and of these more than 80% migrate at night (WebTable 1). Yet most studies of associated risks have focused on terrestrial habitats, underscoring a fun-damental knowledge gap that can be addressed with recent technological (including computational) advances.
Light pollution of the airspace is a relatively recent but growing threat to nocturnally migrating birds (Longcore and Rich 2004; Van Doren et al. 2017; Cabrera-­ Cruz et al. 2018). Increasing urbanization has greatly amplified the amount of artificial light at night (ALAN; Kyba et al. 2017), with almost one-­ half of the contiguous US experiencing substantially photo-­ polluted nights (Falchi et al. 2016). Light sources – including streetlights, safety lights, and extensively lit ­ buildings – can disturb wildlife in a multitude of ways (Gauthreux and Belser 2005; Hölker et al. 2010; Rodríguez et al. 2017). High-­ power light installations like lighthouses and communication towers are known to attract nocturnal migrants and are responsible for substantial mortality (Gauthreux and Belser 2005; Longcore et al. 2012). The numbers of birds attracted to or trapped by illumination depend on light wavelength (Poot et al. 2008) as well as weather factors such as fog and precipita-tion (Gauthreux and Belser 2005). High-­ power light installa-tions can even attract migrants in already heavily photo-­ polluted areas and in skies with clear weather conditions (Van Doren et al. 2017).
An increasing number of artificial structures are now pres-ent in the lowest reaches of the troposphere (Davy et al. 2017), and their continued expansion poses an ever-­ increasing threat to wildlife. In the contiguous US, annual fatal bird collisions with buildings, communication towers, power lines, and wind turbines cumulatively number in the hundreds of millions (Loss et al. 2015). For nocturnally migrating birds, direct ­ mortality as a result of collisions due to attraction to light (Gauthreux and Belser 2005) is the most obvious and direct effect of ALAN, but there are also more subtle effects, such as disrupted orientation (Poot et al. 2008) and changes in habitat selection (McLaren et al. 2018). There is also growing evidence that light pollution alters behavior at regional scales, with migrants occupying urban centers at higher-­ than-­ expected rates as a function of urban illumination (La Sorte et al. 2017). While ALAN acts as an attractant at both large (La Sorte et al. 2017) and local (Van Doren et al. 2017) scales, there is also evidence of migrating birds avoiding strongly lit areas when selecting critical resting sites needed to rebuild energy stores (McLaren et al. 2018).
Challenges to conservation and mitigation To date, mitigating actions to reduce impacts of ALAN have involved directed and specific efforts, including reduc-tions in excess lighting, the periodic switching off of high-­ intensity lights (Van Doren et al. 2017), and adjusting wavelengths in situations where lights cannot be shut down (Poot et al. 2008; Longcore et al. 2018). These actions are Bright lights in the big cities: migratory birds’ exposure to artificial light Kyle G Horton1*, Cecilia Nilsson1, Benjamin M Van Doren2, Frank A La Sorte1, Adriaan M Dokter1, and Andrew Farnsworth1 Many species of migratory birds have evolved the ability to migrate at night, and the recent and rapid expansion of artificial light at night has markedly altered the nighttime sky through which they travel. Migrating birds regularly pass through heavily illumi-nated landscapes, and bright lights affect avian orientation. But risks to migrating birds from artificial light are not spatially or temporally uniform, representing a challenge for mitigating potential hazards and developing action plans to catalog risks at con-tinental scales. We leveraged over two decades of remote-­ sensing data collected by weather surveillance radar and satellite-­ based sensors to identify locations and times of year when the highest numbers of migrating birds are exposed to light pollution in the contiguous US. Our continental-­ scale quantification of light exposure provides a novel opportunity for dynamic and targeted con-servation strategies to address the hazards posed by light pollution to nocturnally migrating birds.
1Cornell Lab of Ornithology, Cornell University, Ithaca, NY *(kgh48@cornell.edu); 2Edward Grey Institute, Department of Zoology, University of Oxford, Oxford, UK Front Ecol Environ doi:10.1002/fee.2029  © The Ecological Society of America ﻿KG﻿ Horto et al.
2 RESEARCH COMMUNICATIONS typically carried out at the scale of individual buildings but occasionally at much larger scales (eg Lights Out Toronto). However, as the intensity and extent of bird migrations vary considerably in space and over time (Van Doren and Horton 2018), so too may exposure risks, requiring detailed and site-­ and time-­ specific considerations when implementing mitigation actions and developing conservation plans. To this end, we used radar to quantify the passage of noctur-nally migrating birds across the contiguous US, identified the areas where the greatest number of migrants are exposed to light pollution, and mapped this exposure across the US, focusing specifically on the 125 largest urban centers.
Methods Weather surveillance radar We used weather surveillance radar (WSR) data from 143 stations from spring (1 March to 31 May) and fall (15 August to 15 November) between spring 1995 and spring 2017 to characterize cumulative migration activity across the contig-uous US. We acquired radar data through the Amazon Web Service portal, extracting data from a 30-­ minute window centered on 3 hours after local sunset. This time period was chosen because it represents the average peak in nocturnal migratory activity (eg Farnsworth et al. 2015; Horton et al. 2015; see Horton et al. [2018] and Van Doren and Horton [2018] for additional details regarding radar processing).
With respect to creating profiles of migration activity, we calculated altitude, speed, and direction using the lowest elevation scans (0.5–4.5°) at distances of 5 km to 37.5 km from the radar station (Farnsworth et al. 2015). We deter-mined migration activity from reflectivity (η, cm2 km−3) and flight direction and groundspeed from radial velocity between 100 m and 3000 m above ground level, at 100-­ m altitudinal bins using the WSRLIB package (Sheldon 2015). We excluded altitudinal bins with velocity azimuth displays with root mean squared error (RMSE) <1 m s−1 to limit con-tamination of radar readings by insects and removed sam-ples with RMSE >5 m s−1 to limit poor fits. In addition, we removed slow-­ flying objects (airspeed <5 m s−1), which are representative of insects (Larkin 1991). To calculate air-speeds, we paired all radar measures of groundspeed and flight direction with wind measures using the North American Regional Reanalysis (NARR). Following these fil-tering procedures, we integrated reflectivity (cm2 km−3) across the column of airspace sampled (100–3000 m) into vertically integrated reflectivity (VIR, cm2 km−2), which rep-resented our measure of migration activity.
To discriminate contaminated scans (ie with precipitation) from precipitation-­ free scans (ie clear or biologically dominated), we designed a random forest classifier (Horton et al. 2019) using the R package “randomForest” (Liaw and Wiener 2002). We trained the classifier on 318,047 (spring: 157,279; fall: 160,768) manually classified nocturnal scans, selected from a 2.5-­ hour period centered on 3 hours after local sunset on 15 March, 15 April, 15 May, 1 September, 1 October, and 1 November. Scans for each radar and for each year were represented in the training set. We extracted derived predictor variables from profiles of reflectivity, groundspeed, and summaries of the number of vol-umes above 35 decibels of reflectivity (dBZ) (a value typical of precipitation). We populated 1000 trees and restricted node size to 50 scans. The algorithm classified a total of 2,176,126 scans (spring: 979,326; fall: 1,196,800) with 5.6% classification error during the spring and 4.5% during the fall, as determined using the manually classified scans. As an additional step to reduce the inclusion of samples classified as clear but containing weather, we used only scans with a confidence of being precipitation-­ free of 75% or higher (rather than a majority rule; ie >50%).
To extrapolate migration activity to areas not sampled by the radars, we relied on a generalized additive model using the R package “mgcv” (Wood 2011; R Core Team 2017). We first cal-culated the average migration activity for each ordinal day across all years and then summed each night through the sea-Figure 1. Log10-­ scaled radiance of artificial light at night (ALAN) meas-ured by the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) on the Suomi-­ NPP satellite of the 125 largest urban centers (by area) in the conti-nental US. The largest urban center area is depicted in the top-­ left corner; the second largest area appears to its immediate right, and so forth, across the top-­ most row. In each successive row, urban center areas ­ continue to decrease in size from left to right.
© The Ecological Society of America  Front Ecol Environ doi:10.1002/fee.2029 Nocturnally migrating birds and artificial light RESEARCH COMMUNICATIONS 3 son to estimate the cumulative migration activity for each radar station. We fit radar station latitude, longitude, and the interac-tion of latitude and longitude with smoothing splines to predict the cumulative seasonal activity across the contiguous US.
Artificial light at night We used the monthly Day/Night Band (DNB) product from the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) onboard the joint National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)/National Aeronautics and Space Administration Suomi-­ ­ NPP satellite to quantify the magnitude of ALAN radiance (Earth Observation Group, NOAA National Geophysical Data Center; https://bit.ly/2nCjqvz). Monthly composites of radiance (nanoWatts per square centimeter per steradian; nW cm−2 sr−1) are projected at 15 arc-­ second geographic resolution and are filtered to exclude data from stray light, lightning, lunar illumination, and cloud cover. However, because these data are not filtered for auroras and fires, we averaged across 3 months (October–December) over 6 years (2012–2017) to dampen the influence of episodic lighting events; these months were chosen because they fall outside the primary storm season in North America, which would obscure radiance measures. As an added step to ensure data quality, we excluded any pixel with fewer than 5 use-­ days prior to averaging monthly composites. Finally, we removed pixels with radiance values greater than 900 nW cm−2 sr−1 to remove wildfires and other ephemeral high-­ intensity lighting events (Kyba et al. 2017).
Exposure index calculation To quantify migrant exposure to ALAN, we summarized exposure at two levels: (1) across the contiguous US and (2) in the top 125 largest urban centers by area (Figure 1). We used the 2017 US Census database to define the bound-aries of these urban centers and used the primary city name in our presentation of urban area (eg Dallas–Fort Worth–Arlington, Texas, is presented as “Dallas”). Across the contiguous US, we calculated exposure as the product of cumulative migration activity × radiance, whereas over urban areas we calculated exposure as the product of cumu-lative migration activity × summed radiance of the entire urban area. To differentiate seasonal differences irrespective of increases in bird populations, we standardized cumulative migratory activity to range between 0 and 1, and standard-ized activity relative to the highest value across the contiguous US. Exposure difference was calculated as the product of log10-­ scaled VIIRS radiance (standardized 0 to 1) and sea-sonal differences in migratory activity.
Results Migration activity Migration activity in spring was greatest in the central US (Figure 2a) and generally more widespread and more easterly in distribution in the fall (Figure 2b). In the western US, we observed greater migratory activity in the spring than in the fall. Furthermore, we observed a 63% increase in cumulative migratory activity from spring to fall. Examining the annual nightly pulses of migratory movements at each radar station, we observed that half of the cumulative migra-tory activity passed each station in 6.2 ± 2.5 (mean ± stand-ard deviation [SD]) nights in spring and 7.1 ± 2.6 nights in fall.
Light pollution The general pattern of nightly radiance showed greater aver-age radiance in the eastern half of the US, with a few notable exceptions from urban areas in the Pacific states, Desert Southwest, and a few Rocky Mountain cities (Figure 2c). As expected, the strongest radiance values were observed Figure 2. Average cumulative distribution of migrant birds during (a) spring and (b) fall migrations from 1995 to 2017 measured by weather surveillance radar (WSR). Circles indicate WSR station locations and are scaled to cumulative migration activity. The magnitudes of spring and fall cumulative movements are standardized to the same range. (c) Log10-­ scaled mean radiance of ALAN measured by the VIIRS on the Suomi-­ NPP satellite.
Front Ecol Environ doi:10.1002/fee.2029  © The Ecological Society of America ﻿KG﻿ Horto et al.
4 RESEARCH COMMUNICATIONS in urban areas. Across the US, 69.5% of the summed linear light radiance came from just 5% of the land area. The top 125 largest urban areas accounted for only 2.1% of total land area and 35.4% of total summed linear radiance.
Continental exposure risk Increased migratory activity during fall was observed in almost all areas, resulting in 53.8% higher total of exposure in the fall. After standardizing for differences in overall migration activity between seasons, we determined that there was still a 13.1% higher sum of exposure in the fall, when migrants moved through more photo-­ polluted airspaces in the eastern half of the US (Figure 3). Departures from this trend were evident in the western half of the country, where spring movements along the Pacific coast led to higher spring exposure (Figure 3).
Urban exposure risk over the 125 largest US cites Mean avian light exposure in cities was 24 times as high as the countrywide average. Larger cities tended toward greater exposure risk (linear regression, spring: F1,123 = 135.8, P < 0.001, R2 = 0.52; fall: F1,123 = 203.1, P < 0.001, R2 = 0.62), but there were notable exceptions, such as Boston (4th in size but 36th and 24th in exposure in spring and fall) and Des Moines (99th in size but 28th and 36th in exposure in spring and fall) (WebTable 2). Regardless of season, the highest levels of exposure to anthropogenic light at night were observed in Chicago, Houston, and Dallas, in descending order (Figure 4; see WebTable 2 for a complete list). These three cities showed exposure magnitudes that were 19 (spring) to 21 (fall) times as high as the median exposure of the remaining 122 cities (Figure 4a). In total, 45 and 74 urban areas exhibited higher spring exposure rankings and higher fall exposure rankings, respectively. Six areas, including Chicago, Houston, and Dallas, showed no change in ranking (Figure 4b). Of the 125 largest US cities, the top 10 greatest changes in seasonal rankings occurred in west-ern states (eg Riverside, San Diego, San Jose; Figure 4b). Of the top 10 risks for exposure, the majority occurred in the central US: seven in spring and six in fall.
Discussion We conducted a quantitative assessment of continent-­ scale exposure of actively migrating birds to nighttime light pollution. The findings leverage recent advances in data access and machine learning to capture new and rich details in characterizing bird movements aloft in relation to radiance from human population centers. With considerations for urban areas and the numbers of migrants flying above them, we can now provide the data necessary to guide con-servation actions to identify locations where ALAN-­ reducing programs may be most effective.
Shifted seasonal distributions Greater abundance of migrants in fall increases the number of birds at risk to ALAN, which was apparent in the gen-eral increase in exposure indices from spring to fall. However, shifts in migratory routes between spring and fall migration also affect the numbers of birds exposed to higher light levels (Figure 2). More easterly fall routes, often described as looped migration (La Sorte et al. 2014), take birds over more heavily photo-­ polluted areas than do spring routes, leading to even higher numbers of birds – and many young birds – exposed to ALAN in fall. At most sites, exposure indices are therefore higher during fall than in spring, indicating that any mitigation efforts (eg lights-­ out cam-paigns) would have a larger effect during the fall, especially with juveniles as they undertake their first migratory jour-ney. However, while the risk of mortality for juveniles is likely to increase in the fall, any effects of ALAN on migrants in the spring will directly affect breeding activities. Birds moving along westerly routes during spring migration are the exception to this general pattern, likely related to their use of more westerly, low-­ elevation routes during spring as compared to fall (La Sorte et al. 2014). For example, the patterns in Los Angeles and other cities in California are the opposite of most East Coast cities, with higher exposure during spring migration (Figures 3 and 4).
Uneven temporal distributions Migration periods may span more than 6 months in total, with hundreds of millions of individual migrants aloft on a Figure 3. Seasonal differences in exposure to ALAN. The magnitude of spring and fall cumula-tive movements were standardized to the same range (0 to 1) to highlight seasonal differences in migratory routes. Exposure difference was calculated as the product of log10-­ scaled VIIRS radiance (standardized 0 to 1) and seasonal differences in migratory activity.
© The Ecological Society of America  Front Ecol Environ doi:10.1002/fee.2029 Nocturnally migrating birds and artificial light RESEARCH COMMUNICATIONS 5 given night; however, their passage occurs in sporadic waves, with a large majority of birds passing individual sites during just a few peak nights. We observed that half of the total number of migrants for each season passed each radar site in just 6.7 ± 2.6 (mean ± SD) nights, a notable finding when paired with the recent capacity to confidently forecast (12–72 hours in advance) these episodic events (Van Doren and Horton 2018). This advance has the potential to offer a detailed and tailored guide for mitigation actions to substantially lower the numbers of birds exposed to risks of ALAN while simul-taneously minimizing adverse effects to stakeholders, including municipalities and industry. In addition, birds disproportion-ately use modified habitats (eg urban areas) during fall migra-tion (Zuckerberg et al. 2016), and because migrants are more numerous and less experienced in fall, an emphasis on fall mitigation efforts is especially important.
Conclusions ALAN continues to increase in many areas globally (Kyba et al. 2017), presenting an ever-­ growing ecological threat to all nocturnally active animals (Longcore and Rich 2004; Guetté et al. 2018), particularly migrating birds. Concerted conservation efforts at local (eg Van Doren et al. 2017) and continental scales are necessary to reduce exposure of migrants to light pollution. The disproportionate relationship between the land area occupied by cities and the amount of ALAN emitted leaves little doubt where conservation action is most needed: urban centers. Such efforts require balance with the needs of stakeholders. ALAN ranges from bright sources to dim stray light, and it remains an open question how conservation action should be prioritized over these widely differing sources. In addition, the extent to which species – or even populations – differentially respond to ALAN remains unclear, but could have important conservation implications. Furthermore, different datasets are available (eg a world atlas of artificial night sky brightness; Falchi et al. 2016), which may provide valuable information for charac-terizing ALAN’s disruptions to aerial organismal biology (eg horizon glow versus upward radiance). Although we did not directly compare different sources of ALAN information with respect to exposure risks, we believe that such com-parisons will be fundamentally important.
Reducing nighttime lights for the benefit of migrants and other wildlife represents yet another instance of anthropogenic and environmental trade-­ offs, in this case among avian safety, human safety, energy expenditure, and societal and psycholog-ical expectations. It is therefore important that conservation efforts and future research are directed to the times and places where they will have the largest impact. An important step in this direction is identifying where the highest numbers of birds are exposed to the highest amounts of ALAN. Here we have shown where the greatest threats exist, and how these threats vary seasonally. The combination of large amounts of noctur-nal illumination and their location in the most trafficked air-space across the US elevate metropolitan Chicago, Houston, and Dallas to the top of the exposure risk ranking. While all urban areas should take care to minimize ALAN, our analysis indicates that actions taken in these particular cities would benefit the largest numbers of birds. Through our analysis, we have identified risk; however, directly linking risk with adverse effects on bird populations is a challenge, and future research is needed to fully understand the impacts of ALAN on migratory species.

args.summary:
This research paper (published in Frontiers in Ecology and the Environment) by Horton, Nilsson, Van Doren, La Sorte, Dokter, and Farnsworth quantifies the continental-scale exposure of nocturnally migrating birds to artificial light at night (ALAN) in the contiguous US. Approximately 80% of North America's ~630 terrestrial bird species are migratory, and over 80% of those migrate at night. The study combined over two decades (spring 1995 to spring 2017) of weather surveillance radar data from 143 stations with satellite-based VIIRS ALAN radiance data to map where and when the highest numbers of migrants are exposed to light pollution, focusing on the 125 largest urban centers.

Key methodology: Radar data from a 30-minute window centered on 3 hours after local sunset were filtered using a random forest classifier (5.6% spring and 4.5% fall classification error) to exclude precipitation scans, with only scans having ≥75% confidence of being precipitation-free retained. Migration activity was measured as vertically integrated reflectivity. ALAN was quantified using monthly VIIRS Day/Night Band composites averaged across October–December 2012–2017.

Key findings: (1) Fall migration had 63% higher cumulative migratory activity than spring, and 53.8% higher total exposure; even after standardizing for migration differences, fall exposure remained 13.1% higher because fall migrants used more easterly (and more photo-polluted) routes. (2) Half of seasonal migratory activity passed each radar site within just 6.7 ± 2.6 nights on average. (3) The top 125 urban areas occupied only 2.1% of total land area but produced 35.4% of total light radiance. (4) Mean avian light exposure in cities was 24 times the countrywide average. (5) Chicago, Houston, and Dallas consistently had the highest exposure risk in both seasons, with exposure magnitudes 19–21 times the median of the other 122 cities. (6) Larger cities generally had greater exposure risk (R² = 0.52 spring, 0.62 fall), but there were notable exceptions like Boston (4th in size but 36th/24th in exposure) and Des Moines (99th in size but 28th/36th in exposure).

Conservation implications: Because migration occurs in concentrated pulses and can now be forecast 12–72 hours in advance, targeted "lights-out" campaigns timed to peak migration nights could reduce bird exposure significantly. Fall mitigation is especially important given the higher numbers of less-experienced juvenile birds. The study identifies urban centers—particularly Chicago, Houston, and Dallas—as the highest-priority locations for ALAN-reducing conservation actions.

<webpage_content>
1 Classification: BIOLOGICAL SCIENCES, Ecology 1 2 Title: High-intensity urban light installation dramatically alters nocturnal bird migration 3 4 Authors: Benjamin M. Van Doren1,3*, Kyle G. Horton1,2*, Adriaan M. Dokter1, Holger Klinck4, Susan B. 5 Elbin5, and Andrew Farnsworth1a. 6 7 Affiliations: 8 1Information Science Program, Cornell Lab of Ornithology, 159 Sapsucker Woods Rd., Ithaca NY, 14850 9 USA 10 2Department of Biology and Oklahoma Biological Survey, University of Oklahoma, 111 E. Chesapeake 11 Street, Norman, OK, 73019 USA 12 3Edward Grey Institute, Department of Zoology, University of Oxford, Oxford, OX1 3PS, UK 13 4Bioacoustics Research Program, Cornell Lab of Ornithology, 159 Sapsucker Woods Rd., Ithaca NY, 14 14850 USA 15 5New York City Audubon, 71 W 23rd St, New York, NY, 10010 USA 16 aCorresponding author: Andrew Farnsworth, 414 E 52nd St Penthouse C, New York, NY 10022, USA. 914 17 672 5971; af27@cornell.edu 18 *These authors contributed equally to this work. 19 20 Keywords: artificial light, nocturnal migration, remote sensing, radar ornithology, flight calls 21 22 2 Abstract: Billions of nocturnally migrating birds move through increasingly photo-polluted skies, 23 relying on cues for navigation and orientation that artificial light at night (ALAN) can impair. Yet 24 no studies have quantified avian responses to powerful ground-based light sources in urban areas. 25 We studied effects of ALAN on migrating birds by monitoring the beams of the National September 26 11 Memorial & Museum's ‘Tribute in Light’ in New York, quantifying behavioral responses with 27 radar and acoustic sensors and modeling disorientation and attraction with simulations. This single 28 light source induced significant behavioral alterations in birds, even in good visibility conditions, in 29 this heavily photo-polluted environment, and to altitudes up to 4 km. We estimate that the 30 installation influenced approximately 1.1 million birds during our study period of seven days over 31 seven years. When the installation was illuminated, birds aggregated in high densities, decreased 32 flight speeds, followed circular flight paths, and vocalized frequently. Simulations revealed a high 33 probability of disorientation and subsequent attraction for nearby birds, and bird densities near 34 the installation exceeded magnitudes 20 times greater than surrounding baseline densities during 35 each year’s observations. However, behavioral disruptions disappeared when lights were 36 extinguished, suggesting that selective removal of light during nights with substantial bird 37 migration is a viable strategy for minimizing potentially fatal interactions among ALAN, 38 structures, and birds. Our results also highlight the value of additional studies describing 39 behavioral patterns of nocturnally migrating birds in powerful lights in urban areas as well as 40 conservation implications for such lighting installations. 41 42 Significance Statement: Artificial light at night is a novel stimulus in the evolutionary history of 43 nocturnal animals. Light pollution can significantly alter these organisms’ behaviors, from migration to 44 foraging to vocal communication. Nocturnally migrating birds are particularly susceptible to artificial 45 light because of adaptations and requirements for navigating and orienting in darkness. However, light’s 46 effects on in-flight behaviors have not been well quantified, especially in urbanized environments. Here 47 we report that an iconic urban light installation dramatically altered multiple behaviors of nocturnally 48 migrating birds—but these effects disappeared when lights were extinguished. We recommend selective 49 removal of light pollution during nights with substantial bird migration to mitigate negative effects on 50 birds, in particular collisions with lighted structures. 51 3 \body 52 53 Introduction: 54 The extent of artificial lighting at night (ALAN) at regional and global scales has increased 5-10% 55 annually in portions of North America and Europe and exponentially in some other regions (1), resulting 56 in sky glow that is often significantly brighter than luminance of the natural sky. ALAN may affect a 57 diverse array of nocturnally active animals, and recent studies have highlighted the need for primary 58 research into these potential impacts (2, 3). The biological effects of anthropogenic light pollution may be 59 especially significant for nocturnally migrating birds (2-6). 60 Birds engage in seasonal migrations that are often global in distribution and span a broad range of 61 spatial and temporal scales (7, 8). Avian migratory movements are often thought of as feats of endurance; 62 some species undertake days-long, nonstop, trans-hemispheric flights, while others embark on complex 63 months-long journeys (9). Failed migration may have detrimental effects at individual and population 64 scales (10, 11). Despite birds’ primarily diurnal activity for the majority of the annual cycle, most 65 migratory movements are nocturnal (7, 8), and the numbers of birds that migrate at night are enormous 66 (e.g. 12, 13). Numerous studies have offered perspectives on factors that govern nocturnal movements 67 (14-18) and insights into adaptations necessary to orient and navigate at night (e.g. 19, 20). 68 Visual cues are essential for navigation during migration (21), and ALAN may alter birds’ 69 abilities to orient and navigate (22, 23). The avian geomagnetic sense, which provides songbirds with a 70 compass to inform their spatial maps (19, 20, 24), may function with a dependency on frequencies of 71 light, and ALAN may interfere with this dependency (e.g. 25, 26-28). Impediments to orientation and 72 navigation senses may prove costly for avian migrants, creating new hazards during an already 73 challenging and dynamic period of the annual cycle (29). Additionally, ALAN can alter the ways birds 74 communicate (30) and avoid predation (31). 75 Accounts of birds’ responses to light are numerous in literary and historical anecdotes, peer-76 reviewed journal articles, and popular media. Mortality at lighted structures has been documented across a 77 wide geographic area and a broad range of species (e.g. 4, 6, 32-44). It is likely that hundreds of millions 78 of birds die annually from nocturnal collisions with buildings (29), representing a diverse array of migrant 79 species (e.g. 32, 33). Understanding the causes of these events is paramount; proposed explanations 80 include that birds exhibit phototaxis and experience light-induced disorientation. 81 Generally, negative impacts of ALAN for birds in flight have been associated with conditions that 82 are already poor for navigation and orientation, such as low cloud ceiling, fog, and stalled or weak frontal 83 boundaries between air masses (e.g. 34-39, 43, 45, 46-48). Experimental field studies are generally rare 84 (e.g. 22, 26, 49-51) and offer limited evidence of the extent and intensity of ALAN’s effects on 85 nocturnally migrating birds, particularly with respect to behaviors in clear sky conditions (but see 48) and 86 urbanized (e.g. heavily photo-polluted) environments. Understanding the disruptive effects of short-term 87 ALAN (e.g. lighting installations, sporting events) on nocturnal bird migration in urbanized and photo-88 polluted areas and identifying the extents of these effects in clear sky conditions are important 89 conservation priorities. 90 We took advantage of a unique opportunity to quantify birds’ responses to ALAN by monitoring 91 numbers, flight patterns and vocalizations of birds aloft during alternating periods of illumination and 92 darkness in the powerful light beams of the National September 11 Memorial & Museum's "Tribute in 93 Light" (TiL) in New York, NY (Fig. 1a). First, we quantified densities and flight speeds of aerial migrants 94 near the light installation using data from the KOKX Brookhaven, NY WSR-88D radar station, revealing 95 how numbers of birds and their rates of passage changed in the presence or absence of illumination. 96 Second, we measured birds’ vocal activity by recording their in-flight vocalizations, or flight calls, from 97 the base of the installation. Increased flight calling activity in nocturnally migrating birds may indicate 98 disorienting or confusing conditions (30, 52). If nocturnally migrating birds were attracted to and 99 disoriented by the lights, we expected to observe higher densities of birds flying at slower flight speeds 100 and vocalizing more frequently during periods of illumination. Finally, we used a flow model to simulate 101 bird behaviors in ALAN conditions for comparison with observed radar data. These spatio-temporal 102 4 distribution simulations investigated three important behavioral parameters to explain bird concentrations 103 at the installation: the probability that the lights affected nearby birds, the distance over which the lights 104 affected birds, and whether disoriented birds showed preferred flight directions towards the display. 105 Together, these parameters determined how long birds remained in the illuminated area. 106 107 Results. 108 We detected large aggregations of circling birds above the installation under clear sky conditions during 109 periods of illumination (Figs. 1b, c; 2a; SI Appendix, Fig. S1, Videos S1-S3). By summing the 110 differences between bird numbers within 5 km of the installation and the number expected in that area 111 given baseline densities, we estimate that approximately 1.1 million birds (95% CI: 0.6-1.6 million) were 112 affected by this single light source during our study period of seven nights over seven years (SI 113 Appendix, Fig. S2). The numbers of birds affected varied by year, in part due to variation in the 114 magnitude of migratory passage through the surrounding area on the study night (SI Appendix, Fig. S3), 115 but all years showed strong increases in bird density with decreasing distance to the light source (Fig. 3; 116 SI Appendix, Fig. S4a). Under illumination, peak bird densities near the installation reached 117 magnitudes 20 times greater than the surrounding baseline during all seven years (see SI Appendix, Fig. 118 S5a), where we defined baseline as the mean density in the area 2-20 km from the site. Peak bird densities 119 exceeded 60 times baseline in five of seven years and 150 times baseline in three years (2008, 2012, 120 2013), but peak densities never exceeded 13 times baseline in the absence of illumination (SI Appendix, 121 Fig. S5a). Vocal activity beneath the lights was intense during periods of aggregation (Fig. 2c; SI 122 Appendix, Fig. S6). Bird densities, flight speeds, and vocal activities all varied closely with illumination 123 (Fig. 2). Removal of illumination resulted in rapid changes in nocturnal migration behaviors, with birds 124 dispersing, increasing flight speeds, decreasing calling activity and moving away from the site in a matter 125 of minutes (Fig. 3c, d). 126 We found a strong effect of illumination on the maximum standardized peak bird density and the 127 maximum number of birds detected within 500 m of the installation during each period of darkness and 128 adjacent periods of illumination. Considering the 0.5º radar elevation angle, maximum standardized bird 129 densities were 14 times greater when the light display was illuminated (t = 5.70, P < 0.0001). Maximum 130 bird numbers averaged 3.4 times greater during lit periods (t = 3.89, P = 0.0003). Remarkably, these 131 effects were also present at high altitudes (1.5º radar elevation angle, sampling altitudes of 2.4-4.1 km): 132 maximum standardized densities increased on average by 3.9x (t = 3.25, P = 0.002) and maximum bird 133 numbers by 3.3x (t = 2.34, P = 0.023) during lit periods at high altitudes. We note that we did not detect 134 many birds congregating in the beams during 2014; this year was not included in the above analyses 135 because the lights were not shut down. We observed a strong effect of light on bird behavior during all 136 other years (SI Appendix, Fig. S7). 137 Considering all radar observations, total numbers of birds within 500 m of the installation 138 averaged 3.4 times higher during illuminated periods (t = 9.34, P < 0.0001). Standardized peak densities 139 showed a similar pattern (factor = 6.4x, t = 3.72, P = 0.0003), with the effect strengthened to 46 times 140 higher during illuminated periods in 2015 (t = 2.91, P = 0.004). Again, these effects were also significant 141 in the high altitude 1.5º radar data (total numbers: factor = 1.9x, t = 3.49, P = 0.0006; std. peak density: 142 factor = 4x, t = 4.00, P < 0.0001). Radial velocities were significantly lower during illuminated periods 143 (main effect = -1.7 m s-1, t = -2.10, P = 0.037), especially during 2012 (effect with interaction = -5.4 m/s, t 144 = -2.38, P = 0.02) and 2015 (effect with interaction = -4.3 m/s, t = -2.52, P = 0.01). Flight call rates 145 recorded beneath the installation were significantly higher during illuminated periods (main effect = 1.4x, 146 t = 4.53, P < 0.0001), especially in 2015 (factor with interaction = 2.9x, t = 6.88, P < 0.0001); the effect 147 was reduced in 2013 (factor with interaction = 1.1x, t = -2.30, P = 0.02). Because our model of vocal 148 activity included bird density as a predictor to account for variation in calling explained by the sheer 149 quantity of birds, the significant increases in calling with illumination can be attributed primarily to 150 behavioral differences. 151 Simulation results showed that birds were highly likely to become disoriented as they approached 152 the installation (SI Appendix, Fig. S8). The model matching radar observations most closely (model 1; 153 5 Fig. 4; SI Appendix, Tables S1 and S2) had disorientation probability a=0.95, indicating a very high 154 likelihood of disorientation near ALAN, and the characteristic disorientation distance (s) was 1500 m. 155 The concentrations of birds observed at the installation could only be explained by including directed 156 flight towards ALAN for disoriented birds (concentration parameter k>0; best model k=0.1). In contrast, 157 simulated birds diffused easily away from ALAN when assuming a non-directional random walk (k=0; 158 model 3 in SI Appendix, Table S1). These results support our visual observations of birds circling around 159 the installation and are indicative of light attraction. 160 The stabilization time to a steady-state increased with disorientation probability (a) and flight 161 directionality towards ALAN (k) (Fig. 4; SI Appendix, Table S1, Videos S4-S8). The stabilization time 162 provides information on the residence time of birds in the beam, as a steady state is only reached over 163 time periods longer than the average residence time. Our model 1, which is conservative in this regard, 164 predicts a stabilization time of 34 minutes. We note that this is the result of average behavior for all birds 165 contributing to the density pattern, and individual residence times may be considerably longer or shorter. 166 Our simulation provides a theoretical framework for explaining our visual and remotely sensed 167 observations, underscoring that the light installation attracted and entrained passage migrants. 168 Finally, direct visual observations showed that birds frequently circled the installation during 169 periods of illumination and decreased speed on approach to the installation (see SI Appendix). Such 170 observations also highlighted a particular hazard that nocturnally migrating birds face in urbanized areas 171 with ALAN: collisions with structures. Observers noted in 2015 and 2016 that many birds collided with 172 the glass windows of a building under construction just north of the lights (50 West St.; Fig 1a). The full 173 extent of mortality was not clear, primarily because of challenges surveying nearby sites, scaffolding 174 preventing birds from falling to ground level, and removal of carcasses by scavengers and building staff. 175 We therefore do not have sufficient data to analyze mortality with respect to illumination and migration 176 intensity. However, existing data are archived at (53). 177 178 Discussion: 179 This is the first study to quantify ALAN-induced changes in multiple behaviors of nocturnally migrating 180 birds. Our data show that the light installation strongly concentrates and disorients migrants flying over a 181 heavily urbanized area, influencing approximately 1.1 million birds during seven nights over seven years. 182 Existing published accounts report attraction to lights almost exclusively under poor-visibility 183 conditions (e.g. 45, 54), but our results show alterations to migrants’ behaviors in clear and mostly clear 184 sky conditions (e.g. after 48). Furthermore, to the best of our knowledge, no previous studies have 185 reported attractive effects of ground-based lights to extend far above the ground, although nocturnally 186 migrating birds will attempt to escape from direct illumination by a searchlight (55). In our study, we 187 found behavioral responses to the installation up to c. 4 km above the ground. The vertical orientation of 188 the light beams may be partly responsible for their high-altitude effects, as illuminated atmospheric 189 moisture, dust, insects, or potentially other birds may attract migrants. We also demonstrated that short-190 term removal of ALAN eliminated its disruptive effects almost instantaneously. Our ground-truthed, 191 direct visual observations of decreases in flight speed and increases in circling behaviors corroborate 192 previous findings that birds shift direction and fly more slowly and erratically in the presence of ALAN 193 (22, 23, 32, 33, 39, 44, 48, 49, 56). Furthermore, the increase in vocal activity that we describe agrees 194 with other studies’ findings, highlighting disorientation due to artificial lighting (23, 30). Finally, 195 although each year exhibited a unique array of atmospheric conditions, we documented a strong 196 concentrating effect of light in all but one of the seven study years (Fig. S7). We conclude that high 197 intensity lights have the ability to greatly impact avian migratory behavior under a wide range of 198 conditions. The fact that we did not document a strong effect during one year (2014) highlights a need for 199 further research on how differing ambient conditions influence birds’ attraction to light sources at night. 200 Light-induced alterations to nocturnal migration behaviors may represent significant energetic 201 expenditures for migrating birds, but the effects of such alterations have not been quantified (57). Our 202 visual observations indicate that bright lights alone can induce unnecessary ascent and descent, long 203 6 periods of circling, and other types of complex and irregular maneuvering in birds close to the ground 204 (see 22); these flight patterns are undoubtedly more energetically expensive than typical straight-path 205 migratory flights. Specific hazards resulting from altered flight behavior may include susceptibility to 206 predation (31), collisions with man-made structures (29), and changes to stopover ecology (58). 207 Importantly, birds entrained for hours (e.g. 39, 41, 42, 56, 59) by artificial lighting expend energy to 208 remain airborne but do not make forward progress. Those that do not die from complications of 209 exhaustion (see 60) may be delayed for days, as it takes time for lean migrants to regain fat stores during 210 migratory stopover (61). Although our best model’s stabilization time of 34 minutes suggests that most 211 birds do not remain at the installation for hours, this model could not explain the largest concentrations 212 we observed; other methods will be necessary to better understand variation in individual birds’ behavior 213 over time in the lights. 214 Further controlled experiments in field and laboratory settings would help determine the causes of 215 attraction and disorientation at local and landscape scales. Studies that varied light intensity locally found 216 that birds respond more strongly with more intense light (62-64). Sampling bird migration at and near 217 light installations of varying intensities may provide additional opportunities to study attraction and 218 disorientation. There are few vertically-pointing light installations of comparable intensity in the US (e.g. 219 Luxor, Las Vegas, NV, USA), but many structures employ similarly powerful horizontal lights (e.g., 220 sports stadia, construction sites, offshore oil rigs). Studies at such locations have not employed multi-221 modal remote sensing to quantify disruptions but have noted behavioral changes similar to those that we 222 observed (e.g., aggregation, circling, and increased vocal activity (58, 65)). 223 Studies of ALAN are revealing large-scale effects on bird behavior that range from flight 224 alterations to changes in stopover habitat usage. There is mounting evidence that migratory bird 225 populations are more likely to occur in urban areas during migration, especially in the autumn (66). Light 226 pollution may explain this relationship, as recent research suggests that birds associate with higher levels 227 of ALAN during migration (67). Given alarming declines in migratory bird populations (68, 69), these 228 studies highlight a need to understand ALAN’s implications for migratory bird populations. 229 Finally, our study highlights a model relationship for collaboration among diverse stakeholders. A 230 hallmark of this project was frequent and public cooperation among the National September 11 Memorial 231 & Museum (NSMM), the Municipal Arts Society, New York City Audubon, the Cornell Lab of 232 Ornithology, and stakeholders with direct interest and responsibility for this event, all of whom 233 acknowledged its potential to negatively impact birds. All parties agreed to keep the display illuminated 234 unless potentially hazardous conditions for birds necessitated a short-term shutdown of the lights. 235 Whereas discontinuing the display would be best for nocturnally migrating birds, such a scenario may not 236 be possible at this time. TiL is arguably one of the world’s most iconic and emotional displays of light. 237 The fact that the event’s organizers and participants were willing to periodically shut down the lights for 238 the benefit of migratory birds is an encouraging acknowledgement of the importance of bird conservation. 239 Moreover, despite occasional confusion and frustration among the tribute’s viewers, media coverage often 240 highlighted a unified message from stakeholders about balancing potential hazards to migrating birds with 241 the intent and spirit of the display. 242 243 Methods: 244 During our seven-year study period, the tribute lights were shut down a total of 22 times, for 245 approximately 20 minutes each. This allowed us to directly contrast birds’ behaviors during adjacent dark 246 and illuminated periods. We note that this study was opportunistic and not a controlled experiment. 247 Furthermore, we note that such an opportunistic approach results in some inevitable challenges in 248 interpretation, for example because we were unable to control for additional factors that could influence 249 the degree to which birds congregate at light sources. Such factors likely include wind speed, wind 250 direction, temperature, cloud cover, and ground-based sources of light and sound. However, because 251 ambient conditions were generally similar within each night, we can still readily measure the additive 252 effect of illumination on bird behavior given each year’s suite of conditions. 253 254 7 Study site and scope. 255 Tribute in Light is an event held annually since 2002 on September 11th to memorialize lives lost during 256 the terrorist attacks of September 11th, 2001 (www.911memorial.org/tribute-light). NSMM currently 257 operates the light installation atop a parking garage near the site of the former World Trade Center in New 258 York City, NY at the southern end of Manhattan Island (40.707°, -74.015°). 259 Massive nocturnal migratory movements of birds regularly occur over our study area during mid-260 September (12, 13, 70, 71). However, since the timing of these movements depends on local and regional 261 weather and wind conditions (e.g. 72, 73-75), the magnitude of migratory passage on the single night of 262 September 11th varies greatly among years. An agreement between New York City Audubon (NYCA) and 263 NSMM governs when to initiate the shutdown procedures: when numbers of birds circling in the beams 264 exceed 1000 individuals, based on visual observations, NYCA requests that lights be extinguished for 265 approximately 20 minutes. These requests originate from observers on site that are directly monitoring 266 birds and their behaviors in the beams. 267 We examined September 11th nights from 2008-2016. High-resolution radar imagery does not 268 exist before 2008, which limited our temporal scope. We excluded 2009 and 2011 because of the presence 269 of precipitation, which interferes with analysis of radar data containing bird migration information. Of the 270 remaining seven years, migration conditions varied from marginal to favorable, assessed based on 271 prevailing atmospheric conditions. Of these seven years, the lights were shut down at least once during 272 five of them; as a result, many of our analyses are restricted to these five years (2010, 2012, 2013, 2015, 273 and 2016). Of the remaining two years, the first (2008) occurred before stakeholders could reach a 274 consensus on a protocol for shutting down the light installation when birds were present and in danger. 275 Organizers did not shut down the installation in 2014 because few birds were present in the lights. 276 277 Local weather conditions. 278 We downloaded hourly local climatic data (LCD) for 11-12 September 2008-2016 (excluding 2009 and 279 2011 as described above) from the closest official National Weather Service station to the installation 280 between evening and morning civil twilight (sun angle 6° below the horizon): WBAN 94728, Central 281 Park, New York, NY at 40.789°, -73.967°; and Meteorological Terminal Aviation Routine Weather 282 Reports (METARS) from Newark Liberty International Airport, the closest such station at 40.690°, -283 74.174°. Based on a review and summary of these data, we classified all nights during our study as clear 284 (see SI Appendix, Tables S3, S4). 285 286 Weather surveillance radar data. 287 We gathered radar data from Brookhaven, NY WSR-88D radar (KOKX; 40.866°, -72.864°) to quantify 288 migrants’ flight behaviors and extracted georeferenced measures of reflectivity (η; cm2 km-3) and radial 289 velocity (m s-1) from the ~0.5° and ~1.5° elevation scales (12, 13, 71, 76, 77). We measured between civil 290 twilight periods within a 20 km radius surrounding the installation (98.5 km from the radar, azimuth 291 260°) and consolidated analyses into 500-m height annuli bins. We dealiased velocities when necessary 292 following (77, 78). We restricted our analyses to data points within 90 minutes of a shutdown period 293 except when described. 294 We studied the effect of light stimuli on migratory birds using several metrics. First, we used the 295 radar sweep with the lowest elevation angle (~0.5º) to estimate the number of birds present in a cylinder 296 centered on the installation with a radius along the ground of 500 m and a height of 1.7 km, the 297 approximate width of the radar beam above the site (79). We calculated total effective scattering area per 298 unit volume (cm2 km-3) of birds in this cylinder using bird density measures from the 0-500 m bin. Then, 299 we converted to numbers of birds using an estimated value of one bird = 8.1 cm2, which is the measured 300 cross sectional area on S-band radar of a small passerine songbird (Common Chiffchaff Phylloscopus 301 collybita (80)). We chose a relatively small cross section value because visual observations at the 302 installation indicated that birds in the lights were predominantly small songbirds. The radar beam set to 303 the 0.5º elevation angle passes above the installation at an altitude of approximately 1.5 km (50% power 304 range 0.7-2.4 km), which is higher than the altitudes at which the greatest migratory activity during this 305 8 season in this region generally occurs (e.g. 81). Therefore, we used an analysis of the entire radar scan to 306 estimate the proportion of migration occurring beneath (or above) the radar beam at the installation, out of 307 sight of the radar. We then adjusted our estimates to account for these undetected birds by multiplying by 308 the necessary correction factor (SI Appendix, Fig. S10). This approach assumes that the light beams did 309 not greatly alter the altitudinal distribution of birds near the installation. The validity of this assumption is 310 supported by direct visual observations at the site, where observers noted descent only by the lowest-311 flying individuals, which would not be detected by radar. Furthermore, any unaccounted-for descent at 312 higher altitudes would render our estimates conservative, because a greater proportion of birds flying 313 below the radar beam than expected would yield a lower estimate of total bird numbers. 314 To complement estimates of the total number of birds in proximity to the installation, we also 315 calculated the extent to which birds were concentrated at high densities in the airspace near the 316 installation, relative to the baseline value in the surrounding airspace. To produce this baseline, we 317 calculated the mean and standard deviation of density values between 2-20 km from the installation. We 318 then found the peak bird density value within 500 m of the installation, and we subtracted the baseline 319 mean density from this peak density and divided the difference by the baseline standard deviation (again, 320 2-20 km from the installation). The resulting value, referred to as “standardized peak density,” represents 321 the number of standard deviations the peak density falls above the baseline density. 322 323 Acoustic data. 324 We collected continuous acoustic data at 32 kHz sampling rates and 16-bit sample sizes during each 325 year’s event with a pressure zone microphone (Old Bird 21c; Old Bird, Ithaca, New York, USA) 326 specifically designed for monitoring avian flight calls, connected to 1) a Nagra ARES-BB+ (2010, 2013) 327 or 2) a custom-built passive acoustic recording system (2015, 2016), comprising a Raspberry Pi 2 Model 328 B (Raspberry Pi Foundation, Caldecote, UK) with a Cirrus Logic Raspberry Pi Audio Card (Cirrus Logic, 329 Austin, Texas, USA). We focused analysis on the 6-9 kHz frequency band to minimize interference from 330 anthropogenic, geophonic, and non-avian biophonic noise and because many of the migrating birds in the 331 New York City area emit flight calls in this frequency band (82). The microphone sensitivity in the 332 relevant frequency band for this study (6-9 kHz) was -33 dB re 1V Pa-1 (± 2 dB). 333 334 Visual Observations. 335 We complemented remote sensing data that characterized behaviors of nocturnally migrating birds above 336 the installation with visual observations. Numerous observers, including one of us (AF) and volunteers 337 from New York City Audubon and the local birdwatching community, made visual counts of nocturnally 338 migrating birds at the installation during the period between civil twilight dusk and dawn. All visual 339 counts made at the installation are archived in the eBird reference database 340 (http://ebird.org/ebird/hotspot/L1744278; (83)). 341 342 Statistics. 343 We used generalized additive models (R package mgcv (84)) to quantify the effects of TiL illumination 344 on birds’ behaviors (see SI Appendix). We tested the categorical factors of light (on/off) and year on four 345 metrics: standardized peak density; the total number of birds present within 500 m of the installation; the 346 radial velocities of birds above the installation; and the number of flight calls recorded beneath the site. 347 For models of time series, we also included smooth terms that accounted for overall variation in densities 348 and behavior through the night. We confirmed that there was negligible temporal autocorrelation of 349 residuals using the acf function in R for all analyses involving time series (see SI Appendix). We log-350 transformed response variables when necessary to reduce residual skewness; for models with log-351 transformed response variables, we express effect size as a multiplicative factor, found by exponentiating 352 the coefficient. Finally, to determine whether the light effects we present in the study are representative of 353 those observed at the installation across years, we compared standardized peak densities across the lighted 354 periods of all seven years, including the two during which no light shutdowns occurred. 355 356 9 Simulations. 357 To understand the dynamic patterns of bird density at the installation, we formulated a spatio-temporal 358 flow model to simulate behavioral changes resulting from exposure to light. In our simulation, birds could 359 transition between two behavioral states: an undisturbed migratory state and a disoriented state induced 360 by ALAN. This is a scientific research paper (Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences) studying the effects of the "Tribute in Light" (TiL) installation at the National September 11 Memorial & Museum in New York City on nocturnally migrating birds. This is the first study to quantify ALAN (artificial light at night)-induced changes in multiple behaviors of nocturnally migrating birds.

Study design: Over seven years (2008-2016, excluding 2009 and 2011 due to precipitation), researchers monitored bird behavior using weather surveillance radar (WSR-88D at Brookhaven, NY), acoustic sensors recording flight calls, and visual observations. The lights were shut down 22 times for approximately 20 minutes each, allowing direct comparison between lit and dark periods. This was an opportunistic study, not a controlled experiment.

Key findings:
- The light installation influenced approximately 1.1 million birds (95% CI: 0.6-1.6 million) during seven nights over seven years
- Bird densities near the installation were up to 20 times greater than baseline densities, exceeding 60 times baseline in five of seven years and 150 times in three years (2008, 2012, 2013)
- Effects were found up to 4 km altitude (3.9x density increase at 1.5° radar elevation angle)
- During illuminated periods: birds aggregated in high densities, decreased flight speeds (by 1.7 m/s), followed circular flight paths, and vocalized more frequently (1.4x increase in flight call rates)
- Maximum standardized bird densities were 14 times greater when lights were illuminated (t=5.70, P<0.0001)
- Total bird numbers within 500m averaged 3.4 times higher during illuminated periods
- Effects were observed under clear sky conditions in a heavily photo-polluted environment – contradicting previous assumptions that light attraction only occurs in poor visibility
- Behavioral disruptions disappeared within minutes when lights were extinguished
- Simulations (flow model with disorientation probability a=0.95 and disorientation distance of 1500 m) revealed high probability of disorientation and attraction, with a stabilization time of 34 minutes
- Observers documented birds colliding with glass windows of a building under construction at 50 West St. in 2015 and 2016

Recommendations: The authors recommend selective removal of light pollution during nights with substantial bird migration to mitigate negative effects, particularly collisions with lighted structures. They note this strategy was successfully implemented through collaboration among the National September 11 Memorial & Museum, New York City Audubon, Cornell Lab of Ornithology, and other stakeholders. The study highlights the value of multimodal remote sensing and the need for further research on how differing ambient conditions influence bird attraction to light sources.

The Cornell Lab of Ornithology builds the eBird global platform for communities and partners around the world to advance data-driven science, education, and conservation.

# eBird Science: Bright lights in the big city—impacts of artificial lighting on bird migration

![](https://s3.amazonaws.com/is-ebird-wordpress-prod-s3/wp-content/uploads/sites/55/image001-2.jpg)

Every year from sunset on September 11th to sunrise on September 12th, the lights of the National September 11 Memorial & Museum’s Tribute in Light are turned on in remembrance of the lives lost during the terrorist attacks of September 11th 2001. Beams from eighty-eight 7500-watt bulbs cast light skyward in two towering pillars as high as the eye can see, noticeable for a 100-mile radius around New York City. And it’s not just people that take notice: nocturnally migrating birds are attracted and disoriented by the lights. At times a close look can reveal tens of thousands ceaselessly circling through the beams. In a new study published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), “[High-intensity urban light installation dramatically alters nocturnal bird migration](http://www.pnas.org/content/early/2017/09/26/1708574114.abstract),” authors from the Cornell Lab of Ornithology, Oxford University, and New York City Audubon quantify the impact of this light installation on nocturnally migrating birds using radar, acoustics, and visual counts [archived on eBird](https://ebird.org/ebird/hotspot/L1744278).

Using weather surveillance radar, the authors estimate that ~1.1 million migrating birds were influenced by the lights over a period of 7 nights over 7 years. While the abundance of migrants in the beams is visually apparent at the site, only by using radar were the authors able to view a full “footprint” of the lights’ impacts on birds, which may extend multiple kilometers from and above the lights themselves.

Working closely with the tribute’s organizers (first the Municipal Arts Society, and now the National September 11 Memorial & Museum), New York City Audubon lobbied from the outset for extinguishing the lights for 20-minute periods when more than 1000 birds were present in the beams or birds were flying dangerously low, an agreement they hoped would support the tribute’s mission while allowing migrants to escape the draw of the lights. The authors’ analysis revealed that birds returned to normal behavior almost immediately after the lights were turned off, suggesting that selectively turning out lights is an effective way to reduce threats to birds in urban areas.

The paper highlights this collaborative effort, which serves as a model for bringing multiple stakeholders together to mitigate human impacts on migratory birds. This is especially important in a world where the night sky is becoming ever more polluted by artificial light.

You can also learn more about this work from recent features by [National Public Radio](http://www.npr.org/2017/10/05/555949789/light-pollution-can-impact-noctural-bird-migration), the [Washington Post](http://washingtonpost.com/news/speaking-of-science/wp/2017/10/02/new-yorks-911-tribute-mesmerizes-birds-and-might-help-save-them), the [New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2017/10/02/science/september-11-tribute-lights-birds.html).

## Abstract

Electromagnetic noise is emitted everywhere humans use electronic devices. For decades, it has been hotly debated whether man-made electric and magnetic fields affect biological processes, including human health. So far, no putative effect of anthropogenic electromagnetic noise at intensities below the guidelines adopted by the World Health Organization has withstood the test of independent replication under truly blinded experimental conditions. No effect has therefore been widely accepted as scientifically proven. Here we show that migratory birds are unable to use their magnetic compass in the presence of urban electromagnetic noise. When European robins, Erithacus rubecula, were exposed to the background electromagnetic noise present in unscreened wooden huts at the University of Oldenburg campus, they could not orient using their magnetic compass. Their magnetic orientation capabilities reappeared in electrically grounded, aluminium-screened huts, which attenuated electromagnetic noise in the frequency range from 50 kHz to 5 MHz by approximately two orders of magnitude. When the grounding was removed or when broadband electromagnetic noise was deliberately generated inside the screened and grounded huts, the birds again lost their magnetic orientation capabilities. The disruptive effect of radiofrequency electromagnetic fields is not confined to a narrow frequency band and birds tested far from sources of electromagnetic noise required no screening to orient with their magnetic compass. These fully double-blinded tests document a reproducible effect of anthropogenic electromagnetic noise on the behaviour of an intact vertebrate.

args.summary: This webpage summarizes a scientific study published in Nature (2014; 509(7500): 353-356) by Engels S, Schneider NL, Lefeldt N, Hein CM, Zapka M, Michalik A, Elbers D, Kittel A, Hore PJ, and Mouritsen H. The study investigates how anthropogenic electromagnetic noise disrupts magnetic compass orientation in migratory birds. The exposure parameters studied included noise in the 50 kHz–9 MHz frequency range, as well as DC, electric field, magnetic field, static magnetic field, geomagnetic field, low frequency, and intermediate frequency exposures, along with shielding/field deprivation. The paper is accessible via Nature (doi:10.1038/nature13290) and PubMed (24805233). A related commentary by Kirschvink JL (2014), titled "Sensory biology: Radio waves zap the biomagnetic compass," provides additional discussion of the findings.

# Man-Made Electromagnetic Noise Disrupts Bird Navigation

**[Item Media](https://interferencetechnology.com/man-made-electromagnetic-noise-disrupts-bird-navigation/)** [Europe](https://interferencetechnology.com/category/europe/), [News](https://interferencetechnology.com/category/news/), [Research](https://interferencetechnology.com/category/markets/research/), [Shielding](https://interferencetechnology.com/category/technologies/shielding/)

![](https://interferencetechnology.com/wp-content/uploads/2014/05/800px-European_Robin_2-resized.jpg)

[![New research suggests electromagnetic noise generated by electronic devices affects migratory birds' ability to navigate. (Photo: Creative Commons)](https://interferencetechnology.com/wp-content/uploads/2014/05/800px-European_Robin_2-300x225.jpg)](https://interferencetechnology.com/wp-content/uploads/2014/05/800px-European_Robin_2.jpg)

New research suggests electromagnetic noise generated by electronic devices affects migratory birds’ ability to navigate. (Photo: Creative Commons)

**Scientists have known for decades that migratory birds orient themselves using the Earth’s magnetic field in order to fly in the right direction. Now, German researchers have documented for the first time that man-made electromagnetic radiation interferes with these birds’ internal compasses.**

The phenomenon was [discovered](http://www.uni-oldenburg.de/en/news-single/art/electrosmog-disrupts-orientation-in-migratory-birds-948/) by Henrik Mouritsen, a professor of neurosensory sciences at the University of Oldenburg , and his colleagues, who had been studying migratory birds—specifically, the European robin—since the early 2000s to determine which part of the brain is used by a migratory bird when aligning itself to the geomagnetic field.

Typically, scientists studying magnetoreception test birds’ navigation abilities in so-called orientation cages often set up in wooden huts at rural sites far away from urban areas. Thermal paper placed on the walls of these funnel-shaped cages records the scratches the birds’ feet make as they scrabble upward in an attempt to escape. In the absence of other navigational cues such as the sun and stars, the birds will orient to the Earth’s magnetic field and take off towards the north, marking the paper as they do so.

However, in 2002 Mouritsen moved his research to the University of Oldenburg, which is located in a city of around 160,000 people. Once there, the robins’ behavior changed.

“We were surprised when robins kept in wooden huts on the Oldenburg University campus were unable to use their magnetic compass,” Mouritsen recounted. “The birds basically jumped in random directions every spring and autumn for three years.”

The scientists altered a number of factors to no avail, including the robins’ food, their cages, the light and the daylight cycle. Finally, a graduate student, Nils-Lasse Schneider, suggested covering the huts and the cages they contained with sheets of aluminum to form a Faraday cage. This did not affect the Earth’s magnetic field influence, but shielded against weaker electromagnetic interference, which Mouritsen calls “electrosmog.” With this solution, the birds’ orientation ability returned.

“Our measurements of the interferences indicated that we had accidentally discovered a biological system that is sensitive to anthropogenic electromagnetic noise generated by humans in the frequency range up to five megahertz,” Mouritsen said. Surprisingly, he noted, the intensity of the interference was below the limits defined by the International Commission on Non-Ionizing Radiation Protection (ICNIRP) and the World Health Organization (WHO).

During an ensuing seven-year investigation, Mouritsen and his team conducted numerous experiments and double-blind studies in order to collect reliable evidence of the observed effect. They discovered that as soon as the grounding of the screens was disconnected or deliberate electromagnetic interference was created inside the Faraday cage, the birds’ magnetic orientation ability was immediately lost again. Furthermore, the researchers found that the disruptive effects were generated by electromagnetic fields that cover a much broader frequency range at a much lower intensity than previous studies had suggested. As expected, the interference is significantly weaker in rural areas and stronger near locations with a high concentration of electronic devices.

“Thus, the effect of anthropogenic electromagnetic noise on bird migration is localized,” Mouritsen said. “However these findings should make us think—both about the survival of migratory birds as well as about the potential effects for human beings, which have yet to be investigated.”

The related study, “[Anthropogenic Electromagnetic Noise Disrupts Magnetic Compass Orientation in a Migratory Bird](http://www.nature.com/nature/journal/v509/n7500/full/nature13290.html),” is published in the online journal *Nature.* In addition to Mouritsen and Schneider, contributing authors include Svenja Engels, Nele Lefeldt, Christine Maira Hein, Manuela Zapka, Andreas Michalik, Dana Elbers, Achim Kittel and P.J. Hore.
