Thus, selection may favor energy-minimizing strategies during both migration bouts in Arctic breeding songbirds. This may also explain the fast and long migra-tion leg of ID4552 from the Central Valley to the coast of Southwest Alaska in spring. Coastal regions are known to be more predictable due to the temperature buffering effect of the ocean, and spring starts earlier. Yet, this individual had three longer stopovers in Alaska before proceeding to its breeding area. A similar pattern has been observed for Golden-crowned Sparrows: individuals migrating north-wards along the coast to coastal breeding sites moved faster than individuals migrating to interior breeding sites (Corm-ier et al. 2016).
Our stable isotope analysis and the few available band recoveries provided further evidence that birds sampled within relatively small areas across the wintering distribu-tion were derived from individuals distributed across the entire breeding range (Fig. 3). This pattern was reinforced by the tracking data, as three individuals headed towards central-north Alaska and ended up relatively close together, but one migrated to the southwestern coastal region about 1500 km distant from the others. These three lines of evi-dence indicate relatively few connections between breed-ing and wintering populations, and thus a low degree of migratory connectivity (Boulet and Norris 2006; Bauer et al. 2016). Similarly, feathers that were molted during the winter but sampled on the breeding grounds at two locations in cen-tral-north Alaska had δ2Hf values that were expected from across the wintering range. Extreme values even indicate potential wintering sites as far south as northern Mexico. At the other extreme, very low δ2Hf values measured in feathers from birds caught in Washington indicating a breeding site just south of Canada. Yet, we have to be careful when inter-preting these extreme values, since they might be outliers, which can be the result of the general problem of including mountainous areas in modeling isoscapes, or the result of micro-habitat effects that do not reflect the large-scale mod-eling result of the maps shown in Fig. 3. Some uncertainties may also result from feathers that were molted outside the regular molting period and the resulting misinterpretation of their origin. However, even if we ignore the extreme values and remain aware of our low sample size, all the data pooled together suggest a leapfrog migration with more southerly wintering groups traveling greater distances to more north-erly breeding grounds than more centrally based groups. The very low δ2Hf values in feathers of individuals from the most southern sites in California indicate that they were exclu-sively long-distance migrants. Birds wintering in the inter-mediate location in Davis show a higher degree of variation with individuals that may breed along the southern coast of Canada, whereas some individuals caught in Washington State might indeed be year-round residents, as suggested by the annual Christmas counts, or perform only very short and potentially altitudinal migration, similar to that of the closely related and sympatric Puget Sound White-crowned Sparrow (Z. leucophrys pugetensis) (Hunn and Beaudette 2014). This leapfrog migration was consistent across our latitudinal sam-pling locations and may be exhibited by other species along this flyway (DeWolfe and Baptista 1995; Bell 1997; but see Fraser et al. 2018). In addition, a detailed analysis of δ2Hf values sampled at the wintering sites also revealed a modest but significant difference between sex classes with females wintering further south. Latitudinal sex differences in the overwintering site is a well-documented pattern in many north temperate migratory species (Ketterson and Nolan 1976). One of the many drivers for this could be that females of smaller body size do not compete well with larger males, and thus tend to migrate further south to avoid competition for resources in winter. This differential could create a geo-graphic separation of sex and sometimes age classes during winter months (Terrill and Ohmart 1984; Terrill 1987; see also Cristol et al. 1999).
The variation in migratory strategies even within the gambelii subspecies suggested by this paper reflects the phenotypic flexibility expressed within the Pacific White-crowned Sparrow complex, and again indicates potentially rapid changes in behavior and physiology (King and Farner 1963; Farner and Wingfield 1978; Morton 2002). While our data are inconclusive and we encourage further investi-gations, taken together with the initial evidence that some Gambel’s White-crowned Sparrows breed as far south as the Cascade Mountains of Washington State (Hunn and Beaudette 2014), we can speculate that wintering and breeding ranges of these birds may even overlap in south-western Canada and northwestern US. There could thus be a continuous gradient of migratory strategies within Gambel’s White-crowned Sparrows with individuals that winter and breed within or close to the potential overlap-ping region being more like the short-distance migrating Puget Sound subspecies than the Gambel’s White-crowned Sparrows that winter further south.

args.key_excerpts: "Results from all three methods, consisting of 79 ring recoveries, four light level geolocator tracks and 388 feather δ2H values, indicate low degrees of migratory connectivity. The isotope data provide evidence for leapfrog migration with the more southerly populations traveling greater distances to the breeding grounds than more centrally wintering individuals."
args.summary:
This peer-reviewed study, published in the Journal of Ornithology (2019), investigates the migration patterns of Gambel's White-crowned Sparrow (Zonotrichia leucophrys gambelii) along the Pacific Flyway in western North America. The researchers used an integrated approach combining three methods: 79 ring recoveries from the USGS Bird Banding Laboratory, four light-level geolocator tracks (from birds tagged in Davis, California in spring 2013), and stable hydrogen isotope (δ2H) analysis of 388 feathers.

Key findings include:
- Low degrees of migratory connectivity between breeding and wintering populations
- Evidence for leapfrog migration, where more southerly wintering populations travel greater distances to northern breeding grounds
- All four tracked individuals migrated to breeding sites in Alaska (3 to central-north Alaska, 1 to far southwestern Alaska)
- Spring migration lasted 22-46 days (mean 32 days) with 2-3 stopovers of 1-12 days; distances ranged from 3,280-4,300 km
- Autumn migration lasted 24-63 days (mean 43.5 days) with 2-6 stopovers of 2-9 days; distances ranged from 3,592-4,666 km
- Round trips ranged from 6,872-8,966 km
- All birds departed the Davis wintering site between April 7-27, departed breeding grounds between August 25-September 3, and arrived back at wintering site between September 27-October 19
- A pronounced clockwise loop migration pattern: while spring routes followed the shortest land route, autumn migrations took an eastern diversion before heading south (circumnavigating the Rocky Mountains)
- Feather isotope analysis showed females winter further south than males (Δδ2Hf = 11.4‰), a pattern attributed to smaller females avoiding competition with larger males
- All three methods confirmed high inter-individual variability in migration distance and strategy

The study concludes that this variation in migratory strategies reflects the phenotypic flexibility within the White-crowned Sparrow complex, and highlights the species' potential for investigating evolutionary adaptations to environmental change. The findings support behavioral evidence of leapfrog migration and seasonal loop migration, with birds potentially taking advantage of seasonal resources and favorable climatic conditions along the eastern slopes of the Rockies during autumn.

Behav Ecol Sociobiol (1991) 28:9-12 Behavioral Ecology and Sociobiology © Springer-Verlag 1991 Inheritance of migratory direction in a bird species: a cross-breeding experiment with SE- and SW-migrating blackcaps (Sylvia atricapilla) Andreas J. Helbig Max-Planck-Institut ffir Verhaltensphysiologie, Vogelwarte Radolfzell, W-7760 M6ggingen, Federal Republic of Germany Received February 27, 1990 / Accepted July 4, 1990 Summary. Young avian migrants of many species are able to find their species- or population-specific winter- ing area without the help of conspecifics. In orientation tests hand-raised birds have been demonstrated to choose appropriate population-specific migratory direc- tions, suggesting a genetic basis to this behaviour. I here report results of a cross-breeding experiment between individuals of two blackcap (Sylvia atricapilla) popula- tions with widely different migratory directions. The ori- entation of the F1 offspring was intermediate between and significantly different from that of both parental populations (Fig. 2). The variance of individual mean directions in the F1 generation did not increase com- pared with the parental groups, and the inheritance of migratory directions was not sex-linked. The data pro- vide direct evidence for a genetic basis of migratory di- rections in birds and demonstrate a phenotypically inter- mediate mode of inheritance. Introduction Many passerine bird species are nocturnal migrants in which young of the year often migrate very long dis- tances individually (without social guidance) to well-de- fined, species- or population-specific wintering areas. A classic large-scale displacement experiment with starlings (Sturnus vulgaris) demonstrated among other things that juveniles on their first migration possess no knowledge about the geographic coordinates of the wintering area (Perdeck 1958). There is substantial evidence that such inexperienced migrants rely largely on innate informa- tion about distance and direction in which to migrate. An approximate measure of distance is encoded in an endogenous circannual programme as the duration of migratory activity per season (Gwinner 1968; Berthold 1973). This behavioural character is known to have a genetic basis (Berthold and Querner 1981) and responds Current address: Zoologisches Institut, Universit/it Frankfurt, Sies- mayerstrasse 70, W-6000 Frankfurt/M, Federal Republic of Ger- many rapidly to selection (Berthold et al. 1990 a). The migrato- ry direction seems to be encoded as an angle with respect to an external reference (Emlen 1969; Wiltschko and Gwinner 1974). The compass mechanisms by which such vector ori- entation is achieved have been subject to intensive re- search during the past 40 years and are reasonably well understood (Wiltschko 1983; Wiltschko and Wiltschko 1988a). However, little is known about the basis of the directional information beyond the assumption that it must be "innate". Young birds of several species have been hand-raised in the laboratory from an early age onward. When tested during their first migration season in circular orientation cages, such inexperienced birds generally chose southerly directions, as expected from ringing recoveries, irrespective of whether they could see the natural sky or not (e.g. Emlen 1969; Wiltschko and Gwinner 1974; Beck and Wiltschko 1982). The geomag- netic field and the rotational center of the starry night sky seem to serve as ontogenetically independent refer- ences in relation to which birds can find a migratory direction (Wiltschko and Wiltschko 1988 b). While such experiments provided strong circumstan- tial evidence that directional information has a genetic basis, the single, more direct support comes from a cross- breeding experiment between migratory and sedentary blackcaps (Sylvia atricapilla): the F1 offspring oriented bimodally in a NE-SW direction, i.e. along the same axis as their migratory parents (Berthold et al. 1990 b). I crossbred blackcaps from two Central European popu- lations which differ considerably in autumn migratory direction to study the mode of inheritance of this behav- ioural trait. The results are one of the very few cases in which the genetic basis as well as the mode of inheri- tance of a behavioural character have been elucidated in a non-domesticated vertebrate species. Material and methods The species. The blackcap is a common and widespread Palearctic representative of the species-rich muscicapid subfamily Sylviinae, 10 , ~:~:i:i:i:i:i::. o ..:: ::::::5'0;iiiii ::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::: # ~:::~ Sylvia ::::!:i:i:i:i: atricapilla :i:i:i:i:i:i: :~:::::;:;;:::::: .
. :::::::::::::::::: -45° ~ ~ ~, 'ii::" - % - -. 0 ~ , Fig. 1. Breeding (stippled) and main over wintering (hatched) areas of the blackcap. Arrows show schematically the autumn migratory directions of central European SW- and SE-migrating populations (after Klein et al. 1973) which were the subjects of this study comprising many long-distance nocturnal migrants. Central Euro- pean populations of this species winter in widely separated areas (western Mediterranean region and NW Africa, East Africa and recently the British Isles) and display within their continuous range a corresponding variety of autumn migratory directions ranging from SE to SW to NW (Klein et al. 1973; Zink 1973; Berthold and Terrill 1986). While the W to NW migrants (a minority) seem to originate from central Europe, a rather distinct migratory divide exists between SE and SW migrants south of 52°N (Fig. 1). Ac- cording to ringing recoveries the initial autumn migratory direc- tions of these two populations differ by about 70 ° (Klein et al. 1973). Raising of test birds and orientation tests. I hand-raised groups of 50 nestlings (up to four siblings per nest) from west of the divide near Frankfurt/M. (50°04'N; 8°41'E) and Radolfzell (47°46'N; 8°59'E), FRG, and from east of the contact zone near Bruck/Leitha and Halbturn (47 ° 46'N; 17 ° 01' E), eastern Austria. Birds were taken out of the nest at 7-8 days of age, i.e. 3-4 days after opening their eyes, and were raised to independence in the laboratory at Radolfzell. Prior to the migration season they were exposed to natural day and night skies by placing them in individ- ual cages in outdoor aviaries. After becoming migratorily active the orientation of each bird was tested 15-20 times outdoors at dusk in round funnel-shaped cages (Emlen and Emlen 1966) lined with typewriter correction paper and covered with clear plexiglass (of. Helbig et al. 1989). Next spring the birds were transferred to outdoor breeding aviaries (2.5 x 2.5 x 2 m) where 35 mixed pairs were formed, comprising one bird each from east and west of the divide. During 1987 and 1988 16 pairs produced a total of 68 F1 offspring (maximum 8 young per pair). These were again hand-raised and their orientation tested during the first autumn of life. Treatment during raising and testing as well as their prior experience of natural skies was exactly the same as for the 2 paren- tal groups. Data analysis and statistics. During the orientation tests birds pro- duced scratches on the typewriter correction paper. Papers were divided into 24 sectors and scratches counted on a light screen. From each recording with a minimum of 40 scratches, a heading (cq) was calculated by vector addition. For treatment of axially bimodal activity distributions see Helbig et al. (1989). For each individual bird a mean vector of orientation was calculated from all its ei values (regardless of the dispersion of hopping activity) during October and November. For each individual and month, the distribution of ei values was checked for axial bimodality by doubling the angles (see Batschelet 1981). If the vector length of the resulting axis exceeded that of the unimodal vector by more than 0.01, the axis of orientation provided a better fit to the data. In such cases the more southerly end of the axis was taken as the bird's mean direction, because over the entire season every individual had more southerly than northerly directional choices. Occasional northerly directional choices probably correspond to reverse orientation, which is frequently observed in nature (Schiiz 1971). The season had to be divided into 2 parts, because 1 parental group changed direction around the end of October (see below). Statistical analysis follows Batschelet (1981). Mean directions were compared between samples using the Watson-Williams test. All samples to which this parametric test was applied had concentra- tion parameters larger than 2 and did not differ significantly from a von-Mises distribution, thus satisfying the underlying assump- tions. Average deviations from the mean angle between 2 samples were compared using the non-parametric Mann-Whitney U test. N • October W • E r $ N November S l~ig. 2. Inner circle, parental generation; solid triangles, birds from the FRG; open triangles, birds from eastern Austria. Outer circles (lull dots), FI generation. Arrowheads, group mean directions. Compare Table 1. Each symbol is based on an average of 8.1 orien- tation tests per bird in the parental generation (data from first and second autumn of life combined) and 6.2 tests per bird and month in the F1 (first autumn only) 11 Table 1. P=0.061 n.s. F1 Oct. vs. Nov. * n.s. P2 October November F~[ October November " For two F1 birds November data are missing (died, escaped) n=number of birds; e=direction, r=length of mean vector. All six samples are significantly oriented (P<0.001 for all cases, Rayleigh test). The right part of the table shows results of pairwise comparisons between samples with respect to differences in mean direction (Watson-Williams test = WW test) and average deviations from the mean direction (Mann-Whitney U test = MW test). * P < 0.05; *** P < 0.001 ; n.s. = not significant Results The birds from eastern Austria (i.e. one of the parental groups) showed a significant shift in orientation during the course of the autumn (P<0.001, Watson-Williams test): individual mean vectors clustered around an over- all mean direction of 134 ° in October and 185 ° in No- vember (Fig. 2). This probably corresponds to a change of direction from SE to S-SSW when the birds fly around the eastern Mediterranean and on toward East Africa (Helbig et al. 1989). The birds from the FRG oriented SW with no difference between months (Table 1). For this population, migration toward its winter quarters in the western Mediterranean region involves no major change of direction (Klein et al. 1973; Zink 1973). During both months of their first migration season, the FI offspring oriented toward mean directions inter- mediate between those of the parental populations. They performed a shift of only 10 ° from October to November (compared with 51 o in the SE migrating parental group). This difference was, however, significant due to the high degree of concentration [F(I; 132)=5.25; P<0.05; Watson-Williams test]. The orientation of the F1 genera- tion differed significantly from both parental popula- tions during October and from the FRG parents in No- vember (Table 1); the difference from the Austrian par- ents in November was suggestive [F(I; 80)=3.70; P= 0.061]. There were no differences in the scatter of mean directions between parental and F1 groups in either month (P>0.05 for all pairwise comparisons; Mann- Table 2. Orientation of FI offspring depending on sex of SW-or- ienfing parent. There are no significant differences in mean direc- tion (Watson-Williams test) or scatter (Mann-Whitney U Test) be- tween any of the six samples (P>> 0.05 in all cases) Period Male parent Female parent n r ~ g/ r ~ October 36 0.913 187 ° 32 0.881 190 ° November 35 0.880 197 ° 31 0.903 202 ° Whole season 36 0.902 190 ° 32 0.925 196 ° Whitney U test). Directional choices of F1 hybrids were not linked to the sex of their respective SE- or SW- migrating parent (Table 2). An analysis of variance showed no greater similarity of mean directions among siblings than among non-siblings [ANOVA: F (15; 52)= 1.32; P=0.228; Kruskal-Wallis test: H=20.96, P= 0.:138], thus revealing no significant genetic component to the variation in individual mean directions. Discussion The results show that the population-specific migratory directions in the blackcap have a genetic basis and can be altered by cross-breeding. The behavior of the F1 generation was phenotypically intermediate between the parental groups with no increase in variance. This sug- gests either a polygenic (polyalMic) basis to the trait or - less likely - a single locus without dominance. The change of direction performed by one but not the other parental population during the course of the season also seems to have been transferred to the offspring but was much smaller in extent. An endogenous basis of intra- seasonal changes of migratory direction had previously been demonstrated for Sylvia borin (Gwinner and Wiltschko 1978) and Ficedula hypoleuca; in the latter, however, changes in magnetic field parameters are also involved in its control (Beck and Wiltschko 1988). Information on the genetics of compass orientation in other organisms is scarce (Scapini 1988). Seaward mi- gration of salmonid fishes has been reported to be based on inherited directional information either with respect to a compass reference or to the water current (Brannon 1972, 1984). As with my Austrian blackcaps, the direc- tions preferred by seaward migrating Oncorhynchus ner- ka fry changed during the season and paralleled the course of rivers the fish are known to follow (Groot 1965). Cross-breeding of positively and negatively rheo- tactic parental populations of the same species resulted in intermediate behaviour in the F1 generation with a strong increase in variance (Brannon 1972). Similarly, Pardi and Scapini (1983) found an intermediate mode 12 of inheritance for the escape direction of the littoral am- phipods Talitrus saltator. My results obtained with blackcaps agree with pre- vious findings that suggest a quantitative genetic basis for other physiological and morphological characters re- lated to migration, such as amount of migratory restless- ness (Berthold and Querner 1981), timing and duration of post-juvenile moult, body weight and wing length (Berthold and Querner 1982). Heritabilities of migratory activity derived from selective breeding experiments were high in the blackcap (Berthold 1988). An important question is how much genetic variability exists with re- spect to migratory directions in natural populations. Among the relatively small sample of birds bred in this experiment, no significant genetic component of the vari- ability could be demonstrated. This may be due to the difficulties of accurately measuring small individual dif- ferences between innate migratory directions with the relatively crude funnel technique. Taken together, the available evidence indicates a rather strong genetic control of migratory adaptations in avian nocturnal migrants. Given sufficient intra-pop- ulation genetic variability, these adaptations may re- spond readily to selection and explain the high degree of population-specific differentiation and rapid rate of evolutionary change observed in some cases (Berthold and Terrill 1988). However, it is at present unclear how the differentiation between (sub)populations with differ- ent migratory directions is maintained in areas of con- tact. args.summary:
This 1991 scientific paper by Andreas J. Helbig (published in Behavioral Ecology and Sociobiology) documents a cross-breeding experiment demonstrating the genetic basis of migratory direction in blackcaps (Sylvia atricapilla). The study crossed two Central European blackcap populations with widely different autumn migratory directions: SW-migrating birds from western Germany (Frankfurt/M and Radolfzell) and SE-migrating birds from eastern Austria (Bruck/Leitha and Halbturn). These populations differ in migratory direction by approximately 70°.

Methodology: Fifty nestlings were hand-raised from each population and tested in circular funnel-shaped orientation cages during their first autumn migration season (15-20 tests per bird). Next spring, 35 mixed pairs were formed (one bird from each side of the migratory divide), producing 68 F1 offspring across 16 pairs in 1987-1988, which were then tested identically.

Key results: The F1 offspring oriented toward mean directions intermediate between (and significantly different from) both parental populations. The eastern Austrian birds shifted direction during the season (134° in October to 185° in November, a 51° shift), corresponding to routing around the eastern Mediterranean toward East Africa, while FRG birds oriented consistently SW (~228-234°). The F1 hybrids showed only a small 10° seasonal shift. The variance of individual mean directions in F1 generation did not increase compared to parental groups, and inheritance of migratory direction was not sex-linked (no difference based on whether the SW-orienting parent was male or female).

Conclusions: The results demonstrate a genetic basis for migratory direction in birds with a phenotypically intermediate (additive/polygenic) mode of inheritance, suggesting either polygenic inheritance or a single locus without dominance. The author suggests F1 hybrids attempting to migrate in intermediate directions would likely cross the Alps, Mediterranean Sea, and parts of the Sahara — formidable barriers both parental populations avoid — significantly lowering hybrid survival chances in the contact zone.

<webpage_content>
Mapping the genomic diversity of the Eurasian blackcap, a songbird with a wide range of migratory behaviour Dissertation in fulfillment of the requirements for the degree Doctor rerum naturalium of the Faculty of Mathematics and Natural Sciences at the Christian Albrechts University of Kiel Submitted by Andrea Bours Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Biology Germany 2025 First examiner: Prof. Dr. Miriam Liedvogel Second examiner: Prof. Dr. Christine Böhmer Date of oral examination: 24.06.2025 5 SUMMARY In this post-genomic era, more and more different sequencing technologies and analysis tools are being created to understand the genomic, transcriptomic and epigenomic variation seen throughout the natural world. Understanding how this variation leads to phenotypic variation has become an integral question for biologists studying phenotypic variation. In response to the increasing knowledge that (and how) these three types of variation affect each other, it is even more important to research the mechanisms underlying genomic, transcriptomic and epigenomic variation, and their evolution. This thesis presents my PhD research focused on understanding the complex behavioural trait of bird migration and its phenotypic variation as seen in the Eurasian blackcap (Sylvia atricapilla). Using genomic and transcriptomic data, to understand (i) the population genomic variation (Chapter 1), (ii) the transcriptomic variation, in different behavioural states, in the bird brain (as a result of epigenetic variation, Chapter 2), and (iii) genome feature variation, in particular transposable elements, in its genome (Chapter 3). The blackcap is a widely used study species for bird migration. In Chapter 1, I investigate the dichotomy between blackcap populations and their propensity to migrate by comparing seasonal migratory populations with year-round residential populations. The residential populations are found in the south of the distribution range, on the Iberian Peninsula (continental residents) and the different archipelagos of Macaronesia: Madeira, Canary Islands, Cape Verde and Azores, and the following islands in the Mediterranean Sea: Mallorca and Crete. By sampling across the distribution range we expanded our previously assembled whole genome sequencing dataset from 110 to 179 individuals. Before we could investigate the genomic variation between the focal resident and migratory phenotypes, population structure analysis was conducted to increase our understanding of where and how often residency evolves in a species considered to be ancestrally migratory. Our revised knowledge now is that residency evolved convergently in the different resident populations on both the continent and the various island systems. This led me to conduct more informed analyses into genomic signatures of selection for residency for each resident population, finding a lack of overlapping genomic regions under selection, further proving the convergent selection for this phenotype. A migrant blackcap alternates between these behavioural states twice a year, during spring migration (to their breeding grounds) and again during autumn migration (to their overwintering grounds). This behavioural change is all-encompassing, a suite of adaptations, as a successful start of migration requires changes in physiology and behavioural traits. These seasonal behavioural changes are not a result of changes to the bases in the genome sequence of the birds, but rather their transcriptome. Using a transcriptomic dataset of three brain regions in birds, either showing migratory behaviour or not (previously studied for gene differential expression). And using the genomic dataset assembled in Chapter 1, I investigated the allele-specific expression (ASE) patterns in these birds. Presenting these results in Chapter 2, I first adjusted my variant calling pipeline to account for RNA sequencing data, followed by using the genome dataset to more confidently recover the genomic variation of these individuals for subsequent use in the ASE analysis. ASE analysis captures cis-regulatory variation of the genome (epigenomic variation), connecting potential genomic regulation with transcriptomic variation. The three focal brain regions show distinct ASE patterns, and the 6 hippocampus and hypothalamus have ASE patterns distinguishable between behavioural states. 92 genes were found to be under ASE across all three brain regions. Of these, two genes: LDHB and Oat, are linked to the circadian clock. The circadian clock molecular mechanism is known for its vital role in migratory behaviour, confirming that our findings are based on behavioural state variation. Up until now, the work I presented has been focused on leveraging genomic base pair variation between individuals, populations and phenotypes. Studying 1) genomic differences on a population scale and what this can say about population structure or selective signals in the genome, and 2) allelic variation in gene expression between migratory behavioural states. However, other genomic features with variation are important to study, too. For example, transposable elements (TEs), mobile genetic elements, move around the genome, resulting in genomic variability which can be researched by itself or across individuals and populations. Chapter 3 presents a high-quality TE annotation for the blackcap genome as a resource for future research. Alongside this TE annotation, my colleagues and I investigated the TE distribution along the genome and how this distribution correlates with other genomic features. Additionally, we classified TEs based on their age into recent and ancient TEs, to understand their specific impact on the genome and its genomic features. A recent accumulation of LTRs in the genome was recovered, previously unseen in the bird genome. Additionally, it was found that recent and ancient TEs interact differently with the four genomic features, recombination rate, gene coverage, CpG island coverage and GC content, included in this study. Together, the work presented in my thesis emphasises the importance of understanding genomic variation at different levels: base pair, structural and allelic variation. This knowledge needs integration and can be used to understand its impact on the genome, transcriptome and epigenome. Furthering the study of complex behavioural traits, such as bird migration. Furthermore, thinking outside of the box when approaching these questions is valuable when researching these complex behavioural traits. 7 ZUSAMMENFASSUNG In der derzeitigen postgenomischen Ära werden immer mehr unterschiedliche Sequenzierungstechnologien und Analysewerkzeuge entwickelt, um genomische, transkriptomische und epigenomische Variation in der Natur zu verstehen. Die Frage, wie genetische Unterschiede zu phänotypischen Variationen führen, ist für Biolog:innen, die phänotypische Variationen untersuchen, zu einem zentralen Thema geworden. In Anbetracht der zunehmenden Erkenntnis, dass sich diese drei Arten der genetischen Variation gegenseitig beeinflussen, ist es umso wichtiger, die Mechanismen zu erforschen, die der genomischen, transkriptomischen und epigenomischen Variation und ihrer Entwicklung zugrunde liegen. Die vorliegende Arbeit befasst sich mit dem Verständnis des komplexen Verhaltens des Vogelzugs und seiner großen Variabilität in der Mönchsgrasmücke (Sylvia atricapilla). Mithilfe von Genom- und Transkriptomdaten möchte ich (i) die genomische Variation der Population (Kapitel 1), (ii) die transkriptomische Variation in verschiedenen Verhaltenszuständen im Gehirn des Vogels (als Ergebnis epigenetischer Variation, Kapitel 2) und (iii) die Variation von genomischen Merkmalen, insbesondere von transponierbaren Elementen, im Genom verstehen (Kapitel 3). Die Mönchsgrasmücke ist eine weit verbreitete Studienart für unterschiedliche Aspekte des Vogelzugs. In Kapitel 1 untersuche und ich die Unterschiede zwischen Mönchsgrasmückenpopulationen bezüglich ihrer Zugneigung, indem wir ziehende Populationen mit sesshaften Populationen vergleichen, die das ganze Jahr über im selben Gebiet aufhalten. Die Brutpulationen befinden sich im Süden des Verbreitungsgebiets, auf der kontinentalen Iberischen Halbinsel und auf verschiedenen Inselgruppen Makaronesiens: Madeira, Kanarische Inseln, Kapverden und Azoren, sowie auf den folgenden Inseln im Mittelmeer: Mallorca und Kreta. Durch zusätzliches Probenmaterial entlang des gesamten Verbreitungsgebiets der Mönchsgrasmücke konnten wir unseren Datensatz individueller Genomdaten von 110 auf 179 Individuen erweitern. Bevor wir die genomische Variation zwischen der beiden im Fokus stehenden Phänotypen untersuchen konnten, haben wir die Art populationsgenetisch charakterisiert, um besser zu verstehen, wo und wie oft sich die Sesshaftigkeit bei einer Art entwickelt, die als ursprünglicher Zugvogel gilt. Nach unseren neuen Erkenntnissen hat sich die Anpassung an einen sesshaften Lebensstil in den verschiedenen sesshaften Populationen sowohl auf dem Kontinent als auch auf den verschiedenen Inselsystemen konvergent entwickelt. Dies hat mich dazu bewogen, die genomischen Signaturen der Selektion und genetischer Anpassung für jede sesshafte Population durchzuführen, und ich konnte feststellen, dass es keine überlappenden genomischen Regionen gibt, die der jeweiligen populationsspezifischen Selektion unterliegen. Dies unterstützt klar die konvergente Selektion dieses Phänotyps. Eine ziehende Mönchsgrasmücke befindet sich zweimal im Jahr in diesem speziellen saisonalen Verhaltenszustand: während des Frühjahrszugs (auf dem Weg in die Brutgebiete) und erneut während der Herbstmigration (in ihre Überwinterungsgebiete). Dieser saisonale Wechsel des Verhaltens umfasst viele koordinierte Anpassungsmechanismen, da ein erfolgreicher Start der Zugs Veränderungen in der Physiologie und in den Verhaltensmerkmalen erfordert. Diese saisonalen Verhaltensänderungen können nicht auf Veränderungen der Genomsequenz der Vögel basieren, sondern müssen regulatorisch auf Ebene des Transkriptom variiert werden. Dies habe ich anhand 8 eines Transkriptom-Datensatzes dreier Hirnregionen bei Vögeln betrachtet, die während und außerhalb der Zugzeit erstellt wurden. Unter Verwendung des in Kapitel 1 zusammengestellten Genomdatensatzes habe ich mir die allelspezifischen Expressionsmuster (ASE) bei diesen Vögeln fokussiert angesehen. Bei der Präsentation dieser Ergebnisse in Kapitel 2 habe ich zunächst meine Pipeline zur charakterisierung genomischer Variation soweit angepasst, dass RNA-Sequenzierungsdaten berücksichtigt werden konnten. Anschließend nutzte ich den Genomdatensatz, um genomische Variation dieser Individuen mit größerer Sicherheit zu bestimmen, damit diese Daten anschließend in der ASE-Analyse verwendet werden konnten. Die ASE-Analyse erfasst die cis-regulatorische Variation des Genoms (epigenomische Variation) und verbindet die potenzielle genomische Regulation mit der transkriptomischen Variation. Die drei im Fokus stehenden Hirnregionen zeigen unterschiedliche ASE-Muster, und der Hippocampus und der Hypothalamus zeigen ASE-Muster, die sich zwischen den Verhaltenszuständen unterscheiden. Ich konnte 92 Gene identifizieren, die in allen drei Hirnregionen unter ASE stehen. Darunter sind zwei Gene: LDHB und Oat, die mit der zirkadianen Rhythmik in Verbindung stehen. Der molekulare Mechanismus der zirkadianen Uhr ist für seine zentrale Bedeutung bei der Koordinierung saisonalen Zugverhalten bekannt, was bestätigt, dass unsere Ergebnisse auf einer Variation des Verhaltenszustands der Vögel beruhen. Bislang konzentrierte sich die von mir vorgestellte Arbeit auf die Nutzung genomischer Variation zwischen Individuen und Populationen. Untersucht werden 1) genomische Unterschiede auf Populationsebene und was dies über die Populationsstruktur oder selektive Signale im Genom aussagen kann, sowie 2) allele Variation in der Genexpression zwischen den einzelnen Verhaltenszuständen. Aber auch andere variable genomische Merkmale sind wichtig zu hierbei zu berücksichtigen. So bewegen sich beispielsweise transponierbare Elemente (TEs), mobile genetische Elemente, im Genom, was zu einer weiteren Ebene genomischer Variabilität führt, die entlang des Genoms characterisiert, aber auch im Vergleich zwischen Individuen und Populationen untersucht werden kann. In Kapitel 3 wird eine präzise TE-Annotation für das Genom der Mönchsgrasmücke vorgestellt, die darüber hinaus auch als wichtige Ressource für zukünftige Forschungsfragen dienen soll. Neben dieser grundlegenden TE-Annotation untersuchten wir die TE-Verteilung entlang des Genoms, und analysierten, wie diese Verteilung mit anderen genomischen Merkmalen korreliert. Außerdem haben wir die TEs anhand ihres Alters in rezente und alte TEs eingeteilt, um ihre spezifischen Auswirkungen auf das Genom und seine Merkmale zu verstehen. Es wurde eine rezente Anhäufung von LTRs im Genom festgestellt, die bisher im Vogelgenom so nicht beobachtet wurde. Darüber hinaus konnten wir feststellen, dass rezente und alte TEs unterschiedlich mit den vier in dieser Studie berücksichtigten Genommerkmalen Rekombinationsrate, Genabdeckung, CpG-Inselabdeckung und GC-Gehalt interagieren. Die in meiner Arbeit vorgestellten Untersuchungen verdeutlichen, wie wichtig es ist, genomische Variation auf verschiedenen Ebenen zu betrachten und diese Variation zu integrieren um unser Verständnis komplexer Verhaltensmerkmale erweitern zu können. In meiner Arbeit habe ich dies auf Ebene der Basenpaare, TEs und allen Variation realisiert. Dieses Wissen kann genutzt werden, um Auswirkungen dieser Variation auf das Genom, Transkriptom und Epigenom zu verstehen. Cambridge dictionary PREFACE In genomics, we use the terms “to map” or “mapping” to describe various concepts. For example, when one studies how different genomic features are distributed across the genome of a species, you are creating a “map”. A commonly used example in genomics of such a “feature map” is a gene annotation. Aside from this, we refer to the practice of aligning small nucleotide sequences to large nucleotide sequences as “mapping”, which is done with specialised mapping software. Often, the “feature map” cannot exist without the practice of mapping, making it an integral tool within a geneticist's toolbox. A gene annotation is created by using software that aligns the inferred DNA sequences of a protein against a longer DNA sequence, which is often the species reference sequence. With the recent advancements in genome sequencing, the practice of mapping has broadened. Now, researchers can easily map the genome sequence of an individual to study how this individual's genome differs from other individuals of the species or, more broadly, how species differ from each other. In this thesis, I present my work mapping the genomic diversity of the Eurasian blackcap (Sylvia atricapilla) and studying the genomics behind their migratory behaviour. 14 Introduction INTRODUCTION The post-genomic era and how did we get here? In the 100 years since Mendelian inheritance was synthesised with Darwin’s theory of evolution (Charlesworth & Charlesworth, 2009), genomic advancements have sped up exponentially. With the discovery of the link between DNA and heredity in the 40s (Avery et al., 1944) and DNA structure discovered in the early ‘50s (Watson & Crick, 1953), it only took 20 years until the first complete gene was sequenced (Jou et al., 1972), rapidly establishing sanger sequencing (Sanger et al., 1977) as a tool indispensable to the field of biology. Following this with the human genome project during the ‘90s, culminating in the first human reference genome assembly around the turn of the millennium (Venter et al., 2001), the genomic era was ushered in. With the continued advancement of sequencing technologies (second-generation sequencing and next-generation sequencing), the 1000 Genomes Project was conducted during the 2000s, resulting in almost double the planned genomes sequenced for the final dataset (Altshuler et al., 2010). This landmark project provided important insights into our genetic diversity as a species and continues to do so. These advancements have led to our current post-genomic era, in which researchers can assemble a good quality reference genome of a species, with moderate resources available, or cheaply sequence 100s to 1000s of individuals of a species to research. As one of these researchers, I am indebted to every woman and man who aided in these endeavours and brought us to where we are today. The advancements in genetic sequencing resulted not only in the field of genomics but also in those of transcriptomics and epigenomics. Transcriptomics is the study of the transcriptome of an organism (Lowe et al., 2017). The transcriptome is the sum of transcription products found in an organism's tissues (ranging from whole organs to single cells), otherwise described as the genetic expression of its genome. Epigenomics is the study of the epigenome (Allis & Jenuwein, 2016), and the epigenome describes the accessibility of the genome for transcription, leading to differences in the transcriptome not attributable to the genome. Together, these lead to the proteome of an organism, resulting in its phenotype (Ritchie et al., 2015). The proteome itself can affect gene expression at the different stages mentioned above. Therefore, to understand a phenotype, one has to use a holistic approach by looking at it from every angle and integrating these angles. The use of different omics techniques and their integration is paramount in the study of complex traits, especially for complex behavioural traits. One such complex behavioural trait is animal migration. Migratory animals are found in all environments, and across many branches of the animal tree of life, for both vertebrates and invertebrates. Migration is characterised by the seasonal movement between two (or more) habitats, reasons for this movement can be (i) alimental: migration for sustenance, facilitating maintenance or growth, (ii) climatic: migration to avoid harsh climate and environments, to ease survival, or (iii) gametic: aiding in breeding purposes, or a combination of the three (Shaw, 2016). One can see, based on this wide variety of reasons for migration, that migration is an evolutionary “solution”, convergently selected for across animals. Our understanding of how this behaviour has evolved and what lies behind it on a genomic level has increased through the use of genomics, transcriptomics and epigenomics. Major advances have been made in insect migration (Freedman & Kronforst, 2023) and bird migration (Gu et al., 2024; Le Clercq et al., 2023), with steps taken to understand the genomics behind the migration in other animals such as the caribou (Cavedon 15 Mapping the genomic diversity of the Eurasian blackcap et al., 2019), sea turtles (Chow et al., 2021) and three-spined stickleback (Kitano et al., 2012). However, a lot of work still has to be done. With the work presented in this thesis, I hope to add to this body of work. The blackcap: a study species for migration Bird migration has fascinated researchers for the past two hundred years. The behavioural syndrome of bird migration encompasses seasonal changes in a bird’s physiology and morphology, and results in changes in sensory and behavioural traits (Merlin & Liedvogel, 2019). These changes occur in response to environmental changes in their habitat, resulting in an escape to more favourable habitats. For birds in the northern hemisphere, this means migrating to warmer, more southern locations during the fall and winter seasons. Putting our focus on songbirds from the western Palearctic, the Eurasian blackcap (Sylvia atricapilla) stands out for its suitability for researching the genomics of migration. The blackcap is a small warbler known for its wide variety of migratory phenotypes, as explained in Box 1. Most importantly, there are decades of research investigating the heritability of these different phenotypes (Berthold et al., 1992; Helbig, 1991; Pulido & Berthold, 2010), with moderate levels of heritability for migratory behavioural and physical traits found (Pulido, 2007). Common garden experiments were foundational to this research. Now, with the advent of easy and cheap genomics technologies, we can take this research into the genomic era. In the past decade, an effort has been made to sequence DNA from birds from across the distribution range and sampling a wide variety of phenotypes, culminating in the first genome-wide study published on the species by Delmore et al. (2020). This study included the compilation of both a reference genome and a gene annotation, as well as the resequencing of 110 individuals. Laying important groundwork for the future by providing a first look into the population history and genomic differences between migrants and residents. Instead of providing answers to understand the genomics of migration for the blackcap, this move into the genomics era has ironically led to more questions. In this thesis, I aim to at least bring a greater understanding to these questions in three ways. Firstly, Delmore et al. (2020) find a strong genomic differentiation between migrant and resident populations. On top of this, the resident populations show strong genomic differentiation based on whether they are on the continent or islands. However, at the time, there were not enough island samples to robustly examine these findings for both within the different resident populations and between resident and migrant phenotypes. Chapter 1 presents a reanalysis of this data with the addition of both more samples of previously included islands and newly resequenced island populations, resulting in an updated population history for the blackcap and a first exploration of genomic signatures for selection of the resident phenotype. Secondly, the study (Delmore et al., 2020) found low levels of genetic differentiation for migratory populations, regardless of migratory direction, and found less than 10 genomic regions under selection for migration. Prompting the question, what if migration evolved through cis-regulatory selective changes? One way to study cis-regulatory activity is by exploring allele-specific expression of genes (Pastinen, 2010). By using the genomic data compiled in Chapter 1 and RNA sequencing data produced from the brains of birds exhibiting migratory traits (Durieux, 2024), a first exploration is presented in Chapter 2. Thirdly, what if single-nucleotide polymorphisms are not the genetic variation causal to the phenotypic variation displayed in the blackcap? Another source of genomic variation 16 Introduction upon which selection can act is transposable elements (TEs) (Romano & Fanti, 2022). However, before one can study the variation of transposable elements in individual genomes of a species, one needs a high-quality TE annotation. This is presented in Chapter 3, alongside an exploration of other genomic features and how they relate to the different TEs found. Together, this research provides new insights and foundational resources to the study of bird migration. BOX 1: The different migratory strategies of the blackcap The species’ migratory behaviour is marked by differences in orientation, migratory distance and propensity to migrate. Firstly, orientation, a migratory divide (across central Europe) separates populations that migrate to the south-east from those migrating to the south-west. A new orientation recently established (during the '50s) has western European birds migrate to the north-west to overwinter. Secondly, the species shows a cline of distance between breeding and overwintering grounds for the birds. With long-distance migrants breeding in Scandinavia/Northern Europe (and migrating to sub-Saharan Africa), medium-distance migrants breeding in western and central Europe (overwintering around the Mediterranean Sea) and short-distance migrants which breed in the North of Spain (to overwinter in the south of Spain). And the last difference with which to characterise the species' migratory strategies is their propensity to migrate. Propensity to migrate is whether an individual will migrate to their wintering grounds. As with migratory distance, the species exhibits this behaviour along a latitudinal cline. In northern Europe, the birds are obligatory migratory, as they have to migrate to survive the harsh winter season. While birds in central Europe tend to remain more often at their breeding ground during winter, resulting in partially migratory populations. Lastly, certain populations in the south of the species’ distribution range do not migrate at all. These resident (or sedentary) populations are located around the Mediterranean basin and its islands, as well as on the different Macaronesian archipelagos situated in the Atlantic Ocean. Figure 1: The blackcap’s distribution range showing the different migratory strategies. The migratory divide in central Europe is characterised by the dotted line. The migratory directions and lengths are visualised using the two-headed arrows. The range map is coloured by species presence during the year. Yellow: pre- and post-breeding migratory season (1 Feb – 7 Jun, and 9 Aug – 29 Nov), blue: non-breeding season (6 Dec – 25 Jan), red: breeding season (14 Jun – 2 Aug) and purpl: year-round. Image provided by eBird (www.ebird.org) and created 28.02.2025 17 Mapping the genomic diversity of the Eurasian blackcap Residency vs “Island syndrome” in the blackcap Birds and residency On first glance, people think of bird migration as something a species does or does not. However, this is a false dichotomy as there are many bird species for which the answer to whether they migrate cannot be given readily. Both partial migrants and non-migratory populations are a common occurrence in migratory species (Reid et al., 2018). There are even bird species for which the migratory status within the individual does not remain constant through their life; an example is the Iberian white stork (Andrade et al., 2025), which in recent decades has shifted to not migrate after its first year of migration. Species, populations or individuals that do not migrate are known as sedentary or resident. Throughout this work, I will use the term resident. As residents remain year-round at their breeding site and do not undertake the strenuous exercise of migrating, the selective pressures have shifted from optimisation for the migratory journey to optimisation for residency. The majority of the research performed on the resident phenotype has been done by comparing fully residential species with fully migratory species. For example, investigating 8 bird families containing both resident and migratory species Phillips et al. (2018) found for each distinct phenotype an evolutionary optimum regarding the morphology of the wings and tail, with residents having rounder wings and longer tails than migrants, optimising them for short-distance foraging flights. Other examples are: morphologically, residents tend to have bigger brains (Sol et al., 2010); behaviourally, residents are more flexible in their response to threats (Morelli et al., 2022); and for life-history, migrants condense their moult time compared to residents (Kiat et al., 2019). These differences are seen at different levels of comparison: species, population and individuals. The blackcap is a species which has resident populations in its southern distribution range, both on the continent and on multiple island systems (see Box 1). Researchers have been studying the differences between these migratory phenotypes of the blackcap for decades. Both by studying the heritability of residency and the rate at which residency can increase in migratory populations (Pulido & Berthold, 2010), and by studying phenological trait differences. The following blackcap-specific trait differences between residents and migrants have been described. Morphologically, resident blackcaps tend to be bigger, have rounder and shorter wings, and larger bill sizes (Tellería & Carbonell, 1999). More specific are the differences seen in the feathers with heavier tail feathers and relatively lower quality primary feathers in residents (de la Hera et al., 2010; Hernández-Téllez et al., 2021), potentially due to longer moult times in residents. Behaviourally, residents are more dominant during the non-breeding months, when wintering migrants are in the same area (Morganti et al., 2017; Tellería et al., 2013). And lastly, acoustic differences in their song have been found for the two phenotypes (Linossier et al., 2016). In summary, the differentiation of resident and migrant populations within the blackcap has led to different selective pressures, which should leave signatures in the genome. Birds and the “island syndrome” Island systems pose an interesting lens for the study of evolution. Due to their limited size and reduced diversity compared to the mainland, islands are “simple” ecosystems to study (Warren et al., 2015; Whittaker et al., 2017). On top of that, archipelagos are interesting as the different islands within an island group can be seen as replicates of the same experiment, with limited differentiation, except across a temporal range. The theory of island biogeography by MacArthur and Wilson, first described 60 years ago (MacArthur & Wilson, 1963), discusses the phenomenon of colonisation and extinction on islands by species as being directly dependent on a) the distance to the mainland and b) the size of 18 Introduction the island. Of course, this is dependent on the intrinsic dispersal ability of the species. For animals, terrestrial species have a lower chance of reaching an island and establishing themselves, compared to aerial and aquatic species. Important to note is that the degree of dispersal for a species is not the only factor in island colonisation (Whittaker et al., 2017). Accessibility of an island is reliant on the changes of the island's biogeography on a macroevolutionary timescale, for example, the formation of a land bridge during an island’s lifetime can aid the colonisation of the island by terrestrial animals. Nevertheless, species worldwide have overcome these barriers and colonised islands many times over. One iconic example of island colonisation and what that can lead to is Darwin’s finches from the Galapagos. Studying the biota of the Galapagos was paramount to the development of the theory of evolution by natural selection by Darwin (Losos & Ricklefs, 2009). Note worthy is the fact that islands were also important for Wallace’s simultaneous development of his theory explaining evolutionary change through natural selection (Van Wyhe & Rookmaker, 2011), during his work and travels across the Malay archipelago. The Darwin’s finches species radiation is a great example of how the island ecosystem can result in unique selective pressures, compared to the mainland. Interestingly, through years of research, it has been found that these unique selective pressures drive selection towards similar traits across species. The collection of these traits resulting from island selective pressures is known as the “island syndrome”. While the “island syndrome” has been described across the tree of life, it must be noted that traits encompassing this syndrome differ between plants and animals, and even between different classes of animals, such as mammals and birds (Jezierski et al., 2024). Research on the “island syndrome” in birds has been reviewed by Jezierski et al. (2024), examples of traits are: morphologically, birds living on island have bigger brains compared to their mainland counterparts; behaviourally, island birds occupy wider niches than non-island dwellers; and for life-history, the combined changes in morphology and behaviour favour the slowing down of their pace of life. Important for the work presented here is the finding that birds develop flightlessness after colonisation of an island (Wright et al., 2016). This flightlessness can range from losing the ability to fly (Sayol et al., 2020) to just a reduction in their degree of dispersal compared to their mainland counterpart (Wright et al., 2016). This reduction is due to shifts in their morphology; for example, the selection for weaker flight muscles makes them less optimal for sustained flight. This list of traits and their difference between mainland and island birds is rather familiar. Similar traits were affected in the comparison between migrant and resident birds, as discussed in the previous section. As mentioned before, the distribution range of the blackcap encompasses multiple island systems, from the different archipelagos of Macaronesia to the islands of the Mediterranean. The Macaronesian island populations show differences from their mainland conspecifics in morphology and behaviour (Dietzen et al., 2008). For example, the populations on the Azores are bigger than those of the continent and have rounder wings than migrants (Andrade et al., 2015). Over the years, there has been more effort made to understand the genetic history of the Macaronesian islands with the continental populations (Delmore et al., 2020; Dietzen et al., 2008; Perez-Tris et al., 2004; Rodrigues et al., 2018). This research suggests rapid range expansion after the last glacial maximum and subsequent colonisation of Macaronesia. Additionally, one study on populations of Corsica found shorter and rounder wings compared to their mainland counterpart, but no genetic differentiation (Linossier et al., 2016). Of course, the most striking difference between island populations and mainland populations is the fact that they are resident. Meaning, if one wants to understand the genetic differentiation behind the resident phenotype, one has to account for the effect of the island habitat in those island populations. 19 Mapping the genomic diversity of the Eurasian blackcap By adding resequencing from samples to the Macaronesian populations and additional island populations (Madeira, Mallorca and Crete), to the dataset from Delmore et al. (2020). A substantial genomic comparison can be made to understand the resident phenotype, regardless of whether the population is from the mainland or an island, which is presented in Chapter 1. By adding islands from the Mediterranean, potential influences from population history connectivity between continental residents and Macaronesia can be accounted for. Furthermore, the reanalysis of population structure, on samples from across the distribution range of the blackcap, shows multiple (convergent) occurrences of the establishment of residency within the blackcap. Through genome-wide selection analysis, population-specific signatures are found for each resident population, narrowing down regions of the genome of interest for possible gene candidates involved in residency. Figure 2: Representation of the resident vs “island syndrome” genomics question. Allele-specific expression in the brains of migratory blackcaps Bird migration is a complex behavioural syndrome, resulting in dramatic shifts in an individual's phenotype on a seasonal basis. While the genome is important to the study of migration, due to its generally unchangeable nature, this cannot be the only avenue of research. One can look at the transcriptomics between different time points (in different tissues) during the life cycle of a migratory bird, linking the genotype with the phenotype (Ritchie et al., 2015). Over the years, transcriptomic studies have resulted in candidate genes for bird migration (Merlin & Liedvogel, 2019). In recent years, there has been a focus on studying the brains and gene expression patterns in migratory birds (Louder et al., 2024; Marasco et al., 2024; Sharma et al., 2021), also in the blackcap (Durieux, 2024). However, gene expression itself is a complex trait and is influenced by (epi)genetic regulation and environmental factors (Pastinen, 2010). Therefore, to fully understand what happens in the transcription of the genotype to the phenotype, one must look at these influences. 20 Introduction Let us focus on (epi)genetic regulation of gene expression. Gene expression regulation can be trans-acting, which means that the acting factor comes from a different part of the genome and acts on both chromosomes; or it is cis-acting, meaning the acting factor comes from nearby the gene and only acts on one chromosome (Wang et al., 2017). Cis-regulatory acting factors are DNA sequences that facilitate the attachment of transcription factors (produced somewhere else in the genome, which is itself an example of trans-acting gene regulation), to start transcription of a nearby gene (Wittkopp & Kalay, 2012). These sequences, also known as enhancers and promoters, can diverge through the basic genetic processes such as mutations, insertions and deletions; this divergence can lead to changes in expression levels on the affected chromosome. To study cis-regulatory variation, one needs to use an allele-specific approach (St Pierre et al., 2022), which uses the heterozygosity found in diploid organisms to quantify expression differences between the two alleles of a gene, also known as allele-specific expression (ASE). ASE is found to affect 30%-56% of genes, and can be tissue-specific. The study system of the three-spined stickleback provides a great example of why studying ASE in a species can be interesting. Mack et al. (2023) investigated the ASE divergence across 7 tissues to better understand the gene expression patterns seen in the adaptive divergence of the species between freshwater and saltwater habitats. Their extensive study found cis-regulatory changes between the two ecotypes, associated with genomic regions previously found to be important in the adaptive evolution of the three-spined stickleback. A promising example for the use of ASE analysis to aid in the understanding of a complex trait. There is a pronounced lack of ASE studies into bird migration, with (at the time of writing) only one example conducted on the Swainson’s thrushes (Louder et al., 2024). More studies using ASE techniques to investigate bird migration are essential to understand this complex behaviour. In Chapter 2, I present such work focusing on the blackcap. By using the growing genomic dataset of the blackcap (produced for Chapter 1) and a recently created dataset of RNA sequencing from brain samples, contrasting the migratory behavioural state during spring migration to that of a bird during the winter season (Durieux, 2024). Using this dataset, I aim to understand the differences in ASE between three brain regions as they pertain to the migratory behavioural state. Overall, 92 genes were found to exhibit ASE in the three brain regions, each brain region showed a unique ASE pattern. Looking at the different behavioural states, we have narrowed this down to 14 genes of interest during spring migration, and a further 11 genes for the winter season. A map of the transposable elements in the blackcap genome Ever since Barbara McClintock (McClintock, 1950) discovered transposable elements (TEs) in the 40s and 50s of the last century, much research has been conducted on them in a wide variety of organisms. TEs are ubiquitous and have been linked to major evolutionary changes in diverse organisms (Romano & Fanti, 2022). Due to specific properties, there are increased levels of difficulty when studying them. The first and most distinguishing property is their ability to move within the genome; in other words, they transpose. Transposition can occur through different mechanisms, upon which their classification is based (Almojil et al., 2021). These “jumping elements” can be seen as individuals of a species within the “ecosystem” of the genome. However, TEs live in an “ecosystem” that actively fights back against their disruptive behaviour and proliferation (Romano & Fanti, 2022). In other words, TEs are similar to mutations; they result in either neutral or deleterious effects on the organism and occasionally have positive effects. Furthermore, one must not discount the importance of TEs to genome evolution. TEs are important to the evolution of genome architecture, for example, they can produce inversions, 21 Mapping the genomic diversity of the Eurasian blackcap and TEs are sources for genomic evolutionary innovation (Sotero-Caio et al., 2017). The study of TEs has been advanced by the post-genomic era, as the ability to assemble a high-quality reference genome for your species of choice (Peona et al., 2021) has led to the ability to produce high-quality TE annotations. These TE annotations provide us with new resources to study both the genome and its evolution, as well as the effect TEs have on both gene transcription and epigenetic variation. The TE content of the avian genome shows both low copy number levels and low levels of diversity, as they make up between 4-10% of the genome, compared to other vertebrates (Sotero-Caio et al., 2017). Generally, the TE landscape and its composition through time are similar across bird species. Looking at what they can tell us about bird evolution, there are different levels of evolution on which they can act. These are: on a phylogenetic scale, a genomic scale and a behavioural trait scale. First, Carotti et al. (2023) studied the TE landscape of 29 bird species, focusing on the potential effects that environmental changes in Australia during the Oligocene have had. They found a burst of TE activity around the time of songbird diversification, suggesting an evolutionary benefit of TE amplification, with this TE amplification driven by climate change. Second, a study comparing the genomes of extant pheasants found chromosome breakage and fusion events linked to a genomic region with high TE density, potentially aiding in the radiation of this lineage (Xu et al., 2024). And lastly, research by Caballero-Lopez et al. (2022) into the genetic bases of migratory phenotypes of the willow warbler found that a previously described candidate locus for migratory direction was characterised by repeat density and TE copy number variation. Hypothesising that the TEs mediated in the rearrangement of the chromosome, resulting in a new migratory phenotype. As you can see, including TEs when studying different biological and evolutionary questions can provide important insights. Therefore, a high-quality TE annotation is an essential accompaniment to a reference genome, similar to a gene annotation. Such a high-quality TE annotation for the blackcap reference genome is presented in Chapter 3. This TE annotation is a new resource for the continued research into the population history and evolution of migratory behaviour within the blackcap. Furthermore, using resources on other genomic features of the blackcap, such as a gene annotation and a recombination rate landscape (Bascón-Cardozo et al., 2024), I aim to bring a better understanding of genomic interactions between these features and TE of different ages. TEs showed different correlation patterns with the genomic features, dependent on age. 22 Introduction SYNTHESIS Thinking outside of the box At first glance, this thesis appears to be asking and answering different questions, with no apparent commonality, except for the study species. And while I presented “mapping” as the commonality across the three chapters that will follow, this “mapping” is only a tool. This is the dissertation of Andrea Bours, completed at the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Biology and the Christian Albrechts University of Kiel (oral examination: 24.06.2025, examiners: Prof. Dr. Miriam Liedvogel and Prof. Dr. Christine Böhmer). The thesis maps genomic diversity in the Eurasian blackcap (Sylvia atricapilla), a songbird with wide migratory behavioral variation, to understand bird migration as a complex behavioral trait through genomic, transcriptomic, and epigenomic data.

The work comprises three chapters:
- **Chapter 1 (Population genomics):** Compared seasonal migratory populations with year-round residential populations (residents found in Southern Iberia, Macaronesia - Madeira, Canary Islands, Cape Verde, Azores - and Mallorca and Crete in the Mediterranean). Whole genome sequencing dataset expanded from 110 to 179 individuals. Population structure analysis revealed that residency evolved convergently multiple times across the different resident populations (both continental and island). Genome-wide selection analyses found no overlapping genomic regions under selection across resident populations, confirming convergent selection for the resident phenotype.
- **Chapter 2 (Transcriptomics/ASE):** Investigated allele-specific expression (ASE) patterns in three brain regions (hippocampus, hypothalamus, and another) comparing birds in migratory vs. non-migratory behavioral states. The variant calling pipeline was adjusted for RNA-seq data. The three brain regions showed distinct ASE patterns, with hippocampus and hypothalamus having ASE patterns distinguishable between behavioral states. 92 genes exhibited ASE across all three brain regions, including LDHB and Oat, which are linked to the circadian clock (known to be vital for migratory behavior).
- **Chapter 3 (Transposable elements):** Presented a high-quality TE annotation for the blackcap genome as a resource, investigating TE distribution along the genome and correlations with recombination rate, gene coverage, CpG island coverage, and GC content. A recent accumulation of LTRs was found - previously unseen in bird genomes. Recent vs. ancient TEs interact differently with the four genomic features studied.

The introduction provides substantial background: the blackcap is a widely used study species for bird migration (decades of heritability research; pivotal genome-wide study by Delmore et al. 2020 which created the reference genome and resequenced 110 individuals). The species shows variation in orientation (migratory divide across central Europe separating SE vs. SW migrants; a new NW orientation established in the 1950s), migratory distance (long-distance Scandinavian birds to sub-Saharan Africa; medium-distance central European birds to the Mediterranean; short-distance northern Spanish birds to southern Spain), and migratory propensity (latitudinal cline from obligatory migration in the north to residency in the south). Residents differ from migrants morphologically (bigger, rounder and shorter wings, larger bills, heavier tail feathers), behaviorally (more dominant during non-breeding months), and acoustically. Island populations exhibit "island syndrome" traits. Only one prior ASE study on bird migration exists (Swainson's thrushes). Avian genomes contain 4-10% TE content, lower than other vertebrates.

## Significance

Seasonal migration is a behavioral response to seasonally changing environments that is exhibited by many taxa and has captured the attention of researchers and laypeople alike. A genetic basis for migration has been suggested for decades but detailed, genome-wide studies have only recently been permitted with advances in tracking and sequencing technology. We capitalized on these advances here, using a natural hybrid zone between songbirds and data on multiple migratory traits from hundreds of individuals to provide one of the most complete genetic characterizations of this behavior to date. Our results can be integrated in future studies to predict organismal ability to adapt to changes in the environment.

## Abstract

Seasonal migration is a widespread behavior relevant for adaptation and speciation, yet knowledge of its genetic basis is limited. We leveraged advances in tracking and sequencing technologies to bridge this gap in a well-characterized hybrid zone between songbirds that differ in migratory behavior. Migration requires the coordinated action of many traits, including orientation, timing, and wing morphology. We used genetic mapping to show these traits are highly heritable and genetically correlated, explaining how migration has evolved so rapidly in the past and suggesting future responses to climate change may be possible. Many of these traits mapped to the same genomic regions and small structural variants indicating the same, or tightly linked, genes underlie them. Analyses integrating transcriptomic data indicate cholinergic receptors could control multiple traits. Furthermore, analyses integrating genomic differentiation further suggested genes underlying migratory traits help maintain reproductive isolation in this hybrid zone.
