## ABSTRACT

Seabirds are highly susceptible to human-induced threats such as light pollution, which alters their behavior and leads to increased mortality rates. Reports of storm-petrels (Hydrobatidae) affected by light pollution exist worldwide, yet the population-level response of this diverse and globally distributed family remains severely understudied. Therefore, we aim to uncover, through an extensive literature review, the current state of evidence regarding the effects of light pollution on seabird populations of the Hydrobatidae family. We conducted a scoping review on Scopus and Web of Science academic platforms and obtained 12 articles that met our search criteria. Our results indicate storm-petrels’ groundings were recorded for almost all Hydrobatidae genera. Although inshore and offshore light pollution sources can lead to storm-petrel disorientation, the artificial light source characteristics (e.g., intensity, spectrum) were generally not quantified. Susceptibility to light pollution is associated with environmental factors (e.g., moon phase) and the storm-petrels’ age, as fallout occurs primarily in fledglings during their first flight leaving the colony. While a limited number of studies assessing light-induced storm-petrel mortality at a population level suggest that it may not be high enough to be deemed as a substantial threat, further research is required to fully understand the extent of light pollution as a potential danger and develop effective conservation measures.

## RÉSUMÉ

Les oiseaux marins sont très sensibles aux menaces d’origine humaine, notamment à la pollution lumineuse. Celle-ci modifie leur comportement et entraîne une augmentation de leur taux de mortalité. Nombre de rapports étudient les conséquences de la pollution lumineuse sur les pétrels-tempête (Hydrobatidae) du monde entier. Toutefois, l’impact sur les populations de cette famille d’oiseaux diversifiée et répartie partout sur le globe reste très insuffisamment étudié. Par conséquent, nous proposons d’analyser méticuleusement la littérature scientifique à la recherche de preuves concernant les effets de la pollution lumineuse sur les populations d’oiseaux marins de la famille des Hydrobatidae. Ainsi, nous avons procédé à une analyse exhaustive des plateformes universitaires Scopus et Web of Science et nous avons sélectionné 12 articles répondant à nos critères de recherche. Nos résultats indiquent que les échouages de pétrels-tempête ont été enregistrés pour presque tous les genres d’Hydrobatidae. Bien que les sources côtières et hauturières de pollution lumineuse puissent entraîner la désorientation des pétrels-tempête, les caractéristiques de ces sources de lumière artificielle (p. ex. : intensité, spectre) n’ont généralement jamais été quantifiées. La sensibilité à la pollution lumineuse est associée à des facteurs environnementaux (p. ex. : les phases lunaires) et à l’ge des pétrels-tempête, car les échouages se produisent principalement chez les oisillons au cours de leur premier vol, au moment de quitter la colonie. Un nombre limité d’études évaluent l’impact des sources de lumière artificielle sur les populations de pétrels-tempête et suggèrent que cette mortalité n’atteint pas des niveaux suffisamment élevés pour constituer une menace substantielle. Toutefois, des recherches supplémentaires sont nécessaires pour comprendre l’étendue et la dangerosité potentielle de la pollution lumineuse et pour développer des mesures de conservation efficaces.

## INTRODUCTION

The order Procellariiformes is among the most endangered seabird groups with the highest number of threatened species of marine birds globally (Croxall et al. 2012, as cited in Rodríguez et al. 2019, Norambuena et al. 2021). Procellariiformes, in general, are highly adapted to the marine environment and spend most of their lives in the open oceans (Rodríguez et al. 2019). They travel long distances for foraging, migration, and dispersal, mostly returning to land only for breeding or at night (Silva et al. 2016, Sausner et al. 2016, Rodríguez et al. 2019).

Within the Procellariiformes order, storm-petrels (Hydrobatidae family) are among the most poorly-known seabird groups (Rodríguez et al. 2019). The limited knowledge of the biology and ecology of storm-petrels, combined with the absence of accurate population estimates, is largely due to their nocturnal, cryptic, and burrow-nesting behavior, as well as the unknown or inaccessible locations of their colonies, which are often found on cliffs or remote islands (Rodríguez et al. 2017, 2019). Of the 22 identified species within the Hydrobatidae family (Nunn and Stanley 1998, Tree of Life Web Project 2008), 12 have declining population trends, and four prove to be Data Deficient (IUCN 2022). Thus, it is important to identify threats and their impact on storm-petrel populations (Norambuena et al. 2021).

Among the documented land-based and marine threats for storm-petrels (e.g. invasive alien species, human disturbance, residential and community development, pollution, mining, and energy farms; Dias et al. 2019; Norambuena et al. 2021), one of the globally increasing threats is light pollution (Kyba et al. 2017). Light pollution is defined as the use of artificial illumination that disrupts natural darkness and the visibility of the night sky (Gaston et al. 2013, Falchi et al. 2016). With the global rise in artificial light due to expanding human settlements driven by population growth (Kyba et al. 2017, United Nations 2019), the ongoing expansion of population centers is expected to escalate light pollution and its effects on storm-petrel populations.

The presence of Artificial Lights at Night (ALAN) may result in the light-induced disorientation of seabirds (i.e., “fallout”), particularly among the youngest. On their first flight away from the colony, fledglings become disoriented by the presence of anthropogenic sources of light (Miles et al. 2010, Wilhelm et al. 2021). As fledglings approach and fly over light sources, they can fall to the ground due to physical exhaustion or collision with man-made structures (Troy et al. 2011), hereby referred to as “grounding.” Storm-petrel fledglings that survive the fall may still die due to an increased risk of predation, starvation, dehydration, drowning, or even collisions with motorized vehicles (Rodríguez et al. 2012, Rodríguez et al. 2014, Rodríguez et al. 2017). Although fallout is considered an important source of mortality for storm-petrel populations (Rodríguez et al. 2017), its mechanism is still unknown. The main hypothesis is that light pollution may outshine natural celestial cues, interfering with storm-petrel navigation systems (Rodríguez et al. 2017). Additional hypotheses like foraging inexperience and an immature visual system have been formulated, but the information is scarce and inconclusive (Imber et al. 1975, Atchoi 2020).

Given the scarce information on the impacts of light pollution on storm-petrel populations, we conducted a scoping review to determine the main impacts of light pollution in the Hydrobatidae family. Through the scoping review, we aim to answer the following research question: What is the current state of evidence on the effects of light pollution on bird populations of the Hydrobatidae family? We expect this review will contribute to the inputs required for the development of adequate management and conservation plans for storm-petrels.

## METHODS

For the scoping review, we limited our efforts to two academic platforms, Scopus and Web of Science. These platforms contain a wide array of scientific content on the selected subject.

### Keyword selection and identification of relevant articles

We limited our search to keywords in two categories: (1) storm-petrel taxa, according to the Tree of Life Project (Nunn and Stanley 1998, Tree of Life Web Project 2008; Appendix 1), and (2) Light pollution (Table 1). All searches were conducted in English, considering that a first exploratory search in Spanish using the SciELO library catalog returned no results. During our search, only one full-text article (Silva et al. 2020) was found in Spanish, although its information in the library catalog was obtained in English. No restrictions were applied on geographical location.

### Article selection process and eligibility criteria

We carried out the literature search on February 16, 2023. Articles published between 01/01/2000 and 31/12/2022 were compiled and uploaded to the Rayyan reference manager (Mourad et al. 2016) for duplicate detection. Articles labeled as duplicates (by the default setting in Rayyan) were individually reviewed by two authors (PS, RM) and removed from the analysis. Article titles and abstracts were screened and excluded if they did not explicitly include light pollution and its effects on Hydrobatidae species or only mentioned unspecified seabirds (Fig. 1). This first screening process was executed by two authors (PS, RM), although in case of discrepancies, all authors discussed whether to exclude or include the article in the next exclusion stage.

The full-text screening was performed using the Zotero reference manager version 6.0.4 (Zotero n.d.). Original research papers that included both light pollution and its effects on Hydrobatidae species were included. Review articles were excluded in this process, except for Silva et al. (2020), as some of their information was published for the first time. At this stage, we also incorporated relevant articles identified within the bibliographies of the originally identified articles. We selected articles from the bibliographies based on title, abstract, and full-text screenings. All studies included in this stage were used for the analysis and literature synthesis presented in the results section.

### Data management and result summarizing

A Microsoft Excel version 16.0. spreadsheet (Microsoft Corporation 2021) was created with all the articles in Zotero after duplicate removal (Appendix 2). Information presented for each article includes publication year, title, journal, DOI, abstract, volume, issue, pages, library catalog, link attachment, status, exclusion stage, and exclusion criteria. Table 2 presents a summary of the relevant content of the included articles.

## RESULTS

### Literature profile and article characteristics

A total of 144 records were identified; 142 were from the database search, and two were added from the bibliographies of articles found in the original search (Appendix 3). After screening titles and abstracts, 20 articles were reviewed in full. Of these, 12 articles published between 2005 and 2022 were included in the final analysis, with half published between 2020 and 2022. Of the 12 articles, six presented data from the southern hemisphere and six from the northern hemisphere. All articles extracted data from locations in the Atlantic Ocean, with only four exceptions: one article from the Mediterranean Sea and three articles from the Pacific Ocean. Most articles included data recovered before the year 2013 (Table 2). In six of the included articles, data collection spanned short periods (< 4 years), while six articles had a more extended data collection period (> 4 years).

Only four articles explicitly focused on Hydrobatidae species; the rest focused on seabirds in general. In these last articles, the percentage of Hydrobatidae species representation was below 45% of all recorded seabird groups. Only two articles used a systematic methodology for data collection (Miles et al. 2010, Wilhelm et al. 2021), while four articles used citizen science (Rodríguez and Rodríguez 2009, Murillo et al. 2013, Rodríguez et al. 2015), and three collected their data from records by vessel crew (Black 2005, Glass and Ryan 2013, Ryan et al. 2021). The remaining articles used previous reports from multiple sources (Silva et al. 2020) or from wildlife centers (Montesdeoca et al. 2017, Gjerdrum et al. 2021, Heswall et al. 2022).

Regarding light pollution, eight articles identified sources of light pollution as inshore, offshore sources, or both. Inshore sources of artificial lights were mentioned in four articles (Miles et al. 2010, Murillo et al. 2013, Wilhelm et al. 2021, Heswall et al. 2022), offshore sources were considered in three articles (Black 2005, Glass and Ryan 2013, Ryan et al. 2021), and only one article included both (Gjerdrum et al. 2021). Merely three articles quantified light pollution levels, two used VIIRS satellite data (Rodríguez et al. 2015, Gjerdrum et al. 2021), while Heswall et al. (2022) used previously measured natural sky brightness in the study area. Additional variables on light pollution effects were evaluated in 9 articles; the remaining articles recorded grounding data (location and date). Environmental variables, such as moon phase and wind, were considered in four (Miles et al. 2010, Murillo et al. 2013, Wilhelm et al. 2021, Gjerdrum et al. 2021) and one article (Wilhelm et al. 2021) respectively. Body condition was assessed in five articles (Black 2005, Murillo et al. 2013, Rodríguez et al. 2015, Wilhelm et al. 2021, Gjerdrum et al. 2021), including body mass, wing length, and plumage condition. Storm-petrel´s age class was recorded in six articles (Rodríguez and Rodríguez 2009, Miles et al. 2010, Rodríguez et al. 2015, Silva et al. 2020, Wilhelm et al. 2021, Heswall et al. 2022), while sex was only determined in 2 (Black 2005, Montesdeoca et al. 2017).

### Article content

#### Grounding records

Grounding records were found for all Hydrobatidae genera except for *Nesofregetta.* Out of the 22 species of the Hydrobatidae family (Tree of Life Web Project 2008, Nunn and Stanley 1998), grounding was recorded in 12 species (Table 3). *O. leucorhoa* and *P. marina* were the most frequently mentioned species, followed by *H. pelagicus*.

#### Age class

Storm-petrel fallout occurs primarily in fledglings during their first flight leaving the colony. Of the articles that included age class in their analysis, five concluded that fledglings comprised a higher percentage of grounding records in comparison with adult storm-petrels (Miles et al. 2010, Rodríguez et al. 2015, Silva et al. 2020, Wilhelm et al. 2021, Heswall et al. 2022). According to a study (Wilhelm et al. 2021), over 99% of all grounded *O. leucorhoa* were fledglings. These results coincide with Silva et al. (2020), in which fledglings account for the majority of grounded individuals of *O. oceanicus*, *O. markhami,* and *G. nereis*. Fledgling fallout rates present seasonal variation and coincide with the storm-petrel´s reproductive season, as found by Rodríguez et al. (2015) and Heswall et al. (2022). Contrary to previously described articles, the publication by Rodríguez and Rodríguez (2009) indicated that 84% of grounded *O. castro* individuals and all of *O. leucorhoa*, *P. marina,* and *H. pelagicus* individuals were adults.

#### Light pollution and additional variables

Storm-petrels can be attracted to terrestrial or marine light pollution sources. Eight articles registered grounding events inshore, but only four mention the inshore light pollution source (Miles et al. 2010, Murillo et al. 2013, Wilhelm et al. 2021, Heswall et al. 2022). Of these, only Wilhelm et al. (2021) specified the type of property where stranded birds were found (e.g., residential, industry, road, highway, business), and Heswall et al. (2022) made a distinction between urban and rural areas. Three articles (Black 2005, Glass and Ryan 2013, Ryan et al. 2021) assessed bird strike events caused by offshore light pollution sources, mainly fishing vessels' deck lights. Only Gjerdrum et al. (2021) considered offshore and inshore light pollution sources, including oil and gas platforms, vessels, construction sites, and municipalities.

Evidence suggests a potential relationship between moon phases and grounding registers (Miles et al. 2010, Murillo et al. 2013, Gjerdrum et al. 2021, Wilhelm et al. 2021). As established by Wilhelm et al. (2021), during the new moon (lowest moon visibility), *O. leucorhoa* had the highest grounding rates. On the other hand, there are few stranding records during the full moon. This lack of records is supported by findings made by Gjerdrum et al. (2021), Miles et al. (2010), and Murillo et al. (2013) in which the largest stranding events of *O. leucorhoa* (Miles et al. 2010, Gjerdrum et al. 2021) and *O. oceanicus* (Gjerdrum et al. 2021) occurred during the moon’s low illumination phase and most of *O. hornbyi* fallouts (Murillo et al. 2013) occurred during the first quarter of the moon or new moon. In addition, Miles et al. (2010) considered the percentage of the night that the moon was above the horizon but found no interactions with the moon phase in the analysis of *O. leucorhoa* grounding rates. Although these articles suggest a potential association between moon phase and groundings, the possibility of a causal link requires further evaluation and is beyond the scope of this study.

#### Population-level impacts and species’ threat status

According to IUCN (2022), among the 12 storm-petrel species mentioned in the articles included in this study, nine have decreasing population trends, two have unknown statuses, and only one is considered stable. Additionally, *O. hornbyi* and *O. markhami* are assessed in the Red List as Near Threatened, *O. leucorhoa* as Vulnerable (*O. leucorhoa*), and *O. gracilis* as Data Deficient. However, the effect of light-induced groundings as a threat to storm-petrel populations is rarely assessed.

Out of the 12 articles included, only five considered the population impact of light pollution (Appendix 3). The articles by Rodríguez and Rodríguez (2009), Ryan et al. (2021), and Rodríguez et al. (2015) found that the percentage of individuals killed annually by fallout is less than 1% of the respective species' population. According to Miles et al. (2010), the number of grounded *O. leucorhoa* and *H. pelagicus* is low compared to their breeding population, and Glass and Ryan (2013) stated that it is unlikely that grounding records of *P. marina* and *Fregetta spp.* have a significant effect at a population level.

## DISCUSSION

This scoping review provides an overview of the state of evidence on the effects of light pollution on storm-petrel (Hydrobatidae) populations worldwide. We discuss the most relevant findings recovered from the analyzed scientific literature, which include (1) the spatial and temporal distribution patterns of light-induced grounding, (2) the implications of these results for future research on light pollution, (3) the knowledge gaps in the reviewed literature, and (4) the limitations encountered during this review.

### Relevance of findings for scientific research and literature

This article is the first global review to focus on light pollution effects on the members of the Hydrobatidae family, aside from broader reviews that include other seabird taxa (Rodríguez et al. 2017, Rodríguez et al. 2019, Dias et al. 2019, Silva et al. 2020). Data for storm-petrels on this subject is scarce, with only twelve scientific articles included in the final analysis of this study. Although there is a trend of increasing research on the effects of light pollution on storm-petrels, most articles used data recovered before 2013, which may be outdated information on light pollution and storm-petrel populations. Furthermore, few articles focused specifically on studying the effects of light pollution on storm-petrels. Most articles treated seabirds as a single group, probably due to methodological limitations or difficulty related to the taxonomic identification of closely related storm-petrel species. Given the specific focus of this scoping review on Hydrobatidae, research articles on light pollution effects on other Procellariiformes (i.e., Procellariidae, Diomedeidae, Pelecanoididae) were not included.

Storm-petrel records are limited mainly to the North American and European coastlines (Fig. 2), even though the eastern Pacific Ocean has the highest storm-petrel diversity due to phylogenetic radiation in the late Miocene (Warheit 1992). This pattern is also noticeable in the number of studies assessing light pollution effects on genera and species. *Oceanodroma*, the most diverse genus within Hydrobatidae, with 13 species out of 22 (Tree of Life Web Project 2008), was evaluated in seven articles. Within this genus, *O. tethys and O. markhami*, present in South America, were the least studied. The limited research on the effects of light pollution on storm-petrels found primarily in the southern hemisphere, and the distribution pattern record centered in the northern hemisphere may be another case of the identified trends of research limitations in the Global South (Dados and Connell 2012, Collyer 2018). This pattern, however, could also be influenced by the elevated levels of light pollution in regions of the northern hemisphere, such as the coastlines of Europe and North America (Falchi et al. 2016).

### Implications for studying light pollution

To determine the extent of light pollution as a threat to the survival of storm-petrel populations, we must first understand which individuals are more susceptible to being disturbed by artificial light sources. One of the variables proven to be fundamental is the age group, as fledglings frequently get disoriented by artificial lights on their first flight toward the sea (Aubrecht et al. 2010, Rodríguez et al. 2017). Six of the evaluated articles considered this variable, and almost all found that storm-petrel fledglings were more frequently grounded by light pollution than adults. These results support evidence from previous studies (Le Corre et al. 2002, Rodríguez and Rodríguez 2009), suggesting that fledgling fallout and mortality may influence population decline (Troy et al. 2011). Even though the reason for fledgling disorientation and attraction toward artificial lights has not been fully established, four main hypotheses have been proposed: (i) inexperienced fledglings may confuse artificial lights with bioluminescent prey (Imber 1975), (ii) storm-petrel fledglings may associate light with a food source since the only light they encounter as nesting chicks is emitted from the burrow entrance used by parents to deliver food (Ainley, personal communication as cited in Rodríguez et al. 2017), (iii) the interplay between an undeveloped visual system and innate behavioral inexperience as fledglings (Atchoi et al. 2020), and (iv) artificial lights may limit their ability to use the moon and stars as navigation cues (Telfer et al. 1987). Understanding the mechanisms of fledgling attraction will allow the proposal of mitigation measures to reduce light pollution effects (Atchoi et al. 2020), particularly during fledgling periods in high-risk areas (Dias et al. 2019).

Among the environmental factors identified in numerous studies to affect storm-petrel susceptibility to light pollution (e.g., wind direction and speed, moon phase, length of time the moon was above the horizon), the moon phase is the most frequently mentioned. An association between grounded storm-petrels’ body condition and subsequent mortality has been established by Wilhelm et al. (2021). However, standardization of data collection may reveal patterns that have remained undetected. Studies performed by Wilhelm et al. (2021), Gjerdrum et al. (2021), Miles et al. (2010), and Murillo et al. (2013) suggest that stranding records focus on nights with the lowest moon visibility, while there are fewer storm-petrel strandings during the full moon (i.e., high moon visibility). In a recent study, Rodríguez et al. (2023) argued that the reduction in strandings during full moon nights may be associated with a lower attraction effect of artificial light when overlapped with natural moonlight. Future studies focusing on storm-petrels’ use of the moon as a navigational cue may reveal the mechanism of disorientation and attraction to artificial lights.

### Knowledge gaps in the reviewed literature

One of the limitations of the current state of evidence on the effects of light pollution on the Hydrobatidae family is that only two of the articles from our study used a systematic methodology for data collection. The accuracy of storm-petrel grounding records depends on the search effort, so systematic searches by qualified personnel are needed to increase the proportion of dead birds found (Rodríguez et al. 2017). However, accurate information is difficult to obtain. Effective monitoring programs need to consider a wide array of factors such as the area of impact, the search area and intensity (Rodríguez et al. 2014, Rodríguez et al. 2017), the probability of a carcass to be found (e.g., due to size, carcass accessibility or time of day; Rodríguez et al. 2017, Malinarich et al. 2018 in Silva et al. 2020), light-induced grounding hotspots (Crymble et al. 2020), proximity to the colony, and how quickly a grounded storm-petrel may disappear due to predation or decay (Rodríguez et al. 2017).

Most data about the magnitude of fallout comes from rescue programs carried out by communities, not necessarily as part of systematic monitoring programs (Rodríguez et al. 2017). The success of rescue campaigns, usually conducted by volunteers, relies on public awareness and successful media campaigns (Crymble et al. 2020). These rescue programs allow the generation of conservation knowledge for rare or poorly-known species, which otherwise would be too expensive or intractable to acquire (Rodríguez et al. 2017). Yet, data obtained through rescue campaigns or volunteering programs generally go underreported and should be interpreted as minimum numbers since (1) some grounded birds could be found by people unaware of the light pollution-seabird problem and hence not be reported (Rodríguez et al. 2015), (2) grounded fledglings tend to hide in dense vegetation, holes or crevices, so an unknown number of grounded birds are never found (Reed et al. 1985), (3) the general public is biased toward the collection of live birds and usually do not report or collect dead birds (Rodríguez et al. 2014, Rodríguez et al. 2015, Crymble et al. 2020), and (4) the effort is inherently greater in highly trafficked areas, leading to a possible sampling bias (Burt et al. 2023). Improved data collection and analysis will arise from combining rescue program information with rigorous scientific methods (Rodríguez et al. 2017). These volunteer rescue campaigns, as part of a citizen science approach, provide the opportunity to gather information that, due to resource and time constraints, would not be possible through traditional scientific methods (Kobori et al. 2016), as it may help to monitor stranding events in a broader geographical scale (Burt et al. 2023). Despite the great potential that citizen science has to advance marine and coastal conservation (Cigliano et al. 2015), awareness and community rescue campaigns still need to be encouraged so that the general public understands the threat of light pollution to seabirds, becomes more involved with conservation efforts, and demands solutions from the local and national governments (Rodríguez and Rodríguez 2009, Burt et al. 2023).

There is a considerable gap in the knowledge of light pollution effects on the Hydrobatidae family, which needs to be addressed to propose appropriate management conservation measures. Although some articles identify light pollution sources, the intensity, and spectrum are generally not quantified. This aspect of light pollution is relevant as the spectrum (wavelengths) and intensity of city lights at night are highly diverse, resulting in a mosaic-like distribution that can affect birds' responses in different magnitudes (Dominoni et al. 2013). Other essential factors to consider on light pollution effects are the temporality of light pollution sources (e.g., time of the day, duration, seasonality), the relationship between gender and incidence of light pollution attraction, and the distance between light pollution sources and the storm-petrel breeding populations or their flight paths (Troy et al. 2011, Silva et al. 2016; Rodríguez et al. 2017, Norambuena et al. 2021, Wilhelm et al. 2021). In fact, a recent study on Leach’s storm-petrels found that even a partial reduction in ALAN resulted in a decrease in strandings of up to 57% (Burt et al. 2024). Understanding the potential relationship between the attributes of light pollution sources such as intensity and distance attracting storm-petrels, may allow to quantify the exposure of dark areas and colonies to light pollution (Rodríguez et al. 2017, Norambuena et al. 2021, Wilhelm et al. 2021, Ryan et al. 2021). These and other previously mentioned gaps in our understanding of the effects of light pollution on storm-petrels, particularly at a population level, need to be addressed in future research, as they hold significant implications for conservation management.

### Limitations of this study

This scoping review has two main limitations. First, our literature search was conducted exclusively in English, with a prior search in Spanish that yielded no results. However, it is possible that relevant articles written in other languages may exist but were not accessible for inclusion in our analysis. Second, we focused exclusively on scientific articles indexed in Scopus and Web of Science platforms. Information from other web search tools, such as Google Scholar, ProQuest, ScienceDirect, and SciELO was not included. Since we also limited our analyses to scientific research papers published between 2000 and 2022, we acknowledge that important information from earlier research or found in the gray literature, such as government reports and environmental impact assessments, was not considered. Yet, focusing solely on academic scientific articles allowed us to identify relevant information gaps and biases in recent light pollution and storm-petrel research.

## CONCLUSIONS AND FUTURE PERSPECTIVES

We identified a series of knowledge gaps that must be further studied to propose effective mitigation measures for light pollution effects on members of the Hydrobatidae family. Future research would benefit from focusing on (1) standardizing data collection of storm-petrel groundings and associated environmental variables, (2) prioritizing systematic collection of grounding data or increasing available information through citizen science programs, (3) assessing the impact of light pollution at a population level to comprehend the effect of light-induced mortality in the species population trends, and (4) characterizing light pollution sources.

As light pollution rapidly increases globally with the expansion of cities, we need to start prioritizing research to determine effects on wildlife and adequately propose management plans and mitigation measures to ensure the well-being of other-than-human beings.

args.key_excerpts: "We aim to uncover, through an extensive literature review, the current state of evidence regarding the effects of light pollution on seabird populations of the Hydrobatidae family."
args.summary:
This is a peer-reviewed research paper published in Avian Conservation and Ecology (2025, Vol. 20, Issue 1, Article 18) titled "Lost in the glow: understanding the impact of light pollution on storm-petrels" by Medina-Franco, Sangiorgi, and Valdés-Velásquez (DOI: 10.5751/ACE-02846-200118).

**Purpose:** The authors conducted the first global scoping review focused specifically on light pollution effects on the Hydrobatidae family (storm-petrels), a poorly-known, nocturnal, burrow-nesting seabird group. The research question was: "What is the current state of evidence on the effects of light pollution on bird populations of the Hydrobatidae family?"

**Methodology:** 
- Literature searched on Scopus and Web of Science (February 16, 2023), covering articles published 2000-2022
- Searches conducted in English (Spanish searches yielded no results)
- Keywords covered storm-petrel taxa and light pollution
- 144 records identified (142 from databases, 2 from bibliographies); 20 reviewed in full; 12 articles (published 2005-2022) included in final analysis
- Half published between 2020 and 2022; six from southern hemisphere, six from northern hemisphere

**Key Results:**
- Grounding records found for all Hydrobatidae genera except *Nesofregetta*; groundings recorded in 12 of 22 Hydrobatidae species
- *O. leucorhoa* and *P. marina* were the most frequently mentioned species, followed by *H. pelagicus*
- Fallout (light-induced grounding) occurs primarily in fledglings during their first flight leaving the colony; over 99% of grounded *O. leucorhoa* were fledglings (per Wilhelm et al. 2021)
- Eight articles identified inshore, offshore, or both light pollution sources; inshore sources included residential, industrial, road, highway, business areas; offshore sources mainly fishing vessel deck lights
- Only three articles quantified light pollution levels (two used VIIRS satellite data, one used natural sky brightness measurements)
- Moon phase associated with groundings: more groundings during new moon (lowest moon visibility), fewer during full moon
- Of 12 species assessed by IUCN, nine have decreasing population trends, two unknown, one stable
- Only five of 12 articles assessed population-level impacts; these found annual fallout mortality was less than 1% of respective species' populations, suggesting light pollution may not currently constitute a substantial population-level threat, though further research is needed

**Hypotheses for fledgling attraction to light:** (1) confusion with bioluminescent prey, (2) association of light with food (burrow entrances), (3) undeveloped visual system and behavioral inexperience, (4) artificial lights limiting navigation by moon and stars.

**Discussion highlights:**
- Data is scarce (only 12 articles) and mostly collected before 2013
- Records limited mainly to North American and European coastlines; eastern Pacific (highest storm-petrel diversity) understudied - potential Global South research bias
- Knowledge gaps: only two articles used systematic data collection; light intensity/spectrum rarely quantified; need for standardized data collection, citizen science programs, population-level impact assessment, and characterization of light pollution sources
- A recent study found even partial reduction in artificial light at night (ALAN) decreased strandings by up to 57% (Burt et al. 2024)

**Study limitations:** English-only search; restricted to Scopus and Web of Science; limited to 2000-2022; gray literature excluded.

**Future research priorities:** (1) standardizing data collection of groundings and environmental variables, (2) systematic data collection or increased citizen science, (3) population-level impact assessment, (4) characterizing light pollution sources.

**Author contributions:** Medina-Franco and Sangiorgi are joint first authors (conceptualization, data curation, analysis, writing); Valdés-Velásquez contributed conceptualization, supervision, editing.

<webpage_content>
Marine oil pollution and beached bird surveys: the development of a sensitive monitoring instrument C.J. Camphuysen a,b,*, M. Heubeck c aNZG/NSO, Ankerstraat 20, 1794 BJ Oosterend, Texel, The Netherlands bNetherlands Institute for Sea Research, PO Box 59, 1790 AB Den Burg, Texel, The Netherlands cDepartment of Biology, University of Aberdeen, c/o AURIS/SOTEAG, Sumburgh Head Lighthouse, Virkie, Shetland ZE3 9JN, Scotland, UK Received 28 July 1999; accepted 1 May 2000 ``Capsule'': After reviewing the eects of oil pollution on seabirds, suggestions for new methods of monitoring marine oil pollution are presented.
Abstract One of the most obvious adverse eects of (chronic) pollution of the world's oceans and seas with mineral oil is the mortality of seabirds. Systematic surveys of beachcast corpses of birds (`beached bird surveys') have been used in many parts of the world to document the eect of oil pollution, but particularly so in Western Europe and in parts of North America. In this paper, the his-tory, current schemes, methods and possible (future) use of beached bird surveys are described and discussed, because the value of beached bird surveys has been hotly disputed. Oil pollution is known since the late 19th century, while the ®rst beached bird surveys were conducted in the 1920s. Due to the amount of man-power needed for these surveys, most beached bird survey programs thrived only through the work of a large number of volunteers. However, most programs have resulted in substantial amounts of high quality data, often covering many consecutive years. One of the main shortcomings of many beached bird survey programs was the emphasis on stranded bird numbers rather than on relative measures, such as oil rates (percentage of corpses oiled of all corpses found). Sources of pollution, particularly so in chronically polluted regions such as the North Sea, the Baltic, the Medi-terranean and the waters around Newfoundland, are insuciently known, but could be studied through a sampling program con-nected to beached bird surveys. Suggestions for standardization of methods are presented, which could lead to a global and highly sensitive monitoring instrument of marine oil pollution. # 2001 Elsevier Science Ltd. All rights reserved.
Keywords: Marine oil pollution; Monitoring instrument; Beached bird surveys; Seabird mortality 1. Introduction The adverse eects of spillages of mineral oil at sea were ®rst recognized in the late 19th and early 20th century, when reports of oil contaminated stranded seabirds were published. Oil pollution was immediately considered to be an unnecessary threat to marine birds and simply to assess the scale of the problem, stretches of beach were searched for birds and `beached bird surveys' were born. Beached bird surveys are counts of stranded corpses on tide-lines, set up in an attempt to quantify numbers of oiled birds washing ashore. Oiled seabirds washed ashore ever since, sometimes in massive numbers, and beached bird surveys have been the most important source of information regarding the adverse eects oil pollution. Yet, the value of beached bird surveys in monitoring trends in seabird mortality or oil pollution has been hotly disputed. In this paper, the history, current schemes, methods and possible (future) use of beached bird surveys are described and discussed and illustrated with some recent results and major trends.
2. History In Europe, the ®rst reports of beached oiled seabirds were published in the late 19th and early 20th centuries (Gray, 1871; Mothersole, 1910), although according to Verwey (1915) in The Netherlands and Wild (1925) in 0269-7491/01/$ - see front matter # 2001 Elsevier Science Ltd. All rights reserved.
PII: S0269-7491(00)00138-X Environmental Pollution 112 (2001) 443±461 www.elsevier.com/locate/envpol * Corresponding author. Tel.: +31-222-318744/369488.
E-mail address: camphuys@nioz.nl (C.J. Camphuysen).
Scotland it was not until the First World War that oiled seabirds became a common phenomenon. These early reports mostly originated from British (Anon., 1922 and 1926; Wild, 1925; Cole, 1929), Dutch (Verwey, 1915; Woltman, 1920; Verwey, 1922; Drijver, 1929) and Baltic coasts (Anon., 1910). Both Britain and The Netherlands then had well developed organisations for the protec-tion of birds which may have led to more published concern over this threat to seabirds than elsewhere.
Local incidents and certain mass strandings prompted people to search a few beaches and some of the counts of dead seabirds were published as short notes in var-ious natural history journals (Verwey, 1915; Hadley, 1930a,b; Brouwer, 1953; Bourne, 1969), or as reports to local authorities or government bodies (e.g. Drijver, 1929; Ampleford and Brown, 1959; Branderhorst, 1979; Heubeck, 1979, 1980, 1982, 1983, 1984, 1986). It was not until the 1950s and 1960s that serious attempts were made to establish and maintain programs for monitor-ing beached (oiled) birds, ®rstly in The Netherlands (Brouwer, 1953; Mo È rzer Bruijns, 1959), Germany (Goethe, 1961), Belgium (Kuyken, 1978a,b) and Britain (Barclay-Smith, 1956; Bourne and Devlin, 1969).
During the 1970s and early 1980s, the number of European countries in which there were organized bea-ched bird surveys gradually increased and the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds in Britain began to co-ordinate results internationally from 1972 onwards (Stowe, 1982a). When the national scheme in Britain was suspended in 1986, this role was taken on by the Danish Ornithological Society (Skov et al., 1989). Cur-rently, beached bird survey schemes operate in 13 Eur-opean countries (Table 1), although these vary considerably in temporal and geographic coverage.
Over the past 30 years beached bird surveys have been particularly intense in Britain (Jones, 1980; Stowe, 1982a,b; Heubeck et al., 1992; Heubeck, 1995), Belgium (Kuyken, 1978a,b; Oringa et al., 1997), The Nether-lands (Camphuysen, 1989, 1997), Germany (Vauk and Reineking, 1980; Averbeck et al., 1992) and France (Debout, 1984; Raevel, 1990). The high level of chronic oiling in the southern North Sea and its approaches, and the frequency with which oiled seabirds occur on beaches has probably helped maintain the interest and commitment of participating volunteers in these long-running schemes, as has concern over the development of North Sea oil ®elds since the 1970s (Dunnet, 1987).
There is no reason to believe that oil pollution was less serious in other parts of the world with high ship-ping densities at the beginning of the 20th century. As early as 1926, an international conference was convened in Washington, DC to discuss oil pollution, from which it can be deduced that the ``oil menace'' had already developed into a global problem (Barclay-Smith, 1930).
The impact of oil pollution on seabirds was noticed in the eastern United States as early as 1919 (Lincoln, 1930), while chronic oil pollution has been a serious problem in eastern Canada since at least the 1940s (Tuck and Livingston, 1959; Gillespie, 1969). Despite this, and some large oiling incidents during the period Table 1 Beached bird surveys in Europe. Arcos, pers. comm.; (16) Pehrsson, 1980; Udde Â n and A Ê hlund, 1984; (17) Dubrovsky, 1959.
444 C.J. Camphuysen, M. Heubeck / Environmental Pollution 112 (2001) 443±461 when beached bird surveys were becoming consolidated in Europe (McTaggart-Cowan et al., 1970; Sims, 1970; Brown et al., 1973; Levy, 1980; Powers and Rummage, 1978), only two schemes have been initiated on the Atlantic coasts of North America, in Newfoundland sporadically since the 1950s (Piatt et al., 1985) and more systematically there since 1984 by the Canadian Wildlife Service (Chardine et al., 1990; Wiese and Ryan, 1999), and at several localities between Massachusetts and Texas during 1974±1983 (Simons, 1985). In the autumn of 1974, observers began counting beached birds at several Atlantic coast localities between Long Island, NY, and Cape Romain, SC. In 1975, the project was extended along the Atlantic coast to southern Florida and to parts of the Florida Gulf coast. In 1977 the Texas Gulf coast was added and coverage was exten-ded to Plum and Nantucket Islands, MA. The results of beached bird surveys in Newfoundland by Environment Canada, the Canadian Coast Guard and Operation Clean Feather (1980±1998) suggested that chronic oil pollution was a more serious threat to sea-birds in these Atlantic waters than for instance along the west coast (see below) or in the Florida Gulf (Simons, 1985; Stenzel et al., 1988; Harvey and Tobin, 1998). Recent analysis showed most alarmingly that the oil rate in beached birds in Newfoundland has consistently increased (Wiese and Ryan, 1999). No systematic beached bird surveys are known to have been organized in the eastern United States since the mid-1980s.
On the western seaboard of North America, oil pollution caused heavy mortality of seabirds o central California in the ®rst decades of the 20th century (Dawson, 1911; Mot and Orr, 1938) and soon deple-ted local breeding populations of some species (Nur et al., 1995). However, it was only after the large oil spill at San Francisco in 1971 (Smail et al., 1972) that Point Reyes Bird Observatory initiated a beached bird survey in central California, the ®rst systematic scheme in North America (Stenzel et al., 1988; Nur et al., 1995).
This ceased in 1985 although other surveys in California have been conducted by the US Fish and Wildlife Service (1980±1986) (Bodkin and Jameson, 1991), and from 1993 to the present by the Gulf of Farallones National Marine Sanctuary (Roletto et al., 1996).
Further north, beached bird surveys have been con-ducted in Oregon and Washington since 1978, focussing especially on post-breeding mortality of Common Murres (Bayer et al., 1991) and in Washington during 1978±1983 by the University of Washington and other groups (Speich and Wahl, 1986). There is little early documented evidence of any eects of oil pollution on seabirds in British Columbian and Alaskan waters, but an increased threat was anticipated following the completion of the Trans-Alaskan pipeline in 1977 and the start of shipments of crude oil from the Valdez Oil Terminal to southern markets (Vermeer and Vermeer, 1975). Indeed both the number and volume of spills in these waters increased markedly between 1974 and 1989 (Burger and Fry, 1993) but as in California, it was only after a serious oil spill involving a large rehabilitation response (the Nestucca incident of December 1988; Rodway et al., 1989) that a beached bird survey scheme was organized in British Columbia. This continued until 1993 (Burger, 1993), but few surveys have been con-ducted since (A.E. Burger, pers. comm.).
In South America, oil spills have caused heavy mortality among penguin populations since at least the early 1970s (Jehl, 1975; Perkins, 1983) and chronic pol-lution has more recently been estimated to kill over 40,000 Magellanic Penguins Spheniscus magellanicus annually along the coast of Chubut Province, Argentina (Boersma, 1995). During the 1980s and 1990s, beached bird surveys have been a powerful tool in demonstrating the impact of chronic oiling on penguins in South America (Knaus, 1990; Carribero et al., 1994; Gandini et al., 1994), while the maintenance of oiled bird reha-bilitation centres in Brazil, Uruguay and Argentina (A.
Chiaradia and G. Becker, pers. comm.) are indications of the public awareness of the problem of oil pollution in the region.
Similarly, a series of serious shipping incidents during the 1970s and 1980s along the coast of South Africa, which caused serious mortality of African Penguins Spheniscus demersus (Morant et al., 1981) prompted the South African Seabird Group and others to establish a program for the rehabilitation of oiled seabirds and, in 1977, to initiate a beached bird survey scheme (Holmes, 1973; Anon., 1975; Berruti, 1978; Avery, 1979, 1980, 1981, 1989; Morant et al., 1981; Randall and Randall, 1986). From these surveys it would appear that apart from penguins, oil rates among other seabird species o South Africa have been relatively low.
Oil incidents and operational discharges have been reported from Australia (e.g. along the Great Barrier Reef) and some of the subantarctic islands but seem to have had little impact on seabirds until 1995, when several thousand Little Penguins Eudyptula minor were oiled in Tasmania (May, 1992; Thoresen and Thomson, 1992; Raaymakers, 1995; C. Hull pers. comm.). However, no beached bird survey scheme has yet been organized in Australia. There has been no major oil spill in New Zealand waters (Knight, 1993) although relatively minor incidents near harbors have aected penguins and shags (Norris, 1965; Robertson and Bell, 1984).
Nevertheless, New Zealand has one of the longest series of beached bird surveys in the world, organized since 1943 by the Ornithological Society of New Zealand primarily to collect information on the occurrence of storm driven birds (Veitch, 1975a, 1975b, 1976, 1977, 1978, 1979, 1980a, 1980b, 1981, 1982; Powlesland and Imber, 1988; Powlesland and Pickard, 1992; Powlesland C.J. Camphuysen, M. Heubeck / Environmental Pollution 112 (2001) 443±461 445 et al., 1992, 1993; Powlesland and Powlesland, 1993).
The results of these surveys suggest that chronic oil pollution is slight around New Zealand with, for exam-ple, only one out of 5000 dead seabirds found in 1994 having an oiled plumage (G. Taylor, pers. comm.).
The only beached bird surveys known to have been organized in Asia were carried out in Japan in the late 1960s and early 1970s (Chiba, 1965, 1974; Kazama, 1968), and the results indicated that chronic oil pollu-tion was a serious threat to seabirds in the Sea of Japan at that time, a situation which appears to have continued (Ohata, 1988; Ohata et al., 1993). Following the Nakhodka oil spill in the Sea of Japan in January 1997, a symposium was held at which Japanese biolo-gists considered a country-wide beached bird survey to monitor oil pollution and help assess impacts on sea-birds (H. Carter, pers. comm.). The environmental threat posed by the rapid development of the oil indus-try in Southeast Asia was discussed at the International Conference of Oil and Gas Development in Vietnam in 1996, and the lack of detailed regulations in many countries in the region was criticized, as was the degree of reporting on environmental impact (Anon., 1995).
This was exempli®ed by the December 1997 Tanjung Karang spill in Malaysia where there was no serious attempt to document the eects on marine life and birds, which were simply left to die on beaches (L.K.
Luensmann pers. comm.).
Despite the long history of oil production and trans-port around the Arabian Peninsula and severe oil pol-lution in the early 1980s during the Iran±Iraq war (Gallagher et al., 1984), it was only after the 1991 Gulf War that organized beached bird surveys were carried out in the region, along the northern Saudi Arabian gulf coast (Symens and Suhaibani, 1993). These surveys were discontinued once levels of oil pollution fell to ``back-ground'' levels (Bourne, 1991; Dipper, 1991; Dorrestein et al., 1991; Haenen, 1991), and chronic oil pollution in the Arabian Gulf, which is usually quite substantial, has thus far received little attention by ornithologists (Bourne, 1989).
In conclusion, the above review shows that while both chronic oil pollution and the major shipping accidents are highly concentrated around the busiest shipping lanes (Couper, 1983), quantitative information on seabird mortality derived from beached bird surveys is largely biased to western Europe, North America, South Africa and New Zealand.
3. Aims of beached bird surveys It is important to distinguish between surveys that are organized in connection with a particular oiling inci-dent, and those that are intended as a monitoring instrument which can be used to detect trends in chronic oil pollution. The former are limited in geographical coverage and in time, since they are simply meant to identify the species aected and to assess the scale of the event. The latter should be organized so that similar coverage and eort is feasible over a number of years.
At a basic level, these beached bird surveys may just have a signaling function, highlighting the adverse eects of oil pollution on seabirds. Initially, this was the aim of most beached bird surveys in the southern North Sea, which were often conducted by individual nat-uralists attempting to demonstrate that oil pollution had not been eliminated despite some international treaties. However, most recent systematic surveys have been set up with two main aims, ®rstly to establish the patterns of occurrence of dead seabirds along a coast-line and the proportions of the dierent species that are oiled, and then to use that data to be able to demonstrate longer-term changes and to identify and assess the scale of particular mortality incidents. Good examples of the monitoring function are the Orkney and Shetland beached bird surveys, set up in late 1970s when oil terminals were established in each of these north British archipelagos, with the aim of monitoring chronic oil pollution around the islands, and in particular that from the terminals and their associated tanker trac (Jones, 1980; Heubeck et al., 1992; Heu-beck, 1995). Elsewhere, beached bird surveys have indicated recent reductions in oil pollution in Poland (Meissner, 1992), Germany (Averbeck et al., 1992) and The Netherlands (Camphuysen, 1997). Despite this, ¯uctuations in numbers of birds washing ashore, and particularly the in¯uence of strong onshore or oshore winds, have led some to conclude that data from beached bird surveys were useless as an instrument for monitoring marine oil pollution. Goals, misconcep-tions, recommendations for survey design and possibilities for future use of beached bird surveys are discussed below.
3.1. Signaling adverse eects of oil on seabirds In many industrialized countries bordering the sea, particularly those with large harbors or with busy coastal shipping lanes, media coverage of smaller and larger oil spillages and accidents at sea is an annual event. In a country like The Netherlands, dramatic photographs and television footage of heavily oiled seabirds appear every single winter, and these casualties are used to bring marine oil pollution to public atten-tion. In fact it is surprising that oiled birds are still newsworthy since the comments in newspapers from the 1950s and 1960s are remarkably similar to those for example in the mid-1990s. Nevertheless, just by showing the oiled birds, or by presenting simple calculations from a series of surveys, this most basic function of beached bird surveys is ful®lled.
446 C.J. Camphuysen, M. Heubeck / Environmental Pollution 112 (2001) 443±461 4. Problems associated with beached bird surveys 4.1. Total numbers of birds stranded The numbers of beached birds can ¯uctuate greatly, whether geographically, seasonally or annually. Several authors have stressed the in¯uence of onshore winds versus oshore winds as an explanation of why numbers of birds washing ashore in one period are much larger than those in later or earlier surveys (e.g. Stowe, 1982a,b). However, very few have examined the eect of ¯uctuations in numbers of seabirds at sea, i.e. the pool of birds from which the beached birds originate. Clear seasonal patterns can be found in seabird numbers washing ashore which are largely the result of seasonal patterns of seabird abundance in coastal or oshore waters. In the southern North Sea, for example, numbers of seabirds at sea are 3 times higher in winter than in summer and the seasonal pattern in deposition rate of beached birds follows these ¯uctuations in sea-bird abundance at sea (Fig. 1). Large scale shifts in the wintering distribution of Common Murres Uria aalge, Razorbills Alca torda and Black-legged Kittiwakes Rissa tridactyla in the early 1980s from the northern North Sea to the south led to a substantial rise in numbers washing ashore in southeast England, Bel-gium, The Netherlands and Germany (Camphuysen, 1989, 1990). In contrast, over a 10 year period with daily surveys in a study area along the Dutch mainland coast, positive correlations between deposition rates and the frequency of onshore winds were only found in pelagic seabirds in winter (Fig. 2). For coastal species and migratory land birds, and for pelagic seabirds in summer, their abundance at sea explained most of the observed variation in deposition rates. Such ¯uctua-tions, in combination with short-term ¯uctuations resulting from shifts in wind direction, limit the ability to monitor changes in oil pollution at sea simply by the number of oiled birds found on beach surveys.
4.2. Total number of birds killed Most accounts of oiling incidents indicate the total number of oiled birds found, and some then try and Fig. 1. (a) Seasonal pattern in seabird abundance in the Dutch sector of the Southern North Sea, based on ship-based surveys 1980±1993 (modi®ed from Camphuysen and Leopold, 1994). Shoen are estimates of total numbers of birds based on the extrapolation of densities over the total area. (b).
Mean deposition rate of seabirds (number of birds per km per month) in a 8km study area at the mainland coast of Noord-Holland, based on daily beached bird surveys between 1 September 1988 and 31 December 1997 (C.J. Camphuysen, unpublished data).
C.J. Camphuysen, M. Heubeck / Environmental Pollution 112 (2001) 443±461 447 estimate the actual number killed by multiplying the body count with a factor to correct for corpses which never washed ashore, taking into account the beached bird survey eort and the volume of oil spilled (where known). However, adequate data on the number of birds at risk in the aected area is rarely available, and the eects of weather and oceanographic conditions on deposition rates of beached birds is not usually considered.
Most estimates of total mortality are therefore seriously open to question (Paine et al., 1996).
A classic estimate, of 275,000±500,000 casualties (mainly Common Scoters) following the grounding of the Danish tanker Gerd Mñrsk in January 1955 in the German Bight (Goethe, 1968), is still cited widely (Bourne, 1969; Reineking and Vauk, 1982; Burger, 1993), yet if the lower end of these ®gures was correct then at least twice the local wintering population of auks, seaduck and loons was wiped out (Skov et al., 1995). Furthermore, there is little evidence of any cor-relation between the amount of oil spilled and numbers of seabirds aected. Burger (1993) found only weak log±log correlations between spill volume and both the numbers of both oiled birds found and the estimated mortality; these relationships could not be used to predict mortality and lost their signi®cance if the case of the Exxon Valdez spill in Alaska was omitted.
Corpses or other objects ¯oating at or near the surface are subject to drift caused by the prevailing wind (Hughes, 1954; Matsumura et al., 1990), and periods of onshore winds obviously lead to more strandings than prolonged periods of oshore winds. Drift experiments have been performed in several places, using bird corp-ses or other ¯oating objects, in an attempt to calculate a common correction factor for bird strandings (Bibby and Lloyd, 1977; Bibby, 1981; Stowe, 1982b; Keijl and Camphuysen, 1992; Hlady and Burger, 1993). Summar-izing the results of these and other experiments (Table 2), it can only be concluded that the results are highly variable and at best location-speci®c. Local situations and weather conditions during these experiments, as well as the type of tags used, led to very dierent results.
It is obvious, however, that seabird mortality following marine oil spills could be greatly underestimated, particularly if the spills occurred far from land or during oshore winds (Threlfall and Piatt, 1983; Keijl and Camphuysen, 1992; Hlady and Burger, 1993). Instead of using a mean derived from the results of these experi-ments, the most sensible option in case of future oil incidents is to set up and perform a drift experiment during the event (cf. Colombe Â et al., 1996).
5. Suggestions for the design of surveys 5.1. Organization, volunteer input Due to the amount of man-power needed for these surveys, most beached bird survey programs thrive only Fig. 2. Camphuysen, unpublished data).

Heubeck / Environmental Pollution 112 (2001) 443±461 through the work of a large number of volunteers, many of whom may have little or no contact with other parti-cipants in the scheme. Maintaining the interest and enthusiasm of a network of volunteers is a considerable task and most beached bird surveys have been orga-nized by a few very motivated people, usually driven by the desire to eliminate oil pollution or at least draw attention to it. Few of these people have been rewarded by a clear reduction in pollution rates and in some cases they lost interest or stopped their work in frustration.
Residence changes and the waxing and waning of enthusiasm among volunteers has usually led to a turn-over in participants and constant recruiting was often necessary to maintain and expand these projects. The result is that many beached bird survey programs have shown a rapid build-up in eort for a number of years, followed by a period of peak activity and the publication of results, and then a decline in eort and in output. The longest running surveys have tended to be those where a degree of contact is maintained between organizers and participants, either personally or through the circulation of reports, analyses and pub-lications so that individual volunteers see that their relatively small contribution helps build a larger, meaningful picture.
5.2. Documentation of oil incidents In oil incidents, the scale of the impact is one of the key issues to be studied by means of beached bird sur-veys. The assessment of total numbers of casualties rather than oil rates of stranded birds require a rather dierent approach than the `ordinary' beached bird surveys that are set up to monitor the eect of chronic oil pollution. To estimate the total number of birds aected in a certain spill we recommend the following activities: . It is essential to immediately assess the area aec-ted by the incident (geographical distribution), to identify its core area, and to reconstruct when the oil reached the coast.
. A drift experiment with tagged, preferably clean and fresh seabird corpses should be set up in the area, during the stranding of casualties, in order to work out a correction factor for stranded num-bers.
. 5.3. Monitoring of chronic oil pollution To monitor the eect of chronic oil pollution on seabirds, there is no urgent need to accurately assess total numbers of birds washing ashore. We propose a system in which a `sucient sample' should be taken each season to allow the calculation of a reliable `oil rate' (fraction of birds oiled of total number of birds found).
5.3.1. Oil rates There is considerable regional and temporal variation in oil rates (the proportion oiled of all birds found stranded). However, for particular areas and seasons, oil rates are clearly species speci®c and indicative of the diering risk of birds (or corpses of birds) to become oiled in certain sea areas (Camphuysen and Franeker, 1992; Camphuysen, 1998). Most beached bird surveys are designed as a monitoring program, ideally using internationally harmonized standard methods so that dierences in the proportion of oiled beached birds and beaches can be easily compared between countries, continents, seasons and years (Camphuysen and Franeker, 1992; Heubeck and Camphuysen, 1992; see below). Several studies have ranked dierent seabird species in an oil vulnerability index according to their behavior, population size, range and dependence on the marine environment (King and Sanger, 1979; Cam-phuysen, 1989, 1998, Williams et al., 1995), and species with a high anticipated vulnerability to oil pollution typically had a higher oil rate among beached birds than those of lower anticipated oil vulnerability (Fig. 3). Oil rates are consistently high for species that spend a lot of time on the sea surface in highly polluted areas, such as loons, seaduck and auks in the southern North Sea, and low for more aerial seabirds such as shearwaters, skuas and terns, especially so in oceanic environments where shipping trac is less dense. A comparison of oil rates between surveys in dierent countries (bordering dierent sea areas) shows that the ranking of species according to their oil rates is often very similar, although the actual level can be quite dierent. For example in Shetland, in the oceanic northwest of the North Sea, Common Murres (13%), Razorbills (12%), and loons (23%) have relatively high oil rates compared to other species, although much lower than for the same species in the southeastern North Sea (Table 3). The oil rate of the Common Murre, the seabird most commonly found on beached bird surveys around the North Sea, clearly re¯ects dierences in shipping intensity of this region. High rates are typical for the Channel area, Southern Bight and Skagerrak region (close to major shipping lanes and large harbors), whereas compara-tively low oil rates are found in the north and northwest and on Atlantic coasts (Stowe, 1982a,b; Furness and Camphuysen, 1997). In North America and Canada, oil rates are apparently more variable (Table 4).
Fig. 3. Oil vulnerability index (see text) of 63 seabirds and coastal birds in the southern North Sea in relation to the observed oil rate (% of birds beached with oil in the feathers) during beached bird surveys in the Netherlands (1977±1997). Data from Camphuysen, 1998.
450 C.J. Camphuysen, M. Heubeck / Environmental Pollution 112 (2001) 443±461 5.3.2. Monitoring oil pollution Under the MARPOL Convention (Annex I), most ships at sea are still permitted to discharge small amounts of waste oil. A recent study has shown that both visible slicks of oil on the sea surface and visible traces of oil on birds must have been caused either by accidental spillages (which should have been reported to the authorities) or illegal discharges of oil (Dahlmann, cited in Camphuysen and Franeker, 1992). A number of countries use aircraft to monitor shipping lanes for oil pollution, but this is costly and slicks are dicult to detect during windy weather and in darkness. Beached bird surveys provide relatively cost-eective additional information on the occurrence of oil and the frequency of illegal spills that could not be collected from the air.
In theory, the oil rate of beached birds should decline if measures to reduce oil pollution are being eective, and should remain stable or increase if they are not, or if pollution levels increase. The statistical power of bea-ched bird survey results has recently been demonstrated for data collected in The Netherlands (1986±1995), indicating that even minor trends in oil rates can be detected with statistical certainty (Camphuysen, 1995, 1997, 1998). The sensitivity of beached bird surveys has also been evident elsewhere in the North Sea, when the eects of speci®c measures taken to reduce illegal dis-charges of oil at sea were soon recorded on beaches the German Bight (Averbeck, 1991) and the northern isles of Scotland (Heubeck, 1991).
Similarly, increased penalties for polluting and the introduction of aerial surveillance of coastal water was re¯ected in a marked reduction in oil rates on Polish beached bird surveys (Meissner, 1992), while a concerted multi-agency eort to combat illegal discharges of oil o Newfoundland coincided with an increase in oil rates on beached bird surveys there (Chardine and Pelly, 1994; Wiese and Ryan, 1999). Total numbers of dead seabirds washing ashore are in¯uenced by many factors (see above), of which an oil spill is only one. Instead of trying to assess the total number of oiled seabirds washing ashore on a coast, the oil rate can be used as an indicator of the risk of a seabird becoming contaminated by oil in that par-ticular sea area. Oil rates can be accurately assessed by recording and describing a large number of beached birds. Oil incidents may suddenly and temporarily ele-vate the oil rate, whereas increased mortality due to natural factors such as food scarcity or severe weather will decrease the oil rate. Over the years, in all countries where long-term trends were analyzed, the oil rate is a reliable ®gure which is consistently dierent in the var-ious species of birds (Andrews and Standring, 1979; Stowe, 1982a; Diego Garcia et al., 1986; Camphuysen, 1989; Reis, 1989; Danielsen et al., 1990; Go Â rski and Antczak, 1990; Jacobsen et al., 1991; Averbeck et al., 1992, 1993; Meissner, 1992; Raevel, 1992; Granadeiro and Silva, 1993; Seys and Meire, 1993; Camphuysen, 1995, 1997, 1998; Heubeck, 1995). Beached bird sur-veys, designed to monitor marine oil pollution in a given area, should provide monthly samples, at least in the winter period but where possible throughout the year, of the abundance of beached birds and the percentage of these birds which are oiled or contaminated with lipophilic compounds. Oil pollution around the Shetland Islands: eective measures to stop vessels from discharging oil Beached bird surveys began in both island groups prior to the opening of the Flotta oil terminal in Orkney in January 1977 and the Sullom Voe terminal in Shet-land in November 1978. Before the ®rst tankers expor-ted oil from these terminals the incidence of oiled birds on beaches was relatively low. Both terminals experi-enced signi®cant oil spills within months of opening, in March 1977 at Flotta (crude, 110 oiled birds found) and December 1978 at Sullom Voe (bunker fuel, 3700 found), but the impacts of both these incidents were relatively localised. A relatively high incidence of oiled birds was recorded in Orkney throughout 1978, with analyses indicating that crude oil and it's residues com-prising 32% of 43 samples taken.
In early December 1978, 10 days after the ®rst ship-ment of oil left the Sullom Voe Terminal in Shetland, hundreds of oiled birds began to wash ashore in Orkney and along the coasts of north-east Mainland Scotland.
During the next 4 months over 4000 oiled birds were found on the coasts of Caithness, Orkney and Shetland in a series of unattributable spills (i.e. excluding the fuel oil spill at Sullom Voe). Sampling during this period in Orkney showed an increased incidence of crude oils (65%, n=26) compared to 1978, with a similar pattern in Shetland (57% crude oils, n=42). Tankers passing the area could not be ruled out as being responsible, but the coincidental timing with the opening of the Sullom Voe terminal led to suspicions that tankers bound there were the main culprits, particularly since the terminal had opened before de-ballasting facilities were completed (these only became operational in November 1979).
In the face of a public outcry and calls for the closure of the Sullom Voe terminal until the deballasting plant was completed, measures were introduced in March 1979 to further discourage de-ballasting at sea by tan-kers bound for Sullom Voe, and to improve naviga-tional safety.
These included (1) dedicated aerial surveillance of tankers and the seas around Shetland; (2) reporting requirements, routing, and areas of avoidance for tankers trading with Sullom Voe; (3) tankers entering Sullom Voe must carry at least 35% ballast, which was sampled to compare with beached oil; (4) preferential chartering of tankers with segregated ballast; (5) tankers failing to comply with these rules would jeopardise their charter contract and may be refused loading facilities at the terminal. Tankers were observed breaking these rules on a number of occasions in 1979 and 1980 and legal actions were taken. However, the percentage of birds found oiled on beached bird surveys decreased in both Orkney and Shetland during 1980 and 1981, and by 1982 crude oil sludges were reduced to 7% and 4% of samples taken in Orkney and Shetland, respectively.

args.summary:
This is a scientific paper by C.J. Camphuysen and M. Heubeck, published in Environmental Pollution (2001), reviewing the history, methods, and future use of beached bird surveys as a monitoring instrument for marine oil pollution. The paper argues that such surveys are a valuable and sensitive tool for detecting chronic oil pollution, despite criticisms about their reliability.

Key points:
- Oil pollution effects on seabirds were first recognized in the late 19th/early 20th century; the first beached bird surveys were conducted in the 1920s, with serious monitoring programs emerging in the 1950s-1960s in the Netherlands, Germany, Belgium, and Britain.
- Currently, beached bird survey schemes operate in 13 European countries, with only two schemes on Atlantic North America (Newfoundland since the 1950s, and Massachusetts-Texas during 1974-1983). Programs exist or have existed in California, Oregon, Washington, British Columbia, South Africa, South America (particularly for Magellanic Penguins), New Zealand, and Japan.
- A major shortcoming of many programs was emphasis on total stranded bird numbers rather than "oil rates" (percentage of corpses oiled). Total numbers fluctuate greatly due to winds, seabird abundance at sea, and seasonal patterns, limiting their use as pollution indicators.
- Estimating total mortality from oil spills is problematic; drift experiments using tagged corpses show highly variable recovery rates (0.3% to 59%) that are location-specific, so correction factors must be developed during actual incidents rather than using mean values.
- The paper recommends that for monitoring chronic pollution, the "oil rate" (fraction oiled of all birds found) should be used, requiring a "sufficient sample" each season. Oil rates are species-specific (high for surface-immersed species like loons, seaduck, auks; low for aerial species like terns and skuas) and reflect shipping intensity in different regions. For example, Common Murre oil rates are 82% in the Netherlands but only 13% in Shetland.
- Statistical power analysis of Dutch data (1986-1995) shows even minor trends in oil rates can be detected within 12-15 years for most species.

Case studies demonstrating effectiveness:
1. Shetland Islands: Surveys showed low pollution before terminal opening (1978), a spike after the Sullom Voe terminal opened (before de-ballasting facilities were ready), and a decline after strict measures were introduced in March 1979 (aerial surveillance, routing requirements, 35% ballast requirement, preferential chartering of segregated-ballast tankers).
2. Southern North Sea: Consistent declines in oil rates over 30 years indicate gradual improvement.
3. German Bight: Drastic decline during an experiment with free harbor oil reception facilities.
4. Newfoundland: Consistent increases in oil rates, indicating worsening pollution.

Methodological recommendations for standardization (for chronic monitoring):
- Choose representative subregions covering the entire coastline; keep standardized over years.
- Surveys preferably done on foot; counts from vehicles not recommended.
- Mark or remove birds to avoid double counting.
- Identify species, age, sex; record corpse condition and oil extent (use only complete corpses for oil rate calculations).
- Record date, place, km surveyed, oil characteristics, observer names, completeness of survey.
- Computerized databases for prompt analysis.
- Separate open coast from sheltered bays/fjords and MARPOL Special Areas in analyses.

For oil incidents, the paper recommends: assessing the affected area immediately, conducting drift experiments during stranding, sampling the entire stranding area with repeated counts, recording live oiled birds, contacting rehabilitation centers and beach cleaners, marking/removing beached birds, and continuing surveys until fresh casualties cease.

Subject Editor: Miguel Araújo Editor-in-Chief: Miguel Araújo Accepted 7 September 2018 42: 876–886, 2019 doi: 10.1111/ecog.04003 Nocturnal avian migration flyways remain an elusive concept, as we have largely lacked meth­ ods to map their full extent. We used the network of European weather radars to investigate nocturnal bird movements at the scale of the European flyway. We mapped the main migra­ tion directions and showed the intensity of movement across part of Europe by extracting biological information from 70 weather radar stations from northern Scandinavia to Portugal, during the autumn migration season of 2016. On average, over the 20 nights and all sites, 389 birds passed per 1 km transect per hour. The night with highest migration intensity showed an average of 1621 birds km–1 h–1 passing the radar stations, but there was considerable geo­ graphical and temporal variation in migration intensity. The highest intensity of migration was seen in central France. The overall migration directions showed strong southwest components. Migration dynamics were strongly related to synoptic wind conditions. A wind-related mass migration event occurred immediately after a change in wind conditions, but quickly dimin­ ished even when supporting winds continued to prevail. This first continental-scale study using the European network of weather radars demonstrates the wealth of information available and its potential for investigating large-scale bird movements, with consequences for ecosystem function, nutrient transfer, human and livestock health, and civil and military aviation.
