--- SOURCE 2: Bruderer & Liechti: Bird migration across the Mediterranean ---
URL: https://www.internationalornithology.org/PROCEEDINGS_Durban/Symposium/S33/S33.5.htm

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific paper by Bruno Bruderer and Felix Liechti (Swiss Ornithological Institute, 1999) examines nocturnal bird migration patterns across the western Mediterranean, Iberian Peninsula, and its relation to the Alps and Sahara as ecological barriers. The study uses three calibrated methods: coordinated moon-watching, passive infrared camera observations, and tracking radar (the 'Superfledermaus'), with primary data collection sites at Malaga (Andalusian coast, 25 km east of Malaga) and southern Mallorca (Balearic Islands).

KEY FINDINGS ON FLYWAY EVOLUTION: Flyways between Europe and Africa evolved at three levels: (1) continent-wide scale following Pleistocene range expansions, (2) medium-scale influenced by ecological barriers (sea, desert, mountains) and weather, and (3) individual behavioral reaction norms. The trade-off between risk-avoidance (avoiding barriers) and time/energy minimization leads to 'guided broad-front migration'.

AUTUMN MIGRATION: Moon-watch data from 42 sites (September 1996, 1749 observations over 145 hours) revealed: west-east variation across upper Italy with westward migration over the Padanian plain, southward shifts along the French Riviera, weak SW migration across the western Mediterranean basin near Rome/Malta/Mallorca, and strong SW migration in southern Spain. At Malaga, 29,866 flight paths were recorded (Aug 11-Oct 24, 1996). Passerine migration peaked in September (trans-Saharan migrants) and again in mid-late October (pre-Saharan migrants like Robin, Black Redstart, Chiffchaff, thrushes, Starling, and Skylark). At Baleares, virtually no migration occurred in August (very weak trans-Saharan passage); September data were contaminated by insects, but clean nights (Sept 26-Oct 3, Oct 14-24) showed massive take-offs from the island with arrivals from the Costa Dorada (~240 km to NW at ~5 hours), Costa Brava (~300 km at ~7 hours), and Camargue (~480 km NNE at ~11 hours).

SPRING MIGRATION: At Malaga (March 22-May 26, 1997; 30,353 flight paths), passerine density averaged about twice that at Mallorca (24,085 flight paths). Wader/waterfowl migration was almost five times stronger at the mainland. At Malaga, peak migration occurred 5 hours after sunset with birds arriving from North Africa (170+ km sea crossing, 40-45 km/h ground speeds), concentrating in a narrow strip along the North African coast. A second April peak ~7 hours after sunset indicated concentrations 100-150 km inland (Atlas mountains). At Baleares, intense evening departures from only ~30 km² of suitable habitat (5-30 birds/ha density) occurred, followed by arrivals from Spain, Ibiza, North Africa, and mainland Europe. Density of spring migration across the Mediterranean basin between Algeria and France was at least 2-3 times lower than across the Iberian Peninsula. Migration traffic rates (MTR) at Cape Trafalgar were 700-2900 birds/km/h, compared to ~600 at Andalusian coast and ~270 on Mallorca (about a third to half).

DISCUSSION: SW and SE migratory directions in Europe (contrasting with North America's southward tendencies) are adaptations to the combined barriers of the Alps, Mediterranean, and Sahara. Trans-Saharan migrants (September) cling strictly to their chosen directions, while pre-Saharan migrants (October) show greater flexibility in direction in response to topography, following coastlines and taking advantage of the land bridge. This flexibility allows refueling before the Sahara crossing and selecting optimal weather. Seaward migration decreases when birds' motivational/physiological state deteriorates. The radar data support a slight concentration of nocturnal migration toward the Strait of Gibraltar in addition to prevailing SW/SSW migration. The proposed hypothesis map (illustrating autumn migration) suggests broad-front NE-SW migration across central Europe with concentrations along the French Mediterranean coast, Italian mainland, and SE coast of Spain, representing convergence of various species' and populations' migratory streams.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"In spite of probable concentration effects over the islands, the recorded density of passerine spring migration at the Baleares is only half of that at Malaga, wader/waterfowl migration only about one fifth; the latter difference emphasises the importance of the flyway along the African Atlantic coast.", "The map suggests broad-front migration on a NE-SW axis across central Europe, with declining density to the SE... the whole assembly being best characterised by the term 'guided broad-front migration'.", "At the Baleares site there was nearly no bird migration in August, indicating very weak passage of trans-Saharan migrants.", "The volume of recorded migration at the Baleares was astonishingly high, i.e. much closer to the volume at Malaga than observed in April and May.", "Migratory directions towards SW and SE combined with an obvious lack of southward migration in central and northern Europe are corroborated by data derived from bird ringing, by cage experiments, and by radar observations."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Favorable winds speed up bird migration in spring but not in autumn ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9339755

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific article, published in Ecology and Evolution (2022, Vol. 12, e9146, doi: 10.1002/ece3.9146), investigates the effect of wind on bird migration speed across western Europe. The study uses the first full-year weather radar dataset of nocturnal bird migration from 37 European weather radars (6.8 million datapoints, Feb 13, 2018 to Jan 1, 2019, 5-minute temporal and 200m altitudinal resolution up to 5km) combined with ERA5 wind reanalysis data. The authors (Raphaël Nussbaumer, Baptiste Schmid, Silke Bauer, and Felix Liechti, from Cornell Lab of Ornithology and Swiss Ornithological Institute) analyzed ground speed, airspeed, wind speed, and wind profit across seasonal, daily, geographical, and altitudinal scales.

Key findings: Wind plays a major role in explaining temporal and spatial variations in ground speed, but airspeed remains remarkably constant across all scales (daily SD=3.1 m/s vs ground speed SD=5.1 m/s; spatial airspeed SD=1.03 m/s vs wind SD=1.35 m/s vs ground SD=2.44 m/s). Spring migration was faster than autumn (ground speed 12.6 vs 9.9 m/s) primarily due to wind profit (4.6 m/s in spring vs 1.1 m/s in autumn), with birds experiencing stronger southwest winds in spring (7.5 vs 5.6 m/s). Average airspeed was only slightly faster in spring (8.7 vs 8.2 m/s, about 5% faster), but this difference was deemed not statistically significant due to measurement biases and limitations. The authors argue this 5% difference falls within the expected 5-15% range from optimal flight theory but is too small to be meaningful given large variance and data quality issues.

Methodology: Airspeed was computed using the triangle of velocities (Vg = √(u²+v²); Va = √((u-U)²+(v-V)²)) with wind speeds linearly interpolated in 4D from ERA5 reanalysis data. Wind profit was calculated as vector projection on assumed migration direction of 225° (NE in spring, SW in autumn). The authors differentiate between experienced wind (density-weighted) and available wind (unweighted).

Discussion of biases includes: weather radar underestimates individual ground speed due to directional scatter (higher in autumn, possibly from inexperience juveniles); insect contamination is more common in autumn and may lower autumn airspeed estimates despite correction methods. The wind profit of 2.0 m/s average speeds up overall migration by 19%, saving approximately 15 hours (2-3 nights) of flight time for a 3000km migration. Within-season airspeed changes (decreasing in spring by 0.53 m/s/month, decreasing in autumn by 0.58 m/s/month) were stronger than between-season differences, possibly reflecting shifts in species composition. Funding was provided by Swiss National Science Foundation (grant no. 191138) and the GloBAM project. Data is available at Zenodo (doi:10.5281/zenodo.3610184) with code on GitHub.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Wind has a significant yet complex effect on bird migration speed. With prevailing south wind, overall migration is generally faster in spring than in autumn."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: [PDF] Nocturnal autumn bird migration at Falsterbo, South Sweden ---
URL: https://lucris.lub.lu.se/ws/files/2778134/624263.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific study published in the Journal of Avian Biology (2001, Vol. 32, pp. 239-248) by Susanna Zehnder, Susanne Åkesson, Felix Liechti, and Bruno Bruderer, investigating nocturnal autumn bird migration at Falsterbo, a coastal peninsula in south-western Sweden (55°23' N, 12°50' E).

**Methodology:** The researchers monitored nocturnal migration using a passive infrared device (LORIS IRTV-445L) positioned at the Falsterbo Lighthouse, 5 m above sea level. Observations were conducted from August 7 to October 28, 1998, covering the main autumn passage. Recordings ran from one hour before sunset to one hour after sunrise (excluding precipitation days), with analyses restricted to periods between civil twilight at dusk and dawn. Video recordings were analyzed using a video peak store for track direction and altitude determination. Birds were classified into seven size classes corresponding to estimated flight altitudes from 0.3 km to 2.1 km. Counts were converted to migration traffic rates (MTR; birds km⁻¹ h⁻¹).

**Key Results:**
- 17,411 flight paths were recorded over 68 nights (632.3 observation hours), covering 51 entire nights (17 nights had some interruptions, 15 nights excluded due to rain)
- Mean nightly MTR ranged from 6 to 6,618 birds km⁻¹ h⁻¹, averaging 1,319 birds km⁻¹ h⁻¹ (median 566); for the full period including zero-filled missing nights, mean was 1,081 birds km⁻¹ h⁻¹
- Intense migration nights (N=16, ≥2% of seasonal passage) accounted for 73% of total passage; intermediate nights (N=20) 21%; low migration nights (N=32) 6%
- Weather factors (wind speed, tailwind component, air pressure, and change in air pressure) explained 66% of variance in migration intensity (R²=0.657)
- Migration was strongest in the second half of September, with low intensities in early season and decline in October

**Flight directions and wind influence:**
- Overall mean track direction was 219° (N=17,411, r=0.62, p<0.001)
- During intense migration nights with weak winds, mean track direction was about 225°, similar to other western European sites (230° in southern Germany/Switzerland, 220° in southern Spain)
- Higher-flight birds showed more southerly and concentrated track directions
- Birds maintained constant headings independent of wind direction, experiencing wind drift; drift coefficients (b) ranged from 0.71 to 0.92, indicating full or near-full drift
- No leading-line effect from the local coastline was found; birds did not compensate for wind drift using topography (coastline orientation of 21°/201° was not within the 95% confidence intervals of mean track directions)
- Later in the night, track directions shifted from SSW toward more westerly directions, likely to shorten the sea crossing to Denmark (closest point 24 km)

**Conclusions:** This was the first estimate of nocturnal migratory intensity in Scandinavia. The number of nocturnal migrants correlated with grounded birds captured the following morning. Migration showed peaks following favorable weather (weak tailwinds, high/rising air pressure). Birds mostly departed from areas over 100 km NE of Falsterbo and began landing after 3-6 hours of flight. Reverse movements were rare. The findings contrast with earlier low-altitude (10-100 m) studies showing coastline-following wind compensation at this site, suggesting that birds flying above 300 m (this study's minimum detection altitude) do not use local topography as a leading line.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"In total 17411 ﬂight paths, including track direction and altitude, of migrating birds were recorded for 68 nights from August to October. Mean migratory trafﬁc rate per night varied between 6 and 6618 birds km−1 h−1, with an average of 1319 birds km−1 h−1."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 7: Orientation of shorebirds in relation to wind: both drift and ... ---
URL: https://www.ottenby.se/wp-content/uploads/message_series/cms_14-s1_260.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific study, published in the Journal of Ornithology (2013, Vol. 154, pp. 385-392) by Grönroos, Green, and Alerstam from Lund University, investigates how arctic shorebirds respond to crosswinds during autumn migration in South Sweden and the southern Baltic Sea. The researchers examined three sites within 200 km of each other: Ottenby (island departure over sea, using visual telescope observations), Vitemölla (coastal site arriving from sea, radar tracking), and Björka (inland site, radar tracking). 

KEY FINDING: The study revealed remarkably different wind responses along this short migratory section. Birds showed almost full drift (Btrack = 0.90) when departing over the sea at Ottenby, partial drift (Btrack = 0.52) at Vitemölla, and almost full compensation (Btrack = 0.30) at higher altitudes over land at Björka. Headings differed between winds from left and right by 0° at Ottenby (no compensation), 13° at Vitemölla, and 23° at Björka.

METHODS: Visual telescope tracking was conducted at Ottenby Bird Observatory (56°12'N, 16°24'E) during 2006-2008 and 2011, tracking low-altitude flocks (2-50 m above sea level, mostly Dunlin comprising 95% of flocks). Radar tracking used X-band mobile tracking radar at Vitemölla (55°42'N, 14°12'E) and Björka (55°39'N, 13°37'E) during 1982-1990, tracking birds at median altitudes of 607 m and 621 m respectively. Heading directions were calculated by vector subtraction of wind velocity. Drift/compensation magnitude was calculated using Green and Alerstam's (2002) methods.

CONCLUSIONS: The initial drift at departure is likely NOT adaptive but rather a result of constraints in compensation capacity—particularly in low-altitude climbing flight over the sea where visual reference cues (seascape/landmarks) may be limited or unavailable. When birds reached higher altitudes with visual landmarks available (at Björka), they compensated almost fully. No significant difference in wind drift was found between adult and juvenile birds, suggesting the drift is not a learned navigation skill deficiency. The study demonstrates that non-adaptive wind drift, alongside adaptive orientation responses, contributes to variability in drift/compensation behavior between places separated by only short distances, depending on local topographic and environmental conditions.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The shorebirds showed clearly different responses to cross-winds along this short section (< 200 km) of the migratory journey, from almost full drift when departing over the sea, followed by partial drift and almost full compensation at higher altitudes over land during later stages."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 9: Experience does not change the importance of wind ... ---
URL: https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c6/Experience_does_not_change_the_importance_of_wind_support_for_migratory_route_selection_by_a_soaring_bird.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific paper (Brønnvik et al., 2022, published in Royal Society Open Science) investigates whether experience changes how European honey buzzards (Pernis apivorus) use wind support and thermal uplift when selecting migratory routes. The researchers tracked 23 juvenile buzzards via GPS during autumn migration from Finland to sub-Saharan Africa over up to 4 years, comparing their route choices with those of adults. Using step-selection functions with Bayesian inference (INLA), they analyzed wind support and two uplift proxies (boundary layer height and vertical velocity of pressure) from ERA5 reanalysis data.

Key findings: Wind support was the most important predictor of route selection across all ages and migrations, and its importance did not change with experience. Contrary to their hypothesis, there was no age-related increase in the use of thermal uplift - neither uplift proxy was an important predictor of route selection for any age. The interaction between uplift and wind support was significant only in the model using boundary layer height, not vertical velocity. The authors attribute the absence of uplift effects possibly to the coarse spatio-temporal scale of the atmospheric data (~30 km resolution) failing to capture fine-scale thermal selection, or to the learning period exceeding the 4-5 year study window. The findings suggest wind support importance is consistent across life stages, with potential implications for the species' resilience to shifting wind patterns from climate change.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"We found that wind support was important in all migrations. However, we did not find an increase in the use of thermal uplifts. This could be due to the species-specific learning period and/or an artefact of the spatio-temporal scale of our uplift proxies.", "Because thermal soaring is a complex flight behaviour that young birds need to learn, we expected that, as individuals gain more experience, their movement decisions will also increasingly favour the best thermal uplift conditions.", "Our finding suggests that wind support is important for migration in all life stages of this species and we suspect that this may be the case in other facultative soaring species as well. This may have consequences for the longevity of the species in the face of shifting wind patterns driven by anthropogenic global warming.", "The atmospheric data measured at roughly 30 km every hour might have failed to capture the uplift conditions that the birds select, which may be on a much finer scale as they glide between thermal columns of varying diameters and strengths."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 10: Bird orientation: compensation for wind drift in migrating ... ---
URL: http://macroecointern.dk/pdf-reprints/BL0300S8.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific paper (Proc. R. Soc. Lond. B (Suppl.) 270, S8–S11, 2003) by Thorup, Alerstam, Hake, and Kjellén investigates how wind drift affects migrating raptors, finding a key age-dependent difference in compensation. The study used satellite-based radio telemetry (Argos system) to track adults and juveniles of two raptor species—osprey (Pandion haliaetus: 11 adults, 2 juveniles) and honey buzzard (Pernis apivorus: 6 adults, 3 juveniles)—during autumn migration between North Europe and Africa. Segments between positions separated by at least 1 day and 100 km were analyzed, yielding 232 segments from 21 birds after excluding aberrant routes. Wind data (NCEP Reanalysis, NOAA-CIRES) at 1000 hPa and 925 hPa pressure levels were used.

Remarkable fidelity is documented — e.g., a barn swallow (Hirundo rustica) traveled between South Africa and a stable in Germany for three years with accuracy of a few metres. - **Solar compass:** Gustav Kramer's orientation cage experiments (Figure 3-5) showed sun position is used as a directional cue. Shifting a bird's internal clock by 6 hours caused a 90° error in flight direction; a 12-hour shift caused 180° reversal (heading north in autumn). Used by diurnal migrants (white storks, large birds of prey), but useless for nocturnal migrants.
- **Night-time compasses (moon and stars):** Franz Sauer (1950s) discovered birds orient using the moon and stars. The "Zugunruhe" (migratory restlessness) behavior at dusk marks migration onset. Franz Sauer and later Stephen T. Emlen (planetarium experiments, Figure 8) demonstrated that birds align with constellations, adjust for their movement during the night, and can be made to "somersault" when the sky was rotated 180°. Birds recalibrate their stellar compass using their magnetic compass, and must "read" new star configurations when crossing the equator.
- **Earth's magnetic field:** Radar studies in the 1950s showed nocturnal migrants oriented correctly even under overcast skies. Kramer proposed a two-stage navigation model (a "mental map" plus a "compass"). Experiments on robins and garden warblers with modified magnetic fields (using coils/magnets to shift magnetic north) provided irrefutable evidence for geomagnetic orientation. Geomagnetism is the only reliable source when all visual references fail.
- **Mental maps:** Birds use geo-topographical landmarks (mountain ranges, river corridors, valleys, passes, coastal strips) as a mosaic of waypoints. Radar observations show wind-driven birds can reorient back to their course after turbulence; birds also exploit favorable winds for massive migratory flows.

The willow warbler (Phylloscopus trochilus) follows a NE-SW course of ~9,000 km, then abruptly changes to north-south at the Iberian Peninsula. Captive garden warblers demonstrated this "pre-programmed" directional change.

**Human use:** Carrier pigeons have been used since Ancient Egypt, sparked 19th-century competitions (notably in the US), and served as messengers in both World Wars, commemorated by a "soldier pigeon" monument in Brussels.

**Key messages:** The navigation model consists of genetically determined mechanisms in rigid sequential order, based on a mental map, astronomical compasses (sun/moon/stars), and a magnetic compass used additionally or exclusively when others fail. Orientation systems work in synergy, birds interpret wind information, and all steps follow a circannual genetically determined internal clock ("tells" birds when to reproduce, moult, migrate).

--- SOURCE 2: [PDF] COMMENTARY Forty years of olfactory navigation in birds - CORE ---
URL: https://core.ac.uk/download/pdf/80243808.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific commentary article by Anna Gagliardo (Department of Biology, University of Pisa, Italy) published in The Journal of Experimental Biology (2013, Vol. 216, pp. 2165-2171) reviewing 40 years of research on olfactory navigation in birds, with a focus on homing pigeons.

**Historical background:** The olfactory navigation hypothesis was formulated in response to experimental findings. About 40 years ago, Floriano Papi and colleagues (1971) conducted experiments in Tuscany showing that pigeons with sectioned olfactory nerves never returned home when released at unfamiliar sites, while intact birds homed successfully. Around the same time, Wallraff's research on pigeons raised in confined aviaries revealed that birds sheltered from winds by glass screens (despite full horizon view) were unable to orient homeward, while birds exposed to winds through a palisade (despite obstructed views) were unimpaired, suggesting an "atmospheric factor" was involved in navigation.

**The olfactory navigation hypothesis (Papi et al., 1972):** Pigeons at their home loft learn windborne environmental odours in association with wind direction. Once at a release site, they recognize local odours and recall from which direction these odours come from at home, allowing them to determine the direction of displacement.

**Key experimental evidence:**
- Benvenuti and Wallraff (1985) demonstrated that birds transported in airtight containers and exposed to air at a "false release site" oriented towards the "false home direction" from that site.
- Anosmia specifically impairs navigation only at unfamiliar sites; anosmic pigeons home normally from familiar locations using visual landscape cues (Biro et al., 2004; Holland, 2003; Gagliardo et al., 2001b).
- Unilateral nostril occlusion combined with unilateral treatments produced impairment only when the plug was placed contralaterally to the treated side (Benvenuti and Gagliardo, 1996).
- Experiments using ZENK immediate early gene expression showed activation of the piriform cortex during navigational tasks from unfamiliar locations but not during homing from familiar sites (Gagliardo et al., 2007; Patzke et al., 2010).
- Trigeminal nerve section (proposed magnetoreceptor pathway) was shown to be neither necessary nor sufficient for navigation; olfactory nerve section impaired homing despite intact trigeminal nerves (Gagliardo et al., 2006). Upper beak iron-containing cells were later shown to be macrophages, not magnetoreceptors (Treiber et al., 2012).
- Wind manipulation experiments (using deflectors or corridor cages with fans) produced predicted deflections in initial orientation. Deflector results were potentially confounded by polarized light effects, but fan-based wind inversion experiments were not.
- Artificial odour experiments (Papi et al., 1974): pigeons exposed to turpentine from north and olive oil from south oriented according to their learned associations, demonstrating that birds can incorporate artificial odours into their olfactory map.
- GPS tracking data showed that birds deprived of environmental olfactory information displayed tortuous tracks and poor homeward orientation, contradicting the "olfactory activation hypothesis" (Gagliardo et al., 2011).

**Structure of the olfactory map:** The olfactory map does not provide exact position/distance like a bicoordinate system but provides information about direction of displacement only. Wallraff and Andreae (2000) collected air samples from 96 sites within 200 km around a loft and found volatile organic compounds distributed along fairly stable spatial gradients. Simulation experiments showed that stable ratios of at least three volatile compounds provide sufficient information for homeward orientation comparable to experimental observations.

**Olfactory navigation in wild species:** Evidence remains at an early stage. Studies showed homing impairment in anosmic swifts (Fiaschi et al., 1974) and anosmic starlings (Wallraff et al., 1995). Holland et al. (2009) tested migrating catbirds (Dumetella carolinensis) in Illinois displaced east to New Jersey. Juvenile catbirds oriented south regardless of manipulation (consistent with first-flight inability to navigate), while anosmic adult catbirds oriented southward instead of westward like controls—providing the first evidence that olfactory cues are involved in wild bird navigation during migration.

**Ongoing debate:** The article addresses the lingering resistance to accepting olfactory navigation, particularly versus the poorly supported idea of magnetic-based position-finding. The author notes that magnetic manipulations do not affect homing performance and that direct experimental evidence for a geomagnetic-based position-finding mechanism is lacking. Open questions include whether olfactory navigation is widespread in birds, whether seabird oceanic navigation depends on olfactory cues, whether olfactory cues are key during migration, what specific chemical compounds are used, and whether birds use odour gradients (Wallraff's model) or patches/mosaic maps (Papi's original model).
</summary>

They explained this phenomenon by developing the olfactory navigation hypothesis: pigeons at the home loft learn the odours carried by the winds in association with wind direction; once at the release site, they determine the direction of displacement on the basis of the odours perceived locally and orient homeward."

Despite over 50 years of research, the field remains contentious, described by some as suffering from a "chronic disease" (Mouritsen & Hore, 2012). 1. True Navigation Definition: First conceptualized by Donald Griffin (1952) as "type III" navigation, with the term "true navigation" adopted by Keeton (1974). The most current definition is "the ability of an animal to return to its original location after displacement to a site in unfamiliar territory, without access to familiar landmarks, goal emanating cues, or information about the displacement route" (Phillips et al., 2006). The review distinguishes "migratory true navigation" as navigating to a specific breeding or wintering area (not just the point of departure) after displacement.

2. Evidence: Perdeck's classic 1958 study demonstrated adult but not juvenile birds can perform migratory true navigation. More recent studies show adult white-crowned sparrows can correct toward their winter area after 3700 km displacement (Thorup et al., 2007), and reed warblers correct for 1000 km displacements (Chernetsov et al., 2008). True navigation is experience-based—adults have learned from previous journeys. However, some studies show failures, including Perdeck's 1967 repeat (no correction in Spain), and white/golden crowned sparrows translocated from the US to Korea failing to return. Limits appear to vary, with evidence of at least 3700 km range but possibly only ~2000 km in starlings.

3. Map and Compass Theory: Kramer's (1953) "map and compass" hypothesis remains the most robust explanation—navigation is a two-step process of determining position (map step) and direction (compass step). True navigation refers specifically to the map step. The bi-coordinate map theory proposes animals learn environmental gradients that vary predictably with latitude and longitude (potentially magnetic field intensity/inclination, sun's arc/sunrise time).

4. Study Methods: Two main approaches are used: (a) laboratory-based migratory restlessness studies (Emlen & Emlen, 1966) using orientation cages, and (b) field-based displacement studies with remote tracking (GPS/satellite telemetry). Both systems have limitations—lab studies lack natural relevance, while field studies suffer from logistical difficulty, lack of statistical power, and expensive tracking technology (GPS telemetry too large for small songbirds, no migratory true navigation study using GPS telemetry yet published).

5. Environmental Cues Examined:
   - Celestial Cues: Sun navigation is generally rejected based on clock-shift experiments in homing pigeons (deflection of ~90° counterclockwise with 6-hour clock shift, consistent with sun compass not sun navigation). Star navigation lacks evidence for time compensation needed for longitude detection. However, a meta-analysis suggests juvenile birds are more likely to correct under starry skies than overcast.
   - Infrasound (0.1-10 Hz): Correlational evidence from pigeon racing disturbances and atmospheric fluctuations (Hagstrum, 2000-2013), but one experiment removing pigeon cochleas showed no homing deficits. No experiment has demonstrated effects on migration.
   - Olfactory Cues: The most controversial and most extensively tested hypothesis (primarily in homing pigeons). Key findings include: olfactory nerve sectioning removes homing ability; "false release site" experiments show birds orient to the original sampling site (Benvenuti & Wallraff, 1985); artificial odour (benzaldehyde) experiments produce orientation consistent with displacement (Ioale et al., 1990). Criticisms include lack of repeatability, potential motivational (activation) rather than navigational roles, and deflector loft effects attributed to polarized light deflection. Stable odour gradients haven't been demonstrated beyond ~200 km, making olfactory navigation hard to reconcile with large migratory displacements. However, a recent experiment (Holland et al., 2009) showed adult catbirds displaced 1000 km lost the ability to correct when olfactory-deprived via zinc sulphate. A neurobiological study found both visual and olfactory brain areas become more active at night during the migratory period (Rastogi et al., 2011).
   - Magnetic Cues: Earth's magnetic field intensity proposed as a latitudinal cue (Viguier, 1882), but only functional over a coarse scale; fine-scale variations mean it may vary with longitude in places, making it a less consistent cue than often portrayed.

The review concludes that true navigation remains one of the great unanswered questions in science, but presents a positive outlook and identifies key remaining questions, emphasizing the need to understand what has been tried, what failed, and what is incomplete to move toward resolution.
</summary>

The article is open access (CC BY license), PMID 41358193, received Feb 12, 2025, accepted Apr 25, 2025.

**Core topic:** The review examines map and compass navigation—a two-step process where animals use a map to determine goalward directions and a compass to orient in those directions—focusing on the mechanisms and ontogeny (development) of animal maps.

**Key framework:** The article deconstructs maps into three components:
1. **Cues**: Environmental properties animals perceive to determine goalward directions. These must be temporally stable and vary predictably in space. Main cue modalities include: magnetic (inclination, intensity, declination), visual (landmarks, geometric relationships, landscape features), and olfactory cues. Other suggested cues include sun arc, Coriolis force, infrasound, and gravity vectors (though with limited controlled experimental evidence).
2. **Structure**: The organization of information used to determine goalward direction. The article distinguishes between **discrete structures** (recognizing distinct places/regions; includes terms like mosaic maps, cognitive maps, signposts) and **continuous structures** (exploiting predictable spatial gradients; includes grid maps, gradient maps, triangulation/trilateration). The structure is limited by underlying cue distributions but also depends on how animals perceive and respond to cues.
3. **Implementation**: Strategies for approaching goals (waypoint navigation vs. direct goalward orientation) and combining multiple map cues. Examples include magnetic+cue combination in turtles, visual+olfactory in pigeons, and gradient combination strategies.

**Ontogeny findings:**
- Some map cues rely on inherited rules (e.g., hatchling loggerhead turtles and salmon inherit responses to magnetic cues), sometimes combined with imprinting on natal site cues.
- Homing pigeons have a sensitive learning period (3-4 months after fledging) for developing olfactory maps, but can also learn cues later when free flying.
- Visual landscape cues are less likely to be developmentally fixed and must be learned through experience.
- Map structures can be inherited (e.g., turtle signposts) or developed through learning (e.g., green turtles displaced up to 100 km appear to use more complex maps).
- Map implementation strategies remain relatively unexplored in terms of their ontogeny.

**Path integration hypothesis:** The authors suggest that path integration (tracking vectors of self-motion through integrating distance and direction, also called dead reckoning) plays an important role in map learning—well documented in mammals over small spatial scales—and could play a similar role in other taxa and over larger spatial scales. This implies path integration may be more taxonomically widespread and play a greater role in navigational learning than currently appreciated.

**Key conclusions:** Learning plays an important role in map ontogeny for many examples, especially those requiring gradient extrapolation or flexible navigation between multiple goals. However, it remains unclear how animals resolve the spatial arrangement of cues to learn maps, particularly over large scales. The review calls for further experimental and correlative studies (aided by advances in animal tracking technology) to better understand map structure, ontogeny, and how animals combine map cues.
</summary>

Notably, the CMF did not correspond to any actual magnetic field on Earth because the real Neftekamsk field has much higher total intensity (~55,510 nT).

A three-axis Helmholtz coil was used to manipulate the magnetic field. Statistical analyses included Rayleigh tests for uniformity, model selection using CircMLE, Moore's paired test, and a generalized additive mixed model (GAMM) to rule out seasonal effects.

- In NMF, 12 birds oriented towards south-southeast (mean direction α = 169°, 95% CI 138–200°, r = 0.651, p = 0.004)
- In CMF, the same birds shifted orientation to WSW (mean direction α = 266°, 95% CI 225–307°, r = 0.544, p = 0.025)

- The WSW re-orientation corresponds to the direction from the virtual displacement site (Neftekamsk) back toward the capture site and matches the response observed when all three cues were changed in the previous 2018 study
- The GAMM model (combining data from 2018, 2019, and 2020) showed no effect of time within season on the east-west component of orientation (χ² = 1.08, p = 0.3), but a significant effect of magnetic condition (χ² = 5.52, p < 0.001)

**Conclusions:** The study demonstrates that magnetic inclination and magnetic declination alone are sufficient for reed warblers to determine their position during migration, even when these cues conflict with total magnetic intensity. --- SOURCE 22: True Navigation: Sensory Bases of Gradient Maps ---
URL: https://pigeon.psy.tufts.edu/asc/Phillips

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific chapter by John B. Phillips, Klaus Schmidt-Koenig, and Rachel Muheim (Virginia Tech & Duke University) reviews the sensory bases of "true navigation" - the ability of animals to home over tens to hundreds of kilometers without relying on familiar landmarks or displacement route information. True navigation requires both a compass (sense of direction) and a map (sense of geographic position).

**Key Concepts:**
- True navigation has been demonstrated in various vertebrates and one invertebrate (spiny lobster; Boles & Lohmann, 2003)
- Vertebrates possess multiple compass systems (sun, star, polarized light, and magnetic compasses), with celestial polarized light patterns serving as the primary calibration reference for the compass in birds
- A navigational map differs from place/bearing/mosaic maps in that it can be extrapolated to unfamiliar sites; gradient maps require learning the alignment and steepness of environmental gradients within the home range and extrapolating beyond familiarity
- Non-parallel gradients of two or more map components enable bicoordinate position fixing

**Theoretical Considerations:**
- Magnetic gradient maps operate over distances >50-75 km (regional gradients) or <5-10 km (local gradients), but are unreliable at intermediate distances (10-20 km to 50-70 km) where local and regional variation are similar in magnitude
- Schmidt-Koenig (1966, 1970) found pigeons showed markedly poorer homing orientation from intermediate distances (30-70 km) compared to closer and farther sites, suggesting different navigational mechanisms for short vs. long-distance homing
- Gradient maps range from complex bicoordinate systems to simple stimulus/response systems that trigger discrete behaviors

**Olfactory Map Evidence:**
- Olfactory deprivation experiments showing effects on homing have often failed to rule out alternative explanations (e.g., effects on trigeminal nerve-mediated magnetoreception, or on distinguishing home from non-home)
- Deflector loft experiments (rotating wind direction) initially appeared to support the olfactory map hypothesis, but four critical experiments demonstrated the effect is caused by rotation of light cues, not wind-borne odors - specifically via polarized-light-based calibration of the sun/magnetic compass
- Split-brain experiments (Foà et al., 1986) showed hemispheric-specific olfactory map effects, but these can be alternatively explained by differently calibrated sun compass systems on each side of the brain
- Conclusion: The literature does not provide compelling evidence for olfactory involvement in a long-distance gradient map; olfactory cues may instead play a role in a short-distance mosaic map, site labeling, or home/non-home recognition

**Magnetic Map Evidence:**
- Magnetic field gradients are extremely weak (only ~5-10 nT/km in total intensity, ~0.01°/km in inclination), requiring extraordinarily sensitive sensory mechanisms
- Magnetic gradients cannot be detected directly but must be derived from multiple point samples; use is experience-dependent with an ontogenetic progression from place maps to gradient maps

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a PubMed abstract page for a scientific article titled "Bird navigation: what type of information does the magnetite-based receptor provide?" published in Proceedings of the Royal Society B (Proc Biol Sci) on November 22, 2006 (Volume 273, Issue 1603, pages 2815-2820). The article has the DOI 10.1098/rspb.2006.3651, PMID 17015316, and PMCID PMC1664630.

AUTHORS: Wolfgang Wiltschko (corresponding author, from Fachbereich Biowissenschaften der J.W.Goethe-Universität, Frankfurt am Main, Germany), Ursula Munro, Hugh Ford, and Roswitha Wiltschko.

METHODOLOGY: The researchers subjected migratory Australian silvereyes (Zosterops lateralis) to a short, strong magnetic pulse and tested their subsequent orientation responses under different magnetic conditions. In the local geomagnetic field, birds preferred easterly headings (a change from their normal migratory direction). When the horizontal component of the magnetic field was shifted 90 degrees anticlockwise, the birds altered their headings accordingly (northwards). In a field with the vertical component inverted, the birds reversed their headings to westwards.

RESULTS AND CONCLUSIONS: The findings demonstrate that although the magnetic pulse strongly affects magnetite particles, it leaves the functional mechanism of the magnetic compass intact, since the birds' directional orientation was still controlled by the normal inclination compass. This indicates that magnetite-based receptors mediate magnetic 'map'-information used for determining position. When affected by the pulse, these receptors provide birds with false positional information, causing them to change their course.

The article includes the abstract, three figures (orientation of silvereyes before pulse treatment, immediately after the pulse and on the following two evenings, and a model illustrating the use of magnetic information by different receptor types in the navigational system), similar articles, and citations. MeSH terms include Animal Migration, Ferrosoferric Oxide chemistry, Flight Animal, Magnetics, Orientation physiology, Passeriformes, and Sensory Receptor Cells. --- SOURCE 2: [PDF] The discovery of the use of magnetic navigational information ---
URL: https://d-nb.info/1242247874/34

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific review article by Roswitha and Wolfgang Wiltschko (published in Journal of Comparative Physiology A, 2021) traces the historical discovery of how animals use magnetic navigational information from Earth's geomagnetic field.

**The avian magnetic compass discovery (mid-1960s):** The first experimental evidence that animals can use magnetic fields for directional orientation came from the Frankfurt group (W. Wiltschko and Merkel 1966), showing that European Robins (Erithacus rubecula) oriented their migratory activity in a test cage according to magnetic North, and shifted headings when magnetic North was deflected by Helmholtz coils. This initial discovery met with great skepticism, partly because earlier prominent scientists like Erwin Stresemann and Donald Griffin had failed to find evidence for magnetoreception. Early attempts to reproduce findings failed due to test cage designs, statistical treatment of circular data, and bird handling. The findings were eventually confirmed when Wallraff (1972) borrowed the Frankfurt cages and confirmed migratory orientation, and when Emlen et al. (1976) confirmed the effects in joint experiments.

**Conditioning challenges:** Magnetic sensitivity was difficult to demonstrate through conditioning because animals did not associate unnatural magnetic stimuli with reinforcers. The magnetic field differs from other stimuli—it is only used for navigation, doesn't change rapidly, and animals don't expect changes. Successful conditioning required setting up the magnetic situation before animals entered the test apparatus and including orientation aspects in tasks. This approach worked for chickens, Zebra Finches, and homing pigeons.

**Sensory mechanisms:** The avian magnetic compass is an inclination compass (not responding to polarity) that works only in a functional window around local magnetic intensity and requires short-wavelength light (UV to green). This suggested the Radical Pair Model (Schulten and Windemuth 1986; Ritz et al. 2000), involving cryptochrome in the eyes. Radio frequency fields (0.64 MHz and above) caused disorientation, and cryptochrome was identified in the outer segments of UV/V cones in retinae (Nießner et al. 2011).

**Widespread occurrence:** Magnetic compass orientation has been demonstrated in all vertebrate classes (birds, amphibians, reptiles, fish, mammals), mollusks (nudibranch Tritonia diomedea), and arthropods (crustaceans, beetles, honeybees, moths, termites, Monarch butterflies, desert ants). Functional modes differ: birds and amphibians use inclination compasses; elasmobranchs, bony fish, and mammals use polarity compasses (magnetite-based in mole-rats and bats).

**Magnetic 'map':** The use of geomagnetic field for determining position was demonstrated after 2000 through magnetically simulated displacements. Spiny lobsters, green sea turtles, bonnethead sharks, and several bird species (Lesser whitethroats, Australian silvereyes, reed warblers) responded to virtual displacements by compensating as if physically displaced. In birds, 'map' information is transmitted via the trigeminal nerve to the trigeminal brainstem complex, based on magnetite-containing structures in the upper beak.

**Magnetic 'sign posts' or triggers:** Specific magnetic conditions elicit spontaneous innate responses. Examples include pied flycatchers initiating the second leg of migration, garden warblers switching from 'equatorward' to 'poleward' after experiencing horizontal magnetic fields, loggerhead sea turtle hatchlings responding to gyre-edge magnetic conditions to stay in favorable oceanic environments, Pacific salmon responding to specific magnetic conditions, and thrush nightingales increasing body mass when exposed to magnetic conditions of Northern Egypt (triggering refueling before Sahara crossing).

The review concludes that the geomagnetic field is a widely used, valuable source of navigational information for mobile animals, used as a compass/reference system, components of a navigational 'map', and 'sign posts' controlling both orientation and physiological functions.
</summary>

"The magnetic field of the Earth provides animals with various kinds of information. Its use as a compass was discovered in the mid-1960s in birds, when it was first met with considerable skepticism, because it initially proved difficult to obtain evidence for magnetic sensitivity by conditioning experiments."

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article, "That Nest of Wires We Call the Imagination: A History of some Key Scientists Behind the Bird Compass Sense" by Lisa Pollack (May 2012, from the Theoretical and Computational Biophysics Group at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign), traces the history of how scientists discovered that birds sense magnetic fields through a quantum biochemical process known as the radical pair reaction. The narrative follows two parallel discovery paths:

The article begins with historical context: homing pigeons were used extensively in WWII (over 16,000 parachuted into Europe, with many receiving the Dickin Medal), and birds like the bar-tailed godwit can fly non-stop up to 7,100 miles. Though conjecture about magnetic sensing existed in the 19th century, experimental proof came only in the 1960s.

The scientific history covers:
- Klaus Schulten, hired in 1974 at the Max Planck Institute in Göttingen, theorized that magnetic fields could affect chemical reactions (explaining "fast triplets" in Albert Weller's experiments). His prediction was confirmed in 1976.
- Independently, Maria-Elisabeth Michel-Beyerle at the Technical University of Munich reached similar conclusions, inspired by Merrifield's 1972 work on magnetic field effects in molecular crystals and the book "The Exciplex." Both published findings in 1976.
- Wolfgang Wiltschko discovered in 1965-66 that European robins use magnetic orientation (his epiphany came on October 12, 1963). He and his wife Roswitha published their first paper together in 1972, proposing an inclination compass.
- Schulten published the first proposal of a chemical compass in 1978 (with Swenberg and Weller), after his paper was rejected by Science. A question from Dudley Herschbach ("where in the bird is the laser?") convinced him the sensor was light-dependent and in the eye.
- The radical pair mechanism works because an external magnetic field causes interconversion between singlet and triplet electron spin states, affecting chemical reaction yields.
- In 2000, Schulten, Thorsten Ritz, and Salih Adem proposed cryptochrome as the candidate molecule in the eye for the avian magnetic compass.
- Key recent findings include Henrik Mouritsen's identification of "cluster N" brain center (whose destruction abolishes magnetic compass but not star/sun orientation), magnetic field effects on cryptochrome-mediated plant systems (Margaret Ahmad), and oscillating magnetic field experiments with fruit flies and birds that provided more evidence for the radical pair mechanism.

The article emphasizes the importance of multi-disciplinary collaboration (behavioral biologists, molecular chemists, physicists) in solving this mystery. It includes several direct quotes from Klaus Schulten, including "The longer you work on a problem the harder it actually gets" and the anecdote about Ed Schlag's remark "What is said over a glass of beer doesn't count."

--- SOURCE 4: [PDF] Magnetic maps in animal navigation - The Lohmann Lab ---
URL: https://lohmannlab.web.unc.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/8154/2023/09/2022_MagneticMapReview_Lohmann_et_al_JCPA.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This review article, published in the Journal of Comparative Physiology A (2022), examines the concept of "magnetic maps" in animal navigation. Earth's magnetic field provides two types of information that animals can exploit: directional (compass) information and positional (map) information, with animals possessing the latter said to have a "magnetic map." The concept has evolved from a contentious hypothesis a generation ago to a well-established tenet of animal navigation, explaining many impressive navigational feats.

Key magnetic parameters that could provide positional information include inclination (the angle at which field lines intersect Earth's surface, varying predictably with latitude), total field intensity, horizontal and vertical field components, and declination (the difference between true north and magnetic north). Small magnetic anomalies from crustal minerals can disrupt this global pattern and may serve as landmarks for some species, though their effects vary.

The first direct evidence of magnetic maps came from experiments with loggerhead turtle hatchlings (Lohmann and Lohmann 1994, 1996a) demonstrating they could detect inclination and intensity. The "magnetic displacement" technique (exposing animals to magnetic fields replicating those at distant locations) has become a powerful tool for demonstrating magnetic maps.

The article identifies two general types of magnetic maps:
1. Inherited maps used by first-time migrants to guide movements along migratory pathways (evidenced in loggerhead sea turtles, Chinook and pink salmon, European eels, and possibly pied flycatchers)
2. Learned maps used for goal navigation (evidenced in juvenile green turtles, bonnethead sharks, and Eurasian reed warblers)

Notable findings include:
- Young loggerhead turtles can distinguish among eight different magnetic fields along their migratory route and can encode longitudinal as well as latitudinal information
- Ocean circulation models show that even 1-3 hours of oriented swimming per day greatly increases young turtles' survival chances
- Young salmon respond to magnetic fields reinforcing survival near range boundaries before ever entering the ocean
- Hatchling pink salmon and European eels respond to magnetic fields that keep them within favorable transport currents
- Thrush nightingales and wheatears use magnetic positional information to adjust food/fuel deposition during migration
- Eurasian reed warblers compensate for both physical and virtual (magnetic) displacements of 1000 km, demonstrating goal-navigation maps
- Birds may use magnetic declination to correct for longitudinal displacements, though not all species appear sensitive to it

The article also discusses geomagnetic imprinting - the process by which sea turtles, salmon, and some birds imprint on the magnetic field of their natal area when young to facilitate return as adults (natal philopatry). Secular variation (gradual changes in Earth's field) is addressed, with strong selective pressure likely maintaining appropriate coupling between animal responses and current magnetic conditions. The review concludes that much remains to be learned about the organization of magnetic maps, their development, and their use in navigation.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"In less than a generation, the idea that animals use Earth's magnetic field as a kind of map has gone from a contentious hypothesis to a well-established tenet of animal navigation."
</key_excerpts>

This is a scientific paper by A.C. Perdeck, published in Ardea in 1958, describing landmark displacement experiments on migrating Starlings (Sturnus vulgaris) and Chaffinches (Fringilla coelebs). The study was the 29th publication of the Foundation "Vogeltrekstation Texel" and aimed to determine whether migrating birds use "one-direction orientation" (maintaining a fixed compass direction) or "true goal orientation" (steering toward a specific geographical location).

The experiment involved catching birds during autumn migration near The Hague, Netherlands, and transporting them by airplane to release points in Switzerland (Basel, Zurich, and Geneva). Between 1949-1953, 11,247 Starlings were transported (3,787 adults and 7,460 juveniles), with 354 recoveries (3.1%). Adults and juveniles were first released separately, then in mixed groups to study age-class influence.

Key findings:
- Adult Starlings, when released separately, flew north-westerly toward their normal winter quarters (Holland, Belgium, N.W. France, S. England, Ireland), demonstrating TRUE GOAL ORIENTATION. - Juvenile Starlings flew in a south-west-by-west direction, roughly parallel to their original migration direction, demonstrating ONE-DIRECTION ORIENTATION. They did not correct for the displacement.
- The preferred autumn migration direction of the Netherlands population was determined to be between W. and W.S.W. based on field observations.
- Juveniles displaced in their first year tended to adopt the region where they first wintered as their permanent wintering area in subsequent years, and showed strong homing to these new winter quarters in later winters—demonstrating that true goal orientation must be learned.
- Adults displaced as juveniles later returned to the shifted wintering area, and recoveries from breeding seasons showed a shift to the eastern part of the normal breeding area.
- Mixed transports (adults and juveniles released together) showed a slight, non-significant tendency for juvenile directions to be more northerly (Wilcoxon test: P between 0.14 and 0.18), so no clear age-class influence was demonstrated.

Authored by Nikita Chernetsov and Gleb Utvenko from the Zoological Institute of the Russian Academy of Sciences, the article reviews decades of research on how juvenile songbirds that migrate solitarily find their wintering grounds.

**Core concept**: The clock-and-compass concept holds that naïve migrants follow an inherited genetic spatio-temporal program—flying in a set compass direction for a predetermined number of days before changing course (a Zugknick)—until they reach their species-specific wintering range. Gustav Kramer's earlier map-and-compass concept distinguished between a positioning system (map) and a compass for direction selection.

**Key historical evidence**:
- Rüppell (1944) displaced 507 hooded crows 750 km west; neither young nor adult birds compensated, consistent with clock-and-compass.
- Perdeck (1958-1967) displaced 11,247 common starlings from the Netherlands to Switzerland. Adults corrected their route and navigated toward winter quarters (map + compass), while young birds continued southwest without correction (compass only). A 2024 re-analysis (Pot et al.) confirmed results couldn't be explained by joining local flocks.
- Thorup et al. (2007) displaced white-crowned sparrows 3,700 km; only adults, not juveniles, compensated for longitudinal displacement.
- Streaked shearwaters: juveniles flew across inhospitable Honshu Island landmasses relying on inherited compass direction, while adults circumvented them.

**Genetic basis**: Research has identified genes involved in migratory direction. VPS13A is linked to wintering region selection in golden-winged and blue-winged warblers. A breakthrough study by Sokolovskis et al. (2023) on willow warblers revealed migration direction is primarily determined by two genes—MARB-a and InvP-Ch1—with MARB-a suppressing InvP-Ch1 through epistasis. Hybrid migration direction can follow parental patterns in some species or be intermediate in others, indicating species-specific inheritance mechanisms.

**Criticisms of the clock-and-compass concept**: Jørgen Rabøl proposed an alternative "navigation by goal area" hypothesis suggesting birds inherit geographic coordinates of destinations. Evidence challenging the simple clock-and-compass model includes:
- Young common cuckoos displaced 1,800 km east returned to their species-specific migration route.
- Young whitethroats, garden warblers, and willow warblers compensated for displacements over 1,000 km.
- Juveniles of several species show route-correction abilities previously thought limited to experienced birds.

**Magnetic field role**: Experiments show first-time migrants use magnetic cues as "beacons":
- Beck and Wiltschko (1988): pied flycatchers needed to experience en route magnetic conditions to display appropriate orientation.
- Fransson et al. (2001): thrush nightingales exposed to simulated northern Egypt magnetic field gained significantly more fuel before crossing the Sahara. A replication (Kullberg et al., 2003) confirmed this in early but not late trials.
- Bulte et al. (2017): northern wheatears showed the opposite—simulated route progression reduced fattening and restlessness.
- Wiltschko and Wiltschko (1992): garden warblers exposed to horizontal magnetic field (simulating magnetic equator crossing) shifted orientation from "toward equator" to "toward pole," though a recent study (Utvenko et al., 2025) found no such shift in marsh warblers.

SUMMARY:
<summary>

Holland, published in the Journal of Zoology (Volume 293, Issue 1, pp. 1-15, first published 16 January 2014, DOI: 10.1111/jzo.12107). The author is from the School of Biological Sciences, Queen's University Belfast, UK (corresponding author, email r.holland@qub.ac.uk).

The review addresses the controversial and unresolved scientific question of how birds achieve true navigation—the ability to return to a known goal from an unfamiliar place. Despite over 50 years of research, the field remains contentious, described by some as suffering from a "chronic disease" (Mouritsen & Hore, 2012). However, significant advances in the last 20 years have come from integrating disciplines including neurobiology, molecular biology, and quantum physics.

KEY CONCEPTS AND FINDINGS:

1. True Navigation Definition: First conceptualized by Donald Griffin (1952) as "type III" navigation, with the term "true navigation" adopted by Keeton (1974). The most current definition is "the ability of an animal to return to its original location after displacement to a site in unfamiliar territory, without access to familiar landmarks, goal emanating cues, or information about the displacement route" (Phillips et al., 2006). The review distinguishes "migratory true navigation" as navigating to a specific breeding or wintering area (not just the point of departure) after displacement.

2. Evidence: Perdeck's classic 1958 study demonstrated adult but not juvenile birds can perform migratory true navigation. More recent studies show adult white-crowned sparrows can correct toward their winter area after 3700 km displacement (Thorup et al., 2007), and reed warblers correct for 1000 km displacements (Chernetsov et al., 2008). True navigation is experience-based—adults have learned from previous journeys. However, some studies show failures, including Perdeck's 1967 repeat (no correction in Spain), and white/golden crowned sparrows translocated from the US to Korea failing to return. Limits appear to vary, with evidence of at least 3700 km range but possibly only ~2000 km in starlings.

3. Map and Compass Theory: Kramer's (1953) "map and compass" hypothesis remains the most robust explanation—navigation is a two-step process of determining position (map step) and direction (compass step). True navigation refers specifically to the map step. The bi-coordinate map theory proposes animals learn environmental gradients that vary predictably with latitude and longitude (potentially magnetic field intensity/inclination, sun's arc/sunrise time).

4. Study Methods: Two main approaches are used: (a) laboratory-based migratory restlessness studies (Emlen & Emlen, 1966) using orientation cages, and (b) field-based displacement studies with remote tracking (GPS/satellite telemetry). Both systems have limitations—lab studies lack natural relevance, while field studies suffer from logistical difficulty, lack of statistical power, and expensive tracking technology (GPS telemetry too large for small songbirds, no migratory true navigation study using GPS telemetry yet published).

5. Environmental Cues Examined:
   - Celestial Cues: Sun navigation is generally rejected based on clock-shift experiments in homing pigeons (deflection of ~90° counterclockwise with 6-hour clock shift, consistent with sun compass not sun navigation). Star navigation lacks evidence for time compensation needed for longitude detection. However, a meta-analysis suggests juvenile birds are more likely to correct under starry skies than overcast.
   - Infrasound (0.1-10 Hz): Correlational evidence from pigeon racing disturbances and atmospheric fluctuations (Hagstrum, 2000-2013), but one experiment removing pigeon cochleas showed no homing deficits. No experiment has demonstrated effects on migration.
   - Olfactory Cues: The most controversial and most extensively tested hypothesis (primarily in homing pigeons). Key findings include: olfactory nerve sectioning removes homing ability; "false release site" experiments show birds orient to the original sampling site (Benvenuti & Wallraff, 1985); artificial odour (benzaldehyde) experiments produce orientation consistent with displacement (Ioale et al., 1990). Criticisms include lack of repeatability, potential motivational (activation) rather than navigational roles, and deflector loft effects attributed to polarized light deflection. Stable odour gradients haven't been demonstrated beyond ~200 km, making olfactory navigation hard to reconcile with large migratory displacements. However, a recent experiment (Holland et al., 2009) showed adult catbirds displaced 1000 km lost the ability to correct when olfactory-deprived via zinc sulphate. A neurobiological study found both visual and olfactory brain areas become more active at night during the migratory period (Rastogi et al., 2011).
   - Magnetic Cues: Earth's magnetic field intensity proposed as a latitudinal cue (Viguier, 1882), but only functional over a coarse scale; fine-scale variations mean it may vary with longitude in places, making it a less consistent cue than often portrayed.

The review concludes that true navigation remains one of the great unanswered questions in science, but presents a positive outlook and identifies key remaining questions, emphasizing the need to understand what has been tried, what failed, and what is incomplete to move toward resolution.

--- SOURCE 22: Inheritance of migratory direction in a bird species ---
URL: https://gwern.net/doc/genetics/selection/artificial/1991-helbig.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This 1991 scientific paper by Andreas J. Helbig (published in Behavioral Ecology and Sociobiology) documents a cross-breeding experiment demonstrating the genetic basis of migratory direction in blackcaps (Sylvia atricapilla). The study crossed two Central European blackcap populations with widely different autumn migratory directions: SW-migrating birds from western Germany (Frankfurt/M and Radolfzell) and SE-migrating birds from eastern Austria (Bruck/Leitha and Halbturn). These populations differ in migratory direction by approximately 70°.

Methodology: Fifty nestlings were hand-raised from each population and tested in circular funnel-shaped orientation cages during their first autumn migration season (15-20 tests per bird). Next spring, 35 mixed pairs were formed (one bird from each side of the migratory divide), producing 68 F1 offspring across 16 pairs in 1987-1988, which were then tested identically.

Key results: The F1 offspring oriented toward mean directions intermediate between (and significantly different from) both parental populations. The eastern Austrian birds shifted direction during the season (134° in October to 185° in November, a 51° shift), corresponding to routing around the eastern Mediterranean toward East Africa, while FRG birds oriented consistently SW (~228-234°). The F1 hybrids showed only a small 10° seasonal shift. The variance of individual mean directions in F1 generation did not increase compared to parental groups, and inheritance of migratory direction was not sex-linked (no difference based on whether the SW-orienting parent was male or female).

Conclusions: The results demonstrate a genetic basis for migratory direction in birds with a phenotypically intermediate (additive/polygenic) mode of inheritance, suggesting either polygenic inheritance or a single locus without dominance. The author suggests F1 hybrids attempting to migrate in intermediate directions would likely cross the Alps, Mediterranean Sea, and parts of the Sahara — formidable barriers both parental populations avoid — significantly lowering hybrid survival chances in the contact zone.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The orientation of the F1 offspring was intermediate between and significantly different from that of both parental populations... the inheritance of migratory directions was not sex-linked. The data provide direct evidence for a genetic basis of migratory directions in birds and demonstrate a phenotypically intermediate mode of inheritance."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 24: Mapping the genomic diversity of the Eurasian blackcap ---
URL: https://d-nb.info/1373599324/34

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is the dissertation of Andrea Bours, completed at the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Biology and the Christian Albrechts University of Kiel (oral examination: 24.06.2025, examiners: Prof. Dr. Miriam Liedvogel and Prof. Dr. Christine Böhmer). The thesis maps genomic diversity in the Eurasian blackcap (Sylvia atricapilla), a songbird with wide migratory behavioral variation, to understand bird migration as a complex behavioral trait through genomic, transcriptomic, and epigenomic data.

The work comprises three chapters:
- **Chapter 1 (Population genomics):** Compared seasonal migratory populations with year-round residential populations (residents found in Southern Iberia, Macaronesia - Madeira, Canary Islands, Cape Verde, Azores - and Mallorca and Crete in the Mediterranean). Whole genome sequencing dataset expanded from 110 to 179 individuals. Population structure analysis revealed that residency evolved convergently multiple times across the different resident populations (both continental and island). Genome-wide selection analyses found no overlapping genomic regions under selection across resident populations, confirming convergent selection for the resident phenotype.
- **Chapter 2 (Transcriptomics/ASE):** Investigated allele-specific expression (ASE) patterns in three brain regions (hippocampus, hypothalamus, and another) comparing birds in migratory vs. non-migratory behavioral states. The variant calling pipeline was adjusted for RNA-seq data. The three brain regions showed distinct ASE patterns, with hippocampus and hypothalamus having ASE patterns distinguishable between behavioral states. 92 genes exhibited ASE across all three brain regions, including LDHB and Oat, which are linked to the circadian clock (known to be vital for migratory behavior).
- **Chapter 3 (Transposable elements):** Presented a high-quality TE annotation for the blackcap genome as a resource, investigating TE distribution along the genome and correlations with recombination rate, gene coverage, CpG island coverage, and GC content. A recent accumulation of LTRs was found - previously unseen in bird genomes. Recent vs. ancient TEs interact differently with the four genomic features studied.

The introduction provides substantial background: the blackcap is a widely used study species for bird migration (decades of heritability research; pivotal genome-wide study by Delmore et al. 2020 which created the reference genome and resequenced 110 individuals). The species shows variation in orientation (migratory divide across central Europe separating SE vs. SW migrants; a new NW orientation established in the 1950s), migratory distance (long-distance Scandinavian birds to sub-Saharan Africa; medium-distance central European birds to the Mediterranean; short-distance northern Spanish birds to southern Spain), and migratory propensity (latitudinal cline from obligatory migration in the north to residency in the south). Residents differ from migrants morphologically (bigger, rounder and shorter wings, larger bills, heavier tail feathers), behaviorally (more dominant during non-breeding months), and acoustically. Island populations exhibit "island syndrome" traits. Only one prior ASE study on bird migration exists (Swainson's thrushes). Avian genomes contain 4-10% TE content, lower than other vertebrates.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 26: Mapping seasonal migration in a songbird hybrid zone -- heritability, genetic correlations, and genomic patterns linked to speciation ---
URL: https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2313442121

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a PNAS research article (DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2313442121) published April 22, 2024, in Vol. 121, Issue 18, examining the genetics of seasonal migration in a hybrid zone between two subspecies of Swainson's thrushes (coastal and inland). Authors: Hannah C. Justen, Wendy E. Easton, and Kira E. Delmore. The article received 3,389 total views and 14 citations.

**Methodology:**
- Fitted archival tags to 333 adult male thrushes over 6 years (data downloaded from 72 birds) and 328 Motus radio tags to juvenile thrushes over 3 years (261 detected)
- Used reference genomes for both subspecies, low-coverage whole genome resequencing, and read-based imputation
- Tracked multiple migratory traits: orientation (4), distance (2), timing (2), plus wing morphology (wing length and Kipp's distance/wing shape)
- Used BSLMMs (bayesian sparse linear mixed models) for heritability estimates, GWAS, multitrait meta-analyses, and transcriptomic integration

**Key Findings:**
1. **Heritability:** Migratory traits show moderate-to-high heritability. Orientation and distance traits had high PVE values (e.g., winter longitude PVE = 0.83, fall distance PVE = 0.78), while timing variables were lower (spring departure PVE = 0.23; fall timing in juveniles = 0.21; wing shape PVE = 0.26). Strong predictive power for orientation/distance traits from GEBVs (r = 0.52 for winter longitude), low for timing/morphological traits.

2. **Genetic correlations:** Traits are strongly genetically correlated, especially orientation and distance (e.g., winter longitude and spring long. 30, r = -0.94; juveniles: fall orientation and wing shape, r = -0.85).

3. **Genomic mapping:** Migratory traits map to shared genomic regions. A large block of association on chromosome 1 (28–96 Mb) for wing length, containing many small structural variants (not large inversions), with reduced recombination and individuals clustering into three groups (consistent with SV heterozygosity). A 430 kb region on chromosome 5 encompassing a single gene (SGCZ - Sarcoglycan Zeta) was associated with fall orientation in juveniles. Two missense exonic SNPs identified in SLC6A19 and ITPRIP genes.

4. **Multitrait GWAS:** After multiple-test correction, 188 SNPs significantly associated with migration (184 adult, 4 juvenile), yielding 192 genes. GO analysis identified cholinergic receptor genes (CHRNB4, CHRNA5, CHRNA3) and thrombin receptor genes (F2R, F2RL2, F2RL1).

5. **Selection and speciation:** Significant SNPs fell in regions of elevated ΔFST (permutation test P < 0.001), indicating divergent selection at migration loci, supporting migration's role in maintaining reproductive isolation between subspecies.

6. **Transcriptomic integration:** Seven of 497 GxE (genotype-by-environment) differentially expressed genes overlapped with GWAS genes (more than expected by chance ~4.9), including CNTN5, CHRNA5, CHRNB4, ARHGEF28, DDX4, IQGAP2, and TLE1. CHRNA5 and CHRNB4 are in a region of elevated genomic differentiation on chromosome 12, with CHRNA5 overexpressed in hypothalamus during migratory period (inland subspecies) and CHRNB4 overexpressed in Cluster N during nonmigratory period (coastal subspecies).

**Background context:** The coastal thrushes migrate along the west coast of North America to Mexico/Guatemala/Honduras; inland thrushes migrate east across the Rocky Mountains through central North America to Colombia/Venezuela. Hybrids take intermediate, ecologically inferior routes. Hybrid zone is narrow with selection against hybrids (s = 0.19–0.40). Migration differences likely maintain reproductive isolation along with song and color differences.

**Relevance:** Results are relevant to genetics of adaptation and speciation (historically dominated by morphological traits) and conservation, since climate change alters selective pressures on migratory behaviors. Authors note their results can be integrated in future studies to predict organismal ability to adapt to environmental changes.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Migration requires the coordinated action of many traits, including orientation, timing, and wing morphology. We used genetic mapping to show these traits are highly heritable and genetically correlated, explaining how migration has evolved so rapidly in the past and suggesting future responses to climate change may be possible."
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:

This is a Perspective article published in Frontiers in Behavioral Neuroscience (21 January 2016, Volume 10, Article 3, doi: 10.3389/fnbeh.2016.00003) by Kira E. The perspective reviews the state of knowledge and future directions for investigating the genetic factors generating and maintaining variation in migratory orientation. Key points include:

- Migratory orientation is facilitated by magnetic and celestial compass systems providing directional and positional information. Quantitative genetic analyses suggest a strong genetic component, though the specific genes remain largely unknown.
- The authors discuss candidate gene analyses (e.g., Clock gene studies showing inconsistent results across taxa, and cryptochromes as the only suggested candidates for orientation specifically), highlighting drawbacks such as inconsistencies across studies and reliance on model organisms that don't migrate.

(2015) studies on Swainson's thrushes, where Delmore et al. found more migration candidates in differentiated regions due to an order of magnitude more variant sites (SNPs). For monarch butterflies, Zhan et al. (2014) used WGS to identify a region differentiating migrants and non-migrants containing collagen IV alpha-1 gene.
- The authors suggest using WGS-based admixture mapping at migratory divides (hybrid zones) as a promising future approach, combining benefits of QTL and association mapping. They note mapping studies for migration have so far been limited to salmonids.
- RNAseq and pathway/GO analyses are highlighted for comparing gene expression between phenotypes. McKinney et al. (2015) used RNAseq to identify differentially expressed genes related to brain growth and development in trout.
- Functional validation methods are discussed including RNAi, genome editing with engineered endonucleases (e.g., in monarch butterflies), and CRISPR/Cas technology, though these may rely on model organisms.

- The importance of accurate phenotype data is stressed, with advances in radar technologies for insects, injectable acoustic transmitters for fish, fluorescent nanoparticle tracking for small organisms, GPS/satellite tags for larger animals, and most notably miniaturized light-level geolocators that can now be fitted to songbirds.
- The authors recommend repeating classic crossbreeding experiments (e.g., Helbig's blackcap studies showing additive inheritance and possible control by few genes of large effect) using NGS tools and new movement ecology methods. They cite Delmore and Irwin (2014) who used geolocators with natural Swainson's thrush hybrids.
- The conclusion emphasizes that migratory divides represent the perfect arena for studying migratory orientation genetics, that epigenetics contributes to variation, and that a complete understanding requires integration across movement ecology, neurogenetics, and neurosensory sciences since orientation relies on visual perception and neuronal integration of celestial and magnetic cues.

The medium-sized songbird connects boreal forests of North America to tropical forests of Central and South America twice a year, joining approximately 200 Nearctic-Neotropical migrant bird species that fly thousands of miles annually, a journey that exists because it increases a bird's fitness (ability to raise young over its lifetime). The article details research on the two Swainson's Thrush subspecies: the "russet-backed" group (C. u. ustulatus) breeding along the Pacific Coast and the "olive-backed" inland group (C. u. swainsoni) breeding in boreal forests. Wintering areas ranged from western Mexico to central South America.
