## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779)Abstract

How animals navigate using single or several sensory modalities remains disputed. Humans often use distant landmarks such as mountain peaks as visual cues for orientation. Whether animals can also rely on distant visual cues while excluding other modalities, such as smell or visual maps, is difficult to test under natural conditions. We investigated this by releasing trained homing pigeons above thick ground fog from a plane. Birds were first trained to home individually from two ground sites, each ~15 km from their loft. Subsequently, trained individuals were released from a plane ~400 m above the terrestrial release sites during sunny conditions. This was followed by two experimental release conditions above continuous ground fog. Above the fog, pigeons cannot use a map or olfactory location cues, but may potentially use magnetic cues. When all landmarks were hidden by ground fog, pigeons showed poor orientation, tortuous flight paths, and descended through the fog within four min, advancing only ~0.1 km (0.1% of the distance) towards home. They subsequently waited for solar cues to continue homing. By contrast, when distant landmarks (alpine mountain tops) were visible, pigeons maintained strong homeward orientation, flying for 20 min and covering 96% of the distance to home, similar to ground-level controls (17 min, 80%). These results demonstrate that when known olfactory cues or local maps are excluded, distant landmarks—but not magnetic cues—enable efficient short-distance homing in experienced pigeons.

**Keywords:**navigation, orientation, _Columba livia_, boundary layer, homing flight, stratus fog, mountain range, Alps, olfactory, magnetic, distant landmarks

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779)1. Introduction

Navigation over large spatial scales often relies on the use of distant landmarks that remain visible across wide areas and provide stable directional information. In humans, distant visual features such as mountain ranges, coastlines, skylines, or prominent geological formations play a central role in large-scale orientation and wayfinding, particularly in unfamiliar or sparsely cued environments [[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B1-life-16-00933),[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B2-life-16-00933),[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B3-life-16-00933),[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B4-life-16-00933),[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B5-life-16-00933),[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B6-life-16-00933),[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B7-life-16-00933),[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B8-life-16-00933)]. Because such landmarks change little with observer position, they provide robust allocentric reference points that can anchor cognitive maps and support long-range route planning across kilometers or more [[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B9-life-16-00933),[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B10-life-16-00933)].

The use of visual landmarks is widespread across animal taxa [[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B11-life-16-00933),[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B12-life-16-00933),[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B13-life-16-00933),[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B14-life-16-00933),[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B15-life-16-00933),[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B16-life-16-00933),[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B17-life-16-00933),[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B18-life-16-00933),[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B19-life-16-00933)]. Mammals navigating open landscapes, marine animals orienting relative to coastlines, and insects using skyline profiles all exploit large-scale visual features that extend beyond the immediate vicinity, e.g., [[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B20-life-16-00933),[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B21-life-16-00933),[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B22-life-16-00933),[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B23-life-16-00933)]. In birds, large-scale visual cues have long been suspected to contribute to orientation and homing, particularly in species that repeatedly travel between fixed locations [[24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B24-life-16-00933)]. However, in free-ranging animals, distant landmarks are almost always embedded within a complex sensory environment that also includes local visual cues, olfactory information, wind-related cues, and geomagnetic signals, making it difficult to isolate their specific role.

Here, we use a novel experimental paradigm to disentangle visual, olfactory and magnetic information during small-scale (local homing) navigation: by releasing homing pigeons above ground fog, we abolish ground visual and known olfactory cues. Birds can only use magnetic cues or distant landmarks if they are available. We can thus directly resolve a long-standing debate, i.e., whether pigeons use magnetic cues or distant landmarks in the absence of potential olfactory cues.

Homing pigeons (_Columba livia_) provide a well-established model for studying large-scale navigation [[25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B25-life-16-00933),[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B26-life-16-00933)]. For many years, most of the investigations on pigeon navigation focused on the nature of the cues used by birds displaced to unfamiliar sites for determining their position with respect to the goal, so that the sensory basis of the navigational map by homing pigeons became a hot debated issue, mainly between the proponents of the olfactory map versus the proponents of the magnetic map [[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B27-life-16-00933),[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B28-life-16-00933),[29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B29-life-16-00933),[30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B30-life-16-00933)]. However, magnetic manipulation of any kind on homing pigeons never affected their homing performance [[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B31-life-16-00933)]. Conversely, a large body of evidence collected both with traditional (recording both initial orientation at the release site and homing performances) and satellite tracking methods supported a critical role of olfactory cues for pigeon homing from unfamiliar sites [[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B26-life-16-00933),[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B31-life-16-00933),[32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B32-life-16-00933),[33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B33-life-16-00933),[34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B34-life-16-00933)]. While pigeons prevented from smelling local odors both at an unfamiliar release site and in flight after release are impaired at homing [[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B26-life-16-00933),[33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B33-life-16-00933),[35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B35-life-16-00933)], the behavior of anosmic pigeons is comparable to that of control birds if they are familiar with the release site [[36](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B36-life-16-00933),[37](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B37-life-16-00933),[38](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B38-life-16-00933)], as familiar visual landmarks provide sufficient navigational information for guiding birds back home.

While the importance of local landmarks of the familiar overflown landscape is well documented [[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B11-life-16-00933),[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B13-life-16-00933),[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B16-life-16-00933)], the contribution of distant visual features—such as mountain ridges or large-scale topographic structures visible from afar—remains less clearly understood. One major reason is that distant and local landmarks are typically perceived together, preventing a clear separation of their respective contributions.

Testing the use of distant landmarks in the wild therefore presents a substantial methodological challenge. To assess their role unambiguously, nearby visual and olfactory cues must be removed to eliminate the use of memory while leaving distant features intact. A rare natural solution to this problem is provided by releases above continuous ground fog. During the occurrence of a dense fog layer, local ground-based visual cues are completely obscured. Depending on the weather conditions, elevated distant features, such as mountain ranges, may remain visible above the fog, allowing long-distance visual landmark use. This creates a natural experimental situation in which distant visual landmarks can be selectively present or absent, without altering the geographic position of the release site itself.

Releases above fog also modify the availability of non-visual navigational cues. Ground fog typically marks the upper limit of the atmospheric boundary layer, above which vertical mixing of air is strongly reduced. As a consequence, olfactory cues originating from the landscape below—known to play a major role in pigeon navigation near the ground—are largely unavailable above the fog layer [[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B26-life-16-00933),[34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B34-life-16-00933)]. In contrast, geomagnetic cues remain accessible and are not disrupted by altitude differences in this magnitude [[39](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B39-life-16-00933)]. Thus, releases above fog provide a unique opportunity to examine visual navigation under conditions in which olfactory information is minimized while magnetic information remains intact.

In the present study, we used this natural separation of sensory cues to test whether homing pigeons can use distant visual landmarks for navigation. Birds were first trained to home from familiar ground-based release sites. They were then transported by aircraft and released above the same sites under three conditions: clear air, fog with distant landmarks visible above the fog, and fog with distant landmarks obscured. By comparing homing performance across these conditions, we directly assessed the contribution of distant visual landmarks to pigeon homing while controlling for release-site familiarity and the availability of non-visual navigational cues.

### Hypotheses and Predictions

We tested the hypothesis that homing pigeons are able to use distant visual landmarks as part of their large-scale navigational system. If distant landmarks contribute to homing, we predicted that pigeons released above fog with visible distant landmarks would show faster homing, more direct routes, or higher homing success than pigeons released above fog when distant landmarks were not visible. Conversely, if distant landmarks are not used, homing performance should not differ between fog conditions, provided that magnetic cues remain available. Additionally, if olfactory cues are essential for navigation at this spatial scale, we predicted an overall reduction in homing performance for all releases above fog compared to ground-based releases, irrespective of distant landmark visibility.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779)2. Materials and Methods

### 2.1. General Setup and Experimental Background

When homing pigeons are trained from a certain location, i.e., when birds home repeatedly from a known point, they orient along specific landmarks such as forest edges or highways ([Figure 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#life-16-00933-f001)A) and become highly efficient in their homing performance. We made use of this situation by allowing birds to home from two terrestrial sites, and then having to home from these sites above a fog layer ([Figure 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#life-16-00933-f001)B) when they did not know (based on ground landmarks) at which site they were located (when released randomly with respect to the release site from the air). After training and experimentally releasing the birds from the ground, we released the pigeons above the atmospheric boundary layer. Under such conditions, there exists a temperature inversion below which intense cloud formation (thick ground fog) occurs ([Figure 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#life-16-00933-f002)B). Above this inversion, which marks the first atmospheric boundary layer, there can be (and always was) bright sunlight and either excellent, or limited visibility ([Figure 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#life-16-00933-f001)B vs. [Figure 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#life-16-00933-f001)C). During excellent visibility conditions, one can see landscape feature up to 200 km distance ([Figure 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#life-16-00933-f002)C), while during limited visibility conditions, distant landscape features are completely occulted ([Figure 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#life-16-00933-f002)B). Under such temperature inversion conditions, one can conduct experiments above the first boundary layer at only several hundred meters above ground, while under non-inversion conditions, the first atmospheric boundary layer is often at least 1500–5000 m above ground ([Figure 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#life-16-00933-f002)A). Interestingly, the air above the first boundary layer is almost never experienced by most birds that fly low to the ground, such as homing pigeons. Thus, the chemical composition of the air above the first boundary layer is not known or familiar to homing pigeons and cannot be used as a potential navigational guidance. However, the sun angle and magnetic information is unaffected by the boundary layer, and if useful for navigation, it could be utilized by the pigeons for navigating home.

### 2.2. Birds and Experimental Procedures

A total of 10 homing pigeons (_Columba livia_), approximately 12–18 months old, were used in this study. All birds were hatched, raised, and housed at a local homing pigeon station near Lake Constance (distance to shore: 300 m) at the village of Fischbach, southern Germany (approx. 47.6705° N, 9.4098° E). Pigeons were maintained as free-flying birds and handled in accordance with German and European regulations governing animal welfare.

The birds were trained to return home individually during sunny, non-windy conditions (wind speed on the ground <5 m/s) by releasing them 10 times on the ground from two different locations during the spring and summer (May to July) of 2014: NW (12 km, 327 degrees) of the loft (approx. 47.7613° N, 9.3213° E), and NE (17 km, 58 degrees) of the loft (approx. 47.7545° N, 9.6112° E). Each bird was then released individually from a Cessna plane flown ca. 400 m over these terrestrial release sites. The time between individual aerial releases was five minutes and that between terrestrial releases was 10 min, to ensure that no grouping of birds during homing flights could occur. The 4-seater Cessna plane (Cessna 172 Skyhawk) took off from Donaueschingen Airfield (EDTD) with two or three people (pilot: M.W., animal handler 1 and 2: various) and 10 pigeons in a transportation crate securely strapped into the passenger seats in the back. Once at the release site, pigeons were removed from the crate and allowed to view the landscape for ca. 5 min ([Video S1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#app1-life-16-00933)). At the moment of the release, the plane was shortly stalled to ca. 50 km/h speed and the bird were then held out of the window. All birds flew off immediately and never had any trouble getting away from the aerial influence of the plane ([Videos S2, S3, S5 and S6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#app1-life-16-00933)). As the plane needed to constantly move in the air, this resulted in release sites for individual birds that were not exactly above the terrestrial release sites, but within a few hundred meters when projected on the ground. For each bird, the release site GPS location was recorded at the time when the pigeon handler released the bird from their hand, holding it out of the Cessna window.

The altitude of 400 m above ground was chosen based on our previous experience representing an altitude with clear conditions above the ground fog that prevails in this lake basin area in fall and winter ([Video S4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#app1-life-16-00933)). Thus, birds were released from the same altitude above the terrestrial release sites during both sunny and foggy conditions ([Video S7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#app1-life-16-00933)). Each bird was released once from above each of the two terrestrial release sites during sunny conditions.

Experimental releases from the air took place during the fall period of 2024 when conditions of complete ground fog in the entire Lake Constance basin prevailed for at least from morning to midday. Individual pigeons were randomly assigned to one of the release sites, and the release order during the flights was randomly chosen. Each bird experienced both fog conditions with or without distant landmarks, but in a random order.

To habituate pigeons to carrying equipment, all birds were fitted with a dummy load 20 days prior to their first terrestrial releases. The dummy was comparable in size, shape, and mass to the GPS data logger used during the experiments. It was attached to the birds’ backs using a Velcro® strip glued to trimmed feathers, allowing secure attachment while minimizing discomfort or interference with flight. Birds flew freely with the dummy during the habituation period, ensuring normal flight behavior at the time of testing. The control homing flights (last flight from the ground training as well as both flights during the sunny condition aerial release) were recorded with GPS data loggers, as were both experimental flights during foggy conditions with and without distant landmarks. As expected for well-trained pigeons, during control flights, each bird flew home almost immediately without stopping along the way. Their return time to the loft or the vicinity of the loft, in case the bird was starting to perch after a continuous flight, was recorded.

### 2.3. GPS Data Loggers

We used miniature GPS data loggers (GPS cell phone loggers built in-house or by the University of Konstanz Technical Engineering workshop; GPS cell phone loggers from Fleetronic GSM, Belgium (company not in existence as of 2024), weight 25 g; sampling rate 1 fix every minute) to record the positional data of flying birds with an accuracy of ~4–10 m [[30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B30-life-16-00933)]. The positional fixes stored by the GPS data loggers include latitude, longitude and time of recording. The devices also provide information about altitude, but with insufficient precision to allow a reliable analysis. The tracks for each pigeon for each recorded release were visualized with Movebank and MapInfo (Dalkeith, UK).

#### Quantitative Analyses and Statistical Procedures

Using each pigeon’s GPS position when the bird was perching down for the first time after release, we calculated five homing performance parameters. Flight duration represents the time between an individual’s release, either on the ground or from the plane, and the time when this individual first perched for more than 5 min. Flight distance was again calculated for each individual based on its release GPS site. On the ground, this was one of two terrestrial release sites. From the air, the release sites differed slightly between individuals as the plane had to be in constant motion; thus, we could not release all birds at the exact location. The flight distance was then calculated as the beeline between the release GPS location and the GPS location of the first perching. From these two parameters, we calculated the homing percentage, i.e., the beeline distance to the first perching location divided by the entire distance to the loft, expressed in percent of the entire distance. Finally, the Distance to home was calculated as the absolute beeline distance between the first perching site and the home loft.

We also used an established homing flight parameter named the homing efficiency index (HEI), which takes into account whether a bird approaches or gets away from home during its flight. The HEI is defined as:

$$
H E I = \frac{a}{l} \times \frac{\left(\right. b - c \left.\right)}{b}
$$

 where a is the beeline between the release site and the last fix recorded, l is the track length (as in [[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B28-life-16-00933),[29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B29-life-16-00933)]), b is the beeline between the release site and home, and c is the beeline between the last fix recorded and home (all in km). Consequently, if the bird failed to approach home, then HEI < 0; if the bird approached home, then HEI > 0; and if the bird homed, HEI = 1. The various values of the three groups were compared with an ANOVA test, and the Dunn’s test was used for multiple comparisons. We used SPSS 31.0 for statistical analysis.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779)3. Results

### 3.1. General Observations

After 10 training flights from two locations located 12 NW or 17 km NE away from the loft, all 10 birds individually showed high homing performance during an experimental terrestrial release ([Figure 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#life-16-00933-f002)A,D). This is expected for trained homing pigeons.

When the same birds were released above thick ground fog ([Figure 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#life-16-00933-f002)B, [Videos S4 and S6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#app1-life-16-00933)), they did not attempt to home but rather descended through the fog layer and landed on the ground. As there was thick fog covering all altitudes down to the ground, the birds did not attempt to fly below the fog (which was not possible), but rather perched almost immediately when they were close to the ground ([Figure 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#life-16-00933-f002)E). All of these birds later returned home to the loft, but only when the sun reappeared and the fog had retracted or disappeared.

In contrast, when distant visual landmarks (the Alpine chain of mountain tops) were visible upon release from the plane ([Figure 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#life-16-00933-f002)C, [Video S3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#app1-life-16-00933)), the birds first descended down to several meters to tens of meters above the fog stratus layer ([Video S7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#app1-life-16-00933)). From there, they continued their homing flights along similar trajectories compared to their previous control flights from the ground ([Figure 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#life-16-00933-f001)). Although their homing was not perfect, most of the pigeons ended up very close to their home loft before perching for the first time after a continuous flight.

### 3.2. Quantifying the Homing Efficiency Index (HEI)

The HEI has been introduced to quantify the homing performance of pigeons and other animals, and was previously employed successfully to characterize such whole-animal performance parameters in natural settings [[30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B30-life-16-00933)]. When our pigeons were released on the ground after 10 training flights from each site, the showed—on average—a very strong and sharply increasing HEI over time ([Figure 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#life-16-00933-f003)A). Not all individuals were equally performant as expressed by their HEI; some individuals, in fact, showed low HEIs for a long time and only appeared to home at a time when the first individuals were already near home or had already reached the loft. Such a variety is, however, expected based on individual performance differences seen in all previous GPS tracking studies on homing in pigeons (for a quantitative comparison between experimental treatments, see [Figure 4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#life-16-00933-f004)). We use analysis of variance to test whether the HEI differs between different experimental settings. Because we randomized the sequence of treatments, we do not include this in the analysis as a covariate, nor do we include potential individual behavioral differences based on body weight, age, or sequence during a release event.

When the individuals were released from the plane above thick ground fog without visible landmarks ([Figure 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#life-16-00933-f003)B), all except one bird showed HEIs close to zero, implying that the birds did not attempt to home and made no spatial advances towards home during the time they were observed (i.e., here until they first perched and thus their GPS position remained stationary within a radius of 20 m).

In contrast, when birds were released from the plane above thick ground fog but with visibility of distant landmarks, they displayed high final HEIs (until they perched for the first time) and steep increases in HEI over time. Again, we observed the expected variability in HEI based on individual homing performance seen in all pigeon homing experiments.

We conclude that trained pigeons can home very efficiently when released 400 m above their release location from a plane.

### 3.3. Statistical Comparison Between Experimental Situations

To quantify the flight and homing performance of pigeons when they were subjected to the experimental situations described above, we performed ANOVA analyses with LSD post hoc comparisons between groups.

The homing efficiency index (HEI) of pigeons during the midpoint of an individual return flight differed between treatments, with the highest HEIs under control conditions and the lowest HEIs—indistinguishable from chance directions—under thick ground fog conditions ([Figure 4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#life-16-00933-f004)A, ANOVA, F = 25.8, df = 30, _p_< 0.001, LSD as indicated). Similarly, maximum HEIs and final HEIs differed between treatments ([Figure 4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#life-16-00933-f004)B, ANOVA, F = 66.1, df = 30, _p_< 0.001, LSD as indicated, and [Figure 4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#life-16-00933-f004)C, respectively, ANOVA, F = 123.9, df = 30, _p_< 0.001, LSD as indicated).

The flight duration of individuals was similar between control and fog-with-landmark conditions, but dramatically declined during fog-no-landmark conditions (ANOVA, F = 19.6, df = 30, _p_< 0.001, LSD significant as indicated in [Figure 5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#life-16-00933-f005), top panel).

Pigeons did not fly long distances when they could not see distant visual landmarks, and rather descended through the ground fog to immediately perch when getting close to the ground layer (2nd panel from top, ANOVA, F = 36.5, df = 30, _p_< 0.001, LSD significant as indicated in [Figure 5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#life-16-00933-f005)).

The homing performance of pigeons, expressed as the percent of distance an individual covered to approach home, was significantly lower in pigeons when they did not see distant landmarks while being released above thick ground fog ([Figure 5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#life-16-00933-f005), 3rd panel). In contrast, pigeons that were exposed to distant visual landmarks were able to show high homing percentages (ANOVA, F = 114.3, df = 30, _p_< 0.001, LSD significant as indicated in [Figure 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#life-16-00933-f003)).

Finally, as the ultimate performance parameter for a homing pigeon, i.e., how far from the home loft the pigeon perched without advancing further during the foggy conditions, it was clear that again the birds exposed to thick ground fog without visible landmarks in the distance did not home well. In contrast, the birds released during sunny control days (ANOVA, F = 85.9, df = 30, _p_< 0.001, LSD significant as indicated in [Figure 5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#life-16-00933-f005), lowest panel).

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779)4. Discussion

### 4.1. Use of Distant Landmarks Above the Fog

The central finding of this study is that homing pigeons are able to orient homeward and reach the home area after aerial release above a continuous fog layer, but only when distant visual landmarks are visible [[38](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B38-life-16-00933)]. When distant landmarks were obscured, pigeons failed to initiate directed homing and instead descended rapidly through the fog layer to the ground. This striking contrast demonstrates that, under these conditions, distant landmarks are not merely auxiliary cues but appear to be essential for establishing a usable navigational solution [[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B15-life-16-00933),[40](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B40-life-16-00933),[41](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B41-life-16-00933),[42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B42-life-16-00933),[43](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B43-life-16-00933),[44](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B44-life-16-00933),[45](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B45-life-16-00933)].

When distant landmarks such as mountain ranges were visible above the fog, pigeons flew home with a precision comparable to control releases under normal ground-based conditions [[46](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B46-life-16-00933),[47](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B47-life-16-00933)]. Flight paths were directed, homing success was high, and birds approached the loft area with remarkable spatial accuracy. This indicates that pigeons can rely on far-distance visual features alone to support large-scale navigation, even in the absence of local landmarks and other ground-based cues. The results thus provide direct experimental evidence that distant landmarks can function as primary navigational references rather than as supplementary cues used only near the goal (c.f.) [[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B18-life-16-00933),[48](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B48-life-16-00933)].

Our results are at first in apparent contrast to Wagner’s [[46](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B46-life-16-00933)] experiments, in which homing pigeons were released above opaque stratus over the Swiss Plateau to determine whether they could locate their loft beneath it. Wagner worked under thermic inversion conditions where the birds had ground visibility below the low stratus layer. Birds above the clouds appeared lost, while those that descended beneath them returned home directly. Wagner inferred, via atmospheric propagation modeling, that infrasonic waves virtually transmitted the location of the loft area. Supposedly, these signals would have been ducted beneath the inversion layer and would not have reached the release sites above it. The absence of homeward infrasonic cues above temperature inversions was used to explain the disorientation of Wagner’s birds, especially if such signals are the predominant cues used by pigeons to home. Because Wagner’s birds had ground visibility below the low stratus, it is expected that they home as soon as they descend through the stratus, exactly as Wagner observed.

### 4.2. Absence of Olfactory Information Above the Boundary Layer

A key aspect of the experimental design is that releases above fog occurred above the atmospheric boundary layer [[49](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B49-life-16-00933),[50](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B50-life-16-00933),[51](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B51-life-16-00933),[52](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B52-life-16-00933)]. Under such conditions, vertical mixing of air masses is strongly reduced, and landscape-derived olfactory cues are effectively unavailable [[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B26-life-16-00933),[34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B34-life-16-00933)]. The complete loss of oriented homing when birds were released above fog without visible landmarks therefore strongly suggests that olfactory navigation cannot operate under these conditions, and birds have to rely upon visual landmarks much more strongly [[38](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B38-life-16-00933)].

This finding reinforces earlier work showing that olfaction is critical for pigeon navigation near the ground but also demonstrates its limitations at higher altitudes. The present results indicate that olfactory cues are not only unnecessary when distant familiar landmarks are available, but also insufficient to support navigation when birds are isolated from the ground-level odor mosaic, as predicted [[29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B29-life-16-00933),[33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B33-life-16-00933),[34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B34-life-16-00933),[53](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B53-life-16-00933),[54](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B54-life-16-00933),[55](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B55-life-16-00933),[56](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B56-life-16-00933)]. Thus, the data provide a rare field-based exclusion of olfactory navigation, achieved without artificial manipulation of the birds themselves [[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B28-life-16-00933),[29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B29-life-16-00933)].

### 4.3. Implications for Magnetic Navigation and the “Map” Problem

The failure of pigeons to orient when released above fog without landmarks also has important implications for magnetic navigation [[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B27-life-16-00933),[57](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B57-life-16-00933),[58](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B58-life-16-00933),[59](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B59-life-16-00933)], which was, e.g., postulated for sea turtles [[60](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B60-life-16-00933)], amphibians [[61](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B61-life-16-00933)], salmon [[62](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B62-life-16-00933)], European eels [[63](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B63-life-16-00933)] and pigeons [[64](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B64-life-16-00933),[65](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B65-life-16-00933)]. Magnetic information—both directional and positional—remains available at altitude and is unaffected by fog. Birds released under landmark-free fog conditions were therefore still able to perceive magnetic field parameters and to maintain a magnetic heading. Nevertheless, they did not initiate consistent homing trajectories.

This strongly suggests that magnetic cues alone do not provide pigeons with sufficient positional (“map”) information under these conditions, c.f. [[66](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B66-life-16-00933)]. If pigeons possessed a functional magnetic map based on spatial gradients or intersections of magnetic parameters (e.g., total intensity, inclination, declination), they should have been able to determine their approximate location and select an appropriate homeward direction, c.f. [[39](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B39-life-16-00933),[60](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B60-life-16-00933)]. The observed behavior instead indicates that, while pigeons may maintain a magnetic compass, they do not know where they are on such a map in the absence of visual or olfactory information. As pigeons experiencing visual landmarks returned home under similar conditions, it is unlikely that any kind of motivational aspect could be involved in their decision to immediately descend into the fog and stay stationary [[67](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B67-life-16-00933)].

This distinction between a compass and a map is critical. The data suggest that pigeons released above fog without landmarks possess orientation mechanisms similar to birds in complete darkness and clouds [[68](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B68-life-16-00933)] but lack positional knowledge. As a consequence, they appear unable to translate directional information into a navigational decision and instead abandon flight at altitude, descending through the fog to regain access to ground-based cues.

#### Descent Behavior and Decision-Making Under Uncertainty

The rapid descent through the fog layer observed in landmark-free conditions provides insight into how pigeons respond to navigational uncertainty [[69](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B69-life-16-00933),[70](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B70-life-16-00933)]. Rather than maintaining altitude and flying in an arbitrary or magnetically defined direction, birds quickly descend to the ground, presumably to re-enter a sensory environment where reliable cues become available. This behavior supports the idea that pigeons actively evaluate cue reliability and switch strategies when navigation becomes unreliable [[71](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B71-life-16-00933)].

In contrast, when distant landmarks were visible, pigeons maintained flight just tens of meters above the fog layer. This altitude appears to represent a compromise between remaining close to the visual horizon and avoiding descent into the fog itself. From this position, distant features such as the Alps were clearly visible on days when fog was restricted to the lowlands, whereas on days when fog extended into higher elevations, no such features were available. This natural variability proved crucial for separating the effects of distant landmark visibility, and is in contrast to the conditions experienced by birds in Wagner’s experiments with low stratus layers [[46](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B46-life-16-00933)].

### 4.4. Precision of Navigation Using Far-Distance Visual Projections

One of the most striking aspects of the results is the spatial precision achieved by pigeons navigating solely with distant landmarks, known from technical systems [[72](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B72-life-16-00933),[73](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B73-life-16-00933),[74](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13300779#B74-life-16-00933)]. args.summary:
This is a peer-reviewed scientific article published in Life (Basel) on June 1, 2026 (DOI: 10.3390/life16060933), investigating whether homing pigeons (Columba livia) use distant visual landmarks for navigation. The study was conducted by researchers from the Max Planck Institute of Animal Behavior (Germany), University of Konstanz, Ohio State University, and University of Pisa, with Martin Wikelski as corresponding author.

**Methodology:** Ten homing pigeons (12-18 months old, housed near Lake Constance, Fischbach, southern Germany) were trained to home individually from two ground sites (~12 km NW and ~17 km NE of the loft) during May-July 2014. They were then released from a Cessna plane ~400 m above the terrestrial release sites under three conditions: (1) clear/sunny air, (2) fog with distant landmarks (Alpine mountain tops) visible above the fog, and (3) fog with no visible landmarks. Releases above fog occur above the atmospheric boundary layer, eliminating olfactory cues while leaving magnetic cues intact. Flight tracking used GPS data loggers (25 g, ~4-10 m accuracy). Homing performance was quantified using flight duration, distance, homing percentage, distance to home, and the Homing Efficiency Index (HEI).

**Key Results:**
- When released above fog WITHOUT visible landmarks, pigeons showed poor orientation, tortuous flight paths, and descended through the fog within 4 minutes, advancing only ~0.1 km (0.1% of distance) toward home. They subsequently waited for solar cues before homing.
- When distant landmarks (Alps) WERE visible above the fog, pigeons maintained strong homeward orientation, flying 20 minutes and covering 96% of the distance home—comparable to ground-level controls (17 min, 80%).
- Statistical analyses (ANOVA) showed significant differences between treatments for HEI (F=25.8 to 123.9, p<0.001), flight duration (F=19.6), flight distance (F=36.5), homing percentage (F=114.3), and distance to home (F=85.9).

**Conclusions:**
1. Distant visual landmarks are essential (not merely auxiliary) for homing when olfactory and local visual cues are unavailable; they can function as primary navigational references.
2. Magnetic cues alone were insufficient for positional ("map") information—despite magnetic cues remaining available above fog, birds did not initiate consistent homing without landmarks. This supports the compass-versus-map distinction.
3. Olfactory cues are unavailable above the boundary layer and are insufficient for navigation at altitude, but this experiment provided a rare field-based exclusion of olfactory navigation without artificial manipulation.
4. Birds displayed rapid descent behavior under uncertainty, suggesting they actively evaluate cue reliability and switch strategies when navigation becomes unreliable.
5. Pigeons achieved remarkable spatial precision using only far-distance visual projections, flying just tens of meters above the fog layer when landmarks were visible.

The article contrasts its findings with Wagner's earlier experiments above opaque stratus over the Swiss Plateau, where infrasonic wave propagation was proposed as a homing cue. This study adds direct experimental evidence to the longstanding debate between olfactory map and magnetic map proponents in pigeon navigation.

**Keywords:** navigation, orientation, Columbia livia, boundary layer, homing flight, stratus fog, mountain range, Alps, olfactory, magnetic, distant landmarks.

--- SOURCE 1: Avian Navigation and Orientation ---
URL: https://avesbiology.com/nav_orient.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage provides a comprehensive scientific overview of avian navigation and orientation mechanisms. It distinguishes between orientation (moving in a compass direction) and true navigation (locating one's position relative to a destination), based on the two-step process first described by Kramer (1953, 1957): determining the correct direction of travel and identifying that direction. Naïve juvenile birds often rely on vector navigation (maintaining a direction for a set time/distance), while experienced adults demonstrate true navigation, as shown in displacement experiments with European Starlings (Perdeck 1958), Common Teal (Wolff 1970), and White-crowned Sparrows (Thorup et al. 2007). Some species' juveniles can compensate for displacement, however. The "clock-and-compass" concept explains how first-time migrants navigate, potentially using magnetic and photoperiodic beacons (Chernetsov and Utvenko 2025). True navigation is likely based on a bi-coordinate grid system using cues that vary along gradients (Thorup and Holland 2009).

The webpage details four compass mechanisms:
1. **Non-compass orientation**: Birds use landmarks and topographic features like coastlines and mountain ridges (e.g., European migrants turning southwest along the Alps).
2. **Star compass**: Emlen's classic planetarium experiments (1967) showed Indigo Buntings learn north by observing stellar rotation around the celestial pole, using Emlen funnels to record orientation. Star-compass use is learned, not innate, and relies on relative constellations rather than specific stars.
3. **Sun compass**: First demonstrated by Kramer (1950); based on the sun's azimuth using an internal clock. Clock-shifting experiments (Schmidt-Koenig 1958) caused 90-degree orientation errors. Learning is tied to the left hippocampus (Gagliardo et al. 2005), with pigeons first able to use it around 12 weeks old.
4. **Polarized light**: Several migratory species (Savannah Sparrows, Swainson's and Gray-cheeked thrushes, White-throated Sparrows) use polarization patterns at sunrise/sunset to calibrate their magnetic compass.
5. **Magnetic cues**: First proposed in 1859 and experimentally demonstrated in 1968 (European Robins). The avian magnetic compass is an inclination compass (distinguishing pole vs. equator, not north vs. south) and is light-dependent, based on cryptochrome molecules in the retina (Mouritsen et al. 2004). Cluster N in the forebrain processes magnetic visual information. Wu and Dickman (2012) identified vestibular brainstem neurons encoding magnetic field direction, intensity, and polarity. Nordmann et al. (2025) traced pigeon magnetoreception to hair cells in inner ear semicircular canals via electromagnetic induction, with signals processed in vestibular nuclei, midbrain cortex, and hippocampus. Iron-oxide magnetoreceptors in the upper beak (maghemite platelets and magnetite clusters) may act as a three-axis magnetometer for detecting field intensity and direction.

For true navigation, birds need "map" information. Mechanisms include visual landmark recognition (used by homing pigeons and food-caching species), path integration (dead reckoning), olfactory cues (studied in homing pigeons with conflicting results; possibly used by tube-nosed seabirds via dimethyl sulfide), and infrasound maps (found implausible due to diffuse sources). The most likely navigational system is bi-coordinate magnetic mapping, using magnetic inclination (for latitude) and intensity (for longitude). A notable example is displaced European Reed Warblers in northwestern Russia that corrected their spring migration direction after longitudinal displacement (Chernetsov et al. 2008), demonstrating use of a magnetic grid map.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"True navigation, as first described by Kramer (1953, 1957), is a two-step process: (1) determining the correct direction of travel, and (2) being able to correctly identify that direction."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: [PDF] COMMENTARY Forty years of olfactory navigation in birds - CORE ---
URL: https://core.ac.uk/download/pdf/80243808.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific commentary article by Anna Gagliardo (Department of Biology, University of Pisa, Italy) published in The Journal of Experimental Biology (2013, Vol. 216, pp. 2165-2171) reviewing 40 years of research on olfactory navigation in birds, with a focus on homing pigeons.

**Historical background:** The olfactory navigation hypothesis was formulated in response to experimental findings. About 40 years ago, Floriano Papi and colleagues (1971) conducted experiments in Tuscany showing that pigeons with sectioned olfactory nerves never returned home when released at unfamiliar sites, while intact birds homed successfully. Around the same time, Wallraff's research on pigeons raised in confined aviaries revealed that birds sheltered from winds by glass screens (despite full horizon view) were unable to orient homeward, while birds exposed to winds through a palisade (despite obstructed views) were unimpaired, suggesting an "atmospheric factor" was involved in navigation.

**The olfactory navigation hypothesis (Papi et al., 1972):** Pigeons at their home loft learn windborne environmental odours in association with wind direction. Once at a release site, they recognize local odours and recall from which direction these odours come from at home, allowing them to determine the direction of displacement.

**Key experimental evidence:**
- Benvenuti and Wallraff (1985) demonstrated that birds transported in airtight containers and exposed to air at a "false release site" oriented towards the "false home direction" from that site.
- Anosmia specifically impairs navigation only at unfamiliar sites; anosmic pigeons home normally from familiar locations using visual landscape cues (Biro et al., 2004; Holland, 2003; Gagliardo et al., 2001b).
- Unilateral nostril occlusion combined with unilateral treatments produced impairment only when the plug was placed contralaterally to the treated side (Benvenuti and Gagliardo, 1996).
- Experiments using ZENK immediate early gene expression showed activation of the piriform cortex during navigational tasks from unfamiliar locations but not during homing from familiar sites (Gagliardo et al., 2007; Patzke et al., 2010).
- Trigeminal nerve section (proposed magnetoreceptor pathway) was shown to be neither necessary nor sufficient for navigation; olfactory nerve section impaired homing despite intact trigeminal nerves (Gagliardo et al., 2006). Upper beak iron-containing cells were later shown to be macrophages, not magnetoreceptors (Treiber et al., 2012).
- Wind manipulation experiments (using deflectors or corridor cages with fans) produced predicted deflections in initial orientation. Deflector results were potentially confounded by polarized light effects, but fan-based wind inversion experiments were not.
- Artificial odour experiments (Papi et al., 1974): pigeons exposed to turpentine from north and olive oil from south oriented according to their learned associations, demonstrating that birds can incorporate artificial odours into their olfactory map.
- GPS tracking data showed that birds deprived of environmental olfactory information displayed tortuous tracks and poor homeward orientation, contradicting the "olfactory activation hypothesis" (Gagliardo et al., 2011).

**Structure of the olfactory map:** The olfactory map does not provide exact position/distance like a bicoordinate system but provides information about direction of displacement only. Wallraff and Andreae (2000) collected air samples from 96 sites within 200 km around a loft and found volatile organic compounds distributed along fairly stable spatial gradients. Simulation experiments showed that stable ratios of at least three volatile compounds provide sufficient information for homeward orientation comparable to experimental observations.

**Olfactory navigation in wild species:** Evidence remains at an early stage. Studies showed homing impairment in anosmic swifts (Fiaschi et al., 1974) and anosmic starlings (Wallraff et al., 1995). Holland et al. (2009) tested migrating catbirds (Dumetella carolinensis) in Illinois displaced east to New Jersey. Juvenile catbirds oriented south regardless of manipulation (consistent with first-flight inability to navigate), while anosmic adult catbirds oriented southward instead of westward like controls—providing the first evidence that olfactory cues are involved in wild bird navigation during migration.

**Ongoing debate:** The article addresses the lingering resistance to accepting olfactory navigation, particularly versus the poorly supported idea of magnetic-based position-finding. The author notes that magnetic manipulations do not affect homing performance and that direct experimental evidence for a geomagnetic-based position-finding mechanism is lacking. Open questions include whether olfactory navigation is widespread in birds, whether seabird oceanic navigation depends on olfactory cues, whether olfactory cues are key during migration, what specific chemical compounds are used, and whether birds use odour gradients (Wallraff's model) or patches/mosaic maps (Papi's original model).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Forty years ago, Papi and colleagues discovered that anosmic pigeons cannot find their way home when released at unfamiliar locations. They explained this phenomenon by developing the olfactory navigation hypothesis: pigeons at the home loft learn the odours carried by the winds in association with wind direction; once at the release site, they determine the direction of displacement on the basis of the odours perceived locally and orient homeward."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: True navigation in birds: from quantum physics to global migration ---
URL: https://zslpublications.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/jzo.12107

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a review article titled "True navigation in birds: from quantum physics to global migration" by R. A. Holland, published in the Journal of Zoology (Volume 293, Issue 1, pp. 1-15, first published 16 January 2014, DOI: 10.1111/jzo.12107). The author is from the School of Biological Sciences, Queen's University Belfast, UK (corresponding author, email r.holland@qub.ac.uk).

The review addresses the controversial and unresolved scientific question of how birds achieve true navigation—the ability to return to a known goal from an unfamiliar place. Despite over 50 years of research, the field remains contentious, described by some as suffering from a "chronic disease" (Mouritsen & Hore, 2012). However, significant advances in the last 20 years have come from integrating disciplines including neurobiology, molecular biology, and quantum physics.

KEY CONCEPTS AND FINDINGS:

1. True Navigation Definition: First conceptualized by Donald Griffin (1952) as "type III" navigation, with the term "true navigation" adopted by Keeton (1974). The most current definition is "the ability of an animal to return to its original location after displacement to a site in unfamiliar territory, without access to familiar landmarks, goal emanating cues, or information about the displacement route" (Phillips et al., 2006). The review distinguishes "migratory true navigation" as navigating to a specific breeding or wintering area (not just the point of departure) after displacement.

2. Evidence: Perdeck's classic 1958 study demonstrated adult but not juvenile birds can perform migratory true navigation. More recent studies show adult white-crowned sparrows can correct toward their winter area after 3700 km displacement (Thorup et al., 2007), and reed warblers correct for 1000 km displacements (Chernetsov et al., 2008). True navigation is experience-based—adults have learned from previous journeys. However, some studies show failures, including Perdeck's 1967 repeat (no correction in Spain), and white/golden crowned sparrows translocated from the US to Korea failing to return. Limits appear to vary, with evidence of at least 3700 km range but possibly only ~2000 km in starlings.

3. Map and Compass Theory: Kramer's (1953) "map and compass" hypothesis remains the most robust explanation—navigation is a two-step process of determining position (map step) and direction (compass step). True navigation refers specifically to the map step. The bi-coordinate map theory proposes animals learn environmental gradients that vary predictably with latitude and longitude (potentially magnetic field intensity/inclination, sun's arc/sunrise time).

4. Study Methods: Two main approaches are used: (a) laboratory-based migratory restlessness studies (Emlen & Emlen, 1966) using orientation cages, and (b) field-based displacement studies with remote tracking (GPS/satellite telemetry). Both systems have limitations—lab studies lack natural relevance, while field studies suffer from logistical difficulty, lack of statistical power, and expensive tracking technology (GPS telemetry too large for small songbirds, no migratory true navigation study using GPS telemetry yet published).

5. Environmental Cues Examined:
   - Celestial Cues: Sun navigation is generally rejected based on clock-shift experiments in homing pigeons (deflection of ~90° counterclockwise with 6-hour clock shift, consistent with sun compass not sun navigation). Star navigation lacks evidence for time compensation needed for longitude detection. However, a meta-analysis suggests juvenile birds are more likely to correct under starry skies than overcast.
   - Infrasound (0.1-10 Hz): Correlational evidence from pigeon racing disturbances and atmospheric fluctuations (Hagstrum, 2000-2013), but one experiment removing pigeon cochleas showed no homing deficits. No experiment has demonstrated effects on migration.
   - Olfactory Cues: The most controversial and most extensively tested hypothesis (primarily in homing pigeons). Key findings include: olfactory nerve sectioning removes homing ability; "false release site" experiments show birds orient to the original sampling site (Benvenuti & Wallraff, 1985); artificial odour (benzaldehyde) experiments produce orientation consistent with displacement (Ioale et al., 1990). Criticisms include lack of repeatability, potential motivational (activation) rather than navigational roles, and deflector loft effects attributed to polarized light deflection. Stable odour gradients haven't been demonstrated beyond ~200 km, making olfactory navigation hard to reconcile with large migratory displacements. However, a recent experiment (Holland et al., 2009) showed adult catbirds displaced 1000 km lost the ability to correct when olfactory-deprived via zinc sulphate. A neurobiological study found both visual and olfactory brain areas become more active at night during the migratory period (Rastogi et al., 2011).
   - Magnetic Cues: Earth's magnetic field intensity proposed as a latitudinal cue (Viguier, 1882), but only functional over a coarse scale; fine-scale variations mean it may vary with longitude in places, making it a less consistent cue than often portrayed.

The review concludes that true navigation remains one of the great unanswered questions in science, but presents a positive outlook and identifies key remaining questions, emphasizing the need to understand what has been tried, what failed, and what is incomplete to move toward resolution.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The most current definition of true navigation is 'the ability of an animal to return to its original location after displacement to a site in unfamiliar territory, without access to familiar landmarks, goal emanating cues, or information about the displacement route' (Phillips et al., 2006)."

"Recently, this problem was described as a 'chronic disease' (Mouritsen & Hore, 2012), suggesting that the field is unhealthy, in a scientific sense, and data should not be trusted."

"The clearest example (Perdeck, 1958) demonstrated that adult but not juvenile birds are capable of migratory true navigation."

"Migratory true navigation is thus experience based, that is an ability to correct and return to a known goal from an unfamiliar place is a consequence of information learned on a previous journey to, or from that goal."

"No aspect of bird navigation contributes to its reputation as a controversial field more than that of the role of olfactory cues in the true navigation map."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 5: Map and compass navigation: the mechanism and ontogeny of animal maps ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7618438

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific review article published in Animal Behaviour (2025), titled "Map and compass navigation: the mechanism and ontogeny of animal maps" by Joe Morford, Joe Wynn, Patrick Lewin, Paris Jaggers, Lewis Lancaster-Reeves, Adelaide Sibeaux, Oliver Padget, and Tim Guilford (University of Oxford, University of Liverpool, and University of Rochester). The article is open access (CC BY license), PMID 41358193, received Feb 12, 2025, accepted Apr 25, 2025.

**Core topic:** The review examines map and compass navigation—a two-step process where animals use a map to determine goalward directions and a compass to orient in those directions—focusing on the mechanisms and ontogeny (development) of animal maps.

**Key framework:** The article deconstructs maps into three components:
1. **Cues**: Environmental properties animals perceive to determine goalward directions. These must be temporally stable and vary predictably in space. Main cue modalities include: magnetic (inclination, intensity, declination), visual (landmarks, geometric relationships, landscape features), and olfactory cues. Other suggested cues include sun arc, Coriolis force, infrasound, and gravity vectors (though with limited controlled experimental evidence).
2. **Structure**: The organization of information used to determine goalward direction. The article distinguishes between **discrete structures** (recognizing distinct places/regions; includes terms like mosaic maps, cognitive maps, signposts) and **continuous structures** (exploiting predictable spatial gradients; includes grid maps, gradient maps, triangulation/trilateration). The structure is limited by underlying cue distributions but also depends on how animals perceive and respond to cues.
3. **Implementation**: Strategies for approaching goals (waypoint navigation vs. direct goalward orientation) and combining multiple map cues. Examples include magnetic+cue combination in turtles, visual+olfactory in pigeons, and gradient combination strategies.

**Ontogeny findings:**
- Some map cues rely on inherited rules (e.g., hatchling loggerhead turtles and salmon inherit responses to magnetic cues), sometimes combined with imprinting on natal site cues.
- Homing pigeons have a sensitive learning period (3-4 months after fledging) for developing olfactory maps, but can also learn cues later when free flying.
- Visual landscape cues are less likely to be developmentally fixed and must be learned through experience.
- Map structures can be inherited (e.g., turtle signposts) or developed through learning (e.g., green turtles displaced up to 100 km appear to use more complex maps).
- Map implementation strategies remain relatively unexplored in terms of their ontogeny.

**Path integration hypothesis:** The authors suggest that path integration (tracking vectors of self-motion through integrating distance and direction, also called dead reckoning) plays an important role in map learning—well documented in mammals over small spatial scales—and could play a similar role in other taxa and over larger spatial scales. This implies path integration may be more taxonomically widespread and play a greater role in navigational learning than currently appreciated.

**Key conclusions:** Learning plays an important role in map ontogeny for many examples, especially those requiring gradient extrapolation or flexible navigation between multiple goals. However, it remains unclear how animals resolve the spatial arrangement of cues to learn maps, particularly over large scales. The review calls for further experimental and correlative studies (aided by advances in animal tracking technology) to better understand map structure, ontogeny, and how animals combine map cues.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 6: Magnetic displacement experiment challenges long-held theories on how migratory birds navigate ---
URL: https://phys.org/news/2024-11-magnetic-displacement-held-theories-migratory.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
A study by Bangor University, published November 13, 2024 in the journal *Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences*, challenges long-held theories about how migratory birds navigate. The research, led by Professor Richard Holland and involving Eurasian reed warblers (Acrocephalus scirpaceus), found that birds use only the Earth's magnetic inclination and declination to determine their position and direction—contradicting the longstanding belief that all components of the Earth's magnetic field, particularly total intensity, are essential for accurate navigation.

METHODOLOGY: In a carefully designed "virtual displacement" experiment, researchers exposed warblers to artificially altered magnetic inclination and declination values that simulated a relocation to a different geographic location, while keeping total magnetic intensity unchanged. Despite the virtual displacement, the birds adjusted their migratory routes as if they were in the new location, demonstrating compensatory behavior.

KEY FINDINGS: The birds were able to extract both positional and directional information from magnetic inclination and declination cues alone, even when these conflicted with other magnetic field components. This provides strong evidence supporting the "map-and-compass" theory of avian navigation while refining the understanding of how the 'map' works. The study suggests birds possess a complex and flexible internal navigation system that allows them to adapt to unfamiliar environmental conditions.

SIGNIFICANCE: The discovery advances understanding of avian navigation, supports the theory of a flexible internal navigation system in birds, and opens new avenues for research into animal navigation with potential implications for broader biological studies on how animals interact with their environment. The paper is authored by Florian Packmor et al., titled "Migratory birds can extract positional information from magnetic inclination and magnetic declination alone."
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"What's interesting is that these findings reveal that the birds don't necessarily need all components of the Earth's magnetic field to determine their position," said Professor Richard Holland, who specializes in animal behavior and led the study. "They can rely solely on inclination and declination, which are also used in compass orientation, to extract their location." "It remains to be seen whether birds use the total intensity of the Earth's magnetic field for navigation in other contexts, but what we've shown is that these two components—magnetic inclination and declination—are enough to provide positional information," explained Richard.

The author is affiliated with the School of Biological Sciences, Queen's University Belfast, UK.

The review addresses true navigation in birds—the ability to return to a known goal from an unfamiliar location—which remains one of the great unanswered questions in science despite over 50 years of research. The field has been described as having a "chronic disease" (Mouritsen & Hore, 2012) due to conflicting results. The review aims to present these conflicting findings and assess the state of the field, particularly from a behavioral biologist's perspective.

Key topics covered:
1. **Migratory true navigation**: Donald Griffin first conceptualized bird navigation (1952), defining "type III" navigation (returning to a goal after displacement). The term "true navigation" was adopted by Keeton (1974). The most current definition (Phillips et al., 2006) is "the ability of an animal to return to its original location after displacement to a site in unfamiliar territory, without access to familiar landmarks, goal emanating cues, or information about the displacement route." Migratory true navigation is defined as navigating to a breeding or wintering area after displacement.

2. **Evidence**: Perdeck's landmark study (1958) demonstrated adult but not juvenile birds are capable of migratory true navigation. White-crowned sparrows corrected for displacements of 3700 km (Thorup et al., 2007), while starlings showed limits around 2000 km. Failures to correct for displacements are also documented (e.g., sparrows translocated from US to Korea did not return).

3. **Theory**: The "map and compass" hypothesis (Kramer, 1953) proposes a two-step process—determining position relative to the goal (map step) and determining direction (compass step). A bi-coordinate gradient map theory suggests animals learn environmental gradients varying predictably with latitude and longitude.

4. **Study methods**: Migratory restlessness in orientation cages provides a laboratory correlate; field-based displacement studies and remote tracking are also used, though tracking devices remain too large for small songbirds, and no study of migratory true navigation using GPS telemetry has yet been published.

5. **Environmental cues assessed**:
   - **Celestial cues** (sun and stars): Generally rejected as navigation maps based on clock-shift experiments with homing pigeons; however, some meta-analyses suggest celestial cues play a role in juvenile corrections.
   - **Infrasound**: Correlational evidence suggests disruption affects pigeon homing, but no experiment has shown infrasound effects on migration; cochlea removal did not produce homing deficits.
   - **Olfactory cues**: The most extensively tested and controversial hypothesis. Olfactory nerve sectioning removes homing ability in pigeons. Key experiments include "false release site" tests and artificial odor (benzaldehyde) experiments showing directional orientation consistent with displacement. However, results suffer from lack of repeatability and competing interpretations (e.g., activation hypothesis vs. navigational cues). Stable olfactory gradients have not been demonstrated beyond approximately 200 km, making it hard to explain long-distance migration displacement experiments. A notable study showed catbirds displaced 1000 km with olfactory deprivation could not correct (Holland et al., 2009).
   - **Magnetic cues**: Earth's magnetic field intensity proposed as a cue over a century ago (Viguier, 1882); potentially indicates latitudinal position but only at coarse scale. Magnets attached to bird heads failed to find homing deficits, although behavioral responses to altered magnetic fields have been demonstrated since the 1960s (Merkel & Wiltschko, 1965).

The review concludes that understanding what has been tried, what has failed, and what is incomplete will aid in resolving the field of true navigation in migratory birds.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific article by Hans G. Wallraff, published in Communicative & Integrative Biology (2014, PMCID: PMC4203629, PMID: 25346789), arguing that pigeon homing from unfamiliar areas relies on olfactory signals. - Atmospheric ratio gradients are moved by winds across birds even when confined in an aviary, solving the problem of how birds learn gradient alignments without exploration flights—a problem other gradient-based hypotheses cannot resolve.

Concluding remarks: A global system (geomagnetism, celestial bodies, gravity) is unlikely to enable goal-oriented navigation over ranges from 20 km to hundreds of kilometers. --- SOURCE 22: True Navigation: Sensory Bases of Gradient Maps ---
URL: https://pigeon.psy.tufts.edu/asc/Phillips

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific chapter by John B. Phillips, Klaus Schmidt-Koenig, and Rachel Muheim (Virginia Tech & Duke University) reviews the sensory bases of "true navigation" - the ability of animals to home over tens to hundreds of kilometers without relying on familiar landmarks or displacement route information. True navigation requires both a compass (sense of direction) and a map (sense of geographic position).

**Key Concepts:**
- True navigation has been demonstrated in various vertebrates and one invertebrate (spiny lobster; Boles & Lohmann, 2003)
- Vertebrates possess multiple compass systems (sun, star, polarized light, and magnetic compasses), with celestial polarized light patterns serving as the primary calibration reference for the compass in birds
- A navigational map differs from place/bearing/mosaic maps in that it can be extrapolated to unfamiliar sites; gradient maps require learning the alignment and steepness of environmental gradients within the home range and extrapolating beyond familiarity
- Non-parallel gradients of two or more map components enable bicoordinate position fixing

**Theoretical Considerations:**
- Magnetic gradient maps operate over distances >50-75 km (regional gradients) or <5-10 km (local gradients), but are unreliable at intermediate distances (10-20 km to 50-70 km) where local and regional variation are similar in magnitude
- Schmidt-Koenig (1966, 1970) found pigeons showed markedly poorer homing orientation from intermediate distances (30-70 km) compared to closer and farther sites, suggesting different navigational mechanisms for short vs. long-distance homing
- Gradient maps range from complex bicoordinate systems to simple stimulus/response systems that trigger discrete behaviors

**Olfactory Map Evidence:**
- Olfactory deprivation experiments showing effects on homing have often failed to rule out alternative explanations (e.g., effects on trigeminal nerve-mediated magnetoreception, or on distinguishing home from non-home)
- Deflector loft experiments (rotating wind direction) initially appeared to support the olfactory map hypothesis, but four critical experiments demonstrated the effect is caused by rotation of light cues, not wind-borne odors - specifically via polarized-light-based calibration of the sun/magnetic compass
- Split-brain experiments (Foà et al., 1986) showed hemispheric-specific olfactory map effects, but these can be alternatively explained by differently calibrated sun compass systems on each side of the brain
- Conclusion: The literature does not provide compelling evidence for olfactory involvement in a long-distance gradient map; olfactory cues may instead play a role in a short-distance mosaic map, site labeling, or home/non-home recognition

**Magnetic Map Evidence:**
- Magnetic field gradients are extremely weak (only ~5-10 nT/km in total intensity, ~0.01°/km in inclination), requiring extraordinarily sensitive sensory mechanisms
- Magnetic gradients cannot be detected directly but must be derived from multiple point samples; use is experience-dependent with an ontogenetic progression from place maps to gradient maps
- Potential problems include local-gradient noise, temporal variation (greatest during daylight), magnetic storms, and long-term field variation
- Route-deprivation studies show newts, juvenile alligators, sea turtles, homing pigeons, and spiny lobsters use map information obtained at testing sites
- The magnetic field appears to be the only potential gradient map source for organisms in forested habitats (e.g., newts) where wind-borne odors are unreliable

**Dual Magnetic Systems:**
- Two distinct magnetoreception mechanisms exist: a light-dependent radical-pair mechanism (compass, in newts via extraocular photoreceptors near the pineal organ; in birds via the right retina) and a magnetite-based mechanism associated with the trigeminal nerve (map component)
- Pulse remagnetization experiments (affecting only magnetite-based receptors) altered orientation of experienced adults navigating with map+compass, but not naive young birds using only compass; affected pigeons only at sites >80 km from the loft, consistent with a large-scale, low-resolution magnetic map

**Simulated Magnetic Displacement:**
- Experiments with newts, sea turtles, and migratory birds exposed subjects to magnetic field component values simulating positions north/south of the testing site; both newts and sea turtles exhibited opposite orientation directions corresponding to the simulated displacements, providing evidence for magnetic field use in gradient map information
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a PubMed abstract page for a scientific article titled "Bird navigation: what type of information does the magnetite-based receptor provide?" published in Proceedings of the Royal Society B (Proc Biol Sci) on November 22, 2006 (Volume 273, Issue 1603, pages 2815-2820). The article has the DOI 10.1098/rspb.2006.3651, PMID 17015316, and PMCID PMC1664630.

AUTHORS: Wolfgang Wiltschko (corresponding author, from Fachbereich Biowissenschaften der J.W.Goethe-Universität, Frankfurt am Main, Germany), Ursula Munro, Hugh Ford, and Roswitha Wiltschko.

METHODOLOGY: The researchers subjected migratory Australian silvereyes (Zosterops lateralis) to a short, strong magnetic pulse and tested their subsequent orientation responses under different magnetic conditions. In the local geomagnetic field, birds preferred easterly headings (a change from their normal migratory direction). When the horizontal component of the magnetic field was shifted 90 degrees anticlockwise, the birds altered their headings accordingly (northwards). In a field with the vertical component inverted, the birds reversed their headings to westwards.

RESULTS AND CONCLUSIONS: The findings demonstrate that although the magnetic pulse strongly affects magnetite particles, it leaves the functional mechanism of the magnetic compass intact, since the birds' directional orientation was still controlled by the normal inclination compass. This indicates that magnetite-based receptors mediate magnetic 'map'-information used for determining position. When affected by the pulse, these receptors provide birds with false positional information, causing them to change their course.

The article includes the abstract, three figures (orientation of silvereyes before pulse treatment, immediately after the pulse and on the following two evenings, and a model illustrating the use of magnetic information by different receptor types in the navigational system), similar articles, and citations. It is a Research Support, Non-U.S. Gov't publication with full text available from Silverchair Information Systems and as a free PMC article. MeSH terms include Animal Migration, Ferrosoferric Oxide chemistry, Flight Animal, Magnetics, Orientation physiology, Passeriformes, and Sensory Receptor Cells. The article has been cited by later works including studies on magnetite-based magnetoreception, repeated pulsing effects, and the interaction of beak-based magnetite receptors with the visual system.
