# New Theory on How Homing Pigeons Find Home

The birds could be using the specific sound signatures of home to navigate.

ByJane J. Lee

Published January 30, 2013

•6 min read

**Homing pigeons** **(*Columba livia*) have been prized for their navigational abilities for thousands of years. They've served as messengers during war, as a means of long-distance communication, and as prized athletes in international races.**

But there are places around the world that seem to confuse these birds—areas where they repeatedly vanish in the wrong direction or scatter on random headings rather than fly straight home, said [Jon Hagstrum](https://profile.usgs.gov/jhag), a geophysicist who authored a study that may help researchers understand how homing pigeons navigate.

Hagstrum's paper, published online Wednesday in the [*Journal of Experimental Biology*](http://jeb.biologists.org/), proposes an intriguing theory for homing pigeon disorientation—that the birds are following ultralow frequency sounds back towards their lofts and that disruptions in their ability to "hear" home is what screws them up.

Called [infrasound](http://www.birds.cornell.edu/brp/elephant/cyclotis/language/infrasound.html), these sound waves propagate at frequencies well below the range audible to people, but pigeons can pick them up, said Hagstrum, who works at the [U.S. Geological Survey](http://www.usgs.gov/) in Menlo Park, California.

"They're using sound to image the terrain [surrounding] their loft," he said. "It's like us visually recognizing our house using our eyes."

**Homeward Bound?**

For years, scientists have struggled to explain carrier pigeons' directional challenges in certain areas, known as release-site biases.

This "map" issue, or a pigeon's ability to tell where it is in relation to where it wants to go, is different from the bird's compass system, which tells it which direction it's headed in. ([Learn about how other animals navigate.](http://ngm.nationalgeographic.com/1991/06/animal-navigations/amos-photography))

"We know a lot about pigeon compass systems, but what has been controversial, even to this day, has been their map [system]," said Cordula Mora, an animal behavior researcher at Bowling Green State University in Ohio who was not involved in the study.

Until now, the two main theories say that pigeons rely either on their sense of smell to find their way home or that they follow the Earth's magnetic field lines, she said.

If something screwed up their sense of smell or their ability to follow those fields, the thinking has been, that could explain why pigeons got lost in certain areas.

But neither explanation made sense to Hagstrum, a geologist who grew interested in pigeons after attending an undergraduate lecture by Cornell biologist William Keeton. Keeton, who studied homing pigeons' navigation abilities, described some release-site biases in his pigeons and Hagstrum was hooked.

"I was just stunned and amazed and fascinated," said Hagstrum. "I understand we don't get dark matter or quantum mechanics, but bird [navigation]?"

So Hagstrum decided to look at Keeton's pigeon release data from three sites in upstate New York. At Castor Hill and Jersey Hill, the birds would repeatedly fly in the wrong direction or head off randomly when trying to return to their loft at Cornell University, even though they had no problems at other locations. At a third site near the town of Weedsport, young pigeons would head off in a different direction from older birds.

There were also certain days when the Cornell pigeons could find their way back home from these areas without any problems.

At the same time, homing pigeons from other lofts released at Castor Hill, Jersey Hill, and near Weedsport, would fly home just fine.

**Sound Shadows**

Hagstrum knew that homing pigeons could hear sounds as low as 0.05 hertz, low enough to pick up infrasounds that were down around 0.1 or 0.2 hertz. So he decided to map out what these low-frequency sound waves would have looked like on an average day, and on the days when the pigeons could home correctly from Jersey Hill.

He found that due to atmospheric conditions and local terrain, Jersey Hill normally sits in a sound shadow in relation to the Cornell loft. Little to none of the infrasounds from the area around the loft reached Jersey Hill except on one day when changing wind patterns and temperature inversions permitted.

That happened to match a day when the Cornell pigeons had no problem returning home.

"I could see how the topography was affecting the sound and how the weather was affecting the sound [transmission]," Hagstrum said. "It started to explain all these mysteries."

The terrain between the loft and Jersey Hill, combined with normal atmospheric conditions, bounced infrasounds up and over these areas.

Some infrasound would still reach Castor Hill, but due to nearby hills and valleys, the sound waves approached from the west and southwest, even though the Cornell loft is situated south-southwest of Castor Hill.

Records show that younger, inexperienced pigeons released at Castor Hill would sometimes fly west while older birds headed southwest, presumably following infrasounds from their loft.

Hagstrum's model found that infrasound normally arrived at the Weedsport site from the south. But one day of abnormal weather conditions, combined with a local river valley, resulted in infrasound that arrived at Weedsport from the Cornell loft from the southeast.

**Multiple Maps**

"What [Hagstrum] has found for those areas are a possible explanation for the [pigeon] behavior at these sites," said Bowling Green State's Mora. But she cautions against extrapolating these results to all homing pigeons.

Some of Mora's work supports the theory that [homing pigeons use magnetic field lines to find their way home](http://rspb.royalsocietypublishing.org/content/276/1671/3295.short).

What homing pigeons are using as their map probably depends on where they're raised, she said. "In some places it may be infrasound, and in other places [a sense of smell] may be the way to go."

Hagstrum's next steps are to figure out how large an area the pigeons are listening to. He's also talking to the Navy and Air Force, who are interested in his work. "Right now we use GPS to navigate," he said. But if those satellites were compromised, "we'd be out of luck." Pigeons navigate from point to point without any problems, he said.

This National Geographic article (published January 30, 2013, by Jane J. Lee) reports on a new theory by geophysicist Jon Hagstrum of the U.S. Geological Survey in Menlo Park, California, explaining why homing pigeons (Columba livia) sometimes get disoriented and fail to find their way home. The theory, published online in the Journal of Experimental Biology, proposes that pigeons navigate using ultralow frequency sounds called infrasound—sound waves at frequencies below human hearing (pigeons can hear as low as 0.05 hertz)—to "image" the terrain surrounding their lofts.

Hagstrum analyzed release data collected by Cornell biologist William Keeton from three sites in upstate New York (Castor Hill, Jersey Hill, and near Weedsport) where Cornell pigeons repeatedly flew in wrong directions or scattered randomly. By mapping how infrasound waves propagated under varying atmospheric conditions and local terrain, Hagstrum found that Jersey Hill normally sits in a "sound shadow" relative to the Cornell loft—infrasounds from the loft area didn't reach the site except on one day when changing wind patterns and temperature inversions allowed transmission, which matched a day when the pigeons found their way home without problems. The model also explained why young pigeons headed west from Castor Hill (where sound arrived from the west/southwest) while older birds flew southwest toward the loft, and how abnormal weather conditions altered infrasound direction at Weedsport.

Researcher Cordula Mora of Bowling Green State University (not involved in the study) said Hagstrum's findings offer a possible explanation for behavior at these specific sites but cautioned against extrapolating to all homing pigeons, noting that some of her work supports the theory that pigeons use magnetic field lines. She suggests pigeons likely use different "maps" depending on where they're raised—infrasound in some places, sense of smell in others. Hagstrum's next steps include determining the size of the listening area and conversing with the Navy and Air Force, who are interested because pigeons navigate without GPS, which could be valuable if satellite navigation were compromised.

Search results: 



--- SOURCE 1: The Magnetic Compass of Birds: The Role of Cryptochrome ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8171495

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific review article titled "The Magnetic Compass of Birds: The Role of Cryptochrome," published in Frontiers in Physiology on May 19, 2021, by Roswitha Wiltschko, Christine Nießner, and Wolfgang Wiltschko (Frankfurt am Main, Germany). The paper reviews the mechanisms behind the avian magnetic compass and the role of cryptochrome as the likely receptor molecule.

KEY FINDINGS:
- The avian magnetic compass is an "inclination compass" that uses the axial course of field lines and their inclination rather than polarity. Birds distinguish "poleward" (field lines tilted downward) and "equatorward" (pointing upward).
- The compass works only within a flexible functional window around local geomagnetic intensity (fields more than ~20-25% weaker/stronger cause disorientation). European Robins kept at 47 μT could adjust to fields from 4 μT to 150 μT, but could not orient at intermediate unexperienced fields.
- The compass is light-dependent, requiring short-wavelength light (UV, blue, turquoise, green). Birds oriented under 373 nm UV, 424 nm blue, 501 nm turquoise, and 565 nm green light, but were disoriented under yellow and red light (568-645 nm).

THE RADICAL PAIR MODEL:
- Proposed by Ritz et al. (2000), this model is based on spin-chemical processes in photo-pigments. Photon absorption forms radical pairs in singlet (antiparallel spin) or triplet (parallel spin) states, with the ratio depending on directional relation to the magnetic field.
- The eyes are proposed as the site of magnetoreception due to light availability and round shape (receptor cells arranged in all spatial directions).
- Experimental support includes: electro-retinographic differences under blue but not red light; radio-frequency fields in the MHz range causing disorientation in birds (diagnostic test for radical pair involvement).

CRYPTOCHROME AND FAD PHOTOCYCLE:
- Cryptochromes use FAD (flavin adenine dinucleotide) as chromophore, undergoing a redox cycle. The oxidized form (FADox) is the dark resting form.
- Photo-reduction forms a radical pair with tryptophan radical (Trp∙); re-oxidation forms a second radical pair (possibly with O2∙).
- Behavioral evidence indicates the radical pair formed during light-independent re-oxidation (not photo-reduction) is crucial for sensing magnetic directions. Birds oriented under green light only transiently (<1 h), requiring prior exposure to photo-reducing light.
- A flickering light/pulsed magnetic field experiment (light 300 ms, field present during darkness) confirmed that sensing can occur in darkness, identifying re-oxidation as the crucial step.

FIVE CRYPTOCHROME TYPES IN BIRD RETINA:
1. Cry1a: Located in outer segments of UV/V (SW1) cones with clear oil droplets; considered the most likely receptor molecule due to location, presence in all spatial directions, and membrane anchoring.
2. Cry1b: In cytosol of ganglion cells and inner segments; expression varies seasonally in night migrants (possibly related to nocturnal activity shifts rather than magnetoreception).
3. Cry2: Found in photoreceptors, ganglion cells, pineal gland; possible clock protein role.
4. Cry4a: In longwave-sensitive cones and double cones; red oil droplets filtering short wavelengths make magnetoreceptive role unlikely.
5. Cry4b: Widespread splice product found in 25+ avian species.

CONCLUSION: Cry1a is identified as the most likely receptor molecule. Open questions remain about how radical pair information is transformed into a biological signal, especially how magnetic and visual information from the same cones are separated and transmitted.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The avian magnetic compass is an inclination compass that uses not the polarity of the magnetic field but the axial course of the field lines and their inclination in space."
</key_excerpts>



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------


--- SOURCE 2: Magnetic Compass of Birds Is Based on a Molecule with Optimal Directional Sensitivity ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2718301

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article published in the Biophysical Journal (2009 Apr 22;96(8):3451–3457; doi:10.1016/j.bpj.2008.11.072) titled "Magnetic Compass of Birds Is Based on a Molecule with Optimal Directional Sensitivity." The study was conducted by Thorsten Ritz (UC Irvine, Department of Physics and Astronomy), Roswitha and Wolfgang Wiltschko (J.W. Goethe-Universität, Frankfurt), and PJ Hore, Christopher T Rodgers, and Christiane R Timmel (University of Oxford, Department of Chemistry). 

**Background:** The avian magnetic compass is an "inclination compass" based on the inclination of magnetic field lines rather than polarity, and its operation requires short-wavelength light. The "radical pair" model postulates that specialized photopigments in the retina undergo light-induced electron transfer to create spin-correlated radical pairs (with singlet and triplet states), whose reaction yields depend on the orientation of the radical pair relative to the external magnetic field.

**Methodology:** The researchers used a multidisciplinary approach, subjecting migratory European robins (Erithacus rubecula) to oscillating magnetic fields combined with static fields and using their orientation responses as a criterion for unhindered magnetoreception. Birds were tested in funnel-shaped cages under 565 nm green light during spring migration from 2003 to 2006 at the Zoological Institute of the University Frankfurt (50°08′N, 8°40′E). The local geomagnetic field was 46.0–47.4 μT with 66° inclination; in 2006, tests were also performed in a 92 μT static field (approximately twice the local field) using Helmholtz coils.

**Key Results:**
- Birds were tested at eight frequencies from 0.01 MHz to 7.0 MHz with intensities of 470–480 nT. At 0.01 and 0.03 MHz, birds oriented normally; at 0.10 and 0.50 MHz they showed weak axial responses; at 0.658 MHz and higher frequencies they were disoriented.
- The onset of oscillating field effects allowed estimation of the radical pair lifetime at 2–10 μs (relatively long).
- Testing at the Larmor frequency (νL = γeB0/2π; numerically νL in MHz = 0.028 × B0 in μT, giving 1.315 MHz in the local field) revealed an extraordinarily sensitive resonance: robins were disoriented at 1.315 MHz even at 15 nT, while 0.658 MHz and 2.63 MHz required 480 nT to cause disorientation.
- In the 92 μT static field (double intensity), the birds became most sensitive to 2.63 MHz (15 nT disrupting orientation), confirming the resonance scales with the Larmor frequency and arises from the Zeeman interaction.

**Conclusions:** An intense resonance at the Larmor frequency indicates a radical pair in which one radical is devoid of hyperfine interactions—an electron spin that is magnetically isolated, with no magnetic interactions other than with the geomagnetic field. Simulations showed this resonance is 30–50 times stronger than at other frequencies. Such a radical pair design is optimal as a biological compass because: (1) it is more sensitive to weak external fields, (2) it maximizes anisotropy of the magnetic field effect crucial for directional sensitivity, (3) it avoids cancellation of hyperfine anisotropic effects, and (4) it allows slow spin relaxation.

**Proposed Mechanism:** The radical pair design might be realized by cryptochrome photoreceptors (blue-light photoreceptor proteins with flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) as chromophore) if paired with molecular oxygen as a reaction partner—specifically, a flavin-superoxide radical pair formed during dark reversion where the superoxide radical (O2•−) is devoid of hyperfine couplings. The radical pairs found in the forward photoactivation reaction alone cannot explain the resonance data. The authors note the mechanism is likely common to all birds (a radical-pair-based inclination compass has been demonstrated in domestic chickens as well), while crustaceans, fish, and some mammals use magnetite-based polarity compasses, and the magnetite structure in birds' beaks is not involved in the magnetic compass mechanism described.

**Two Main Models:** The two competing models for avian magnetoreception are: (1) a magnetite-based model involving magnetic particles in the bird's head, and (2) a radical-pair-based model in which a chemical reaction in the bird's eye produces radical pairs whose spin dynamics are influenced by magnetic fields. The protein binds FAD (flavin adenine dinucleotide) and undergoes photoactivation via a chain of three tryptophans (Trp324, Trp377, Trp400). Blue light converts FAD to excited FAD*, which is protonated to FADH+, and electron transfers through the tryptophan chain form radical pairs (FADH + Trp400+, FADH + Trp377+, FADH + Trp324+). The lecture focuses on the physics of how migratory songbirds sense the Earth's magnetic field via a chemical compass.

**Core Mechanism:**
- The proposal (dating to 1978, by Klaus Schulten) is that a chemical reaction in birds contains short-lived intermediates called radical pairs, which are sensitive to magnetic fields as weak as the Earth's (~50 microTesla).
- Radical pairs (lasting ~1 microsecond) can either revert to reactants (singlet) or form products. The branching ratio depends on the strength and direction of the Earth's magnetic field, making it a direction-sensing compass rather than just an intensity sensor.
- The mechanism is light-dependent—blue and green photons provide energy to create the radicals.
- The key energetic paradox: the magnetic interaction with Earth's field is ~10 million times smaller than thermal energy (kT), yet the mechanism works because it applies tiny energy at a precisely non-equilibrium moment (analogous to a fly landing on a balanced stone block), influencing spin dynamics.

**Physics Background:**
- Electrons have quantum spin (quantum number s=1/2) and associated magnetic moments.
- Radicals are molecules with unpaired electrons and are therefore magnetic.
- Radical pairs exist in singlet states (opposite spins, total spin 0) or triplet states (parallel spins, total spin 1).
- Organic radical reactions conserve spin, so singlet radical pairs must come from singlet precursors, and triplet products can only form from triplet radical pairs.
- Hyperfine interactions between electron spins and nuclear spins (of hydrogen and nitrogen, which have ~100% natural abundance) are essential. Carbon-12 and oxygen-16 have no nuclear spin.
- Anisotropic hyperfine interactions (particularly from nitrogen atoms in the central rings of flavin) enable direction sensitivity, with interaction strengths ranging from microTesla to milliTesla—many stronger than the Earth's field.
- For flavin and tryptophan radicals, hyperfine interactions are in the milliTesla range, compared to Earth's field at ~0.05 milliTesla.

**Spin Dynamics:**
- Hyperfine interactions cause coherent oscillations between singlet and triplet states at frequencies determined by interaction strengths (typically ~10 MHz).
- The Larmor frequency for a free electron in Earth's field (50 microTesla) is 1.4 MHz, corresponding to a 700-nanosecond period.
- A magnetic field shifts energy levels and changes oscillation frequencies, with differences becoming visible after ~0.1 microsecond; direction matters because of anisotropy.
- Earth's field effects (~10^-7 of kT) arise from the "low field effect"—pairs of degenerate energy levels split slightly by the field, adding a slow oscillation pathway (a 1.4 MHz beat).
- The final product yield integrates over the radical pair lifetime and thus depends on field presence and direction.

**Key Points on the Mechanism:**
- The mechanism is consistent with birds having an axial compass (not polarity-sensitive), and with light-dependence (evidenced by Wiltschko's findings that blue/green light is required).
- The chemistry is well established—hundreds of radical pair reactions in laboratories are known to be magnetically sensitive at 1 milliTesla or more. The big question is whether it is the actual mechanism in birds.
- In 2002, Ritz and Schulten proposed cryptochrome as the protein hosting this chemistry, likely located in the retina, with aligned/immobilized molecules needed for direction sensing.

**Magnetite Alternative:**
- Magnetite (Fe3O4) is the principal competing mechanism, based on iron atoms' magnetic moments.
- Particle properties depend on size/shape: small crystals (<30-40 nm) are superparamagnetic (fluctuating moments); larger crystals can be single-domain (permanent moments acting like compass needles); too large and they become multi-domain (moments cancel).

- Magnetite is considered less likely for birds (they sense rather than passively respond, and would need enormous numbers of particles to align their bodies), but cannot yet be ruled out.

--- SOURCE 11: The magnetite-based receptors in the beak of birds and their role in avian navigation ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3552369

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article, published in the Journal of Comparative Physiology A (2012, Vol 199, p. 89, doi:10.1007/s00359-012-0769-3) by R. Wiltschko and W. Wiltschko of J.W. Goethe-Universität Frankfurt, reviews the evidence for magnetite-based magnetoreceptors in the beaks of birds and their role in avian navigation.

Key findings:
- Iron-rich structures have been described in the beaks of homing pigeons, chickens, and migratory birds (including Bobolinks, Australian Silvereyes, European Robins, and Reed Warblers), and were initially interpreted as magnetoreceptors.
- The trigeminal system (ophthalmic nerve) mediates magnetic information, with electrophysiological recordings from Bobolinks suggesting these convey information on magnetic intensity (with a logarithmic relationship between spike rate and intensity).
- Behavioral studies using strong, short magnetic pulses (0.5 Tesla, <5 ms) demonstrate the involvement of magnetite in these receptors. Pulsed Silvereyes showed ~90° directional shifts, and Bobolinks deviated in direction-dependent ways. Anesthetics applied to the ophthalmic nerve or upper beak suppressed these pulse effects.
- Crucially, the magnetite-based beak receptors are NOT part of the avian magnetic compass—which is a separate system based on radical-pair processes in the eye. When the compass is disrupted by certain light conditions (darkness, red light, green+yellow combinations), birds show 'fixed direction' polar responses that originate from the beak receptors.
- The natural function of these receptors appears to be recording magnetic intensity, providing one component of the multi-factorial navigational 'map' used by homing pigeons and migrants.
- Evidence for this map function includes: only experienced (not juvenile) migrants respond to pulses (suggesting a learned, experience-based system); pigeons released in magnetic anomalies (e.g., Vogelsberg anomaly) showed confusion and slower departures unless their beaks were anesthetized; pigeons respond to geomagnetic fluctuations on the order of 20 nT.
- The exact location of the receptors is debated—Hanzlik et al. (2000) and Fleissner et al. (2003) identified superparamagnetic magnetite nanocrystal clusters in the upper beak skin, but Treiber et al. (2012) challenged these findings, claiming the structures were merely macrophages. Findings from chicken beak-tip removal and localized anesthesia effects suggest receptors may be further forward in the beak.
- Whether the particles are single-domain or superparamagnetic remains unresolved; the short-lived recovery from pulsing (~8-10 days) and second-pulse responses suggest superparamagnetic clusters.
- Parallel cases were noted in rainbow trout, where trigeminal nerve responses convey intensity (not direction) information.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Behavioral studies support the involvement of magnetite and the trigeminal system in magnetoreception, but clearly show that the inclination compass normally used by birds represents a separate system."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 1: The sun compass revisited - PMC ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222775

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an ideas paper by Tim Guilford and Graham K Taylor (Oxford University, Animal Behaviour Research Group) published in an Elsevier journal (PMC ID 4222775), revisiting the concept of the sun compass in animal (particularly bird) navigation. The paper argues that the traditional paradigm of the time-compensated sun compass, validated by clock shift experiments, obscures several other ways solar information could be used in animal orientation.

KEY ARGUMENTS:
1. The authors distinguish between the sun as a compass (providing absolute geographical direction, e.g. north) versus as a heading indicator (detecting/maintaining heading changes, like a gyroscope in an aircraft). These may be separate mechanisms serving different functions (navigation vs. steering).
2. A solar compass need not be fully time-compensated to be useful. Animals might use time-dependent solar information in associatively acquired, time-limited ways rather than through full time compensation.
3. A solar heading indicator used on short timescales needs no time compensation at all. At an average solar azimuth rate of 15°/hour, a bird flying a constant heading to the sun would trace a circular arc of ~229 km radius at 60 km/h — curvature indiscernible over a few minutes of flight. Applying a constant offset correction of π/12 radians/h (15°/h) could maintain an almost straight heading for hours without true time compensation.
4. Solar-derived cues (e.g. shadows) can also be involved in navigation in position-dependent, non-compass ways — giving directionality to landmarks or acting as time-dependent landmarks for place recognition.

CONCLUSION: Clock shift experiments alone are neither necessary nor sufficient to identify all conceivable uses of solar information in animal orientation. A predictable response to clock shift should not be regarded as an acid test of solar information use in navigation.

KEY MECHANISMS DISCUSSED:
- Sun as compass functions: compass for navigation (map-and-compass, mosaic map), compass for racing (repeated training from single direction, e.g. pigeon racing 'north road'/'south road' birds)
- Solar heading indicator for steering: maintaining constant heading, path integration, compensating for crosswind drift
- Time-compensated landmarks: time-dependent visual appearance of scenes (illustrated by Van Gogh and Monet paintings)
- Directed landmarks: shadows conferring directional sense to landscape features

Notable studies cited: Kramer (1950, 1952), Schmidt-Koenig (1958), Budzynski et al. (2000) showing pigeons can learn sun compass at unfamiliar times of day, Fuller et al. (1983) showing large clock shift deviation after 55 releases from a single site, McDonald (1972) showing pigeons use shadow patterns, Bingman & Ioalè (1989) showing clock-shifted birds only deviate with intact olfactory sense.

The paper received June 27, 2014, revised July 15, 2014, accepted August 8, 2014, and is open access under CC BY-NC-ND license.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"We distinguish between the known use of the sun's azimuth to provide absolute geographical direction (compass mechanism) and its possible use to detect changes in heading (heading indicator mechanism). Just as in an aircraft, these two kinds of information may be provided by separate mechanisms and used for different functions, for example for navigation versus steering."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: [PDF] New Experiments on the Effect of Clock Shifts on Homing in Pigeons ---
URL: https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19720017428/downloads/19720017428.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific paper by Klaus Schmidt-Koenig reports on experiments extending previous research on the effect of clock shifts on homing in pigeons, presented at an animal orientation and navigation symposium. The research tests the "Sun azimuth compass" hypothesis, where clock shifts introduce predictable errors in initial orientation. Key experiments and findings include:

1. **Distance of release experiments (6-hr clock shifts):** Releases were conducted from 15 km and 200 km from the cardinal compass directions in Durham, N.C. Results confirmed that 6-hr clockwise and counterclockwise shifts (imposed for at least 4 days) produced roughly 90° deviations in initial orientation from controls, with significantly inferior homing performance (p<0.01). No significant difference was found between 15 km and 200 km releases, indicating the Sun compass is utilized at both short and long distances.

2. **Small clock shift experiments (2-hr and 30-min counterclockwise shifts):** The logic of this test was that if the Sun were used as a compass, a 2-hr shift should produce only ~30° deviation (and a 30-min shift ~8°), but if the Sun were used for navigation (as suggested by Matthews), a 2-hr shift should be interpreted as a longitudinal displacement of ~2000 km and a 30-min shift as ~700 km, causing birds to head east. Results showed NO significant difference in initial orientation for 2-hr shifts (though homing performance was significantly different, p<0.01 by χ² test) and no significant difference for 30-min shifts. These results "clearly support and considerably strengthen previous evidence that the Sun is used for compass orientation and not for navigation."

3. **Methodology:** Pigeons were placed in closed rooms with automated timers controlling illumination; 6-hr shifts required 4 days to complete, so all birds (including 30-min shift birds) were subjected to 4 days of shifting. Controls experienced artificial conditions with no shift. Release times were restricted to the overlap period between artificial and natural days.

4. **Discussion highlights:** Schmidt-Koenig reported that initial orientation of normal pigeons is a function of distance from home, deteriorating beyond 200 km (with particularly poor orientation at 300 km in German repeats of the North Carolina "dead belt" experiments). However, Keeton reported completing nearly 175 releases involving ~2550 birds and finding NO distance effect, with clock-shift results being consistent at 32, 48, 64, 80 km and even ~2 km distances (as long as the loft was not visible). Keeton also reported that birds allowed to merely see the Sun in an aviary during shifting remained effectively shifted, but birds permitted to fly during overlap periods became confused and oriented randomly (preliminary results). Regarding overcast, Keeton found birds could orient at 160-240 km under overcast only if they had prior short-distance (4.8-16 km) training flights under overcast conditions.

5. **Night releases:** Releasing pigeons at night produced large scatter, with some indication that pigeons "think" the Sun goes counterclockwise at night (unlike bees); these experiments were discontinued.

The experiments in the U.S. were supported by the Office of Naval Research, National Science Foundation (grant GB 2952), and NASA (contract NER 34401-019), and in Germany by the Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft. The discussion also notes acknowledgments of P. H. Klopfer for support and hospitality.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 5: Mouritsen: Birds' use of compasses during migration ---
URL: https://www.internationalornithology.org/PROCEEDINGS_Durban/Symposium/S17/S17.1.htm

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific paper by Henrik Mouritsen addresses whether young night-migrating passerines use a simple "clock-and-compass" strategy or true navigation during their first autumn migration. The author argues strongly for the clock-and-compass hypothesis, concluding that young birds are equipped with compasses and an internal clock but no map.

**Key evidence presented for the clock-and-compass hypothesis:**

1. **Mathematical model**: Mouritsen developed a model predicting directional distributions of ringing recoveries assuming birds accumulate errors (no navigation) rather than correct them.

2. **Ringing recovery data**: Scandinavian Pied Flycatchers (Ficedula hypoleuca, n=1138 recoveries) showed directional distributions matching model predictions. The r-value after one migratory step (approx. 125 km) was 0.665 (angular SD of ~52°). Model predicted 66% of recoveries within a parabola; actual data showed 65%, an extremely close fit. Statistical test (Wilcoxon signed rank, P>0.20) confirmed no significant difference.

3. **Displacement experiment**: 48 young Pied Flycatchers were tested at Christians, Denmark (oriented south-southwest), then split into three groups: one displaced ~500 km south, one ~400 km west, one control. All groups showed the same orientation with overlapping confidence intervals, showing no compensatory orientation.

4. **Literature review**: Re-evaluation of all previous displacement experiments (summarized in Table 1) found only two studies weakly supporting navigation, both with methodological flaws. The south-east orientation at Blavand (Denmark) was reinterpreted as a local anomaly rather than evidence for compensation.

**The clock-and-compass model**: Describes migration as a series of unrelated migratory steps in an almost constant direction (compass) under a predetermined time schedule (clock). Distinguishing from 'Goal Area Navigation' hypothesis (Rabøl) which posits true navigational ability requiring both compass AND map.

**Perdeck's (1958) experiment**: Thousands of European Starlings displaced from Netherlands to Switzerland showed juvenile birds continued on the same SW course (ending in southern France/Spain) rather than compensating, while adults corrected and reached normal wintering grounds — strong evidence for clock-and-compass in juveniles. However, the author cautions this cannot be directly generalized since starlings migrate in flocks (potentially learning from adults) while night-migrating passerines migrate alone.

**Emergency plans proposed**: 
- Plan A: If over water at dawn in autumn, turn ~90° toward sunrise (from SW to SE heading) until land is encountered (supported by radar observations of thrushes over the North Sea by Myres 1964).
- Plan B: If wind too strong for Plan A, fly with wind until land encountered.

**Regarding adult birds**: The author acknowledges adult and naive birds likely gain navigational abilities through learning, citing high site fidelity and familiar landmarks. Adults migrating at 300-2000 m altitude can see a wide area for landmark navigation up to 160 km from goals.

**Conclusion**: Young night-migrating passerines on first autumn migration appear to rely solely on two inherited compasses (magnetic and celestial), an endogenous time schedule, and emergency plans — no map sense is needed. The author calls for carefully designed future displacement experiments with large samples of single species, clear predictions, and meticulous controls, while avoiding coastal test sites like Blavand.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 6: Navigation and Orientation ---
URL: http://web.stanford.edu/group/stanfordbirds/text/essays/Navigation.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage (copyright 1988 by Paul R. Ehrlich, David S. Dobkin, and Darryl Wheye) explains how birds navigate and orient during migration. It frames the question as two puzzles: (1) how birds navigate thousands of miles between breeding and wintering sites, and (2) how they find their way back to precise nesting/roosting sites (homing behavior). Birds must both orient (determine compass direction) and navigate (judge position while traveling).

Key content: Birds find their way using various cues in a hierarchical fashion, with different species prioritizing cues differently. The five primary directional information sources are: (1) topographic features (including wind direction influenced by landforms), (2) stars, (3) sun, (4) Earth's magnetic field, and (5) odors.

Notable experiments and findings include:
- Behavioral ecologist Stephen Emlen used Indigo Buntings in a planetarium, exploiting their "migratory restlessness." Birds oriented correctly via projected stellar cues, shifted orientation when stars were shifted, and learned a "sky map" by watching star rotation as they matured. Young birds exposed to a false sky rotating around Betelgeuse acted as if it were the North Star.
- On overcast nights, birds set course by the setting sun. When both stars and sun are obscured, they orient by wind direction (not always correctly). Ornithologist Kenneth Able used radar and portable ceilometers and found birds frequently flew in the wrong direction when using wind as a cue without stars.
- Contrary to common belief, there is little evidence that birds use topographic features (mountains, rivers, buildings) for navigation, though most ornithologists believe they do near the home site.
- Pigeons can detect Earth's magnetic field for orientation and possibly navigation; the mechanism for sensing weak electromagnetic fields is not understood, and its prevalence among other bird species is unknown.
- Homing pigeons also use smell for short-distance orientation to their loft. Leach's Storm-Petrels (and possibly other "tubenoses") may use smell to locate nest burrows but rely on other cues to find the colony.
- Shearwaters performed spectacular homing: taken from nest burrows off England's coast, transported across the Atlantic, released near Boston, some returned to their burrows 12.5 days later—clearly not by smell.

Conclusion: Birds do not rely on a single source of information; they use redundant cues from a variety of sources, shaped over evolutionary time, enabling navigation under most routine conditions.
</summary>

Originally appeared in Birds of North America with content partner American Ornithological Society. The protonym is Tanagra cyanea (Linnaeus, 1766), type locality in Carolina (restricted to South Carolina).

**Migration Overview**: A complete migrant leaving breeding grounds in eastern U.S. for wintering areas from southern Florida to northern South America. Most birds cross the Gulf of Mexico (based on arrival date sequences from Galveston to northern Florida), while flocks in Veracruz, Mexico indicate some move around the Gulf to avoid overwater crossings.

**Fall migration**: Birds leave northern breeding areas in September; migrants common in southeastern U.S. in late September and October; nearly all have departed breeding grounds by mid-October; first arrivals in Neotropics in mid-September. Migration moves on a broad front, not along mountain ridges.

**Spring migration**: Leave wintering areas late April-May, arrive on breeding grounds late April to early June. Males generally arrive earlier than females (two-week difference in first arrival dates). Adult males arrive earlier than yearling males on average. Some individuals remain on wintering grounds in Guatemala through April; others appear in Louisiana late March through early May.

**Band recovery data**: Of 149,738 buntings banded from 1927 through 2002 (~2,000/year), only 340 were re-encountered, and only 116 (0.078%) recovered away from their banding site. Recoveries demonstrate that eastern and midwestern breeding populations remain geographically separate into winter, with longitudinal order of breeding and wintering sites closely correlated (rs = 0.93, P < 0.01), showing strong migratory connectivity. Spring migration recoveries traced northeastward movement (rs = 0.89, P < 0.01). Banding recoveries suggest buntings fly downwind both crossing the Gulf and in overland migration (winds from southeast over Gulf, southwest over continent).

**Migratory behavior**: Nocturnal migrant. Feeding rate increases before migration as birds deposit fat. Flight speed estimated at ~32 km/hour. Birds become active at night in migration season and use star patterns in the night sky for orientation (as shown by planetarium tests by Emlen). Magnetic fields may also influence orientation but this is uncertain.

**Physiology**: Autumn migrants accumulate fat deposits, reaching up to 26g (50% increase in mass). A bunting needs ~30% of body mass in fat to complete the nearly 1,000 km flight from northern Florida across the Gulf of Mexico. Birds ≥18g may have sufficient fuel for unaided trans-Gulf flight. In Jamaica, mean male mass increases from 14.5g in January to 18-19g in April before migrating. Birds arriving after Gulf crossings stop (mean 4 days) to feed near the Louisiana coast.

--- SOURCE 12: Wiltschko & Wiltschko: Celestial and magnetic cues in conflict ---
URL: https://www.internationalornithology.org/PROCEEDINGS_Durban/Symposium/S17/S17.4.htm

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific paper by Roswitha Wiltschko and Wolfgang Wiltschko (1999) reviews experiments testing migrating birds under conflicting magnetic and celestial orientation cues. The paper examines how the mature orientation system rates and ranks available cues during the second phase of migratory orientation (actual migration en route), as distinct from the pre-migratory period.

KEY FINDINGS ON CUE-CONFLICT EXPERIMENTS:
- When birds were tested only ONCE under the natural sky with magnetic North deflected: 48% followed celestial cues, 24% became disoriented/bimodal, 19% showed compromise directions, and 10% (2 of 21 samples, Snow Buntings) responded to the magnetic deflection.
- When birds were tested REPEATEDLY under conflicting cues: All 11 samples across species (European warblers, European Robins, Dunnocks, Silvereyes, Yellow-faced Honeyeaters) ultimately followed magnetic cues.
- Response timing varied: some species (robins) showed delayed responses to magnetic deflection, changing direction only after 2 exposures, while others (warblers, Snow Buntings) responded immediately.
- Silvereyes showed both immediate and delayed responses depending on the direction of magnetic North shift, indicating asymmetry related to the relationship between celestial rotation and deflection direction (with reversed patterns between Northern and Southern Hemispheres).

MANIPULATING CELESTIAL CUES:
- Indigo Buntings, Savannah Sparrows, and Robins tested once or twice followed celestial cues or became disoriented.
- Bobolinks tested repeatedly under reversed planetarium skies preferred magnetic cues.
- European Starlings were the only day migrants showing significant response to clock-shift.
- Homing Pigeons paralleled migrant behavior: single clock-shift releases showed sun compass dominance, but repeated exposure led them to abandon the sun compass.

AFTER-EFFECTS:
- After repeated exposure to conflicting cues, celestial cues (both stars and sunset/polarized light cues) were recalibrated to match the experimental magnetic field, restoring agreement between cue systems.
- No difference was found between recalibration of star compass vs. sunset cues.
- Magnetic compass courses remained unaffected in Silvereyes after recalibration.
- The single contradictory study (Able & Able 1995, Savannah Sparrows) suggested celestial dominance over magnetic cues, but differed in methodology (birds on breeding grounds, steep magnetic inclination).

CONCLUSION: During actual migration, the magnetic field is the dominant cue on a long-term basis, with celestial cues recalibrated to match magnetic information. This contrasts sharply with the pre-migratory period, where celestial rotation dominates. The paper suggests this shift may occur because celestial cues change with latitude during migration, while the magnetic field becomes more regular at lower latitudes, providing more reliable directional information.
</summary>

This is a PubMed record for a scientific article titled "Polarized light cues underlie compass calibration in migratory songbirds," published in Science on August 11, 2006 (Volume 313, Issue 5788, pages 837-839, DOI: 10.1126/science.1129709). The authors are Rachel Muheim (Department of Animal Ecology, Lund University, Lund, Sweden), John B. Phillips, and Susanne Akesson. The research was supported by non-U.S. government and U.S. government (non-P.H.S.) grants.

The study investigates how migratory Savannah sparrows calibrate their compass systems. Migratory songbirds use the geomagnetic field, stars, the Sun, and polarized light patterns to determine their migratory direction, and these compass systems must be calibrated to a common reference to prevent navigational errors. The researchers demonstrated that migratory Savannah sparrows use polarized light cues from the region of sky near the horizon to recalibrate their magnetic compass at both sunrise and sunset. They propose that skylight polarization patterns are used to derive an absolute (geographic) directional system that serves as the primary calibration reference for all the compasses of migratory songbirds.

--- SOURCE 16: Behavioural and physiological mechanisms of polarized light sensitivity in birds ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3049006

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article is a scientific review by Rachel Muheim (Lund University, Sweden), published in Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B (2011, Vol. 366, pp. 763–771, doi: 10.1098/rstb.2010.0196), examining the behavioural and physiological mechanisms of polarized light (PL) sensitivity in birds. The review finds that while PL sensitivity is well-studied in invertebrates and some fish, the mechanism in birds remains a major mystery in sensory biology. The article concludes that the evidence for PL cues being part of the time-compensated avian sun compass is very weak, with most studies indicating that a direct view of the Sun's disc is necessary for sun-compass orientation. Instead, cue-conflict and cue-calibration experiments demonstrate that the skylight polarization pattern near the horizon at sunrise and sunset provides birds with a seasonally and latitudinally independent compass calibration reference, used to recalibrate their magnetic compass. Direct experimental evidence for PL sensitivity in birds remains largely lacking—of the direct conditioning experiments attempted, only two (with homing pigeons by Delius et al. and Kreithen & Keeton) were successful, while others with pigeons, Japanese quails, and European starlings failed, potentially due to light intensity/reflectance artefacts and inappropriate testing contexts. Avian double cones are proposed as putative PL receptors (similar to the mechanism in fish retinas), but detailed anatomical and physiological evidence is still needed. The review highlights intriguing parallels between the functional and physiological properties of PL reception and light-dependent magnetoreception (mediated by radical-pair mechanisms in cryptochromes), suggesting the possibility of a common receptor system. Key points include: skylight polarization arises from scattering of sunlight, with maximum polarization at 90° from the Sun; the e-vector is always perpendicular to the scattering plane; birds only use PL cues near the horizon at sunrise/sunset when the e-vector is vertically aligned; and a view of the horizon (lowest 5°–10° of the polarization pattern) is crucial for compass calibration.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"In birds, the available evidence for an involvement of the skylight polarization pattern in sun-compass orientation is very weak. Instead, cue-conflict and cue-calibration experiments have shown that the skylight polarization pattern near the horizon at sunrise and sunset provides birds with a seasonally and latitudinally independent compass calibration reference."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 17: [PDF] Timing avian long-distance migration - Enlighten Publications ---
URL: https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/145118/7/145118.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific review article examining how long-distance migratory birds time their migrations using internal clock mechanisms (circadian and circannual rhythms) in interplay with environmental conditions across the annual cycle. Published in Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B in 2017, the review was authored by researchers from Lund University, the Royal Netherlands Institute for Sea Research, Moscow State University, the Netherlands Institute of Ecology, and the University of Glasgow.

The paper identifies several timing challenges faced by migrating birds:
1. Departing in time for spring and autumn migration in anticipation of future environmental conditions — For long-distance migrants crossing the equator, photoperiodism alone cannot explain timely returns since day length is nearly constant at the equator. Research by Gwinner showed circannual programming (endogenous internal year rhythms) enables timely homeward departure even under constant conditions, though these rhythms free-run and drift without environmental synchronization cues.
2. Using clocks en route for orientation, navigation, and stopover — Birds use time-compensated sun compasses (requiring circadian clock adjustments for time-of-day solar azimuth) and geomagnetic inclination compasses. Migratory birds down-regulate nightly melatonin as part of migration, weakening the clock for easier resetting, while melatonin increases during stopover for fat accumulation.
3. Fitting activities into the annual cycle with flexibility while staying on time — Birds balance flexibility against consistency, showing carry-over effects between life-cycle stages and compensating via acceleration/deceleration of activities or phase adjustments.
4. Keeping pace with global environmental change — Climate change has advanced breeding phenology in many species, but birds relying on endogenous rhythms and photoperiodism may be too inflexible to accommodate changes, creating timing mismatches with food availability.

Three case studies are presented:
- CASE STUDY 1: Circannual programming in waders (red knots Calidris canutus islandica) — 20-year captive observations showed spring life-cycle stages (pre-alternate moult, spring body mass gain) retained robust circannual cycles under constant conditions (free-running with periods near 365 days), while post-breeding stages drifted more rapidly. This differential rigidity fits the seasonal life of red knots, which breed in the High Arctic, depart the Wadden Sea in early May, stop in Iceland, and arrive at breeding grounds in early June, preparing by moulting into breeding plumage and gaining mass in late March.
- CASE STUDY 2: Songbirds' endogenous spatio-temporal programs and navigation — Individually migrating songbirds like the thrush nightingale (Luscinia luscinia) respond to geomagnetic field information triggering extensive fueling before Sahara barrier crossings. Birds have three biological compasses based on sun/skylight polarization, stars, and geomagnetic field. The paddyfield warbler (Acrocephalus agricola) has expanded its breeding range from Central Asia to the western Black Sea coast but still winters in Pakistan and India, circumventing the Black and Caspian Seas, requiring new migration directions and a 3h 20min time shift from longitude crossing (vs. 1h 40min for the thrush nightingale).
- CASE STUDY 3: Globetrotting lifestyles in terrestrial and marine migrants — Wandering albatrosses (Diomedea exulans) at Crozet Islands (~46°S) show sex-specific movement patterns (males ~3,600 km vs. females ~1,500 km), sabbatical years between breeding events, and at least four movement strategies. Palaearctic-African migrants gradually move from Sahel Zone stopovers in early autumn to southern wintering areas later in winter, tracking rainfall-driven vegetation changes from the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ).

Key conclusions include that annual cycle components can be independently modified within circannual programs, with differential rigidity between spring (more punctual) and autumn (more flexible) stages, and that birds differentially prioritize information from endogenous clocks, photoperiod-response systems, and non-photic environmental cues based on the balance between required flexibility and rigidity.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Migratory birds regularly perform impressive long-distance flights, which are timed relative to the anticipated environmental resources at destination areas that can be several thousand kilometres away. </key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 18: Magnetic orientation in migratory birds ---
URL: http://oops.uni-oldenburg.de/83/1/liemag06.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This document is the Ph.D. thesis of Miriam Liedvogel (defended September 13, 2006 at Carl von Ossietzky Universität Oldenburg, supervised by PD Dr. Henrik Mouritsen and Prof. Dr. Karl-Wilhelm Koch), titled "Magnetic orientation in migratory birds – linking behavioural phenomena with underlying molecular and neuronal mechanisms."

The thesis investigates how night-migratory birds perceive directional information from the Earth's magnetic field and how this information is processed in the brain. Using an integrative approach combining behavioral observation, molecular biology, biochemistry, biophysics, and neuroanatomy, Liedvogel's research covered the full process from the primary receptor molecule to higher brain integration centers.

KEY FINDINGS:

1. **Head-scanning behavior (Paper I):** Using a custom-built experimental setup allowing real-time monitoring under controllable magnetic field conditions, garden warblers (Sylvia borin) showed clear south-westerly orientation under natural magnetic fields but oriented randomly in zero-magnetic fields. Birds nearly tripled their head-scanning frequency in a fully compensated zero magnetic field, and showed significant increases in head-scanning just before initiating migratory restlessness. This indicated the magnetic compass sensor is in the head, and that scanning likely facilitates detection of the magnetically modulated visual pattern on the retina.

2. **Cryptochrome identification (Paper II):** Four cryptochrome family members were identified, cloned, and sequenced in the retina of migratory garden warblers: Cry1a, Cry1b, Cry2, and Cry4. Cry1a is predominantly expressed in the cytosol of ganglion cells, displaced ganglion cells, and photoreceptors. Striking differences were found between migratory and non-migratory birds: Cry1a expression was highest at night in night-migratory birds but decreased to background levels at night in non-migratory control species. Neuronal activity markers colocalized perfectly with Cry1a during night-time magnetic orientation - the first experimental demonstration of a putative light-mediated primary magnetoreceptor molecule in a bird's eye.

3. **Biophysical characterization (Paper III):** Garden warbler cryptochromes were recombinantly expressed as holoproteins (with built-in flavin cofactor) in a baculovirus/Sf9 cell system - the first successful expression of an animal cryptochrome holoprotein in a heterologous eukaryotic system. This required a novel on-column denaturation/refolding step to overcome known difficulties. Garden warbler cryptochromes are light-excited, absorb in the blue spectral range (matching wavelengths known to elicit magnetic orientation in behavioral experiments), and form radical pairs lasting approximately 10 milliseconds - sufficiently long-lived to detect Earth-strength magnetic fields.

4. **Cluster N identification (Paper IV):** Behavioral molecular mapping identified a distinct forebrain area in night-migratory birds, termed "Cluster N" ("N" for night), showing high neuronal activation at night during magnetic orientation but not during the day. Cluster N was inactive in non-migratory zebra finches (Taeniopygia guttata) and canaries (Serinus canaria). Located adjacent to or as part of the visual Wulst, covering birds' eyes with light-tight covers significantly reduced Cluster N activation to near baseline, demonstrating it is active specifically during night-vision in night-migratory birds.

5. **Lateralization and further tests (Paper V, VI):** European robins (Erithacus rubecula) showed significant dominance of Cluster N activation in the right hemisphere. Garden warblers tested under different magnetic field conditions and monochromatic red light showed no significant differences in Cluster N activation, so a definitive role in magnetic compass processing could not be confirmed. Additional analysis found positive correlations between movement and activity levels in 10 cerebral regions and parts of the cerebellum, supporting the hypothesis that vocal learning brain systems evolved from a pre-existing motor pathway.

METHODS: Experiments relied on careful behavioral observation (especially the final 60 minutes before tissue collection), followed by brain dissection, cryostat sectioning, radioactive in situ hybridization for neuronal activity mapping (using immediate early genes like c-Fos and ZENK), and immunohistochemistry for retinal tissue. Primary study species were garden warblers and European robins; control species were zebra finches, canaries, and Sardinian warblers (Sylvia melanocephala).

CONCLUSION: All findings support a light-mediated magnetoperception mechanism in night-migratory birds, consistent with the hypothesis that magnetically modulated intensity patterns are perceived by the visual system - i.e., night-migratory birds may literally "see" the direction of the Earth's magnetic field. The thesis comprises six manuscripts (three published, one submitted, one under review, one near submission) plus supplementary materials on cryptochrome cloning methodology.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Migratory birds use head scans to detect the direction of the Earth's magnetic field" (Paper I title); "During my Ph.D. studies, I identified, cloned and sequenced four different members of the cryptochrome family in the retina of migratory garden warblers: Cry1a, Cry1b, Cry2 and Cry4."; "This was the first successful expression of an animal cryptochrome in a heterologous cell-system with its flavin cofactor built in (holoprotein)... light-excitation leads to radical pair formation and that these radicals are very long lived (~ 10 milliseconds) and therefore very well suited for detecting the direction of Earth-strength magnetic fields."; "In other words, night-migratory birds may literally 'see' the direction of the Earth's magnetic field."; "Cluster N is a brain area active specifically during night-vision in night-migratory birds" and "Covering up the birds' eyes strongly reduced neuronal activity in Cluster N."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 19: Re-calibration of the magnetic compass in hand-raised European robins (Erithacus rubecula) ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4585702

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific article published in Scientific Reports (2015, vol. 5, article 14323, doi: 10.1038/srep14323) by Bianca Alert, Andreas Michalik, Nadine Thiele, Michael Bottesch, and Henrik Mouritsen from the University of Oldenburg, Germany. The study investigates whether hand-raised European robins (Erithacus rubecula) that never developed a functional magnetic compass before or during their first autumn migration could re-learn to orient if exposed to natural celestial cues during the subsequent winter and spring.

METHODS: 41 European robin nestlings were collected near Oldenburg, Lower Saxony, Germany (13 in 2010, 13 in 2011, 15 in 2013) and hand-raised in a windowless room with no access to natural celestial cues. During their first summer, they were exposed to artificial celestial rotation but did not develop appropriate orientation. In subsequent spring seasons (late February onward), approximately half of the birds (experimental group) were transferred to an outdoor aviary with access to natural celestial cues, while control birds remained indoors. Orientation was tested in Emlen funnels within magnetically-controlled huts simulating the local geomagnetic field (48,880 nT, 67.5° inclination).

RESULTS: During first autumn migration, none of the birds showed significant magnetic orientation (Rayleigh test: r = 0.17, n = 41, P = 0.295). However, in the following spring, the experimental group (n = 22) significantly oriented in their species-specific north-easterly spring migratory direction (mean = 56°, r = 0.43, P = 0.004; V test P = 0.004), while control birds (n = 19) remained disoriented (r = 0.08, P = 0.895). The concentration of the experimental group was significantly higher than controls (P = 0.002). Similar results were observed across three different years, with the means not differing between seasons (Watson-Williams F test: F = 1.307, P = 0.294). CONCLUSIONS: European robins remain capable of establishing a functional orientation system after their first autumn migration, suggesting avian compass systems are more flexible than previously believed. The results contrast with earlier findings (Able & Able) which suggested re-gained dominance of an inherited magnetic preference, and with Emlen's work suggesting star compass learning was limited to a sensitive juvenile period. This webpage is an Academia.edu paper page for the 1976 scientific article "Interrelation of magnetic compass and star orientation in night-migrating birds" by Wolfgang Wiltschko, published in the Journal of Comparative Physiology A. --- SOURCE 21: Historical Series:  Magnetic Sense of Birds ---
URL: https://www.ks.uiuc.edu/History/magnetoreception

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article, "That Nest of Wires We Call the Imagination: A History of some Key Scientists Behind the Bird Compass Sense" by Lisa Pollack (May 2012, from the Theoretical and Computational Biophysics Group at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign), traces the history of how scientists discovered that birds sense magnetic fields through a quantum biochemical process known as the radical pair reaction. The narrative follows two parallel discovery paths:

The article begins with historical context: homing pigeons were used extensively in WWII (over 16,000 parachuted into Europe, with many receiving the Dickin Medal), and birds like the bar-tailed godwit can fly non-stop up to 7,100 miles. Though conjecture about magnetic sensing existed in the 19th century, experimental proof came only in the 1960s.

The scientific history covers:
- Klaus Schulten, hired in 1974 at the Max Planck Institute in Göttingen, theorized that magnetic fields could affect chemical reactions (explaining "fast triplets" in Albert Weller's experiments). His prediction was confirmed in 1976.
- Independently, Maria-Elisabeth Michel-Beyerle at the Technical University of Munich reached similar conclusions, inspired by Merrifield's 1972 work on magnetic field effects in molecular crystals and the book "The Exciplex." Both published findings in 1976.
- Wolfgang Wiltschko discovered in 1965-66 that European robins use magnetic orientation (his epiphany came on October 12, 1963). He and his wife Roswitha published their first paper together in 1972, proposing an inclination compass.
- Schulten published the first proposal of a chemical compass in 1978 (with Swenberg and Weller), after his paper was rejected by Science. A question from Dudley Herschbach ("where in the bird is the laser?") convinced him the sensor was light-dependent and in the eye.
- The radical pair mechanism works because an external magnetic field causes interconversion between singlet and triplet electron spin states, affecting chemical reaction yields.
- In 2000, Schulten, Thorsten Ritz, and Salih Adem proposed cryptochrome as the candidate molecule in the eye for the avian magnetic compass.
- Key recent findings include Henrik Mouritsen's identification of "cluster N" brain center (whose destruction abolishes magnetic compass but not star/sun orientation), magnetic field effects on cryptochrome-mediated plant systems (Margaret Ahmad), and oscillating magnetic field experiments with fruit flies and birds that provided more evidence for the radical pair mechanism.

The article emphasizes the importance of multi-disciplinary collaboration (behavioral biologists, molecular chemists, physicists) in solving this mystery. It includes several direct quotes from Klaus Schulten, including "The longer you work on a problem the harder it actually gets" and the anecdote about Ed Schlag's remark "What is said over a glass of beer doesn't count."
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"What was a surprise for everybody, including myself, was that this quantum process would actually lead to a very significant change in the chemical reaction," says Klaus Schulten.
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 1: Birds May Use 'Sound Maps' To Navigate Huge Distances : NPR ---
URL: https://www.npr.org/2013/02/01/170884694/birds-may-use-sound-maps-to-navigate-huge-distances

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This NPR "All Things Considered" segment (aired February 1, 2013) features an interview between host Melissa Block and Jonathan Hagstrum, a geophysicist with the U.S. Geological Survey, about his hypothesis that homing pigeons use "infrasound" (very low-frequency sound below human hearing) as a navigational map. Hagstrum's study was published in the Journal of Experimental Biology.

Key points from the interview:
- Infrasound is defined as sound below human hearing (~20 Hz). Pigeons can hear down to 0.05 Hz.
- Hagstrum theorizes that deep ocean waves constantly produce acoustic energy that travels through the Earth as seismic energy, is reradiated at the landscape back into the atmosphere, and that pigeons (and other birds) listen to this reradiated infrasound to navigate home.
- While birds use the sun, stars, and geomagnetic field as compasses, the long-standing mystery has been what serves as the "map" — how birds know where they are relative to home.
- Hagstrum's research began after reading about pigeon races in the eastern United States where birds got lost on perfectly sunny days, which he traced to sonic booms from the Concorde affecting their infrasound cues.
- He used a large database of pigeon-release data from Cornell University (1967-1980, spanning 14 years), a computer program modeling sound movement through the atmosphere, and weather data for release days to test his theory.
- His findings showed that on days when pigeons were confused or couldn't leave a release site, the sound was being bent up and over by the temperature and wind structure of the atmosphere, preventing it from reaching the birds. On days when they returned home successfully, the sound was reaching the release site.
- Hagstrum suggests the broader implications could extend to whales, sea turtles, and migrating birds (including those flying nonstop from Alaska to New Zealand), which might all use infrasound. He notes that unlike GPS with its massive satellite infrastructure, this natural navigation method works by simply listening.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Infrasound is very low-frequency sound. And infra means it's below human hearing. So pigeons can hear down to 0.05 hertz, and humans can hear down to about 20 hertz." — Jonathan Hagstrum, "There are waves in the deep ocean that are constantly producing acoustic energy. And that acoustic energy travels through the Earth as seismic energy, and then is reradiated at the landscape back into the atmosphere. And I think pigeons and other birds probably are listening to that reradiated infrasound, and using that to find their way home." — Jonathan Hagstrum, "In order to get home from some location, you need a map and a compass. And we know what the compass senses are, in birds. They use the stars, the position of the sun and the geomagnetic field, as compasses. But what the big mystery has been for a long time - has been, what is the map?" — Jonathan Hagstrum, "I was able to get a very large database of pigeon-release data from Cornell University; where pigeons had been released for 14 years, between 1967 and 1980." — Jonathan Hagstrum
</key_excerpts>

PURPOSE/CONCLUSION: The paper proposes a framework to explore the importance of infrasound (low-frequency inaudible sound, 3.3 mHz–20 Hz) for seabird navigation. Seabirds cross vast, featureless oceans, and existing navigational mechanisms (visual, olfactory, magnetic) do not fully explain their long-distance homing abilities. The authors argue infrasound may provide additional navigational cues and propose three hypotheses for how seabirds could use infrasound—as an acoustic beacon, landmark, or gradient.

KEY FACTS:
- Infrasound is ubiquitous in the marine environment and can propagate thousands of kilometers (even globally for powerful signals like the 2013 Chelyabinsk meteor airburst).
- Sound propagates at ~334 m/s at ~15°C; infrasound frequency range is 3.3 mHz to 20 Hz (below the human audible threshold).
- Marine infrasound sources include: microbaroms (0.1–1.0 Hz, from standing ocean waves, quasi-continuous), surf (above 1.0 Hz near coastlines), and transient sources (severe weather, earthquakes, meteor explosions, volcanic eruptions). Infrasound can radiate from underwater sources into the atmosphere.
- The seasonal reversal of the circumpolar vortex and downwind propagation efficiency cause seasonal variations in long-range infrasound; downwind birds would experience higher sound levels than upwind birds.
- Of >9,000 bird species, hearing has been tested in <50 species; only five have been measured at low frequencies, with four of five demonstrating hearing below 20 Hz (infrasound range). Only one seabird species hearing measured... actually no seabird infrasonic sensitivities have been tested empirically.
- Domestic chickens have infrasonic hearing thresholds comparable to Indian elephants.
- Homing pigeons can perceive infrasound at frequencies as low as 0.05 Hz (Kreithen and Quine, 1979).
- Pigeon thresholds for frequency shift detection increased from 1% to 7% as frequencies lowered from 20 Hz to 1 Hz (Quine and Kreithen, 1981).
- Seabird flight speeds (40 km/h / 11 m/s) could produce a 3% Doppler frequency shift of a 1 Hz signal—potentially sufficient for a detectable frequency shift.

THREE PROPOSED HYPOTHESES:
1. BEACON: A target location (e.g., the colony) is the infrasound source the bird detects and moves toward (requires direction perception or detecting approach/retreat via field intensity variations).
2. LANDMARK: Multiple infrasound sources (e.g., islands) create a unique acoustic signature at a location via combinations of signals; birds compare power spectra to locate themselves within a frame of reference.
3. GRADIENT: Large-scale infrasonic amplitude gradient fields (e.g., from microbaroms or surf) provide a functional coordinate reference system; intersecting gradients could serve as a bi-coordinate map.

THREE PROPOSED DETECTION MECHANISMS:
1. Interaural time/level differences via middle ear coupling (interaural canals as pressure difference receivers).
2. Doppler effect frequency shifts during flight.
3. Direct perception of particle motion via otolithic vestibular organs (saccule, utricle, lagena), with 180° ambiguity possibly resolved by phase-difference neural computation.

DETECTION LIMITATIONS: Bird infrasonic hearing thresholds below 20 Hz are generally >50 dB relative to 20 μPa SPL, increasing toward lower frequencies. Wavelengths of infrasound are much larger than interaural distance, limiting directional cues. Auditory systems encode infrasound frequency changes better than amplitude changes.

FUTURE DIRECTIONS: The authors suggest testing hypotheses by combining conceptual navigation models with empirical seabird movement data and in-situ infrasound measurements. Recommended approaches include:
- Electrophysiological sensitivity tests to infrasonic vibration in 3D (e.g., auditory brainstem response).
- Correlating movement decisions with infrasound along foraging trips, comparing outbound/return legs.
- Constructing agent-based conceptual models of navigation.
- Using natural extreme events (volcanic eruptions, hurricanes) as quasi-experimental opportunities.
- Deploying mobile infrasound loggers and miniature multidisciplinary sensor platforms with biologging devices (GPS, accelerometers, magnetometers).
- The global International Monitoring System (IMS) infrasound array network (54 of eventual 60 arrays installed since 2001, under the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty) provides global infrasound observations.

--- SOURCE 7: Olfactory navigation - Wikipedia ---
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olfactory_navigation

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Olfactory navigation is a hypothesis proposing that homing pigeons use their sense of smell for navigation and homing. The article discusses two principal versions of this hypothesis: Papi's mosaic model, which proposes that pigeons construct an odour map from the distribution of environmental odours within a radius of 70–100 kilometres (learning to associate wind-borne scents like pine forests, coastlines, and city pollution with locations), and Wallraff's gradient theory, which proposes long-range, stable atmospheric odour gradients that pigeons compare against home loft concentrations. However, meteorologists deny that such predictable odour gradients exist in nature, and the evidence for an 'olfactory map' is not conclusive.

Background: Homing requires both a compass sense (direction) and a map sense (location). Magnetic orientation and the sun have been proposed as compass mechanisms. In 1972, Papi and colleagues first reported that anosmic pigeons were severely impaired in orientation and homing, leading to the olfactory navigation hypothesis.

Empirical evidence: Experiments manipulating wind direction (e.g., rearing pigeons with wind carrying olive oil from the south and turpentine from the north) produced results supporting the olfactory hypothesis in Italy, where pigeons flew in directions consistent with their learned odour associations. However, these results failed to replicate in Germany, Italy, and the United States. Deflector loft experiments, which shifted apparent wind direction by 90°, produced consistent ~90° orientation errors, but anosmic pigeons showed the same degree of error, suggesting results may reflect non-odour factors like wind responses or light reflection. Notably, pigeons lack highly developed nasal apparatus and associated brain functions. A consistent finding is that anosmic pigeons released from familiar sites are essentially unaffected.

Other sensory cues: The Earth's magnetic field is a potential map cue. Keeton (1971) and Ioalé (1984) reported magnets caused disorientation under overcast conditions. Magnetic storms shift initial bearings, and magnetic anomalies cause disorientation even in sunny conditions. The sun's predictable 15° per hour movement also serves as a celestial compass, demonstrated in migratory European starlings and reproduced in some pigeon studies.

Conclusion: The fundamental question remains whether pigeons can smell. While empirical evidence shows homing can be compromised by interfering with the olfactory environment, variability in effects indicates odours are not the sole navigational cue. Map sense appears to rely on comparison of multiple available cues, and physical limitations combined with inconsistent findings render the olfactory hypothesis questionable, though odour may play a highly variable role among multiple navigational factors.
</summary>

**Methods:** Thirty-six inexperienced pigeons (~15-18 months old) from the Arnino field station (Pisa, Italy) were transported in air-tight containers to release sites 53 km (Bolgheri) and 61 km (Montespertoli) from home. Three experimental groups were tested: 
- Control (C) group: exposed to natural environmental air
- Pure Air (PA) group: exposed to charcoal-filtered pure air
- Artificial Odour (AO) group: exposed to pure air plus puffs of artificial plant-based odours (eucalyptus, orange, jasmine, rose, lavender)
Before release, all pigeons received nasal anaesthesia (Xylocaine through the choanae) and were fitted with 1 Hz GPS data loggers (Technosmart and E-obs devices). - Within the first hour after release, both AO and PA pigeons (receiving no environmental odours) showed impaired navigational performances at each release site.
- Control birds showed significantly oriented mean vector distributions at both sites, with directions close to home.
- AO pigeons showed the most severe impairment: tortuous flight paths, poor homeward orientation (median tortuosity 0.24 vs. C=0.69; homeward component +0.08 vs. C=+0.48), and significantly lower efficiency index than controls.
- AO pigeons circled near the release site and remained in its vicinity even one hour after release.
- At Bolgheri, control pigeons were significantly closer to home (median 29.9 km) than AO pigeons (median 53.5 km) within the first hour.
- Homing performance at Bolgheri: C pigeons were significantly faster (median homing speed 7.97 km/h) than both PA and AO groups.
- The effect of artificial odours appeared even more detrimental than pure air deprivation, possibly because artificial odours impregnated in feathers confounded/environmental odour perception even after anaesthesia wore off.

**Conclusions:** The data support the olfactory navigation hypothesis and contradict the olfactory activation hypothesis. Pigeons only navigate well when they perceive intact environmental odours. The authors argue that artificial non-sense odours act as a disturbing factor, and that accepting the activation hypothesis would require the implausible admission that pigeons are never impaired by direct manipulation of the navigational mechanism itself—only by manipulation of the olfactory system that activates it. The GPS tracking of non-homing birds proved critically important, as virtual vanishing bearings alone did not always correspond with en-route behaviour (notably at Montespertoli).
