Vol.:(0123456789) Journal of Ornithology https://doi.org/10.1007/s10336-024-02234-4 REVIEW In‑flight reactions of nocturnally migrating birds to winds Bruno Bruderer1 · Pius Korner1 · Dieter Peter1 Received: 5 May 2024 / Revised: 12 October 2024 / Accepted: 29 October 2024 © The Author(s) 2024 Abstract Available knowledge on in-flight reactions of nocturnal bird migrants to winds is reviewed, with emphasis on the challeng-ing topographical and meteorological conditions in Western Europe, and differences from the situation in North America discussed. Conclusions drawn are used for a new approach: using individual radar tracks of nocturnal migrants (mainly pas-serines) as well as winds measured at their flight altitudes, we defined the basic direction (BD = average flight direction of all migrants tracked under negligible wind influence) as a reference. For two altitudinal zones above a radar site near Nuremberg, we modelled the deviations of tracks and headings from BD for increasing wind from six 60° sectors. A comparison of birds’ air speeds Va with winds from four 90°-sectors confirmed that Va increased with opposing winds from ~ 11 to 13 (14) m/s; a similar increase occurred with side winds. An expected, slight decrease of Va with increasing following winds was only indicated for high-flying, not for low-flying birds. A predicted increase in average Va due to decreasing air density with increasing height was not observed; possible explanations (birds climbing to high altitudes in following, but not in strong opposing winds) are discussed. Over the whole autumn migration season, headings were concentrated in a sector of ± 30° around 230° in both altitudinal zones. Prevailing winds from 230 to 320° (SW–NW, i.e. opposing from right) led to widely scattered tracks primarily between 190° and 270°, but additional ones in the SE sector (mainly 100°–170°). The analysis of tracks and headings relative to BD revealed the following features. (1) Overcompensation was frequently observed at low wind speeds (< 3 m/s); (2) under all wind conditions, but particularly with opposing winds and at low flight levels, tracks were widely scattered, including birds deviating more than 90° from BD. (3) Under opposing and side winds from the right compensatory efforts led to partial drift compensation up to wind speeds of ~ 8–10 m/s. Because efforts to compensate drift dwindled with increasing wind speeds, birds were fully drifted. Many even shifted their heading to due south and, hence, overdrifted. (4) Opposing and side winds from the left induced partial compensation at low flight levels and full drift above 1500 m asl. (5) The lateral components of the rare and weak following winds led to tracks close to expected minimal drift (without important compensation needed). In general, migrants compensated less for deviations by wind force than expected. The tendency of birds to maintain headings close to BD under opposing winds was so strong that many individuals continued migration with minimal progress over ground or even with retrograde migration as an extreme. On the other hand, there was an omnipresent fraction of birds with tracks far from seasonally favourable directions, including reverse migration.
Keywords Bird migration · Tracking radar · Basic direction · Drift · Compensation · Track · Heading · Flight altitude Zusammenfassung Reaktionen nachts ziehender Vögel auf aktuelle Windbedingungen Vorhandene Publikationen über die Reaktionen nächtlich ziehender Vögel auf Windeinflüsse wurden – mit Fokus auf den herausfordernden topografischen und meteorologischen Bedingungen im westlichen Europa – zusammengefasst und Unterschiede zu den Verhältnissen in Nordamerika diskutiert. Daraus abgeleitete Folgerungen führten zu einem neuen Communicated by A. Hedenström. * Bruno Bruderer bruno.bruderer@vogelwarte.ch 1 Swiss Ornithological Institute/Schweizerische Vogelwarte, Seerose 1, 6204 Sempach, Switzerland Journal of Ornithology methodischen Ansatz: Wir nutzten die individuellen Flugwege von Nachtziehern (mehrheitlich Singvögel) sowie auf der Flughöhe der Vögel gemessene Winddaten, um eine Basisrichtung (BD = mittlere Flugrichtung von bei vernachlässigbaren Windstärken ziehenden Vögeln) als Referenz zu definieren. Zunehmende Rückenwinde induzierten dagegen keine eindeutige Reduktion von Va. Eine aufgrund abnehmender Luftdichte erwartete Zunahme von Va mit der Höhe konnte nicht festgestellt werden; wahrscheinlich, weil die Vögel bei starkem Gegenwind das Aufsteigen in den oberen Höhenbereich vermieden. – Über die ganze Herbstzugperiode waren die Eigenrichtungen in beiden Höhenbereichen konzentriert in einem Sektor von ± 30° um 230°. Vorherrschende Winde von 230–320° (SW-NW, d.h. Gegenwind von rechts) führten zu weit gestreuten Flugrichtungen vor allem zwischen 190° und 270° und zusätzlich Richtungen gegen den SE-Sektor (100°-170°). – Die Analyse von Flug- und Eigenrichtungen relativ zu BD deckte folgende Merkmale auf: (1) Überkompensation trat häufig auf bei geringen Windgeschwindigkeiten (< 3 m/s). (2) Unter allen Windbedingungen, aber speziell bei Gegenwinden auf geringen Flughöhen waren die Flugrichtungen weit gestreut und schlossen Vögel ein, die mehr als 90° von BD abwichen. (3) Bei Seiten- und Gegenwinden von rechts erzielten die Vögel Teilkompensation bis zu Windgeschwind von ~ 8–10 m/s. Abnehmende Kompensationsanstrengungen der Vögel mit zunehmender Windgeschwindigkeit führten zu vollständiger Verdriftung. Viele drehten ihre Körperachse gegen Süden und erreichten damit Über-Drift. (4) Seiten- und Gegenwinden von links führten zu Teilkompensation auf geringen Flughöhen und zu voller Drift oberhalb von 1500 m über Meer. (5) Die lateralen Komponenten der seltenen und schwachen Winden von hinten erlaubten Flugrichtungen nahe bei der erwarteten minimalen Drift, ohne wesentliche Kompensation. – Generell kompensierten die Vögel weniger für windbedingte Abweichungen als erwartet. Die Tendenz von Zugvögeln, die Ausrichtung ihrer Körperachse nahe bei BD zu halten, war so stark, dass viele Individuen ihren Zug fortsetzen, auch wenn sie bei starkem Gegenwind nur minim über Grund vorankamen oder als Extrem sogar vom Wind rückwärts getrieben wurden. Anderseits gab es einen beinahe ständig vorhandenen Anteil an Vögeln, die stark von saison-konformen Richtungen abwichen und dabei auch Umkehrzug zeigten.
Introduction and review Migrating birds move with the body of air in which they fly. The movements of this medium have enormous effects on the time and energy budget of the migrants, and they may cause major problems for orientation (e.g., Shamoun-Baranes et al. 2017). The effects of strong adverse winds can be reduced by avoiding flights under such conditions. How-ever, because westerly and south-westerly winds occur fre-quently in the western half of Europe, autumn migrants need to fly under such conditions to keep with their time schedule and, thus, are forced to implement means to cope with wind influence aloft (Erni et al. 2005). Once in flight, the birds can increase their air speed Va or modify their heading ­ Ra to mitigate deviations of their tracks Rg by wind. Counteracting adverse wind effects becomes increasingly demanding and essential for survival with increasing wind force. The vital importance of such behaviour has stimulated numerous stud-ies in this field, particularly since radar facilitated the meas-urement of directions and speeds of nocturnally migrating birds. However, the circular distribution of winds and migra-tory movements implied major challenges for the analysis of available data. We will, therefore, provide a brief review of pertinent studies as a background for our own approach.
Our focus is on nocturnal migration in Western Europe, because topography and frequent unfavourable winds for autumn migration require challenging adaptations. Limited considerations about the conditions in North America are included in the discussion.
Historical overview Basic ideas about the influence of winds on migratory direc-tions were provided by Alerstam (1976). He defined full wind drift (flying with a fixed heading), complete drift com-pensation (flying along a fixed track), and partial compen-sation (either compensating with respect to moving waves over water, or incomplete compensation of wind above land). The term “pseudo-drift” was used for wind-induced shifts in the observed mean flight directions (tracks) due to the supposed participation of different species or populations profiting from following winds to reach different intermedi-ate goals. As a universal measure of drift, he suggested the linear regression coefficient b of track directions on α (the angle between track and heading directions). In a second part, he critically reviewed radar (mainly surveillance radar, thus not altitudinally differentiated) information on migra-tory movements and their relation to simultaneous wind situations (presented in publications from 1957 till 1975) and drew the following conclusions: (1) all the observed movements showed at least partial compensation for wind Journal of Ornithology drift; (2) ample evidence demonstrated the birds’ capability for complete drift compensation, while most instances of observed drift appeared to be explainable by pseudo-drift; (3) some cases, however, indicated partial drift effects that could not completely be explained by pseudo-drift. Addi-tionally, he stated that birds were extremely rarely overpow-ered by winds exceeding the birds’ air speed. None of the studies suggested the existence of overcompensation (nega-tive drift).
Besides immediate reactions to wind effects, Alerstam (1979a, b) suggested that birds might tolerate drift in the early phases of migration far from their goal by flying at high altitudes with relatively strong winds. Descending to lower flight levels with weaker winds towards the end of their flight would allow them to correct for previous drift. A different approach to estimate the influence of wind on track and heading directions was applied by Bruderer and Liechti (1990). They defined site-specific basic directions (BD) under minimal wind influence (VW < 5 m/s) as refer-ence directions to quantify wind-induced deviations from the bearing towards the assumed intermediate goals (along the BD). At Nuremberg in southern Germany, estimated BD for autumn migration was ~ 230° in the lowest 1000 m agl, and ~ 218° above, with only minor deviations due to differ-ent wing-beat classes or the progress of the season. In weak to moderate opposing winds from W, birds headed into the wind, but—apart from a slight increase in air speed—they did not augment their efforts to compensate for increasing wind force. Thus, drift increased with increasing wind speed. With very high wind speeds, the birds shifted their body axis southward. This was considered as tolerated southward or south-eastward drift, and not as pseudo-drift (see Liechti 1993 below).
Bruderer and Jenni (1990) found (based on the analysis of ringing recoveries of passerines crossing Switzerland and on birds caught in the Swiss Lowlands and on Alpine passes) that the mean recruiting directions shifted from 220 to 230° for short-distance migrants with low fat scores towards 200° for trans-Sahara migrants with high fat scores. Southerly directions and high fat stores suggested a provenience from northern populations and trans-Sahara migration, thus pro-viding a plausible interpretation of the tracking radar data showing more southerly directions among high-flying birds.
Reviewing publications up to 1990, Richardson (1991) concluded that birds developed many adaptations to cope with wind effects: Particularly, high-flying birds may allow crosswinds to drift their tracks laterally from the preferred direction, while many low-flying birds compensate for drift, and may even overcompensate to make up for previous drift. Tolerating partial drift at high flight levels in the early stages of migration and overcompensating later by flying at low levels against weaker winds may even be considered an optimal strategy (Alerstam 1979a, b). Compensation may be more common where there are prominent topographical features. Other adaptations include reduction of drift by fly-ing at times and/or altitudes without strong crosswinds. The significance of pseudo-drift was put into perspective, but was still considered a major complication for the interpreta-tion of field data.
Liechti (1993) analysed tracking radar data from the area of Nuremberg and showed that an increase in south-erly tracks with altitude (in addition to the generally SW-oriented movements) was mainly due to winds. Under strong headwinds, the proportion of southerly headings increased and resulted in tracks towards SE or even E (at all heights). These SE movements were not considered as pseudo-drift, because SE flights were the result of drift with winds from W, but not downwind flights with NW winds. Partial com-pensation for wind drift by nocturnal migrants seemed to occur mainly in relation to wind direction rather than wind speed. Birds apparently adapted their drift compensation to relatively low wind speed at low flight levels. Thereby they were able to compensate completely for side wind speeds of less than 20% of their own air speed (i.e. about 2.4 m/s for small passerines); this means that average track directions remain ± constant under weak winds of all directions, but show increasing drift at higher wind speeds, resulting in diminishing partial compensation.
The relation between flight power and air speed of birds can be used to predict maximum range speed Vmr (Penny-cuick 1972). This optimal air speed for minimizing cost of transport is modified by winds. Calculations of such modifi-cations based on field data were based on head- and tailwind components (e.g. Bruderer 1971), while Liechti et al. (1994) demonstrated that side winds had an additional effect on Vmr. Vmr depends not only on the effect of wind on the bird’s ground speed, but also on the bird’s angle of compensation for side wind. Optimal air speeds should be faster in side winds than in pure tail- and headwinds. Critical tests of this prediction are, however, only possible if the goal direction is known and birds compensate completely for wind drift (i.e. only at very low wind speeds!).
A goal-oriented migrant optimizing energy expenditure during flight should adjust not only its heading, but also its air speed with respect to wind. Liechti (1995) introduced a model combining simultaneous modifications of headings and air speed in an optimal strategy (using a garden war-bler Sylvia borin with a theoretical maximum range speed Vmr = 10.5 m/s as a model bird). According to this model, the angle of compensation culminates with side winds from behind (~ 60°), while adjustments in air speed are strongest with opposing winds. Increasing air speed under opposing winds results in a considerable reduction of drift.
Tracking-radar samples from the area of Lund led Bäck-mann and Alerstam (2003) conclude that wind drift was the dominant cause of the large scatter of track directions, Journal of Ornithology especially during the autumn season. Besides drift, they detected partial drift compensation in spring, but not in autumn. In situations with low wind speeds, headings seemed to be slightly more concentrated in spring than in autumn, suggesting less accurate orientation in autumn, when a large proportion of the migrants are naïve juveniles. According to the presented data, we may also think of alter-native interpretations: (1) birds are closer to their destination in spring and may—according to Alerstam (1979a,b)—cor-rect for previous drift when approaching their goal areas; (2) considering that fast flying birds with wing-beat frequencies below 11.5 Hz were the dominating category of migrants, particularly in spring, and showed the highest concentra-tion of heading directions, we may suggest that waders and waterfowl contributed to the reduction of drift in spring.
Liechti (2006) summarized studies on flight behaviour of migratory birds in relation to winds published during the 15 years since Richardson’s (1991) review. These studies corroborate that birds select favourable wind conditions for departure as well as aloft to save energy. For some long-distance migrants, tailwind may even be an indispensable support to cross large barriers. A new aspect was brought into discussion by proposing a simple method for drift detec-tion by the migrants: A flying bird may determine the angle between its body axis (heading) and flight direction (track) by observing the angular velocity of landmarks to the left and right below its flight path. Maximum angular velocity is always right-angled to the flight direction (irrespective of heading). Without lateral drift, the maximum angular veloc-ity of landmarks occurs also at right angles to both sides of the body axis. With increasing drift, maximum angular velocities deviate increasingly from the body axis: on the lee (downwind) side, landmarks in front of the bird move faster, while on the windward side, the landmarks on a diagonal behind the bird move faster. Obviously, the effectiveness of such a procedure decreases with increasing height above ground. Compensation for lateral wind drift reduces the risk that the flight routes would mainly be shaped by the wind conditions experienced en route. Hence, a migratory bird should be able to detect the varying wind forces aloft and react adequately to either profit from wind or at least avoid costly wind effects.
Green and Alerstam (2002) evaluated four methods that had been used to quantitatively estimate wind drift or com-pensation. They found that the original method of Aler-stam (1976) provided robust and reliable results. In con-trast, regressions of individual flight directions in relation to α (in this case, the angle between track and heading for individually tracked targets) proved to produce biased and spurious results, overestimating compensation under fol-lowing winds, while overestimating drift under opposing winds. The authors state that “comparing mean directions for cases with winds from the left and right in relation to individual flight directions also gives biased and spurious results unless there is full variation in wind directions or an equal distribution of crosswinds from left and right”. As an alternative, we suggest considering the influence of winds from different sectors separately.
A general background to the present study is given by the publications of Bruderer & Peter (2022) on the direc-tions of autumn migration between Europe and the West African savannas and Bruderer et al. (2018) on the vertical distribution of bird migration between the Baltic Sea and the Sahara.
Aim Instead of analysing the problem of drift vs compensation for entire migratory movements (as suggested by Thomas Alerstam and colleagues), we wanted to know how indi-vidual nocturnal migrants react to winds of varying speeds and incident angles. To avoid the problems arising due to the circular distribution of winds and migratory directions (mentioned by Green and Alerstam 2002), we analysed the reactions of birds to winds from different sectors. The inci-dent angles were measured relative to a site-specific basic direction (BD), where BD is the average travel direction of birds migrating under negligible wind influence through a given area in a migratory season.
Nocturnal migrants (mainly passerines) tend to engage in migration when their position relative to cyclones and anticyclones is optimal (Richardson 1990), usually when winds follow and the probability for rain is low (Erni et al. 2002). Once airborne, the birds move with the air mass in which they fly. This “physical drift” (passive displacement by wind) reduces a bird’s progress with respect to its inter-mediate or final goal; thus, it would be meaningful for the bird to either land or optimize its flight behaviour to miti-gate negative effects, e.g. by choosing flight altitudes with less unfavourable wind, or by adjusting its air speed and/ or heading. The wind vector and the bird’s own movement together result in the track of the bird. We used the differ-ence between physical drift (i.e. zero compensation) and the average track directions of the birds per wind sector to quantify the effectiveness of the migrants to mitigate the effects of wind. The reactions of the birds were visualized by comparing the theoretical heading required for full com-pensation under increasing wind force with the averages of measured headings in each sector.
The ideas on wind-dependent reactions of migrating birds presented in the reviewed publications lead us to the follow-ing hypotheses: (H1)Air speeds of birds increase with opposing and side winds, and slightly decrease in following winds.
Journal of Ornithology – As suggested by Pennycuick (1972) by the curve of power versus speed, predicting that the speed of maxi-mum range Vmr (minimising energy cost per unit dis-tance travelled) increases with opposing winds and decreases with following winds.
(H2)Air speeds of birds increase with altitude.
– This according to flight aerodynamic theory predicting that air speed increases with decreasing air density.
(H3) Opposing and side winds (relative to BD) are fully compensated at low wind speeds, while higher wind speeds lead to increasing drift.
– Testing Liechti’s (1993) conclusion that average track directions remain ± constant under weak winds from all directions, but show increasing drift at higher wind speeds.
(H4) High wind speeds (close to or exceeding the birds’ air speed) lead to full drift or even overdrift.
– Verifying the observation of Bruderer and Liechti (1990) that besides drift increasing with wind speed, birds seemed to shift their body axis southward at very high wind speeds, thus augmenting southward or south-eastward drift.
(H5) Winds from the right (in autumn from W and NW) favour more drift than side winds from the left (in autumn S).
– Because in Western Europe southward drift (by winds from W and NW) brings autumn migrants closer to their southern destinations than drift towards the right (NW).
(H6) Reverse migration occurs in most nights, but is favoured by winds opposite to preferred migratory direc-tions (which are towards SW in autumn).
– Re-considering a statement of Komenda-Zehnder et al. (2002) that a small proportion of reverse migration is an intrinsic feature of nocturnal bird migration, and its volume is not explainable by weather factors (in the trade-wind zone of Israel).
(H7) Retrograde migration (birds flying backwards, i.e. tail-on with the wind) can be observed under opposing winds surmounting the birds’ flight capacities.
– Richardson (1991) mentioned the occurrence of “ret-rograde migration” of birds being blown backwards by headwinds exceeding their air speed.
(H8) Downwind flights towards SE (towards south-east-ern goal areas and thus pseudo-drift) are rare.
– Pseudo-drift (due to varying proportions of birds with differing goal areas) is often mentioned, but is suggested to be rare in southern Germany by Liechti (1993).
(H9) Following winds do not require much compensation due to concentrating wind effects. Within the expected nar-row range, we expect similar reactions as suggested under points 3 and 4.
– Despite minimal requirement of compensation, residual reactions are expected.
In the results, we refer to these hypotheses by the number of the hypothesis (Hx) and an indication whether the results agree fully (H +), partially (H ±), or not at all (H -) with the corresponding hypothesis.
Methods The present study is based on the data of a complete autumn season at Lehrberg near Nuremberg (10° 31′ E/49°29′ N, 450 m asl, 30 July–30 Oct 1987). This allowed us to analyse the flight behaviour of nocturnal migrants above a landscape without pronounced topographical features. Continuously flapping birds made up only 6.4% of all tracked birds. Thus, the results reflect mainly the behaviour of intermittently flap-ping passerines.
The tracking radar “Superfledermaus” was used to track migrating birds and pilot balloons (to measure wind vectors) over the last 50 years; technical improvements comprised mainly recording techniques and signal processing (Bruderer 1971, 2020; Bloch et al. 1981; Bruderer et al. 2012). Since 1991, the polar coordinates of the tracked objects (birds or pilot balloons) provided by the radar at intervals of 1 s were digitized, transformed into Cartesian coordinates, and aver-aged over 20 s. These averages were used to calculate the mean flight direction (track), heading, height above radar, ground speed, and air speed as well as vertical speed per individual.
For detailed studies, birds tracked between 20 and 05 h were included in the standard analysis (provided their air speed Va was > 5 and < 25 m/s, and their vertical speed Vz > −5 and < 3 m/s; thus excluding a few unrealis-tic extremes). Whenever possible, the wind measurement at midnight (with the best preconditions for undisturbed Journal of Ornithology laminar air currents and least time difference to the indi-vidual bird tracks) was used for the calculation of headings and air speeds of all night migrants. In the rare cases when this measurement was lacking, the wind data of the nearest evening or morning pilot balloon was used. For altitudinal comparisons, we defined two altitudinal zones below and above 1500 m asl (corresponding to < 1000 and > 1000 m agl in the relatively flat area roughly 500 m asl, aiming at comparable numbers of tracked birds per height bin).
We defined the basic direction (BD) as the mean direction of the tracks recorded in the considered area under minimal wind influence, over the entire observation period (Bruderer and Liechti 1990). As BD may differ between altitudes, we calculated it for the two altitudinal zones, using the track directions of all individuals flying in weak following winds (VW < 5 m/s) or in even weaker opposing and side winds (VW < 3 m/s). The resulting BD was 230.56° below 1500 m asl, and 216.54° in the upper height bin. We bear in mind that BD is a convention that includes considerable uncer-tainty due to individual variation of migratory directions, thus calculating decimals is a matter of mathematics, not of biology.
We assigned wind directions to six sectors (wind catego-ries, Fig. 1) and analysed the deviations of tracks and head-ings from BD per wind sector. The track directions represent vector additions of a bird’s own movement and the wind vec-tor. To visualize the difference between passive transport and the birds’ own efforts, we calculated curves of physical drift with increasing wind speed for each wind sector. Physical drift is the deviation of a bird that flies with an average air speed exactly in the basic direction under the wind direction in the centre of the sector in question with a speed that can be read from the Y-axis (Fig. 2a).
The deviations of the bird’s headings from BD show (within the defined wind sectors) the reactions of the birds to increasing wind speed. The headings needed to fully com-pensate the actual winds from six different sectors provide a basis for the comparison of the birds’ reactions with perfect compensation (Fig. 2b).
Fig. 1 Six wind sectors of 60° each, arranged to both sides of the basic direction BD (= 230.56° below 1500 m asl). The sectors repre-sent opposing, following, and side winds from left and right, respec-tively Fig. 2 a Resulting physical drift with increasing wind speed from six sectors (according to Fig. 1), with full lines for the lower and dot-ted lines for the upper altitudinal zone (< 1500 m and > 1500 m asl, respectively) b Average headings needed to fully compensate drift with increasing speed of winds from six sectors (according to Fig. 1). Full lines for altitudes below and dotted lines above 1500 m asl Journal of Ornithology We compared the physical drift with the observed drift in relation to wind speed. We also compared the deviations of the bird;s headings (bearing of the body axis) from BD with increasing wind speed, to show the reactions of the birds to winds. The mean of heading is compared with the line showing full compensation. To estimate mean drift and mean heading, we fitted robust general additive models per wind sector and flight level (using a Student-t data distribu-tion; separate models for drift and heading), modelling a smoothed effect of wind speed and including a temporal autocorrelation. The model was fitted by the functions brm (package brms, Bürkner 2017; 24000 draws retained after warmup) and s (for the smoothing; package mgcv, Wood 2017; using the default for the degree of smoothing). For the tracks, we also present the medians of raw data per 1.5 m/s increase of wind speed.
Terms, definitions, and abbreviations: Va = air speed (speed relative to the surrounding air).
Ra = heading = bearing = direction of the body axis.
VW = wind speed (speed of moving air masses).
RW = wind direction (provenience of moving air masses).
Vg = ground speed (speed relative to the ground).
Rg = track = direction or flight path over ground = vec-tor addition of Ra + RW (arrow above for vector)Vmr = air speed Va allowing a bird to cover the maximum range by minimizing the energy cost per unit distance travelled.
Basic direction = BD = average track direction of the migrants flying under negligible wind influence.
Overcompensation = birds shift their body axis more than expected for full compensation of the actual side wind com-ponents (leading to negative drift).
Overdrift occurs when compensation is negative, result-ing in tracks being deflected more than expected by physical drift.
Recruiting direction = direction where the migrants come from.
Retrograde migration = birds are blown backwards by strong opposing winds.
Reverse migration = migration opposite to the directions expected for the season.
Physical drift = displacement of an airborne object (like a balloon) with the moving air = full drift.
Pseudo-drift = changes in the spectrum of migratory directions due to differential use of following winds by populations or species with different intermediate goals.
Wind drift = drift = resulting movement of a bird, based on physical drift and the reaction of the bird.
Sectors denoting the origin of winds relative to BD: fr, fl = front-right, front-left, sr, sl = side-right, side-left, br, bl = back-right, back-left.
Wind directions relative to the birds: side winds from right and left (sr, sl), opposing (fr, fl), following (br, bl).
agl = above ground level; asl = above sea level.
Two altitudinal zones (above or below ~ 1500 m asl) = height bins (above or below ~ 1000 m agl) = flight levels.

Figures 3a–d provide a general overview of the available winds and those used by the migrants, leading to first conclusions about selective behaviour of the birds.
While tracks were widely scattered between 100° and 310° (i.e. from ESE to NW) at low flight levels and 110°–270° higher up, headings were concentrated around the basic direction BD, mainly between 200° and 260° in the lower altitudinal zone, and slightly more S at the upper level (roughly 200°–260°). The concentrated headings con-trasting with the scattered tracks reveal important wind drift (Fig. 3a).
The diagram of the available and used wind directions (Fig. 3b) shows that most birds had to fly with opposing winds from the right of their body axis. Winds were used according to availability, except an overproportional use of SE winds and a concentration of high-flying birds in the central part (260°–290°) of the available wind directions. Winds from E and particularly W were on average stronger than those from S and particularly N, but the average wind speed was astonishingly low, i.e. < 5.3 m/s.
The directional distribution of available and used wind speeds (Fig. 3c) reveals that the low-flying migrants avoided the strongest opposing winds from the right of BD (fr, ~ 230°–270°), while preferring strong following winds from the left (bl, ~ 50°–100°). A consequence of head-wind avoidance was that opposing side winds from WNW (280°–330°) and from SW (200°–220°) got more relative importance than the strongest and most frequent (but avoided) winds from sector WSW in our data set. In the upper height bin, the available winds from the W (230°–330°) were stronger than in the lower bin, as expected according to wind pattern in the lower troposphere. Wind speeds from due W averaged over the whole season reached 13.24 m/s. The averaged used wind speeds towards this directions were, however, only 4.9 m/s. This indicates a pronounced selectivity for low wind speeds under opposing winds (at both flight levels).
For a better understanding of the directional and altitu-dinal distribution of the tracked individuals, Fig. 3d shows Journal of Ornithology the number of recorded flightpaths for each third of a sector: according to the distribution of available winds, most birds flew in the sector with winds from W–SW (fr), most of them in the lower altitudinal zone, but with increasing proportions of highfliers towards the right of the sector. The increasing proportion of high-flying birds continued into the sector NW (sr) and persisted throughout this sector as well as in sector br (with rare winds from N–NE). Black arrows = BD. Full lines below 1500 m asl, and dotted lines above 1500 m asl. b Distribution of wind directions (directions of origin) during autumn 1987 near Nurem-berg. Within the sector fr, the proportion of high flights increased; this prevailing of high flights continued across the sectors sr, br, and partially bl. While the general distribution of tracks was due to the availability of winds, the altitudinal distribution may indicate that more birds were prepared to climb to the upper flight level with wind components from the right and from behind.
Prospects and limits of drift compensation To get an idea of the range and intensity of the birds’ reac-tions to winds, Fig. 4 exemplifies theoretically (based on flight-path recordings and associated winds from three sec-tors to the right of BD up to an altitude of 1500 m asl) the course of three flight parameters with increasing wind speed and full compensation (black line: ­ Ra; purple line: mean Va; orange line: resulting ground speed Vg).
The left graph in Fig. 4 shows that winds from front-right (fr) increasing from 0 to 25 m/s could be compensated completely by shifting headings (Ra, black line) continu-ously from 0° to about 30°, the resulting ground speed drop-ping to zero at VW = 12 m/s. The air speed Va (purple line) increased from 11 m/s to roughly 14 m/s with wind speed increasing from 0 to 25 m/s (corroborating Pennycuick’s 1972 prediction about maximum range speed Vmr, H1 +), while the resulting ground speed Vg (orange line) decreased linearly from 11 to 0 m/s.
Middle graph (with same colour code as left graph): With side winds from the right (sr), Va increased from 10.5 to about 12.5 m/s for an increase of VW from 0 to 25 m/s (H1 +). Headings needed for full compensation increased towards 90°; ground speed declining steeply towards 0 at VW = 11.5 m/s.
Right graph: With following winds from the right (br), headings for full compensation approached 90° at wind speeds close to 24 m/s, while ground speed increased up to VW = 24 m/s, then decreased to about VW = 22 m/s. Va increased only slightly from 11 to 12 m/s (H1 ±).
Variation of air speed with wind speed One option of a bird to compensate for wind effects is by increasing air speed (Va)—as suggested by the purple line in Fig. 4.
Figure 5 visualizes the variation of mean air speeds with increasing wind force ­ (VW) from four sectors of incident wind (opposing, following, and side winds from left and right) at two flight levels. According to Fig. 5, mean air speeds showed increasing trends with increasing speed of opposing and side winds in both altitudinal zones (H1 +) as expected according to Pennycuick’s (1972) model on the influence of wind on maximum range speed Vmr. The highest average Va reached about 13 m/s under high wind speeds. An expected slight decrease of ­ Va with increasing following winds was only indicated for high-flying, not for low-flying birds (H1 ±). Under weak winds (VW < 3 m/s), the all-over average of Va from both altitudinal zones was ~ 11 m/s. Under these weak winds, Va was marginally higher with opposing winds than with other wind directions. The average increase of Va per step of 3 m/s increase of opposing winds varied around 0.4 m/s, indicating that the birds compensated roughly 10–20% of weak to moderate opposing winds. An unexpected lack of higher air speeds at high compared to low flight levels (H2 ±) will be commented in the discussion.

The graphs in the left column show the tracks, and those in the right column the headings. The raw data (small cir-cles in each graph) show the full scatter of directions as well as the distribution of the recorded birds along the wind axis. Green lines in the left graphs indicate full drift for a bird flying with average speed and zero compensa-tion, and green lines in the right graphs represent headings needed for full compensation (given average flight speed). Accordingly, mean estimated tracks often follow rather closely the lines of full drift. Opposing winds from front-left (fl) low: winds from this sector were rather rare according to Fig. 3b. Reverse migration was prominent (H6 +). Birds flying against headwinds stronger than their maximum air speed prove the occurrence of retrograde migration (H7 +).

Reverse migration was massive under the given conditions (H6 +), quite some headings indicating downwind flights.
Opposing winds from front-right (fr) high: the regression line of headings suggests compensation or overcompensa-tion with wind speeds VW < 3 m/s, tracks indicating negative drift up to VW ~ 7 m/s). At wind speeds above 3 m/s, com-pensation diminished towards zero, while tracks approached full drift (H3 +), minimal overdrift indicated by the medians under wind speeds of 12–14 m/s (H4 + , H5 +).
Side winds from left (sl) low: headings indicate slight overcompensation at lowest wind speeds, going over to par-tial compensation and insufficient increase with wind speed, tracks indicating partial drift up to VW ~ 15 m/s (H3 ±); few tracks above this limit may suggest overdrift (H4 + , H5−).
Side winds from left (sl) high: headings indicate slight compensation at lowest wind speeds, shifting to zero com-pensation above VW ~ 4 m/s (H3 +); tracks show full drift up to VW = 11 m/s (H4 +) and possible overdrift above (contra-dicting H5 as in the lower height bin).
Side winds from right (sr) low: headings indicate over-compensation at very low wind speeds, resulting in negative Fig. 5 Mean air speeds Va (with standard error) of migrants flying in two altitudinal zones with winds from four sectors, arranged accord-ing to six wind speed classes. Weak compensation remained nearly constant with increasing wind speed, thus leading to par-tial drift up to VW ~ 8 m/s, shifting towards full drift and even overdrift above (H3 + , H4 +). The graphs to do not indicate more drift with winds from the right than from the left (H5−).

With higher wind speeds, the regression lines of headings and tracks shift towards partial compensation/ drift up to VW ~ 9 m/s. Above this wind speed compensa-tory efforts decreased, and tracks shifted to overdrift (H3 + , H4 + , H5 +). The exceptionally high number of tracks in the upper height bin is explained by Fig. 3d.
Following winds from back-left (bl) low: headings and tracks indicate compensation or overcompensation up to VW ~ 3 m/s. Compensation efforts did not increase suffi-ciently with increasing wind speed; thus, tracks approached full drift with wind speeds VW = 5–9 m/s (H9 + , H3 +), and slight overdrift above (H4 + , H5 ±).

Directional devia-tions are similar at low and hight altitudes, tendentially with reduced compensation higher up.
Figure 7 visualizes the results of Fig. 6 in circular dia-grams, and thus a presentation closer to our spatial percep-tion. These diagrams allow a general comparison of the directional distributions between the two altitudinal zones and the six wind sectors (which slightly differ between the zones according to differing BD): the directional distribu-tions of the headings differed less between the height bins than the calculated BD. Headings showed the strongest com-pensation under side winds from the right (sr), the resulting tracks scattered around SSW at low levels and SSE higher up; birds were thus somewhat more efficient when closer to the ground. Compensatory efforts were less pronounced or even comprised overdrift with opposing winds from the right (fr), leading to pronounced shifts of most tracks towards SE, particularly at low levels (H5 +). Low wind speeds in the sector with side winds from left (sl) induced moderate drift with little scatter. Following winds (bl and br) were associ-ated with increased scatter of headings and weak signs of drift.
Conclusions and discussion This re-analysis of the radar tracks of migrants from Nurem-berg confirm and refine earlier analyses by Liechti (1993). The general finding is that in a relatively flat area of south-ern Germany, full compensation or overcompensation was the prevailing reaction of nocturnal bird migrants to deviat-ing winds with speeds of less than 3 m/s. Under stronger winds, the radar-tracked birds showed insufficient or even decreasing compensation, so that drift became the predomi-nant feature of migration under moderate to strong winds. Southward overdrift was conspicuous under the frequent winds from front-right. Despite some omnipresent reverse migration, we found no support for the idea that songbird migrants tend to fly downwind irrespective of wind direction as suggested, e.g. by Gauthreaux and Able (1970) for North America. We assume that reactions to winds are similar on both continents, but the frequently available northerly winds may allow autumn migrants in the northern USA (north of about 35° N) more drift tolerance than the birds in Central Europe that are confronted with predominant westerly winds (Fig. 3b). Some North American studies are reconsidered below.
Methodological limits Tracking pilot balloons to get information on wind condi-tions at the flight altitudes of individually tracked birds is the most exact method to study the reactions of individual nocturnal migrants to winds. Nevertheless, temporal differ-ences of up to several hours and ± 100 m in altitude between wind measurements and bird tracks induce some uncertain-ties. A mixture of species in our samples is an additional source of scatter. Fortunately, earlier studies showed that only about 6–7% of the tracked birds in Central Europe con-sist of continuously flapping birds, considered as waders or waterfowl (Bruderer 1971; Liechti 1993). The proportion of swifts was only relevant in the first half of August (with about 20%), then declined rapidly. Most of the birds were intermittently flapping passerines (averaged over the whole season 93.6%, with 71% small and 22.6% large passerines), the relative importance of large passerines increasing in October (Liechti 1993). This is a peer-reviewed scientific review article published in the Journal of Ornithology (2024) by Bruno Bruderer, Pius Korner, and Dieter Peter of the Swiss Ornithological Institute, examining how nocturnally migrating birds react to winds in flight.

**Study Design:** The authors reviewed available knowledge on in-flight reactions of nocturnal bird migrants to winds, focusing on the challenging conditions in Western Europe versus North America. They then conducted a new analysis using tracking radar data from a complete autumn season (30 July–30 October 1987) at Lehrberg near Nuremberg, Germany, at an altitude of 450 m asl. Using the "Superfledermaus" tracking radar, they tracked individual nocturnal migrants (93.6% intermittently flapping passerines) and measured winds using pilot balloons at the birds' flight altitudes.

**Key Methods:** They defined a "basic direction" (BD) as the average flight direction of migrants under negligible wind influence (mean ±30° around 230°). Track and heading deviations from BD were modeled for two altitudinal zones (above/below 1500 m asl) against winds from six 60° sectors. Statistical analysis used robust general additive models with a Student-t distribution.

**Key Results:**
- Air speeds (Va) increased from ~11 to 13 (14) m/s with opposing and side winds (supporting H1); a slight decrease with following winds was only observed in high-flying birds
- No expected increase in air speed with altitude due to decreasing air density (H2 unsupported)
- Overcompensation was frequent at low wind speeds (<3 m/s); birds compensated fully or overcompensated for winds under 3 m/s
- Under opposing and side winds from the right, birds achieved partial drift compensation up to ~8–10 m/s, then were fully drifted (H3, H4)
- Winds from the right (W/NW) caused more drift at low levels; results for H5 were ambiguous
- Retrograde migration (birds blown backwards by headwinds exceeding air speed) was observed (H7)
- Reverse migration occurred on most nights (H6)
- Migrants compensated less for wind deviations than expected; many maintained headings close to BD even when making minimal ground progress or moving backwards
- General conclusion: full compensation or overcompensation prevailed for winds <3 m/s, but drift became predominant under moderate to strong winds

This is a Google Scholar profile page for Felix Liechti, an ornithologist specializing in bird migration research. His citation metrics show 11,186 total citations (4,491 since 2021), an h-index of 59 (36 recent), and an i10-index of 149 (109 recent).

His most highly cited publications include:
- "Birds: blowin' by the wind?" (2006, Journal of Ornithology) - 615 citations
- "The natural link between Europe and Africa–2.1 billion birds on migration" (2009, Oikos) - 374 citations
- "Bird migration flight altitudes studied by a network of operational weather radars" (2010) - 323 citations
- "Atmospheric conditions create freeways, detours and tailbacks for migrating birds" (2017) - 251 citations
- "The relevance of wind for optimal migration theory" (1998) - 245 citations

His research focuses heavily on:
- The influence of wind and atmospheric conditions on bird migration
- Radar-based quantification of bird migration
- Migration across the Sahara and between Europe and Africa
- Use of light-level geolocators for tracking small migrants
- Nocturnal migration behavior and flight altitudes

Notable work includes "First evidence of a 200-day non-stop flight in a bird" (2013, Nature Communications) and research on the painted lady butterfly's multi-generational migration (2013). He has collaborated extensively with researchers including B. Bruderer, B. Erni, H. Schmaljohann, and others. Publications span from 1995 to 2017, appearing in journals such as Journal of Ornithology, Ibis, Oikos, Nature Communications, and Proceedings of the Royal Society B.

You are tasked with summarizing the raw content of a webpage retrieved from a web search. Your goal is to create a summary that preserves the most important information from the original web page. This summary will be used by a downstream research agent, so it's crucial to maintain the key details without losing essential information.

Here is the raw content of the webpage:

<webpage_content>
Temporal and Spatial Pattern of Nocturnal Bird Migration across the Western Mediterranean Sea Studied by Radar Diploma Thesis by Simon Speich Zoological Institute University of Basel, Switzerland July 1999 Supervised by Professor Dr. Bruno Bruderer and Dr. Felix Liechti Swiss Ornithological Institute, Sempach 2 Content I. General Introduction p. 4 II. Part A: Diurnal and Seasonal Schedule of Spring Migration over Mallorca p. 8 III. Part B: Direction, Speed and Origin of Spring Migrants Arriving on Mallorca: p. 26 Why did Nocturnal Migrants Arrive in a Wave? IV. Acknowledgements and appendix: time table, figures and Access Basic module p. 46 Pictures: Wood Sandpiper (Tringa glareola) p. 3, Little Egrett (Egretta garzetta) p. 7, Black-winged Stilt (Himantopus himantopus) p. 25, Audouin’s Gull (Larus audouinii) p. 45. 3 I 4 General Introduction Migratory birds have to cross or circumvent two vast areas, the Sahara Desert and the Mediterreanean Sea, during their migratory journey between their breeding areas in Europe and their wintering areas in Africa. A lot of day migrants such as raptors, herons and storks avoid crossing the Mediterranean Sea and concentrate at the Straits of Gibraltar and Bosporus. But most birds migrate by night and until recently relatively little was known about how and to what extent these night migrants cross the Mediterranean Sea and the Sahara. It was supposed that they fly on a more or less broad front across the Mediterranean and the Sahara during night and day (Moreau 1972, Curry-Lindahl 1981). Early radar and visual observations gave no evidence for concentrations along the shortest routes, such as Gibraltar, Sicily or Malta (Casement 1966) and many surveillance radar studies suggested no deviations in tracks when birds flew across coastlines (Eastwood 1967). In recent years however, field observations have shown that mountain ridges can lead to local concentrations of the migratory stream (Bruderer 1996) and that coasts can influence the flight behaviour of migrants (Alerstam, 1977). It was argued that at least some of the birds maintained their temporal pattern of flying by night and resting during the day even over a large ecological barrier such as the Sahara (Biebach et al. 1986, Bairlein 1988). Therefore, the Swiss Ornithological Institute carried out a study supported by the Swiss National Science Foundation, where bird migration across the western Mediterranean was investigated in autumn 1996 and spring 1997. The aim of this study was to find out if the the migratory stream occurs over a broad front across the Mediterranean Sea and if islands such as the Balearic Islands, in particular the coastlines, influence the migratory stream. Two tracking radars were operated, one on the southern tip of the island Mallorca, the other near Malaga at the coast on the Spanish mainland. Moon and infrared observations along the French and Spanish coast provided additional information over a larger scale. This diploma thesis was part of the project. It focused on the temporal and spatial pattern of nocturnal bird migration over Mallorca during the spring season as recorded by radar. The thesis was divided into two themes which were analysed and discussed in detail: 1) the temporal and seasonal schedule of the migration intensities and 2) the direction, speed, and potential recruiting areas of the migrants. 5 Cited Literature Alerstam, T. 1977. Why do migrating birds fly along coastlines? – J. Theor. Biol. 65: 699 - 712. Bairlein, F. 1988. How do migratory songbirds cross the Sahara? - TREE 3: 191 - 194. Biebach, H. W. Friedrich & G. Heine 1986. Interaction of bodymass, fat, foraging and stopover period in trans-Sahara migrating passerine birds. - Oecologia 69: 370 - 379. Bruderer, B. 1996. Vogelzugforschung im Bereich der Alpen 1980-1995. - Orn. Beob. 93: 119 - 130. Bruderer, B & F. Liechti (in press). Bird migration across the Mediterranean. - In: Adams, N. & E. Slotow (eds), Proc. Int. Orn. Congr., Durban, University of Natal: yyy - zzz. Casement, M. B. 1966. Migration across the Mediterranean observed by radar. - Ibis 108: 461 - 491. Curry-Lindahl, K. 1981. Bird migration in Africa. - Academic Press, London/New York. Eastwood, E. 1967. Radar ornithology. - Methuen, London. Moreau, R. E. 1972. The Paleartic-African bird migration Systems. - Academic Press, London/New York 6 II 7 Diurnal and Seasonal Schedule of Spring Migration over Mallorca Summary The diurnal and seasonal schedule of nocturnal bird migration over Mallorca in spring was investigated by means of a tracking radar. The diurnal course showed two phases of high activity with a gap in between. The take-off phase on the island started shortly before sunset and lasted for 2 to 4 hours. The peak intensity was reached within one hour after sunset. The main mass of birds from Africa arrived on Mallorca eight hours after sunset. On average at least one third of the migrants landed soon after crossing the coast every night. This pattern is supported by a fair correlation between the number of birds arriving during the night and the number of birds taking off the next evening. This correlation suggests short resting periods of only one day. Among all tracked birds the proportion of birds with a passerine-type wing-beat pattern was almost 50% at the beginning of April and decreased to 18% by the end of May. The proportion of birds with a continuously flapping wing-beat pattern stayed approximately constant, while the proportion of birds with a swift-type wing-beat pattern increased from 6% to more than 40% over the same period. The temporal variation in the number of birds was high, presumably due to different weather conditions. The diurnal pattern showed that the take-off was confined to a short period after sunset and that the main mass of birds landed somewhere in North Africa before crossing the Mediterranean Sea. Keywords bird migration, Mediterranean, Mallorca, temporal pattern, seasonal pattern, take off, landing, spring Introduction Every year in Europe about 5 billion birds (Moreau 1972) leave their breeding areas in autumn and migrate to Africa in order to spend the winter in regions which offer more favourable environmental conditions. In spring they return to Europe to make use of the abundant food for raising their broods. On their migratory journey they either circumvent the Mediterranean or cross it (Bruderer & Liechti in press). Those making the shortcut across the sea between southern France and the Algerian coast have to fly a distance of about 600 km 8 without the possibility to land. The eastern and western straits, Bosporus and Gibraltar, are famous for their massive concentrations of day migrants such as raptors, herons and storks. But most species migrate by night and until recently relatively little was known about how and to what extent these night migrating birds cross the Mediterranean and the Sahara. Early radar and visual observations indicated no concentrations at the narrows of Gibraltar, Sicily or Malta (Steinbacher 1954, Moreau 1961, Casement 1966,). It was supposed that the birds crossed the Mediterranean on a broad front and that the migrants performed non-stop flights over the Sahara and in autumn even directly over the Mediterranean without landing (Moreau 1972, Curry-Lindahl 1981, Lövei 1989). In recent years, however, it was shown that mountain ridges can lead to local concentrations and deviations from the migratory stream (Bruderer & Jenni 1990, Bruderer 1996, Liechti et al. 1996) and it was argued that at least some of the birds maintained their temporal pattern of flying by night and resting during the day even over a large ecological barrier such as the Sahara (Biebach et al. 1986, Bairlein 1988, Biebach et al. 1991). This schedule was maintained in the Negev desert in southern Israel (Bruderer 1994). A recent review of bird migration across the Mediterranean, including radar, infrared and moon watching data, showed considerable concentration of nocturnal bird migration to the east and west of the Mediterranean Sea and a high degree of separation between diurnal and nocturnal migration in spring and autumn (Bruderer & Liechti in press). From previous studies in different parts of Europe and North America it is known that migration starts prior to or within the first hour after sunset and reaches a peak of migratory activity 1 to 4 hours after sunset (Parslow 1968, Hebrard 1971, Bolshakov 1975, Alerstam 1976, Richardson 1978, Dolnik 1987, Biebach et al. 1991, Åkesson et al. 1996, Bruderer 1997, Liechti et al. 1997). But it is not well known how long the take-off phase is. Studies in which radio transmitters were attached to birds showed that some birds took off much later in the night (Cochran et al. 1967, Åkesson et al. 1996, Moore & Aborn 1996). In this paper, I would like to present the seasonal course and the exact time schedule of nocturnal bird migration over Mallorca. Owing to the unique geographical situation which the island offers and the radar site near the southern coast, it was possible to investigate the timing and length of the take-off phase. Because the birds could not take off from the sea, the actual take-off by birds in the small area around and south of the radar could be monitored. The birds which had taken off in North Africa arrived only later in the night, after crossing a distance of 300 km over water. By means of the observed temporal pattern of migration it will be shown: 1) Whether the take-off phase is confined to the beginning of the night or whether birds take off at any time throughout the night; 2) Whether the birds adhere to the pattern of migrating by night and resting during 9 the day, even when crossing a large ecological barrier such as the Mediterranean Sea. Then the local schedule of migration can be used to show if non-stop flights over the Mediterranean and the Sahara are the prevailing strategy or if most birds take advantage of the possibility to land and refuel in North Africa before crossing the Mediterranean Sea. Materials and Methods This radar study was conducted in spring 1997 on the island of Mallorca, Spain. The radar was located in the south of the island (39° 18´ N, 3° 4´ E) 20 m above sea level next to the Salines de Salobrar about 8 km NW and 2 km NE from the southern coast (fig. 1). The radar used was an X-band (3.3 cm wavelength) tracking radar with 2.2° nominal beam width, 150 kW peak pulse power and 0.3 µs pulse length. Data was obtained on 64 nights between 24-03-97 and 26-05-97. Every half hour from 20:30 h to 04:30 h and every hour from 05:30 h to 11:30 h a quantitative measurement of the spatial distribution was made by conically scanning within a half-sphere of 4 km radius. All time indications are local summer time, which is UTC + 2 h. From 13-04-97 to 26-05-97 at the same site a second radar was operated, which automatically made the quantitative measurements every 10 minutes, 24 hours a day. With these measurements, the density of the birds was calculated as number of birds·km-3 according to the procedure described by Bruderer et al. (1995). Fig. 1. Map of the western Mediterranean. The radar site is marked with a cross. MALLORCA 10 During the time between two measurements, the operator manually locked on single targets to register their flight tracks for 40 s each. The wind was measured by tracking a meteorological balloon up to at least 4 km height above ground level at noon and then every 4 hours. By combining the data of the wind measurements with the tracking data of the birds (e.g. ground speed, vertical speed, altitude and track), heading and air speed were calculated. The fluctuations of the radar signal (echo-signatures) allowed the identification of wing-beat patterns, which were classified into 4 groups (Bloch et al 1981): CF: continuously flapping birds, corresponding mainly to wader-/waterfowl-type birds, but also to continuously beating swifts and others IF: intermittently flapping birds, corresponding mainly to passerines SW: swifts (apus) UD: undetermined pattern; flocks, bats, insects, echoes interfering with ground clutter For the present analysis I worked with two datasets. For the period from 27-03-97 to 13-04-97, I used the data from the first radar (N = 14 nights); from 13-04-97 to 26-05-97, I also took the measurements from the second radar (N = 35 nights). For those times when data from both radars was available, I took the average of the two. In the analysis some nights are lacking due to missing measurements or technical problems. In order to express the temporal pattern quantitatively, I wrote a computer program in Access Basic (appendix). It went through all measurements of the densities one by one and calculated the following: 1) the maxima and minima of the density curve over time. In the case of the first radar, a value was defined as a maximum if the two measurements before and the two measurements after were smaller than the actual value, and as a minimum if they were larger. For the second radar, the definition of a maximum or a minimum was slightly different, because more measurements were available. In that case a value was defined as a maximum if all values one hour before and one hour after it were smaller, and as a minimum if they were larger; 2) the duration was calculated as the time between two minima; 3) the sum of all densities from one minimum to the next was computed and used to calculate the MTR (Migration Traffic Rate = theoretical number of birds crossing a front of one kilometre per hour, Lowery 1951. Originally one mile). All measurements from one minimum to the next will be referred to as a phase. The phase from the first minimum around sunset to the following minimum was considered to be the take-off phase (TP), characterised by one maximum in between. All the phases from this second minimum onwards to the first minimum which followed after the last maximum before sunrise were defined as the night phase (NP). A special case occurred when the density after the take-off phase remained low and no maximum could be 11 detected between two minima. In such cases the night phase was defined to start at the minimum before the next maximum after the minimum of the take-off phase. By multiplying the MTR with the length of the night phase or the take-off phase and weighting it with the proportion of tracks with wing-beat classes of CF and IF, the number of birds arriving or leaving the area south and around the radar per front of one kilometre was calculated. For this entity the term weighted Migration Traffic (MT) will be used. Results Diurnal schedule Nocturnal migration showed two more or less distinctive phases separated by a gap, caused by the lack of migrants taking-off from the sea. The first phase consisted of birds departing from the island; the second phase of those arriving from North Africa later in the night. In the relatively short gap only few birds were recorded (fig. 2, for figures and time tables of all nights separately, see appendix). The take-off phase began on average 13 ± 25 min before sunset (standard error of the mean SE = ± 4 min, N = 49 nights), reached the maximum only 64 minutes later (mean M = 51 ± 13 min, SE ± 2 min) and came to an end 200 ± 62 min after sunset (SE = ± 9). The relationship of the take-off phase to sunset and civil twilight (sun 6° below horizon) over the observation period is shown in figure 3. At this latitude the civil twilight bears a constant relationship to the time of sunset. Discussion The take-off phase on Mallorca started shortly before sunset, which is at least half an hour earlier than reported in other papers (for a summary of take-off times see table 2 in Åkesson et al.1996). It is not clear if this is a relevant difference or just a matter of method, because the methods compared are widely different and sometimes very crude in determining the take-off time. Surveillance radars in particular might miss the first departures (example Fig. 8. in Gauthreaux 1971, where the first birds seemed to be cut off.). If the decision of a bird to take off is related to light intensity, then this variation in take-off times could be an effect of relating the take-off times to sunset (instead of light intensity itself), because light intensity around sunset depends on the time of year and geographical latitude and it varies with local weather and cloud conditions. Species with a continuously flapping wing-beat pattern departed earlier than the passerines. Richardson (1979) found general take-off times of shorebirds of even more than one hour before sunset. The peak intensity of the take-off phase was reached within one hour after sunset and the whole take-off phase lasted only 2 to 4 hours. Published data on the exact duration of the take off-phase is scarce. It has been reported that migratory activity declined during the later part of the night and ceased more or less before sunrise (Alerstam 1976, Bruderer 1994, Bruderer 1995). But this does not really show the length of the take-off phase, because birds which had taken off further from the observation site flew over the observation site later in the night. Using data from a ceilometer study with visual observations of migrants taking off (Hebrard, 1971), I calculated a mean duration of the take-off phase of 83 ± 29 minutes. Gauthreaux (1971) reported a take-off pattern which is very similar in shape to the one of the present analysis. The duration was at least 4 hours but the data in the presented graph is not arranged according to sunset, probably increasing the duration of the take-off time. Parslow (1968) inferred from his own data that the take-off phase could be as short as 10 minutes. But studies in which radio transmitters were attached to the birds showed that some birds took off much later in the night (Cochran et al. 1967, Åkesson et al. 1996, Moore & Abborn 1996). These studies, however, are very limited in the number of tracked birds and might only be valid for the observed species and could therefore not be taken as the general pattern. Furthermore, the late take-off times were not observed directly but inferred from not relocating the birds the next day. It can not be excluded that the handling of the birds influenced the decision of the birds to take off. Nonetheless, they can indicate that there could be differences in the take-off times between species and latitudes. The radar situated at the southern tip of Mallorca offered a special opportunity to investigate the time period during which the migrants took off, because the area south of the radar site was very limited in size (approximately 65 km2). The data was based on a high number of observed migrants and lasted over several days. It is evident that the take-off on Mallorca was confined to 2 to 4 hours after sunset and that the take-off times and take-off peaks were related to sunset. Even the widely scattered ending times of the take-off phase were related to sunset. The high number of birds taking off south and around the radar site every evening reflected a high attractiveness of the island. The temporal pattern suggested that on average at least one third of the birds which arrived on Mallorca landed, especially around sunrise (and probably during the first morning hours). The birds which did not land and continued to fly over the radar site before sunrise still had a flight of more than one hour to cross the island. According to an infrared study in the north of Mallorca most migrants did not fly out to sea after sunrise (Holzgang pers. comm.). Therefore, the proportion of birds which landed on the whole island must have been much higher than one third. 18 It is generally assumed that most migrants cross the Mediterranean in one non-stop flight. Based on their physiology it is estimated that birds can easily fly distances of 400 - 600 km without landing (Biebach 1992). In spring the competition for good breeding sites, which may simply depend on who arrives first at the breeding grounds, and the possibility to raise additional broods could create a strong pressure to be back as early as possible. This could result in a more rapid migration than in autumn (Safriel & Lavee 1988). Why then should the birds land instead of covering the whole sea-crossing in one flight? Possible reasons include: 1) The risk of depleting energy reserves by omitting a possibility to land and refuel could be high, especially if some migrants already had low energy reserves when they left the coast in North Africa. 2) The selection for flying by night must be stronger than selection for time minimising. This could explain why the vertical speeds on Mallorca suddenly became more negative around sunrise, indicating that landings could be a reaction to increasing light intensity. The present results showed that in spring a non-stop flight over the Sahara and the Mediterranean Sea is not the case for most birds. The pattern with two waves and a gap in between showed that the birds had landed in North Africa before crossing the Mediterranean Sea. This is consistent with the findings of Bairlein (1988) and Biebach et al. (1991) suggesting that an unknown proportion of birds uses an intermittent strategy when crossing the Sahara. Also Moreau (1961) supposed that in spring the Atlas Mountains in North Africa could offer good resting sites because of the Mediterranean climate with its rainy season in winter and spring. It can of course not be excluded that some birds flew over the Mediterranean non-stop, but they were quantitatively not relevant. The declining proportions of passerine type wing-beat frequencies and the highest migration intensities between mid-April and the beginning of May was in agreement with the findings of Finlayson (1992) at Gibraltar, where the highest densities of trans-Saharan migrants occurred in April and to a lesser extent in May. The highest densities of the pre-Saharan migrants in Gibraltar were recorded already in February and March and were even higher than the density of the trans-Saharan migrants in April. But the densities on Mallorca were low in the last third of March. This could indicate that the pre-Saharan migrants either did not cross the Mediterranean in large numbers and instead circumvented it or they had already passed in February or during the first two thirds of March. The second possibility is highly probable, because Bruderer & Liechti (in press) recorded highest densities of autumn migrants over Mallorca during the passage of pre-Saharan migrants in October. Trapping was carried out on Cabrera, a small island SSW of the radar site from 16-04 to 15-05-1993 (Montemaggiori et al. 1993). The seasonal peak of the number of captures was in the beginning of May, which was later than the seasonal peak of the radar data in mid-April. This difference could be an indication that trapping on an island is biased if the species differed in their decision to land at the first occasion while 19 flying over the sea. The most frequently trapped night migrants on Cabrera were the following species, which might also be represented in the passerine-type wing-beat class: Pied Flycatcher (Ficedula hypoleuca), Spotted Flycatcher (Musciapa striata), Willow Warbler (Phylloscopus trochilus), Redstart (Phoenicurus phoenicurus), Whinchat (Saxicola rubetra), Whitethroat (Sylvia communis) and Garden Warbler (S. borin). Wader species were not captured. For examples of possible species see observations of Kestenholz & Peter (1998). During the whole observation period, migration intensity fluctuated heavily from night to night. This variation was much higher in the night phase than in the take-off phase. A possible explanation could be that the island functioned as a buffer for the number of birds. The variability in the number of birds in the night phase could be a consequence of the weather in northern Algeria, whereas the number of birds in the take-off phase could be more influenced by the local weather situation on Mallorca itself. The migrants which arrived in the second half of the night had only left the coast in north Africa and continued their migration over the sea when winds were not too unfavourable. In contrast, the migrants on Mallorca would take off irrespective of winds and land again later when winds were too bad to continue migration. In some nights (especially from 03-04 to 06-04 and 01-05 to 02-05) more birds departed from the island than arrived during the night before. This is explainable by an accumulation of birds and a following mass departure. The high number of departing birds in the nights from 03-04 to 06-04 could be a consequence of the high number of birds which arrived in the night of 28-03 and almost no departures in the evenings of the two following nights. The same situation holds true for the nights from 01-05 to 02-05, which followed after the nights from 25-04 to 27-04 with very high numbers of arriving birds. Both mass departures took place after an evening with very strong opposing winds with velocities of more than 10 m·s-1 in migration direction. This was in the same magnitude as the birds own airspeed (part B of diploma thesis), probably keeping them on the ground (data from wind measurements at 20:00 h). This buffer effect seems to be the reason why no direct correlation between the number of birds in the night phase and the number of birds in the take-off phase was found. Two groups were created, one in which the weighted MT in the take-off phase was higher than in the night phase, the other in which it was lower. Then the correlation within both groups became highly significant. This suggests that a lot of birds stayed only for a short time, probably not more than one day. This is supported by findings of Gauthreaux (1971), Biebach et al. (1986), Safriel & Lavee (1988), Kuenzi et al. (1991) and Moore & Aborn (1996), where the stopover times of most birds were usually not longer than one day. Another explanation of these mass departures could be that in the preceding nights most migrants arrived after sunrise on Mallorca. They immediately landed unmeasured south of the radar site 20 and were therefore not included in the night phase, thereby increasing the number of birds taking off the next evening. The daily course of migration was not included, because the measured densities during the day were not reliable due to the following reasons: 1. Local birds, which became active soon after sunrise, could not be separated from migrating birds. These were mostly Yellow-legged Gulls (Larus cachinnans), which could be visually observed up to great heights almost every day, circling over the radar site in large flocks. This increased the number of birds in the air during the day to values much larger than during the night, although the gulls were the only birds around on most days. Tracking was often continued into the day until 12:00 h. The decline of the density and of the proportion of tracks with a songbird or continuously flapping wing-beat pattern around sunrise showed that the birds did not continue to fly over the island after sunrise (although the decline of the density and the increase of the proportion of undetermined tracks around sunrise may have been to some extent due to building flocks and not to landing). Furthermore, it was possible to check the tracked bird visually with a telescope. But we could not detect single migrating birds or flocks. This indicates that migration across Mallorca is confined to the night. It cannot be excluded that some birds still arrived on the island during the day and landed undetected in front of the radar if they were flying at very low altitudes and/or landed very quickly. It seems that the main mass of birds followed the pattern of migrating by night and resting during the day. The birds did not continue to fly across Mallorca during the day, which would have forced them to fly another 300 km over water, taking them to the southern coast of France.
