Summary Direction and speed of nocturnal bird migration was investigated with a tracking radar over Mallorca in spring 1997. The mean flight direction was 18° during take-off and 10° during the arrivals from North Africa. The average ground speed of the migrating birds was 12 m·s-1. Birds with a passerine-type wing-beat pattern had a more than 2 m·s-1 higher ground speed than birds with an uninterrupted wing-beat pattern. Nocturnal migrants from Africa arrived in a wave at different times in the second half of the night. This pattern occurred because most migrants did not fly non-stop over the Sahara and the Mediterranean Sea, but landed somewhere in North Africa. With the direction and speed of the migrants during the arrivals, it was possible to calculate the potential previous take-off areas for each night. The distribution of the take-off areas suggested that the migrants were not predominantly concentrated along the coast before they crossed the sea. Instead they departed, at least in some nights, from different places further inland in the Atlas Highlands. Some migrants could even have departed south of the Atlas mountains. It seems likely that the migrants, after having crossed the Sahara, landed as soon as they detected the first potential resting areas around dawn. Those migrants finding themselves still over the Sahara continued their flights until they reached promising habitats in the Atlas highlands increasing the number of migrants there but not near the coast. The island seemed to have no important concentration effect in attracting migrants from different directions. Keywords bird migration, Mediterranean, flight speed, air speed, flight direction, stopover, north Africa, radar, recruiting areas, intermittent flight strategy, Sahara Introduction The knowledge about the Paleartic-African bird migration system was discussed in comprehensive reviews by Moreau (1961, 1972). But the incomplete data available at that time was difficult to handle, particularly 26 because quantitative data on flight behaviour and volume of migration were lacking. He concluded that most autumn migrants flew non-stop over the Mediterranean Sea and the adjacent Sahara Desert on a broad front. On the birds’ journey back to the breeding grounds, the Atlas mountains and the coastal region in the western part of the Mediterranean offered good resting areas in spring because of the rainy season during the preceding winter. A more recent review of bird migration across the Mediterranean, including infrared and moon watching data, showed considerable concentration of nocturnal bird migration to the east and west of the Mediterranean Sea and a high degree of separation between diurnal and nocturnal migration in spring and autumn (Bruderer und Liechti in press). In central Europe autumn migration occurs on a broad front with basic directions around SW (Bruderer 1997). Moonwatching (Liechti et al. 1996) and observations by radar (Bruderer & Jenni 1990) have shown that in the area of the Alps most of the migrants are deflected by the mountains towards WSW. In northern Italy and southern France the main directions are even more westerly. Over the Iberian Peninsula the general flow of migrants takes place on a more NNE-SSW axis. The migrants flying over the Mediterranean Sea had more southerly directions (Bruderer & Liechti 1998a). Until now, reliable quantitative data of flight directions and flight speeds of nocturnal migrants across the western Mediterranean Sea in spring has been lacking. First indications of directions were given in an early radar study by Casement (1966) suggesting directions around NE; while some more recent data suggests mainly NNE directions (Rivera & Bruderer 1998). The temporal pattern of nocturnal bird migration on Mallorca showed that the take-off time was confined to 3 hours after sunset. Migration intensities increased again in the second half of the night, after a period when only few birds were recorded. The gap occurred because no birds could have taken off from the Mediterranean Sea. The pattern showed that most birds did not fly non-stop over the Mediterranean Sea, but must have landed somewhere in North Africa after having crossed the Sahara Desert (diploma thesis part A). This paper presents data about directions and speeds of nocturnal migrants arriving at Mallorca in spring. Information about directions and speeds is used as a basis to calculate potential recruiting areas of the migrants in North Africa. Two possible distributions of the potential resting areas previous to Mallorca will be presented and the following questions will be discussed: 1) Where did the migrants come from? On the one hand the migrants could have taken off from only a narrow strip along the coast leading to a wave in arrivals on Mallorca. On the other hand they could have departed from anywhere in North Africa. 2) Was Mallorca an important stepping stone or just an accidental stopover site? If the island attracted birds, this would imply a higher scatter of directions during the arrivals compared to the departures and an increase in scatter and possibly a shift in the general migration direction towards the end of night. 27 Materials and Methods This radar study was conducted in spring 1997 on the island of Mallorca, Spain. The radar was located in the south of the island (39° 2´ N, 3° 4´ E) 20 m above sea level next to the Salines de Salobrar about 8 km NW and 2 km NE from the southern coasts (fig. 1). The radar used was an X-band (3.3 cm wavelength) tracking radar with 2.2° nominal beam width, 150 kW peak pulse power and 0.3 µs pulse length. Data was obtained on 64 nights between 24-03-97 and 26-05-97. Every half hour from 20:30 h to 04:30 h and every hour from 05:30 h to 11:30 h a quantitative measurement of the spatial distribution was made by conically scanning within a half-sphere of 4 km radius. All time indications are local summer time, which is UTC + 2 h. From 13-04-97 to 26-05-97 at the same site a second radar was operated, which automatically made the quantitative measurements every 10 minutes, 24 hours a day. With these measurements, the density of the birds was calculated as number of birds·km-3 according to the procedure described by Bruderer et al. (1995). During the time between two measurements, the operator manually locked on single targets to register their flight tracks for 40 s each. The wind was measured by tracking a meteorological balloon up to at least 4 km height above ground level at noon and then every 4 hours. By combining the data of the wind measurements with the tracking data of the birds (e.g. ground speed, vertical speed, altitude and track) heading and air speed were calculated. The fluctuations of the radar signal (echo-signatures) allowed the identification of wing-beat patterns, which were classified into 4 groups (Bloch et al 1981): Fig. 1. args.summary:
This is a diploma thesis by Simon Speich from the Zoological Institute of the University of Basel, Switzerland (July 1999), supervised by Prof. Dr. Bruno Bruderer and Dr. Felix Liechti of the Swiss Ornithological Institute. It studies bird migration across the western Mediterranean Sea using tracking radar on Mallorca, Spain, during spring 1997 (March 24 to May 26).

**Part A: Diurnal and Seasonal Schedule of Spring Migration over Mallorca**

The study used an X-band (3.3 cm wavelength) tracking radar located in southern Mallorca (39°18'N, 3°4'E), about 8 km from the southern coast. Data was collected on 64 nights. Wing-beat patterns were classified into four groups: CF (continuously flapping, mainly waders/waterfowl), IF (intermittently flapping, mainly passerines), SW (swifts), and UD (undetermined).

Key findings on diurnal pattern:
- Nocturnal migration showed two distinct phases separated by a gap (no birds taking off from the sea): a take-off phase (birds departing from the island) and a night phase (birds arriving from North Africa).
- Take-off began on average 13 ± 25 min before sunset (SE=±4 min, N=49 nights), reached peak intensity within one hour after sunset (average 51 ± 13 min after sunset), and ended 200 ± 62 min after sunset.
- The fastest birds arrived from Africa 229 ± 81 min after sunset; the main mass arrived 485 ± 94 min after sunset (roughly 8 hours after sunset).
- Night phase ended on average 8 ± 59 min after sunrise.
- Continuously flapping birds took off earlier than intermittently flapping (passerine) birds (Mann-Whitney U = 126, p < 0.046).
- On average, at least one third of migrants landed after crossing the coast each night (estimate between 27% and 37%).

Seasonal course:
- Migration intensity increased steeply from early April to mid-April, then slowly declined by end of May; highest intensity was between mid-April and beginning of May.
- Passerine-type wing-beat proportion was ~48% early in April (almost 50%), declining to 18% by end of May.
- Swift-type wing-beat proportion increased from 6% (early April) to over 40% by late May, causing the clear separation between take-off and night phases to disappear (swifts sleep in the air).
- No significant direct correlation between night phase and take-off phase migration traffic was found (Spearman R=0.2389, p=0.0983), but when nights were divided into two groups (where take-off MT was higher vs. lower than night phase MT), correlations became highly significant (R=0.8951, p<0.001, N=12; and R=0.4520, p=0.0107, N=35). This suggests most birds rested only about one day ("short resting periods of only one day").

**Part B: Direction, Speed and Origin of Spring Migrants Arriving on Mallorca**

- Mean flight direction was 18° during take-off and 10° during arrivals from North Africa (roughly NNE).
- Average ground speed of migrating birds was 12 m·s⁻¹; passerine-type wing-beat birds had ground speeds more than 2 m·s⁻¹ higher than continuously flapping birds.
- Nocturnal migrants from Africa arrived "in a wave" at different times in the second half of the night because most did NOT fly non-stop over the Sahara and Mediterranean, but landed somewhere in North Africa first.
- Using direction and speed, potential previous take-off areas in North Africa were calculated; migrants were NOT predominantly concentrated along the coast but departed, at least some nights, from further inland in the Atlas Highlands, and some possibly even south of the Atlas mountains.
- It appears migrants landed as soon as they detected potential resting areas around dawn after crossing the Sahara; those still over the Sahara continued to the Atlas highlands, increasing numbers there but not near the coast.
- Mallorca seemed to have no important concentration effect attracting migrants from different directions.

**Overall conclusion:** The two-wave pattern (take-off phase, gap, night phase) demonstrated that most spring migrants do NOT fly non-stop over the Sahara and Mediterranean; instead, they land and rest in North Africa before the sea crossing, adhering to a night-flying/day-resting strategy even across large ecological barriers. Migration over Mallorca is confined to the night. Possible reasons for landing instead of non-stop flight include avoiding depletion of energy reserves and stronger selection for night-flying than for time-minimizing.

The study was part of a larger Swiss National Science Foundation-supported project by the Swiss Ornithological Institute investigating whether bird migration across the Mediterranean occurs on a broad front and whether islands like the Balearics influence migration. Two tracking radars were used: one on Mallorca and one near Malaga on the Spanish mainland, with moon and infrared observations along French and Spanish coasts.

In a recent review of the cue conflict literature (Muheim et al. [2006a](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR10 "Muheim R, Moore FR, Phillips JB (2006a) Calibration of magnetic and celestial compass cues in migratory birds—a review of cue-conflict experiments. J Exp Biol 209:2–17")), we summarized all of the published studies in which migratory birds were exposed to a shifted magnetic field relative to the natural celestial cues. We concluded that the birds recalibrated the magnetic compass with respect to celestial cues if they had a view of the sky down to the horizon at sunrise or sunset. When the view of the horizon was obstructed during exposure (e.g., when exposure to the cue conflict was carried out in an orientation funnel or automatic registration cage), the birds recalibrated the celestial cues with respect to the magnetic field. We found no other variables, e.g., migratory phase (before vs. during migration), season, species or location, that could explain the otherwise highly variable and seemingly contradictory results from the different studies. In all of the studies cited by Wiltschko et al. as contradictory to our theory (Wiltschko and Wiltschko [1975a](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR18 "Wiltschko W, Wiltschko R (1975a) The integration of stars and magnetic field in the orientation system of night migrating birds. I. Autumn experiments with European warblers (Gen. Sylvia). Z Tierpsychol 37:337–355"), [b](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR19 "Wiltschko W, Wiltschko R (1975b) The integration of stars and magnetic field in the orientation system of night migrating birds. II. Spring experiments with European robins, Erithacus rubecula. Z Tierpsychol 39:265–282"); Bingman [1987](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR6 "Bingman VP (1987) Earth’s magnetism and the nocturnal orientation of migratory European robins. Auk 104:523–525"); Bingman and Wiltschko [1988](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR7 "Bingman VP, Wiltschko W (1988) Orientation of dunnocks, Prunella modularis, at sunset. Ethology 77:1–9"); Wiltschko et al. [1998](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR21 "Wiltschko W, Wiltschko R, Munro U, Ford H (1998) Magnetic versus celestial cues: cue-conflict experiments with migrating silvereyes at dusk. J Comp Physiol A 182:521–529"); Sandberg et al. [2000](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR15 "Sandberg R, Bäckman J, Moore FR, Lõhmus M (2000) Magnetic information calibrates celestial cues during migration. Anim Behav 60:453–462")), the birds were exposed to the cue conflict in funnels or registration cages, restricting the view of the horizon, the section of sky that we suggest is critical for magnetic compass calibration. It is likely that the birds could obtain a view of the horizon in some of the funnel/cage designs when hovering near the top of the cage. However, our survey of the literature suggests that recalibration of the magnetic compass does not occur under these conditions, perhaps because birds must remain stationary during the calibration process.

To test the conclusions of our literature survey, that polarized light cues present at sunrise and sunset provide the calibration reference used to recalibrate the magnetic compass, we carried out orientation experiments with Savannah Sparrows, _Passerculus sandwichensis_, in Alaska (Muheim et al. [2006b](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR11 "Muheim R, Phillips JB, Åkesson S (2006b) Polarized light cues underlie compass calibration in migratory songbirds. Science 313:837–839"), [2007](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR12 "Muheim R, Åkesson S, Phillips JB (2007) Magnetic compass of migratory Savannah sparrows is calibrated by skylight polarization at sunrise and sunset. J Ornithol 148(Suppl 2):485–494")). We exposed birds caught during migration to a shifted artificial polarization pattern at sunrise or sunset and tested their magnetic compass orientation. The comparison between each bird’s initial control orientation and its orientation after the exposure clearly showed that Savannah Sparrows recalibrate their magnetic compass after a 1-h exposure to a rotated polarization axis at either sunrise or sunset. The results supported earlier findings by Able and Able ([1995](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR3 "Able KP, Able MA (1995) Interactions in the flexible orientation system of a migratory bird. Nature 375:230–232")) and Cochran et al. ([2004](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR8 "Cochran WW, Mouritsen H, Wikelski M (2004) Migrating songbirds recalibrate their magnetic compass daily from twilight cues. Science 304:405–408")) that also reported recalibration of the magnetic compass when the birds were exposed to a rotated magnetic field while simultaneously provided with a view of sunset cues down to the horizon. We have recently corroborated these results with White-throated Sparrows, _Zonotrichia albicollis_, in New York State, showing that these sparrows recalibrate their magnetic compass after exposure to either a shifted artificial polarization pattern in the ambient (unshifted) geomagnetic field or a shifted magnetic field under natural celestial cues (R Muheim, ME Deutschlander, JB Phillips, unpublished data). These experiments were carried out during both spring and autumn migration and confirm that migratory season and phase do not explain the difference between studies, and that there is no difference in the response of the birds to a cue conflict produced by rotating an artificial polarization pattern versus one produced by rotating the magnetic field.

Wiltschko et al. argue that the paper by Cochran et al. ([2004](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR8 "Cochran WW, Mouritsen H, Wikelski M (2004) Migrating songbirds recalibrate their magnetic compass daily from twilight cues. Science 304:405–408")) cannot be regarded as support for recalibration of the magnetic compass, since the experiments were not carried out in orientation funnels, but instead are based on release experiments. This argument strongly contradicts a study by Sandberg et al. ([2000](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR15 "Sandberg R, Bäckman J, Moore FR, Lõhmus M (2000) Magnetic information calibrates celestial cues during migration. Anim Behav 60:453–462")), who exposed four species of birds to a shifted magnetic field while they were tested in orientation funnels during sunset, and then released these birds and observed their vanishing bearings. In agreement with the overall pattern found in the literature (Muheim et al. [2006a](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR10 "Muheim R, Moore FR, Phillips JB (2006a) Calibration of magnetic and celestial compass cues in migratory birds—a review of cue-conflict experiments. J Exp Biol 209:2–17")), the birds did not recalibrate their magnetic compass, since their view of the celestial cues near the horizon was obscured by the funnels during the exposure. Instead, two species recalibrated their celestial compasses in the funnel experiments, while the other two species did not show a reaction to the exposure (Sandberg et al. [2000](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR15 "Sandberg R, Bäckman J, Moore FR, Lõhmus M (2000) Magnetic information calibrates celestial cues during migration. Anim Behav 60:453–462")). In the release experiments that occurred within 1 h after the funnel experiments, the departure directions of the birds of all four groups showed that they had recalibrated their celestial compasses. Neither the funnel experiments nor the subsequent release experiments provided evidence for recalibration of the magnetic compass, nor was there evidence that birds show opposite responses in funnel and release experiments. Thus, the results of Sandberg et al. and Cochran et al. are in full agreement with our interpretation. Wiltschko et al. ([1983](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR20 "Wiltschko W, Wiltschko R, Keeton WT, Madden R (1983) Growing up in an altered magnetic field affects the initial orientation of young homing pigeons. Behav Ecol Sociobiol 12:135–142")) also argue that the findings from the study by Cochran et al. ([2004](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR8 "Cochran WW, Mouritsen H, Wikelski M (2004) Migrating songbirds recalibrate their magnetic compass daily from twilight cues. Science 304:405–408")) cannot be interpreted as evidence for recalibration of the magnetic compass because the birds may have been “overcompensating” after exposure to the cue conflict, citing their earlier work on homing pigeons. They exposed homing pigeons to a rotated magnetic field in a home loft which provided an undisturbed view of celestial cues. When first tested under the sun, the birds shifted in a direction consistent with calibration of the sun compass relative to the magnetic field, but then “overcompensated” (i.e., shifted in the opposite direction), presumably as a result of the feedback they received during their first flight under the sun. Interpretation of these findings is complicated by the fact that the same deflection of the initial orientation would result from the magnetic compass being calibrated relative to celestial cues if the pigeons used magnetic compass cues to determine the direction of displacement (Phillips and Waldvogel [1988](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR13 "Phillips JB, Waldvogel JA (1988) Celestial polarized patterns as a calibration reference for sun compass of homing pigeons. J Theor Biol 131:55–67")). Regardless of the explanation for the magnetic loft experiments, there is no reason to believe that these findings suggest a reinterpretation of Cochran et al.’s findings, since these birds were tracked on their first release after exposure to the cue conflict, and showed the deflected orientation immediately upon release. In conclusion, it is inappropriate to exclude Cochran et al.’s ([2004](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR8 "Cochran WW, Mouritsen H, Wikelski M (2004) Migrating songbirds recalibrate their magnetic compass daily from twilight cues. Science 304:405–408")) results when discussing cue conflict experiments.

The paper by Wiltschko et al. shows interesting new findings that appear to contradict our results. They report that Australian Silvereyes, _Zosterops lateralis_, did not show recalibration of the magnetic compass after exposure to a shifted magnetic field for 90 min at sunset and for 90 min the following sunrise, even though the birds has access to natural celestial cues, including the horizon. Instead, their birds oriented in the same direction as before the exposure, which is interpreted by the authors as a demonstration of that polarized light cues are not the primary compass cues, but instead that the magnetic field calibrates the celestial compasses during migration. Unfortunately, Wiltschko et al. did not test whether the silvereyes had recalibrated their celestial compasses. Since the birds were held in an outdoor aviary for about two weeks prior to the start of the experiments (see below), they may have completed calibration of their compass systems prior to the cue conflict exposures. Previous studies have shown that once calibration of a compass system is completed, updating the calibration (e.g., when the birds are exposed to a new cue conflict) may require several days of exposure (Bingman [1987](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR6 "Bingman VP (1987) Earth’s magnetism and the nocturnal orientation of migratory European robins. Auk 104:523–525"); Wiltschko and Wiltschko [1975b](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR19 "Wiltschko W, Wiltschko R (1975b) The integration of stars and magnetic field in the orientation system of night migrating birds. II. Spring experiments with European robins, Erithacus rubecula. Z Tierpsychol 39:265–282")).

In their recent paper, Wiltschko et al. discuss a number of possible explanations for their contradictory results that we would like to address:

FormalPara _Different bird species_
Wiltschko et al. point out that species-specific differences in the control of migration could explain the differences observed between the Savannah Sparrows in North America and Silvereyes in Australia, i.e., that birds of different phylogenetic origin may have evolved different migration strategies. To date, published records of recalibration of the magnetic compass has been shown for the following species: Savannah Sparrow (Bingman [1983](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR4 "Bingman VP (1983) Magnetic field orientation of migratory Savannah sparrows with different first summer experience. Behaviour 87:43–51"); Able and Able [1990](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR1 "Able KP, Able MA (1990) Ontogeny of migratory orientation in the Savannah sparrow, Passerculus sandwichensis: calibration of the magnetic compass. Anim Behav 39:905–913"), [1993](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR2 "Able KP, Able MA (1993) Daytime calibration of magnetic orientation in a migratory bird requires a view of skylight polarization. Nature 364:523–525"), [1995](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR3 "Able KP, Able MA (1995) Interactions in the flexible orientation system of a migratory bird. Nature 375:230–232"); Muheim et al. [2006b](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR11 "Muheim R, Phillips JB, Åkesson S (2006b) Polarized light cues underlie compass calibration in migratory songbirds. Science 313:837–839"), [2007](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR12 "Muheim R, Åkesson S, Phillips JB (2007) Magnetic compass of migratory Savannah sparrows is calibrated by skylight polarization at sunrise and sunset. J Ornithol 148(Suppl 2):485–494")), Pied Flycatcher, _Ficedula hypoleuca_ (Weindler and Liepa [1999](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR16 "Weindler P, Liepa V (1999) The influence of premigratory experience on the migratory orientation of birds. In: Adams NJ, Slotow RH (eds) Proceedings of the 22nd International Ornithological Congress, Durban, 1998. Birdlife South Africa, Johannesburg, pp 979–987"); Prinz and Wiltschko [1992](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR14 "Prinz K, Wiltschko W (1992) Migratory orientation of pied flycatchers: interaction of stellar and magnetic information during ontogeny. Anim Behav 44:539–545")) and Swainson’s and Gray-cheeked Thrush, _Catharus ustulatus_ and _minimus_ (Cochran et al. [2004](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR8 "Cochran WW, Mouritsen H, Wikelski M (2004) Migrating songbirds recalibrate their magnetic compass daily from twilight cues. Science 304:405–408")). Moreover, Bingman ([1984](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR5 "Bingman VP (1984) Night sky orientation of migratory pied flycatchers raised in different magnetic fields. Behav Ecol Sociobiol 15:77–80")) (Pied Flycatcher) and Able and Able ([1997](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR22 "Able KP, Able MA (1997) Development of sunset orientation in a migratory bird: no calibration by the magnetic field. Anim Behav 53:363–368")) (Savannah Sparrow) reported no recalibration of the celestial compasses when testing birds in a vertical magnetic field after exposure to a shifted magnetic field in an open cage, indicating that the magnetic field is likely to have been recalibrated instead. Thus, a variety of species from both North America and Europe recalibrated their magnetic compass when exposed to a cue conflict with access to polarized light cues near the horizon. Further work is needed to determine whether Silvereyes are an exception to this general pattern or, instead, whether methodological differences can account for the difference in the responses of the birds in the experiments carried out by Wiltschko et al. (see earlier discussion and below).

FormalPara _Different phases of migration_
Contrary to the conclusions of earlier authors that birds use celestial cues to recalibrate their magnetic compass before the onset of migration, but then switch to using the magnetic compass to recalibrate the celestial compasses during migration (Wiltschko and Wiltschko [1999](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR17 "Wiltschko R, Wiltschko W (1999) Celestial and magnetic cues in experimental conflict. In: Adams NJ, Slotow RH (eds) Proceedings of the 22nd International Ornithological Congress, Durban, 1998. Birdlife South Africa, Johannesburg, pp 988–1004")), we did not find that the phase of migration was a factor in our review of the cue conflict literature (Muheim et al. [2006a](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR10 "Muheim R, Moore FR, Phillips JB (2006a) Calibration of magnetic and celestial compass cues in migratory birds—a review of cue-conflict experiments. J Exp Biol 209:2–17")). This was based on two studies (Able and Able [1995](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR3 "Able KP, Able MA (1995) Interactions in the flexible orientation system of a migratory bird. Nature 375:230–232"); Cochran et al. [2004](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR8 "Cochran WW, Mouritsen H, Wikelski M (2004) Migrating songbirds recalibrate their magnetic compass daily from twilight cues. Science 304:405–408")) that showed recalibration of the magnetic compass during migration. Cochran et al. ([2004](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR8 "Cochran WW, Mouritsen H, Wikelski M (2004) Migrating songbirds recalibrate their magnetic compass daily from twilight cues. Science 304:405–408")) tested long-distance migrants captured en route during spring migration, and so they used birds that were well underway in their migratory journey. Able and Able ([1995](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR3 "Able KP, Able MA (1995) Interactions in the flexible orientation system of a migratory bird. Nature 375:230–232")) used both juvenile and adult birds captured at their breeding site before migration, but did not start with the exposures and experiments before later during the migration season. Wiltschko et al. argue that both Able and Able’s and our study was carried out at the start of the migratory season, with birds that had not previously experienced changing relationships between compass cues. This is surprising, because the Silvereyes used in their study were captured near the northern edge of their wintering area two weeks before the start of spring migration. The Savannah Sparrows we tested in Alaska (Muheim et al. [2006b](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR11 "Muheim R, Phillips JB, Åkesson S (2006b) Polarized light cues underlie compass calibration in migratory songbirds. Science 313:837–839")) had all accumulated subcutaneous fat, a clear sign of migratory disposition, and it is very likely that they had been migrating up to several 100 km before reaching our research station. When considered along with the study by Cochran et al. ([2004](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR8 "Cochran WW, Mouritsen H, Wikelski M (2004) Migrating songbirds recalibrate their magnetic compass daily from twilight cues. Science 304:405–408")), showing recalibration of the magnetic compass during migration, these findings make it unlikely that phase of migration or migratory disposition can explain the discrepancies between the studies. The argument that the Silvereyes might have used true navigation and therefore did not recalibrate their compasses might be a valid interpretation of the current results, but then adult birds tested in both our and Able and Able’s study would also have been expected to show a different response to that of the juvenile birds, which they did not. Therefore, further consideration should be given to the possibility that the Silvereyes in Wiltschko et al.’s study calibrated their compasses during the two weeks they were held in the outdoor aviary (a significant departure from the other studies) and did not calibrate their compasses again when exposed to the shifted magnetic field in the familiar environment. If this explanation is correct, we would expect that there would be no recalibration of the magnetic or celestial compasses. Another departure from most, if not all, previous studies is that Wiltschko et al. held birds between exposure to the cue conflicts and testing in a room with a window that provided a partial view of the outside world, although not a direct view of the sky. Further work will be needed to determine whether a view of previously calibrated landmarks and/or indirect sun information might have interfered with the calibration of one or more of the birds’ compass systems.

FormalPara _Different regions of the Earth_
We agree that the rapid changes of magnetic declination experienced in Alaska (11 min/year in the year of the experiments) compared to 0.2 min/year in eastern Australia could result in the evolution of an orientation system that primarily relies on celestial, rather than magnetic cues. However, magnetic declination does not change as dramatically in central North America (New York and Illinois, 3 and 7 min/year, respectively; changes that are similar to those observed in Germany, 7 min/year). Thus, if variation in declination in different regions of the Earth rather than access to celestial cues near the horizon explains the differences between studies, birds from central North America and Europe should use the same primary calibration cues. However, there are large discrepancies between studies carried out in regions with similar annual changes in declination, both within central North America (e.g., Able and Able [1995](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR3 "Able KP, Able MA (1995) Interactions in the flexible orientation system of a migratory bird. Nature 375:230–232") and Cochran et al. [2004](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR8 "Cochran WW, Mouritsen H, Wikelski M (2004) Migrating songbirds recalibrate their magnetic compass daily from twilight cues. Science 304:405–408") versus Sandberg et al. [2000](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR15 "Sandberg R, Bäckman J, Moore FR, Lõhmus M (2000) Magnetic information calibrates celestial cues during migration. Anim Behav 60:453–462")) and between Europe and central North America (e.g., Wiltschko and Wiltschko [1975a](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR18 "Wiltschko W, Wiltschko R (1975a) The integration of stars and magnetic field in the orientation system of night migrating birds. I. Autumn experiments with European warblers (Gen. Sylvia). Z Tierpsychol 37:337–355"), [b](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR19 "Wiltschko W, Wiltschko R (1975b) The integration of stars and magnetic field in the orientation system of night migrating birds. II. Spring experiments with European robins, Erithacus rubecula. Z Tierpsychol 39:265–282"); Bingman [1987](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR6 "Bingman VP (1987) Earth’s magnetism and the nocturnal orientation of migratory European robins. Auk 104:523–525"); Bingman and Wiltschko [1988](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR7 "Bingman VP, Wiltschko W (1988) Orientation of dunnocks, Prunella modularis, at sunset. Ethology 77:1–9") and Wiltschko et al. [1998](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR21 "Wiltschko W, Wiltschko R, Munro U, Ford H (1998) Magnetic versus celestial cues: cue-conflict experiments with migrating silvereyes at dusk. J Comp Physiol A 182:521–529") versus Able and Able [1995](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR3 "Able KP, Able MA (1995) Interactions in the flexible orientation system of a migratory bird. Nature 375:230–232") and Cochran et al. [2004](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR8 "Cochran WW, Mouritsen H, Wikelski M (2004) Migrating songbirds recalibrate their magnetic compass daily from twilight cues. Science 304:405–408")). Therefore, different regions of the Earth with different magnetic properties are unlikely to explain why the Silvereyes in Wiltschko et al.’s experiments responded differently to the cue conflict.

FormalPara _Circumstances of experiments_
As mentioned earlier, the birds in the experiments reported in Muheim et al. ([2006b](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR11 "Muheim R, Phillips JB, Åkesson S (2006b) Polarized light cues underlie compass calibration in migratory songbirds. Science 313:837–839")) had accumulated fat and showed migratory restlessness with a clear directional tendency (Mouritsen and Larsen [1998](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR9 "Mouritsen H, Larsen ON (1998) Evaluating alternative methods for the analysis of Emlen funnel data. In: Mouritsen H (ed) Compasses and orientational strategies of night migrating Passerine birds. Center of Sound Communication, Institute of Biology, Odense University, Odense, pp 115–124")), which suggests that the birds were in migratory condition. In addition, most Savannah Sparrows had left the area in the second part of the experimental period, indicating that the experiments were carried out during the migratory period of the population of Savannah Sparrows migrating in this area.

Wiltschko et al.’s comparison of the exposures to polarizing filters in our study (Muheim et al. [2006b](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR11 "Muheim R, Phillips JB, Åkesson S (2006b) Polarized light cues underlie compass calibration in migratory songbirds. Science 313:837–839"), [2007](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR12 "Muheim R, Åkesson S, Phillips JB (2007) Magnetic compass of migratory Savannah sparrows is calibrated by skylight polarization at sunrise and sunset. J Ornithol 148(Suppl 2):485–494")) with other studies fails to mention one important difference: while birds in the studies cited by Wiltschko et al. aligned their behavior along the e-vector axis of the polarizers, birds did not do this in our experiments (which would have resulted in a fixed axis of orientation relative to the polarization filter). Instead, individual birds in our study reoriented their direction of orientation relative to the magnetic field by an amount corresponding to the difference between the natural polarization pattern and the rotated pattern produced with the polarization filters; a consistent axis of orientation was only observed when each bird’s direction of orientation after exposure to the cue conflict was plotted as a deviation from their direction of orientation prior to the cue conflict exposure. Thus, unlike earlier studies using artificial polarization filters, the birds’ orientation cannot be attributed to a fixed (i.e., parallel) alignment relative to the artificial polarization axis as Wiltschko et al. suggest, nor can an artifact resulting from the use of an unnaturally strong polarized light stimulus explain the results of experiments by Cochran et al. ([2004](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR8 "Cochran WW, Mouritsen H, Wikelski M (2004) Migrating songbirds recalibrate their magnetic compass daily from twilight cues. Science 304:405–408")) and Able and Able ([1995](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3#ref-CR3 "Able KP, Able MA (1995) Interactions in the flexible orientation system of a migratory bird. Nature 375:230–232")), in which cue conflicts were created by exposing birds to natural celestial cues in a rotated magnetic field.

## Conclusions

In conclusion, we believe that the most likely explanation for the reported failure of Silvereyes to respond in the same manner as the other species tested to date lies in differences in the exposure protocol and/or the experiences of birds before or after exposure to the cue conflict, rather than in the arguments listed by Wiltschko et al. Their birds may have had ample opportunity to familiarize themselves with the surroundings and to recalibrate their compasses during the two weeks they spent in the outdoor aviary. They may not have updated the calibration of their compass systems when later exposed to the shifted magnetic field in the familiar surroundings if the aviary was situated close to the exposure site used later. The role of a familiar environment in the compass calibration process remains an interesting area of future research. Future studies might also examine other methodological differences between the studies. For example, if birds are exposed to a conflict between celestial and magnetic cues during successive day/night transitions, does the order of these exposures matter (e.g., for a nocturnal migrant, a typical daytime stopover would result in the bird experiencing a sunrise followed by a sunset at the same location)? Clearly, much is yet to be learned about the detailed mechanisms of compass calibration, especially in different species and geographic areas, and it remains a challenging area of future exploration.

args.summary:
This is a scientific commentary article published in the Journal of Ornithology (Volume 149, pages 659-662, 2008) responding to a paper by R. Wiltschko et al. that presented contradictory results on the role of polarized light in compass calibration in migratory songbirds. The article is authored by Rachel Muheim, Susanne Åkesson, and John B. Phillips, and published July 25, 2008 (DOI: 10.1007/s10336-008-0337-3), with 13 citations and over 1000 accesses.

The authors defend their earlier literature review (Muheim et al. 2006a) which concluded that migratory birds recalibrate their magnetic compass relative to celestial cues when they have a view of the sky down to the horizon at sunrise or sunset. When the horizon view was obstructed (e.g., in orientation funnels or registration cages), birds instead recalibrated celestial cues relative to the magnetic field.

Key methodological points and arguments include:
- Their own experiments with Savannah Sparrows (Passerculus sandwichensis) in Alaska and White-throated Sparrows (Zonotrichia albicollis) in New York State demonstrated that a 1-hour exposure to a rotated polarization axis at sunrise or sunset caused recalibration of the magnetic compass.
- The authors argue that Cochran et al. (2004) results showing daily recalibration of magnetic compass from twilight cues should not be excluded, contrary to Wiltschko et al.'s argument. They reference Sandberg et al. (2000) in support.
- They address Wiltschko et al.'s claim about "overcompensation" in homing pigeons, noting alternative interpretations via Phillips and Waldvogel (1988).
- The paper addresses four possible explanations for discrepancies: (1) different bird species - noting that recalibration of the magnetic compass has been shown in Savannah Sparrows, Pied Flycatchers, and Swainson's and Gray-cheeked Thrushes, but Silvereyes may be an exception; (2) different phases of migration - arguing that migratory phase does not explain differences since birds in multiple studies were actively migrating; (3) different regions of the Earth with varying magnetic declination changes - noting that differences in declination changes cannot fully explain discrepancies; (4) circumstances of experiments - highlighting methodological differences including the two-week outdoor aviary habituation period for Silvereyes before experiments.

Conclusion: The authors believe the different results from Silvereyes are most likely due to differences in exposure protocol or prior/post-exposure experiences of birds, rather than the arguments offered by Wiltschko et al. The birds may have already completed compass calibration during two weeks in an outdoor aviary, and may not have updated calibration in a familiar environment. Future research should examine the role of familiar environments in compass calibration and other methodological differences (e.g., order of sunrise/sunset exposures).

# A Stellar Migrant

## Indigo Bunting

This update was written by Smithsonian Migratory Bird Center scientist Mary Deinlein

![brightly-colored bird](/sites/default/files/styles/max_1300x1300/public/conservation/migratory-birds/news/inbu11.jpg?itok=Seb7wICh)

One constellation most people can recognize is the Big Dipper. Did you know that the two stars farthest from the handle of the Big Dipper point toward the Little Dipper, and that the last star in the handle of the Little Dipper is the North Star? Did you also know that the North Star is the star around which all other stars rotate, and that it is a reliable reference point for due north?

This is the kind of information that indigo buntings learn and rely on to get their bearings for migration. Read on to find out how this was discovered…

In the summertime, the high-pitched, persistent [**song**](http://www.mbr-pwrc.usgs.gov/id/framlst/Song/h5980so.mp3) of the dazzling male indigo bunting is a common roadside sound throughout the eastern United States and southeastern Canada. Because of an increase in this species' preferred habitat of abandoned fields, forest clearings, and brushy woodland edges (such as along roads and power line clearings), it is more abundant now than when the Mayflower docked at Plymouth Rock. Since the 1940's, its range has also been expanding into the southwestern United States.

As is typical in the bird world, the male indigo bunting is the more dapper and conspicuous of the sexes. Whereas it is not easy to catch a glimpse of the secretive, dull-brown female, it's hard to miss the cobalt blue male that often belts out his strident song from an exposed perch high in the tree tops.

Interestingly, the brilliant blue of male indigo buntings results not from pigment but rather from the diffraction of light through the structure of the feathers. This accounts for why in some lighting the males appear exquisitely turquoise blue, while in others they appear to be almost black.

Older male buntings are first to arrive on their North American breeding grounds in late April to mid May. They will have already staked out their territories by the time the females arrive about 2 weeks later. Within a day or two, each female will select a mate and settle on a particular territory where she will most likely remain throughout the season. Together each pair will raise as many as 3 broods.

Despite the appearances of monogamy, recent advances in genetic analyses have revealed that 20-40% of the buntings born in a season are fathered by males other than the holder of the territory in which the young are born.

Another fly in the pudding of nuclear family life is that about 15% of breeding males will have as many as 4 females on their territory, either simultaneously or over a season.

The females do most if not all of the feeding and caring for the young for the 9 to 12 days they are in the nest, although the male defends the nest against intruders. Once the young have fledged the males will tend to them, particularly if the female is busy building a new nest for the next brood.

If you've ever tried to learn to identify birds by song, you know that there is a lot of variation between the songs of individual birds within a species. You may never hear a bird in the wild that sounds exactly like the song recording you listened to repeatedly on your store-bought CD or tape. The individual differences in birds songs enable male birds within some species to distinguish one another.

For example, experiments have shown that territorial males respond differently to hearing tape recordings of a neighbor's song versus that of a stranger's song. In addition to individual variation there are also regional dialects which are detectable differences in songs within a species in different geographical locations.

In the case of indigo buntings, 80% of males learn their particular song by imitating an older male with an established territory during their first spring. Alluding to the adaptive value of this pattern of song learning, males that match an older, territorial neighbor's song their first year are more successful in attracting mates and fledging young.

Most likely this is because they are able to trick their competitors (other first year males) into mistaking them for the older, established male. Combined with the fact that males usually return to the same breeding territory each year, this song mimicry gives rise to local dialects in which the sequence of notes in the songs of neighbors is similar, and different from that of birds in other areas.

Between mid-August and November, with their breeding duties over for the year, indigo buntings group together in large flocks and abandon their northern quarters for the tropics. Traveling up to 2,000 miles, most indigo buntings settle for the winter anywhere from southern Mexico and the West Indies to northern South America.

A smaller number will spend the winter in southernmost Florida. At this time of year, the indigo buntings' alter-ego takes over. The males give their syrinxes (equivalent to human vocal chords) a few months hiatus, and they no longer sport their namesake shock of blue feathers. Instead they assume an overall brown plumage with few streaks of blue remaining, thus resembling the females.

Whereas their social life on the breeding grounds revolves around defended territories occupied by a single male and one or more females, loose flocks composed of hundreds or thousands of birds roost together by night and forage together by day while in the tropics. The main food of choice becomes seeds and buds, rather than insects and spiders which are the staple during the breeding season.

Studies of indigo buntings have shed light on one of the many mysteries surrounding bird migration—how birds select the appropriate direction in which to fly. In the 1960's, Stephen Emlen cleverly demonstrated in experiments conducted outdoors and in a planetarium that indigo buntings, like sailors of yore, use the pattern of the stars as a compass.

In his experiments, Emlen took advantage of a behavior pattern shown by migratory birds in captivity during the periods of time when their normal spring and fall migrations occur. Termed Zugunruhe, a German word meaning migratory restlessness, this behavior is characterized by increased activity, mainly hopping and fluttering of the wings.

By placing captive buntings in cages made out of a funnel of blotting paper with an ink pad as a floor and a see-through top, Emlen was able to determine that buntings with a view of the night sky oriented their Zugunruhe activity in the appropriate direction in which they would be migrating, i.e. northward under a spring sky and southward under a fall sky.

Without a view of the night sky, the birds activity became randomly oriented. This orientation of activity was apparent in the pattern of inked footprints left on the blotting paper sides of the cages.

By systematically covering up parts of the night sky within a planetarium, Emlen went on to show that the birds gauge direction using the pattern of stars nearest the North Star, the pivot around which all the stars rotate and a reliable reference for due north. He also was able to conclude that young buntings learn this pattern during their first summer.

Experiments done since then on a variety of species have revealed that the stars are but one of several cues that birds rely on for orientation. Other sources of information include the position of the setting sun and the pattern of polarized light it creates, the earth's magnetic field, odors, wind, and topographic features such as mountains and bodies of water.

One of the last birds to stop singing as the summer months draw to a close, the indigo bunting is one of our best known songbirds. As the subject of an impressive amount of scientific research, this stellar migrant has enabled us to advance our limited understanding of the mind-boggling capabilities of migratory birds, and allowed us to enhance our view into the curious world of avian social life.

*Song recorded by John R. Sauer, USGS Patuxent Wildlife Research Center*

This is a Smithsonian National Zoo & Migratory Bird Center article (written by scientist Mary Deinlein) about the Indigo Bunting, a migratory songbird of the eastern United States and southeastern Canada. Key facts include:

- The male indigo bunting is brilliant cobalt blue, but this color results not from pigment but from diffraction of light through feather structure (appearing turquoise in some light, almost black in others); females are dull brown.
- Its range has expanded since the 1940s and it is more abundant now than when the Mayflower docked, due to its preference for abandoned fields, forest clearings, and brushy woodland edges.
- Older males arrive first (late April to mid May), stake out territories, and females arrive about 2 weeks later. Pairs raise up to 3 broods per season.
- Despite appearing monogamous, genetic analyses show 20-40% of buntings are fathered by males other than the territory holder, and about 15% of breeding males have up to 4 females on their territory.
- 80% of males learn their song by imitating an older territorial male during their first spring; matching a neighbor's song increases mating and fledging success, creating regional dialects.
- Between mid-August and November, they migrate up to 2,000 miles to winter in southern Mexico, the West Indies, and northern South America (some in southernmost Florida). In winter they lose their blue plumage, molt to brown, and switch diet from insects/spiders to seeds and buds, forming large flocks.
- Scientific significance: In the 1960s, Stephen Emlen demonstrated (using outdoor and planetarium experiments, and the Zugunruhe migration restlessness behavior) that indigo buntings use the pattern of stars near the North Star as a compass for migration. Young buntings learn this pattern during their first summer. Later experiments on various species revealed birds also use other cues: position of the setting sun and polarized light, the earth's magnetic field, odors, wind, and topographic features.

URL: https://aeroecolab.com/s/Horton_et_al-2019-Frontiers_in_Ecology_and_the_Environment.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This research paper (published in Frontiers in Ecology and the Environment) by Horton, Nilsson, Van Doren, La Sorte, Dokter, and Farnsworth quantifies the continental-scale exposure of nocturnally migrating birds to artificial light at night (ALAN) in the contiguous US. Approximately 80% of North America's ~630 terrestrial bird species are migratory, and over 80% of those migrate at night. The study combined over two decades (spring 1995 to spring 2017) of weather surveillance radar data from 143 stations with satellite-based VIIRS ALAN radiance data to map where and when the highest numbers of migrants are exposed to light pollution, focusing on the 125 largest urban centers.

Key methodology: Radar data from a 30-minute window centered on 3 hours after local sunset were filtered using a random forest classifier (5.6% spring and 4.5% fall classification error) to exclude precipitation scans, with only scans having ≥75% confidence of being precipitation-free retained. Migration activity was measured as vertically integrated reflectivity. ALAN was quantified using monthly VIIRS Day/Night Band composites averaged across October–December 2012–2017.

Key findings: (1) Fall migration had 63% higher cumulative migratory activity than spring, and 53.8% higher total exposure; even after standardizing for migration differences, fall exposure remained 13.1% higher because fall migrants used more easterly (and more photo-polluted) routes. (2) Half of seasonal migratory activity passed each radar site within just 6.7 ± 2.6 nights on average. (3) The top 125 urban areas occupied only 2.1% of total land area but produced 35.4% of total light radiance. (4) Mean avian light exposure in cities was 24 times the countrywide average. (5) Chicago, Houston, and Dallas consistently had the highest exposure risk in both seasons, with exposure magnitudes 19–21 times the median of the other 122 cities. (6) Larger cities generally had greater exposure risk (R² = 0.52 spring, 0.62 fall), but there were notable exceptions like Boston (4th in size but 36th/24th in exposure) and Des Moines (99th in size but 28th/36th in exposure).

Conservation implications: Because migration occurs in concentrated pulses and can now be forecast 12–72 hours in advance, targeted "lights-out" campaigns timed to peak migration nights could reduce bird exposure significantly. Fall mitigation is especially important given the higher numbers of less-experienced juvenile birds. The study identifies urban centers—particularly Chicago, Houston, and Dallas—as the highest-priority locations for ALAN-reducing conservation actions.
</summary>

"Across the US, 69.5% of the summed linear light radiance came from just 5% of the land area. The top 125 largest urban areas accounted for only 2.1% of total land area and 35.4% of total summed linear radiance."

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research paper (Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences) studying the effects of the "Tribute in Light" (TiL) installation at the National September 11 Memorial & Museum in New York City on nocturnally migrating birds. This is the first study to quantify ALAN (artificial light at night)-induced changes in multiple behaviors of nocturnally migrating birds.

Study design: Over seven years (2008-2016, excluding 2009 and 2011 due to precipitation), researchers monitored bird behavior using weather surveillance radar (WSR-88D at Brookhaven, NY), acoustic sensors recording flight calls, and visual observations. The lights were shut down 22 times for approximately 20 minutes each, allowing direct comparison between lit and dark periods. This was an opportunistic study, not a controlled experiment.

Key findings:
- The light installation influenced approximately 1.1 million birds (95% CI: 0.6-1.6 million) during seven nights over seven years
- Bird densities near the installation were up to 20 times greater than baseline densities, exceeding 60 times baseline in five of seven years and 150 times in three years (2008, 2012, 2013)
- Effects were found up to 4 km altitude (3.9x density increase at 1.5° radar elevation angle)
- During illuminated periods: birds aggregated in high densities, decreased flight speeds (by 1.7 m/s), followed circular flight paths, and vocalized more frequently (1.4x increase in flight call rates)
- Maximum standardized bird densities were 14 times greater when lights were illuminated (t=5.70, P<0.0001)
- Total bird numbers within 500m averaged 3.4 times higher during illuminated periods
- Effects were observed under clear sky conditions in a heavily photo-polluted environment – contradicting previous assumptions that light attraction only occurs in poor visibility
- Behavioral disruptions disappeared within minutes when lights were extinguished
- Simulations (flow model with disorientation probability a=0.95 and disorientation distance of 1500 m) revealed high probability of disorientation and attraction, with a stabilization time of 34 minutes
- Observers documented birds colliding with glass windows of a building under construction at 50 West St. in 2015 and 2016

Recommendations: The authors recommend selective removal of light pollution during nights with substantial bird migration to mitigate negative effects, particularly collisions with lighted structures. They note this strategy was successfully implemented through collaboration among the National September 11 Memorial & Museum, New York City Audubon, Cornell Lab of Ornithology, and other stakeholders. The study highlights the value of multimodal remote sensing and the need for further research on how differing ambient conditions influence bird attraction to light sources.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific paper (published in Nature) reports that anthropogenic electromagnetic noise (EMN) disrupts the magnetic compass orientation of migratory European robins (Erithacus rubecula). The study found that birds tested in unscreened wooden huts at the University of Oldenburg campus could not orient using their magnetic compass due to background electromagnetic noise, but regained full orientation capabilities when the huts were shielded with grounded aluminium screens that attenuated EMN in the 50 kHz–5 MHz range by ~2 orders of magnitude. 

Methodology: The researchers conducted extensive double-blinded experiments over 7 years. Key findings include: (1) When the aluminium screen grounding was removed, birds again became disoriented; (2) Deliberately introduced broadband EMN (2 kHz–9 MHz) at intensities similar to background urban noise caused disorientation, while very weak noise did not; (3) The disruptive effect was not confined to a single frequency band—both 20 kHz–450 kHz and 600 kHz–3 MHz ranges prevented orientation; (4) At a rural location ~7.5 km from the university where EMN was much weaker, birds oriented normally without screening.

Key quantitative data: Anthropogenic EMN peak magnetic field intensity at single frequencies was ~0.1–50 nT, with total time-dependent field summed over 10 kHz–5 MHz of ~200–1100 nT (still far weaker than Earth's magnetic field of ~49,000 nT). The effects occurred at intensities well below WHO/ICNIRP guidelines (reference levels of 6,000 nT at 150 kHz to 180 nT at 5 MHz). Effects were not attributed to power lines (16.7/50 Hz), mobile phone signals (GHz), or frequencies below 2 kHz or above 5 MHz. 

Conclusions and implications: The results could impact migratory bird conservation, as disorientation may reduce survival during migration, especially in overcast conditions when sun/star compass cues are unavailable. The effect appears localized to urban areas with high electronic device usage. The mechanism is unclear but may involve radical-pair (cryptochrome-based) magnetoreception or iron-containing particle clusters—the possibility of effects on quantum spin dynamics at such weak intensities is noted as remarkable. This study represents the first fully double-blinded, reproducible demonstration of an effect of anthropogenic electromagnetic fields (much weaker than current guidelines) on an intact vertebrate's behavior.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Interference Technology reports research led by Henrik Mouritsen, a professor of neurosensory sciences at the University of Oldenburg, Germany, which documented for the first time that man-made electromagnetic radiation interferes with migratory birds' internal magnetic compasses. While scientists have long known migratory birds navigate using Earth's magnetic field, this study found that anthropogenic electromagnetic noise ("electrosmog") disrupts this ability.

The researchers had studied European robins since the early 2000s using orientation cages with thermal paper to record the birds' movements. When Mouritsen moved his research to the University of Oldenburg (a city of about 160,000 people) in 2002, the robins lost their ability to use their magnetic compass and jumped in random directions for three years. After exhausting other explanations (food, cages, light, daylight cycle), a graduate student named Nils-Lasse Schneider suggested covering the huts and cages with aluminum sheets to form a Faraday cage, which shielded against weaker electromagnetic interference. This restored the birds' orientation ability without affecting Earth's magnetic field.

The study found the interference (in the frequency range up to 5 MHz) was below the limits set by the International Commission on Non-Ionizing Radiation Protection (ICNIRP) and the World Health Organization (WHO). Over a seven-year investigation involving double-blind studies, the team confirmed that when Faraday cage grounding was disconnected or deliberate electromagnetic interference was created inside, the birds immediately lost their magnetic orientation again. The disruptive electromagnetic fields cover a broader frequency range at much lower intensity than previous studies suggested. The interference is significantly weaker in rural areas and stronger near concentrations of electronic devices, meaning the effect is localized. The team noted potential implications both for migratory bird survival and for human beings, which remain uninvestigated.

The study, "Anthropogenic Electromagnetic Noise Disrupts Magnetic Compass Orientation in a Migratory Bird," was published in Nature (vol. 509, no. 7500), with contributing authors including Svenja Engels, Nele Lefeldt, Christine Maira Hein, Manuela Zapka, Andreas Michalik, Dana Elbers, Achim Kittel, and P.J. Hore.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article from the Journal of Comparative Physiology A (published September 1995, Volume 177, pages 363–369) by W. Wiltschko and R. Wiltschko (Fachbereich Biologie der Universität Frankfurt a. M., Germany). The study tested alternative hypotheses of magnetoreception in migratory European Robins (Erithacus rubecula) — specifically whether magnetoreception is based on photopigments or on magnetite.

Methodology: Migratory robins were tested under light of different wavelengths, then subjected to a brief, strong magnetic pulse designed to alter the magnetization of single domain magnetite.

Key results:
- Under "white" (control) light, birds preferred the normal, seasonally appropriate migratory direction.
- Under 571 nm green light, birds remained well oriented in the migratory direction.
- Under 633 nm red light, their behavior was not different from random.
- The magnetic pulse had a significant effect on migratory orientation, but responses varied between individuals: some showed a persistent directional shift, others exhibited a change in scatter, and one bird was seemingly unaffected.

Conclusion: The findings indicate a light-dependent process and suggest an involvement of magnetizable material in migratory orientation. The results are consistent with a model of a light-dependent compass combined with a magnetite-based 'map,' although some questions concerning the magnetic pulse effect remain open.

Key words include: Bird migration, Magnetic compass, Photopigments, Magnetite European robin, Erithacus rubecula. --- SOURCE 12: Magnetic orientation in migratory birds ---
URL: http://oops.uni-oldenburg.de/83/1/liemag06.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This document is the Ph.D. thesis of Miriam Liedvogel (defended September 13, 2006 at Carl von Ossietzky Universität Oldenburg, supervised by PD Dr. Henrik Mouritsen and Prof. Dr. Karl-Wilhelm Koch), titled "Magnetic orientation in migratory birds – linking behavioural phenomena with underlying molecular and neuronal mechanisms."

The thesis investigates how night-migratory birds perceive directional information from the Earth's magnetic field and how this information is processed in the brain. Using an integrative approach combining behavioral observation, molecular biology, biochemistry, biophysics, and neuroanatomy, Liedvogel's research covered the full process from the primary receptor molecule to higher brain integration centers.

KEY FINDINGS:

1. **Head-scanning behavior (Paper I):** Using a custom-built experimental setup allowing real-time monitoring under controllable magnetic field conditions, garden warblers (Sylvia borin) showed clear south-westerly orientation under natural magnetic fields but oriented randomly in zero-magnetic fields. Birds nearly tripled their head-scanning frequency in a fully compensated zero magnetic field, and showed significant increases in head-scanning just before initiating migratory restlessness. This indicated the magnetic compass sensor is in the head, and that scanning likely facilitates detection of the magnetically modulated visual pattern on the retina.

2. **Cryptochrome identification (Paper II):** Four cryptochrome family members were identified, cloned, and sequenced in the retina of migratory garden warblers: Cry1a, Cry1b, Cry2, and Cry4. Cry1a is predominantly expressed in the cytosol of ganglion cells, displaced ganglion cells, and photoreceptors. Striking differences were found between migratory and non-migratory birds: Cry1a expression was highest at night in night-migratory birds but decreased to background levels at night in non-migratory control species. Neuronal activity markers colocalized perfectly with Cry1a during night-time magnetic orientation - the first experimental demonstration of a putative light-mediated primary magnetoreceptor molecule in a bird's eye.

3. **Biophysical characterization (Paper III):** Garden warbler cryptochromes were recombinantly expressed as holoproteins (with built-in flavin cofactor) in a baculovirus/Sf9 cell system - the first successful expression of an animal cryptochrome holoprotein in a heterologous eukaryotic system. This required a novel on-column denaturation/refolding step to overcome known difficulties. Garden warbler cryptochromes are light-excited, absorb in the blue spectral range (matching wavelengths known to elicit magnetic orientation in behavioral experiments), and form radical pairs lasting approximately 10 milliseconds - sufficiently long-lived to detect Earth-strength magnetic fields.

4. **Cluster N identification (Paper IV):** Behavioral molecular mapping identified a distinct forebrain area in night-migratory birds, termed "Cluster N" ("N" for night), showing high neuronal activation at night during magnetic orientation but not during the day. Cluster N was inactive in non-migratory zebra finches (Taeniopygia guttata) and canaries (Serinus canaria). Located adjacent to or as part of the visual Wulst, covering birds' eyes with light-tight covers significantly reduced Cluster N activation to near baseline, demonstrating it is active specifically during night-vision in night-migratory birds.

5. **Lateralization and further tests (Paper V, VI):** European robins (Erithacus rubecula) showed significant dominance of Cluster N activation in the right hemisphere. Garden warblers tested under different magnetic field conditions and monochromatic red light showed no significant differences in Cluster N activation, so a definitive role in magnetic compass processing could not be confirmed. Additional analysis found positive correlations between movement and activity levels in 10 cerebral regions and parts of the cerebellum, supporting the hypothesis that vocal learning brain systems evolved from a pre-existing motor pathway.

METHODS: Experiments relied on careful behavioral observation (especially the final 60 minutes before tissue collection), followed by brain dissection, cryostat sectioning, radioactive in situ hybridization for neuronal activity mapping (using immediate early genes like c-Fos and ZENK), and immunohistochemistry for retinal tissue. Primary study species were garden warblers and European robins; control species were zebra finches, canaries, and Sardinian warblers (Sylvia melanocephala).

CONCLUSION: All findings support a light-mediated magnetoperception mechanism in night-migratory birds, consistent with the hypothesis that magnetically modulated intensity patterns are perceived by the visual system - i.e., night-migratory birds may literally "see" the direction of the Earth's magnetic field. The thesis comprises six manuscripts (three published, one submitted, one under review, one near submission) plus supplementary materials on cryptochrome cloning methodology.
</summary>

</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 14: ‘Fixed direction’-responses of birds in the geomagnetic field - PMC ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2686356

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific article by Roswitha Wiltschko and Wolfgang Wiltschko (published in Communicative & Integrative Biology, 2009;2(2):100–103, DOI: 10.4161/cib.7622, PMC2686356) examining "fixed direction"-responses in migratory birds' geomagnetic orientation. It serves as an addendum to their earlier paper on light-dependent magnetoreception under dim red light.

**Background:** Migratory birds exhibit spontaneous migration orientation — heading south in autumn and north in spring — which serves as a stable baseline for orientation testing. The avian magnetic compass, studied since the 1970s in European Robins (Erithacus rubecula), functions as an "inclination compass" based on the axial course and inclination of magnetic field lines rather than field polarity.

**The 'Fixed Direction' Response:** A distinct type of directional response has been observed in European Robins and Australian Silvereyes (Zosterops l. lateralis) under specific light conditions. Under dim 645nm red light, birds exhibit a persistent westerly tendency that does not vary with season—a "fixed direction" response that is a polar (not axial) response, contrasting sharply with the normal compass behavior. Other fixed direction responses were observed under bright monochromatic 565nm green light, 502nm turquoise light, bichromatic light combinations, and even in total darkness.

**Key differences (Table 1):**
- Compass orientation: axial/inclination compass, requires short-wavelength light, disrupted by oscillating fields, not affected by upper beak anesthesia, based on radical pair mechanism, receptors in right eye, transmitted via optic nerve, can indicate any direction
- Fixed direction responses: polar, occur even in total darkness, NOT affected by oscillating fields, disrupted by upper beak anesthesia, magnetite-based mechanism, receptors in skin of upper beak, transmitted via branch of trigeminal nerve, only one specific fixed direction depending on light regime

**Physical mechanisms:** The avian magnetic compass operates via radical pair processes (confirmed by disorientation from MHz range oscillating fields, consistent with the Ritz model where photon absorption forms radical pairs whose singlet-triplet ratio depends on magnetic field alignment). Compass orientation requires light from short wavelengths up to 565nm green. In contrast, fixed direction responses originate from superparamagnetic magnetite-based receptors in the upper beak skin, are unaffected by oscillating fields, and are disrupted by upper beak anesthesia.

**Interactions with visual system:** The light-dependence of fixed direction responses suggests complex interactions between beak-derived directional information and the visual system at higher processing levels. Monochromatic or bichromatic test lights activate only one or two color cones simultaneously—an unnatural condition, as natural light is always polychromatic. Higher light intensities (beyond ~8 quanta/s m² for compass orientation) trigger fixed direction responses, possibly due to cone activation imbalance disrupting the compass magnetoreception system. Notably, fixed direction responses are only observed under laboratory conditions not occurring in nature.

**Fixed direction vs disorientation:** Under oscillating fields, long-wavelength light, or right-eye occlusion (which disrupt radical pair processes) birds become disoriented rather than showing fixed directions, even though beak magnetite receptors remain functional — suggesting interference at the peripheral physical process level differs fundamentally from disruption at the transmitting/processing level involving visual input.

**Significance:** The compass allows birds to orient toward any chosen direction (migratory, home, or acquired), while fixed direction responses appear forced by the stimulus. The magnetite-based beak receptors normally provide magnetic intensity information as part of the navigational "map." Their role in fixed direction responses is surprising and unclear. The authors suggest it may represent a phylogenetic relict—an ancient function of magnetite-based receptors (found in all vertebrate groups) superseded in modern birds by the radical-pair-based avian compass.
</summary>

Magnetite is found in all vertebrate groups, and e.g., in mammals, it is discussed as basis for a magnetic compass."

This webpage contains three scientific research papers published in Nature (Vol 429, 13 May 2004), all as "letters to nature."

**1. Community disassembly and extinction paper (Ives et al.):**
The authors modeled how communities respond to environmental stressors, showing that the species with the lowest tolerance di(N) goes extinct first. They developed a method to calculate community equilibrium under stress using equations ri + ais + Σj bi,j x*j(s) = 0. They used various community topologies including plant-herbivore-predator food webs, competitive communities, arbitrary topologies (45% competitors, 45% prey/predators, 10% mutualists), and random food webs. Intraspecific interactions were constrained to negative values to avoid unrealistic positive abundances under stress. The assumption that lowest-tolerance species go extinct first was validated by full model simulations, categorizing species as extinct when reduced by a factor of 10^-3 in abundance. **2. Avian magnetic compass via radical-pair mechanism (Ritz et al.):**
This study tested competing hypotheses for the avian magnetic compass: magnetite-based versus radical-pair chemical reaction mechanisms. European robins (Erithacus rubecula) were tested under 565 nm light in the local geomagnetic field (46 μT, 66° inclination). Birds were disoriented when exposed to broadband (0.1–10 MHz, 0.085 μT) or single-frequency (7 MHz, 0.47 μT) oscillating fields. The effect is consistent with resonance effects on singlet–triplet transitions, supporting a radical-pair mechanism. A 7 MHz field would require 285 μT to affect magnetite receptors, far stronger than the 0.47 μT used. The paper presents EpiSims, a large-scale agent-based simulation tool built on TRANSIMS (a Los Alamos National Laboratory transportation simulation), using census, land-use, and population-mobility data to model disease spread in urban areas. The dynamic bipartite contact graph shows the person contact network is strongly connected small-world-like with a well-defined degree distribution scale, while the locations graph is scale-free, enabling efficient outbreak detection by placing sensors in location hubs. Analysis of smallpox mitigation strategies suggests outbreaks can be contained by targeted vaccination combined with early detection, without mass vaccination.
