--- SOURCE 5: Temporal and Spatial Pattern of Nocturnal Bird Migration ... ---
URL: https://speich.net/about/diplomarbeit.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a diploma thesis by Simon Speich from the Zoological Institute of the University of Basel, Switzerland (July 1999), supervised by Prof. Dr. Bruno Bruderer and Dr. Felix Liechti of the Swiss Ornithological Institute. It studies bird migration across the western Mediterranean Sea using tracking radar on Mallorca, Spain, during spring 1997 (March 24 to May 26).

**Part A: Diurnal and Seasonal Schedule of Spring Migration over Mallorca**

The study used an X-band (3.3 cm wavelength) tracking radar located in southern Mallorca (39°18'N, 3°4'E), about 8 km from the southern coast. Data was collected on 64 nights. Wing-beat patterns were classified into four groups: CF (continuously flapping, mainly waders/waterfowl), IF (intermittently flapping, mainly passerines), SW (swifts), and UD (undetermined).

Key findings on diurnal pattern:
- Nocturnal migration showed two distinct phases separated by a gap (no birds taking off from the sea): a take-off phase (birds departing from the island) and a night phase (birds arriving from North Africa).
- Take-off began on average 13 ± 25 min before sunset (SE=±4 min, N=49 nights), reached peak intensity within one hour after sunset (average 51 ± 13 min after sunset), and ended 200 ± 62 min after sunset.
- The fastest birds arrived from Africa 229 ± 81 min after sunset; the main mass arrived 485 ± 94 min after sunset (roughly 8 hours after sunset).
- Night phase ended on average 8 ± 59 min after sunrise.
- Continuously flapping birds took off earlier than intermittently flapping (passerine) birds (Mann-Whitney U = 126, p < 0.046).
- On average, at least one third of migrants landed after crossing the coast each night (estimate between 27% and 37%).

Seasonal course:
- Migration intensity increased steeply from early April to mid-April, then slowly declined by end of May; highest intensity was between mid-April and beginning of May.
- Passerine-type wing-beat proportion was ~48% early in April (almost 50%), declining to 18% by end of May.
- Swift-type wing-beat proportion increased from 6% (early April) to over 40% by late May, causing the clear separation between take-off and night phases to disappear (swifts sleep in the air).
- No significant direct correlation between night phase and take-off phase migration traffic was found (Spearman R=0.2389, p=0.0983), but when nights were divided into two groups (where take-off MT was higher vs. lower than night phase MT), correlations became highly significant (R=0.8951, p<0.001, N=12; and R=0.4520, p=0.0107, N=35). This suggests most birds rested only about one day ("short resting periods of only one day").

**Part B: Direction, Speed and Origin of Spring Migrants Arriving on Mallorca**

- Mean flight direction was 18° during take-off and 10° during arrivals from North Africa (roughly NNE).
- Average ground speed of migrating birds was 12 m·s⁻¹; passerine-type wing-beat birds had ground speeds more than 2 m·s⁻¹ higher than continuously flapping birds.
- Nocturnal migrants from Africa arrived "in a wave" at different times in the second half of the night because most did NOT fly non-stop over the Sahara and Mediterranean, but landed somewhere in North Africa first.
- Using direction and speed, potential previous take-off areas in North Africa were calculated; migrants were NOT predominantly concentrated along the coast but departed, at least some nights, from further inland in the Atlas Highlands, and some possibly even south of the Atlas mountains.
- It appears migrants landed as soon as they detected potential resting areas around dawn after crossing the Sahara; those still over the Sahara continued to the Atlas highlands, increasing numbers there but not near the coast.
- Mallorca seemed to have no important concentration effect attracting migrants from different directions.

**Overall conclusion:** The two-wave pattern (take-off phase, gap, night phase) demonstrated that most spring migrants do NOT fly non-stop over the Sahara and Mediterranean; instead, they land and rest in North Africa before the sea crossing, adhering to a night-flying/day-resting strategy even across large ecological barriers. Migration over Mallorca is confined to the night. Possible reasons for landing instead of non-stop flight include avoiding depletion of energy reserves and stronger selection for night-flying than for time-minimizing.

The study was part of a larger Swiss National Science Foundation-supported project by the Swiss Ornithological Institute investigating whether bird migration across the Mediterranean occurs on a broad front and whether islands like the Balearics influence migration. Two tracking radars were used: one on Mallorca and one near Malaga on the Spanish mainland, with moon and infrared observations along French and Spanish coasts.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"On average at least one third of the migrants landed soon after crossing the coast every night." "The take-off phase began on average 13 ± 25 min before sunset... reached the maximum only 64 minutes later and came to an end 200 ± 62 min after sunset." "The main mass of birds did not reach the island until 256 minutes later than the fastest birds (M = 485 ± 94 min, SE = ± 13 min)." "Among all tracked birds the proportion of birds with a passerine-type wing-beat pattern was almost 50% at the beginning of April and decreased to 18% by the end of May. The proportion of birds with a swift-type wing-beat pattern increased from 6% to more than 40% over the same period." "The pattern with two waves and a gap in between showed that the birds had landed in North Africa before crossing the Mediterranean Sea... it can of course not be excluded that some birds flew over the Mediterranean non-stop, but they were quantitatively not relevant."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 6: Geomagnetic disturbance associated with increased vagrancy in migratory landbirds | Scientific Reports ---
URL: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-022-26586-0

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific article (published in Scientific Reports, 2023) investigates the association between geomagnetic disturbance and avian vagrancy in migratory landbirds. The researchers hypothesized that errors in orientation or navigation caused by disruption to the Earth's magnetic field could lead birds astray, as migratory birds use magnetoreception—sensing the Earth's magnetic field via specialized magnetoreceptor structures—to traverse long distances.

METHODOLOGY: The study analyzed 2,226,936 banding records of 152 migratory landbird species in North America (150 species in fall, 124 in spring) from 1960 to 2019, combining USGS Bird Banding Lab data with eBird Status and Trends weekly species abundance maps. Instead of using binary vagrancy classification, they created a continuous "vagrancy index" measuring the spatiotemporal rarity of each banding record relative to modeled expected species ranges. Using hierarchical Bayesian random-effects models, they tested associations with geomagnetic disturbance (global Ap index) and solar activity (American relative sunspot number).

KEY RESULTS:
- Strong positive association between geomagnetic disturbance and vagrancy during fall migration (posterior median = 0.109; 95% CrI = 0.077–0.142; p(>0) = 1). Typically, a two-standard-deviation increase in geomagnetic disturbance is associated with a 24% increase in median predicted vagrancy index and a 250% increase in the number of spatiotemporally rare banding records (from 2% to 5% of records).
- 83% of species showed positive sensitivity to geomagnetic disturbance in fall.
- Sensitivity to geomagnetic disturbance was stronger among longer-distance migrants (supporting the hypothesis that long-distance migrants rely more on magnetoreception), but no effect of breeding latitude was found.
- Hatch-year (juvenile) birds showed higher baseline fall vagrancy than adults, but were NOT more sensitive to geomagnetic disturbance.
- Only weak or no evidence for associations during spring migration, potentially due to sampling biases (banding sites preferentially capture birds near breeding sites late in migration).
- Contrary to hypotheses, increased solar activity was negatively associated with fall vagrancy (potential mitigation effect). An interaction model showed strong evidence for a negative interaction during fall—during high solar activity, birds are less sensitive to geomagnetic disturbance, suggesting radiofrequency noise disables magnetoreception, causing birds to pause migration or switch to other cues.
- Diurnal migrants (24% of fall species) were more sensitive to solar activity than nocturnal migrants, possibly because solar radiofrequency noise affects the sunlit side of Earth; this may explain previously observed negative effects of solar activity on crane migration.

IMPLICATIONS: Geomagnetic disturbance and solar activity explained a median of 5.9% of variance in vagrancy (species-specific range 0.3–30%), meaning other factors (weather, population fluctuations, etc.) explain 70% to >99% depending on species. The authors note geomagnetic disturbance may have downstream ecological consequences, as vagrants may experience increased mortality or facilitate range expansions of avian populations and the organisms they disperse. The findings provide macroecological evidence supporting the widespread importance of magnetoreception in migratory landbirds.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
Using data from 2 million captures of 152 landbird species in North America over 60 years, we demonstrate a strong association between disruption to the Earth's magnetic field and avian vagrancy during fall migration., We found, with high confidence, that vagrancy across North American landbirds is associated with increased geomagnetic disturbance in the fall migration season (posterior median ωfall,geom. dist. = 0.109; 95% credible interval (CrI) = 0.077 to 0.142; proportion of posterior p(> 0) = 1)., For the typical species... an increase in geomagnetic disturbance of two standard deviations above average conditions is associated with a 24% increase in the median predicted vagrancy index of all records and a 250% increase in the number of spatiotemporally rare banding records (from 2% of all records at average geomagnetic disturbance to 5% under elevated conditions)., Results from this interaction model provide strong evidence for a negative interaction during fall migration, suggesting that during periods of high solar activity, birds are less sensitive to the effect of geomagnetic disturbance (posterior median μωfall = − 0.025; 95% CrI = − 0.047 to − 0.003; p(< 0) = 0.99).
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 7: Space Weather Disrupts Nocturnal Bird Migration, Study Finds - Climate and Space Sciences and Engineering ---
URL: https://clasp.engin.umich.edu/2023/10/10/space-weather-disrupts-nocturnal-bird-migration-study-finds

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article reports on a University of Michigan study, published online October 9, 2023, in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), that found correlational evidence linking geomagnetic disturbances (space weather) to disruptions in nocturnal bird migration. Researchers used massive long-term datasets from 37 NEXRAD Doppler weather radar stations in the U.S. Great Plains central flyway (spanning over 1,000 miles from Texas to North Dakota) and ground-based magnetometer data from the superMAG network to test this connection.

Key findings include a 9%-17% reduction in the number of migrating birds during severe space weather events in both spring and fall, with birds that did migrate experiencing more difficulty navigating, especially under overcast conditions in autumn. The final datasets included 1.7 million radar scans from fall and 1.4 million from spring, spanning 23 years. The bird community studied was primarily composed of perching birds (Passeriformes, 73%), shorebirds (Charadriiformes, 12%), and waterfowl (Anseriformes, 9%).

The researchers used two complementary statistical models that controlled for weather, temporal, and geographic variables. SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific article from the Encyclopedia of the Environment (by Jacques Blondel, published January 17, 2025) explains how migratory birds orient themselves during migrations that can span nearly 10,000 km. The core premise is that bird orientation relies on a combination of genetically determined mechanisms, including an "internal calendar" and an "internal compass."

**Basic principles:** Navigation involves setting and maintaining a heading regardless of hazards. Very young birds migrate alone in their first year, proving orientation mechanisms are innate/genetically determined. Remarkable fidelity is documented — e.g., a barn swallow (Hirundo rustica) traveled between South Africa and a stable in Germany for three years with accuracy of a few metres. Most small migratory passerines fly at night, covering 300–600 km per night at 40–50 km/h, relying on a magnetic compass as their basic tool effective in all weather.

**Orientation mechanisms** (discovered through experiments beginning in the 1950s):
- **Solar compass:** Gustav Kramer's orientation cage experiments (Figure 3-5) showed sun position is used as a directional cue. Shifting a bird's internal clock by 6 hours caused a 90° error in flight direction; a 12-hour shift caused 180° reversal (heading north in autumn). Used by diurnal migrants (white storks, large birds of prey), but useless for nocturnal migrants.
- **Night-time compasses (moon and stars):** Franz Sauer (1950s) discovered birds orient using the moon and stars. The "Zugunruhe" (migratory restlessness) behavior at dusk marks migration onset. Franz Sauer and later Stephen T. Emlen (planetarium experiments, Figure 8) demonstrated that birds align with constellations, adjust for their movement during the night, and can be made to "somersault" when the sky was rotated 180°. Birds recalibrate their stellar compass using their magnetic compass, and must "read" new star configurations when crossing the equator.
- **Earth's magnetic field:** Radar studies in the 1950s showed nocturnal migrants oriented correctly even under overcast skies. Kramer proposed a two-stage navigation model (a "mental map" plus a "compass"). Experiments on robins and garden warblers with modified magnetic fields (using coils/magnets to shift magnetic north) provided irrefutable evidence for geomagnetic orientation. Geomagnetism is the only reliable source when all visual references fail.
- **Mental maps:** Birds use geo-topographical landmarks (mountain ranges, river corridors, valleys, passes, coastal strips) as a mosaic of waypoints. Radar observations show wind-driven birds can reorient back to their course after turbulence; birds also exploit favorable winds for massive migratory flows.
- **Positioning in time and space:** Two genetically integrated programmes exist: a temporal programme (correct orientation for a given journey duration) and a spatial programme (appropriate direction that can change along the way). The willow warbler (Phylloscopus trochilus) follows a NE-SW course of ~9,000 km, then abruptly changes to north-south at the Iberian Peninsula. Captive garden warblers demonstrated this "pre-programmed" directional change.

**Human use:** Carrier pigeons have been used since Ancient Egypt, sparked 19th-century competitions (notably in the US), and served as messengers in both World Wars, commemorated by a "soldier pigeon" monument in Brussels.

**Key messages:** The navigation model consists of genetically determined mechanisms in rigid sequential order, based on a mental map, astronomical compasses (sun/moon/stars), and a magnetic compass used additionally or exclusively when others fail. Orientation systems work in synergy, birds interpret wind information, and all steps follow a circannual genetically determined internal clock ("tells" birds when to reproduce, moult, migrate).
</summary>

--- SOURCE 13: Magnetic orientation in migratory birds ---
URL: http://oops.uni-oldenburg.de/83/1/liemag06.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This document is the Ph.D. thesis of Miriam Liedvogel (defended September 13, 2006 at Carl von Ossietzky Universität Oldenburg, supervised by PD Dr. Henrik Mouritsen and Prof. Dr. Karl-Wilhelm Koch), titled "Magnetic orientation in migratory birds – linking behavioural phenomena with underlying molecular and neuronal mechanisms."

The thesis investigates how night-migratory birds perceive directional information from the Earth's magnetic field and how this information is processed in the brain. Using an integrative approach combining behavioral observation, molecular biology, biochemistry, biophysics, and neuroanatomy, Liedvogel's research covered the full process from the primary receptor molecule to higher brain integration centers.

KEY FINDINGS:

1. **Head-scanning behavior (Paper I):** Using a custom-built experimental setup allowing real-time monitoring under controllable magnetic field conditions, garden warblers (Sylvia borin) showed clear south-westerly orientation under natural magnetic fields but oriented randomly in zero-magnetic fields. Birds nearly tripled their head-scanning frequency in a fully compensated zero magnetic field, and showed significant increases in head-scanning just before initiating migratory restlessness. This indicated the magnetic compass sensor is in the head, and that scanning likely facilitates detection of the magnetically modulated visual pattern on the retina.

2. **Cryptochrome identification (Paper II):** Four cryptochrome family members were identified, cloned, and sequenced in the retina of migratory garden warblers: Cry1a, Cry1b, Cry2, and Cry4. Cry1a is predominantly expressed in the cytosol of ganglion cells, displaced ganglion cells, and photoreceptors. Striking differences were found between migratory and non-migratory birds: Cry1a expression was highest at night in night-migratory birds but decreased to background levels at night in non-migratory control species. Neuronal activity markers colocalized perfectly with Cry1a during night-time magnetic orientation - the first experimental demonstration of a putative light-mediated primary magnetoreceptor molecule in a bird's eye.

3. **Biophysical characterization (Paper III):** Garden warbler cryptochromes were recombinantly expressed as holoproteins (with built-in flavin cofactor) in a baculovirus/Sf9 cell system - the first successful expression of an animal cryptochrome holoprotein in a heterologous eukaryotic system. This required a novel on-column denaturation/refolding step to overcome known difficulties. Garden warbler cryptochromes are light-excited, absorb in the blue spectral range (matching wavelengths known to elicit magnetic orientation in behavioral experiments), and form radical pairs lasting approximately 10 milliseconds - sufficiently long-lived to detect Earth-strength magnetic fields.

4. **Cluster N identification (Paper IV):** Behavioral molecular mapping identified a distinct forebrain area in night-migratory birds, termed "Cluster N" ("N" for night), showing high neuronal activation at night during magnetic orientation but not during the day. Cluster N was inactive in non-migratory zebra finches (Taeniopygia guttata) and canaries (Serinus canaria). Located adjacent to or as part of the visual Wulst, covering birds' eyes with light-tight covers significantly reduced Cluster N activation to near baseline, demonstrating it is active specifically during night-vision in night-migratory birds.

5. **Lateralization and further tests (Paper V, VI):** European robins (Erithacus rubecula) showed significant dominance of Cluster N activation in the right hemisphere. Garden warblers tested under different magnetic field conditions and monochromatic red light showed no significant differences in Cluster N activation, so a definitive role in magnetic compass processing could not be confirmed. Additional analysis found positive correlations between movement and activity levels in 10 cerebral regions and parts of the cerebellum, supporting the hypothesis that vocal learning brain systems evolved from a pre-existing motor pathway.

METHODS: Experiments relied on careful behavioral observation (especially the final 60 minutes before tissue collection), followed by brain dissection, cryostat sectioning, radioactive in situ hybridization for neuronal activity mapping (using immediate early genes like c-Fos and ZENK), and immunohistochemistry for retinal tissue. Primary study species were garden warblers and European robins; control species were zebra finches, canaries, and Sardinian warblers (Sylvia melanocephala).

CONCLUSION: All findings support a light-mediated magnetoperception mechanism in night-migratory birds, consistent with the hypothesis that magnetically modulated intensity patterns are perceived by the visual system - i.e., night-migratory birds may literally "see" the direction of the Earth's magnetic field. The thesis comprises six manuscripts (three published, one submitted, one under review, one near submission) plus supplementary materials on cryptochrome cloning methodology.

The authors defend their earlier literature review (Muheim et al. 2006a) which concluded that migratory birds recalibrate their magnetic compass relative to celestial cues when they have a view of the sky down to the horizon at sunrise or sunset. --- SOURCE 23: Avian Navigation and Orientation ---
URL: https://avesbiology.com/nav_orient.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage provides a comprehensive scientific overview of avian navigation and orientation mechanisms. It distinguishes between orientation (moving in a compass direction) and true navigation (locating one's position relative to a destination), based on the two-step process first described by Kramer (1953, 1957): determining the correct direction of travel and identifying that direction. Naïve juvenile birds often rely on vector navigation (maintaining a direction for a set time/distance), while experienced adults demonstrate true navigation, as shown in displacement experiments with European Starlings (Perdeck 1958), Common Teal (Wolff 1970), and White-crowned Sparrows (Thorup et al. 2007). Some species' juveniles can compensate for displacement, however. The "clock-and-compass" concept explains how first-time migrants navigate, potentially using magnetic and photoperiodic beacons (Chernetsov and Utvenko 2025). True navigation is likely based on a bi-coordinate grid system using cues that vary along gradients (Thorup and Holland 2009).

The webpage details four compass mechanisms:
1. **Non-compass orientation**: Birds use landmarks and topographic features like coastlines and mountain ridges (e.g., European migrants turning southwest along the Alps).
2. **Star compass**: Emlen's classic planetarium experiments (1967) showed Indigo Buntings learn north by observing stellar rotation around the celestial pole, using Emlen funnels to record orientation. Star-compass use is learned, not innate, and relies on relative constellations rather than specific stars.
3. **Sun compass**: First demonstrated by Kramer (1950); based on the sun's azimuth using an internal clock. Clock-shifting experiments (Schmidt-Koenig 1958) caused 90-degree orientation errors. Learning is tied to the left hippocampus (Gagliardo et al. 2005), with pigeons first able to use it around 12 weeks old.
4. **Polarized light**: Several migratory species (Savannah Sparrows, Swainson's and Gray-cheeked thrushes, White-throated Sparrows) use polarization patterns at sunrise/sunset to calibrate their magnetic compass.
5. **Magnetic cues**: First proposed in 1859 and experimentally demonstrated in 1968 (European Robins). The avian magnetic compass is an inclination compass (distinguishing pole vs. equator, not north vs. south) and is light-dependent, based on cryptochrome molecules in the retina (Mouritsen et al. 2004). Cluster N in the forebrain processes magnetic visual information. Wu and Dickman (2012) identified vestibular brainstem neurons encoding magnetic field direction, intensity, and polarity. Nordmann et al. (2025) traced pigeon magnetoreception to hair cells in inner ear semicircular canals via electromagnetic induction, with signals processed in vestibular nuclei, midbrain cortex, and hippocampus. Iron-oxide magnetoreceptors in the upper beak (maghemite platelets and magnetite clusters) may act as a three-axis magnetometer for detecting field intensity and direction.

For true navigation, birds need "map" information. Mechanisms include visual landmark recognition (used by homing pigeons and food-caching species), path integration (dead reckoning), olfactory cues (studied in homing pigeons with conflicting results; possibly used by tube-nosed seabirds via dimethyl sulfide), and infrasound maps (found implausible due to diffuse sources). The most likely navigational system is bi-coordinate magnetic mapping, using magnetic inclination (for latitude) and intensity (for longitude). A notable example is displaced European Reed Warblers in northwestern Russia that corrected their spring migration direction after longitudinal displacement (Chernetsov et al. 2008), demonstrating use of a magnetic grid map.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"True navigation, as first described by Kramer (1953, 1957), is a two-step process: (1) determining the correct direction of travel, and (2) being able to correctly identify that direction."
</key_excerpts>

# Using artificial intelligence to track birds' dark-of-night migrations

by [University of Massachusetts Amherst](http://umass.edu/)

[Add as preferred source](https://google.com/preferences/source?q=https%3A%2F%2Fphys.org%2F)

![Using artificial intelligence to track birds' dark-of-night migrations](https://scx1.b-cdn.net/csz/news/800a/2019/5-usingartific.jpg "Map colors indicate estimates of migration traffic from measurements at 143 radar stations. Map colors indicate estimates of migration traffic from measurements at 143 radar stations. Locations are indicated by white circles, with size proportional to migration traffic at the station. The central corridor of the U.S. receives particularly intense migration. Estimated numbers of birds crossing different latitudes are shown to the right. Credit: Courtesy of the authors and Kyle G. Horton

On many evenings during spring and fall migration, tens of millions of birds take flight at sunset and pass over our heads, unseen in the night sky. Though these flights have been recorded for decades by the National Weather Services' network of constantly scanning weather radars, until recently these data have been mostly out of reach for bird researchers.

That's because the sheer magnitude of information and lack of tools to analyze it made only limited studies possible, says artificial intelligence (AI) researcher Dan Sheldon at the University of Massachusetts Amherst.

Ornithologists and ecologists with the time and expertise to analyze individual radar images could clearly see patterns that allowed them to discriminate precipitation from birds and study migration, he adds. But the massive amount of information—over 200 million images and hundreds of terabytes of data—significantly limited their ability to sample enough nights, over enough years and in enough locations to be useful in characterizing, let alone tracking, seasonal, continent-wide migrations, he explains.

Clearly, a [machine learning system](https://phys.org/tags/machine+learning+system/) was needed, Sheldon notes, "to remove the rain and keep the birds."

Now, with colleagues from the Cornell Lab of Ornithology and others, senior authors Sheldon and Subhransu Maji and lead author Tsung-Yu Lin at UMass's College of Information and Computer Sciences unveil their new tool "MistNet." In Sheldon's words, it's the "latest and greatest in machine learning" to extract bird data from the radar record and to take advantage of the treasure trove of bird migration information in the decades-long radar data archives. The tool's name refers to the fine, almost invisible, "mist nets" that ornithologists use to capture migratory songbirds.

MistNet can "automate the processing of a massive data set that has measured bird migration over the continental U.S. for over two decades," Sheldon says. "This is a really important advance. Our results are excellent compared with humans working by hand. It allows us to go from limited 20th-century insights to 21st-century knowledge and conservation action." He and co-authors point out, "Deep learning has revolutionized the ability of computers to mimic humans in solving similar recognition tasks for images, video and audio."

For this work, supported in part by a National Science Foundation grant to Sheldon to design and test new mathematical approaches and algorithms for such applications, the team conducted a large-scale validation of MistNet and competing approaches using two evaluation data sets. Their new paper also presents several case studies to illustrate MistNet's strengths and flexibility. Details appear in the current issue of *Methods in Ecology and Evolution*.

MistNet is based on neural networks for images and includes several architecture components tailored to the unique characteristics of radar data, the authors point out. Radar ornithology is advancing rapidly and leading to significant discoveries about continent-scale patterns of bird movements, they add.

The team made maps of where and when migration occurred over the past 24 years and animated these to illustrate, for example, "the most intensive migration areas in the continental United States," Sheldon explains—a corridor roughly along and just west of the Mississippi River. MistNet also allows researchers to estimate flying velocity and traffic rates of migrating birds.

Discover the latest in science, tech, and space with over **100,000 subscribers** who rely on Phys.org for daily insights. Sign up for our [free newsletter](https://sciencex.com/help/newsletter/) and get updates on breakthroughs, innovations, and research that matter—**daily or weekly**.

MistNet, designed to address one of the "long-standing challenges in radar aero-ecology," the authors note, comes just in time to help scientists better use not only existing weather [radar](https://phys.org/tags/radar/) data, but the "explosion" of large new data sets generated by citizen science projects such as eBird, animal tracking devices and earth observation instruments, say Sheldon and colleagues.

"We hope MistNet will enable a range of science and conservation applications. For example, we see in many places that a large amount of migration is concentrated on a few nights of the season," Sheldon says. "Knowing this, maybe we could aid [birds](https://phys.org/tags/birds/) by turning off skyscraper lights on those nights." Another question the ornithologists are interested in is the historical timing, or phenology, of bird [migration](https://phys.org/tags/migration/) and whether it, and timely access to food, have shifted with climate change.

# Record-breaking Night of Bird Migration Detected with Radar

September 26, 2025

_Ithaca, NY_—A record-breaking night of bird migration was detected last night by [BirdCast](http://birdcast.org/), a platform that uses the same weather radar technology behind daily forecasts to track migrating birds.

On its live migration map, BirdCast tracked more than 1.2 billion birds streaming south to their wintering grounds after sunset Thursday—the largest single-night total ever recorded since the collaborative research project began mapping live migrations in 2018. This surge surpasses the previous milestone of one billion birds, first observed in October 2023.

## More Cornell Lab News

*   ![Image 19](https://www.birds.cornell.edu/home/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/YellowBelliedSapsucker_StevenHunter.jpeg) [News Room](https://www.birds.cornell.edu/home/news/)  

“These numbers are almost inconceivable,” said Andrew Farnsworth, a visiting scientist at the Cornell Lab of Ornithology and longtime BirdCast researcher. “They’re enormous. They grab your attention, even for people that study migration regularly. The scale of how many organisms that this represents, it is just mind blowing.”

Farnsworth said this seemingly rare night captured about 10% of the continent’s birds in flight at the same time. On an average fall night during peak migration, only about 400 million birds are detected in flight at the same time above the United States, but on this night, the number was three times that. “It’s really unbelievable,” he said.

![Image 20: Map of the United States showing large numbers of migrating birds in bright yellow across the US.](https://www.birds.cornell.edu/home/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/IMG_4790.jpg)
While astonishing to both birders and scientists, Farnsworth said this event was not random. It resulted from a combination of ideal migrating conditions coinciding with the peak of fall migration.

Thursday night’s weather was perfect for travel, he explained, with calm winds—including tail winds that helped push the birds along their migratory paths across much of the center of the country and the Mississippi River valley.

BirdCast is a collaborative research project that uses weather radar and machine learning to track and forecast bird migration patterns, with research contributions from the Cornell Lab of Ornithology, Purdue University, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, and University of Massachusetts Amherst.

Farnsworth said this record-breaking migration—documented by radar technology that was never intended to track birds—is a chance to not only to marvel at the immense magnitude of bird migration but also a chance to remind the public that the data is freely available and accessible in real time. The technology at [BirdCast.org](http://birdcast.org/) allows anyone to view forecast maps that predict the number of birds migrating while live migration maps show migration happening in real time. Both tools let people know when birds are moving nearby, so they can take necessary precautions to protect them.

“BirdCast gives the ability for more people to engage in and participate in this incredible spectacle,” Farnsworth said, “and understand that it’s happening.”

It’s also a timely reminder that people across the continent can help make birds’ journeys safer. Every year, more than one billion birds die in collisions with windows in the United States.

Bright lights can disorient birds migrating at night, drawing them into areas where collisions with glass are common. To help, turn off nonessential lights at night and add bird friendly film or other markings spaced no more than two inches apart on the outside of windows. Learn more at [stopbirdcollisions.org.](https://www.stopbirdcollisions.org/)

The thesis investigates how night-migratory birds perceive directional information from the Earth's magnetic field and how this information is processed in the brain. Using an integrative approach combining behavioral observation, molecular biology, biochemistry, biophysics, and neuroanatomy, Liedvogel's research covered the full process from the primary receptor molecule to higher brain integration centers.

KEY FINDINGS:

1. **Head-scanning behavior (Paper I):** Using a custom-built experimental setup allowing real-time monitoring under controllable magnetic field conditions, garden warblers (Sylvia borin) showed clear south-westerly orientation under natural magnetic fields but oriented randomly in zero-magnetic fields. Birds nearly tripled their head-scanning frequency in a fully compensated zero magnetic field, and showed significant increases in head-scanning just before initiating migratory restlessness. This indicated the magnetic compass sensor is in the head, and that scanning likely facilitates detection of the magnetically modulated visual pattern on the retina.

2. **Cryptochrome identification (Paper II):** Four cryptochrome family members were identified, cloned, and sequenced in the retina of migratory garden warblers: Cry1a, Cry1b, Cry2, and Cry4. Cry1a is predominantly expressed in the cytosol of ganglion cells, displaced ganglion cells, and photoreceptors. Striking differences were found between migratory and non-migratory birds: Cry1a expression was highest at night in night-migratory birds but decreased to background levels at night in non-migratory control species. Neuronal activity markers colocalized perfectly with Cry1a during night-time magnetic orientation - the first experimental demonstration of a putative light-mediated primary magnetoreceptor molecule in a bird's eye.

3. **Biophysical characterization (Paper III):** Garden warbler cryptochromes were recombinantly expressed as holoproteins (with built-in flavin cofactor) in a baculovirus/Sf9 cell system - the first successful expression of an animal cryptochrome holoprotein in a heterologous eukaryotic system. This required a novel on-column denaturation/refolding step to overcome known difficulties. Garden warbler cryptochromes are light-excited, absorb in the blue spectral range (matching wavelengths known to elicit magnetic orientation in behavioral experiments), and form radical pairs lasting approximately 10 milliseconds - sufficiently long-lived to detect Earth-strength magnetic fields.

4. **Cluster N identification (Paper IV):** Behavioral molecular mapping identified a distinct forebrain area in night-migratory birds, termed "Cluster N" ("N" for night), showing high neuronal activation at night during magnetic orientation but not during the day. Cluster N was inactive in non-migratory zebra finches (Taeniopygia guttata) and canaries (Serinus canaria). Located adjacent to or as part of the visual Wulst, covering birds' eyes with light-tight covers significantly reduced Cluster N activation to near baseline, demonstrating it is active specifically during night-vision in night-migratory birds.

5. **Lateralization and further tests (Paper V, VI):** European robins (Erithacus rubecula) showed significant dominance of Cluster N activation in the right hemisphere. Garden warblers tested under different magnetic field conditions and monochromatic red light showed no significant differences in Cluster N activation, so a definitive role in magnetic compass processing could not be confirmed. This is a scientific article published in Nature (volume 364, pages 525-527, 1993) by Wolfgang Wiltschko, Ursula Munro, Hugh Ford, and Roswitha Wiltschko, titled "Red light disrupts magnetic orientation of migratory birds." The paper reports the first orientation tests on migratory birds under light of different wavelengths, providing evidence for a light-dependent magnetoreception process in birds.

The article addresses the ongoing scientific debate about the mechanisms of magnetoreception in birds, focusing on two main hypotheses: small particles of magnetite, and biochemical bi-radical reactions of excited macromolecules. The bi-radical hypothesis suggested magnetic resonance phenomena in the retina as primary processes, raising the question of whether magnetoreception was light-dependent.

Prior evidence included homing experiments and electrophysiological evidence from pigeons supporting such a mechanism, and a study showing that in newts, magnetic compass orientation was maintained under blue light (450 nm and below) but shifted roughly 90° counterclockwise under wavelengths at or above 500 nm. This study's results suggest a light-dependent process in migratory birds that appears to differ from that reported in newts.

The authors are affiliated with the Fachbereich Biologie der Universität Frankfurt a.M., Zoologie, Germany (Wiltschko and Wiltschko) and the Department of Zoology, University of New England, Armidale, New South Wales, Australia (Munro and Ford). The article has been cited 292 times and has 2732 accesses. Related literature cited includes work on magnetite biomineralization, the bi-radical mechanism, previous homing experiments, and studies on newt orientation under different light wavelengths.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 14: ‘Fixed direction’-responses of birds in the geomagnetic field - PMC ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2686356

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific article by Roswitha Wiltschko and Wolfgang Wiltschko (published in Communicative & Integrative Biology, 2009;2(2):100–103, DOI: 10.4161/cib.7622, PMC2686356) examining "fixed direction"-responses in migratory birds' geomagnetic orientation. It serves as an addendum to their earlier paper on light-dependent magnetoreception under dim red light.

**Background:** Migratory birds exhibit spontaneous migration orientation — heading south in autumn and north in spring — which serves as a stable baseline for orientation testing. The avian magnetic compass, studied since the 1970s in European Robins (Erithacus rubecula), functions as an "inclination compass" based on the axial course and inclination of magnetic field lines rather than field polarity.

**The 'Fixed Direction' Response:** A distinct type of directional response has been observed in European Robins and Australian Silvereyes (Zosterops l. lateralis) under specific light conditions. Under dim 645nm red light, birds exhibit a persistent westerly tendency that does not vary with season—a "fixed direction" response that is a polar (not axial) response, contrasting sharply with the normal compass behavior. Other fixed direction responses were observed under bright monochromatic 565nm green light, 502nm turquoise light, bichromatic light combinations, and even in total darkness.

**Key differences (Table 1):**
- Compass orientation: axial/inclination compass, requires short-wavelength light, disrupted by oscillating fields, not affected by upper beak anesthesia, based on radical pair mechanism, receptors in right eye, transmitted via optic nerve, can indicate any direction
- Fixed direction responses: polar, occur even in total darkness, NOT affected by oscillating fields, disrupted by upper beak anesthesia, magnetite-based mechanism, receptors in skin of upper beak, transmitted via branch of trigeminal nerve, only one specific fixed direction depending on light regime

**Physical mechanisms:** The avian magnetic compass operates via radical pair processes (confirmed by disorientation from MHz range oscillating fields, consistent with the Ritz model where photon absorption forms radical pairs whose singlet-triplet ratio depends on magnetic field alignment). Compass orientation requires light from short wavelengths up to 565nm green. In contrast, fixed direction responses originate from superparamagnetic magnetite-based receptors in the upper beak skin, are unaffected by oscillating fields, and are disrupted by upper beak anesthesia.

**Interactions with visual system:** The light-dependence of fixed direction responses suggests complex interactions between beak-derived directional information and the visual system at higher processing levels. Monochromatic or bichromatic test lights activate only one or two color cones simultaneously—an unnatural condition, as natural light is always polychromatic. Higher light intensities (beyond ~8 quanta/s m² for compass orientation) trigger fixed direction responses, possibly due to cone activation imbalance disrupting the compass magnetoreception system. Notably, fixed direction responses are only observed under laboratory conditions not occurring in nature.

**Fixed direction vs disorientation:** Under oscillating fields, long-wavelength light, or right-eye occlusion (which disrupt radical pair processes) birds become disoriented rather than showing fixed directions, even though beak magnetite receptors remain functional — suggesting interference at the peripheral physical process level differs fundamentally from disruption at the transmitting/processing level involving visual input.

**Significance:** The compass allows birds to orient toward any chosen direction (migratory, home, or acquired), while fixed direction responses appear forced by the stimulus. The magnetite-based beak receptors normally provide magnetic intensity information as part of the navigational "map." Their role in fixed direction responses is surprising and unclear. The authors suggest it may represent a phylogenetic relict—an ancient function of magnetite-based receptors (found in all vertebrate groups) superseded in modern birds by the radical-pair-based avian compass.
</summary>

Magnetite is found in all vertebrate groups, and e.g., in mammals, it is discussed as basis for a magnetic compass."

<summary>
This webpage contains three scientific research papers published in Nature (Vol 429, 13 May 2004), all as "letters to nature."

**1. Community disassembly and extinction paper (Ives et al.):**
The authors modeled how communities respond to environmental stressors, showing that the species with the lowest tolerance di(N) goes extinct first. They developed a method to calculate community equilibrium under stress using equations ri + ais + Σj bi,j x*j(s) = 0. They used various community topologies including plant-herbivore-predator food webs, competitive communities, arbitrary topologies (45% competitors, 45% prey/predators, 10% mutualists), and random food webs. Intraspecific interactions were constrained to negative values to avoid unrealistic positive abundances under stress. The assumption that lowest-tolerance species go extinct first was validated by full model simulations, categorizing species as extinct when reduced by a factor of 10^-3 in abundance. Funding from the US National Science Foundation; correspondence directed to A.R.I. (arives@wisc.edu).

**2. Avian magnetic compass via radical-pair mechanism (Ritz et al.):**
This study tested competing hypotheses for the avian magnetic compass: magnetite-based versus radical-pair chemical reaction mechanisms. European robins (Erithacus rubecula) were tested under 565 nm light in the local geomagnetic field (46 μT, 66° inclination). Birds were disoriented when exposed to broadband (0.1–10 MHz, 0.085 μT) or single-frequency (7 MHz, 0.47 μT) oscillating fields. In a 7 MHz field, disorientation depended on the angle between the oscillating and geomagnetic fields: birds oriented normally when fields were parallel, but were disoriented at 24° and 48° angles. The effect is consistent with resonance effects on singlet–triplet transitions, supporting a radical-pair mechanism. A 7 MHz field would require 285 μT to affect magnetite receptors, far stronger than the 0.47 μT used. Model calculations showed that a resonant oscillating field of 0.033 μT (a thousandth of Earth's field strength) could produce a detectable effect. The study establishes oscillating magnetic fields as a diagnostic tool for identifying radical-pair magnetoreception, applicable to other animal groups. Magnetite is suggested as a separate magnetic-intensity ('map') sensor, not compass orientation. Experiments conducted January 13–February 17, 2003, in Frankfurt am Main, Germany; correspondence to T.R. (tritz@uci.edu).

**3. Modeling disease outbreaks in urban social networks (Eubank et al.):**
The paper presents EpiSims, a large-scale agent-based simulation tool built on TRANSIMS (a Los Alamos National Laboratory transportation simulation), using census, land-use, and population-mobility data to model disease spread in urban areas. The dynamic bipartite contact graph shows the person contact network is strongly connected small-world-like with a well-defined degree distribution scale, while the locations graph is scale-free, enabling efficient outbreak detection by placing sensors in location hubs. Analysis of smallpox mitigation strategies suggests outbreaks can be contained by targeted vaccination combined with early detection, without mass vaccination. By 2030, more than 60% of the world's population is estimated to live in cities, making such high-resolution epidemic modeling important for policy decisions.

--- SOURCE 1: Migration Monitoring with Automated Technology ---
URL: https://research.fs.usda.gov/download/treesearch/32078.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper, presented at the Third International Partners in Flight Conference (March 20-24, 2002, Asilomar, California), examines how automated technology can supplement ground-based methods of migration monitoring. The author, Rhonda L. Millikin, argues that automated technology can provide: (1) unbiased and automated sampling; (2) independent validation of current methods; (3) a larger sample area for landscape-level analysis of stopover habitat selection; and (4) an opportunity to study flight behavior. Specifically, radar-acoustic sensor fusion can provide species-specific landing behavior data to indicate what portion of the population passing over a site is available for ground-based monitoring via mist-net capture or census.

The paper reviews five key technologies: long-range radar (e.g., WSR-88D weather radar with 230 km range), short-range radar (X-band surveillance radar with 0-5 km range and individual bird resolution), acoustic-sensing (e.g., BirdCast® for traffic rates), acoustic-location (for landing/nesting sites and flight paths), and infrared. Each has limitations (e.g., no species info for radar, non-vocal individuals missed by acoustics, weather limitations for infrared/acoustic).

Key findings from the author's research at Prince Edward Point, Ontario (August-September 1999) include: most migration occurred below 300m; a larger proportion of birds flew below 300m at dawn but many also flew below 200m at midnight; 13% of midnight migrants flew in a reversed northerly direction (indicating landing behavior); and birds dispersing straight up at dusk reached heights up to 660m. Using radar-acoustic fusion, the author demonstrated that Swainson's Thrushes experienced Lake Ontario as a barrier and reversed direction to land at Prince Edward Point.

Methods and applications: Short-range radar was adapted (patented) to provide height information using a tilted antenna and neutral regression. Acoustic-location was co-located with radar tracks—of 129 tracks, 28 were co-located with acoustic calls. Data showed passerines migrate in loosely spaced, multi-species flocks, with same-species birds flying together showing greater similarity in flight speed.

Recommended approach for migration monitoring networks: (1) use long-range radar to determine funneling routes; (2) use short-range radar fused with acoustic-location to identify preferred landing sites of priority species; (3) situate mist-nets and census routes within the range of the radar-acoustic system. Costs of adding automated radar-acoustic data would be 1-3 times the cost of a volunteer-based mist-netting program (sensor fusion estimated at $85K CDN vs $27K for traditional mist-netting; relative cost of 3 vs 1).

Capture rate analysis showed very low mist-net capture rates for Partners in Flight-Canada priority species (e.g., Bicknell's Thrush at 0.042/100 net-hours across 4 stations), suggesting automation could significantly augment population samples. Key literature contributions include Zehnder et al. (2001) finding weather explained two-thirds of variation in migration intensity, and Nisbet et al. (1995) showing 19 of 25 papers supporting transoceanic Blackpoll Warbler flights came from radar studies.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Automated technology can supplement ground-based methods of migration monitoring by providing: (1) unbiased and automated sampling; (2) independent validation of current methods; (3) a larger sample area for landscape-level analysis of habitat selection for stopover, and (4) an opportunity to study flight behavior."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Bird migration flight altitudes studied by a network of operational weather radars ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3024816

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific article published in the Journal of the Royal Society Interface (2010 Jun 2;8(54):30, doi: 10.1098/rsif.2010.0116) titled "Bird migration flight altitudes studied by a network of operational weather radars." Authors: Adriaan M. Dokter (Royal Netherlands Meteorological Institute, De Bilt), Felix Liechti, Herbert Stark (Swiss Ornithological Institute, Sempach), Laurent Delobbe (Royal Meteorological Institute of Belgium, Brussels), Pierre Tabary (Météo France, Toulouse), and Iwan Holleman (Royal Netherlands Meteorological Institute). PMC3024816, PMID 20519212.

**Purpose/Methodology:** The researchers developed a fully automated method using operational C-band Doppler weather radar to detect and quantify bird migration, measuring bird density, speed, and direction as a function of altitude. The algorithm uses the volume velocity profiling (VVP) technique and relies on high radial velocity standard deviation (σr > 2 m/s) to distinguish birds from wind-borne scatterers like insects and hydrometeors. Non-bird echoes (precipitation, insects) are filtered out using reflectivity thresholds (>20 dBZ masked), cell-finding algorithms with radial velocity variance criteria (σcell < 5 m/s or Zcell > 15 dBZ removed), and for one polarimetric radar (Trappes, France), correlation coefficient ρHV > 0.9 (hydrometeors) and differential reflectivity ZDR > 3.0 dB (insects) criteria. The algorithm produces vertical profiles of bird density, speed, and direction every 5-15 minutes at 200 m altitude resolution using data from the 5-25 km range.

**Validation:** Weather radar observations were validated against a high-accuracy dedicated X-band 'Superfledermaus' bird radar stationed in the measurement volume of weather radars in The Netherlands (19 Aug–16 Sep 2007), Belgium (18 Sep–22 Oct 2007), and France (10 Mar–9 May 2008), totaling 118 days of data covering a full migration season (autumn 2007 and spring 2008).

**Key Results:** 
- The weather radar system achieved a high probability of detection (POD = 97%) for bird presence; for high bird density events (reflectivity > -5 dBZ), POD = 100% with only 3% false alarm ratio (FAR), while overall FAR was 42% (mostly at very low densities).
- A strong linear correlation (R² = 0.73) was found between weather radar reflectivity and bird radar density.
- An effective median bird radar cross section at C-band of σbird = 11 ± 6 cm² was determined.
- Seasonal trends in cross section reflect changing passerine species composition: increasing from 7 to 15 cm² in autumn (as larger Turdus thrushes arrive in October) and decreasing from 16 to 10 cm² in spring.
- Weather radar closely reproduced the altitude profiles measured by dedicated bird radar, including height-integrated densities.
- The algorithm could observe mesoscale variability in how weather conditions structure migration timing and altitude profiles within single nights, including multi-layer bird density profiles explained by distinct wind conditions at different take-off sites.

**Applications/Conclusions:** Consistently lower bird densities were recorded in The Netherlands compared with sites in France and eastern Belgium, revealing the spatial extent of the dominant Scandinavian flyway over continental Europe. The authors conclude that Doppler weather radar can serve as a reliable operational sensor for quantifying bird densities aloft, and extending this approach to multiple radars enables mapping and continuous monitoring of bird migration flyways. Applications include improving aviation safety (particularly military low-level flying and bird strike warnings), and warning systems to reduce bird collisions with wind farms and offshore platforms. The paper notes that existing operational weather radar networks (like Europe's OPERA network) could be repurposed as bird migration sensor networks with unprecedented coverage.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"We show that weather radar can extract near real-time bird density altitude profiles that closely correspond to the density profiles measured by dedicated bird radar."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Weather Radar Predicts Nighttime Bird Migrations | American Association for the Advancement of Science (AAAS) ---
URL: https://www.aaas.org/news/weather-radar-predicts-nighttime-bird-migrations

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from AAAS (published around September 2018, reporting on findings in the September 14 issue of Science) describes a new forecasting model that uses weather radar data combined with machine learning to predict nighttime bird migrations across North America up to a week in advance. The study, led by Benjamin Van Doren of the University of Oxford with co-author Kyle Horton of Cornell University, used the meteorological Next-Generation Radar (NEXRAD) network combined with climate models to accurately predict the timing, intensity, and location of nocturnal migration events, as well as estimate nightly bird numbers. In early May, when temperatures warm, more than 500 million migratory songbirds take flight each night in North America.

The researchers combed through 23 years of spring migration radar data, using machine learning to automate the identification of bird signatures amid chaotic background signals like precipitation and insect swarms. The model's predictions could reduce bird deaths from human activities—over 630 million birds die annually in the U.S. from collisions with buildings, towers, and vehicles, and bird strikes cause at least $1.2 billion in annual aircraft damage worldwide (including the 2009 "miracle on the Hudson" incident). Predictions could also help wind turbine operators shut down turbines or turn off lights during large flights, and help track the spread of avian-borne diseases.

Most North American songbirds (warblers, sparrows, thrushes) migrate at night to take advantage of cooler, more stable atmospheres, allowing daylight hours for foraging at stopover sites. Migratory bird populations in North America are in decline, mostly due to habitat loss. The study demonstrates the value of "big data" ecology research in understanding the complex drivers of avian migration, which involve navigation, timing, wind, food availability, and environmental conditions like temperature, atmospheric pressure, and precipitation.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Birds must navigate accurately using multiple cues, time their journeys precisely, deal with winds that may blow them off course, find food in transient and unfamiliar environments, and often re-engineer their bodies to store energy and save weight," said Van Doren.
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: Radar Ornithology – BirdCast ---
URL: https://birdcast.org/science-center/radar-technology

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from BirdCast provides an overview of radar ornithology—the use of weather radar to study bird migration. 

**Historical Development:** The page traces the field's history chronologically: (1) Heinrich Hertz discovered solid objects reflect radio waves in the 1880s; (2) Christian Hülsmeyer refined radar applications in the early 1900s; (3) radar rapidly developed in the 1930s for detecting enemy aircraft; (4) During WWII, unexplained radar targets dubbed "angels" were identified as birds by ornithologist David Lack and entomologist George Varley, who found Northern Gannets (Morus bassanus) were responsible—their seminal publication in 1945 (Lack and Varley) marked the beginning of radar ornithology; (5) The first U.S. weather surveillance radar (WSR-1) operated in the late 1940s at Washington, D.C., followed by WSR-57 radars along the Gulf of Mexico (starting in Miami in 1959); (6) Dr. Sidney A. Gauthreaux used WSR-57 data for foundational work on trans-Gulf migration in Louisiana; (7) The 1980s NEXRAD/WSR-88D brought digital and Doppler technology that allowed radar ornithology to truly take flight; (8) Dual polarization upgrades in 2012–2014 further enhanced bird tracking and target discrimination. Today, an operational network of over 140 weather surveillance radars covers the atmosphere above the contiguous U.S. (plus Alaska, Hawaii, and Korea).

**Applications & Classification:** Radar can detect anything scattering microwave energy—meteorological phenomena, aircraft, Saharan dust, insects, and fire smoke. BirdCast uses archived weather surveillance data and machine learning to distinguish migrating birds from other atmospheric objects, converting radar data into information about bird numbers, flight directions, speeds, and altitudes.

Key classification distinctions include:
- **Non-biological targets:** Meteorological objects (rain, snow, sleet) are primary NEXRAD targets; quality control filters remove false echoes from ground clutter.
- **Biological targets:** Harder to remove automatically; birds, bats, and insects are BirdCast's focus.
- **Birds vs. bats:** Distinguished by size, shape, and intensity of radar returns. Species-specific behavior helps—e.g., Purple Martins form massive nocturnal roosts producing a unique "ring" similar to bats leaving caves. Seasonality helps: birds initiate migration ~30–45 minutes after local sunset in spring and fall, while many bats forage in summer months.
- **Birds vs. insects:** Insects are generally more reliant on wind and drift with it, while birds can fly across or against winds—radar targets moving differently than winds are more readily attributed to birds.

**Scientific Team:** BirdCast is made possible by participating scientists from several institutions and many contributors.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"With the seminal publication of these findings in Lack and Varley (1945), so began the era of radar ornithology.", "The advent of digital technology and Doppler capabilities was game changing for meteorology and ornithology.", "For meteorologists, dual-pol data provide an ability to distinguish partially frozen sleet from droplets of rain; for ornithologists, they allow us to more easily separate birds from precipitation and other flying creatures.", "Birds initiate migration activity around 30–45 minutes after local sunset during spring and fall, whereas many bats set out on their foraging flights during the summer months.", "Using meteorologists' 'discarded' data, we meticulously attempt to characterize the biology of the atmosphere and to distinguish birds from insects and bats."
</key_excerpts>

KEY RESULTS:
- 37 out of 277 fledglings (13.4%) were grounded by artificial lights and recovered during rescue campaigns
- Birds with higher down abundance had higher probability of being grounded
- Probability of grounding was positively related to flight tortuosity and overflown light pollution levels
- Birds with slower flights were more likely to be grounded
- Tortuosity increased with light pollution levels but decreased with moon luminance
- All birds oriented flights towards low-altitude coastal areas, following the most light-polluted regions
- Significance: flights covered 18.7 ± 10.8 km and lasted 47.3 ± 45.3 min on average
- Control birds (8.2% grounding rate) were grounded less often than GPS-tagged (19.5%) and tape-labelled (13%) birds, suggesting control birds were overlooked during rescue due to small metal rings being less visible than artificial marks

The GPS devices with remote download represented a substantial improvement over previous studies requiring recapture. Intrinsic factors (down abundance indicating younger/less developed birds) and extrinsic factors (light pollution, moon luminance, flight speed) influence grounding probability. The most dangerous light-polluted areas in southern Tenerife were identified, where more than 50% of island-wide rescued birds are grounded. URL: https://archimer.ifremer.fr/doc/00851/96289/104542.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This research note by Airam Rodríguez and colleagues (published in Conservation Science and Practice, October 2023) addresses why fewer seabird fledglings are grounded (rescued) by artificial light during full moon nights. The authors conclude that during full moon nights, a higher proportion of fledglings safely reach the sea than during moonless nights, reducing light pollution-induced mortality. URL: https://ace-eco.org/vol20/iss1/art18

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed research paper published in Avian Conservation and Ecology (2025, Vol. 20, Issue 1, Article 18) titled "Lost in the glow: understanding the impact of light pollution on storm-petrels" by Medina-Franco, Sangiorgi, and Valdés-Velásquez (DOI: 10.5751/ACE-02846-200118).

The research question was: "What is the current state of evidence on the effects of light pollution on bird populations of the Hydrobatidae family?"

**Methodology:** 
- Literature searched on Scopus and Web of Science (February 16, 2023), covering articles published 2000-2022
- Searches conducted in English (Spanish searches yielded no results)
- Keywords covered storm-petrel taxa and light pollution
- 144 records identified (142 from databases, 2 from bibliographies); 20 reviewed in full; 12 articles (published 2005-2022) included in final analysis
- Half published between 2020 and 2022; six from southern hemisphere, six from northern hemisphere

**Key Results:**
- Grounding records found for all Hydrobatidae genera except *Nesofregetta*; groundings recorded in 12 of 22 Hydrobatidae species
- *O. leucorhoa* and *P. marina* were the most frequently mentioned species, followed by *H. pelagicus*
- Fallout (light-induced grounding) occurs primarily in fledglings during their first flight leaving the colony; over 99% of grounded *O. leucorhoa* were fledglings (per Wilhelm et al. 2021)
- Eight articles identified inshore, offshore, or both light pollution sources; inshore sources included residential, industrial, road, highway, business areas; offshore sources mainly fishing vessel deck lights
- Only three articles quantified light pollution levels (two used VIIRS satellite data, one used natural sky brightness measurements)
- Moon phase associated with groundings: more groundings during new moon (lowest moon visibility), fewer during full moon
- Of 12 species assessed by IUCN, nine have decreasing population trends, two unknown, one stable
- Only five of 12 articles assessed population-level impacts; these found annual fallout mortality was less than 1% of respective species' populations, suggesting light pollution may not currently constitute a substantial population-level threat, though further research is needed

**Hypotheses for fledgling attraction to light:** (1) confusion with bioluminescent prey, (2) association of light with food (burrow entrances), (3) undeveloped visual system and behavioral inexperience, (4) artificial lights limiting navigation by moon and stars.

**Discussion highlights:**
- Data is scarce (only 12 articles) and mostly collected before 2013
- Records limited mainly to North American and European coastlines; eastern Pacific (highest storm-petrel diversity) understudied - potential Global South research bias
- Knowledge gaps: only two articles used systematic data collection; light intensity/spectrum rarely quantified; need for standardized data collection, citizen science programs, population-level impact assessment, and characterization of light pollution sources
- A recent study found even partial reduction in artificial light at night (ALAN) decreased strandings by up to 57% (Burt et al. 2024)

**Study limitations:** English-only search; restricted to Scopus and Web of Science; limited to 2000-2022; gray literature excluded.

**Future research priorities:** (1) standardizing data collection of groundings and environmental variables, (2) systematic data collection or increased citizen science, (3) population-level impact assessment, (4) characterizing light pollution sources.

**Author contributions:** Medina-Franco and Sangiorgi are joint first authors (conceptualization, data curation, analysis, writing); Valdés-Velásquez contributed conceptualization, supervision, editing.

--- SOURCE 17: Marine oil pollution and beached bird surveys ---
URL: https://eurowa.eu/web/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/Marine-oil-pollution-and-beached-bird-surveys-CJcamphuysenMHeubeck.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific paper by C.J. Camphuysen and M. Heubeck, published in Environmental Pollution (2001), reviewing the history, methods, and future use of beached bird surveys as a monitoring instrument for marine oil pollution. The paper argues that such surveys are a valuable and sensitive tool for detecting chronic oil pollution, despite criticisms about their reliability.

Key points:
- Oil pollution effects on seabirds were first recognized in the late 19th/early 20th century; the first beached bird surveys were conducted in the 1920s, with serious monitoring programs emerging in the 1950s-1960s in the Netherlands, Germany, Belgium, and Britain.
- Currently, beached bird survey schemes operate in 13 European countries, with only two schemes on Atlantic North America (Newfoundland since the 1950s, and Massachusetts-Texas during 1974-1983). Programs exist or have existed in California, Oregon, Washington, British Columbia, South Africa, South America (particularly for Magellanic Penguins), New Zealand, and Japan.
- A major shortcoming of many programs was emphasis on total stranded bird numbers rather than "oil rates" (percentage of corpses oiled). Total numbers fluctuate greatly due to winds, seabird abundance at sea, and seasonal patterns, limiting their use as pollution indicators.
- Estimating total mortality from oil spills is problematic; drift experiments using tagged corpses show highly variable recovery rates (0.3% to 59%) that are location-specific, so correction factors must be developed during actual incidents rather than using mean values.
- The paper recommends that for monitoring chronic pollution, the "oil rate" (fraction oiled of all birds found) should be used, requiring a "sufficient sample" each season. Oil rates are species-specific (high for surface-immersed species like loons, seaduck, auks; low for aerial species like terns and skuas) and reflect shipping intensity in different regions. For example, Common Murre oil rates are 82% in the Netherlands but only 13% in Shetland.
- Statistical power analysis of Dutch data (1986-1995) shows even minor trends in oil rates can be detected within 12-15 years for most species.

Case studies demonstrating effectiveness:
1. Shetland Islands: Surveys showed low pollution before terminal opening (1978), a spike after the Sullom Voe terminal opened (before de-ballasting facilities were ready), and a decline after strict measures were introduced in March 1979 (aerial surveillance, routing requirements, 35% ballast requirement, preferential chartering of segregated-ballast tankers).
2. Southern North Sea: Consistent declines in oil rates over 30 years indicate gradual improvement.
3. German Bight: Drastic decline during an experiment with free harbor oil reception facilities.
4. Newfoundland: Consistent increases in oil rates, indicating worsening pollution.

Methodological recommendations for standardization (for chronic monitoring):
- Choose representative subregions covering the entire coastline; keep standardized over years.
- Surveys preferably done on foot; counts from vehicles not recommended.
- Mark or remove birds to avoid double counting.
- Identify species, age, sex; record corpse condition and oil extent (use only complete corpses for oil rate calculations).
- Record date, place, km surveyed, oil characteristics, observer names, completeness of survey.
- Computerized databases for prompt analysis.
- Separate open coast from sheltered bays/fjords and MARPOL Special Areas in analyses.

For oil incidents, the paper recommends: assessing the affected area immediately, conducting drift experiments during stranding, sampling the entire stranding area with repeated counts, recording live oiled birds, contacting rehabilitation centers and beach cleaners, marking/removing beached birds, and continuing surveys until fresh casualties cease.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"One of the main shortcomings of many beached bird survey programs was the emphasis on stranded bird numbers rather than on relative measures, such as oil rates (percentage of corpses oiled of all corpses found)."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 1: Revealing patterns of nocturnal migration using the European ... ---
URL: https://www.flysafe-birdtam.eu/files/Nilsson_et_al-2019-Ecography.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific article published in Ecography (2019, vol. 42, pp. 876-886) describing the first continental-scale study of nocturnal avian migration across Europe using a network of weather radars during autumn 2016.

**Methods:**
- Data was extracted from 70 weather radar stations (out of 84 processed, from Sweden to Portugal) operated by meteorological agencies of Sweden, Germany, Finland, France, the Netherlands, Czech Republic, Slovenia, Poland, Belgium, Portugal, Catalonia, and Bulgaria
- The study period covered 19 September to 9 October 2016 (peak passerine migration season)
- Data was processed using the vol2bird algorithm (in the R bioRad package), with radar cross-section of 11 cm² per bird assumed
- Only C-band radars were used; the lowest altitude bin (up to 200m a.g.l.) was excluded to avoid ground clutter
- Migration Traffic Rate (MTR) was calculated as birds passing a theoretical 1-km transect per hour

**Key findings:**
- Overall average: 389 birds passed per 1 km transect per hour across all sites and nights
- The highest migration intensity night (4 October) showed an average of 1621 birds km⁻¹ h⁻¹
- The highest nightly mean MTR was recorded at Eisberg, south-eastern Germany (7,282 birds km⁻¹ h⁻¹ on 4-5 October)
- The site with the highest mean MTR was Bordeaux, France (1,292 birds km⁻¹ h⁻¹)
- Highest intensity of migration was seen in central France; birds funneled between the Alps and the Atlantic Ocean
- Migration directions showed strong southwest components (overall mean 212 degrees), indicating migration passes through Iberia rather than over the Alps
- MTR generally increased from north to south (though southern coastal sites in Portugal and Catalonia showed lower values)
- 74% of sites had an r-value of 0.7 or higher (little directional variation)

**Weather effects:**
- Migration dynamics were strongly related to synoptic wind conditions; a mass migration event occurred immediately after wind conditions improved (3 October) but quickly diminished even while supporting winds continued
- Model results: for every 1 m/s increase in tailwind component, approximately 33 more birds pass a 1-km transect per hour; +10 birds/h from tailwind change from previous night; +3 from interaction
- Migration peaked as soon as winds turned supportive, supporting the 'sit-and-wait' hypothesis of optimal migration
- Peak migration dates were earlier at higher latitudes and later at lower latitudes, showing a large-scale migration wave moving north to south

**Conclusions and implications:**
- The study demonstrates weather radar networks are a valuable tool for large-scale bird movement research
- Findings have consequences for ecosystem function, nutrient transfer, human and livestock health, and civil/military aviation safety
- Applications include targeted conservation efforts (shutting down wind turbines, reducing artificial lights, altering aviation flight plans)
- Future priorities include expanding data coverage to include Spain, Italy, Balkan Peninsula countries, and eastern Europe
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"On average, over the 20 nights and all sites, 389 birds passed per 1 km transect per hour. The night with highest migration intensity showed an average of 1621 birds km–1 h–1 passing the radar stations, but there was considerable geographical and temporal variation in migration intensity." , "Overall, most sites have a clear south-west migration direction (overall mean 212 degrees), indicating that the main part of the flyway down through Europe passes through Iberia, rather than over the Alps." , "A wind-related mass migration event occurred immediately after a change in wind conditions, but quickly diminished even when supporting winds continued to prevail." , "This first continental-scale study using the European network of weather radars demonstrates the wealth of information available and its potential for investigating large-scale bird movements, with consequences for ecosystem function, nutrient transfer, human and livestock health, and civil and military aviation." , "Our results indicate that, on average, for every 1 m s–1 increase in tailwind component, approximately 33 more birds will pass a 1 km transect per hour."
</key_excerpts>
