--- SOURCE 2: Bruderer & Liechti: Bird migration across the Mediterranean ---
URL: https://www.internationalornithology.org/PROCEEDINGS_Durban/Symposium/S33/S33.5.htm

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific paper by Bruno Bruderer and Felix Liechti (Swiss Ornithological Institute, 1999) examines nocturnal bird migration patterns across the western Mediterranean, Iberian Peninsula, and its relation to the Alps and Sahara as ecological barriers. The study uses three calibrated methods: coordinated moon-watching, passive infrared camera observations, and tracking radar (the 'Superfledermaus'), with primary data collection sites at Malaga (Andalusian coast, 25 km east of Malaga) and southern Mallorca (Balearic Islands).

KEY FINDINGS ON FLYWAY EVOLUTION: Flyways between Europe and Africa evolved at three levels: (1) continent-wide scale following Pleistocene range expansions, (2) medium-scale influenced by ecological barriers (sea, desert, mountains) and weather, and (3) individual behavioral reaction norms. The trade-off between risk-avoidance (avoiding barriers) and time/energy minimization leads to 'guided broad-front migration'.

AUTUMN MIGRATION: Moon-watch data from 42 sites (September 1996, 1749 observations over 145 hours) revealed: west-east variation across upper Italy with westward migration over the Padanian plain, southward shifts along the French Riviera, weak SW migration across the western Mediterranean basin near Rome/Malta/Mallorca, and strong SW migration in southern Spain. At Malaga, 29,866 flight paths were recorded (Aug 11-Oct 24, 1996). Passerine migration peaked in September (trans-Saharan migrants) and again in mid-late October (pre-Saharan migrants like Robin, Black Redstart, Chiffchaff, thrushes, Starling, and Skylark). At Baleares, virtually no migration occurred in August (very weak trans-Saharan passage); September data were contaminated by insects, but clean nights (Sept 26-Oct 3, Oct 14-24) showed massive take-offs from the island with arrivals from the Costa Dorada (~240 km to NW at ~5 hours), Costa Brava (~300 km at ~7 hours), and Camargue (~480 km NNE at ~11 hours).

SPRING MIGRATION: At Malaga (March 22-May 26, 1997; 30,353 flight paths), passerine density averaged about twice that at Mallorca (24,085 flight paths). Wader/waterfowl migration was almost five times stronger at the mainland. At Malaga, peak migration occurred 5 hours after sunset with birds arriving from North Africa (170+ km sea crossing, 40-45 km/h ground speeds), concentrating in a narrow strip along the North African coast. A second April peak ~7 hours after sunset indicated concentrations 100-150 km inland (Atlas mountains). At Baleares, intense evening departures from only ~30 km² of suitable habitat (5-30 birds/ha density) occurred, followed by arrivals from Spain, Ibiza, North Africa, and mainland Europe. Density of spring migration across the Mediterranean basin between Algeria and France was at least 2-3 times lower than across the Iberian Peninsula. Migration traffic rates (MTR) at Cape Trafalgar were 700-2900 birds/km/h, compared to ~600 at Andalusian coast and ~270 on Mallorca (about a third to half).

DISCUSSION: SW and SE migratory directions in Europe (contrasting with North America's southward tendencies) are adaptations to the combined barriers of the Alps, Mediterranean, and Sahara. Trans-Saharan migrants (September) cling strictly to their chosen directions, while pre-Saharan migrants (October) show greater flexibility in direction in response to topography, following coastlines and taking advantage of the land bridge. This flexibility allows refueling before the Sahara crossing and selecting optimal weather. Seaward migration decreases when birds' motivational/physiological state deteriorates. The radar data support a slight concentration of nocturnal migration toward the Strait of Gibraltar in addition to prevailing SW/SSW migration. The proposed hypothesis map (illustrating autumn migration) suggests broad-front NE-SW migration across central Europe with concentrations along the French Mediterranean coast, Italian mainland, and SE coast of Spain, representing convergence of various species' and populations' migratory streams.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"In spite of probable concentration effects over the islands, the recorded density of passerine spring migration at the Baleares is only half of that at Malaga, wader/waterfowl migration only about one fifth; the latter difference emphasises the importance of the flyway along the African Atlantic coast.", "The map suggests broad-front migration on a NE-SW axis across central Europe, with declining density to the SE... the whole assembly being best characterised by the term 'guided broad-front migration'.", "At the Baleares site there was nearly no bird migration in August, indicating very weak passage of trans-Saharan migrants.", "The volume of recorded migration at the Baleares was astonishingly high, i.e. much closer to the volume at Malaga than observed in April and May.", "Migratory directions towards SW and SE combined with an obvious lack of southward migration in central and northern Europe are corroborated by data derived from bird ringing, by cage experiments, and by radar observations."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Favorable winds speed up bird migration in spring but not in autumn ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9339755

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific article, published in Ecology and Evolution (2022, Vol. 12, e9146, doi: 10.1002/ece3.9146), investigates the effect of wind on bird migration speed across western Europe. The study uses the first full-year weather radar dataset of nocturnal bird migration from 37 European weather radars (6.8 million datapoints, Feb 13, 2018 to Jan 1, 2019, 5-minute temporal and 200m altitudinal resolution up to 5km) combined with ERA5 wind reanalysis data. The authors (Raphaël Nussbaumer, Baptiste Schmid, Silke Bauer, and Felix Liechti, from Cornell Lab of Ornithology and Swiss Ornithological Institute) analyzed ground speed, airspeed, wind speed, and wind profit across seasonal, daily, geographical, and altitudinal scales.

Key findings: Wind plays a major role in explaining temporal and spatial variations in ground speed, but airspeed remains remarkably constant across all scales (daily SD=3.1 m/s vs ground speed SD=5.1 m/s; spatial airspeed SD=1.03 m/s vs wind SD=1.35 m/s vs ground SD=2.44 m/s). Spring migration was faster than autumn (ground speed 12.6 vs 9.9 m/s) primarily due to wind profit (4.6 m/s in spring vs 1.1 m/s in autumn), with birds experiencing stronger southwest winds in spring (7.5 vs 5.6 m/s). Average airspeed was only slightly faster in spring (8.7 vs 8.2 m/s, about 5% faster), but this difference was deemed not statistically significant due to measurement biases and limitations. The authors argue this 5% difference falls within the expected 5-15% range from optimal flight theory but is too small to be meaningful given large variance and data quality issues.

Methodology: Airspeed was computed using the triangle of velocities (Vg = √(u²+v²); Va = √((u-U)²+(v-V)²)) with wind speeds linearly interpolated in 4D from ERA5 reanalysis data. The core premise is that bird orientation relies on a combination of genetically determined mechanisms, including an "internal calendar" and an "internal compass."

**Basic principles:** Navigation involves setting and maintaining a heading regardless of hazards. Very young birds migrate alone in their first year, proving orientation mechanisms are innate/genetically determined. Remarkable fidelity is documented — e.g., a barn swallow (Hirundo rustica) traveled between South Africa and a stable in Germany for three years with accuracy of a few metres. Most small migratory passerines fly at night, covering 300–600 km per night at 40–50 km/h, relying on a magnetic compass as their basic tool effective in all weather.

**Orientation mechanisms** (discovered through experiments beginning in the 1950s):
- **Solar compass:** Gustav Kramer's orientation cage experiments (Figure 3-5) showed sun position is used as a directional cue. Shifting a bird's internal clock by 6 hours caused a 90° error in flight direction; a 12-hour shift caused 180° reversal (heading north in autumn). Used by diurnal migrants (white storks, large birds of prey), but useless for nocturnal migrants.
- **Night-time compasses (moon and stars):** Franz Sauer (1950s) discovered birds orient using the moon and stars. The "Zugunruhe" (migratory restlessness) behavior at dusk marks migration onset. Franz Sauer and later Stephen T. Emlen (planetarium experiments, Figure 8) demonstrated that birds align with constellations, adjust for their movement during the night, and can be made to "somersault" when the sky was rotated 180°. Birds recalibrate their stellar compass using their magnetic compass, and must "read" new star configurations when crossing the equator.
- **Earth's magnetic field:** Radar studies in the 1950s showed nocturnal migrants oriented correctly even under overcast skies. Kramer proposed a two-stage navigation model (a "mental map" plus a "compass"). Experiments on robins and garden warblers with modified magnetic fields (using coils/magnets to shift magnetic north) provided irrefutable evidence for geomagnetic orientation. Geomagnetism is the only reliable source when all visual references fail.
- **Mental maps:** Birds use geo-topographical landmarks (mountain ranges, river corridors, valleys, passes, coastal strips) as a mosaic of waypoints. Radar observations show wind-driven birds can reorient back to their course after turbulence; birds also exploit favorable winds for massive migratory flows.
- **Positioning in time and space:** Two genetically integrated programmes exist: a temporal programme (correct orientation for a given journey duration) and a spatial programme (appropriate direction that can change along the way). Phillips, titled "Calibration of magnetic and celestial compass cues in migratory birds – a review of cue-conflict experiments." The paper reviews cue-conflict experiments designed to determine how migratory birds integrate multiple compass systems (geomagnetic field, sun, skylight polarization patterns, and star patterns) and which cues have primacy during different periods.

Key findings:
1. **Premigratory period**: Celestial cues (especially sunset polarized light patterns near the horizon) serve as the primary calibration reference, and both juvenile and adult birds use these to recalibrate their magnetic compass. In 5 out of 6 experiments with access to sunrise/sunset cues, the magnetic compass was recalibrated.

2. **Migratory period**: A majority of experiments suggest birds rely primarily on the magnetic field and use it to calibrate celestial compass cues—the relative saliency of magnetic and celestial cues is reversed during migration.

3. **Alternative explanation**: The authors propose that access to celestial cues, rather than timing of exposure (premigratory vs. migratory), determines whether magnetic compass recalibration occurs. Birds with a full view of the sky down to the horizon (8 of 9 studies) recalibrated the magnetic compass regardless of season. Birds with restricted views (95-160° centered on zenith from funnels/registration cages) did not recalibrate the magnetic compass in 28 of 29 studies.

4. **Methodology**: The authors analyzed 76 experiments divided into three groups: (1) after-effects of premigratory exposure to cue conflict (12 experiments), (2) effects of exposure during migration (46 experiments), and (3) after-effects of exposure during migration (18 experiments). Only experiments shifting the horizontal magnetic field relative to natural celestial cues were included; artificial polarization filter, mirror, and artificial star sky experiments were excluded.

5. **Directional asymmetry**: During migration, birds showed asymmetric responses to clockwise vs. counterclockwise (and "with sun" vs. "against sun") magnetic field shifts. CW/WS shifts produced less variable responses (IQR=13.0°, N=10-12) compared to CCW/AS shifts (IQR=39-42°, N=6-8; P=0.04-0.05). Birds reacted to AS shifts less readily, with lower accuracy and consistency.

6. **Proposed explanations for asymmetry**: (a) lateral asymmetry in right/left eye involvement in light-dependent magnetic compass orientation, and (b) interference from spectral and intensity distribution of skylight at sunset with the light-dependent magnetic compass response.

7. **Study quality considerations**: The authors re-analyzed some previous studies, including reinterpreting Able and Able (1990b) by using a more appropriate "natural day sky" control group, and explaining apparent contradictions in Alerstam and Högstedt (1983) due to reversed magnetic field direction at nest box entrances from coil placement.

8. **Conclusion**: The authors suggest that under natural conditions, there may be a single calibration reference for all compass systems of migratory birds, derived from sunset (and possibly sunrise) polarized light cues from the region of sky near the horizon. This contradicts earlier reviews suggesting more complex calibration schemes (Able, 1993; Åkesson, 1994; Wiltschko et al., 1997, 1998a).

--- SOURCE 18: Magnetic orientation in migratory birds ---
URL: http://oops.uni-oldenburg.de/83/1/liemag06.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This document is the Ph.D. thesis of Miriam Liedvogel (defended September 13, 2006 at Carl von Ossietzky Universität Oldenburg, supervised by PD Dr. Henrik Mouritsen and Prof. Dr. Karl-Wilhelm Koch), titled "Magnetic orientation in migratory birds – linking behavioural phenomena with underlying molecular and neuronal mechanisms."

The thesis investigates how night-migratory birds perceive directional information from the Earth's magnetic field and how this information is processed in the brain. Using an integrative approach combining behavioral observation, molecular biology, biochemistry, biophysics, and neuroanatomy, Liedvogel's research covered the full process from the primary receptor molecule to higher brain integration centers.

KEY FINDINGS:

1. **Head-scanning behavior (Paper I):** Using a custom-built experimental setup allowing real-time monitoring under controllable magnetic field conditions, garden warblers (Sylvia borin) showed clear south-westerly orientation under natural magnetic fields but oriented randomly in zero-magnetic fields. Birds nearly tripled their head-scanning frequency in a fully compensated zero magnetic field, and showed significant increases in head-scanning just before initiating migratory restlessness. This indicated the magnetic compass sensor is in the head, and that scanning likely facilitates detection of the magnetically modulated visual pattern on the retina.

2. **Cryptochrome identification (Paper II):** Four cryptochrome family members were identified, cloned, and sequenced in the retina of migratory garden warblers: Cry1a, Cry1b, Cry2, and Cry4. Cry1a is predominantly expressed in the cytosol of ganglion cells, displaced ganglion cells, and photoreceptors. Striking differences were found between migratory and non-migratory birds: Cry1a expression was highest at night in night-migratory birds but decreased to background levels at night in non-migratory control species. Neuronal activity markers colocalized perfectly with Cry1a during night-time magnetic orientation - the first experimental demonstration of a putative light-mediated primary magnetoreceptor molecule in a bird's eye.

3. **Biophysical characterization (Paper III):** Garden warbler cryptochromes were recombinantly expressed as holoproteins (with built-in flavin cofactor) in a baculovirus/Sf9 cell system - the first successful expression of an animal cryptochrome holoprotein in a heterologous eukaryotic system. This required a novel on-column denaturation/refolding step to overcome known difficulties. Garden warbler cryptochromes are light-excited, absorb in the blue spectral range (matching wavelengths known to elicit magnetic orientation in behavioral experiments), and form radical pairs lasting approximately 10 milliseconds - sufficiently long-lived to detect Earth-strength magnetic fields.

4. **Cluster N identification (Paper IV):** Behavioral molecular mapping identified a distinct forebrain area in night-migratory birds, termed "Cluster N" ("N" for night), showing high neuronal activation at night during magnetic orientation but not during the day. Cluster N was inactive in non-migratory zebra finches (Taeniopygia guttata) and canaries (Serinus canaria). Located adjacent to or as part of the visual Wulst, covering birds' eyes with light-tight covers significantly reduced Cluster N activation to near baseline, demonstrating it is active specifically during night-vision in night-migratory birds.

5. **Lateralization and further tests (Paper V, VI):** European robins (Erithacus rubecula) showed significant dominance of Cluster N activation in the right hemisphere. Garden warblers tested under different magnetic field conditions and monochromatic red light showed no significant differences in Cluster N activation, so a definitive role in magnetic compass processing could not be confirmed. Additional analysis found positive correlations between movement and activity levels in 10 cerebral regions and parts of the cerebellum, supporting the hypothesis that vocal learning brain systems evolved from a pre-existing motor pathway.

METHODS: Experiments relied on careful behavioral observation (especially the final 60 minutes before tissue collection), followed by brain dissection, cryostat sectioning, radioactive in situ hybridization for neuronal activity mapping (using immediate early genes like c-Fos and ZENK), and immunohistochemistry for retinal tissue. Primary study species were garden warblers and European robins; control species were zebra finches, canaries, and Sardinian warblers (Sylvia melanocephala).

CONCLUSION: All findings support a light-mediated magnetoperception mechanism in night-migratory birds, consistent with the hypothesis that magnetically modulated intensity patterns are perceived by the visual system - i.e., night-migratory birds may literally "see" the direction of the Earth's magnetic field. The thesis comprises six manuscripts (three published, one submitted, one under review, one near submission) plus supplementary materials on cryptochrome cloning methodology.

--- SOURCE 21: Avian Navigation and Orientation ---
URL: https://avesbiology.com/nav_orient.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage provides a comprehensive scientific overview of avian navigation and orientation mechanisms. It distinguishes between orientation (moving in a compass direction) and true navigation (locating one's position relative to a destination), based on the two-step process first described by Kramer (1953, 1957): determining the correct direction of travel and identifying that direction. Naïve juvenile birds often rely on vector navigation (maintaining a direction for a set time/distance), while experienced adults demonstrate true navigation, as shown in displacement experiments with European Starlings (Perdeck 1958), Common Teal (Wolff 1970), and White-crowned Sparrows (Thorup et al. 2007). Some species' juveniles can compensate for displacement, however. The "clock-and-compass" concept explains how first-time migrants navigate, potentially using magnetic and photoperiodic beacons (Chernetsov and Utvenko 2025). True navigation is likely based on a bi-coordinate grid system using cues that vary along gradients (Thorup and Holland 2009).

The webpage details four compass mechanisms:
1. **Non-compass orientation**: Birds use landmarks and topographic features like coastlines and mountain ridges (e.g., European migrants turning southwest along the Alps).
2. **Star compass**: Emlen's classic planetarium experiments (1967) showed Indigo Buntings learn north by observing stellar rotation around the celestial pole, using Emlen funnels to record orientation. Star-compass use is learned, not innate, and relies on relative constellations rather than specific stars.
3. **Sun compass**: First demonstrated by Kramer (1950); based on the sun's azimuth using an internal clock. Clock-shifting experiments (Schmidt-Koenig 1958) caused 90-degree orientation errors. Learning is tied to the left hippocampus (Gagliardo et al. 2005), with pigeons first able to use it around 12 weeks old.
4. **Polarized light**: Several migratory species (Savannah Sparrows, Swainson's and Gray-cheeked thrushes, White-throated Sparrows) use polarization patterns at sunrise/sunset to calibrate their magnetic compass.
5. **Magnetic cues**: First proposed in 1859 and experimentally demonstrated in 1968 (European Robins). The avian magnetic compass is an inclination compass (distinguishing pole vs. equator, not north vs. south) and is light-dependent, based on cryptochrome molecules in the retina (Mouritsen et al. 2004). Cluster N in the forebrain processes magnetic visual information. Wu and Dickman (2012) identified vestibular brainstem neurons encoding magnetic field direction, intensity, and polarity. Nordmann et al. (2025) traced pigeon magnetoreception to hair cells in inner ear semicircular canals via electromagnetic induction, with signals processed in vestibular nuclei, midbrain cortex, and hippocampus. Iron-oxide magnetoreceptors in the upper beak (maghemite platelets and magnetite clusters) may act as a three-axis magnetometer for detecting field intensity and direction.

For true navigation, birds need "map" information. Mechanisms include visual landmark recognition (used by homing pigeons and food-caching species), path integration (dead reckoning), olfactory cues (studied in homing pigeons with conflicting results; possibly used by tube-nosed seabirds via dimethyl sulfide), and infrasound maps (found implausible due to diffuse sources). The most likely navigational system is bi-coordinate magnetic mapping, using magnetic inclination (for latitude) and intensity (for longitude). A notable example is displaced European Reed Warblers in northwestern Russia that corrected their spring migration direction after longitudinal displacement (Chernetsov et al. 2008), demonstrating use of a magnetic grid map.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: Microsoft Word - _App_Flys.doc ---
URL: https://www.shastacounty.gov/media/7311

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This document is an evaluation of the nocturnal bird migration study conducted by ABR, Inc. on Hatchet Ridge (Shasta County, California) for the proposed Hatchet Ridge wind power project. The evaluation was authored by Dr. Kenneth P. Able (Professor Emeritus, University at Albany, SUNY) on behalf of the Wintu Audubon Society of Redding, California, as an appendix to the project's Environmental Impact Report (EIR).

**Context and Study Details:**
- Wintu Audubon originally criticized the draft EIR for lacking studies of actively migrating birds (day and night), especially under adverse weather conditions when collision risk with turbines is highest.
- The ABR study used marine radar stationed at two ridge sites (the "Saddle site" and "North site") over 36 nights between September 7 and October 15, 2007.
- The evaluator concludes the equipment, methods, data collection, analysis, and interpretations are "generally in line with current standards," mostly straightforward and reasonably conservative.

**Key Limitations Identified:**
1. **Radar identity limitations**: Radar provides little information on bird identity (cannot distinguish a single large bird from a flock of small birds), and provides no reliable count of birds since multiple reflectors within a radar pulse volume produce the same target.
2. **Low-altitude detection problems**: Ground clutter can obscure birds flying at low altitudes where turbine collisions occur. Although the report claims ground clutter was minimal, no radar photos document this, and the antenna was elevated 15° making low-altitude estimates unreliable and biased low. The study does not present data on detectability of birds at the lowest altitudes.
3. **Timing and weather conditions**: The study period (Sept-Oct) preceded the main migration of large, flocked waterbirds (sandhill cranes, tundra swans, geese, ducks, shorebirds) which migrate late in fall and into winter to Central Valley overwintering sites. It is argued these species face the greatest collision risk. Data were collected entirely under good weather conditions, missing the critical periods when low clouds or fog coincide with large migrations—conditions most likely to cause major mortality.
4. **Missing complementary technologies**: Thermal imaging, night vision, or audio recordings of flight calls would have provided independent verification of bird identity and flock sizes.

**Recommended Studies:**
- Studies should cover the entire fall (extending through December/January) and spring migration seasons.
- Both nocturnal and diurnal migration need examination (cranes migrate by day; swans and geese migrate both day and night).
- Emphasis on flight behavior under poor visibility conditions at ridge-top.
- Visual observation or audio recording would be needed since radar is ineffective when clouds contain moisture or precipitation.
- Future work should concentrate at the Saddle site, which is near the center of the proposed turbine array and showed larger numbers of birds.

The document concludes with the extensive curriculum vitae of Dr. Kenneth P. Able, detailing his education (B.A. and M.S. from University of Louisville, Ph.D. from University of Georgia), career at University at Albany (1971-2003, Professor Emeritus thereafter), honors including the William Brewster Medal (American Ornithologists' Union, 1996), extensive NSF grant support for bird migration orientation research, numerous invited lectures and symposia, and a lengthy publication record spanning from 1962 to 2007 focused on avian migration, orientation, and navigation.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"A target that appears large on the radar screen could be the reflection of a single large bird or the reflection of a large flock of small birds. In short, one cannot be certain whether one is detecting swans or sparrows."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Weather Radar Predicts Nighttime Bird Migrations ---
URL: https://www.aaas.org/news/weather-radar-predicts-nighttime-bird-migrations

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from AAAS (published around September 2018, reporting on findings in the September 14 issue of Science) describes a new forecasting model that uses weather radar data combined with machine learning to predict nighttime bird migrations across North America up to a week in advance. The study, led by Benjamin Van Doren of the University of Oxford with co-author Kyle Horton of Cornell University, used the meteorological Next-Generation Radar (NEXRAD) network combined with climate models to accurately predict the timing, intensity, and location of nocturnal migration events, as well as estimate nightly bird numbers. In early May, when temperatures warm, more than 500 million migratory songbirds take flight each night in North America.

The researchers combed through 23 years of spring migration radar data, using machine learning to automate the identification of bird signatures amid chaotic background signals like precipitation and insect swarms. The model's predictions could reduce bird deaths from human activities—over 630 million birds die annually in the U.S. from collisions with buildings, towers, and vehicles, and bird strikes cause at least $1.2 billion in annual aircraft damage worldwide (including the 2009 "miracle on the Hudson" incident). Predictions could also help wind turbine operators shut down turbines or turn off lights during large flights, and help track the spread of avian-borne diseases.

Most North American songbirds (warblers, sparrows, thrushes) migrate at night to take advantage of cooler, more stable atmospheres, allowing daylight hours for foraging at stopover sites. Migratory bird populations in North America are in decline, mostly due to habitat loss. The study demonstrates the value of "big data" ecology research in understanding the complex drivers of avian migration, which involve navigation, timing, wind, food availability, and environmental conditions like temperature, atmospheric pressure, and precipitation.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Birds must navigate accurately using multiple cues, time their journeys precisely, deal with winds that may blow them off course, find food in transient and unfamiliar environments, and often re-engineer their bodies to store energy and save weight," said Van Doren.
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This blog post from the National Archives' Textual Records Division (The Text Message) documents how the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) shut down U.S. airspace on September 11, 2001, in response to the terrorist attacks. Written by Megan Dwyre, Special Access and FOIA Program Archivist at the National Archives at College Park, MD, the post recounts key events chronologically: the day began as "severe clear" with over 4,500 aircraft in the air; by 9:03 AM, after two planes hit the World Trade Center towers, the FAA issued the first national ground stop in U.S. history prohibiting all civilian aircraft departures; following the Pentagon strike at 9:37 AM, the FAA ordered all aircraft to land at the nearest airport in the first-ever unplanned shutdown of U.S. airspace; at 11:06 AM, FAA Advisory 036 suspended operations in the National Airspace System; and by 12:16 PM—three-and-a-half hours after the first plane hit—the airspace was clear of all commercial and private flights. A week later, the Director of Air Traffic Control issued a memo to employees thanking them for their strength and dedication, noting that two days later the system was restarted "a little at a time, in accordance with national security interests," closing with "We will recover and we will build a stronger and better system." The post notes that air travel "would never be the same" after the attacks. All documents cited are from the series "Open Files Relating to September 11, 2001 Terrorist Attacks" (NAID 7419198), Record Group 237: Records of the Federal Aviation Administration, at the National Archives at College Park, MD.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 7: Space Weather Disrupts Nocturnal Bird Migration, Study Finds ---
URL: https://clasp.engin.umich.edu/2023/10/10/space-weather-disrupts-nocturnal-bird-migration-study-finds

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article reports on a University of Michigan study, published online October 9, 2023, in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), that found correlational evidence linking geomagnetic disturbances (space weather) to disruptions in nocturnal bird migration. Researchers used massive long-term datasets from 37 NEXRAD Doppler weather radar stations in the U.S. Great Plains central flyway (spanning over 1,000 miles from Texas to North Dakota) and ground-based magnetometer data from the superMAG network to test this connection.

Key findings include a 9%-17% reduction in the number of migrating birds during severe space weather events in both spring and fall, with birds that did migrate experiencing more difficulty navigating, especially under overcast conditions in autumn. The final datasets included 1.7 million radar scans from fall and 1.4 million from spring, spanning 23 years. The bird community studied was primarily composed of perching birds (Passeriformes, 73%), shorebirds (Charadriiformes, 12%), and waterfowl (Anseriformes, 9%).

The researchers used two complementary statistical models that controlled for weather, temporal, and geographic variables. They also found that migrating birds drift with the wind more frequently during fall geomagnetic disturbances, with "effort flying" against the wind reduced by 25% under cloudy skies during strong solar storms—suggesting that a combination of obscured celestial cues and magnetic disruption hinders navigation.

Lead author Eric Gulson-Castillo (doctoral student, U-M Department of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology) conducted the study as part of his dissertation. Senior author Ben Winger is an assistant professor in the U-M Department of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology and a curator of birds at the U-M Museum of Zoology. Additional authors include Benjamin Van Doren (Cornell), Kyle Horton (Colorado State), Jing Li, Mark Moldwin, and Kerby Shedden (U-M), and Michelle Bui (formerly UT Arlington). U-M Climate & Space Assistant Professor Daniel Welling and Michelle Bui compiled the space weather data and designed the geomagnetic disturbance index. Funding was provided by a U-M MCubed grant, NSF fellowships, and other sources.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Our findings highlight how animal decisions are dependent on environmental conditions—including those that we as humans cannot perceive, such as geomagnetic disturbances—and that these behaviors influence population-level patterns of animal movement," said study lead author Eric Gulson-Castillo, a doctoral student in the U-M Department of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology.
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 8: Space weather disrupts nocturnal bird migration ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10589677

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article titled "Space weather disrupts nocturnal bird migration," published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS) on October 9, 2023 (DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2306317120). The study was conducted by Eric R. Gulson-Castillo and colleagues from the University of Michigan, Cornell University, University of Texas at Arlington, and Colorado State University.

STUDY PURPOSE AND METHODS: The researchers investigated whether space weather geomagnetic disturbances affect bird migration at a macroecological scale. They leveraged 22 years of Doppler radar (NEXRAD) data to characterize nightly migration dynamics of nocturnally migrating North American avifauna, and used concurrent magnetometer data to develop a local magnetic disturbance index (ΔBmax) associated with each radar station. They used two complementary statistical approaches: nonlinear mixed effects (NLME) models and machine learning decision tree (MLT) models, while controlling for atmospheric weather and spatiotemporal patterns. The final datasets included 1,725,415 radar scans in fall and 1,392,826 in spring.

KEY FINDINGS:
1. Migration Intensity: Severe space weather events were associated with a 9-17% decrease in migration intensity in both spring (11.2% decrease in MLT model; 17.4% in NLME model) and fall (8.9% decrease in MLT model). Decreases were predicted at geomagnetic disturbances greater than ~500 nT. These large disturbances occurred on 81 (3.32%) unique nights in fall and 50 (2.28%) in spring over the 23-year dataset, with 75.5% linked to registered geomagnetic storms.

2. Effort Flying Against Wind: During fall migration, there was evidence for decreases in effort flying against the wind during geomagnetic disturbances. The fall NLME model predicted a 25.4% decrease in the crosswind component at 100% cloud cover and high ΔBmax, while the MLT model showed a 7.6% decrease. This suggests birds drift more with the wind during geomagnetic disturbances, indicating navigation difficulties. No such effects were found in spring models. The seasonal differences may relate to fall migration containing many inexperienced juvenile birds that depend on simpler "clock and compass" magnetic orientation strategies.

3. Flight Altitude: Little support was found for an effect of geomagnetic disturbances on the mean altitude of migrants aloft.

4. Comparison with Atmospheric Weather: Atmospheric weather had larger effects on migration than space weather (e.g., warm spring temperatures associated with 45.2% increase in migration intensity; north fall winds with ~43.1% increase), but log-likelihood tests supported the inclusion of ΔBmax.

LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE DIRECTIONS: The study provides correlational evidence and explicitly controlled for atmospheric weather, addressing limitations of previous studies. Finer-scale patterns such as species-specific responses cannot be studied with the current dataset, but future research could combine radar with citizen science or bird banding efforts. The work implies that longer-term impacts to Earth's magnetic field (e.g., the 11-year solar cycles) could also affect bird migration.

The article notes that the study was received April 18, 2023, and accepted August 22, 2023.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Our results suggest that fewer birds migrate during strong geomagnetic disturbances and that migrating birds may experience more difficulty navigating, especially under overcast conditions in autumn."

--- SOURCE 12: Insufficient adaptation to climate change alters avian ... ---
URL: https://www.rug.nl/staff/c.both/both_chapter_birds_habitats.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific book chapter by Christiaan Both (University of Groningen) exploring how insufficient adaptation to climate change alters avian habitat quality and habitat selection, with a focus on phenological mismatch in long-distance migratory birds.

**Background/Observations:** The chapter opens with the author's observation that pied flycatchers (Ficedula hypoleuca) prefer nest-boxes already occupied by tits, despite the risk of being killed by great tits (with brains eaten) - this demonstrates reliance on information from other species for habitat selection. An experiment in 2000 (an exceptionally warm April) showed flycatchers arriving exceptionally late (April 20 vs. normal April 10) but breeding at high speed, an early sign of climate-driven phenological disruption.

**Core Findings on Phenological Mismatch:** Since about 1980, laying dates in many populations have advanced, with rates strongly correlated with local spring warming. In Dutch habitats, caterpillars advanced more than passerine hatching dates, causing increasing fitness penalties for late breeding and making habitats less suitable. However, responses varied geographically: in Wytham Woods (UK) birds became better timed with food peaks; in the Czech Republic synchrony was maintained. Unequal trophic responses can also be beneficial - Dutch tits and flycatchers escape some predation by sparrowhawks (Accipiter nisus) whose phenology changed less. Climate can also affect nest predation through increased mast seeding frequency increasing rodent overwinter survival.

**Habitat Differences:** Dutch pied flycatcher populations declined strongly in deciduous (oak) stands on fertile soils from the late 1980s, while coniferous/mixed forests thrived. Population trends were strongly negative in areas with early food peaks but unchanged in areas with late food peaks. Great tit trends were unrelated to food peak dates, and absolute caterpillar densities were highest in early-peak areas. In spring 2009, mass chick mortality occurred when caterpillars were so abundant they defoliated trees and starved before flycatcher eggs hatched (tits breeding ten days earlier were hardly affected).

**Mechanisms:** Pied flycatchers' inflexibility in arrival timing (males have not advanced arrival in western/central Europe over three decades) relates to photoperiod-controlled annual cycles and environmental constraints during migration, though they have advanced passage through North Africa. Long-distance migrants generally responded less to warming than short-distance migrants. By the end of the twentieth century, species with the smallest advancement in spring arrival declined most. Comparing Dutch forests (narrow food peaks) with marshlands (extended insect availability) revealed all forest long-distance migrants declined (up to 85% in icterine warblers), while marshland migrants did not; later-arriving species declined most.

**Dispersal as Adaptation:** The chapter discusses whether dispersal to areas with better phenological matches (e.g., more northerly sites) is a viable adaptation. Evidence for directional dispersal in response to phenological mismatch is largely non-existent. Members discuss: immigrant fitness generally lower than philopatric individuals (though immigrants can benefit inbred populations), latitudinal variation in migration timing possibly having genetic basis, spatial variation in phenology changes (Swedish birds likely not mismatched), and the American redstart example showing winter habitat quality affects departure date and dispersal direction.

**Local Adaptation and Dispersal:** Studies show young fledged in poor condition or born late in the season are more likely to disperse. In the author's pied flycatcher study, chicks born later dispersed further, especially in areas with early tree phenology - suggesting maladapted young emigrate. Eight of 11 studies on lifetime reproductive success reported fitness declines in dispersers for at least one sex. The chapter proposes translocation experiments (successfully performed with pied flycatchers) to test fitness consequences of alternative breeding sites and whether long-distance dispersal is a viable adaptation.

**Conclusions:** Climate change affects habitat suitability through phenological changes, with trophic mismatches expected to become more frequent (invertebrate phenology advances more than vertebrate phenology). Population consequences are most evident in long-distance migrants in seasonal habitats. Habitat selection changes may occur at small spatial scales (only temporary solution) or larger scales, but more data on long-distance dispersal frequency and fitness consequences of phenological match versus local adaptation costs are needed. Technological tracking (e.g., stable isotopes) and translocation experiments will help predict adaptive ability of species to climate change.
</summary>

Probably as a consequence, the fitness penalty of late breeding increased over the years, as late nests became progressively more mismatched with the food peak." --- SOURCE 13: Can long-distance migratory birds adjust to the ... ---
URL: https://www.ucm.es/data/cont/media/www/pag-33468/2008_GlobChangeBiol_14_2516.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific paper (Coppack et al., 2008, Global Change Biology) investigates whether the pied flycatcher (Ficedula hypoleuca), a long-distance Palaearctic-Afrotropical migratory bird, can adjust to the advancement of spring under climate change by shortening its migration distance. The study experimentally exposed hand-raised male pied flycatchers (collected from broods near Erlangen, Germany) to simulated photoperiodic conditions representing different wintering latitudes (10°N, 20°N, 30°N, 37.5°N, and 50°N) and measured the timing of prenuptial moult, spring migratory activity (Zugunruhe), and gonadal/testicular growth.

Key findings: A moderate northward displacement of the current wintering grounds (from 10°N to 20°N, roughly 1,100 km) resulted in significant advancement of the termination of prenuptial moult (18–23 days earlier), the onset of spring migration (25–33 days earlier), and gonadal growth. However, no further advancement occurred under higher simulated wintering latitudes, indicating a critical photoperiodic threshold or steep gradual response within the narrow geographical range between 10°N and 20°N. The onset and duration of prenuptial moult were not affected by photoperiodic treatment. Testis size was significantly larger only in the northernmost groups (37.5°N and 50°N); a significant family-by-latitude interaction effect was found for gonadal development, indicating genetic variation in photoperiodic response.

The authors conclude that the pied flycatcher's photoperiodic response to latitudinal changes is not linear. Since the species' current wintering range is restricted to a narrow band along the West African coast (near equator to approximately 15°N), and since desertification in the Sahel region is progressing rapidly due to climate change and human activity, the potential for this species to adapt to changing climatic conditions by gradually shortening migration distance is likely limited. The research could not distinguish between a threshold reaction norm versus a gradual one within the critical 10°N–20°N range, and the authors recommend smaller-scale follow-up experiments. The study also compares the pied flycatcher's response to related species (collared flycatcher, garden warbler, common redstart), suggesting that species with broader wintering ranges may have shallower photoperiodic reaction norms, and highlights that the rate of adaptation will depend on the additive genetic variation underlying photoperiodic reaction norms.
</summary>

"We experimentally show that a moderate northward displacement of the pied flycatcher's current wintering grounds by 10 degrees would result in a clear advancement of the termination of prenuptial moult and the initiation of spring migratory activity and gonadal growth. However, we found no further advancement under conditions simulating higher wintering latitudes, suggesting the existence of a critical photoperiodic threshold or a steep gradual response within a narrow geographical range between 10 degrees and 20 degrees northern latitude.", "Compared with the control group held at a photoperiodic regime at 10N, birds ended prenuptial moult significantly earlier (by 18–23 days) and advanced migration onset (by 25–33 days) in all experimental groups. However, there were no significant differences in the termination of moult and the onset of migration among birds kept under photoperiodic conditions beyond 10N latitude, indicating a threshold response to latitudinal photoperiodic variation.", "Because habitat conditions in this area are deteriorating rapidly, the potential for pied flycatchers to adjust their life cycle to changing climatic conditions by shortening the migration distance may be limited in the future.", "The finding that the latitudinal shift from 10N to 20N elicited a pronounced advancement of moult and migration indicates that an adaptive advancement of migration and reproduction by a change in wintering area may be limited in the pied flycatcher."

--- SOURCE 1: In-flight reactions of nocturnally migrating birds to winds ---
URL: https://d-nb.info/1356231144/34

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific review article published in the Journal of Ornithology (2024) by Bruno Bruderer, Pius Korner, and Dieter Peter of the Swiss Ornithological Institute, examining how nocturnally migrating birds react to winds in flight.

**Study Design:** The authors reviewed available knowledge on in-flight reactions of nocturnal bird migrants to winds, focusing on the challenging conditions in Western Europe versus North America. They then conducted a new analysis using tracking radar data from a complete autumn season (30 July–30 October 1987) at Lehrberg near Nuremberg, Germany, at an altitude of 450 m asl. Using the "Superfledermaus" tracking radar, they tracked individual nocturnal migrants (93.6% intermittently flapping passerines) and measured winds using pilot balloons at the birds' flight altitudes.

**Key Methods:** They defined a "basic direction" (BD) as the average flight direction of migrants under negligible wind influence (mean ±30° around 230°). Track and heading deviations from BD were modeled for two altitudinal zones (above/below 1500 m asl) against winds from six 60° sectors. Statistical analysis used robust general additive models with a Student-t distribution.

**Key Results:**
- Air speeds (Va) increased from ~11 to 13 (14) m/s with opposing and side winds (supporting H1); a slight decrease with following winds was only observed in high-flying birds
- No expected increase in air speed with altitude due to decreasing air density (H2 unsupported)
- Overcompensation was frequent at low wind speeds (<3 m/s); birds compensated fully or overcompensated for winds under 3 m/s
- Under opposing and side winds from the right, birds achieved partial drift compensation up to ~8–10 m/s, then were fully drifted (H3, H4)
- Winds from the right (W/NW) caused more drift at low levels; results for H5 were ambiguous
- Retrograde migration (birds blown backwards by headwinds exceeding air speed) was observed (H7)
- Reverse migration occurred on most nights (H6)
- Migrants compensated less for wind deviations than expected; many maintained headings close to BD even when making minimal ground progress or moving backwards
- General conclusion: full compensation or overcompensation prevailed for winds <3 m/s, but drift became predominant under moderate to strong winds
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The general finding is that in a relatively flat area of southern Germany, full compensation or overcompensation was the prevailing reaction of nocturnal bird migrants to deviating winds with speeds of less than 3 m/s. Under stronger winds, the radar-tracked birds showed insufficient or even decreasing compensation, so that drift became the predominant feature of migration under moderate to strong winds." — From Conclusions and discussion

"Despite some omnipresent reverse migration, we found no support for the idea that songbird migrants tend to fly downwind irrespective of wind direction as suggested, e.g. by Gauthreaux and Able (1970) for North America."

"Overcompensation was frequently observed at low wind speeds (<3 m/s)" — Abstract

"The tendency of birds to maintain headings close to BD under opposing winds was so strong that many individuals continued migration with minimal progress over ground or even with retrograde migration as an extreme." — Abstract

"In general, migrants compensated less for deviations by wind force than expected." — Abstract
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Google Scholar profile page for Felix Liechti, an ornithologist specializing in bird migration research. His citation metrics show 11,186 total citations (4,491 since 2021), an h-index of 59 (36 recent), and an i10-index of 149 (109 recent).

His most highly cited publications include:
- "Birds: blowin' by the wind?" (2006, Journal of Ornithology) - 615 citations

- "Bird migration flight altitudes studied by a network of operational weather radars" (2010) - 323 citations
- "Atmospheric conditions create freeways, detours and tailbacks for migrating birds" (2017) - 251 citations
- "The relevance of wind for optimal migration theory" (1998) - 245 citations

His research focuses heavily on:
- The influence of wind and atmospheric conditions on bird migration
- Radar-based quantification of bird migration
- Migration across the Sahara and between Europe and Africa

- Nocturnal migration behavior and flight altitudes

Notable work includes "First evidence of a 200-day non-stop flight in a bird" (2013, Nature Communications) and research on the painted lady butterfly's multi-generational migration (2013). He has collaborated extensively with researchers including B. Bruderer, B. Erni, H. Schmaljohann, and others. Publications span from 1995 to 2017, appearing in journals such as Journal of Ornithology, Ibis, Oikos, Nature Communications, and Proceedings of the Royal Society B.

--- SOURCE 3: [PDF] Revealing patterns of nocturnal migration using the European ... ---
URL: https://www.flysafe-birdtam.eu/files/Nilsson_et_al-2019-Ecography.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific article published in Ecography (2019, vol. 42, pp. 876-886) describing the first continental-scale study of nocturnal avian migration across Europe using a network of weather radars during autumn 2016.

**Methods:**
- Data was extracted from 70 weather radar stations (out of 84 processed, from Sweden to Portugal) operated by meteorological agencies of Sweden, Germany, Finland, France, the Netherlands, Czech Republic, Slovenia, Poland, Belgium, Portugal, Catalonia, and Bulgaria
- The study period covered 19 September to 9 October 2016 (peak passerine migration season)
- Data was processed using the vol2bird algorithm (in the R bioRad package), with radar cross-section of 11 cm² per bird assumed
- Only C-band radars were used; the lowest altitude bin (up to 200m a.g.l.) was excluded to avoid ground clutter
- Migration Traffic Rate (MTR) was calculated as birds passing a theoretical 1-km transect per hour

**Key findings:**
- Overall average: 389 birds passed per 1 km transect per hour across all sites and nights
- The highest migration intensity night (4 October) showed an average of 1621 birds km⁻¹ h⁻¹
- The highest nightly mean MTR was recorded at Eisberg, south-eastern Germany (7,282 birds km⁻¹ h⁻¹ on 4-5 October)
- The site with the highest mean MTR was Bordeaux, France (1,292 birds km⁻¹ h⁻¹)
- Highest intensity of migration was seen in central France; birds funneled between the Alps and the Atlantic Ocean
- Migration directions showed strong southwest components (overall mean 212 degrees), indicating migration passes through Iberia rather than over the Alps
- MTR generally increased from north to south (though southern coastal sites in Portugal and Catalonia showed lower values)
- 74% of sites had an r-value of 0.7 or higher (little directional variation)

**Weather effects:**
- Migration dynamics were strongly related to synoptic wind conditions; a mass migration event occurred immediately after wind conditions improved (3 October) but quickly diminished even while supporting winds continued
- Model results: for every 1 m/s increase in tailwind component, approximately 33 more birds pass a 1-km transect per hour; +10 birds/h from tailwind change from previous night; +3 from interaction
- Migration peaked as soon as winds turned supportive, supporting the 'sit-and-wait' hypothesis of optimal migration
- Peak migration dates were earlier at higher latitudes and later at lower latitudes, showing a large-scale migration wave moving north to south

**Conclusions and implications:**
- The study demonstrates weather radar networks are a valuable tool for large-scale bird movement research
- Findings have consequences for ecosystem function, nutrient transfer, human and livestock health, and civil/military aviation safety
- Applications include targeted conservation efforts (shutting down wind turbines, reducing artificial lights, altering aviation flight plans)
- Future priorities include expanding data coverage to include Spain, Italy, Balkan Peninsula countries, and eastern Europe
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"On average, over the 20 nights and all sites, 389 birds passed per 1 km transect per hour. The night with highest migration intensity showed an average of 1621 birds km–1 h–1 passing the radar stations, but there was considerable geographical and temporal variation in migration intensity." , "Overall, most sites have a clear south-west migration direction (overall mean 212 degrees), indicating that the main part of the flyway down through Europe passes through Iberia, rather than over the Alps." , "A wind-related mass migration event occurred immediately after a change in wind conditions, but quickly diminished even when supporting winds continued to prevail." , "This first continental-scale study using the European network of weather radars demonstrates the wealth of information available and its potential for investigating large-scale bird movements, with consequences for ecosystem function, nutrient transfer, human and livestock health, and civil and military aviation." , "Our results indicate that, on average, for every 1 m s–1 increase in tailwind component, approximately 33 more birds will pass a 1 km transect per hour."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: Bruderer & Liechti: Bird migration across the Mediterranean ---
URL: https://www.internationalornithology.org/PROCEEDINGS_Durban/Symposium/S33/S33.5.htm

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific paper by Bruno Bruderer and Felix Liechti (Swiss Ornithological Institute, 1999) examines nocturnal bird migration patterns across the western Mediterranean, Iberian Peninsula, and its relation to the Alps and Sahara as ecological barriers. The study uses three calibrated methods: coordinated moon-watching, passive infrared camera observations, and tracking radar (the 'Superfledermaus'), with primary data collection sites at Malaga (Andalusian coast, 25 km east of Malaga) and southern Mallorca (Balearic Islands).

KEY FINDINGS ON FLYWAY EVOLUTION: Flyways between Europe and Africa evolved at three levels: (1) continent-wide scale following Pleistocene range expansions, (2) medium-scale influenced by ecological barriers (sea, desert, mountains) and weather, and (3) individual behavioral reaction norms. The trade-off between risk-avoidance (avoiding barriers) and time/energy minimization leads to 'guided broad-front migration'.

AUTUMN MIGRATION: Moon-watch data from 42 sites (September 1996, 1749 observations over 145 hours) revealed: west-east variation across upper Italy with westward migration over the Padanian plain, southward shifts along the French Riviera, weak SW migration across the western Mediterranean basin near Rome/Malta/Mallorca, and strong SW migration in southern Spain. At Malaga, 29,866 flight paths were recorded (Aug 11-Oct 24, 1996). Passerine migration peaked in September (trans-Saharan migrants) and again in mid-late October (pre-Saharan migrants like Robin, Black Redstart, Chiffchaff, thrushes, Starling, and Skylark). At Baleares, virtually no migration occurred in August (very weak trans-Saharan passage); September data were contaminated by insects, but clean nights (Sept 26-Oct 3, Oct 14-24) showed massive take-offs from the island with arrivals from the Costa Dorada (~240 km to NW at ~5 hours), Costa Brava (~300 km at ~7 hours), and Camargue (~480 km NNE at ~11 hours).

SPRING MIGRATION: At Malaga (March 22-May 26, 1997; 30,353 flight paths), passerine density averaged about twice that at Mallorca (24,085 flight paths). Wader/waterfowl migration was almost five times stronger at the mainland. At Malaga, peak migration occurred 5 hours after sunset with birds arriving from North Africa (170+ km sea crossing, 40-45 km/h ground speeds), concentrating in a narrow strip along the North African coast. A second April peak ~7 hours after sunset indicated concentrations 100-150 km inland (Atlas mountains). At Baleares, intense evening departures from only ~30 km² of suitable habitat (5-30 birds/ha density) occurred, followed by arrivals from Spain, Ibiza, North Africa, and mainland Europe. Density of spring migration across the Mediterranean basin between Algeria and France was at least 2-3 times lower than across the Iberian Peninsula. Migration traffic rates (MTR) at Cape Trafalgar were 700-2900 birds/km/h, compared to ~600 at Andalusian coast and ~270 on Mallorca (about a third to half).

DISCUSSION: SW and SE migratory directions in Europe (contrasting with North America's southward tendencies) are adaptations to the combined barriers of the Alps, Mediterranean, and Sahara. Trans-Saharan migrants (September) cling strictly to their chosen directions, while pre-Saharan migrants (October) show greater flexibility in direction in response to topography, following coastlines and taking advantage of the land bridge. This flexibility allows refueling before the Sahara crossing and selecting optimal weather. Seaward migration decreases when birds' motivational/physiological state deteriorates. The radar data support a slight concentration of nocturnal migration toward the Strait of Gibraltar in addition to prevailing SW/SSW migration. The proposed hypothesis map (illustrating autumn migration) suggests broad-front NE-SW migration across central Europe with concentrations along the French Mediterranean coast, Italian mainland, and SE coast of Spain, representing convergence of various species' and populations' migratory streams.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"In spite of probable concentration effects over the islands, the recorded density of passerine spring migration at the Baleares is only half of that at Malaga, wader/waterfowl migration only about one fifth; the latter difference emphasises the importance of the flyway along the African Atlantic coast.", "The map suggests broad-front migration on a NE-SW axis across central Europe, with declining density to the SE... the whole assembly being best characterised by the term 'guided broad-front migration'.", "At the Baleares site there was nearly no bird migration in August, indicating very weak passage of trans-Saharan migrants.", "The volume of recorded migration at the Baleares was astonishingly high, i.e. much closer to the volume at Malaga than observed in April and May.", "Migratory directions towards SW and SE combined with an obvious lack of southward migration in central and northern Europe are corroborated by data derived from bird ringing, by cage experiments, and by radar observations."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 5: Temporal and Spatial Pattern of Nocturnal Bird Migration ... ---
URL: https://speich.net/about/diplomarbeit.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a diploma thesis by Simon Speich from the Zoological Institute of the University of Basel, Switzerland (July 1999), supervised by Prof. Dr. Bruno Bruderer and Dr. Felix Liechti of the Swiss Ornithological Institute. It studies bird migration across the western Mediterranean Sea using tracking radar on Mallorca, Spain, during spring 1997 (March 24 to May 26).

**Part A: Diurnal and Seasonal Schedule of Spring Migration over Mallorca**

The study used an X-band (3.3 cm wavelength) tracking radar located in southern Mallorca (39°18'N, 3°4'E), about 8 km from the southern coast. Data was collected on 64 nights. Wing-beat patterns were classified into four groups: CF (continuously flapping, mainly waders/waterfowl), IF (intermittently flapping, mainly passerines), SW (swifts), and UD (undetermined).

Key findings on diurnal pattern:
- Nocturnal migration showed two distinct phases separated by a gap (no birds taking off from the sea): a take-off phase (birds departing from the island) and a night phase (birds arriving from North Africa).
- Take-off began on average 13 ± 25 min before sunset (SE=±4 min, N=49 nights), reached peak intensity within one hour after sunset (average 51 ± 13 min after sunset), and ended 200 ± 62 min after sunset.
- The fastest birds arrived from Africa 229 ± 81 min after sunset; the main mass arrived 485 ± 94 min after sunset (roughly 8 hours after sunset).
- Night phase ended on average 8 ± 59 min after sunrise.
- Continuously flapping birds took off earlier than intermittently flapping (passerine) birds (Mann-Whitney U = 126, p < 0.046).
- On average, at least one third of migrants landed after crossing the coast each night (estimate between 27% and 37%).

Seasonal course:
- Migration intensity increased steeply from early April to mid-April, then slowly declined by end of May; highest intensity was between mid-April and beginning of May.
- Passerine-type wing-beat proportion was ~48% early in April (almost 50%), declining to 18% by end of May.
- Swift-type wing-beat proportion increased from 6% (early April) to over 40% by late May, causing the clear separation between take-off and night phases to disappear (swifts sleep in the air).
- No significant direct correlation between night phase and take-off phase migration traffic was found (Spearman R=0.2389, p=0.0983), but when nights were divided into two groups (where take-off MT was higher vs. lower than night phase MT), correlations became highly significant (R=0.8951, p<0.001, N=12; and R=0.4520, p=0.0107, N=35). This suggests most birds rested only about one day ("short resting periods of only one day").

**Part B: Direction, Speed and Origin of Spring Migrants Arriving on Mallorca**

- Mean flight direction was 18° during take-off and 10° during arrivals from North Africa (roughly NNE).
- Average ground speed of migrating birds was 12 m·s⁻¹; passerine-type wing-beat birds had ground speeds more than 2 m·s⁻¹ higher than continuously flapping birds.
- Nocturnal migrants from Africa arrived "in a wave" at different times in the second half of the night because most did NOT fly non-stop over the Sahara and Mediterranean, but landed somewhere in North Africa first.
- Using direction and speed, potential previous take-off areas in North Africa were calculated; migrants were NOT predominantly concentrated along the coast but departed, at least some nights, from further inland in the Atlas Highlands, and some possibly even south of the Atlas mountains.
- It appears migrants landed as soon as they detected potential resting areas around dawn after crossing the Sahara; those still over the Sahara continued to the Atlas highlands, increasing numbers there but not near the coast.
- Mallorca seemed to have no important concentration effect attracting migrants from different directions.

**Overall conclusion:** The two-wave pattern (take-off phase, gap, night phase) demonstrated that most spring migrants do NOT fly non-stop over the Sahara and Mediterranean; instead, they land and rest in North Africa before the sea crossing, adhering to a night-flying/day-resting strategy even across large ecological barriers. Migration over Mallorca is confined to the night. Possible reasons for landing instead of non-stop flight include avoiding depletion of energy reserves and stronger selection for night-flying than for time-minimizing.

The study was part of a larger Swiss National Science Foundation-supported project by the Swiss Ornithological Institute investigating whether bird migration across the Mediterranean occurs on a broad front and whether islands like the Balearics influence migration. Two tracking radars were used: one on Mallorca and one near Malaga on the Spanish mainland, with moon and infrared observations along French and Spanish coasts.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"On average at least one third of the migrants landed soon after crossing the coast every night." "The take-off phase began on average 13 ± 25 min before sunset... reached the maximum only 64 minutes later and came to an end 200 ± 62 min after sunset." "The main mass of birds did not reach the island until 256 minutes later than the fastest birds (M = 485 ± 94 min, SE = ± 13 min)." "Among all tracked birds the proportion of birds with a passerine-type wing-beat pattern was almost 50% at the beginning of April and decreased to 18% by the end of May. The proportion of birds with a swift-type wing-beat pattern increased from 6% to more than 40% over the same period." "The pattern with two waves and a gap in between showed that the birds had landed in North Africa before crossing the Mediterranean Sea... it can of course not be excluded that some birds flew over the Mediterranean non-stop, but they were quantitatively not relevant."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 6: Geomagnetic disturbance associated with increased vagrancy in migratory landbirds | Scientific Reports ---
URL: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-022-26586-0

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific article (published in Scientific Reports, 2023) investigates the association between geomagnetic disturbance and avian vagrancy in migratory landbirds. The researchers hypothesized that errors in orientation or navigation caused by disruption to the Earth's magnetic field could lead birds astray, as migratory birds use magnetoreception—sensing the Earth's magnetic field via specialized magnetoreceptor structures—to traverse long distances.

METHODOLOGY: The study analyzed 2,226,936 banding records of 152 migratory landbird species in North America (150 species in fall, 124 in spring) from 1960 to 2019, combining USGS Bird Banding Lab data with eBird Status and Trends weekly species abundance maps. Instead of using binary vagrancy classification, they created a continuous "vagrancy index" measuring the spatiotemporal rarity of each banding record relative to modeled expected species ranges. Using hierarchical Bayesian random-effects models, they tested associations with geomagnetic disturbance (global Ap index) and solar activity (American relative sunspot number).

KEY RESULTS:
- Strong positive association between geomagnetic disturbance and vagrancy during fall migration (posterior median = 0.109; 95% CrI = 0.077–0.142; p(>0) = 1). Typically, a two-standard-deviation increase in geomagnetic disturbance is associated with a 24% increase in median predicted vagrancy index and a 250% increase in the number of spatiotemporally rare banding records (from 2% to 5% of records).
- 83% of species showed positive sensitivity to geomagnetic disturbance in fall.
- Sensitivity to geomagnetic disturbance was stronger among longer-distance migrants (supporting the hypothesis that long-distance migrants rely more on magnetoreception), but no effect of breeding latitude was found.
- Hatch-year (juvenile) birds showed higher baseline fall vagrancy than adults, but were NOT more sensitive to geomagnetic disturbance.
- Only weak or no evidence for associations during spring migration, potentially due to sampling biases (banding sites preferentially capture birds near breeding sites late in migration).
- Contrary to hypotheses, increased solar activity was negatively associated with fall vagrancy (potential mitigation effect). An interaction model showed strong evidence for a negative interaction during fall—during high solar activity, birds are less sensitive to geomagnetic disturbance, suggesting radiofrequency noise disables magnetoreception, causing birds to pause migration or switch to other cues.
- Diurnal migrants (24% of fall species) were more sensitive to solar activity than nocturnal migrants, possibly because solar radiofrequency noise affects the sunlit side of Earth; this may explain previously observed negative effects of solar activity on crane migration.

IMPLICATIONS: Geomagnetic disturbance and solar activity explained a median of 5.9% of variance in vagrancy (species-specific range 0.3–30%), meaning other factors (weather, population fluctuations, etc.) explain 70% to >99% depending on species. The authors note geomagnetic disturbance may have downstream ecological consequences, as vagrants may experience increased mortality or facilitate range expansions of avian populations and the organisms they disperse. The findings provide macroecological evidence supporting the widespread importance of magnetoreception in migratory landbirds.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
Using data from 2 million captures of 152 landbird species in North America over 60 years, we demonstrate a strong association between disruption to the Earth's magnetic field and avian vagrancy during fall migration., We found, with high confidence, that vagrancy across North American landbirds is associated with increased geomagnetic disturbance in the fall migration season (posterior median ωfall,geom. dist. = 0.109; 95% credible interval (CrI) = 0.077 to 0.142; proportion of posterior p(> 0) = 1)., For the typical species... an increase in geomagnetic disturbance of two standard deviations above average conditions is associated with a 24% increase in the median predicted vagrancy index of all records and a 250% increase in the number of spatiotemporally rare banding records (from 2% of all records at average geomagnetic disturbance to 5% under elevated conditions)., Results from this interaction model provide strong evidence for a negative interaction during fall migration, suggesting that during periods of high solar activity, birds are less sensitive to the effect of geomagnetic disturbance (posterior median μωfall = − 0.025; 95% CrI = − 0.047 to − 0.003; p(< 0) = 0.99).
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 7: Space Weather Disrupts Nocturnal Bird Migration, Study Finds - Climate and Space Sciences and Engineering ---
URL: https://clasp.engin.umich.edu/2023/10/10/space-weather-disrupts-nocturnal-bird-migration-study-finds

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article reports on a University of Michigan study, published online October 9, 2023, in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), that found correlational evidence linking geomagnetic disturbances (space weather) to disruptions in nocturnal bird migration. Researchers used massive long-term datasets from 37 NEXRAD Doppler weather radar stations in the U.S. Great Plains central flyway (spanning over 1,000 miles from Texas to North Dakota) and ground-based magnetometer data from the superMAG network to test this connection.

Key findings include a 9%-17% reduction in the number of migrating birds during severe space weather events in both spring and fall, with birds that did migrate experiencing more difficulty navigating, especially under overcast conditions in autumn. The final datasets included 1.7 million radar scans from fall and 1.4 million from spring, spanning 23 years. The bird community studied was primarily composed of perching birds (Passeriformes, 73%), shorebirds (Charadriiformes, 12%), and waterfowl (Anseriformes, 9%).

The researchers used two complementary statistical models that controlled for weather, temporal, and geographic variables. They also found that migrating birds drift with the wind more frequently during fall geomagnetic disturbances, with "effort flying" against the wind reduced by 25% under cloudy skies during strong solar storms—suggesting that a combination of obscured celestial cues and magnetic disruption hinders navigation.

Lead author Eric Gulson-Castillo (doctoral student, U-M Department of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology) conducted the study as part of his dissertation. Senior author Ben Winger is an assistant professor in the U-M Department of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology and a curator of birds at the U-M Museum of Zoology. Additional authors include Benjamin Van Doren (Cornell), Kyle Horton (Colorado State), Jing Li, Mark Moldwin, and Kerby Shedden (U-M), and Michelle Bui (formerly UT Arlington). U-M Climate & Space Assistant Professor Daniel Welling and Michelle Bui compiled the space weather data and designed the geomagnetic disturbance index. Funding was provided by a U-M MCubed grant, NSF fellowships, and other sources.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Our findings highlight how animal decisions are dependent on environmental conditions—including those that we as humans cannot perceive, such as geomagnetic disturbances—and that these behaviors influence population-level patterns of animal movement," said study lead author Eric Gulson-Castillo, a doctoral student in the U-M Department of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology.
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 8: "Sunset and the Orientation Behaviour of Migrating Birds" by Frank R. Moore ---
URL: https://aquila.usm.edu/fac_pubs/14912

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a repository record from The Aquila Digital Community (University of Southern Mississippi) for the academic paper "Sunset and the Orientation Behaviour of Migrating Birds" by Frank R. Moore, published in Biological Reviews in February 1987 (Volume 62, Issue 1, pages 65-86).

**Key details:**
- **Author:** Frank R. Moore, University of Southern Mississippi, Department of Biological Sciences
- **Document type:** Article
- **Publication:** Biological Reviews, Vol. 62, Issue 1, pp. 65-86, February 1987

**Main findings/conclusions from the abstract:**
1. Migratory birds integrate directional information prior to departure, likely during the daylight-to-darkness transition, when information from the sun and other references becomes especially valuable. This is based on cage experiments with nocturnal migrants interpreted alongside field observations.
2. How migrants integrate information in selecting/maintaining a direction is not well understood—the relationship between magnetic stimuli and solar cues at sunset, and the contribution of skylight polarization patterns, remain unresolved. After selecting a heading, birds likely use stars or winds aloft to maintain it.
3. The paper proposes path analysis (a statistical method by Sewall Wright) for graphically displaying causal relations among orientation cues, noting its heuristic value and its requirement to make explicit the theoretical framework. It could help study redundancy in orientation, competing causal models, and ontogenetic changes in orientation relationships.
4. Migrants likely redetermine preferred directions after landing or before next departure rather than while aloft; solar-related information may be involved in morning orientation and re-determination of direction after night-time displacement.
5. Evidence is unclear on whether migrants use constant-angle (menotaxis) or constant-azimuth orientation at sunset.
6. How migrants identify sunset as a reference stimulus is unresolved—possibly based on spectral distribution, illumination pattern, or skylight polarization patterns.
7. Several lines of evidence suggest migrants learn to use the setting sun and associated skylight features as orientation cues.
8. The setting sun functions both as a source of directional information and as an environmental stimulus influencing the likelihood of migratory activity.

**Citation:** Moore, F. R. (1987). Sunset and the Orientation Behaviour of Migrating Birds. Biological Reviews, 62(1), 65-86. Available at: https://aquila.usm.edu/fac_pubs/14912

Full text available at: https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1469-185X.1987.tb00626.x
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
Migratory birds integrate information from a wide array of environmental sources. As our knowledge of migratory orientation depends heavily upon the results of cage‐experiments with nocturnal migrants, it is essential that the results of these cage studies be interpreted in the light of field observations of migratory behaviour and experiments with free‐flying migrants. When this is done, the impression emerges that night‐migrating birds integrate directional information prior to departure, probably during the transition between daylight and darkness.
</key_excerpts>
