--- SOURCE 9: Migrating birds: Disturbances in magnetic field suspected when birds go astray ---
URL: https://phys.org/news/2023-01-migrating-birds-disturbances-magnetic-field.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
A new study by UCLA ecologists, published January 13, 2023 in Scientific Reports, explores how disturbances to Earth's magnetic field can cause migrating birds to go astray—a phenomenon called "vagrancy"—even in perfect weather, particularly during fall migration. The research was led by doctoral student Benjamin Tonelli, with corresponding author Morgan Tingley (UCLA associate professor of ecology and evolutionary biology) and postdoctoral researcher Casey Youngflesh. The team compared data from 2.2 million birds (152 species) captured and released between 1960 and 2019 under a US Geological Survey tracking program, against historic records of geomagnetic disturbances and solar activity. They found a strong correlation between birds captured far outside their expected range and geomagnetic disturbances during both fall and spring migrations, with the effect most pronounced in fall. Notably, while the researchers expected heightened solar activity to increase vagrancy, they found solar activity actually reduced it—possibly because radiofrequency activity from solar disturbances makes birds' magnetoreceptors unusable, causing birds to either pause migration or switch to other navigation cues. Daytime-migrating birds were an exception, being more affected by solar activity. Geomagnetic disturbances affected both young and older birds equally, suggesting similar reliance on geomagnetism regardless of migration experience. Understanding vagrancy is important because with North America's bird populations declining, it helps scientists understand threats birds face and adaptation mechanisms—while vagrancy can harm birds in unfamiliar territory, it may also benefit species whose traditional habitats are becoming uninhabitable due to climate change. The methods could also help explain why other migratory species, such as whales, become stranded (the research was inspired by whale strandings). Tonelli developed a web-based tool (bentonelli.github.io/rarebirdforecast/) that tracks geomagnetic conditions and predicts vagrancy in real time. Publication: Benjamin A. Tonelli et al., "Geomagnetic disturbance associated with increased vagrancy in migratory landbirds," Scientific Reports (2023), DOI: 10.1038/s41598-022-26586-0.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"There's increasing evidence that birds can actually see geomagnetic fields," said Morgan Tingley, the paper's corresponding author and a UCLA associate professor of ecology and evolutionary biology. "In familiar areas, birds may navigate by geography, but in some situations it's easier to use geomagnetism."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 10: The orientation of migratory birds ---

Experiments on robins and garden warblers with modified magnetic fields (using coils/magnets to shift magnetic north) provided irrefutable evidence for geomagnetic orientation. --- SOURCE 13: Magnetic orientation in migratory birds ---
URL: http://oops.uni-oldenburg.de/83/1/liemag06.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This document is the Ph.D. thesis of Miriam Liedvogel (defended September 13, 2006 at Carl von Ossietzky Universität Oldenburg, supervised by PD Dr. Henrik Mouritsen and Prof. Dr. Karl-Wilhelm Koch), titled "Magnetic orientation in migratory birds – linking behavioural phenomena with underlying molecular and neuronal mechanisms."

The thesis investigates how night-migratory birds perceive directional information from the Earth's magnetic field and how this information is processed in the brain. Using an integrative approach combining behavioral observation, molecular biology, biochemistry, biophysics, and neuroanatomy, Liedvogel's research covered the full process from the primary receptor molecule to higher brain integration centers.

KEY FINDINGS:

1. **Head-scanning behavior (Paper I):** Using a custom-built experimental setup allowing real-time monitoring under controllable magnetic field conditions, garden warblers (Sylvia borin) showed clear south-westerly orientation under natural magnetic fields but oriented randomly in zero-magnetic fields. Birds nearly tripled their head-scanning frequency in a fully compensated zero magnetic field, and showed significant increases in head-scanning just before initiating migratory restlessness. This indicated the magnetic compass sensor is in the head, and that scanning likely facilitates detection of the magnetically modulated visual pattern on the retina.

2. **Cryptochrome identification (Paper II):** Four cryptochrome family members were identified, cloned, and sequenced in the retina of migratory garden warblers: Cry1a, Cry1b, Cry2, and Cry4. Cry1a is predominantly expressed in the cytosol of ganglion cells, displaced ganglion cells, and photoreceptors. Striking differences were found between migratory and non-migratory birds: Cry1a expression was highest at night in night-migratory birds but decreased to background levels at night in non-migratory control species. Neuronal activity markers colocalized perfectly with Cry1a during night-time magnetic orientation - the first experimental demonstration of a putative light-mediated primary magnetoreceptor molecule in a bird's eye.

3. **Biophysical characterization (Paper III):** Garden warbler cryptochromes were recombinantly expressed as holoproteins (with built-in flavin cofactor) in a baculovirus/Sf9 cell system - the first successful expression of an animal cryptochrome holoprotein in a heterologous eukaryotic system. This required a novel on-column denaturation/refolding step to overcome known difficulties. Garden warbler cryptochromes are light-excited, absorb in the blue spectral range (matching wavelengths known to elicit magnetic orientation in behavioral experiments), and form radical pairs lasting approximately 10 milliseconds - sufficiently long-lived to detect Earth-strength magnetic fields.

4. **Cluster N identification (Paper IV):** Behavioral molecular mapping identified a distinct forebrain area in night-migratory birds, termed "Cluster N" ("N" for night), showing high neuronal activation at night during magnetic orientation but not during the day. Cluster N was inactive in non-migratory zebra finches (Taeniopygia guttata) and canaries (Serinus canaria). Located adjacent to or as part of the visual Wulst, covering birds' eyes with light-tight covers significantly reduced Cluster N activation to near baseline, demonstrating it is active specifically during night-vision in night-migratory birds.

5. **Lateralization and further tests (Paper V, VI):** European robins (Erithacus rubecula) showed significant dominance of Cluster N activation in the right hemisphere. Garden warblers tested under different magnetic field conditions and monochromatic red light showed no significant differences in Cluster N activation, so a definitive role in magnetic compass processing could not be confirmed. Additional analysis found positive correlations between movement and activity levels in 10 cerebral regions and parts of the cerebellum, supporting the hypothesis that vocal learning brain systems evolved from a pre-existing motor pathway.

METHODS: Experiments relied on careful behavioral observation (especially the final 60 minutes before tissue collection), followed by brain dissection, cryostat sectioning, radioactive in situ hybridization for neuronal activity mapping (using immediate early genes like c-Fos and ZENK), and immunohistochemistry for retinal tissue. Primary study species were garden warblers and European robins; control species were zebra finches, canaries, and Sardinian warblers (Sylvia melanocephala).

CONCLUSION: All findings support a light-mediated magnetoperception mechanism in night-migratory birds, consistent with the hypothesis that magnetically modulated intensity patterns are perceived by the visual system - i.e., night-migratory birds may literally "see" the direction of the Earth's magnetic field. The thesis comprises six manuscripts (three published, one submitted, one under review, one near submission) plus supplementary materials on cryptochrome cloning methodology.

The authors defend their earlier literature review (Muheim et al. 2006a) which concluded that migratory birds recalibrate their magnetic compass relative to celestial cues when they have a view of the sky down to the horizon at sunrise or sunset. When the horizon view was obstructed (e.g., in orientation funnels or registration cages), birds instead recalibrated celestial cues relative to the magnetic field.

Key methodological points and arguments include:
- Their own experiments with Savannah Sparrows (Passerculus sandwichensis) in Alaska and White-throated Sparrows (Zonotrichia albicollis) in New York State demonstrated that a 1-hour exposure to a rotated polarization axis at sunrise or sunset caused recalibration of the magnetic compass.

- They address Wiltschko et al.'s claim about "overcompensation" in homing pigeons, noting alternative interpretations via Phillips and Waldvogel (1988).

--- SOURCE 23: Avian Navigation and Orientation ---
URL: https://avesbiology.com/nav_orient.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage provides a comprehensive scientific overview of avian navigation and orientation mechanisms. It distinguishes between orientation (moving in a compass direction) and true navigation (locating one's position relative to a destination), based on the two-step process first described by Kramer (1953, 1957): determining the correct direction of travel and identifying that direction. Naïve juvenile birds often rely on vector navigation (maintaining a direction for a set time/distance), while experienced adults demonstrate true navigation, as shown in displacement experiments with European Starlings (Perdeck 1958), Common Teal (Wolff 1970), and White-crowned Sparrows (Thorup et al. 2007). Some species' juveniles can compensate for displacement, however. The "clock-and-compass" concept explains how first-time migrants navigate, potentially using magnetic and photoperiodic beacons (Chernetsov and Utvenko 2025). True navigation is likely based on a bi-coordinate grid system using cues that vary along gradients (Thorup and Holland 2009).

The webpage details four compass mechanisms:
1. **Non-compass orientation**: Birds use landmarks and topographic features like coastlines and mountain ridges (e.g., European migrants turning southwest along the Alps).
2. **Star compass**: Emlen's classic planetarium experiments (1967) showed Indigo Buntings learn north by observing stellar rotation around the celestial pole, using Emlen funnels to record orientation. Star-compass use is learned, not innate, and relies on relative constellations rather than specific stars.
3. **Sun compass**: First demonstrated by Kramer (1950); based on the sun's azimuth using an internal clock. Clock-shifting experiments (Schmidt-Koenig 1958) caused 90-degree orientation errors. Learning is tied to the left hippocampus (Gagliardo et al. 2005), with pigeons first able to use it around 12 weeks old.
4. **Polarized light**: Several migratory species (Savannah Sparrows, Swainson's and Gray-cheeked thrushes, White-throated Sparrows) use polarization patterns at sunrise/sunset to calibrate their magnetic compass.
5. **Magnetic cues**: First proposed in 1859 and experimentally demonstrated in 1968 (European Robins). The avian magnetic compass is an inclination compass (distinguishing pole vs. equator, not north vs. south) and is light-dependent, based on cryptochrome molecules in the retina (Mouritsen et al. 2004). Cluster N in the forebrain processes magnetic visual information. Wu and Dickman (2012) identified vestibular brainstem neurons encoding magnetic field direction, intensity, and polarity. Nordmann et al. (2025) traced pigeon magnetoreception to hair cells in inner ear semicircular canals via electromagnetic induction, with signals processed in vestibular nuclei, midbrain cortex, and hippocampus. Iron-oxide magnetoreceptors in the upper beak (maghemite platelets and magnetite clusters) may act as a three-axis magnetometer for detecting field intensity and direction.

For true navigation, birds need "map" information. Mechanisms include visual landmark recognition (used by homing pigeons and food-caching species), path integration (dead reckoning), olfactory cues (studied in homing pigeons with conflicting results; possibly used by tube-nosed seabirds via dimethyl sulfide), and infrasound maps (found implausible due to diffuse sources). The most likely navigational system is bi-coordinate magnetic mapping, using magnetic inclination (for latitude) and intensity (for longitude). A notable example is displaced European Reed Warblers in northwestern Russia that corrected their spring migration direction after longitudinal displacement (Chernetsov et al. 2008), demonstrating use of a magnetic grid map.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"True navigation, as first described by Kramer (1953, 1957), is a two-step process: (1) determining the correct direction of travel, and (2) being able to correctly identify that direction."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 24: A Stellar Migrant | Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute ---
URL: https://nationalzoo.si.edu/migratory-birds/news/stellar-migrant

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Smithsonian National Zoo & Migratory Bird Center article (written by scientist Mary Deinlein) about the Indigo Bunting, a migratory songbird of the eastern United States and southeastern Canada. Key facts include:

- The male indigo bunting is brilliant cobalt blue, but this color results not from pigment but from diffraction of light through feather structure (appearing turquoise in some light, almost black in others); females are dull brown.
- Its range has expanded since the 1940s and it is more abundant now than when the Mayflower docked, due to its preference for abandoned fields, forest clearings, and brushy woodland edges.
- Older males arrive first (late April to mid May), stake out territories, and females arrive about 2 weeks later. Pairs raise up to 3 broods per season.
- Despite appearing monogamous, genetic analyses show 20-40% of buntings are fathered by males other than the territory holder, and about 15% of breeding males have up to 4 females on their territory.
- 80% of males learn their song by imitating an older territorial male during their first spring; matching a neighbor's song increases mating and fledging success, creating regional dialects.
- Between mid-August and November, they migrate up to 2,000 miles to winter in southern Mexico, the West Indies, and northern South America (some in southernmost Florida). In winter they lose their blue plumage, molt to brown, and switch diet from insects/spiders to seeds and buds, forming large flocks.
- Scientific significance: In the 1960s, Stephen Emlen demonstrated (using outdoor and planetarium experiments, and the Zugunruhe migration restlessness behavior) that indigo buntings use the pattern of stars near the North Star as a compass for migration. Young buntings learn this pattern during their first summer. Later experiments on various species revealed birds also use other cues: position of the setting sun and polarized light, the earth's magnetic field, odors, wind, and topographic features.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The brilliant blue of male indigo buntings results not from pigment but rather from the diffraction of light through the structure of the feathers." "20-40% of the buntings born in a season are fathered by males other than the holder of the territory in which the young are born." "80% of males learn their particular song by imitating an older male with an established territory during their first spring." "In the 1960's, Stephen Emlen cleverly demonstrated in experiments conducted outdoors and in a planetarium that indigo buntings, like sailors of yore, use the pattern of the stars as a compass." "The stars are but one of several cues that birds rely on for orientation. Other sources of information include the position of the setting sun and the pattern of polarized light it creates, the earth's magnetic field, odors, wind, and topographic features such as mountains and bodies of water."
</key_excerpts>

URL: https://www.birdwatching.com/stories/indigobunting-stars.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Birdwatching Dot Com, written by Diane Porter, explains how Indigo Buntings navigate during migration using the stars. The piece begins with the author's personal observation of an Indigo Bunting leaving her Iowa yard for Central America in fall, while winter birds like Purple Finches, Red-breasted Nuthatches, and Dark-eyed Juncos arrive and return to familiar spots. The core scientific content focuses on a 1967 study by ornithologist Stephen Emlen, who raised baby Indigo Buntings in a planetarium. Instead of rotating the artificial sky around the Pole Star, Emlen rotated it around Betelgeuse in Orion. When the buntings matured, they felt impelled to fly away from Betelgeuse, behaving as if they had formed a concept of "south" as the direction opposite Betelgeuse's position. Emlen concluded that baby Indigo Buntings naturally study the night sky from their nests, noticing that stars near the Pole Star move slowest and trace small circles around it, giving them a lifelong map and compass for migration. The article closes with the author's hope that young migrating buntings will successfully return north, find mates, and raise young.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"In 1967, ornithologist Stephen Emlen published his study of how Indigo Buntings learn to navigate. He raised baby Indigo Buntings in a planetarium. Instead of circling the Pole Star, Emlen's artificial night sky rotated about Betelgeuse, a star in Orion." "When his baby Indigo Buntings grew up, and the time for migration approached, they felt impelled to fly away from Betelgeuse. They behaved as if they had formed a concept of 'south,' as the direction opposite the place that Betelgeuse occupied in the sky." "They notice that the stars close to the Pole Star move the slowest, tracing the path of a small circle around that star. From then on, the night sky is map and compass for them." "Many birds navigate by the sun. Others use landmarks, such as lakes. Birds who migrate at night, however, must rely on darker devices."

--- SOURCE 1: Migration Monitoring with Automated Technology ---
URL: https://research.fs.usda.gov/download/treesearch/32078.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper, presented at the Third International Partners in Flight Conference (March 20-24, 2002, Asilomar, California), examines how automated technology can supplement ground-based methods of migration monitoring. The author, Rhonda L. Millikin, argues that automated technology can provide: (1) unbiased and automated sampling; (2) independent validation of current methods; (3) a larger sample area for landscape-level analysis of stopover habitat selection; and (4) an opportunity to study flight behavior. Specifically, radar-acoustic sensor fusion can provide species-specific landing behavior data to indicate what portion of the population passing over a site is available for ground-based monitoring via mist-net capture or census.

The paper reviews five key technologies: long-range radar (e.g., WSR-88D weather radar with 230 km range), short-range radar (X-band surveillance radar with 0-5 km range and individual bird resolution), acoustic-sensing (e.g., BirdCast® for traffic rates), acoustic-location (for landing/nesting sites and flight paths), and infrared. Each has limitations (e.g., no species info for radar, non-vocal individuals missed by acoustics, weather limitations for infrared/acoustic).

Key findings from the author's research at Prince Edward Point, Ontario (August-September 1999) include: most migration occurred below 300m; a larger proportion of birds flew below 300m at dawn but many also flew below 200m at midnight; 13% of midnight migrants flew in a reversed northerly direction (indicating landing behavior); and birds dispersing straight up at dusk reached heights up to 660m. Using radar-acoustic fusion, the author demonstrated that Swainson's Thrushes experienced Lake Ontario as a barrier and reversed direction to land at Prince Edward Point.

Methods and applications: Short-range radar was adapted (patented) to provide height information using a tilted antenna and neutral regression. Acoustic-location was co-located with radar tracks—of 129 tracks, 28 were co-located with acoustic calls. Data showed passerines migrate in loosely spaced, multi-species flocks, with same-species birds flying together showing greater similarity in flight speed.

Recommended approach for migration monitoring networks: (1) use long-range radar to determine funneling routes; (2) use short-range radar fused with acoustic-location to identify preferred landing sites of priority species; (3) situate mist-nets and census routes within the range of the radar-acoustic system. Costs of adding automated radar-acoustic data would be 1-3 times the cost of a volunteer-based mist-netting program (sensor fusion estimated at $85K CDN vs $27K for traditional mist-netting; relative cost of 3 vs 1).

Capture rate analysis showed very low mist-net capture rates for Partners in Flight-Canada priority species (e.g., Bicknell's Thrush at 0.042/100 net-hours across 4 stations), suggesting automation could significantly augment population samples. Key literature contributions include Zehnder et al. (2001) finding weather explained two-thirds of variation in migration intensity, and Nisbet et al. (1995) showing 19 of 25 papers supporting transoceanic Blackpoll Warbler flights came from radar studies.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Automated technology can supplement ground-based methods of migration monitoring by providing: (1) unbiased and automated sampling; (2) independent validation of current methods; (3) a larger sample area for landscape-level analysis of habitat selection for stopover, and (4) an opportunity to study flight behavior."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Space Weather Disrupts Nocturnal Bird Migration, Study Finds ---
URL: https://clasp.engin.umich.edu/2023/10/10/space-weather-disrupts-nocturnal-bird-migration-study-finds

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article reports on a University of Michigan study, published online October 9, 2023, in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), that found correlational evidence linking geomagnetic disturbances (space weather) to disruptions in nocturnal bird migration. Researchers used massive long-term datasets from 37 NEXRAD Doppler weather radar stations in the U.S. Great Plains central flyway (spanning over 1,000 miles from Texas to North Dakota) and ground-based magnetometer data from the superMAG network to test this connection.

Key findings include a 9%-17% reduction in the number of migrating birds during severe space weather events in both spring and fall, with birds that did migrate experiencing more difficulty navigating, especially under overcast conditions in autumn. The final datasets included 1.7 million radar scans from fall and 1.4 million from spring, spanning 23 years. The bird community studied was primarily composed of perching birds (Passeriformes, 73%), shorebirds (Charadriiformes, 12%), and waterfowl (Anseriformes, 9%).

The researchers used two complementary statistical models that controlled for weather, temporal, and geographic variables. They also found that migrating birds drift with the wind more frequently during fall geomagnetic disturbances, with "effort flying" against the wind reduced by 25% under cloudy skies during strong solar storms—suggesting that a combination of obscured celestial cues and magnetic disruption hinders navigation.

Lead author Eric Gulson-Castillo (doctoral student, U-M Department of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology) conducted the study as part of his dissertation. Senior author Ben Winger is an assistant professor in the U-M Department of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology and a curator of birds at the U-M Museum of Zoology. Additional authors include Benjamin Van Doren (Cornell), Kyle Horton (Colorado State), Jing Li, Mark Moldwin, and Kerby Shedden (U-M), and Michelle Bui (formerly UT Arlington). U-M Climate & Space Assistant Professor Daniel Welling and Michelle Bui compiled the space weather data and designed the geomagnetic disturbance index. Funding was provided by a U-M MCubed grant, NSF fellowships, and other sources.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Our findings highlight how animal decisions are dependent on environmental conditions—including those that we as humans cannot perceive, such as geomagnetic disturbances—and that these behaviors influence population-level patterns of animal movement," said study lead author Eric Gulson-Castillo, a doctoral student in the U-M Department of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology.
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Weather Radar Predicts Nighttime Bird Migrations ---
URL: https://www.aaas.org/news/weather-radar-predicts-nighttime-bird-migrations

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from AAAS (published around September 2018, reporting on findings in the September 14 issue of Science) describes a new forecasting model that uses weather radar data combined with machine learning to predict nighttime bird migrations across North America up to a week in advance. The study, led by Benjamin Van Doren of the University of Oxford with co-author Kyle Horton of Cornell University, used the meteorological Next-Generation Radar (NEXRAD) network combined with climate models to accurately predict the timing, intensity, and location of nocturnal migration events, as well as estimate nightly bird numbers. In early May, when temperatures warm, more than 500 million migratory songbirds take flight each night in North America.

The researchers combed through 23 years of spring migration radar data, using machine learning to automate the identification of bird signatures amid chaotic background signals like precipitation and insect swarms. The model's predictions could reduce bird deaths from human activities—over 630 million birds die annually in the U.S. from collisions with buildings, towers, and vehicles, and bird strikes cause at least $1.2 billion in annual aircraft damage worldwide (including the 2009 "miracle on the Hudson" incident). Predictions could also help wind turbine operators shut down turbines or turn off lights during large flights, and help track the spread of avian-borne diseases.

Most North American songbirds (warblers, sparrows, thrushes) migrate at night to take advantage of cooler, more stable atmospheres, allowing daylight hours for foraging at stopover sites. Migratory bird populations in North America are in decline, mostly due to habitat loss. The study demonstrates the value of "big data" ecology research in understanding the complex drivers of avian migration, which involve navigation, timing, wind, food availability, and environmental conditions like temperature, atmospheric pressure, and precipitation.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Birds must navigate accurately using multiple cues, time their journeys precisely, deal with winds that may blow them off course, find food in transient and unfamiliar environments, and often re-engineer their bodies to store energy and save weight," said Van Doren.
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: Using artificial intelligence to track birds' dark-of-night migrations ---
URL: https://phys.org/news/2019-08-artificial-intelligence-track-birds-dark-of-night.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On August 28, 2019, researchers from the University of Massachusetts Amherst and the Cornell Lab of Ornithology announced the development of "MistNet," a new machine learning tool (based on convolutional neural networks) designed to extract bird migration data from the massive archive of National Weather Service weather radar data. For decades, tens of millions of birds have flown at night during spring and fall migrations and been recorded by constantly scanning weather radars, but the sheer volume of data—over 200 million images and hundreds of terabytes spanning more than two decades—made analysis nearly impossible for ornithologists.

Led by UMass AI researchers Dan Sheldon (senior author), Subhransu Maji (senior author), and Tsung-Yu Lin (lead author), the team built MistNet to "remove the rain and keep the birds," effectively automating the discrimination between precipitation and birds in radar images. The tool automates processing of radar data that has measured bird migration over the continental U.S. for over two decades.

Key features and findings of the work, published in Methods in Ecology and Evolution (DOI: 10.1111/2041-210X.13280):
- MistNet was validated through a large-scale comparison against competing approaches using two evaluation datasets, and its results compare excellently with human analysis.
- The tool allowed researchers to create maps of where and when migration occurred over the past 24 years, identifying the most intensive migration corridor roughly along and just west of the Mississippi River, based on measurements at 143 radar stations.
- MistNet also enables estimation of flying velocity and traffic rates of migrating birds.
- The work was partly supported by a National Science Foundation grant to Sheldon.

Researchers hope MistNet will enable conservation applications, such as turning off skyscraper lights on the few nights of the season when migration is concentrated, and studying the phenology of bird migration to understand whether timing and access to food have shifted with climate change. The tool also helps scientists use the "explosion" of large new datasets from citizen science projects like eBird, animal tracking devices, and earth observation instruments.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"This is a really important advance. Our results are excellent compared with humans working by hand. It allows us to go from limited 20th-century insights to 21st-century knowledge and conservation action." - AI researcher Dan Sheldon at UMass Amherst. "Deep learning has revolutionized the ability of computers to mimic humans in solving similar recognition tasks for images, video and audio." - Sheldon and co-authors. "We hope MistNet will enable a range of science and conservation applications. For example, we see in many places that a large amount of migration is concentrated on a few nights of the season... Knowing this, maybe we could aid birds by turning off skyscraper lights on those nights." - Dan Sheldon.
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 5: Record-breaking Night of Bird Migration Detected with Radar ---
URL: https://www.birds.cornell.edu/home/record-breaking-night-of-bird-migration

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On September 25-26, 2025, a record-breaking night of bird migration was detected using radar by BirdCast, a collaborative platform using weather radar and machine learning to track migrating birds. BirdCast tracked more than 1.2 billion birds streaming south to their wintering grounds after sunset Thursday—the largest single-night total ever recorded since the project began mapping live migrations in 2018. This surpasses the previous milestone of one billion birds, first observed in October 2023.

According to Andrew Farnsworth, a visiting scientist at the Cornell Lab of Ornithology and longtime BirdCast researcher, this seemingly rare night captured about 10% of the continent's birds in flight at the same time, roughly three times the average of 400 million birds detected on typical fall nights during peak migration. Farnsworth noted the event was not random but resulted from a combination of ideal migrating conditions coinciding with the peak of fall migration, including calm winds and tail winds that helped push birds along their migratory paths across much of the center of the country and the Mississippi River valley.

BirdCast is a collaborative research project involving the Cornell Lab of Ornithology, Purdue University, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, and University of Massachusetts Amherst. The platform provides freely accessible real-time data, with forecast maps predicting bird migration numbers and live migration maps showing migration in real time, allowing the public to take precautions to protect birds.

The article also serves as a reminder about bird safety: every year, more than one billion birds die in collisions with windows in the United States. Bright lights can disorient birds migrating at night, drawing them into areas where collisions with glass are common. Recommended measures include turning off nonessential lights at night and adding bird-friendly film or markings spaced no more than two inches apart on the outside of windows. More information is available at stopbirdcollisions.org.

Media contact: Kathi Borgmann, Cornell Lab of Ornithology, (607) 254-2137, klb274@cornell.edu.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"These numbers are almost inconceivable," said Andrew Farnsworth, a visiting scientist at the Cornell Lab of Ornithology and longtime BirdCast researcher. "They're enormous. They grab your attention, even for people that study migration regularly. The scale of how many organisms that this represents, it is just mind blowing." "It's really unbelievable," he said. "BirdCast gives the ability for more people to engage in and participate in this incredible spectacle," Farnsworth said, "and understand that it's happening."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 6: Geomagnetic disturbance associated with increased vagrancy in migratory landbirds | Scientific Reports ---
URL: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-022-26586-0

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific article (published in Scientific Reports, 2023) investigates the association between geomagnetic disturbance and avian vagrancy in migratory landbirds. The researchers hypothesized that errors in orientation or navigation caused by disruption to the Earth's magnetic field could lead birds astray, as migratory birds use magnetoreception—sensing the Earth's magnetic field via specialized magnetoreceptor structures—to traverse long distances.

METHODOLOGY: The study analyzed 2,226,936 banding records of 152 migratory landbird species in North America (150 species in fall, 124 in spring) from 1960 to 2019, combining USGS Bird Banding Lab data with eBird Status and Trends weekly species abundance maps. Instead of using binary vagrancy classification, they created a continuous "vagrancy index" measuring the spatiotemporal rarity of each banding record relative to modeled expected species ranges. Using hierarchical Bayesian random-effects models, they tested associations with geomagnetic disturbance (global Ap index) and solar activity (American relative sunspot number).

KEY RESULTS:
- Strong positive association between geomagnetic disturbance and vagrancy during fall migration (posterior median = 0.109; 95% CrI = 0.077–0.142; p(>0) = 1). Typically, a two-standard-deviation increase in geomagnetic disturbance is associated with a 24% increase in median predicted vagrancy index and a 250% increase in the number of spatiotemporally rare banding records (from 2% to 5% of records).
- 83% of species showed positive sensitivity to geomagnetic disturbance in fall.
- Sensitivity to geomagnetic disturbance was stronger among longer-distance migrants (supporting the hypothesis that long-distance migrants rely more on magnetoreception), but no effect of breeding latitude was found.
- Hatch-year (juvenile) birds showed higher baseline fall vagrancy than adults, but were NOT more sensitive to geomagnetic disturbance.
- Only weak or no evidence for associations during spring migration, potentially due to sampling biases (banding sites preferentially capture birds near breeding sites late in migration).
- Contrary to hypotheses, increased solar activity was negatively associated with fall vagrancy (potential mitigation effect). An interaction model showed strong evidence for a negative interaction during fall—during high solar activity, birds are less sensitive to geomagnetic disturbance, suggesting radiofrequency noise disables magnetoreception, causing birds to pause migration or switch to other cues.
- Diurnal migrants (24% of fall species) were more sensitive to solar activity than nocturnal migrants, possibly because solar radiofrequency noise affects the sunlit side of Earth; this may explain previously observed negative effects of solar activity on crane migration.

IMPLICATIONS: Geomagnetic disturbance and solar activity explained a median of 5.9% of variance in vagrancy (species-specific range 0.3–30%), meaning other factors (weather, population fluctuations, etc.) explain 70% to >99% depending on species. The authors note geomagnetic disturbance may have downstream ecological consequences, as vagrants may experience increased mortality or facilitate range expansions of avian populations and the organisms they disperse. The findings provide macroecological evidence supporting the widespread importance of magnetoreception in migratory landbirds.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
Using data from 2 million captures of 152 landbird species in North America over 60 years, we demonstrate a strong association between disruption to the Earth's magnetic field and avian vagrancy during fall migration., We found, with high confidence, that vagrancy across North American landbirds is associated with increased geomagnetic disturbance in the fall migration season (posterior median ωfall,geom. dist. = 0.109; 95% credible interval (CrI) = 0.077 to 0.142; proportion of posterior p(> 0) = 1)., For the typical species... an increase in geomagnetic disturbance of two standard deviations above average conditions is associated with a 24% increase in the median predicted vagrancy index of all records and a 250% increase in the number of spatiotemporally rare banding records (from 2% of all records at average geomagnetic disturbance to 5% under elevated conditions)., Results from this interaction model provide strong evidence for a negative interaction during fall migration, suggesting that during periods of high solar activity, birds are less sensitive to the effect of geomagnetic disturbance (posterior median μωfall = − 0.025; 95% CrI = − 0.047 to − 0.003; p(< 0) = 0.99).
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 7: "Sunset and the Orientation Behaviour of Migrating Birds" by Frank R. Moore ---
URL: https://aquila.usm.edu/fac_pubs/14912

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a repository record from The Aquila Digital Community (University of Southern Mississippi) for the academic paper "Sunset and the Orientation Behaviour of Migrating Birds" by Frank R. Moore, published in Biological Reviews in February 1987 (Volume 62, Issue 1, pages 65-86).

**Key details:**
- **Author:** Frank R. Moore, University of Southern Mississippi, Department of Biological Sciences
- **Document type:** Article
- **Publication:** Biological Reviews, Vol. 62, Issue 1, pp. 65-86, February 1987

**Main findings/conclusions from the abstract:**
1. Migratory birds integrate directional information prior to departure, likely during the daylight-to-darkness transition, when information from the sun and other references becomes especially valuable. This is based on cage experiments with nocturnal migrants interpreted alongside field observations.
2. How migrants integrate information in selecting/maintaining a direction is not well understood—the relationship between magnetic stimuli and solar cues at sunset, and the contribution of skylight polarization patterns, remain unresolved. After selecting a heading, birds likely use stars or winds aloft to maintain it.
3. The paper proposes path analysis (a statistical method by Sewall Wright) for graphically displaying causal relations among orientation cues, noting its heuristic value and its requirement to make explicit the theoretical framework. It could help study redundancy in orientation, competing causal models, and ontogenetic changes in orientation relationships.
4. Migrants likely redetermine preferred directions after landing or before next departure rather than while aloft; solar-related information may be involved in morning orientation and re-determination of direction after night-time displacement.
5. Evidence is unclear on whether migrants use constant-angle (menotaxis) or constant-azimuth orientation at sunset.
6. How migrants identify sunset as a reference stimulus is unresolved—possibly based on spectral distribution, illumination pattern, or skylight polarization patterns.
7. Several lines of evidence suggest migrants learn to use the setting sun and associated skylight features as orientation cues.
8. The setting sun functions both as a source of directional information and as an environmental stimulus influencing the likelihood of migratory activity.

**Citation:** Moore, F. R. (1987). Sunset and the Orientation Behaviour of Migrating Birds. Biological Reviews, 62(1), 65-86. Available at: https://aquila.usm.edu/fac_pubs/14912

Full text available at: https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1469-185X.1987.tb00626.x
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
Migratory birds integrate information from a wide array of environmental sources. As our knowledge of migratory orientation depends heavily upon the results of cage‐experiments with nocturnal migrants, it is essential that the results of these cage studies be interpreted in the light of field observations of migratory behaviour and experiments with free‐flying migrants. When this is done, the impression emerges that night‐migrating birds integrate directional information prior to departure, probably during the transition between daylight and darkness.
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 8: Migrating birds: Disturbances in magnetic field suspected when birds go astray ---
URL: https://phys.org/news/2023-01-migrating-birds-disturbances-magnetic-field.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
A new study by UCLA ecologists, published January 13, 2023 in Scientific Reports, explores how disturbances to Earth's magnetic field can cause migrating birds to go astray—a phenomenon called "vagrancy"—even in perfect weather, particularly during fall migration. The research was led by doctoral student Benjamin Tonelli, with corresponding author Morgan Tingley (UCLA associate professor of ecology and evolutionary biology) and postdoctoral researcher Casey Youngflesh. The team compared data from 2.2 million birds (152 species) captured and released between 1960 and 2019 under a US Geological Survey tracking program, against historic records of geomagnetic disturbances and solar activity. They found a strong correlation between birds captured far outside their expected range and geomagnetic disturbances during both fall and spring migrations, with the effect most pronounced in fall. Notably, while the researchers expected heightened solar activity to increase vagrancy, they found solar activity actually reduced it—possibly because radiofrequency activity from solar disturbances makes birds' magnetoreceptors unusable, causing birds to either pause migration or switch to other navigation cues. Daytime-migrating birds were an exception, being more affected by solar activity. Geomagnetic disturbances affected both young and older birds equally, suggesting similar reliance on geomagnetism regardless of migration experience. Understanding vagrancy is important because with North America's bird populations declining, it helps scientists understand threats birds face and adaptation mechanisms—while vagrancy can harm birds in unfamiliar territory, it may also benefit species whose traditional habitats are becoming uninhabitable due to climate change. The methods could also help explain why other migratory species, such as whales, become stranded (the research was inspired by whale strandings). Tonelli developed a web-based tool (bentonelli.github.io/rarebirdforecast/) that tracks geomagnetic conditions and predicts vagrancy in real time. Publication: Benjamin A. Tonelli et al., "Geomagnetic disturbance associated with increased vagrancy in migratory landbirds," Scientific Reports (2023), DOI: 10.1038/s41598-022-26586-0.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"There's increasing evidence that birds can actually see geomagnetic fields," said Morgan Tingley, the paper's corresponding author and a UCLA associate professor of ecology and evolutionary biology. "In familiar areas, birds may navigate by geography, but in some situations it's easier to use geomagnetism."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 9: The orientation of migratory birds ---
URL: https://www.encyclopedie-environnement.org/en/life/orientation-migratory-birds

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific article from the Encyclopedia of the Environment (by Jacques Blondel, published January 17, 2025) explains how migratory birds orient themselves during migrations that can span nearly 10,000 km. The core premise is that bird orientation relies on a combination of genetically determined mechanisms, including an "internal calendar" and an "internal compass."

**Basic principles:** Navigation involves setting and maintaining a heading regardless of hazards. Very young birds migrate alone in their first year, proving orientation mechanisms are innate/genetically determined. Remarkable fidelity is documented — e.g., a barn swallow (Hirundo rustica) traveled between South Africa and a stable in Germany for three years with accuracy of a few metres. Most small migratory passerines fly at night, covering 300–600 km per night at 40–50 km/h, relying on a magnetic compass as their basic tool effective in all weather.

**Orientation mechanisms** (discovered through experiments beginning in the 1950s):
- **Solar compass:** Gustav Kramer's orientation cage experiments (Figure 3-5) showed sun position is used as a directional cue. Shifting a bird's internal clock by 6 hours caused a 90° error in flight direction; a 12-hour shift caused 180° reversal (heading north in autumn). Used by diurnal migrants (white storks, large birds of prey), but useless for nocturnal migrants.
- **Night-time compasses (moon and stars):** Franz Sauer (1950s) discovered birds orient using the moon and stars. The "Zugunruhe" (migratory restlessness) behavior at dusk marks migration onset. Franz Sauer and later Stephen T. Emlen (planetarium experiments, Figure 8) demonstrated that birds align with constellations, adjust for their movement during the night, and can be made to "somersault" when the sky was rotated 180°. Birds recalibrate their stellar compass using their magnetic compass, and must "read" new star configurations when crossing the equator.
- **Earth's magnetic field:** Radar studies in the 1950s showed nocturnal migrants oriented correctly even under overcast skies. Kramer proposed a two-stage navigation model (a "mental map" plus a "compass"). Experiments on robins and garden warblers with modified magnetic fields (using coils/magnets to shift magnetic north) provided irrefutable evidence for geomagnetic orientation. Geomagnetism is the only reliable source when all visual references fail.
- **Mental maps:** Birds use geo-topographical landmarks (mountain ranges, river corridors, valleys, passes, coastal strips) as a mosaic of waypoints. Radar observations show wind-driven birds can reorient back to their course after turbulence; birds also exploit favorable winds for massive migratory flows.
- **Positioning in time and space:** Two genetically integrated programmes exist: a temporal programme (correct orientation for a given journey duration) and a spatial programme (appropriate direction that can change along the way). 2. **Cryptochrome identification (Paper II):** Four cryptochrome family members were identified, cloned, and sequenced in the retina of migratory garden warblers: Cry1a, Cry1b, Cry2, and Cry4. Cry1a is predominantly expressed in the cytosol of ganglion cells, displaced ganglion cells, and photoreceptors. Striking differences were found between migratory and non-migratory birds: Cry1a expression was highest at night in night-migratory birds but decreased to background levels at night in non-migratory control species. Introduction 1 Hatchet Ridge Nocturnal Migration Study INTRODUCTION Wind energy is one of the fastest growing sources of energy production in the United States (GAO 2005). Studies examining the impacts of windfarms on birds in the United States and Europe suggest that fatalities and behavioral modifications (e.g., avoidance of windfarms) occur in some, but not all, locations (Winkelman 1995, Anderson et al. 1999, Erickson et al. 2001). In the United States both resident and migratory birds sometimes collide with wind turbines (Erickson 2004, NWCC 2004) with the overall fatality rate being similar (~2.3–3.5 avian fatalities/MW/yr) on a regional scale in the United States (NRC 2007).
The makeup of these fatalities varies for some species groups, although passerines (“songbirds”) comprise ~ 70–85% of the known bird collisions at wind power developments throughout the US (Erickson et al. 2001, Strickland and Johnson 2006). Neotropical migratory species of passerines such as thrushes (Turdidae), vireos (Vireonidae), and warblers (Parulidae) have a long history of colliding with above-ground structures (Kerlinger 2000, Longcore et al. 2005) and seem to be the most vulnerable to collisions during their nocturnal migrations (Manville 2005). This pattern also holds true at wind-energy developments, with ~50% of the fatalities at windfarms involving nocturnal passerine migrants (Erickson et al.
2001). This makes sense both because of poorer visibility at night and because passerines tend to migrate at lower altitudes than do other groups of birds (e.g., shorebirds, waterfowl; Kerlinger 1995, Alerstam 1990).
The paucity of general information on nocturnal bird migration in most areas has generated interest in conducting preconstruction studies of nocturnal migration at the growing number of proposed wind power developments throughout the country (CEC guidelines, Kunz et al. 2007a). Consideration of potential wind power impacts on nocturnal bird migration is particularly important because more birds migrate at night than during the daytime (Gauthreaux 1975, Kerlinger 1995) and frequently a large proportion (ranging from 0–80%) of the fatalities at wind-energy developments are from nocturnal passerine migrants (Erickson et al. 2001).
Bat fatalities have also occurred at wind farms in the United States with recent data from Appalachian ridgetops in the eastern US (Arnett 2005, Erickson 2004, Kerns 2004, Kunz et al.
2007a), the Tug Hill Plateau region in New York (Jain et al. 2007), prairie locations in both the US and Canada (see references in Barclay et al. 2007, Kunz et al. 2007a), indicating that substantial bat kills are possible at some wind power projects.
Most of the bat fatalities documented at windfarms have been associated with migratory tree-roosting species during seasonal periods of dispersal and migration and the majority of these collisions occurred during the late summer and fall migratory periods (Arnett 2005, Barclay et al. 2007, Kunz et al. 2007a). There are many hypotheses as to why bats may collide with wind turbines (Kunz et al.
2007a) and ongoing research may yield patterns at a later point in time.
Hatchet Ridge Wind, LLC proposes to develop the Hatchet Ridge Wind Project (HRWP), a ~100 MW wind power development in Shasta County in northern California (Fig. 1). The development would consist of ~42 wind turbines, each with a generating capacity of up to ~2.4 MW.
Characteristics of the proposed wind turbines include a monopole tower ~80 m in height and three rotor blades each extending ~47.5 m equating to a rotor area ~95 m in diameter. Thus, the total maximal height of each turbine will be ~127.5 m with a blade in the vertical position.
The proposed HRWP is located in a region with little information on the migratory pathways of nocturnal migrants such as passerines and bats.
Within ~100–150 km to the north-northeast of the proposed development are a series of lakes and wildlife refuges (Fig. 1) that provide habitat for large numbers of migratory waterfowl, shorebirds, and songbirds (USFWS 1995) raising the possibility that birds from these regions may pass over HRWP en route to the Sacramento Valley and other over wintering areas during fall migration.
We conducted the current study to provide baseline information on nocturnal migrants at the proposed HRWP during fall 2007.

Objectives 3 Hatchet Ridge Nocturnal Migration Study OBJECTIVES The primary goal of this study was to collect information on the nocturnal migration patterns of targets (i.e., birds and bats) during the peak period of fall passerine migration at the proposed Hatchet Ridge Wind Project (HRWP). Specifically, the objectives of this study were to: (1) collect baseline information on migration characteristics (i.e., flight direction, migration passage rates, and flight altitudes) of nocturnal migrants; and (2) determine the number of targets that would pass within the rotor-swept area of the proposed wind turbines during the migratory season. We also evaluated the influence of weather on migration passage rates and flight altitudes.
STUDY AREA The proposed Hatchet Ridge Wind Project (HRWP) is located along Hatchet Ridge in a rural area of Shasta County in northern California (Fig. 1). The development is located ~8 km west of the town of Burney, California and ~64 km northeast of Redding, California. Highway 299 runs along the southern boundary of the project area. Hatchet Ridge is situated along the southern edge of the Cascade Range. The general orientation of the ridgeline is northwest to southeast and elevations within the project area range from ~1,670 m asl in the northwest section to ~1,310 m asl in the southern portion near Hatchet Mountain Pass. The topography of the project area is primarily flat, broad ridge-top with moderate to steep side slopes. Average annual rain fall is ~127 cm and the average annual temperature is ~6°C.
The natural dominant vegetation community is mixed conifer that includes a combination of white fir (Abies concolor), incense cedar (Calocedrus decurrens), sugar pine (Pinus lambertiana), ponderosa pine (Pinus ponderosa), Douglas-fir (Pseudotsuga menziesii), and black oak (Quercus velutina). Large portions of the ridgeline and project area burned in the Fountain Fire of 1992 and areas were replanted in 1996 with white fir and ponderosa pine.
Our study included two radar sampling stations located in open areas along Hatchet Ridge within the area of the proposed development (Fig. 2). The North station (N40.90863, W121.82530 WGS84) was located ~1,683 m asl in the northwest section of the development whereas the Saddle station (N40.88871, W121.79435 WGS84) was lower in elevation, ~1,541 m asl, and situated in the central portion of the proposed development.
METHODS STUDY DESIGN We conducted nightly radar observations at both sampling stations on 39 nights during fall 2007 (7 September to 15 October) during the general peak of passerine migration in this region (Harris 2005). This timing was chosen when it would be expected that many birds would be migrating through the area including passerines, shorebirds, waterfowl, and potentially bats.
We obtained useable data from radar observations during 36 and 34 nights at the North and Saddle stations, respectively. On the remaining nights, we were unable to conduct radar observations because of inclement weather (rain and snow). Each night we split sampling time between the two sampling stations to capture potential spatial variation in migration characteristics in the project area and we alternated the starting location on a nightly basis to reduce bias. Sampling started ~45 min after sunset and continued for a total of 7 h/night on most nights.
Our sampling schedule provided coverage during the peak hours of nocturnal passerine migration within a night (Lowery 1951, Gauthreaux 1971, Alerstam 1990, Kerlinger 1995, Mabee et al., 2006a). RADAR EQUIPMENT Our mobile radar laboratory consisted of a marine radar that was mounted on the roof of a van and that functioned as both a surveillance and vertical radar. When the antenna was in the horizontal position (i.e., in surveillance mode), the radar scanned the area surrounding the lab (Fig. 3), and we manually recorded information on flight direction, flight behavior, passage rates, and groundspeeds of targets. When the antenna was placed in the vertical position (i.e., in vertical mode), the radar scanned the area in an arc across the top of the lab (Fig. 4), and we manually measured flight altitudes of targets with an index Methods Hatchet Ridge Nocturnal Migration Study 4 Figure 2.
