--- SOURCE 5: Record-breaking Night of Bird Migration Detected with Radar ---
URL: https://www.birds.cornell.edu/home/record-breaking-night-of-bird-migration

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On September 25-26, 2025, a record-breaking night of bird migration was detected using radar by BirdCast, a collaborative platform using weather radar and machine learning to track migrating birds. BirdCast tracked more than 1.2 billion birds streaming south to their wintering grounds after sunset Thursday—the largest single-night total ever recorded since the project began mapping live migrations in 2018. This surpasses the previous milestone of one billion birds, first observed in October 2023.

According to Andrew Farnsworth, a visiting scientist at the Cornell Lab of Ornithology and longtime BirdCast researcher, this seemingly rare night captured about 10% of the continent's birds in flight at the same time, roughly three times the average of 400 million birds detected on typical fall nights during peak migration. Farnsworth noted the event was not random but resulted from a combination of ideal migrating conditions coinciding with the peak of fall migration, including calm winds and tail winds that helped push birds along their migratory paths across much of the center of the country and the Mississippi River valley.

BirdCast is a collaborative research project involving the Cornell Lab of Ornithology, Purdue University, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, and University of Massachusetts Amherst. The platform provides freely accessible real-time data, with forecast maps predicting bird migration numbers and live migration maps showing migration in real time, allowing the public to take precautions to protect birds.

The article also serves as a reminder about bird safety: every year, more than one billion birds die in collisions with windows in the United States. Bright lights can disorient birds migrating at night, drawing them into areas where collisions with glass are common. Recommended measures include turning off nonessential lights at night and adding bird-friendly film or markings spaced no more than two inches apart on the outside of windows. More information is available at stopbirdcollisions.org.

Media contact: Kathi Borgmann, Cornell Lab of Ornithology, (607) 254-2137, klb274@cornell.edu.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"These numbers are almost inconceivable," said Andrew Farnsworth, a visiting scientist at the Cornell Lab of Ornithology and longtime BirdCast researcher. "They're enormous. They grab your attention, even for people that study migration regularly. The scale of how many organisms that this represents, it is just mind blowing." "It's really unbelievable," he said. "BirdCast gives the ability for more people to engage in and participate in this incredible spectacle," Farnsworth said, "and understand that it's happening."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 6: Geomagnetic disturbance associated with increased vagrancy in migratory landbirds | Scientific Reports ---
URL: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-022-26586-0

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific article (published in Scientific Reports, 2023) investigates the association between geomagnetic disturbance and avian vagrancy in migratory landbirds. The researchers hypothesized that errors in orientation or navigation caused by disruption to the Earth's magnetic field could lead birds astray, as migratory birds use magnetoreception—sensing the Earth's magnetic field via specialized magnetoreceptor structures—to traverse long distances.

METHODOLOGY: The study analyzed 2,226,936 banding records of 152 migratory landbird species in North America (150 species in fall, 124 in spring) from 1960 to 2019, combining USGS Bird Banding Lab data with eBird Status and Trends weekly species abundance maps. Instead of using binary vagrancy classification, they created a continuous "vagrancy index" measuring the spatiotemporal rarity of each banding record relative to modeled expected species ranges. SUMMARY:

This scientific article from the Encyclopedia of the Environment (by Jacques Blondel, published January 17, 2025) explains how migratory birds orient themselves during migrations that can span nearly 10,000 km. The core premise is that bird orientation relies on a combination of genetically determined mechanisms, including an "internal calendar" and an "internal compass."

**Basic principles:** Navigation involves setting and maintaining a heading regardless of hazards. Very young birds migrate alone in their first year, proving orientation mechanisms are innate/genetically determined. Remarkable fidelity is documented — e.g., a barn swallow (Hirundo rustica) traveled between South Africa and a stable in Germany for three years with accuracy of a few metres. Most small migratory passerines fly at night, covering 300–600 km per night at 40–50 km/h, relying on a magnetic compass as their basic tool effective in all weather.

**Orientation mechanisms** (discovered through experiments beginning in the 1950s):
- **Solar compass:** Gustav Kramer's orientation cage experiments (Figure 3-5) showed sun position is used as a directional cue. Shifting a bird's internal clock by 6 hours caused a 90° error in flight direction; a 12-hour shift caused 180° reversal (heading north in autumn). Used by diurnal migrants (white storks, large birds of prey), but useless for nocturnal migrants.
- **Night-time compasses (moon and stars):** Franz Sauer (1950s) discovered birds orient using the moon and stars. The "Zugunruhe" (migratory restlessness) behavior at dusk marks migration onset. Franz Sauer and later Stephen T. Emlen (planetarium experiments, Figure 8) demonstrated that birds align with constellations, adjust for their movement during the night, and can be made to "somersault" when the sky was rotated 180°. Birds recalibrate their stellar compass using their magnetic compass, and must "read" new star configurations when crossing the equator.
- **Earth's magnetic field:** Radar studies in the 1950s showed nocturnal migrants oriented correctly even under overcast skies. Kramer proposed a two-stage navigation model (a "mental map" plus a "compass"). Experiments on robins and garden warblers with modified magnetic fields (using coils/magnets to shift magnetic north) provided irrefutable evidence for geomagnetic orientation. Geomagnetism is the only reliable source when all visual references fail.
- **Mental maps:** Birds use geo-topographical landmarks (mountain ranges, river corridors, valleys, passes, coastal strips) as a mosaic of waypoints. Radar observations show wind-driven birds can reorient back to their course after turbulence; birds also exploit favorable winds for massive migratory flows.
- **Positioning in time and space:** Two genetically integrated programmes exist: a temporal programme (correct orientation for a given journey duration) and a spatial programme (appropriate direction that can change along the way). The willow warbler (Phylloscopus trochilus) follows a NE-SW course of ~9,000 km, then abruptly changes to north-south at the Iberian Peninsula. Captive garden warblers demonstrated this "pre-programmed" directional change.

**Human use:** Carrier pigeons have been used since Ancient Egypt, sparked 19th-century competitions (notably in the US), and served as messengers in both World Wars, commemorated by a "soldier pigeon" monument in Brussels.

**Key messages:** The navigation model consists of genetically determined mechanisms in rigid sequential order, based on a mental map, astronomical compasses (sun/moon/stars), and a magnetic compass used additionally or exclusively when others fail. Orientation systems work in synergy, birds interpret wind information, and all steps follow a circannual genetically determined internal clock ("tells" birds when to reproduce, moult, migrate).
</summary>

5. **Directional asymmetry**: During migration, birds showed asymmetric responses to clockwise vs. counterclockwise (and "with sun" vs. "against sun") magnetic field shifts. 1. **Head-scanning behavior (Paper I):** Using a custom-built experimental setup allowing real-time monitoring under controllable magnetic field conditions, garden warblers (Sylvia borin) showed clear south-westerly orientation under natural magnetic fields but oriented randomly in zero-magnetic fields. Birds nearly tripled their head-scanning frequency in a fully compensated zero magnetic field, and showed significant increases in head-scanning just before initiating migratory restlessness. This indicated the magnetic compass sensor is in the head, and that scanning likely facilitates detection of the magnetically modulated visual pattern on the retina.

2. **Cryptochrome identification (Paper II):** Four cryptochrome family members were identified, cloned, and sequenced in the retina of migratory garden warblers: Cry1a, Cry1b, Cry2, and Cry4. Cry1a is predominantly expressed in the cytosol of ganglion cells, displaced ganglion cells, and photoreceptors. Striking differences were found between migratory and non-migratory birds: Cry1a expression was highest at night in night-migratory birds but decreased to background levels at night in non-migratory control species. Neuronal activity markers colocalized perfectly with Cry1a during night-time magnetic orientation - the first experimental demonstration of a putative light-mediated primary magnetoreceptor molecule in a bird's eye.

3. **Biophysical characterization (Paper III):** Garden warbler cryptochromes were recombinantly expressed as holoproteins (with built-in flavin cofactor) in a baculovirus/Sf9 cell system - the first successful expression of an animal cryptochrome holoprotein in a heterologous eukaryotic system. This required a novel on-column denaturation/refolding step to overcome known difficulties. Garden warbler cryptochromes are light-excited, absorb in the blue spectral range (matching wavelengths known to elicit magnetic orientation in behavioral experiments), and form radical pairs lasting approximately 10 milliseconds - sufficiently long-lived to detect Earth-strength magnetic fields.

4. **Cluster N identification (Paper IV):** Behavioral molecular mapping identified a distinct forebrain area in night-migratory birds, termed "Cluster N" ("N" for night), showing high neuronal activation at night during magnetic orientation but not during the day. Cluster N was inactive in non-migratory zebra finches (Taeniopygia guttata) and canaries (Serinus canaria). Located adjacent to or as part of the visual Wulst, covering birds' eyes with light-tight covers significantly reduced Cluster N activation to near baseline, demonstrating it is active specifically during night-vision in night-migratory birds.

5. **Lateralization and further tests (Paper V, VI):** European robins (Erithacus rubecula) showed significant dominance of Cluster N activation in the right hemisphere. Garden warblers tested under different magnetic field conditions and monochromatic red light showed no significant differences in Cluster N activation, so a definitive role in magnetic compass processing could not be confirmed. --- SOURCE 1: A radar study of nocturnal bird and bat migration at the ... ---
URL: https://nrm.dfg.ca.gov/FileHandler.ashx?DocumentID=23982

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a final report on radar studies of nocturnal bird and bat migration conducted from 7 September to 15 October 2007 (39 nights) at the proposed Hatchet Ridge Wind Project (HRWP) in Shasta County, California. The ~100 MW project would consist of ~42 wind turbines (each ~2.4 MW, with 80-m towers and ~95-m diameter rotors, totaling ~127.5 m max height). The study used Furuno FR-1510 MKIII marine radar (X-band, 9.410 GHz, 12 kW peak power) in both surveillance and vertical modes at two stations (North and Saddle). The primary goal was to collect baseline data on nocturnal migration characteristics and estimate the number of targets passing within the rotor-swept area.

Key results:
- Mean nocturnal flight direction was 191° at North, 196° at Saddle, and 194° combined (southerly, perpendicular to ridge orientation).
- Mean nocturnal passage rates: 231 ± 31 targets/km/h at North, 351 ± 39 at Saddle, 290 ± 26 combined. Nightly rates ranged 31–1,159 targets/km/h.
- Mean flight altitudes: 474 ± 5 m agl at North, 463 ± 4 m agl at Saddle, 468 ± 3 m combined (range 50–1,206 m).
- Percentage of targets below 125 m agl: 7% at North, 9% at Saddle, 8% combined.
- Low-altitude (<125 m agl) passage rates: 17 ± 3 targets/km/h at North, 39 ± 7 at Saddle, 28 ± 4 combined (range 0–171).
- Estimated turbine passage rates (assuming 10 nocturnal h/day): 41–389 migrants/turbine at North, 94–898 at Saddle, 67–640 combined over the 39-day study, equating to daily indices of 1.1–10.0, 2.4–23.0, and 1.7–16.4 migrants/turbine/day respectively.

Passage rates were significantly higher at Saddle than North and increased later in the season. Flight altitudes increased under favorable synoptic conditions (tailwinds). Targets were mostly individual passerines (only 3.6% were "large" targets likely shorebirds/waterfowl). Targets with airspeeds <6 m/s (16.2% overall) were excluded to eliminate insect contamination. Weather effects were modeled using linear mixed models and AICc model selection. Passage rates did not vary among nocturnal sampling hours, and flight altitudes did not differ significantly between stations.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The mean nocturnal passage rate was 231 ± 31 targets/km/h and 351 ± 39 targets/km/h at North and Saddle respectively. The overall mean passage rate at the combined stations was 290 ± 26."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Listening to Migrating Birds at Night May Help Ensure Their Safety | Audubon ---
URL: https://www.audubon.org/magazine/listening-migrating-birds-night-may-help-ensure-their-safety

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Audubon Magazine article (September-October 2013, by T. Edward Nickens) explores the emerging field of acoustic monitoring of nocturnal bird migration—the recording and analysis of "night flight calls" (NFCs) that migrating birds make while flying in darkness.

KEY POINTS:
- **The phenomenon**: On spring and autumn nights, hundreds of thousands to millions of birds migrate across North America. Most birds migrate at night for stability (free of daytime thermals), cooler temperatures, navigational aid from stars, and to avoid daytime predators. While largely unseen, this migration is not silent—birds vocalize in flight with short, faint calls (NFCs).
- **Technology**: Specialized acoustic monitoring equipment (microphones calibrated for high-frequency high-altitude calls) can now record, analyze, and identify these calls. The best microphones can capture a warbler flying 1,000 feet overhead or a grosbeak at twice that distance. Automated sound-recognition software (including free tools) has made analysis more feasible.
- **History**: The first quantified record came in 1896 when Orin Libby tallied 3,600 night flight calls from a hill near Madison, Wisconsin (published 1899). First audio recordings came in the 1950s (using reel-to-reel recorders inside hay bale rings). A voice-activated system was developed in 1987. In 2002, Bill Evans and Michael O'Brien published a CD with calls and spectrograms of 211 North American terrestrial bird species, helping launch modern research.
- **Research applications**: 
  - Rachel Bricklin (Fordham Ph.D. candidate) monitors bird activity at Mianus River Gorge Preserve (suburban) and the Bronx Zoo (urban), testing birds for corticosterone (stress hormone) to understand how stopover birds in city parks respond to stressful urban conditions.
  - Cornell, with Oregon State, UMass-Amherst, Microsoft, and NOAA, plans automated recording stations across the Northeast and Gulf Coast; Andrew Farnsworth leads BirdCast migration forecasting and developed the "Rosetta Stone for warblers" (spectrograms of 48 warbler NFCs).
  - German researchers in the North Sea recorded calls near offshore wind turbines to study collisions; acoustic systems could serve as real-time collision risk alarms.
  - A 2012 Philadelphia art installation with 24 robotic searchlights (25 nights during peak migration) was monitored; radar tracked over 735,000 migrating birds and acoustic recordings found six times more NFCs near the lights than at a nearby station.
  - J. Alan Clark (Fordham) counted over 300,000 targets in just 10 nights in May 2010 over two 550-yard-wide transects of New York City.
  - High school student Jessica Fleischman recorded 20,500+ nocturnal flight calls over 84 nights comparing suburban and rural sites, winning awards for showing wind speed and precipitation affect calling rates.
- **Why birds call at night**: Scientists believe NFCs help birds stay with flocks (more frequent in rough weather/headwinds) and may warn of fatal crashes with tall lit structures. High call rates coincide with mass collisions at towers and skyscrapers.
- **The calls**: Most are shorter than half a second (e.g., hooded warbler's is ~1/20 second). Spectrograms reveal unique "auditory fingerprints" per species. Examples: hooded warbler (cup-shaped, 6-7.5 kHz), dickcissel vs. painted bunting vs. blue grosbeak buzzes, swamp sparrow's buzzy 'zee' vs. hermit thrush whistle. Some species are grouped into call "complexes" when not individually identifiable.
- **Future applications**: Data could create "risk maps" of urban landscapes, identifying high- and low-threat zones for bird collisions, and inform bird-friendly urban design.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"This is making the invisible visible. We are now able to peek into those dark skies and quantify and clarify nocturnal migration in ways that will make the world safer for birds." — J. Alan Clark, Fordham biology professor
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Record-breaking Night of Bird Migration Detected with Radar ---
URL: https://www.birds.cornell.edu/home/record-breaking-night-of-bird-migration

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On September 25-26, 2025, a record-breaking night of bird migration was detected using radar by BirdCast, a collaborative platform using weather radar and machine learning to track migrating birds. BirdCast tracked more than 1.2 billion birds streaming south to their wintering grounds after sunset Thursday—the largest single-night total ever recorded since the project began mapping live migrations in 2018. This surpasses the previous milestone of one billion birds, first observed in October 2023.

According to Andrew Farnsworth, a visiting scientist at the Cornell Lab of Ornithology and longtime BirdCast researcher, this seemingly rare night captured about 10% of the continent's birds in flight at the same time, roughly three times the average of 400 million birds detected on typical fall nights during peak migration. Farnsworth noted the event was not random but resulted from a combination of ideal migrating conditions coinciding with the peak of fall migration, including calm winds and tail winds that helped push birds along their migratory paths across much of the center of the country and the Mississippi River valley.

BirdCast is a collaborative research project involving the Cornell Lab of Ornithology, Purdue University, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, and University of Massachusetts Amherst. The platform provides freely accessible real-time data, with forecast maps predicting bird migration numbers and live migration maps showing migration in real time, allowing the public to take precautions to protect birds.

The article also serves as a reminder about bird safety: every year, more than one billion birds die in collisions with windows in the United States. Bright lights can disorient birds migrating at night, drawing them into areas where collisions with glass are common. Recommended measures include turning off nonessential lights at night and adding bird-friendly film or markings spaced no more than two inches apart on the outside of windows. More information is available at stopbirdcollisions.org.

Media contact: Kathi Borgmann, Cornell Lab of Ornithology, (607) 254-2137, klb274@cornell.edu.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"These numbers are almost inconceivable," said Andrew Farnsworth, a visiting scientist at the Cornell Lab of Ornithology and longtime BirdCast researcher. "They're enormous. They grab your attention, even for people that study migration regularly. The scale of how many organisms that this represents, it is just mind blowing." "It's really unbelievable," he said. "BirdCast gives the ability for more people to engage in and participate in this incredible spectacle," Farnsworth said, "and understand that it's happening."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: Weather Radar Predicts Nighttime Bird Migrations ---
URL: https://www.aaas.org/news/weather-radar-predicts-nighttime-bird-migrations

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from AAAS (published around September 2018, reporting on findings in the September 14 issue of Science) describes a new forecasting model that uses weather radar data combined with machine learning to predict nighttime bird migrations across North America up to a week in advance. The study, led by Benjamin Van Doren of the University of Oxford with co-author Kyle Horton of Cornell University, used the meteorological Next-Generation Radar (NEXRAD) network combined with climate models to accurately predict the timing, intensity, and location of nocturnal migration events, as well as estimate nightly bird numbers. In early May, when temperatures warm, more than 500 million migratory songbirds take flight each night in North America.

The researchers combed through 23 years of spring migration radar data, using machine learning to automate the identification of bird signatures amid chaotic background signals like precipitation and insect swarms. The model's predictions could reduce bird deaths from human activities—over 630 million birds die annually in the U.S. from collisions with buildings, towers, and vehicles, and bird strikes cause at least $1.2 billion in annual aircraft damage worldwide (including the 2009 "miracle on the Hudson" incident). Predictions could also help wind turbine operators shut down turbines or turn off lights during large flights, and help track the spread of avian-borne diseases.

Most North American songbirds (warblers, sparrows, thrushes) migrate at night to take advantage of cooler, more stable atmospheres, allowing daylight hours for foraging at stopover sites. Migratory bird populations in North America are in decline, mostly due to habitat loss. The study demonstrates the value of "big data" ecology research in understanding the complex drivers of avian migration, which involve navigation, timing, wind, food availability, and environmental conditions like temperature, atmospheric pressure, and precipitation.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Birds must navigate accurately using multiple cues, time their journeys precisely, deal with winds that may blow them off course, find food in transient and unfamiliar environments, and often re-engineer their bodies to store energy and save weight," said Van Doren.
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 6: In-flight reactions of nocturnally migrating birds to winds ---
URL: https://d-nb.info/1356231144/34

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific review article published in the Journal of Ornithology (2024) by Bruno Bruderer, Pius Korner, and Dieter Peter of the Swiss Ornithological Institute, examining how nocturnally migrating birds react to winds in flight.

**Study Design:** The authors reviewed available knowledge on in-flight reactions of nocturnal bird migrants to winds, focusing on the challenging conditions in Western Europe versus North America. They then conducted a new analysis using tracking radar data from a complete autumn season (30 July–30 October 1987) at Lehrberg near Nuremberg, Germany, at an altitude of 450 m asl. Using the "Superfledermaus" tracking radar, they tracked individual nocturnal migrants (93.6% intermittently flapping passerines) and measured winds using pilot balloons at the birds' flight altitudes.

**Key Methods:** They defined a "basic direction" (BD) as the average flight direction of migrants under negligible wind influence (mean ±30° around 230°). Track and heading deviations from BD were modeled for two altitudinal zones (above/below 1500 m asl) against winds from six 60° sectors. Statistical analysis used robust general additive models with a Student-t distribution.

**Key Results:**
- Air speeds (Va) increased from ~11 to 13 (14) m/s with opposing and side winds (supporting H1); a slight decrease with following winds was only observed in high-flying birds
- No expected increase in air speed with altitude due to decreasing air density (H2 unsupported)
- Overcompensation was frequent at low wind speeds (<3 m/s); birds compensated fully or overcompensated for winds under 3 m/s
- Under opposing and side winds from the right, birds achieved partial drift compensation up to ~8–10 m/s, then were fully drifted (H3, H4)
- Winds from the right (W/NW) caused more drift at low levels; results for H5 were ambiguous
- Retrograde migration (birds blown backwards by headwinds exceeding air speed) was observed (H7)
- Reverse migration occurred on most nights (H6)
- Migrants compensated less for wind deviations than expected; many maintained headings close to BD even when making minimal ground progress or moving backwards
- General conclusion: full compensation or overcompensation prevailed for winds <3 m/s, but drift became predominant under moderate to strong winds
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The general finding is that in a relatively flat area of southern Germany, full compensation or overcompensation was the prevailing reaction of nocturnal bird migrants to deviating winds with speeds of less than 3 m/s. Under stronger winds, the radar-tracked birds showed insufficient or even decreasing compensation, so that drift became the predominant feature of migration under moderate to strong winds." — From Conclusions and discussion

"Despite some omnipresent reverse migration, we found no support for the idea that songbird migrants tend to fly downwind irrespective of wind direction as suggested, e.g. by Gauthreaux and Able (1970) for North America."

"Overcompensation was frequently observed at low wind speeds (<3 m/s)" — Abstract

"The tendency of birds to maintain headings close to BD under opposing winds was so strong that many individuals continued migration with minimal progress over ground or even with retrograde migration as an extreme." — Abstract

"In general, migrants compensated less for deviations by wind force than expected." — Abstract
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific article published in Ecography (2019, vol. 42, pp. 876-886) describing the first continental-scale study of nocturnal avian migration across Europe using a network of weather radars during autumn 2016.

**Methods:**
- Data was extracted from 70 weather radar stations (out of 84 processed, from Sweden to Portugal) operated by meteorological agencies of Sweden, Germany, Finland, France, the Netherlands, Czech Republic, Slovenia, Poland, Belgium, Portugal, Catalonia, and Bulgaria
- The study period covered 19 September to 9 October 2016 (peak passerine migration season)

- Only C-band radars were used; the lowest altitude bin (up to 200m a.g.l.) was excluded to avoid ground clutter
- Migration Traffic Rate (MTR) was calculated as birds passing a theoretical 1-km transect per hour

**Key findings:**

- The highest migration intensity night (4 October) showed an average of 1621 birds km⁻¹ h⁻¹
- The highest nightly mean MTR was recorded at Eisberg, south-eastern Germany (7,282 birds km⁻¹ h⁻¹ on 4-5 October)

- Peak migration dates were earlier at higher latitudes and later at lower latitudes, showing a large-scale migration wave moving north to south

- The study demonstrates weather radar networks are a valuable tool for large-scale bird movement research
- Findings have consequences for ecosystem function, nutrient transfer, human and livestock health, and civil/military aviation safety

--- SOURCE 8: Enhanced forecasting of bird nocturnal migration intensity in relation to previous days and synoptic weather patterns ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12178967

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific article, published in the International Journal of Biometeorology (April 19, 2025), presents a framework for enhancing forecasts of nocturnal bird migration intensity by incorporating previous days' weather conditions and synoptic (large-scale) weather patterns. The research was conducted by Amédée Roy (France Energies Marines), Thibault Désert (Météo-France), Vincent Delcourt (Biotope), Cécile Bon (France Energies Marines), and Baptiste Schmid (Swiss Ornithological Institute).

METHODOLOGY: Bird densities were estimated using 9 dual-polarized weather radars from the French Meteorological Institute (Abbeville, Bordeaux, Bourges, Falaise, Nancy, Nîmes, St-Nizier, Toulouse, Treillières) using the vol2bird algorithm, covering nights from February-May and July-November over 2017-2022. Vertical profiles were log-transformed and interpolated on a 0-3000m scale. Weather data came from two Météo-France models: AROME (1.3km resolution, local scale) and ARPEGE (global, synoptic scale). Dimensionality reduction was performed using Functional Principal Component Analysis (FPCA) for bird density and local weather profiles, and Empirical Orthogonal Functions (EOF) for synoptic weather maps. Gradient-boosted regression trees (LightGBM) with Tree-structured Parzen Estimator hyperparameter optimization, SHAP values for feature interpretation, and separate spring/autumn models were used.

KEY RESULTS: The model explained approximately 47% of variance in spring and 60% in autumn bird densities. The naïve phenology-based forecast explained 35% and 51% respectively. The new approach improved explained variance by 12% and 10% over phenology models (vs. 9% and 4% for the Van Doren & Horton 2018 framework), explaining 1.3x (spring) and 2.25x (autumn) more non-phenology variance. The model significantly improved identification of migration peaks (F1-score improvements) in both seasons, though it still underestimates highest density values.

FPCA identified two principal components (88% variance explained): PC1 (70.7%) for migration intensity and PC2 (17.4%) for flight altitude. Migration intensity was higher in autumn, while flight altitudes were higher in spring.

KEY FINDINGS: Wind (zonal and meridional) had the most significant impact on predicting migration intensity and flight altitude. Spring relied more on temperature and pressure; autumn on humidity and cloudiness. Local and instantaneous weather data had the highest overall contribution, but previous days' weather (particularly in autumn) and synoptic data were crucial for detecting migration peaks. Local instantaneous data mainly helped forecast nights with no/few migrations. Favorable conditions for both seasons were associated with low supportive winds preceded by 1-3 days of strong headwinds. In spring, favorable conditions involved a high-pressure system over the Mediterranean creating South-West winds over France; in autumn, high pressure over the UK with North-East winds in France.

CONCLUSIONS: The study demonstrates that incorporating previous days' local conditions and synoptic weather dynamics substantially improves bird migration forecasting, particularly for peak events. The authors recommend the combined use of dimension reduction tools (FPCA/EOF) and explainable regression trees with SHAP values as a transferable framework for complex ecological systems. Limitations include underestimation of peak densities, potential underestimation of precipitation effects due to rain-contaminated profile removal, and the need for species/population-level data for further improvements.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Our main contribution is in the characterization and quantification of the contribution of local weather conditions as well as synoptic weather patterns from previous days on forecast models."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 16: Gauthreaux & Belser: Migration at the Gulf of Mexico ---
URL: https://www.internationalornithology.org/PROCEEDINGS_Durban/Symposium/S33/S33.1.htm

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## Bird Migration in the Region of the Gulf of Mexico

This is a scientific paper by Sidney A. Gauthreaux, Jr. and Carroll G. Belser (Clemson University), presented at the 22nd International Ornithological Congress in Durban (1999), examining the flight strategies of migratory birds around and across the Gulf of Mexico.

### Historical Context & Debate
Since the early 1900s, there has been debate about whether birds cross the Gulf directly (trans-Gulf migration) or fly around it (circum-Gulf migration):
- **Cooke (1904)** and **Lowery (1945)** argued many species fly across the Gulf in spring
- **Williams (1945)** proposed most birds migrated around the Gulf
- **Lowery (1946)** used moon-watching at Progresso, Yucatan to document northward trans-Gulf migration in spring, firmly re-establishing the trans-Gulf hypothesis
- **Stevenson (1957)** examined 164 species; while some fly circum-Gulf, 40 species are certainly trans-Gulf migrants based on abundance patterns along the Gulf coast

### Research Methods
Multiple techniques have been employed across different eras:
- Field observations and museum specimens (early studies, e.g., Cooke 1904)
- Bird-banding with mist nets at coastal stations (data on species composition and physiological condition)
- Moon-watching and vertical telescopes
- **Weather surveillance radar** (WSR-57 from 1965, then the more sensitive WSR-88D Doppler radar) since the mid-1960s to detect, quantify, and monitor migration
- Fixed vertical-beam marine radar for measuring altitudinal distribution
- Satellite radio telemetry (Argos platform) for mapping raptor migration pathways

### Spring Migration Findings
- Occurs from mid-March to late May, peaking in late April/early May, greatly reduced by the third week of May
- Arrival timing strongly influenced by Julian date and synoptic weather conditions over the Gulf
- **Arrival pattern on the upper Texas/southwestern Louisiana coast**: begins in morning with moderate south winds (5-10 ms⁻¹ at 767-1489 m altitude), peaks in the afternoon, essentially finished by nightfall
- Peak arrival time occurs later as spring progresses and earlier at more southerly stations
- Peak arrival is strongly correlated with velocity of winds aloft
- Most migrants fly over coastal areas to make landfall in bottomland forests inland; only during adverse weather (hard rain or strong north winds) do substantial numbers land in coastal woodlands
- **Exodus**: 30-40 minutes after sunset, migrants depart stopover areas; exodus rarely exceeds 3 hours for central northern Gulf stations, but continues most of the night along the Texas coast (includes birds moving up from eastern Mexico)
- Winds aloft over the Gulf are critically important; March winds often influenced by continental polar air masses (east winds), with south-to-north crossings only possible during southerly return flow of maritime tropical air
- Powerful cold fronts in late April/early May cause spectacular fallouts on offshore oil rigs, fishing boats, and coastal woodlands—birds often exhausted, without fat reserves, with catabolized breast muscle; many don't survive
- **Spatial extent**: trans-Gulf flights can arrive over approximately one-third of the 2250 km coastline from Brownsville, TX to Key West, FL

### Altitudinal Distribution
- Trans-Gulf migrants fly considerably higher than most daytime songbird movements over land
- Layer thickness typically 1500-2000 m, ranging from 400 to 3000 m
- Distribution depends on winds aloft; one instance of migrants flying at 3657-4572 m (12,000-15,000 ft) above a shallow cold front
- When powerful cold fronts force migrants lower, they fly just above the Gulf waters (below radar coverage)
- Insect echoes can contaminate data up to 500 m during daytime arrivals

### WSR-88D Radar Network Findings
The network of 10 WSR-88D radars from Brownsville, TX to Key West, FL has provided detailed temporal and spatial patterns:
- **Key West, FL radar** monitors nightly exodus of migrants from Cuba
- Gulf coast of Florida (except northwestern coast) rarely receives trans-Gulf migrations
- Western Gulf radars reveal trans-Gulf flights originating on the Gulf coast of Tamaulipas and south Texas moving NE over the Gulf to landfall on upper Texas/southwestern Louisiana coast (occur when winds ahead of slow-moving cold fronts are from southwest)
- In spring, circum-Gulf migrants may fly NE from Brownsville, TX and Tamaulipas, Mexico coasts, crossing the northwestern Gulf

### Autumn Migration
Much less studied than spring migration:
- **Able (1972)** analysis of 34 nights of fall data at Lake Charles, LA: weather conditions in fall are generally NOT favorable for trans-Gulf migration; frequency of cold fronts to assist crossing is low until late in season; strong net flow of songbirds toward southwest assisted by prevailing northeast winds
- **Buskirk (1980)** found high-magnitude trans-Gulf migrations occur under post-cold-front conditions, with most migrants crossing late September through first three weeks of October
- Northerly winds over the northern Gulf coast occur on approximately 10% of September dates and 25-30% of October dates, increasing to 39% and 51% in early and late November
- WSR-88D data since fall 1995 shows fall trans-Gulf flights are closely associated with frontal systems penetrating the Gulf; in absence of cold fronts, migrants follow the Texas coast or move down the Florida peninsula
- Flights following weak cold fronts are often directed SW toward south Texas and upper Mexican coast
- In fall, migrants occasionally depart southward, turn WSW offshore, and make landfall on the lower Texas coast (strongly dependent on wind patterns)

### Research Gaps
- Little known about the departure phase of trans-Gulf flights from Mexico and western Cuba (only Lowery's pioneering studies)
- Relatively little published on fall migration along the northern Gulf coast
- Late Lowery & Newman (1966) suggested a sizeable proportion of migrants may detour the Gulf in fall, moving westward and southwestward

The paper was supported by the Legacy Resource Management Program of the US Department of Defense and acknowledges assistance from National Weather Service personnel.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 21: Gwinner: circadian and circannual programs ---
URL: https://www.internationalornithology.org/PROCEEDINGS_Durban/Symposium/S40/S40.2.htm

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific paper by Eberhard Gwinner (published in 1999 in the Proceedings of the 22nd International Ornithological Congress) examining how circadian (daily) and circannual (annual) endogenous rhythms allow birds to adapt to periodic environmental changes. The central thesis is that these biological clocks contain both rigid, "hard-wired" elements and flexible elements that provide temporal frameworks within which organisms can adjust behavior according to circumstances.

KEY FINDINGS ON CIRCANNUAL PROGRAMS:
- Circannual rhythms control reproduction, moult, migration, body weight, and other functions in birds. They have been mainly studied in tropical species and temperate-zone long-distance migrants.

STONECHAT STUDIES (East African Stonechats, Saxicola torquata axillaris):
- Annual rhythms of gonadal size and moult persist for up to ten years even under constant 12.25h equatorial photoperiod and controlled conditions, proving their endogenous nature.
- Circannual rhythms are both endogenous AND innate - normal rhythms develop even in birds raised from embryonic life in constant laboratory conditions.
- The reproductive "window" (duration of reproductively active phase) is rigid and insensitive to nutritional conditions and social factors (mate presence). Paired and unpaired birds showed gonadal growth/regression at the same times.
- However, within this window, birds are flexible: paired birds bred twice (and even three times in one case) versus free-living Kenyan Stonechats that usually breed only once. Double-broodedness is common in a Tanzanian population 250 km south.
- Subspecies-specific timing: East African birds take longer to moult than European conspecifics; F1-hybrids show intermediary patterns.

WARBLER MIGRATION STUDIES (Garden Warblers, Sylvia borin):
- Migratory activity and fat deposition are controlled by genetically determined species/population-specific circannual programs. F1-hybrids between long- and short-distance migrants show intermediary patterns.
- These programs are rigid: preventing fat deposition, starvation, or suppressing nocturnal activity did not alter the timing of beginning or end of migratory restlessness.
- But food availability modifies intensity of nocturnal activity within the rigid framework: food-deprived birds show increased migratory restlessness; refeeding interrupts it (helps birds cope with changing nutritional conditions).
- The response to food withdrawal is phase-dependent - high early in the migratory season, declining to zero at season's end (when moulting begins).

LEARNING AND MODIFICATION:
- Wintering-site fidelity shows learning can supplement or replace endogenous timing programs. Perdeck's starling experiments showed adult birds compensated for experimental displacement to migrate to their normal wintering area, while young first-time migrants flew in their original direction, ending in "wrong" wintering sites. Some recovered birds returned to their displaced wintering sites in later years, proving they had learned the position.
- Gregarious migrants (waders, ducks, geese, cranes) develop population or family traditions for migratory routes. Experiments imprinting goslings onto light airplanes as surrogate parents have proven successful.

CIRCADIAN TIME-PLACE LEARNING:
- Bees and birds can memorize times of day when food is available at certain places (first observed by Forel in 1910; called a "time sense" by von Frisch). Wenger et al. (1991) demonstrated the circadian basis in birds.

- Enright suggests circadian rhythms act like a "circa-24-h closed loop on a tape recorder" on which daily events can be recorded and recalled, representing "the primary adaptive significance of biological clocks for higher animals."

- Circadian/circannual rhythms provide rigid temporal frameworks for reproduction and migration, within which birds show flexible, environment-dependent responses.
- Daily time-place learning exists; comparable circannual time-place learning likely exists too (migratory birds may associate spatial information with phases of an endogenous annual clock) but has not been rigorously tested.
- The author notes that while molecular and physiological bases of rhythms are increasingly revealed, studies on adaptive significance are becoming scarcer, which is critical for proper biological interpretation.
</summary>

## Fully Comprehensive Findings

### LANDMARK FINDING ON THE 9/11 "TRIBUTE IN LIGHT" (B): Van Doren et al. 2017 PNAS

The central paper on artificial light at night (ALAN) disrupting nocturnal migration is **Van Doren, B.M., Horton, K.G., Dokter, A.M., Klinck, H., Elbin, S., & Farnsworth, A. (2017). "High-intensity urban light installation dramatically alters nocturnal bird migration." Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, October 2, 2017 (DOI: 10.1073/pnas.1708574114)**, which studied the "Tribute in Light" (TiL) installation at the National September 11 Memorial & Museum in New York City — the first study to quantify ALAN-induced changes in multiple behaviors of nocturnally migrating birds [1][2][3][4].

Study design and methods:
- Over seven years (2008–2016, excluding 2009 and 2011 due to precipitation), birds were monitored using weather surveillance radar (WSR-88D at Brookhaven, NY), acoustic sensors recording flight calls, visual observations, and computer simulations. This was an opportunistic study, not a controlled experiment [2].
- The installation is described as beams from **eighty-eight 7500-watt bulbs** shining skyward over New York City every September 11th, with authors from Cornell Lab of Ornithology, Oxford University, and New York City Audubon [4].
- The lights were shut down **22 times for approximately 20 minutes each** during the study, allowing direct comparison between lit and dark periods [2][3].

Key quantitative findings:
- **The installation influenced approximately 1.1 million birds (95% CI: 0.6–1.6 million) during 7 nights over 7 years** [1][2][3][4].
- Bird densities near the installation were **up to 20 times greater than baseline densities**, exceeding 60 times baseline in five of seven years and **150 times baseline in three years (2008, 2012, 2013)**; densities never exceeded 13 times baseline when lights were off [2][3].
- Effects were found **up to 4 km altitude** (3.9x density increase at 1.5° radar elevation angle) [2][3].
- **Maximum standardized bird densities were 14 times greater during illuminated periods** (t=5.70, P<0.0001); maximum bird numbers within 500 m averaged **3.4 times higher** during illumination (t=3.89, P=0.0003) [2][3].
- During illuminated periods birds aggregated in high densities, **decreased flight speeds (by 1.7 m/s)**, followed circular flight paths, and **vocalized more frequently (1.4x increase in flight call rates)** (radial velocity main effect −1.7 ms⁻¹, t=−2.10, P=0.037; flight call rates t=4.53, P<0.0001) [2][3].
- Effects occurred **under clear sky conditions in a heavily photo-polluted environment** — contradicting previous assumptions that light attraction only occurs in poor visibility [2][3].
- **Behavioral disruptions disappeared within minutes when lights were extinguished** [1][2][4].
- Simulations (flow model with disorientation probability a=0.95 and disorientation distance of 1500 m) revealed high probability of disorientation and attraction, with a stabilization time of **34 minutes**; bird concentrations could only be explained by directed flight toward the light for disoriented birds [2][3].
- Observers documented **birds colliding with glass windows of a building under construction at 50 West St. in 2015 and 2016** [2][3].

Conservation recommendations: Selective removal of lights during nights with substantial bird migration is a "viable strategy for minimizing potentially fatal interactions among ALAN, structures, and birds" [1]. The lights were extinguished when more than 1,000 birds were in the beams or flying dangerously low, following lobbying by the Municipal Arts Society (now National September 11 Memorial & Museum) and New York City Audubon [4]. The paper highlights this collaboration (National September 11 Memorial & Museum, NYC Audubon, Cornell Lab of Ornithology) as a model for mitigation [4]. The paper contains 4 figures, 292 citations (per Semantic Scholar), and 89 references [1].

Related works noted on the paper's citation page: blue light attracts nocturnally migrating birds (suggesting switching to longer wavelength lights could reduce collisions); ALAN confounds broad-scale habitat use by migrating birds; light pollution is greatest within migration passage areas worldwide [1]. The Van Doren Google Scholar profile also lists: "A continental system for forecasting bird migration" (Science, 2018, 290 citations); "Bright lights in the big cities: migratory birds' exposure to artificial light" (Frontiers in Ecology, 2019, 202 citations); "Drivers of fatal bird collisions in an urban center" (PNAS, 2021, 170 citations); "Holding steady: Little change in intensity or timing of bird migration over the Gulf of Mexico" (Global Change Biology, 2019, 121 citations); and "MistNet: Measuring historical bird migration in the US using archived weather radar data and convolutional neural networks" (2019, 120 citations) [6].

The eBird Science article adds: "Only by using radar were the authors able to view a full 'footprint' of the lights' impacts on birds, which may extend multiple kilometers from and above the lights themselves." [4]

### 9/11 AIRSPACE SHUTDOWN CONTEXT

Note: Searches for a peer-reviewed radar study of birds using the September 11, 2001 airspace shutdown did **not** surface a dedicated primary paper in the returned results. However, the following relevant documentation was found:

- The National Archives blog "Shutting Down the Sky: The Federal Aviation Administration on 9/11" documents: the day began as "severe clear"; over 4,500 aircraft were in the air; at 9:03 AM the FAA issued the **first national ground stop in U.S. history** prohibiting all civilian aircraft departures; following the Pentagon strike at 9:37 AM the FAA ordered all aircraft to land at the nearest airport (first-ever unplanned shutdown of U.S. airspace); at 11:06 AM FAA Advisory 036 suspended operations in the National Airspace System; **by 12:16 PM — three-and-a-half hours after the first plane hit — the airspace was clear of all commercial and private flights**. Documents come from the series "Open Files Relating to September 11, 2001 Terrorist Attacks" (NAID 7419198), Record Group 237: Records of the FAA, National Archives at College Park, MD [19].
- A Facebook post shows a photograph of the FAA Notice to Airmen (NOTAM) from 9/11/2001 grounding all aircraft/all airports [20].

### CONTINENTAL-SCALE ALAN EXPOSURE: Horton et al. 2019 Frontiers in Ecology and the Environment

**Horton, K.G., Nilsson, C., Van Doren, B.M., La Sorte, F.A., Dokter, A.M., & Farnsworth, A. (2019). "Bright lights in the big cities: migratory birds' exposure to artificial light." Frontiers in Ecology and the Environment.** Key findings [5]:
- Approximately **80% of North America's ~630 terrestrial bird species are migratory, and over 80% of those migrate at night**.
- Combined over two decades (spring 1995 to spring 2017) of weather surveillance radar data from **143 stations** with satellite-based VIIRS ALAN radiance data, focusing on the **125 largest urban centers**. Radar data from a 30-minute window centered on 3 hours after local sunset were filtered using a random forest classifier (5.6% spring and 4.5% fall classification error). Migration activity was measured as vertically integrated reflectivity; ALAN quantified using monthly VIIRS Day/Night Band composites averaged across October–December 2012–2017.
- **Fall migration had 63% higher cumulative migratory activity than spring, and 53.8% higher total exposure**; even after standardizing, fall exposure remained 13.1% higher because fall migrants used more easterly (and more photo-polluted) routes.
- **Half of seasonal migratory activity passed each radar site within just 6.7 ± 2.6 nights on average.**
- **The top 125 urban areas occupied only 2.1% of total land area but produced 35.4% of total light radiance**; across the US, 69.5% of summed linear light radiance came from just 5% of the land area.
- **Mean avian light exposure in cities was 24 times the countrywide average.**
- **Chicago, Houston, and Dallas consistently had the highest exposure risk in both seasons, with exposure magnitudes 19–21 times the median of the other 122 cities.**
- Larger cities generally had greater exposure risk (R² = 0.52 spring, 0.62 fall), with exceptions like Boston (4th in size but 36th/24th in exposure) and Des Moines (99th in size but 28th/36th in exposure).
- Because migration occurs in concentrated pulses and can now be forecast 12–72 hours in advance, targeted "lights-out" campaigns timed to peak migration nights could reduce exposure significantly; fall mitigation is especially important given higher numbers of less-experienced juvenile birds.

### PROCELLARIFORMES / SEABIRD LIGHT ATTRACTION (OFFSHORE PLATFORMS, VESSELS, LIGHTHOUSES, ISLAND LIGHTS)

**Reed, J.R., Sincock, J.L., & Hailman, J.P. (1985). "Light attraction in endangered procellariiform birds: reduction by shielding upward radiation." The Auk** (Digital Commons USF, 179 citations) [7]: **Shielding (of upward radiation) decreased attraction by nearly 40%. Most attraction occurred 1–4 hours after sunset. Full moon dramatically decreased attraction.**

**Rodríguez, A., & Rodríguez, B. (2009). "Attraction of petrels to artificial lights in the Canary Islands: effects of the moon phase and age class." Ibis 151(2):299–310 (138 citations)** [8][9].

**Wiese, F., Montevecchi, W.A., et al. (2001). "Seabirds at risk around offshore oil platforms in the northwest Atlantic." Marine Pollution Bulletin 42: 1285–1290 (273 citations)** [10][11][12][13][14]: **"Seabirds aggregate around oil drilling platforms and rigs in above average numbers due to night lighting, flaring, food and other visual cues."**

**Merkel, F.R., & Johansen, K.L. (2011). "Light-induced bird strikes on vessels in Southwest Greenland." Marine Pollution Bulletin 62(11), 2330–2336 (113 citations)** [10].

**Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution (January 18, 2022). "Tracking Flights to Investigate Seabird Mortality Induced by Artificial Lights."** — Original research tracking **Cory's shearwater (Calonectris borealis)** fledglings on Tenerife, Canary Islands, 2017–2019 [15]:
- More than **56 burrow-nesting petrel species, some critically endangered, are affected by lights** (citing Rodríguez et al., 2017; Silva et al., 2020); "Every fledging season, on islands where humans and petrels coexist, thousands of fledglings of different species are grounded by light pollution."
- Used GPS-GSM transmitters to track **277 experimentally released fledglings** from an inland release site (8 km inland at 900 m elevation); treatments: GPS-tagged (87), tape-labelled (92), control (98).
- **37 of 277 fledglings (13.4%) were grounded by artificial lights**; birds with higher down abundance had higher grounding probability; grounding probability was positively related to flight tortuosity and overflown light pollution levels; slower flights were more likely to be grounded; tortuosity increased with light pollution levels but decreased with moon luminance.
- All birds oriented flights towards low-altitude coastal areas, following the most light-polluted regions; flights covered 18.7 ± 10.8 km and lasted 47.3 ± 45.3 min on average.
- Control birds (8.2% grounding) were grounded less often than GPS-tagged (19.5%) and tape-labelled (13%) birds, suggesting control birds were overlooked during rescue due to small metal rings being less visible.
- The most dangerous light-polluted areas in southern Tenerife were identified, where more than 50% of island-wide rescued birds are grounded. Funding: European Commission project INTERREG MAC/4.6d/157 LuMinAves.

**Rodríguez, A., et al. (2023). "Moonlight diminishes seabird attraction to artificial light." Conservation Science and Practice** [16]:
- Rescue programs report fewer fledglings grounded during full moon nights. The authors evaluate two hypotheses: (1) reduced strandings because birds are less attracted/disoriented by light pollution during full moon; (2) reduced fledging activity (chicks avoiding departure during bright moonlight as anti-predator behavior). Evidence supports the first but not the second.
- Evidence includes: annual stranding numbers lower when full moon coincides with mean peak fledging date; biometric data from **8,954 Cory's shearwater fledglings in the Azores (2016–2021) and 267 from Tenerife** showing no evidence of delayed fledging after full moon nights; multiple studies showing cavity-nesting seabirds fledge regardless of moon phase (Newell's shearwaters via camera traps, Leach's storm-petrels, Barau's petrels via radar surveys); GPS tracking showing fledglings fly straighter over light-polluted areas during full moon and reach the ocean more successfully.
- **At least 73 seabird species, mostly cavity-nesting Procellariiformes, have been documented in light pollution-induced mortality events, with approximately 60% showing population declines and 28 globally threatened by IUCN criteria.**
- Proposed mechanisms: reduced relative glare of artificial lights, ability to see obstructions, orientation toward the moon instead of artificial lights, and potential visual system development benefits from moonlight exposure.

**Medina-Franco, Sangiorgi, & Valdés-Velásquez (2025). "Lost in the glow: understanding the impact of light pollution on storm-petrels." Avian Conservation and Ecology 20(1), Art. 18 (DOI: 10.5751/ACE-02846-200118)** — first global scoping review on light pollution effects on Hydrobatidae (storm-petrels) [17]:
- 12 articles (published 2005–2022) included from 144 records; half published 2020–2022; six southern hemisphere, six northern.
- **Grounding records found for all Hydrobatidae genera except *Nesofregetta*; groundings recorded in 12 of 22 Hydrobatidae species**; *O. leucorhoa* and *P. marina* most frequently mentioned, followed by *H. pelagicus*.
- **Fallout occurs primarily in fledglings during their first flight leaving the colony; over 99% of grounded *O. leucorhoa* were fledglings** (per Wilhelm et al. 2021).
- Inshore sources: residential, industrial, road, highway, business areas; offshore sources: mainly fishing vessel deck lights.
- **Moon phase associated with groundings: more groundings during new moon, fewer during full moon.**
- Of 12 species assessed by IUCN, nine have decreasing population trends, two unknown, one stable.
- Only five of 12 articles assessed population-level impacts; these found **annual fallout mortality was less than 1% of respective species' populations**.
- Hypotheses for fledgling attraction to light: (1) confusion with bioluminescent prey; (2) association of light with food (burrow entrances); (3) undeveloped visual system and behavioral inexperience; (4) artificial lights limiting navigation by moon and stars.
- A recent study found **even partial reduction in artificial light at night (ALAN) decreased strandings by up to 57%** (Burt et al. 2024).
- Knowledge gaps: only two articles used systematic data collection; eastern Pacific (highest storm-petrel diversity) understudied; light intensity/spectrum rarely quantified.

### OTHER ALAN/NIGHT-MIGRATION MONITORING CONTEXT (Audubon Magazine, Sept–Oct 2013):

- History: first quantified record in **1896 by Orin Libby tallying 3,600 night flight calls near Madison, Wisconsin**; first audio recordings in the 1950s; voice-activated system developed 1987; in 2002 Bill Evans and Michael O'Brien published a CD with calls/spectrograms of **211 North American terrestrial bird species** [18].
- Research applications: Rachel Bricklin (Fordham) monitors activity at Mianus River Gorge Preserve and the Bronx Zoo testing corticosterone; Cornell with Oregon State, UMass-Amherst, Microsoft, NOAA planning automated recording stations; Andrew Farnsworth developed the "Rosetta Stone for warblers" (spectrograms of 48 warbler NFCs); German researchers recorded calls near offshore wind turbines in the North Sea.
- **A 2012 Philadelphia art installation with 24 robotic searchlights (25 nights during peak migration): radar tracked over 735,000 migrating birds and acoustic recordings found six times more NFCs near the lights than at a nearby station.**
- J. Alan Clark (Fordham) counted over 300,000 targets in just 10 nights in May 2010 over two 550-yard-wide transects of New York City.
- High school student Jessica Fleischman recorded 20,500+ nocturnal flight calls over 84 nights comparing suburban and rural sites, showing wind speed and precipitation affect calling rates.
- Why birds call at night: NFCs help birds stay with flocks (more frequent in rough weather/headwinds) and may warn of fatal crashes with tall lit structures; high call rates coincide with mass collisions at towers and skyscrapers. Most calls are shorter than half a second (hooded warbler's is ~1/20 second).

### ANTHROPOGENIC ELECTROMAGNETIC NOISE / RADIOFREQUENCY FIELDS (B): Engels et al. 2014 Nature

**Engels, S., Schneider, N.-L., Lefeldt, N., Hein, C.M., Zapka, M., Michalik, A., Elbers, D., Kittel, A., Hore, P.J., & Mouritsen, H. (2014). "Anthropogenic electromagnetic noise disrupts magnetic compass orientation in a migratory bird." Nature 509(7500):353–356 (May 15, 2014; DOI: 10.1038/nature13290; Epub May 7, 2014; PMID: 24805233)** [23][24][25][26][27]. Affiliations: University of Oldenburg (Institute for Biology and Environmental Sciences, Research Centre for Neurosensory Sciences, Institute of Physics) and University of Oxford (Physical and Theoretical Chemistry Laboratory) [23].

Key findings:
- **"Here we show that migratory birds are unable to use their magnetic compass in the presence of urban electromagnetic noise"** — tested on European robins (*Erithacus rubecula*) [23][25][26].
- Birds in unscreened wooden huts at the University of Oldenburg campus could not orient using their magnetic compass; **their magnetic orientation abilities reappeared in electrically grounded, aluminium-screened huts that attenuated EM noise in the 50 kHz to 5 MHz range by approximately two orders of magnitude** [23][26].
- **When grounding was removed or broadband electromagnetic noise (2 kHz–9 MHz) was deliberately generated inside the screened and grounded huts at intensities similar to background urban noise, birds again lost their magnetic orientation capabilities**; very weak noise did not cause disorientation [23][26].
- **The disruptive effect of radiofrequency electromagnetic fields was not confined to a narrow frequency band** — both 20 kHz–450 kHz and 600 kHz–3 MHz ranges prevented orientation [23][26].
- **Birds tested far from sources of electromagnetic noise (a rural location ~7.5 km from the university) required no screening to orient with their magnetic compass** [23][26].
- "These fully double-blinded tests document a reproducible effect of anthropogenic electromagnetic noise on the behaviour of an intact vertebrate" — noted as significant because previous claimed effects below WHO guidelines had not withstood independent replication under blinded conditions [23][26].

Quantitative details:
- Anthropogenic EMN peak magnetic field intensity at single frequencies was ~0.1–50 nT, with total time-dependent field summed over 10 kHz–5 MHz of ~200–1100 nT (still far weaker than Earth's magnetic field of ~49,000 nT) [26].
- **Effects occurred at intensities well below WHO/ICNIRP guidelines** (reference levels of 6,000 nT at 150 kHz to 180 nT at 5 MHz) [26].
- Effects were **not** attributed to power lines (16.7/50 Hz), mobile phone signals (GHz), or frequencies below 2 kHz or above 5 MHz [26].
- Exposure parameters listed as 50 kHz–9 MHz, DC, electric field, magnetic field, static magnetic field, geomagnetic field, low frequency, intermediate frequency, shielding/field deprivation [24].
- Mechanism unclear but may involve radical-pair (cryptochrome-based) magnetoreception or iron-containing particle clusters; the possibility of effects on quantum spin dynamics at such weak intensities is noted as remarkable [26].
- Implications: disorientation may reduce survival during migration, especially in overcast conditions when sun/star compass cues are unavailable; effect appears localized to urban areas with high electronic device usage [26].
- The paper lists a commentary: **Kirschvink, J.L. (2014). "Sensory biology: Radio waves zap the biomagnetic compass." Nature 2014;509:296–7** [23][24]. The paper has 374 citations and 44 references per Semantic Scholar [25].
- Semantic Scholar lists key citing papers: a **2016 study showing weak broadband electromagnetic fields are more disruptive to European robin magnetic compass orientation than strong narrow-band fields**; a **2017 paper questioning whether the radical-pair model can explain the behavioral findings**; a **2019 study indicating 0.1–100 kHz RF fields did not disrupt blackcap orientation, suggesting radical pair spin coherence lifetimes of 2–10 µs**; and a **2026 Science paper on disruptive effects of brief radiofrequency noise on migratory bat navigation** [25].

Background from the Interference Technology article (interview with Henrik Mouritsen) [27]:
- Researchers had studied European robins since the early 2000s using orientation cages with thermal paper. When Mouritsen moved to the University of Oldenburg (population ~160,000) in 2002, "the robins basically jumped in random directions every spring and autumn for three years." After exhausting other explanations (food, cages, light, daylight cycle), graduate student Nils-Lasse Schneider suggested covering huts and cages with aluminum sheets to form a Faraday cage, which restored orientation without affecting Earth's magnetic field.
- "Our measurements of the interferences indicated that we had accidentally discovered a biological system that is sensitive to anthropogenic electromagnetic noise generated by humans in the frequency range up to five megahertz."
- The interference was below ICNIRP/WHO limits; over a seven-year investigation with double-blind studies, when Faraday cage grounding was disconnected or deliberate interference created, birds immediately lost orientation again.
- "Thus, the effect of anthropogenic electromagnetic noise on bird migration is localized. However these findings should make us think — both about the survival of migratory birds as well as about the potential effects for human beings, which have yet to be investigated."

### RESONANCE EFFECTS AND THE RADICAL-PAIR MECHANISM (SENSORY MECHANISM): Ritz et al. 2004 Nature

**Ritz, T., Thalau, P., Phillips, J.B., Wiltschko, R., & Wiltschko, W. (2004). "Resonance effects indicate a radical-pair mechanism for avian magnetic compass." Nature 429(6988):177–180 (May 13, 2004; DOI: 10.1038/nature02534; PMID: 15141211)** [28][29][30][31][32].

Key findings:
- European robins (*Erithacus rubecula*) were tested under 565 nm light in the local geomagnetic field (46 µT, 66° inclination). **Robins were disoriented when exposed to a vertically aligned broadband (0.1–10 MHz) field (0.085 µT) or a single-frequency 7-MHz field (0.47 µT)** in addition to the geomagnetic field [20/29/32].
- **In the 7-MHz oscillating field, the effect depended on the angle between the oscillating and geomagnetic fields: birds exhibited seasonally appropriate migratory orientation when the field was parallel to the geomagnetic field, but were disoriented when presented at a 24° or 48° angle** [28][29][32].
- "These results are consistent with a resonance effect on singlet–triplet transitions and suggest a magnetic compass based on a radical-pair mechanism" [29].
- The 7 MHz field would require 285 µT to affect magnetite receptors, far stronger than the 0.47 µT used; model calculations showed a resonant oscillating field of 0.033 µT (a thousandth of Earth's field strength) could produce a detectable effect [32].
- Magnetite is suggested as a separate magnetic-intensity ('map') sensor, not for compass orientation [32].
- The study establishes oscillating magnetic fields as a diagnostic tool for identifying radical-pair magnetoreception, applicable to other animal groups [19/32]. Experiments conducted January 13–February 17, 2003, in Frankfurt am Main, Germany; 12 test birds [31][32].
- The Academia.edu page notes: rodent compasses (e.g., mole-rats) are NOT disrupted by the same fields and likely use magnetite-based mechanisms; the wood mouse (*Apodemus sylvaticus*) showed first evidence of a radical-pair mechanism in a mammal [31].

### LIGHT-DEPENDENT MAGNETORECEPTION — RED LIGHT DISRUPTION: Wiltschko, Munro, Ford & Wiltschko 1993 Nature

**Wiltschko, W., Munro, U., Ford, H., & Wiltschko, R. (1993). "Red light disrupts magnetic orientation of migratory birds." Nature 364:525–527 (292 citations, 2732 accesses)** [33]. This reports the **first orientation tests on migratory birds under light of different wavelengths**, providing evidence for a light-dependent magnetoreception process.

- The discussion on magnetoreception in birds focuses mainly on two mechanisms: small particles of magnetite, and "biochemical bi-radical reactions of excited macromolecules."
- Prior evidence: bi-radical hypothesis suggested magnetic resonance phenomena in the retina as primary processes; homing experiments and electrophysiological evidence from pigeons supported this; a study showed that in newts, magnetic compass orientation was maintained under blue light (450 nm and below) but shifted roughly 90° counterclockwise under wavelengths at or above 500 nm.
- The results suggest a light-dependent process in migratory birds "that appears to differ from that reported in newts."

**Wiltschko, W., & Wiltschko, R. (1995). "Migratory orientation of European Robins is affected by the wavelength of light as well as by a magnetic pulse." Journal of Comparative Physiology A 177:363–369 (DOI: 10.1007/BF00192425; 136 citations)** [34]:
- Under "white" (control) light, robins preferred the normal, seasonally appropriate migratory direction; **under 571 nm green light they remained well oriented, whereas under 633 nm red light their behavior was not different from random**.
- A brief, strong magnetic pulse had a significant effect on migratory orientation but responses varied between individuals: some showed a persistent directional shift, others a change in scatter, one bird seemingly unaffected.
- "These findings indicate a light-dependent process and, at the same time, suggest an involvement of magnetizable material in migratory orientation. They are in agreement with the model of a light-dependent compass and a magnetite-based 'map'."
- The paper references Wiltschko & Wiltschko's **1972 discovery of the magnetic compass in European robins (Science 176:62–64)** and their 1993 red-light finding.

**Wiltschko, R., Ritz, T., Stapput, K., Thalau, P., & Wiltschko, W. (2005). "Two Different Types of Light-Dependent Responses to Magnetic Fields in Birds." Current Biology 15(16):1518–1523** [35]:
- Under 502 nm turquoise light, birds showed normal migratory orientation (inclination compass) at a quantal flux of **8×10^15 quanta m−2 s−1**, but under brighter light (54×10^15 quanta m−2 s−1) they showed a **fixed northward tendency based on magnetic polarity** rather than the inclination compass.
- When exposed to a weak oscillating field that interferes with radical pair processes, the inclination compass response was disrupted while the magnetic polarity response remained unaffected.
- Demonstrates that the normal inclination compass relies on a radical-pair mechanism, while the fixed direction represents a novel type of light-dependent orientation based on a different mechanism.

**Wiltschko, R., & Wiltschko, W. (2009). "'Fixed direction'-responses of birds in the geomagnetic field." Communicative & Integrative Biology 2(2):100–103 (PMC2686356; DOI: 10.4161/cib.7622)** [36]:
- The avian magnetic compass "works as an 'inclination compass' — it is based on the axial course of the field lines and their inclination rather than on the polarity of the magnetic field."
- The 'Fixed Direction' response: under **dim 645 nm red light**, European Robins and Australian Silvereyes (Zosterops l. lateralis) exhibit a persistent westerly tendency that does not vary with season — a polar (not axial) response contrasting with normal compass behavior. Other fixed direction responses occurred under bright monochromatic 565 nm green light, 502 nm turquoise light, bichromatic light combinations, and even in total darkness.
- Key differences (Table 1): Compass orientation = axial/inclination compass, requires short-wavelength light, disrupted by oscillating fields, not affected by upper beak anesthesia, based on radical pair mechanism, receptors in right eye, transmitted via optic nerve, can indicate any direction. Fixed direction responses = polar, occur even in total darkness, NOT affected by oscillating fields, disrupted by upper beak anesthesia, magnetite-based mechanism, receptors in skin of upper beak, transmitted via branch of trigeminal nerve, only one specific fixed direction depending on light regime.
- Higher light intensities (beyond ~8 ×10^15 quanta s−1 m−2 for compass orientation) trigger fixed direction responses, possibly due to cone activation imbalance. **Fixed direction responses are only observed under laboratory conditions not occurring in nature.**
- Under oscillating fields, long-wavelength light, or right-eye occlusion, birds become disoriented rather than showing fixed directions.
- The magnetite-based beak receptors normally provide magnetic intensity information as part of the navigational "map." The authors suggest fixed direction may be "a phylogenetic relict — an ancient function of magnetite-based receptors (found in all vertebrate groups) superseded in modern birds by the radical-pair-based avian compass."

### SENSORY MECHANISM DETAILS: Liedvogel 2006 PhD Thesis (Oldenburg)

**Liedvogel, M. (2006). "Magnetic orientation in migratory birds – linking behavioural phenomena with underlying molecular and neuronal mechanisms." PhD thesis, Carl von Ossietzky Universität Oldenburg** [37]:
- Garden warblers (*Sylvia borin*) oriented south-westerly under natural magnetic fields but randomly in zero-magnetic fields; birds nearly **tripled their head-scanning frequency in a fully compensated zero magnetic field**, indicating the magnetic compass sensor is in the head.
- Four cryptochrome family members identified/cloned/sequenced in the retina of migratory garden warblers: **Cry1a, Cry1b, Cry2, Cry4**. Cry1a predominantly expressed in cytosol of ganglion cells, displaced ganglion cells, and photoreceptors; **Cry1a expression was highest at night in night-migratory birds but decreased to background levels at night in non-migratory control species**; neuronal activity markers colocalized perfectly with Cry1a during night-time magnetic orientation — "the first experimental demonstration of a putative light-mediated primary magnetoreceptor molecule in a bird's eye."
- Garden warbler cryptochromes are light-excited, absorb in the blue spectral range (matching wavelengths known to elicit magnetic orientation behaviorally), and **form radical pairs lasting approximately 10 milliseconds** — sufficiently long-lived to detect Earth-strength magnetic fields. First successful expression of an animal cryptochrome holoprotein in a heterologous eukaryotic system (baculovirus/Sf9).
- **"Cluster N"** ("N" for night): a distinct forebrain area in night-migratory birds showing high neuronal activation at night during magnetic orientation but not during the day; inactive in non-migratory zebra finches (*Taeniopygia guttata*) and canaries (*Serinus canaria*); located adjacent to or as part of the visual Wulst; **covering birds' eyes with light-tight covers significantly reduced Cluster N activation to near baseline**.
- European robins showed significant dominance of Cluster N activation in the right hemisphere.
- Conclusion: "night-migratory birds may literally 'see' the direction of the Earth's magnetic field."

Science (DOI: 10.1126/science.854743; 57 citations)** [38]: "The results indicate that such disturbances do influence the orientation of free-flying migrants, but the evidence is not sufficient to show that geomagnetism is a cue in their orientation system."

Notable citing works listed on the Semantic Scholar page [38]:
