### 4. Infrasound-Based Map Hypotheses and Topographical/Landmark Recognition

#### 4.1 Infrasound
**Pigeon hearing of infrasound (Kreithen & Quine 1979, J Comp Physiol 129:1–4).** "Homing pigeons could detect extremely low frequency sounds (infrasounds) as low as 0.05 Hz in a sound isolation chamber"; "classically conditioned heart rate changes were used as a behavioral measure of sensitivity"; "an audiogram of thresholds was determined for 13 frequencies between 0.05 Hz and 200 Hz"; "below 10 Hz, the pigeons are at least 50 dB more sensitive than humans"; "surgical removal of middle ear or inner ear structures reduced or eliminated the infrasound responses"; "natural infrasounds come from many sources including weather patterns, topographic features, and ocean wave activity. Infrasounds propagate long distances and can be detected hundreds or even thousands of km away from their sources" [70][71]. (The pigeon hearing range is ~40 Hz to 8.5 kHz, most sensitive near 1 kHz, with exceptional infrasound sensitivity documented to ~0.05 Hz [72].) Earlier Cornell tests (Kreithen and Yodlowski; Quine) extended detection down to 0.05 Hz (one cycle every twenty seconds), with pigeons "more than 200 times more sensitive in this range than humans" [73].

**Hagstrum's infrasound map model (Hagstrum 2000, JEB 203:1103–1111; 2001, J Navigation).** "Pigeons can hear infrasound down to 0.05 Hz, and an acoustic avian map is proposed consisting of infrasonic cues radiated from steep-sided topographic features. The source of these infrasonic signals is microseisms continuously generated by interfering oceanic waves" (6 s period, ~0.14 Hz), transformed into audible infrasound radiated from topography; a coplanar source larger than the infrasound wavelength (~2.4 km) amplifies in-phase signals along a line normal to the source, providing directional information [65][66][67]. "Four recent disrupted pigeon races in Europe and the north-eastern USA intersected infrasonic shock waves from the Concorde supersonic transport": June 29, 1997 RPRA race of 60,000+ pigeons from Nantes to England; July 31, 1998 races from Bergerac (42,845 birds) and Soustons (13,610 birds) to the Netherlands (<10% of Soustons birds returned by evening; 60% still missing by Wednesday); October 5, 1998 races in Virginia and Pennsylvania (first birds returned after 8+ hours instead of 3). Supporting evidence: "site-release biases at Cornell lofts (Ithaca, NY) and Wilhelmshaven, Germany showed consistent patterns (clockwise offsets northeast, anticlockwise southwest) explained by southerly winds deflecting infrasonic map cues northward"; Jersey Hill (132 km west of Ithaca) showed random orientations explained by strong tropospheric winds impeding infrasonic waves—except August 13, 1969 when calm winds allowed normal homing; annual fluctuations in homing performance (Gronau and Schmidt-Koenig, 1970) correlate with winter microbarom atmospheric noise; birds with perforated tympana (raising hearing threshold 35–45 dB) had more homing difficulty [65]. "Having an acoustic map might also allow clock-shifted birds to test their homeward progress and select between their magnetic and solar compasses" [67]. Sight was ruled out as the long-range map cue since "pigeons with frosted contact lenses can return within 500m of their loft" [65].

**Hagstrum's 2013 analysis (NPR, JEB).** Hagstrum (USGS geophysicist) analyzed 14 years (1967–1980) of Cornell pigeon-release data combined with a computer model of sound propagation and weather: "when sound was bent up and over by temperature and wind structure, pigeons became confused; when sound reached the site, they returned home"; he modeled infrasound emanation from 200 sites around Cornell (~45,000 pigeons released over 14 years); at Jersey Hill "infrasound waves from that location didn't reach their Cornell home loft" on bad days. "It could mean that a lot of these animals—say, like whales or sea turtles, who swim across the ocean without any apparent problem; there are even birds that migrate from Alaska to New Zealand nonstop—I think they might well be using infrasound," Hagstrum said [68][69].

**Rejection evidence.** "With their cochleae removed, however, pigeons homed from unfamiliar areas over a distance of 150–160 km at the same speeds as control birds and their initial bearings were clearly oriented toward home" [58]. The Holland 2014 review: "Correlational evidence from pigeon racing disturbances and atmospheric fluctuations (Hagstrum, 2000-2013), but one experiment removing pigeon cochleas showed no homing deficits. No experiment has demonstrated effects on migration" [3]. The avesbiology.com overview calls infrasound maps "found implausible due to diffuse sources" [1]. The 2025 Animal Behaviour review lists infrasound among cues "with limited controlled experimental evidence" [4]. The 2026 Wikelski et al. study (below) notes Wagner's earlier experiments above opaque stratus over the Swiss Plateau proposed infrasonic propagation as a homing cue, but its authors found landmarks, not infrasound, explained successful homing above fog [77][78].

#### 4.2 Topographical/landscape landmark recognition
**Familiar-area navigation and route fidelity.** Biro, Meade & Guilford (2004, PNAS 101:17440–17443): nine pigeons from Oxford's Wytham station, trained through 20 releases from two sites (Weston Wood, 10.7 km; High Cogges, 9.4 km), tracked with GPS (1-second fixes, ±4 m). Birds developed "narrow flight corridors averaging 151 ± 60 m wide (Weston Wood) and 176 ± 33 m wide (High Cogges)"; routes were "strikingly inefficient—even after 20 releases, birds flew on average 18-25% extra distance to reach home (track efficiency 0.85 at Weston Wood, 0.80 at High Cogges)"; when released from novel "off-route" sites 1,000–1,500 m away, "in 76% of off-route releases, birds made contact with their established training tracks... deflecting dramatically toward their routes from distances of up to 1,500 m"; birds reached established routes "significantly earlier than expected (4.4 km earlier at Weston Wood, 2.5 km earlier at High Cogges)"; "59 of 66" rejoined routes "downstream" (closer to home); birds "selectively followed linear landscape features (roads, railways) that oriented homeward." Conclusion: pigeons use a "route map" of memorized visual landmarks or waypoints, supporting "visual pilotage (steeple-chasing—direct visual attraction to successive landmarks)" rather than a compass-based "mosaic map" [74]. Related: "In the local area pigeons potentially have access to a powerful navigational aid—a memorized landscape map. Current opinion suggests that landmarks are used..." [75]. "Pigeons navigate with an olfactory map and sun compass from unfamiliar areas and, in familiar areas, are largely guided by visual landscape cues, following stereotyped and idiosyncratic routes" [119].

**Distant landmarks as primary navigational references (Wikelski et al. 2026, Life 16:933).** Ten homing pigeons (~12–18 months) trained to home from two ground sites ~12 km NW and ~17 km NE of a loft near Lake Constance, then released from a Cessna ~400 m above the sites under three conditions: clear air, fog with distant Alpine landmarks visible, and fog with no landmarks. Results: "When all landmarks were hidden by ground fog, pigeons showed poor orientation, tortuous flight paths, and descended through the fog within four min, advancing only ~0.1 km (0.1% of the distance) towards home. They subsequently waited for solar cues to continue homing. By contrast, when distant landmarks (alpine mountain tops) were visible, pigeons maintained strong homeward orientation, flying for 20 min and covering 96% of the distance to home, similar to ground-level controls (17 min, 80%)." ANOVA: HEI (F=25.8 to 123.9, p<0.001), flight duration (F=19.6), flight distance (F=36.5), homing percentage (F=114.3), distance to home (F=85.9). Conclusions: "distant landmarks—but not magnetic cues—enable efficient short-distance homing in experienced pigeons"; "when known olfactory cues or local maps are excluded, distant landmarks are not merely auxiliary cues but appear to be essential for establishing a usable navigational solution"; "Magnetic information—both directional and positional—remains available at altitude and is unaffected by fog... Nevertheless, they did not initiate consistent homing trajectories. This strongly suggests that magnetic cues alone do not provide pigeons with sufficient positional ('map') information under these conditions" [77][78].

**Non-compass orientation by landmarks in migrants.** "Birds use landmarks and topographic features like coastlines and mountain ridges (e.g., European migrants turning southwest along the Alps)" [1]. "Visual landmark recognition" is used by homing pigeons and food-caching species; path integration (dead reckoning) is an additional mechanism [1].

**Passive exposure is insufficient for navigational learning in pigeons (Morford et al. 2024, Animal Behaviour).** 49 first-year pigeons exposed to environmental (visual and olfactory) cues at one of two release sites (Castelfranco di Sotto, 34.2 km; Cecina, 39.3 km) for 2 hours while caged, released the next day from the same or a different site: "We found no differences in the directional distributions, mean vector lengths, virtual vanishing times, efficiency indices or homing efficiency indices between birds that had and had not previously visited the site... passive exposure to the cues at a novel site was sufficient to facilitate a detectable improvement in navigational performance" was not supported. Explanations offered: weak effect below detection power; passive exposure insufficient (possibly because it "fails to sufficiently activate the hippocampal formation"); or pigeons learn but don't rely on the information [119].

**Ontogeny of maps (Morford et al. 2025).** "Some map cues rely on inherited rules (e.g., hatchling loggerhead turtles and salmon inherit responses to magnetic cues), sometimes combined with imprinting on natal site cues"; "homing pigeons have a sensitive learning period (3-4 months after fledging) for developing olfactory maps, but can also learn cues later when free flying"; "visual landscape cues are less likely to be developmentally fixed and must be learned through experience"; "map structures can be inherited (e.g., turtle signposts) or developed through learning (e.g., green turtles displaced up to 100 km appear to use more complex maps)" [4].

### 5. Integration and Weighting of Multiple Cues: Calibration Hierarchies, Redundancy, and Current Debates

#### 5.1 Compass calibration hierarchy
"Migratory birds use several different sources of orientation information. They have at least three compass systems based on different cues: the sun and polarized light, the stars and their constellations, and the geomagnetic field. The concurrent information obtained from these three compasses is redundant, therefore the compasses need to have a hierarchy and must be calibrated relative to each other" [87].

**Muheim, Moore & Phillips (2006, JEB 209:2–17)** reviewed 76 cue-conflict experiments (12 premigratory after-effects; 46 during-migration effects; 18 post-migration after-effects): 
- "During the premigratory season, celestial information is given the greatest salience and used to recalibrate the magnetic compass by both juvenile and adult birds. Sunset polarized light patterns from the region of the sky near the horizon appear to provide the calibration reference for the magnetic compass." In 5 of 6 cases where birds had access to sunrise/sunset cues during premigratory exposure, the magnetic compass was recalibrated.
- "During the migratory period: a majority of experiments suggest birds rely primarily on the magnetic field and use it to calibrate celestial compass cues—the relative saliency of magnetic and celestial cues is reversed during migration."
- Key pattern: "Birds with a full view of the sky down to the horizon (8 of 9 studies) recalibrated the magnetic compass regardless of season. Birds with restricted views (95-160° centered on zenith from funnels/registration cages) did not recalibrate the magnetic compass in 28 of 29 studies."

Proposed explanations: "(a) lateral asymmetry in right/left eye involvement in light-dependent magnetic compass orientation, and (b) interference from spectral and intensity distribution of skylight at sunset."

## Fully Comprehensive Findings

### LANDMARK FINDING ON THE 9/11 "TRIBUTE IN LIGHT" (B): Van Doren et al. 2017 PNAS

The central paper on artificial light at night (ALAN) disrupting nocturnal migration is **Van Doren, B.M., Horton, K.G., Dokter, A.M., Klinck, H., Elbin, S., & Farnsworth, A. (2017). "High-intensity urban light installation dramatically alters nocturnal bird migration." Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, October 2, 2017 (DOI: 10.1073/pnas.1708574114)**, which studied the "Tribute in Light" (TiL) installation at the National September 11 Memorial & Museum in New York City — the first study to quantify ALAN-induced changes in multiple behaviors of nocturnally migrating birds [1][2][3][4].

Study design and methods:
- Over seven years (2008–2016, excluding 2009 and 2011 due to precipitation), birds were monitored using weather surveillance radar (WSR-88D at Brookhaven, NY), acoustic sensors recording flight calls, visual observations, and computer simulations. This was an opportunistic study, not a controlled experiment [2].
- The installation is described as beams from **eighty-eight 7500-watt bulbs** shining skyward over New York City every September 11th, with authors from Cornell Lab of Ornithology, Oxford University, and New York City Audubon [4].
- The lights were shut down **22 times for approximately 20 minutes each** during the study, allowing direct comparison between lit and dark periods [2][3].

Key quantitative findings:
- **The installation influenced approximately 1.1 million birds (95% CI: 0.6–1.6 million) during 7 nights over 7 years** [1][2][3][4].
- Bird densities near the installation were **up to 20 times greater than baseline densities**, exceeding 60 times baseline in five of seven years and **150 times baseline in three years (2008, 2012, 2013)**; densities never exceeded 13 times baseline when lights were off [2][3].
- Effects were found **up to 4 km altitude** (3.9x density increase at 1.5° radar elevation angle) [2][3].
- **Maximum standardized bird densities were 14 times greater during illuminated periods** (t=5.70, P<0.0001); maximum bird numbers within 500 m averaged **3.4 times higher** during illumination (t=3.89, P=0.0003) [2][3].
- During illuminated periods birds aggregated in high densities, **decreased flight speeds (by 1.7 m/s)**, followed circular flight paths, and **vocalized more frequently (1.4x increase in flight call rates)** (radial velocity main effect −1.7 ms⁻¹, t=−2.10, P=0.037; flight call rates t=4.53, P<0.0001) [2][3].
- Effects occurred **under clear sky conditions in a heavily photo-polluted environment** — contradicting previous assumptions that light attraction only occurs in poor visibility [2][3].
- **Behavioral disruptions disappeared within minutes when lights were extinguished** [1][2][4].
- Simulations (flow model with disorientation probability a=0.95 and disorientation distance of 1500 m) revealed high probability of disorientation and attraction, with a stabilization time of **34 minutes**; bird concentrations could only be explained by directed flight toward the light for disoriented birds [2][3].
- Observers documented **birds colliding with glass windows of a building under construction at 50 West St. in 2015 and 2016** [2][3].

Conservation recommendations: Selective removal of lights during nights with substantial bird migration is a "viable strategy for minimizing potentially fatal interactions among ALAN, structures, and birds" [1]. The lights were extinguished when more than 1,000 birds were in the beams or flying dangerously low, following lobbying by the Municipal Arts Society (now National September 11 Memorial & Museum) and New York City Audubon [4]. The paper highlights this collaboration (National September 11 Memorial & Museum, NYC Audubon, Cornell Lab of Ornithology) as a model for mitigation [4]. The paper contains 4 figures, 292 citations (per Semantic Scholar), and 89 references [1].

Related works noted on the paper's citation page: blue light attracts nocturnally migrating birds (suggesting switching to longer wavelength lights could reduce collisions); ALAN confounds broad-scale habitat use by migrating birds; light pollution is greatest within migration passage areas worldwide [1]. The Van Doren Google Scholar profile also lists: "A continental system for forecasting bird migration" (Science, 2018, 290 citations); "Bright lights in the big cities: migratory birds' exposure to artificial light" (Frontiers in Ecology, 2019, 202 citations); "Drivers of fatal bird collisions in an urban center" (PNAS, 2021, 170 citations); "Holding steady: Little change in intensity or timing of bird migration over the Gulf of Mexico" (Global Change Biology, 2019, 121 citations); and "MistNet: Measuring historical bird migration in the US using archived weather radar data and convolutional neural networks" (2019, 120 citations) [6].

The eBird Science article adds: "Only by using radar were the authors able to view a full 'footprint' of the lights' impacts on birds, which may extend multiple kilometers from and above the lights themselves." [4]

### CONTINENTAL-SCALE ALAN EXPOSURE: Horton et al. 2019 Frontiers in Ecology and the Environment

**Horton, K.G., Nilsson, C., Van Doren, B.M., La Sorte, F.A., Dokter, A.M., & Farnsworth, A. (2019). "Bright lights in the big cities: migratory birds' exposure to artificial light." Frontiers in Ecology and the Environment.** Key findings [5]:
- Approximately **80% of North America's ~630 terrestrial bird species are migratory, and over 80% of those migrate at night**.
- Combined over two decades (spring 1995 to spring 2017) of weather surveillance radar data from **143 stations** with satellite-based VIIRS ALAN radiance data, focusing on the **125 largest urban centers**. Radar data from a 30-minute window centered on 3 hours after local sunset were filtered using a random forest classifier (5.6% spring and 4.5% fall classification error). Migration activity was measured as vertically integrated reflectivity; ALAN quantified using monthly VIIRS Day/Night Band composites averaged across October–December 2012–2017.
- **Fall migration had 63% higher cumulative migratory activity than spring, and 53.8% higher total exposure**; even after standardizing, fall exposure remained 13.1% higher because fall migrants used more easterly (and more photo-polluted) routes.
- **Half of seasonal migratory activity passed each radar site within just 6.7 ± 2.6 nights on average.**
- **The top 125 urban areas occupied only 2.1% of total land area but produced 35.4% of total light radiance**; across the US, 69.5% of summed linear light radiance came from just 5% of the land area.
- **Mean avian light exposure in cities was 24 times the countrywide average.**
- **Chicago, Houston, and Dallas consistently had the highest exposure risk in both seasons, with exposure magnitudes 19–21 times the median of the other 122 cities.**
- Larger cities generally had greater exposure risk (R² = 0.52 spring, 0.62 fall), with exceptions like Boston (4th in size but 36th/24th in exposure) and Des Moines (99th in size but 28th/36th in exposure).
- Because migration occurs in concentrated pulses and can now be forecast 12–72 hours in advance, targeted "lights-out" campaigns timed to peak migration nights could reduce exposure significantly; fall mitigation is especially important given higher numbers of less-experienced juvenile birds.

### PROCELLARIFORMES / SEABIRD LIGHT ATTRACTION (OFFSHORE PLATFORMS, VESSELS, LIGHTHOUSES, ISLAND LIGHTS)

**Reed, J.R., Sincock, J.L., & Hailman, J.P. (1985). "Light attraction in endangered procellariiform birds: reduction by shielding upward radiation." The Auk** (Digital Commons USF, 179 citations) [7]: **Shielding (of upward radiation) decreased attraction by nearly 40%. Most attraction occurred 1–4 hours after sunset. Full moon dramatically decreased attraction.**

**Rodríguez, A., & Rodríguez, B. (2009). "Attraction of petrels to artificial lights in the Canary Islands: effects of the moon phase and age class." Ibis 151(2):299–310 (138 citations)** [8][9].

**Wiese, F., Montevecchi, W.A., et al. (2001). "Seabirds at risk around offshore oil platforms in the northwest Atlantic." Marine Pollution Bulletin 42: 1285–1290 (273 citations)** [10][11][12][13][14]: **"Seabirds aggregate around oil drilling platforms and rigs in above average numbers due to night lighting, flaring, food and other visual cues."**

**Merkel, F.R., & Johansen, K.L. (2011). "Light-induced bird strikes on vessels in Southwest Greenland." Marine Pollution Bulletin 62(11), 2330–2336 (113 citations)** [10].

**Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution (January 18, 2022). "Tracking Flights to Investigate Seabird Mortality Induced by Artificial Lights."** — Original research tracking **Cory's shearwater (Calonectris borealis)** fledglings on Tenerife, Canary Islands, 2017–2019 [15]:
- More than **56 burrow-nesting petrel species, some critically endangered, are affected by lights** (citing Rodríguez et al., 2017; Silva et al., 2020); "Every fledging season, on islands where humans and petrels coexist, thousands of fledglings of different species are grounded by light pollution."
- Used GPS-GSM transmitters to track **277 experimentally released fledglings** from an inland release site (8 km inland at 900 m elevation); treatments: GPS-tagged (87), tape-labelled (92), control (98).
- **37 of 277 fledglings (13.4%) were grounded by artificial lights**; birds with higher down abundance had higher grounding probability; grounding probability was positively related to flight tortuosity and overflown light pollution levels; slower flights were more likely to be grounded; tortuosity increased with light pollution levels but decreased with moon luminance.
- All birds oriented flights towards low-altitude coastal areas, following the most light-polluted regions; flights covered 18.7 ± 10.8 km and lasted 47.3 ± 45.3 min on average.
- Control birds (8.2% grounding) were grounded less often than GPS-tagged (19.5%) and tape-labelled (13%) birds, suggesting control birds were overlooked during rescue due to small metal rings being less visible.
- The most dangerous light-polluted areas in southern Tenerife were identified, where more than 50% of island-wide rescued birds are grounded. Funding: European Commission project INTERREG MAC/4.6d/157 LuMinAves.

**Rodríguez, A., et al. (2023). "Moonlight diminishes seabird attraction to artificial light." Conservation Science and Practice** [16]:
- Rescue programs report fewer fledglings grounded during full moon nights. The authors evaluate two hypotheses: (1) reduced strandings because birds are less attracted/disoriented by light pollution during full moon; (2) reduced fledging activity (chicks avoiding departure during bright moonlight as anti-predator behavior). Evidence supports the first but not the second.
- Evidence includes: annual stranding numbers lower when full moon coincides with mean peak fledging date; biometric data from **8,954 Cory's shearwater fledglings in the Azores (2016–2021) and 267 from Tenerife** showing no evidence of delayed fledging after full moon nights; multiple studies showing cavity-nesting seabirds fledge regardless of moon phase (Newell's shearwaters via camera traps, Leach's storm-petrels, Barau's petrels via radar surveys); GPS tracking showing fledglings fly straighter over light-polluted areas during full moon and reach the ocean more successfully.
- **At least 73 seabird species, mostly cavity-nesting Procellariiformes, have been documented in light pollution-induced mortality events, with approximately 60% showing population declines and 28 globally threatened by IUCN criteria.**
- Proposed mechanisms: reduced relative glare of artificial lights, ability to see obstructions, orientation toward the moon instead of artificial lights, and potential visual system development benefits from moonlight exposure.

**Medina-Franco, Sangiorgi, & Valdés-Velásquez (2025). "Lost in the glow: understanding the impact of light pollution on storm-petrels." Avian Conservation and Ecology 20(1), Art. 18 (DOI: 10.5751/ACE-02846-200118)** — first global scoping review on light pollution effects on Hydrobatidae (storm-petrels) [17]:
- 12 articles (published 2005–2022) included from 144 records; half published 2020–2022; six southern hemisphere, six northern.
- **Grounding records found for all Hydrobatidae genera except *Nesofregetta*; groundings recorded in 12 of 22 Hydrobatidae species**; *O. leucorhoa* and *P. marina* most frequently mentioned, followed by *H. pelagicus*.
- **Fallout occurs primarily in fledglings during their first flight leaving the colony; over 99% of grounded *O. leucorhoa* were fledglings** (per Wilhelm et al. 2021).
- Inshore sources: residential, industrial, road, highway, business areas; offshore sources: mainly fishing vessel deck lights.
- **Moon phase associated with groundings: more groundings during new moon, fewer during full moon.**
- Of 12 species assessed by IUCN, nine have decreasing population trends, two unknown, one stable.
- Only five of 12 articles assessed population-level impacts; these found **annual fallout mortality was less than 1% of respective species' populations**.
- Hypotheses for fledgling attraction to light: (1) confusion with bioluminescent prey; (2) association of light with food (burrow entrances); (3) undeveloped visual system and behavioral inexperience; (4) artificial lights limiting navigation by moon and stars.
- A recent study found **even partial reduction in artificial light at night (ALAN) decreased strandings by up to 57%** (Burt et al. 2024).
- Knowledge gaps: only two articles used systematic data collection; eastern Pacific (highest storm-petrel diversity) understudied; light intensity/spectrum rarely quantified.

### OTHER ALAN/NIGHT-MIGRATION MONITORING CONTEXT (Audubon Magazine, Sept–Oct 2013):

- History: first quantified record in **1896 by Orin Libby tallying 3,600 night flight calls near Madison, Wisconsin**; first audio recordings in the 1950s; voice-activated system developed 1987; in 2002 Bill Evans and Michael O'Brien published a CD with calls/spectrograms of **211 North American terrestrial bird species** [18].
- Research applications: Rachel Bricklin (Fordham) monitors activity at Mianus River Gorge Preserve and the Bronx Zoo testing corticosterone; Cornell with Oregon State, UMass-Amherst, Microsoft, NOAA planning automated recording stations; Andrew Farnsworth developed the "Rosetta Stone for warblers" (spectrograms of 48 warbler NFCs); German researchers recorded calls near offshore wind turbines in the North Sea.
- **A 2012 Philadelphia art installation with 24 robotic searchlights (25 nights during peak migration): radar tracked over 735,000 migrating birds and acoustic recordings found six times more NFCs near the lights than at a nearby station.**
- J. Alan Clark (Fordham) counted over 300,000 targets in just 10 nights in May 2010 over two 550-yard-wide transects of New York City.
- High school student Jessica Fleischman recorded 20,500+ nocturnal flight calls over 84 nights comparing suburban and rural sites, showing wind speed and precipitation affect calling rates.
- Why birds call at night: NFCs help birds stay with flocks (more frequent in rough weather/headwinds) and may warn of fatal crashes with tall lit structures; high call rates coincide with mass collisions at towers and skyscrapers. Most calls are shorter than half a second (hooded warbler's is ~1/20 second).

### ANTHROPOGENIC ELECTROMAGNETIC NOISE / RADIOFREQUENCY FIELDS (B): Engels et al. 2014 Nature

**Engels, S., Schneider, N.-L., Lefeldt, N., Hein, C.M., Zapka, M., Michalik, A., Elbers, D., Kittel, A., Hore, P.J., & Mouritsen, H. (2014). "Anthropogenic electromagnetic noise disrupts magnetic compass orientation in a migratory bird." Nature 509(7500):353–356 (May 15, 2014; DOI: 10.1038/nature13290; Epub May 7, 2014; PMID: 24805233)** [23][24][25][26][27]. Affiliations: University of Oldenburg (Institute for Biology and Environmental Sciences, Research Centre for Neurosensory Sciences, Institute of Physics) and University of Oxford (Physical and Theoretical Chemistry Laboratory) [23].

Key findings:
- **"Here we show that migratory birds are unable to use their magnetic compass in the presence of urban electromagnetic noise"** — tested on European robins (*Erithacus rubecula*) [23][25][26].
- Birds in unscreened wooden huts at the University of Oldenburg campus could not orient using their magnetic compass; **their magnetic orientation abilities reappeared in electrically grounded, aluminium-screened huts that attenuated EM noise in the 50 kHz to 5 MHz range by approximately two orders of magnitude** [23][26].
- **When grounding was removed or broadband electromagnetic noise (2 kHz–9 MHz) was deliberately generated inside the screened and grounded huts at intensities similar to background urban noise, birds again lost their magnetic orientation capabilities**; very weak noise did not cause disorientation [23][26].
- **The disruptive effect of radiofrequency electromagnetic fields was not confined to a narrow frequency band** — both 20 kHz–450 kHz and 600 kHz–3 MHz ranges prevented orientation [23][26].
- **Birds tested far from sources of electromagnetic noise (a rural location ~7.5 km from the university) required no screening to orient with their magnetic compass** [23][26].
- "These fully double-blinded tests document a reproducible effect of anthropogenic electromagnetic noise on the behaviour of an intact vertebrate" — noted as significant because previous claimed effects below WHO guidelines had not withstood independent replication under blinded conditions [23][26].

Quantitative details:
- Anthropogenic EMN peak magnetic field intensity at single frequencies was ~0.1–50 nT, with total time-dependent field summed over 10 kHz–5 MHz of ~200–1100 nT (still far weaker than Earth's magnetic field of ~49,000 nT) [26].
- **Effects occurred at intensities well below WHO/ICNIRP guidelines** (reference levels of 6,000 nT at 150 kHz to 180 nT at 5 MHz) [26].
- Effects were **not** attributed to power lines (16.7/50 Hz), mobile phone signals (GHz), or frequencies below 2 kHz or above 5 MHz [26].
- Exposure parameters listed as 50 kHz–9 MHz, DC, electric field, magnetic field, static magnetic field, geomagnetic field, low frequency, intermediate frequency, shielding/field deprivation [24].
- Mechanism unclear but may involve radical-pair (cryptochrome-based) magnetoreception or iron-containing particle clusters; the possibility of effects on quantum spin dynamics at such weak intensities is noted as remarkable [26].
- Implications: disorientation may reduce survival during migration, especially in overcast conditions when sun/star compass cues are unavailable; effect appears localized to urban areas with high electronic device usage [26].
- The paper lists a commentary: **Kirschvink, J.L. (2014). "Sensory biology: Radio waves zap the biomagnetic compass." Nature 2014;509:296–7** [23][24]. The paper has 374 citations and 44 references per Semantic Scholar [25].
- Semantic Scholar lists key citing papers: a **2016 study showing weak broadband electromagnetic fields are more disruptive to European robin magnetic compass orientation than strong narrow-band fields**; a **2017 paper questioning whether the radical-pair model can explain the behavioral findings**; a **2019 study indicating 0.1–100 kHz RF fields did not disrupt blackcap orientation, suggesting radical pair spin coherence lifetimes of 2–10 µs**; and a **2026 Science paper on disruptive effects of brief radiofrequency noise on migratory bat navigation** [25].

Background from the Interference Technology article (interview with Henrik Mouritsen) [27]:
- Researchers had studied European robins since the early 2000s using orientation cages with thermal paper. When Mouritsen moved to the University of Oldenburg (population ~160,000) in 2002, "the robins basically jumped in random directions every spring and autumn for three years." After exhausting other explanations (food, cages, light, daylight cycle), graduate student Nils-Lasse Schneider suggested covering huts and cages with aluminum sheets to form a Faraday cage, which restored orientation without affecting Earth's magnetic field.
- "Our measurements of the interferences indicated that we had accidentally discovered a biological system that is sensitive to anthropogenic electromagnetic noise generated by humans in the frequency range up to five megahertz."
- The interference was below ICNIRP/WHO limits; over a seven-year investigation with double-blind studies, when Faraday cage grounding was disconnected or deliberate interference created, birds immediately lost orientation again.
- "Thus, the effect of anthropogenic electromagnetic noise on bird migration is localized. However these findings should make us think — both about the survival of migratory birds as well as about the potential effects for human beings, which have yet to be investigated."

### RESONANCE EFFECTS AND THE RADICAL-PAIR MECHANISM (SENSORY MECHANISM): Ritz et al. 2004 Nature

**Ritz, T., Thalau, P., Phillips, J.B., Wiltschko, R., & Wiltschko, W. (2004). "Resonance effects indicate a radical-pair mechanism for avian magnetic compass." Nature 429(6988):177–180 (May 13, 2004; DOI: 10.1038/nature02534; PMID: 15141211)** [28][29][30][31][32].

Key findings:
- European robins (*Erithacus rubecula*) were tested under 565 nm light in the local geomagnetic field (46 µT, 66° inclination). **Robins were disoriented when exposed to a vertically aligned broadband (0.1–10 MHz) field (0.085 µT) or a single-frequency 7-MHz field (0.47 µT)** in addition to the geomagnetic field [20/29/32].
- **In the 7-MHz oscillating field, the effect depended on the angle between the oscillating and geomagnetic fields: birds exhibited seasonally appropriate migratory orientation when the field was parallel to the geomagnetic field, but were disoriented when presented at a 24° or 48° angle** [28][29][32].
- "These results are consistent with a resonance effect on singlet–triplet transitions and suggest a magnetic compass based on a radical-pair mechanism" [29].
- The 7 MHz field would require 285 µT to affect magnetite receptors, far stronger than the 0.47 µT used; model calculations showed a resonant oscillating field of 0.033 µT (a thousandth of Earth's field strength) could produce a detectable effect [32].
- Magnetite is suggested as a separate magnetic-intensity ('map') sensor, not for compass orientation [32].
- The study establishes oscillating magnetic fields as a diagnostic tool for identifying radical-pair magnetoreception, applicable to other animal groups [19/32]. Experiments conducted January 13–February 17, 2003, in Frankfurt am Main, Germany; 12 test birds [31][32].
- The Academia.edu page notes: rodent compasses (e.g., mole-rats) are NOT disrupted by the same fields and likely use magnetite-based mechanisms; the wood mouse (*Apodemus sylvaticus*) showed first evidence of a radical-pair mechanism in a mammal [31].

### LIGHT-DEPENDENT MAGNETORECEPTION — RED LIGHT DISRUPTION: Wiltschko, Munro, Ford & Wiltschko 1993 Nature

**Wiltschko, W., Munro, U., Ford, H., & Wiltschko, R. (1993). "Red light disrupts magnetic orientation of migratory birds." Nature 364:525–527 (292 citations, 2732 accesses)** [33]. This reports the **first orientation tests on migratory birds under light of different wavelengths**, providing evidence for a light-dependent magnetoreception process.

- The discussion on magnetoreception in birds focuses mainly on two mechanisms: small particles of magnetite, and "biochemical bi-radical reactions of excited macromolecules."
- Prior evidence: bi-radical hypothesis suggested magnetic resonance phenomena in the retina as primary processes; homing experiments and electrophysiological evidence from pigeons supported this; a study showed that in newts, magnetic compass orientation was maintained under blue light (450 nm and below) but shifted roughly 90° counterclockwise under wavelengths at or above 500 nm.
- The results suggest a light-dependent process in migratory birds "that appears to differ from that reported in newts."

**Wiltschko, W., & Wiltschko, R. (1995). "Migratory orientation of European Robins is affected by the wavelength of light as well as by a magnetic pulse." Journal of Comparative Physiology A 177:363–369 (DOI: 10.1007/BF00192425; 136 citations)** [34]:
- Under "white" (control) light, robins preferred the normal, seasonally appropriate migratory direction; **under 571 nm green light they remained well oriented, whereas under 633 nm red light their behavior was not different from random**.
- A brief, strong magnetic pulse had a significant effect on migratory orientation but responses varied between individuals: some showed a persistent directional shift, others a change in scatter, one bird seemingly unaffected.
- "These findings indicate a light-dependent process and, at the same time, suggest an involvement of magnetizable material in migratory orientation. They are in agreement with the model of a light-dependent compass and a magnetite-based 'map'."
- The paper references Wiltschko & Wiltschko's **1972 discovery of the magnetic compass in European robins (Science 176:62–64)** and their 1993 red-light finding.

**Wiltschko, R., Ritz, T., Stapput, K., Thalau, P., & Wiltschko, W. (2005). "Two Different Types of Light-Dependent Responses to Magnetic Fields in Birds." Current Biology 15(16):1518–1523** [35]:
- Under 502 nm turquoise light, birds showed normal migratory orientation (inclination compass) at a quantal flux of **8×10^15 quanta m−2 s−1**, but under brighter light (54×10^15 quanta m−2 s−1) they showed a **fixed northward tendency based on magnetic polarity** rather than the inclination compass.
- When exposed to a weak oscillating field that interferes with radical pair processes, the inclination compass response was disrupted while the magnetic polarity response remained unaffected.
- Demonstrates that the normal inclination compass relies on a radical-pair mechanism, while the fixed direction represents a novel type of light-dependent orientation based on a different mechanism.

**Wiltschko, R., & Wiltschko, W. (2009). "'Fixed direction'-responses of birds in the geomagnetic field." Communicative & Integrative Biology 2(2):100–103 (PMC2686356; DOI: 10.4161/cib.7622)** [36]:
- The avian magnetic compass "works as an 'inclination compass' — it is based on the axial course of the field lines and their inclination rather than on the polarity of the magnetic field."
- The 'Fixed Direction' response: under **dim 645 nm red light**, European Robins and Australian Silvereyes (Zosterops l. lateralis) exhibit a persistent westerly tendency that does not vary with season — a polar (not axial) response contrasting with normal compass behavior. Other fixed direction responses occurred under bright monochromatic 565 nm green light, 502 nm turquoise light, bichromatic light combinations, and even in total darkness.
- Key differences (Table 1): Compass orientation = axial/inclination compass, requires short-wavelength light, disrupted by oscillating fields, not affected by upper beak anesthesia, based on radical pair mechanism, receptors in right eye, transmitted via optic nerve, can indicate any direction. Fixed direction responses = polar, occur even in total darkness, NOT affected by oscillating fields, disrupted by upper beak anesthesia, magnetite-based mechanism, receptors in skin of upper beak, transmitted via branch of trigeminal nerve, only one specific fixed direction depending on light regime.
- Higher light intensities (beyond ~8 ×10^15 quanta s−1 m−2 for compass orientation) trigger fixed direction responses, possibly due to cone activation imbalance. **Fixed direction responses are only observed under laboratory conditions not occurring in nature.**
- Under oscillating fields, long-wavelength light, or right-eye occlusion, birds become disoriented rather than showing fixed directions.
- The magnetite-based beak receptors normally provide magnetic intensity information as part of the navigational "map." The authors suggest fixed direction may be "a phylogenetic relict — an ancient function of magnetite-based receptors (found in all vertebrate groups) superseded in modern birds by the radical-pair-based avian compass."

### SENSORY MECHANISM DETAILS: Liedvogel 2006 PhD Thesis (Oldenburg)

**Liedvogel, M. (2006). "Magnetic orientation in migratory birds – linking behavioural phenomena with underlying molecular and neuronal mechanisms." PhD thesis, Carl von Ossietzky Universität Oldenburg** [37]:
- Garden warblers (*Sylvia borin*) oriented south-westerly under natural magnetic fields but randomly in zero-magnetic fields; birds nearly **tripled their head-scanning frequency in a fully compensated zero magnetic field**, indicating the magnetic compass sensor is in the head.
- Four cryptochrome family members identified/cloned/sequenced in the retina of migratory garden warblers: **Cry1a, Cry1b, Cry2, Cry4**. Cry1a predominantly expressed in cytosol of ganglion cells, displaced ganglion cells, and photoreceptors; **Cry1a expression was highest at night in night-migratory birds but decreased to background levels at night in non-migratory control species**; neuronal activity markers colocalized perfectly with Cry1a during night-time magnetic orientation — "the first experimental demonstration of a putative light-mediated primary magnetoreceptor molecule in a bird's eye."
- Garden warbler cryptochromes are light-excited, absorb in the blue spectral range (matching wavelengths known to elicit magnetic orientation behaviorally), and **form radical pairs lasting approximately 10 milliseconds** — sufficiently long-lived to detect Earth-strength magnetic fields. First successful expression of an animal cryptochrome holoprotein in a heterologous eukaryotic system (baculovirus/Sf9).
- **"Cluster N"** ("N" for night): a distinct forebrain area in night-migratory birds showing high neuronal activation at night during magnetic orientation but not during the day; inactive in non-migratory zebra finches (*Taeniopygia guttata*) and canaries (*Serinus canaria*); located adjacent to or as part of the visual Wulst; **covering birds' eyes with light-tight covers significantly reduced Cluster N activation to near baseline**.
- European robins showed significant dominance of Cluster N activation in the right hemisphere.
- Conclusion: "night-migratory birds may literally 'see' the direction of the Earth's magnetic field."

Science (DOI: 10.1126/science.854743; 57 citations)** [38]: "The results indicate that such disturbances do influence the orientation of free-flying migrants, but the evidence is not sufficient to show that geomagnetism is a cue in their orientation system."

### SPACE WEATHER DISRUPTS NOCTURNAL BIRD MIGRATION: Gulson-Castillo et al. 2023 PNAS

**Gulson-Castillo, E.R., Van Doren, B.M., Bui, M.X., Horton, K.G., Li, J., Moldwin, M.B., Shedden, K., Welling, D.T., & Winger, B.M. (2023). "Space weather disrupts nocturnal bird migration." PNAS 120(42):e2306317120 (October 9, 2023; DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2306317120)** [39][40][41][42][43].

Methodology:
- 23-year (1995–2018) dataset of bird migration from **37 NEXRAD Doppler weather radar stations in the central flyway of the US Great Plains** (spanning over 1,000 miles from Texas to North Dakota), chosen to minimize topographic/coastal variation.
- Final datasets: **1,725,415 radar scans in fall and 1,392,826 in spring**.
- Concurrent magnetometer data from the superMAG database; a local magnetic disturbance index (ΔBmax, maximum hourly change in nT from background) developed for each radar station by Daniel Welling and Michelle Bui.
- Two complementary statistical models: nonlinear mixed effects (NLME) and machine learning decision tree (MLT), controlling for atmospheric weather and spatiotemporal patterns.
- Migrating bird community: primarily Passeriformes (73%), Charadriiformes (12%), Anseriformes (9%).

Key findings:
- **Migration intensity decreased 9–17% in both spring and fall during severe space weather events**: Spring MLT residual model: 11.2% decrease; Spring NLME model: 17.4% reduction; Fall MLT residual model: 8.9% decrease. Decreases were predicted at geomagnetic disturbances greater than ~500 nT.
- **Large disturbances (>~500 nT) occurred on 81 (3.32%) unique nights in fall and 50 (2.28%) unique nights in spring over the 23-year dataset; 75.5% of large disturbances were directly linked to registered geomagnetic storms.**
- **During fall migration, evidence showed decreases in effort flying against the wind (crosswind component of airspeed): the fall NLME model predicted a 25.4% decrease at 100% cloud cover and high ΔBmax; MLT model showed a 7.6% decrease** — birds drift more with the wind during geomagnetic disturbances, indicating navigation difficulties.
- No significant effects found on flight altitude; no crosswind effects in spring — potentially because fall migration contains many inexperienced juveniles migrating for the first time who depend on simpler "clock and compass" magnetic orientation strategies.
- Atmospheric weather had larger effects than space weather (e.g., warm spring temperatures associated with 45.2% increase in migration intensity; north fall winds with ~43.1% increase), but log-likelihood tests supported inclusion of ΔBmax.
- Quote: "Our results suggest that fewer birds migrate during strong geomagnetic disturbances and that migrating birds may experience more difficulty navigating, especially under overcast conditions in autumn."
- The study provides correlational evidence and explicitly controlled for atmospheric weather, addressing limitations of previous studies. Paper received April 18, 2023, accepted August 22, 2023; edited by Pablo Marquet (Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile). Funding: U-M MCubed grant, NSF fellowships.

### GEOMAGNETIC DISTURBANCE AND VAGRANCY: Tonelli, Youngflesh & Tingley 2023 Scientific Reports

**Tonelli, B.A., Youngflesh, C., & Tingley, M.W. (2023). "Geomagnetic disturbance associated with increased vagrancy in migratory landbirds." Scientific Reports (DOI: 10.1038/s41598-022-26586-0)** [44][45]:
- Analyzed **2,226,936 banding records of 152 migratory landbird species in North America (150 in fall, 124 in spring) from 1960 to 2019**, combining USGS Bird Banding Lab data with eBird Status and Trends weekly species abundance maps.
- Created a continuous "vagrancy index" measuring the spatiotemporal rarity of each banding record relative to modeled expected ranges; tested associations with geomagnetic disturbance (global Ap index) and solar activity (American relative sunspot number) using hierarchical Bayesian random-effects models.
- **Strong positive association between geomagnetic disturbance and vagrancy during fall migration (posterior median = 0.109; 95% CrI = 0.077–0.142; p(>0) = 1). A two-standard-deviation increase in geomagnetic disturbance is associated with a 24% increase in median predicted vagrancy index and a 250% increase in the number of spatiotemporally rare banding records (from 2% to 5% of records).**
- **83% of species showed positive sensitivity to geomagnetic disturbance in fall.**
- Sensitivity was stronger among longer-distance migrants (supporting the hypothesis that long-distance migrants rely more on magnetoreception); no effect of breeding latitude; hatch-year (juvenile) birds showed higher baseline fall vagrancy but were NOT more sensitive.
- Only weak or no evidence for associations during spring migration (possibly sampling bias).
- **Contrary to hypotheses, increased solar activity was negatively associated with fall vagrancy**: the interaction model showed strong evidence of a negative interaction during fall (posterior median μωfall = −0.025; 95% CrI = −0.047 to −0.003; p(<0) = 0.99) — during high solar activity, birds are less sensitive to geomagnetic disturbance, "suggesting radiofrequency noise disables magnetoreception, causing birds to pause migration or switch to other cues."
- **Diurnal migrants (24% of fall species) were more sensitive to solar activity than nocturnal migrants**, possibly because solar radiofrequency noise affects the sunlit side of Earth; may explain previously observed negative effects of solar activity on crane migration.
- Geomagnetic disturbance and solar activity explained a median of **5.9% of variance in vagrancy** (species-specific range 0.3–30%).
- Phys.org reports: the effect was most pronounced in fall; solar activity actually reduced vagrancy (possibly by making magnetoreceptors unusable, causing birds to pause or switch cues); geomagnetic disturbances affected both young and older birds equally; research was inspired by whale strandings; Tonelli developed a web-based rare-bird forecast tool (bentonelli.github.io/rarebirdforecast/). Quote from Morgan Tingley: "In familiar areas, birds may navigate by geography, but in some situations it's easier to use geomagnetism." [45]

### NATURALLY SHIFTING MAGNETIC DECLINATION AND TRUE NAVIGATION (A)

**Chernetsov, N., Pakhomov, A., Kobylkov, D., Kishkinev, D., Holland, R.A., & Mouritsen, H. (2017). "Migratory Eurasian Reed Warblers Can Use Magnetic Declination to Solve the Longitude Problem." Current Biology, August 21, 2017 (DOI: 10.1016/j.cub.2017.07.024)** [46][47]:
- First time in history that birds have been proven to measure the difference between magnetic and geographical north; resolves the "longitude problem" (west–east direction) in animal navigation.
- Experiments with adult and young Eurasian reed warblers (*Acrocephalus scirpaceus*, nesting in the Baltics, wintering in West Africa) at the Curonian Spit, Kaliningrad region, in circular arenas where birds demonstrated eagerness to migrate south-west.
- Researchers rotated magnetic north **8.5° anticlockwise while keeping magnetic intensity and inclination the same** — equivalent to a virtual displacement to southeast Scotland. **Adult birds compensated by turning southeast to return to their normal migratory route; younger, inexperienced migrants were disoriented**, indicating the ability to measure declination is acquired, not innate.
- The navigation map is thus "magnetic-astronomical" rather than strictly magnetic. ScienceDaily adds: mature birds oriented as if migrating from Aberdeen, Scotland (with actual declination of 8°), approximately 900 miles away from their actual location; immature birds were confounded, suggesting the magnetic map is learned by experience [47]. Comment from Richard Holland: "How birds have resolved the longitudinal problem has been a scientific mystery... It seems that a bird as unassuming as the reed warbler, may have a geographic map or memory that enables it to identify its longitudinal position on the globe, only by detecting the magnetic north pole and its variance from true north."

**Kishkinev, D., et al. (2021). "Navigation by extrapolation of geomagnetic cues in a migratory songbird." Current Biology (April 12, 2021)** [48]:
- Tested the "gradient map" (extrapolated map) hypothesis with experienced Eurasian reed warblers captured at Lake Neusiedl, Illmitz, south-eastern Austria, in modified Emlen funnels inside a 3D magnetic coil system during fall migration.

- All other environmental cues (local stars, sun, odors) were unchanged, yet birds responded to the magnetic field changes, indicating magnetic cues play a dominant role in this species' navigation map. - The setting sun functions both as a source of directional information and as an environmental stimulus influencing the likelihood of migratory activity.

Birds recalibrate their stellar compass using their magnetic compass, and must "read" new star configurations when crossing the equator.

# Avian Migratory Navigation: Sensory Mechanisms, Map-Based Position Determination, Cue Integration, and Disrupting Factors

## 1. Introduction

Bird migration requires solving two distinct navigational problems: knowing **which direction** to fly (compass/heading information) and knowing **where you are** relative to the destination (map/positional information). This two-step "map-and-compass" framework, first formalized by Gustav Kramer in the 1950s, remains the conceptual foundation of the field [1][3]. The evidence accumulated over six decades of behavioral experiments, radar studies, and more recently GPS tracking and virtual-reality magnetic manipulations shows that birds possess multiple, partially redundant compass systems — geomagnetic, solar, stellar, and polarized-light based — as well as several candidate "map" systems based on magnetic field parameters, atmospheric odors, and possibly infrasound [1][2][3].

The picture that emerges is one of hierarchical, experience-dependent integration: innate magnetic compass information is calibrated early in life by celestial rotation, then recalibrated on a daily basis from twilight cues during migration; experienced adults add learned map-based navigation that allows true goal-directed correction, while first-time migrants rely on inherited "clock-and-compass" programs [2][30][46]. The relative weighting of cues shifts with ontogeny, time of day, geography, and weather, and this finely balanced system is vulnerable to both natural perturbations (geomagnetic storms, weather) and anthropogenic disturbances (artificial light at night, electromagnetic noise, habitat change) [52][54][57].

---

## 2. Compass Mechanisms: How Birds Obtain Directional (Heading) Information

### 2.1 The Geomagnetic Compass

**Discovery and basic properties.** The avian magnetic compass was discovered in the 1960s by Wolfgang Wiltschko, who showed that European Robins (*Erithacus rubecula*) orient their migratory restlessness (*Zugunruhe*) according to the direction of the ambient magnetic field; the landmark 1972 *Science* paper by Wiltschko & Wiltschko formalized the "inclination compass" concept [4][5]. Unlike a human-built polarity compass, the avian magnetic compass is **axial**: birds do not distinguish magnetic "north" from magnetic "south." Instead, they sense the **inclination** of the field lines — the angle at which they dip relative to gravity — and use the distinction between "poleward" (field lines pointing downward in the Northern Hemisphere) and "equatorward" (pointing upward) as the directional reference [4][6]. This was demonstrated by inverting the vertical component of the field, which reverses the birds' preferred heading, whereas inverting the horizontal component does not [5][6].

The compass operates only within a "functional window" of field intensities near the local value: European Robins kept at Frankfurt's ~46 µT field oriented at 43 and 54 µT but became disoriented at 34 and 60 µT, although they could adapt to a wider range with prolonged exposure [4]. The compass is also strictly **light-dependent**: birds orient under UV, blue, turquoise, and green light but are disoriented under yellow and red light — the classic 1993 *Nature* experiment showed robins orienting normally under 571 nm green light but randomly under 633 nm red light [7][8]. Covering the right eye abolishes magnetic compass orientation, indicating strong lateralization to the right eye/left hemisphere [4][6].

**The radical-pair mechanism.** The leading mechanistic explanation for the light-dependent compass is the **radical-pair hypothesis**, originally proposed by Schulten et al. (1978) and developed by Ritz, Adem & Schulten (2000), which proposes that cryptochrome proteins in the retina form spin-correlated radical pairs whose singlet/triplet reaction ratio is modulated by the geomagnetic field [4][9]. Key requirements and predictions of the model — anisotropic hyperfine coupling, spin coherence lasting >1 µs, and aligned receptor molecules — are laid out in Rodgers & Hore's 2009 *PNAS* review [9]. Behavioral support comes from resonance experiments: Ritz, Wiltschko, Hore and colleagues (2009, *Biophysical Journal*) showed that European Robins tested in Frankfurt (local field ~46–47 µT, Larmor frequency 1.315 MHz) were disoriented by oscillating fields at the Larmor frequency at intensities as low as 15 nT, and that this sensitivity scaled with field intensity (in a 92 µT field, birds became most sensitive at 2.63 MHz) — implying a magnetically isolated electron spin, consistent with a flavin–superoxide radical pair in cryptochrome [10]. The earlier 2004 *Nature* paper by Ritz et al. demonstrated that a 7 MHz oscillating field of only 0.47 µT disoriented robins when applied at 24° or 48° to the geomagnetic field, but not when parallel — a diagnostic resonance effect that magnetite-based receptors could not produce [11].

**Cryptochrome and the visual pathway.** Five cryptochrome types (Cry1a, Cry1b, Cry2, Cry4a, Cry4b) have been identified in bird retinas. Cry1a is located in the outer segments of UV/V-cones and is considered the most likely magnetoreceptor molecule; Cry4 is expressed more strongly in the migratory season [4][12]. Garden warbler cryptochromes, recombinantly expressed, form radical pairs lasting ~10 milliseconds — long enough to detect Earth-strength fields — and absorb in the blue spectral range matching the wavelengths that support behavioral orientation [13]. Mouritsen et al. (2004, *Current Biology*) showed that caged migratory garden warblers perform characteristic **head-scanning** movements before choosing a direction, and that in a zero-magnetic field they nearly tripled scanning frequency and then oriented randomly — demonstrating that the sensor is in the head and that scanning is used to locate the magnetic reference direction [14]. Molecular mapping identified **Cluster N**, a visual forebrain area (part of the Wulst) that is active at night during magnetic orientation in night-migratory birds but inactive in non-migratory species [13][15]. Surgically deactivating Cluster N in European Robins abolished magnetic compass orientation while leaving sun and star compasses intact — and, critically, cutting the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve had no effect on the compass, disproving the hypothesis that iron-mineral receptors in the beak mediate the compass [15][16]. The current consensus is that birds effectively **"see" the magnetic field** as a visual modulation pattern superimposed on the retina [4][15].

**Magnetite-based receptors and the "map" component.** A second magnetoreception system, based on iron-mineral (magnetite/maghemite) particles, is located in the upper beak and innervated by the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve. Fleissner and colleagues described elaborate iron-containing dendrites in the beak skin of pigeons, robins, garden warblers, and chickens [60], and Heyers et al. (2010, *PNAS*) showed that magnetic field changes activate the trigeminal brainstem complex (PrV/SpV) in robins [18]. However, the interpretation of these structures as magnetoreceptors has been challenged: a 2012 *Nature* paper by Treiber et al. argued the iron-rich beak cells are macrophages, not neurons [5][17]. Despite this controversy, the behavioral evidence that the trigeminal system carries **positional** (map) rather than compass information is strong. Magnetic pulse experiments — brief 0.5 T pulses that remagnetize magnetite but leave radical-pair chemistry unaffected — cause experienced (but not naive) migratory birds such as Australian Silvereyes to shift direction by ~90°, an effect lasting days and interpreted as false positional information [17][19]. Similarly, in homing pigeons, local anesthesia of the beak suppressed the disorienting effect of a magnetic anomaly, implicating beak receptors in magnetic map perception [17]. A series of "virtual displacement" experiments in Eurasian Reed Warblers (section 3.2) confirmed that an intact trigeminal nerve is necessary for magnetic-map-based reorientation [20]. The current consensus, summarized by Wiltschko & Wiltschko (2019), is that birds have two magnetic senses: a light-dependent radical-pair compass in the eye (optic nerve → Cluster N) and a magnetite-based intensity/map sensor in the beak region (trigeminal nerve → brainstem), although the exact receptor structures remain debated [6][17].

### 2.2 The Sun Compass

Gustav Kramer's orientation-cage experiments with starlings in the 1950s established that birds can use the **sun's azimuth** as a compass, compensating for the sun's ~15°/hour apparent movement using an internal circadian clock [21][22]. The time-compensated nature of the sun compass was proven by **clock-shift experiments**: shifting a bird's circadian clock by 6 hours causes a ~90° error in heading, and a 12-hour shift causes a 180° reversal [22][23]. Schmidt-Koenig's systematic releases of clock-shifted homing pigeons at 15–200 km confirmed that 6-hour shifts produce ~90° deviations while 2-hour shifts (predicting ~30° error) produce none — exactly as the compass hypothesis predicts, and ruling out a navigational (map) role for the sun [23]. The sun compass is **learned**, not innate: young birds must observe the sun's arc, and its use is tied to the hippocampus and circadian pacemaker systems (pineal, SCN, retina) [1][21]. Guilford & Taylor have argued that the traditional "time-compensated compass" paradigm may obscure other ways solar information is used — e.g., as a simple heading indicator (gyroscope) or via constant-offset corrections that need not be fully time-compensated [24]. The sun compass is primarily a tool of **diurnal** migrants (starlings, pigeons, raptors, storks); it is useless to nocturnal migrants flying after sunset [22].

### 2.3 The Star Compass

Franz Sauer's planetarium experiments in the 1950s first demonstrated stellar orientation in nocturnal migrants, but the definitive work came from Stephen Emlen, who raised Indigo Buntings (*Passerina cyanea*) in a planetarium and showed that they learn a **star compass** by watching the rotation of the night sky during their juvenile period [22][25]. Emlen's classic experiments (1967, *Auk*; 1970, *Science*) revealed that buntings do not innately know which star is "north": young birds exposed to a false sky rotating around Betelgeuse treated Betelgeuse as the celestial pole and learned their migratory direction relative to it [25][26]. The star compass is therefore a **learned sky map** based on the geometry of constellations around the axis of celestial rotation, not on individual stars, and it is not time-compensated (the same star pattern indicates the same direction all night) [1][25]. Emlen also showed that celestial rotation is only effective if the stars move in the natural direction — reversing the rotation prevented learning [26]. The star compass is of primary importance to nocturnal passerine migrants, though its relative weight versus the magnetic compass varies (section 4).

### 2.4 Polarized Light and Twilight Cues

At sunrise and sunset, the pattern of skylight polarization near the horizon provides a reliable, geography-independent reference to the solar meridian, and several lines of evidence indicate that birds use these patterns to **calibrate their other compasses**. Phillips & Moore (1992) showed that migratory warblers exposed to a rotated polarized-light pattern at sunset shifted their orientation accordingly, and that polarized light, not the sun's disc position per se, was the effective calibration stimulus [28]. Muheim, Phillips & Åkesson (2006, *Science*) demonstrated that Savannah Sparrows use polarized light from the sky region near the horizon to recalibrate their magnetic compass at both sunrise and sunset, proposing that skylight polarization provides the primary absolute directional reference for all compass systems of migratory songbirds [27]. Muheim's 2011 review details the physical basis — the e-vector of skylight is always perpendicular to the scattering plane, with maximum polarization at 90° from the sun — and notes that birds need a view of the lowest 5–10° of sky near the horizon for calibration, which is why Emlen funnels that restrict the sky view can produce misleading results [29]. The exact receptor mechanism for polarized light (likely double cones) remains less well characterized than magnetoreception [29].

### 2.5 Olfactory Cues

Floriano Papi's 1971–72 experiments in Tuscany showed that homing pigeons with sectioned olfactory nerves failed to return from unfamiliar release sites, launching the olfactory navigation hypothesis — the most controversial topic in bird navigation [31][32]. Two versions exist: Papi's **mosaic model** (birds learn a map of local wind-borne odors around the loft) and Wallraff's **gradient model** (birds compare concentrations of volatile compounds that vary along stable spatial gradients, allowing bicoordinate position fixing) [31][43]. Wallraff's experiments with pigeons raised in screened aviaries demonstrated that an "atmospheric factor" (wind-borne odors) is necessary for developing the navigational map [32].

The modern evidence, from Anna Gagliardo's group using GPS tracking, strongly supports a true olfactory map role rather than a mere motivational "activation" effect. In 2011, pigeons transported in air-tight containers and exposed to artificial fragrances (eucalyptus, rose, lavender) showed severely impaired homing — tortuous tracks, poor homeward orientation, and low homing efficiency — whereas control birds exposed to natural air oriented correctly [34]. In 2016, pigeons allowed to smell environmental air before being made anosmic (via zinc sulfate) still oriented homeward, while birds that never smelled natural air did not — showing that local odors at the release site are critical for determining the direction of displacement [35]. In 2018, Gagliardo, Pollonara & Wikelski confirmed that only natural local odors, not artificial ones, allow homeward orientation [33]. In free-ranging seabirds, anosmic Scopoli's Shearwaters showed impaired homeward orientation during pelagic homing (>40 km from coast) but normal coastal navigation, indicating an olfactory map used specifically over the open sea [37].

The chemical identity of the navigational odors remained unknown for 40 years until Zannoni et al. (2020, *Scientific Reports*) measured volatile organic compounds (VOCs) around a pigeon loft in Pisa, identifying three regional gradients — dimethyl sulfide (marine), aromatic compounds (anthropogenic), and monoterpenes (biogenic) — sloping in different directions, theoretically sufficient for triangulating the home direction [36]. This is the first direct measurement of candidate olfactory map cues, and the authors note that climate change may be altering VOC emission patterns, potentially degrading olfactory maps [36].

### 2.6 Infrasound

Kreithen & Quine (1979) demonstrated that homing pigeons can hear infrasound down to 0.05 Hz — frequencies far below human hearing — using classically conditioned heart-rate responses [38]. Jonathan Hagstrum (a geophysicist at the USGS) built on this to propose that birds navigate using **infrasonic "acoustic maps"**: microseisms generated by interfering ocean waves are reradiated as infrasound from topographic features, and birds listen to these signals to determine their position relative to home [39]. Hagstrum's 2000 *Journal of Experimental Biology* paper supported this with correlational evidence, including the remarkable observation that four major pigeon races in Europe and the northeastern US were disrupted in 1997–98, each coinciding with Concorde supersonic shock waves [39]. In 2013, he used atmospheric propagation modeling of 14 years of Cornell pigeon-release data to show that on days when pigeons were disoriented at particular release sites, infrasonic signals from the loft area were being bent away by temperature inversions and wind structure; when the sound reached the release site, pigeons oriented normally [40][41]. The infrasound hypothesis has been extended to seabirds, where Patrick et al. (2021) proposed three testable mechanisms (beacon, landmark, and gradient models) and noted that infrasonic cues propagate thousands of kilometers in the marine environment [42]. However, the hypothesis remains controversial: pigeons with cochleae removed have homed normally from 150–160 km, and no experiment has directly demonstrated infrasonic map use in wild migrants [42][43].

### 2.7 Landscape and Topographic Landmarks

Visual landmarks are undoubtedly important, especially for experienced birds in familiar areas. GPS tracking of homing pigeons has revealed that individuals develop idiosyncratic, stereotyped "route maps," following narrow flight corridors (often along linear features such as roads and railways) and deflecting toward their established routes from up to 1.5 km away when released off-route (Biro, Meade & Guilford 2004, *PNAS*) [1]. A 2026 study by Wikelski et al. released trained pigeons from a Cessna under clear skies, fog with distant Alpine landmarks visible, and fog with no landmarks: birds with distant mountain landmarks visible flew homeward (covering 96% of the distance in 20 minutes), while birds with all landmarks hidden showed poor orientation and descended through the fog — demonstrating that distant landscape features can be essential for homing when other cues are unavailable [1]. Even in long-distance migration, topographic "leading lines" (coastlines, mountain ridges, river valleys) serve as waypoints and guides [22]. However, passive exposure to a novel site's visual/olfactory cues is insufficient for pigeons to learn its navigational information (Morford et al. 2024, *Animal Behaviour*) — active exploration appears necessary [59].

---

## 3. Positional ("Map") Information: How Birds Know Where They Are

### 3.1 The Map-and-Compass Framework and True Navigation

Kramer's model separates the compass (direction) from the map (position), and Donald Griffin's classification distinguished Type II orientation (maintaining a direction) from Type III "true navigation" — the ability to return to a goal from unfamiliar territory without familiar landmarks or route information [1][3]. True navigation requires a map that can be extrapolated beyond the animal's familiar range, and the most widely accepted implementation is a **bicoordinate gradient map** using two or more environmental variables that vary predictably with latitude and longitude [3]. Displacement experiments provide the behavioral gold standard: Perdeck's (1958) mass displacement of European Starlings from the Netherlands to Switzerland showed that juveniles continued on their inherited southwest heading (clock-and-compass) while adults corrected their course toward their normal wintering grounds (true navigation) [2][3]. Similar true-navigation responses have been documented in displaced Manx Shearwaters (5,150 km), Laysan Albatrosses (6,630 km), White Storks (2,269 km), and White-crowned Sparrows (3,860 km) [3].

### 3.2 The Magnetic Map

The Earth's magnetic field offers several parameters that vary predictably in space: **total intensity**, **inclination** (varying mainly with latitude), and **declination** (the angle between magnetic and true north, varying mainly with longitude) [48][51]. The magnetic map hypothesis proposes that birds learn the local pattern of these parameters and use them to determine position. Direct evidence comes from "virtual displacement" experiments, in which birds are placed in a magnetic coil system that reproduces the field of a distant location while all other cues remain unchanged.

**Reed warblers.** In 2008, Chernetsov, Kishkinev & Mouritsen physically displaced Eurasian Reed Warblers (*Acrocephalus scirpaceus*) 1,000 km eastward during spring migration; the birds reoriented from northeast to northwest, compensating correctly for the displacement [48]. In 2017, Chernetsov et al. (*Current Biology*) rotated the magnetic declination by 8.5° while keeping intensity and inclination constant — a virtual displacement to Scotland, ~1,450 km away. Experienced adult reed warblers changed their heading by 151° (from WSW to ESE), consistent with compensating for the virtual displacement, while juveniles became randomly oriented [48][49]. This was the first demonstration that birds can use **magnetic declination** to solve the "longitude problem" — the east-west component of position [48][49]. The 2021 study by Kishkinev et al. went further: experienced reed warblers at Lake Neusiedl, Austria, exposed to a magnetic field matching Neftekamsk, Russia (~2,700 km northeast, beyond the species' range), reoriented southwest — the correct direction back toward their migratory corridor — providing direct evidence that birds can **extrapolate magnetic map information beyond their previous experience**, as a true gradient map requires [50]. A 2024 *Proceedings of the Royal Society B* study (Packmor et al.) showed that changing only inclination and declination (while keeping intensity constant) is sufficient to trigger compensatory reorientation, suggesting total intensity may not be a necessary map component in this species [50].

**Trigeminal necessity.** Pakhomov et al. (2018, *Scientific Reports*) combined virtual displacement with nerve surgery: sham-operated reed warblers exposed to the Zvenigorod field (1,000 km east) reoriented northwest, but birds with bilaterally sectioned ophthalmic branches of the trigeminal nerve (V1) did not — demonstrating that the trigeminal nerve carries essential magnetic map information [20]. This fits the two-system model (radical-pair compass in the eye; magnetite/trigeminal intensity sensor in the beak) described in section 2.1 [6][17][18].

**Age dependence and other taxa.** Magnetic map responses are consistently **experience-dependent**: juveniles without an established navigational map fail to respond to virtual displacements (reed warblers [48]) and to magnetic pulse treatments (silvereyes [19]). The review literature identifies two classes of magnetic maps: **inherited** signpost maps used by first-time migrants (e.g., thrush nightingales increasing fuel deposition when exposed to the magnetic field of northern Egypt before the Sahara crossing) and **learned** gradient maps used for goal navigation [17][51]. Not all species appear sensitive to declination, however — European Robins and Garden Warblers did not respond to declination shifts in a 2020 study — indicating significant variation in navigational map organization across taxa [48]. A simulation study of greater white-fronted geese using daily geomagnetic field models found that a simple "geomagnetic taxis" (compass-type) strategy reproduced observed GPS trajectories better than map-based bicoordinate strategies, though multifactorial mechanisms were still indicated [51].

### 3.3 The Olfactory Map

As detailed in section 2.5, the olfactory map is the best-supported map system for **homing pigeons**, with 40 years of nerve-section, anosmia, air-filtration, and GPS-tracking experiments showing that pigeons need access to natural environmental odors to determine the home direction from unfamiliar sites [32][33][34][35]. Wallraff (2014) argues forcefully that no other cue system has survived experimental scrutiny for pigeon homing, and that olfactory navigation is not a redundant component but a necessary one [43]. The Zannoni et al. (2020) VOC analysis showed that pigeons could in principle triangulate position from three stable chemical gradients (DMS, aromatics, monoterpenes), although the mosaic model of unique site-specific odor signatures was not supported [36]. In wild migratory species, olfactory map use has been suggested by experiments on anosmic Gray Catbirds displaced 1,000 km (which failed to correct westward) and on Lesser Black-backed Gulls translocated 850–1,000 km (olfactory-nerve-sectioned birds could not compensate) [32]. Critics note that stable odor gradients beyond ~200 km have not been demonstrated, that deflector-loft results may be confounded by polarized-light effects, and that olfactory navigation is hard to reconcile with trans-oceanic migrations [3][31]. The field remains polarized, with Wallraff on one side, Gagliardo's GPS-tracking evidence on the other, and calls for standardized collaborative experiments [32].

### 3.4 The Infrasound Map

Hagstrum's infrasound hypothesis (section 2.6) is explicitly a **map** hypothesis: birds use the direction and pattern of arrival of low-frequency acoustic signals reradiated from topography to determine their position relative to home [39]. The atmospheric propagation modeling (Hagstrum 2013) provides a mechanistic explanation for long-standing anomalies in pigeon homing data, including why birds are disoriented at specific sites on specific days, and why young pigeons sometimes head in the opposite direction from home [40][41]. However, the cochlea-removal experiments and the absence of direct tests in migratory species keep the hypothesis at the level of a plausible but unproven mechanism [42][43]. Patrick et al. (2021) provide a testable framework for seabirds, proposing beacon, landmark, and gradient variants and discussing plausible detection mechanisms (interaural time/level differences, Doppler shifts, vestibular particle-motion sensing) [42].
